# Converted Devanāgarī → IAST with sanscript on 2026-09-23 (Kengo Harimoto / Claude); XML notes dropped; the *Vidhiviveka* mūla is embedded in the commentary as in the source. Avagraha appears as an apostrophe.
Now begins the *Vidhiviveka*.
Homage to the illustrious Gaṇeśa!
Those who know the three Vedas maintain that [injunction] is the means for achieving the goals of human life.
Since awakening depends upon the ritual procedure, that [procedure] is now being analyzed.
Now, the *Nyāyakaṇikā*: Homage to the illustrious Sarasvatī.
The Blessed One, who has never been touched by afflictions in any way whatsoever—

We bow to that Viṣṇu, the teacher even of the teachers of the gods, who— neither by merit nor by demerit, nor by the three types of fruition, nor by those two— is the supreme reality of words, which he causes one to realize through the syllable "Om."
Salutations to you, the destroyer of the fear of worldly existence, the architect who ordains the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the universe, and the slayer of even the three cities,
[who are] Earth, Fire, Consciousness, Water, Wind, and Moon— *Note: The final line appears to be incomplete in the source text.*
Salutations to you, O Bhava, who bear the eight forms beginning with Sthāṇu, Vidyut, and Āditya.

Salutation to the Guru, the tree of knowledge, the progenitor and sovereign lord, who has brought forth this beautiful Nyāyamañjarī, which subdues the darkness of ignorance and overcomes adversaries. || 3 ||
Even the speech of those like us, though devoid of the refined composition of a teacher,
purifies like the falling current of the Gaṅgā purifying the water in a street.

At the commencement of this treatise, he states the purpose— which consists in the discernment of the subject matter and its scope, serving as a prerequisite for the engagement of a discerning person and being caused by the subject and the purpose:
"Those who know the three Vedas maintain that [the means] for the human goal is in the practice."
Since awakening depends upon the ritual procedure, that [procedure] is now being analyzed.

On this point, some say: that which has no purpose as its object is not within the scope of the activity of a discerning person, just like the examination of a crow’s teeth. And so is this treatise on Mīmāṃsā; thus, there is the perception of a property incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*).

Nor is this [reason] unestablished (*asiddha*). For the purpose of an injunction here is either the establishment of the Veda’s authority, or the cognition of the connection between word-meanings, or the comprehension of the means for achieving the beneficial or the harmful as the cause for engagement or withdrawal. First, it is not the establishment of authority, because that is possible even without an injunction.

The prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa): This might be so. In the absence of an injunction, there would be a lack of a task to be accomplished; consequently, because it would merely comprehend an already existing state of affairs (bhūtārtha), and because such an existing state is the object of other means of knowledge, the Veda’s authority would be undermined due to its dependence upon them, just like the speech of a human being. That, however, is untenable. To this, you must explain when asked: as for this [speech of a] human being...

Regarding the dependence of verbal statements upon other means of knowledge: is this due to their referring to an already existing state of affairs (*bhūtārthatā*), or rather because they originate from human intellect? It cannot be due to their referring to an existing state of affairs; for that would entail the loss of validity for perception and the other means of knowledge, since they too indeed refer to existing states of affairs. Furthermore, a statement such as "one should worship the *caitya*," which expresses a task to be accomplished (*kāryārtha*), would [otherwise] be independent [of other means of knowledge].

Because that would entail [the Veda] being a means of valid cognition [only through human agency]. Furthermore, the claim that "this [Vedic text] refers merely to the application [of a mantra] and not to an action to be performed" is a manifestation of mere faith in an independent tenet and is not authoritative; this will be demonstrated later. Therefore, the very fact of originating from the cognition of a speaker is the cause of dependence. And since that [originating from a speaker's cognition] does not exist even in the case of a Vedic text whose subject matter is an already established fact (*bhūtārtha*), there is no [dependence].

[Objection: There is dependence [on other means of knowledge], and that applies even to the words of a person whose purpose is the accomplishment of an action. [Reply: That is not so; the establishment of validity is not the purpose of an injunction (*vidhi*), nor is the cognition of the connection between word-meanings. For even without an injunction, one says, "He cooks rice in a pot."

For the cognition of the connection between word-meanings is established in the case of [the sentence] "Caitra. If it should be thought that human utterances depend upon the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*), and that intention depends upon the determination of another means of knowledge (*mānāntara*), and that this other means of knowledge has as its object the connection between word-meanings rather than the word-meanings alone— then that other means of knowledge, by virtue of its authority, would also [be present] in the person.

[The opponent argues: "Only [ordinary] words refer to the connection between word-meanings (*padārthasaṃsarga*); however, since Vedic sentences are not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*), an injunction (*vidhi*) must be sought for the sake of establishing that connection between word-meanings. This is incorrect, because even in the case of an injunction, that [connection] is untenable.
If it is argued that "when that injunction exists, the relation of the word-meanings is based on the requirement (*ākāṅkṣā*) for that injunction," then—
If it is argued that doubt itself [does not arise] because that [injunction] does not terminate [without them], we say no; for the same applies to action (*kriyā*) and the rest as well.

For just as an injunction (*vidhi*) expressed by a word does not reach its completion without an object (*viṣaya*), an instigator (*niyojya*), and so forth, so too do the categories such as action and the like not reach their completion without factors such as the *kārakas*. Thus, these very [factors] are supplied by the words themselves.

Since the words—conjoined with [the factors of] semantic competency (*yogyatā*) and proximity (*sannidhi*)—will bring about the cognition of the syntactic relation (*saṃsarga*), there is no need for an injunction (*vidhi*). Furthermore, the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) of words is known in the world to be prompted by the desire to convey a qualified meaning;
and since the Vedic cognition of meaning is understood to have that worldly usage as its means, [an injunction is redundant].
Nor is it possible for the understanding of something as a means to achieve what is beneficial or harmful to be its purpose;

for even from a statement concerning the present— such as "the sprinkling of water relieves the heat of one who is scorched" and "embracing a mass of blazing flames burns"— one understands that they are respectively means to achieve the beneficial and the harmful.

Consequently, since engagement and withdrawal are established through desire to acquire and desire to avoid—as they are by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth—an injunction (*vidhi*) would be useless;
thus, the perception of a factor incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*) is proven. Therefore, this treatise need not be commenced.

To those [who hold such a view], he replies: "Those who know the three Vedas (trayīvidas) maintain that the understanding of the means to the human goal (puruṣārtha-sādhana) is dependent upon the injunction (vidhi). Let there be no other purposes for the injunction; however, the realization that it is a means to the human goal is based on the injunction. For indeed...

In the injunction "one desiring heaven should sacrifice," if it were not for this injunction, heaven could not be the object to be produced (*bhāvya*) by the efficient force (*bhāvanā*). For that [force] requires only something to be produced;

and while both the sacrificer and sacrifices such as the *yāga* are things that come into being (*bhavitṛ*), [heaven alone is the object] because it is mentioned in the same word and because it is the meaning of the verbal root.

Since it is understood that the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) is indeed colored by that [result], and since heaven is established as a qualification of the person— being denoted by another word— the *bhāvanā* would abandon that [heaven] and grasp only the sacrifice and other such acts as the object to be accomplished (*bhāvya*). However, this *bhāvanā*, its limits being constrained by the injunction (*vidhi*) which consists in the means sought by the agent, remains identical [to the original].
Although the word "foot" (*padā*) is mentioned first and is understood, it is set aside because it causes suffering and is not required by the agent;

instead, the text relies solely on "heaven" (*svarga*) as the *bhāvya* (the end to be accomplished), for heaven is required even though it is not mentioned in the same syntactical unit (*asamāna-pada-upādāna*), is a qualification of the person (*puruṣa-viśeṣaṇa*), and has been obtained as such a *bhāvya*. And [once] such a *bhāvya* has been secured, sacrifices and the like are taken as the instruments (*karaṇa*).

By accepting [the injunctions], it is established that they are means for achieving the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*). How, then, is the status of being a means for human goals understood in the world from present-day instructions? It is through the force of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), not through the inherent power of the word itself.
This is just as stated in the passages "In the case of substances, preparatory rites, and actions... and "But it is not a proof, because it is for that purpose."
The Teacher himself will explain and establish this while commenting.

Now, is this injunction well-known from verbal testimony or not? If it is well-known, it need not be propounded by this treatise, because that which is already understood through verbal testimony is not something one seeks to understand further.

Because once the action has been accomplished, the means of accomplishment can no longer function therein; and if [the meaning] were unestablished, it would be all the more impossible for it to be established as the meaning of the Veda. Therefore, this section concerning that subject matter is useless. To this he says: "Therefore, that is being analyzed.
It is true that an injunction, though cognizable through words, is subject to dispute because of the presence of supporting and subverting arguments.
In the absence of valid means of knowledge, one who has fallen into doubt regarding what is to be understood examines it through both logical possibility and impossibility;
having excluded the forms of mere suspicion and false attribution, it is established as it truly is. This is what is meant by the statement: "it is discerned" (*vivicyate*).

Now, one might object: "But since a discrimination (*viveka*) of this [subject] has already been made by the author of the *Vārttika* and others, that too is surely useless. To this he says: "pra" (and so forth). Although a discrimination was made by them, it is as if not made at all, because of their use of confused terminology such as "they say there is an *abhidhā-bhāvanā*. Here, however, [the definition is given as] "that which is the means to what is desired by the agent."
Is that distinction [of the object] indeed a difference in the word, or an excellence in its function, or a difference in the object itself— such that by virtue of being denoted,
the word too may be designated in that same way?
Because it is a means of valid cognition, because activity occurs without restriction, because it relies on consciousness,
and because it is uttered in syntactic coordination, a word is not an injunction, since it merely brings about the conceptualization of what is to be done.

For verbal testimony is accepted as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and a means of valid cognition is that which makes something known. In this regard, a word attains the status of a means of valid cognition as an injunction (*codanā*) only when it conveys some specific excellence of an object that serves as a cause for activity. However, if it were itself the efficient cause (*kāraka*) of the activity, it would forfeit that status as a means of valid cognition; for that which is an efficient cause is not a means of valid cognition.
Rather, it is indicative;
for since that [distinction] is expressed by extracting [it from the general], and since its excellence is established through its exposition, this section is indeed meaningful.
In that regard, he first states the doubt which is the cause of conflicting views: "Is that indeed a difference in words?"

The "distinction" (bheda) consists in the fact that the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth are distinct from other words. For that optative suffix and the like, there must be accepted either: (1) an excellence (*atiśaya*) born of the very nature of the thing, like a magnet, by which it impels the conscious being as iron does;
or (2) an excellence of its operation; or (3) a distinction in its object (*arthabheda*), which is the distinction to be described as the cause of activity.

If there is a difference in meaning, how then can it be said that "codanā" is the statement that impels one toward action, as in the principle "but because it forms a single syntactical unit with the injunction"?
To this, he says: "Because it denotes that [action], the word itself may also be designated in that way.
Regarding this, he first negates the status of being an injunction for the mere form of the word:
Because it possesses authority, because activity occurs without restriction, because it relies upon consciousness,
and because of its co-occurrence [with other words], a word is not an injunction (vidhi) due to the conceptualization of an effect.

He explains the verse: "For it is declared that verbal testimony is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), in the statement: 'Dharma is a matter characterized by Vedic injunction (*codanā*). And a means of valid cognition is that which makes something known; it is that which generates a cognition of an object that is uncontradicted, not already known, and free from doubt. In this regard, verbal testimony possesses the status of a means of valid cognition as an injunction (*codanā*) when it brings about the understanding of some particular excellence of an object that serves as a cause for action."

In the view of those who maintain that the nature of the word itself is the injunction (*vidhi*), [the word] would abandon its status as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it is the cause of an activity that is itself invalid. Now, one might ask: why is the cause of an invalid activity not a means of valid cognition?

To this he says: "For a cause that is merely a producer (*kāraka*) is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Let it not be the case that seeds and the like, which are the producers of sprouts and so forth, [are considered means of valid cognition].
[The opponent asks: "What then is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)? To this he replies: "Rather, it is an indicator (jñāpaka), because [this is] the case with the sense organs and so forth.
[The opponent objects: "Granted that one might not speak of some excellence of the object as the cause of activity; let the word [be the means of cognition]."

It is itself the cause of activity. Even so, if it is argued that there is no fault because the person’s cognition of the object—wherein activity is to be produced by this [cognition]—is directed toward that very object, we say: no, for that alone exists elsewhere as well.

Because [the two cases] are equal; for the accepted principle that "dharma is a purpose characterized by a Vedic injunction" (codanā-lakṣaṇa) would become meaningless. Furthermore, if the word were independent, there would necessarily be an obligatory engagement [in action]. And thus, the scriptural statement "one who does not perform the enjoined rite" would be rendered devoid of subject matter. For at such a time, even the will [of the agent] would not exist, just as in the case of one being driven by a powerful torrent of wind and water.

With respect to activity, the *tantra* (the Vedic injunction) is the motivator for the person; furthermore, as an indicator, it requires knowledge of its own nature, its function, and its object. Since the nature of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth is the cause of activity, it would follow that activity would arise even in a person who lacks knowledge of the nature, function, and object of that [suffix], which are otherwise irrelevant.

If it is argued that the operation (*vyāpāra*) is what is understood, and thus the status of being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) will be established for the efficient cause (*kāraka-hetu*) as well—since it generates valid cognition regarding its object, just as the cause consisting of cooking and so forth makes its own cause known through the sprout—the opponent objects:
"There is no fault, because [the cause] brings about the cognition of the object. He refutes this: "No. Why? Because of that alone...

This [objection] applies equally elsewhere, even in cases where there is a statement of an existing state, such as "Caitra cooks," for in those cases too, the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) is not unperceived. To the objection, "Let there be equality; what loss is that to us?", he says:

because it would result in the futility of the accepted principle that "Dharma is a purpose characterized by an injunction" (*codanā*). For the nature of an injunction (*codanātva*) consists in being an impeller (*pravartakatva*).

An [injunction] attains its status as a means of valid knowledge (*prāmāṇya*) by making known some specific excellence of an object that serves as a cause for activity, and not merely by expressing a mental disposition (*bhāvanā*), because that [mere expression of a disposition] is common even elsewhere [such as in poetry]. Therefore, in the form in which it is a means of valid knowledge, it is not an injunction;
and in the form in which it is an injunction, it does not possess that status as a means of valid knowledge, because of its being a causal factor (*kāraka*) with respect to activity.

This is the meaning. Having explained the reason "because it is a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇatvāt*), he explains [the phrase] "due to the lack of necessity for activity" (*aniyamāt pravṛtteḥ*):

if the word were independent [in its power to impel], then there would necessarily be activity on the part of the person by force of that injunction (*niyogataḥ*). [The opponent asks: "Let it be so; what is the fault? To this he replies: "And thus, 'one who does not perform the prescribed action'—this is the statement of the authors of the *Dharmasūtras*."
It would be without an object.

Now, since the activity of persons is dependent upon desire, and since that [desire] is only occasional, there is no rule of necessity regarding activity even when something is enjoined; thus, it is possible for [the injunction] to be without an object due to the non-performance of what has been enjoined.

Because of this, he says: "For at that time, even the will of the person is not the primary factor regarding activity, just as in the case of one being driven by a powerful wind or a mass of water. He explains [the phrase] "because it rests upon consciousness" as follows:
"And the indicator (liṅādi) requires knowledge of its own nature, its function, and the relationship between them as its object; however, it is not a causal agent."

Furthermore, since the very nature of activity is its cause, it would follow that activity would occur even for a person who lacks the cognition of the object related to that action and its nature, which are irrelevant to the purpose. What is meant is this: [the self] is the locus of consciousness regarding its own effect by way of being the knower.

But might this not be like the sound of a conch? For just as it is only those who possess the cognition of the relationship between the specific nature [of the sound] and its application—namely, that "one should act upon the sound of the conch"—who proceed to act, and no others; and yet the sound of the conch is not the denoter of the activity, nor of any other cause for activity, such that it would function as an indicator (*jñāpaka*).
This is not correct.

For the sound of a conch is not the cause of activity by virtue of being a convention useful for engagement, such that one would think "one should act because of the sound of the conch"; rather, it is "one should act.

When there is a difference in the intention of the person to be enjoined regarding the meaning of the suffix—which is distinct from the meaning of the verbal root—the convention established therein reminds him of that [intention].

It is pervaded [by the probans], because such is observed in the case of smoke and the like, and because it is not perceived in the case of seeds and the like. Therefore, in this instance, non-perception in the form of the perception of a cause contradictory to that [consciousness] would itself negate the state of being the substratum of consciousness.
He raises an objection: "But might this not be like the sound of a conch? He clarifies this very point: "For just as..."

One should act upon the sound of a conch; it is only those who possess the cognition of the essential nature and its relation [to action], which are conducive to engagement, that proceed, and not others. Nor does this [sound] function as a signifier (*jñāpaka*) in that regard, because it does not denote [the action]; rather, it is indeed a causal factor (*kāraka*).
Thus he says: "And the sound of the conch is not a denoter of engagement, nor of anything else related to engagement."

Because there would be no reason by which it could be a communicator (*jñāpaka*). Even though the sound of a conch shell is not a motivator for activity, it is indeed a communicator, since it makes known the specific intention of the person to be obeyed, which is the cause of activity; thus, there is no deviation [from the rule]. He refutes this: "This is trivial. For the sound of a conch shell is not actually useful for activity."

The reason for its occurrence is its being associated [with the action]. Why? Because from the statement "people proceed from the sound of the conch," it is understood that this [sound] possesses causality toward the commencement of its own effect. This is because the ablative case is prescribed in the sense of a cause (*hetu*). Consequently, in this manner, from the very sound of the conch, whose own effect has been known, a specific intention [is inferred].
Because there would otherwise be the undesirable consequence of activity proceeding from what is established merely by inference. To the question, "How then does activity proceed from it? he says:

rather, in the case of a verbal suffix whose meaning exceeds that of the verbal root—as in the case of an injunction (*ājñā*) and so forth, which are varieties of the intention of one who is to be followed—the suffix, having established a connection through convention (i.e., having had its linguistic usage fixed), causes one to recall that specific intention. That particular intention...

"Having made it the object of observation" means for the purpose of inferring; that is to say, it causes one to remember the relationship. Therefore, it is from the sound of the conch itself—assisted by the recollection of the established relationship—that the inference of the specific intention is accomplished.
In some readings, it says: "It first causes one to recollect the established relationship; then, that recollection..."

It should be understood that the collaborator (sahakārī) leads to the inference of a difference in intention (*abhiprāyabheda*). By this, it is shown that there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) because the sound of a conch is merely indicative (*jñāpaka*). [Objection: Let this be so; but from what does the activity (*pravṛtti*) arise? To this he says: "From that inferred difference in intention, those who conform to it proceed."

Consequently, they proceed in accordance with that. It is also false to claim that those who have not understood the convention do not act because they are unaware of the object; for this consequence would apply even to one who knows only the connection between that [word] and its referent. [This is so] because there is no cognition...

Furthermore, in the case of activity (*pravṛtti*) being dependent on sound (*śabda*), the cognition of the object is useless; for one who is driven by a strong wind, such as a blind man or a lame person, cognition is not a factor for activity. Even a causal agent (*kāraka*) residing in a living being, such as a snake-bite, requires knowledge [of its cause]. This is not so; for in that case, it is knowledge itself that acts as the causal agent. Even without a snake-bite...
For death is observed even through the poison of mere suspicion.

Furthermore, as for the one who says: "Just as a word, though it is an efficient cause (*kāraka-hetu*) with respect to the cognition of its denoted object, requires the knowledge of its capacity (*śakti*), so too does it require the awareness of the capacity for action (*pravṛtti-śakti-saṃvit*)," even by him [it is admitted] that this is not the case elsewhere than in the case of an indicator (*jñāpaka*).

The dependence upon knowledge is demonstrated; for only that which produces knowledge is designated as a "cognizer" (jñāpaka). Now, let it be granted that [the Veda] is the producer of activity; however, the object toward which a person is to be prompted by it cannot become an object of activity if it is unknown. Therefore, in that case, the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth must be admitted to be the cognizer.

Thus, its status as the locus of consciousness is established; for even that which causes activity possesses authority regarding the object of that activity. To this he says: [the claim] that "persons do not act upon words such as the optative (*liṅ*), even though they cause activity, because the objects are unknown and the convention has not been apprehended," is also false. Why?
For even one who merely knows the connection between that [word] and its object would face the consequence of acting upon it. He states another objection:
furthermore, since activity based on a word is independent of prior experience, the cognition of the object is useless. Why is it useless?
To this he says: for one driven by a powerful wind, such as a blind man or a lame person, cognition is not a factor in their activity.

The opponent objects: Even the agent [of death] residing in a living being, such as the bite of a snake, depends upon cognition; thus, there is a deviation from the rule. The author replies: It is not so, because in that case, cognition itself is the cause. Why? Because death is observed even without a snake-bite, through the poison of mere suspicion. If the bite itself were the cause of death, then in its absence, [death would not occur].
One should not die from the poison of fear. A seed-consciousness never produces a sprout in the absence of a seed.

It must be understood that even for children, death occurs because fear arises when there is the cognition of being bitten by a snake, due to the awakening of latent impressions (*bhāvanā*) from a previous existence.

As for the one who says: "Just as a word, though it is a productive cause (*kāraka-hetu*) with respect to the cognition of a specific denotable object, requires the knowledge of its capacity (*śakti*), so too does it require the awareness of the capacity for [linguistic] activity (*pravṛtti-śakti-saṃvit*)," even by him no requirement for cognition other than that of a signifier (*jñāpaka*) is demonstrated; for a signifier is defined precisely as that which is a producer of cognition (*jñāna-kāraka*).

The point is that there is no deviation (vyabhicāra) from the similar instance (sapakṣa). Thinking that every indicator (jñāpaka) possesses the capacity to produce an effect because it is established as being based on the awareness of its own nature and power, the deluded person objects: "But surely...

[Objection: But surely the eye and other sense organs, though they are producers of cognition, do not depend upon the cognition of their own capacity. [Reply: What follows from this? It would follow that the word is not a producer [of cognition]. This is another fault. [Question: From what, then, does the comprehension of meaning arise? [Answer: From repeated practice (*abhyāsa*), like a whip or a goad. And it has been said:
In brief, every word is a cause of intuitive insight (*pratibhā*) through repeated practice,
just as it brings about the comprehension of meaning for children and even for animals.

Even the eyes and other sense organs, though they are producers of cognition, do not depend upon a cognition of their own power (*śakti*). To resolve this, [the author], with a hidden intention, asks: "What follows from this? Internally, [the opponent] brings forward a reductio ad absurdum: it would follow that sound is not a producer of cognition, because it lacks the characteristics of the eyes and other organs which are producers of cognition. Immediately following this—

With that [objection], he first offers a reply to one standing nearby: "This is another fault. We are not Mīmāṃsakas, such that we would assert an inherent relationship between word and meaning"—this is the sense. Now, if the word is non-expressive, how then does the cognition of the meaning arise? Nor should it be said that it does not exist, because of your own statement.

The sense is that it would follow that [the scripture] would not function for the purpose of our own instruction. The answer is: "Due to superimposition (adhyāsa), like the strike of a whip or a goad. The comprehension of an object from a word does not depend on its denotation;
rather, it depends on superimposition. For indeed, just as the strikes of a whip or a goad, though not expressive [in themselves], [produce a response through association].

By repeatedly practicing [the use of] horses, elephants, and so forth, people cultivate an intuition (*pratibhā*) that has the appearance of an object and serves as the cause for spontaneous engagement or withdrawal;

thus, they become motivators or deterrents. In short, the meaning is that every word generates such [intuition] here for those who are proficient as well as for those who are not. And it has been said:

In brief, every word is the cause of intuition (*pratibhā*) through practice; for those who are proficient, however, it functions through the expression of meaning. By the term "practice," he refers to the mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) produced by practice, because the cause is metaphorically attributed to the effect. And this [intuition] is the result of practice from a previous life.
He provides an example for the fact that this must necessarily be accepted: "Just as in the case of conveying meaning to children and animals—
for indeed, their comprehension of an object, which serves as the cause for engagement or withdrawal, cannot occur without the latent impressions (*bhāvanā*) from a previous birth."

The possibility of the arising of a semblance (*pratibhā*) consists in the appearance of an object; and by producing the semblance of an object, the communication of that object is said to occur. This will be explained in detail according to our established doctrine (*siddhānta*).
"And that practice is held by some to be the convention (*samaya*) which has no [prior] source.
We do not say that every indicator depends upon cognition; rather, it is only that [specific one], and not any other, because such dependence is not observed in the case of seeds and the like.
Nor can there be a postulation of a nature contrary to what is observed on the grounds that the suffixes such as the optative (*liṅ*) would otherwise be inexplicable;

for they are indeed explicable even in accordance with such [a nature]. Furthermore, the suffix is expressed either together with the stem or by way of reiterating it, and that repetition is not derived from scripture.

"Āgama" means a cause (*kāraṇa*), because it is that from which [something] is approached or attained. That in which no *āgama* exists is "anāgama," meaning it is beginningless (*anādi*). This is the position held by some.

He states that "convention" (*samaya*) and so forth denote a beginning. For the Naiyāyikas and others declare that the relationship between a word and its meaning, which is the creation of God, is convention; and since that is the object of practice (*abhyāsa*), that is to say, cultivation (*bhāvanā*), it is called "practice.
Having thus refuted the objection from the side, he provides the answer to the original challenger: "And we do not say..."
Every indicator (jñāpaka) depends upon knowledge; however, it is that alone which is an indicator, and not any other causal agent (kāraka).

Why? Because such dependence on knowledge is not observed in the case of seeds and the like, which are causal agents for sprouts and so forth; thus, it is determined that [the indicator] is indeed an indicator. By this, the hidden intention has been revealed.

Now, even though their status as indicators (*jñāpaka*) is equal, some produce knowledge without depending on consciousness, such as the eyes and so forth; whereas others depend on consciousness, such as smoke and the like, which produce the cognition of fire and so forth.
Thus, although other causal factors (*kāraka-hetu*) are independent of consciousness with respect to the production of their own effects, nevertheless—
Even that which causes the application of words must depend upon consciousness; otherwise, the occurrence of such application would be untenable. To this, he says:
"Nor can the nature of the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth be assumed to be contrary to what is observed on the grounds of their inexplicability otherwise.
Why? Because they are also tenable by following what is observed, namely, their being indicators of an object that serves as a cause for activity. [End of fragment] Prakṛti...

The two suffixes are denoted together. And thus, because they are denoted together, the suffix deserves to be uttered in syntactic contiguity with the base, and not otherwise. He shows the manner of this joint denotation: "Or, by way of restating that" (p.
Alternatively, it deserves to be used in co-utterance with that [number] either because it illuminates it, or because it denotes another meaning related to it.

However, such co-utterance is not appropriate for an expressive word that functions as a *kāraka* (grammatical participant) which lacks a denotative function. If it is argued that this [co-utterance] is based on other denoted meanings such as number (*saṃkhyā*) and so forth?

Let it be so. But how can there be a connection with activity (*pravṛtti*) for that activity which is not conveyed by the suffix (*pratyaya*)? If it is argued that activity, as colored by the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), is indeed denoted by the suffix through its primary denotative function (*abhidhā*), we reply: it cannot be said by the proponents of the verbal injunction (*śabdavidhivādin*) that the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) is denoted by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth in the form of an effect (*kārya*). In that case, [what is denoted]?

The connection of such suffixes as the optative (*liṅ*) and others is by way of being *kārakas* (grammatical factors). Their co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*), however, is due to the restatement (*anuvāda*) of the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*). This is as in the cases "one," "two," or "many. Alternatively, it is because they manifest that [meaning], or because they manifest the meaning of the base;
for example, the feminine suffix *ī* in "kumārī" manifests femininity. This is because it denotes another meaning related to that [base].

Just as in the case of "the cook cooks" or "the staff-bearer," according to the *Trikasūtra*, the *bhāvanās* qualified by the meanings of the verbal roots have the purpose of connecting them with an agent; let that be so. To the question, "What follows from this in the present context? he says: "But for an [injunctive suffix] such as the optative (*liṅ*), which is not expressive [of an agent], it is not logical for there to be a co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) with a factor of action (*kāraka*), because [the agent] is not denoted together [with it]."
Because it is possible. He raises an objection: "If it is argued that this [co-utterance] is based on a different denotable object?

We do not, indeed, claim that the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth are entirely devoid of a denotable object, such that co-utterance with the verbal base would be impossible due to the impossibility of simultaneous denotation. Rather, [it concerns] the agent, number, and so forth.

For these [words] are its denotata, and since they are somehow connected through their function (*kṛtya*), the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) is established; such is the meaning. He refutes this: "Let there be mere co-occurrence, but the specific point is not proven," he says: "But as for activity (*pravṛtti*), which is an effect not conveyed by the suffix..."

How is there a connection with the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛti*)? Indeed, it is not merely the co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) of the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth with the verbal root that is understood; rather, they denote the productive urge (*pravṛttibhāvanā*)—which has its limits defined by the state of being something to be done (*kartavyatā*)—as qualified by the meaning of the verbal root. And this distinction cannot be established even when there is the expression of the agent’s number and so forth.

The meaning is "it is worthy. He raises an objection: "If it is argued that *bhāvanā*—the activity of the suffix as colored by the meaning of the stem—is indeed the denotation [of the suffix], and therefore the specific co-occurrence [with the stem] is logically established? He refutes this: "First of all, those who maintain that the nature of the word itself is the injunction (*vidhi*) cannot claim that *bhāvanā*, in the form of an action to be accomplished, is denoted by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth."

Since it is only the *bhāvanā* (productive operation) in the form of "that which is to be done" (*kartavyatā*) that serves as the cause for activity, it is illogical for the mere verbal form [of the suffix] to possess the nature of an injunction (*vidhi*). Therefore, they must admit that the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth is merely activity (*pravṛtti*), and not its form as "that which is to be done. And thus, in that case, regarding such activity in the form of "that which is to be done"—

The connection of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth is by way of being a causal factor (*kāraka*), and not by way of being an expressive denoter (*abhidhāyaka*); thus, that which is characterized as an effect (*kārya*)—whether directly expressed or indicated—as colored by the meaning of the verbal root, enters into such a relationship. For it is impossible for two things that have not been cognized to be joined together. This applies to the case of the effect...

However, regarding the commencement [of action], there exists no restrictive cause for that which is inexpressible and serves as the motive for engagement. Furthermore, in cases where results are not heard, there is the supply of a result; in some instances, there is the postulation of assistance to the sacrifice;

and even in the case of heaven and so forth which are explicitly heard, there is the determination of their status as results—all this greatness belongs to the injunction (*vidhi*), and it is the power of the word.
It is untenable in its absence; for at that time, what is not understood from the word itself cannot be understood otherwise.

It is not the case that the very nature of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth is inexplicable otherwise. If it is argued that this refers to the instigator [of action], we say no; for even that is possible—just as in the case of wind and the like—even without a causal factor in the form of a fruit. Therefore, the injunction is not the word itself.

Or, it is the function of the word itself, by way of its form as that which expresses the manifestation of the object. But from what does this specific co-utterance arise, and why is it without a cause? To this he says: "The expressed or the indicated [meaning], by means of such an expressed or indicated meaning."

[The word] attains a [semantic] relation, because a connection between two things not cognized from the word itself is impossible. For in the case of verbal cognition (*śābda-pramāṇa*), only the activity (*pravṛtti*) is the denotable object (*abhidheya*). However, in the case of an activity that is to be performed—which has the form of "that which ought to be done" (*kartavyatā*)—and which is not itself denotable, there exists no cause for restriction, nor any cause consisting in a specific syntactic juxtaposition (*samabhivyāhāra*), since [the activity] is not denotable.

In the view of those who maintain that the nature of the word itself is the injunction for an already existing qualified object of denotation, he explains [the necessity] of postulating an effect (kārya) regarding the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth, which serve as the cause for engagement:
"Furthermore, in cases such as the Piṇḍapitṛyajña where no fruit is heard mentioned, there is the superimposition (*adhyāhāra*) of a fruit such as heaven."

In some cases, such as with the *samidh* and other [subsidiary rites], there is the conceptualization of assistance to the sacrifice; and even in the case of heaven (*svarga*) and the like, which are mentioned [in the texts] as qualifiers of the person, they are determined to be the fruit. All this majesty belongs to the injunction (*vidhi*). That [majesty] is untenable if the word [itself] lacks the nature of an injunction. Why? Because in that case, it would not be possible to derive [the meaning] from the word.

Otherwise, some result would have to be understood as being independent of the assistance provided by the sacrifice. That which is understood from the word and is otherwise inexplicable (anupapadyamāna) without a result or the like would serve as the basis for the postulation of such a result. Let it not be that there is no "otherwise-unexplicability" regarding what is understood from the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth. If it is argued that the optative suffix itself constitutes that [basis], he says in response: "For it is not the case that [the requirement] belongs to the very nature of the optative suffix and so forth..."

It is because it cannot be otherwise established (*anyathānupapatti*). For when that [word] whose form is perceivable by the ear is present, the fruit and so forth do not exist such that they would be impossible without it. An objection is raised: "If it is argued that it is the inciter [of action]? Indeed, the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and others are the inciters of persons. And these are not able to incite a person toward something that is fruitless; therefore, [the word's meaning] is established through its impossibility otherwise.

The meaning is: "the postulation of a result. He refutes this: "No; for even that [scripture] can function as an instigator, just like the wind and so forth. For it is not the case that everything which instigates action requires a result; since we observe that things such as the wind, though they instigate action, do not depend upon one," such is the meaning. He concludes the sense of the verse: "Therefore, the cause..."
The word is not an injunction (*vidhi*), nor is its operation an injunction.

For this very reason, these faults apply only when [the injunction] is not denotable; however, if it were indeed denotable, then for words such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, the person (*puruṣa*)— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The instigation (*pravartanā*) is one's own activity corresponding to the activity of the prompter (*prayojaka*). For it has been stated thus: "The optative suffixes (*liṅ* etc. express a distinct *abhidhā-bhāvanā* (verbal productive operation). And in this way, its status as a means of valid cognition (*prāmāṇya*) arises from its being an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Having understood the cause of engagement, a person acts by virtue of their own desire; furthermore, there is a requirement for the cognition of the relationship, namely the relationship with the denoted meaning (*abhidheya-sambandha*).

And [it is argued that] there is a restrictive rule (niyama) because [the word] has a denotable meaning; for one must postulate an effect [in the form of an injunction] since the application [of the word] as understood would otherwise be inexplicable.
This is not sound, because [the injunction] cannot be determined through usage, because it is redundant, and because of the aforementioned defects.

Because there is no activity [of the soul], because of the impossibility of a fruit [without it], and because of the scriptural statement regarding its form, the activity belongs to the Śruti (the Veda).

The term "injunction" (*vidhi*) is supplied [from the previous context]. For it is not the case that the word’s operation—characterized by instigation (*preraṇā*), entreaty (*adhyeṣaṇā*), or permission (*abhyanujñā*)—incites anyone. But surely, these previously mentioned defects apply if the operation of the word is not denotable; however, the operation of words such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*) toward a person who is being prompted is indeed denotable with respect to the person who is the agent of the action.

The instigation (*pravartanā*) belongs to [the Vedic word] itself. And to show that this is not merely his own invention, he says: "For it has been stated thus: 'The optative suffixes (*liṅ* etc. express a distinct *bhāvanā* of denotation (*abhidhā*).

And there is a restriction regarding the relationship between the denotata. The meaning is that because there is a restriction on the relationship between the two denotata—the meaning of the verbal root and the meaning of the suffix, namely *pravartanā* (the impulsion)—the specific co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) of the base and the suffix is also logically established. Why?
Because *pravartanā* is the denotatum. And the verbal operation (*śabdavyāpāra*), once denoted, acts as an auxiliary to the [agent's] desire (*icchā*) to impel.

Regarding the statement "it acts": he says that even the postulation of an effect (kārya) is tenable—"the postulation of an effect [is made] because the instigation understood from the word would otherwise be inexplicable. He refutes this: "This is not sound. For:
[it is so] because the application [of the word] cannot be determined, because it is redundant, and because of the aforementioned defect."
Activity [of the self] does not occur because it is incompatible with [the nature of] a result; rather, activity belongs to the scripture because of its description of form.
The term "impeller" (*vedhi*) is supplied [from the previous context]. And that [impelling] is denied on the grounds that it is not an activity, because it is a direct scriptural statement (*śruti*).
He explains this by stating: "Because its application cannot be determined"—for [impelling] does not consist of commanding, requesting, or permitting.

The activity (*vyāpāra*) is being examined, because that [activity] is a property of the person (*puruṣadharma*). Nor is there another [activity] characterized by performing what is conducive to that [result], as in the case of cow-dung fuel (*kārīṣa*) and so forth; for such a thing is not perceived. Furthermore, perception [of it] based on that very [inference] is incorrect, because it depends upon a [logical] connection (*sambandha*). Nor do the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and others denote a mere performance of what is conducive to the result, distinct from an injunction (*preṣaṇa*) and so forth, as they do in the case of the causative suffix (*ṇic*).

The applications [of words] have been described. However, substances such as cow-dung cakes (*kārīṣa*) are causes for engagement by producing capacity through the removal of cold and so forth; but it is not yet determined how the word [functions].
Rather, the application—that is, the operation—of the word is being described. Now, one might object: since the understanding of that [meaning] follows immediately after the utterance of the word...
To the question, "Since it has been stated thus, why is the application of words—characterized by commanding and so forth—not defined?", he replies:

"Because that is a property of the person. It is true that [commanding] is perceived immediately after the cognition of the word; however, it does not belong to the word itself, because it is a distinction of intention (*abhiprāya-bheda*). The meaning is that since commanding and the like are insentient, they are impossible in the case of a word.

Now, let it not be that [functions such as] commanding and so forth are properties of a person residing in the word; rather, just as the *kārīṣa* fire— by producing for the student the removal of cold, which is capable of inducing the activity of studying—
instigates the person toward study, so too do the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and others produce some assistance capable of instigating activity.

Thinking that [the agent] might set others in motion by performing his own activity, he says: "Nor is there another [activity] characterized by the performance of what is capable of that [result], such as [the activity of] cow-dung fires and so forth, other than commanding and the like. Why? Because it is not perceived through any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

If it should be argued that "let it not be known by another means of valid cognition; rather, that operation shall be understood from the word itself," to this he says: "From that very [word], the apprehension is incorrect. Why? Because it depends upon the grasping of a relationship (*sambandha*). This is the meaning: a word indeed makes its own object known only when its relationship [to that object] has been grasped.

Furthermore, the cognition of a relation is dependent upon the perception of the related entities. If the related object were to be understood from the word alone, an insurmountable circularity would result: the word causes the understanding of the object once the relation is known, yet the knowledge of the relation occurs only when that object is understood. Now, one might argue that it is just as with the *ṇic* suffix [which indicates causation] in the case of words such as *kārīṣa*.

[The author] states that [the suffixes] denote an activity conducive to the commencement of meditation; likewise, the optative (*liṅ*) and other suffixes denote their own operation, namely "incitement" (*pravartanā*), which is conducive to a person's engagement. Therefore, he says: "And the optative and other suffixes are not observed through other means of knowledge to be used in the sense of mere performance of what is capable [of the action], as distinct from 'command' (*preṣaṇā*) and so forth, in the same way as the causative (*ṇic*)."

It has been stated that the operation (*vyāpāra*) of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and others is not perceived. However, the operation denoted by the causative suffix (*ṇic*), as in the case of *kārīṣa* (cow-dung fire) and so forth, is not like that; therefore, he says: "But *kārīṣa* and the like, by removing cold and so forth, bring about capacity and thus become the cause of activity. But how the word [itself acts] is not investigated, because it would be redundant."

It might be thought: "The optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth impel a person, just as wind and the like do. That is incorrect, because the denotative function would be rendered useless; for even though its operation is not perceived, it would [impel] by its very nature, just as wind and the like do.

Because [the word] is an instigator; and because the aforementioned defects would ensue. For if the word is an operative factor (*kāraka*) with respect to activity, then even its denotation of that operation is not a contributing factor (*aṅga*). This is because the word remains an operative factor even when its operation is not denoted, since an operative factor does not depend upon its being known. Even granting, however, the usage of the word...

We reply: No, one should not act merely because of a word, for even a word that prompts action is not something to be followed blindly. For the activity of discerning people does not occur toward every prompter; rather, it occurs toward one who is to be obeyed.
And the cause for such obedience—namely, the attainment of benefit or the avoidance of harm—is not present in a word as it is in a master or similar authority.

If it is argued that [the injunction] is frustrated because activity proceeds from the result, and that it is not futile precisely because the result is understood from that very [injunction], we say: no. He raises an objection to refute this: "It might be thought that the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth impel a person just as the wind does;
why then should there be a grasping of its operation through another means of knowledge? He refutes this: "That is incorrect, because of the denotation..."

Because it would be purposeless. Why? Because even if its operation (*vyāpāra*) were not cognized, the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth would, by their very nature, be instigating agents like the wind; furthermore, this would entail the previously mentioned defects. The meaning is that it would result in such defects as invalidity (*apramāṇatva*). Now, it might be argued: "These defects apply when the operation is not denotable, but not when it is denotable. To this, [the author replies: "Therefore..."

He says: Even if the word possesses the capacity to produce activity (*pravṛtti-kārakatva*), its denotation of that operation is not a factor with respect to the activity, because it functions as a causal factor (*kāraka*) even when its operation is not denoted. Why?
Because a causal factor does not depend upon being known. By this, [the arguments] "because of futility" and "because of the previous fault" are also explained.

He explains [the reason] for "non-engagement": "Even granting the use of words, we say that a person would not engage. Why? Because even a word that prompts [action] is not something to be followed. For among discerning people, engagement does not occur toward every prompter; rather, it occurs toward one who is to be obeyed. Now, is the word something to be obeyed?"

Why does it not [function] by that? To this he says: "And there exists in the word, as there is in the case of a master (*svāmī*) and so forth, no cause for conforming to the attainment of a purpose or the avoidance of what is not a purpose. By the two uses of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), compassion and the suffering of others are included. If it were argued that the attainment of a result (*phala*) is the cause for conformity, to that he says: "The result..."
If [the word] were to function toward that [activity], it would be useless. The word "that" refers to the operation of the word. He raises an objection:
if it is argued that there is no futility because the result is understood from that very operation of the word, since the manifestation is produced by the word [itself], we say:
no, because of the impossibility of a result through the manifestation produced by its own operation while the word remains a mere instigator.

He states the impossibility of there being a fruit [of action] in such a case: for when the authoritative person (*āpta*) is one who acts with confidence and is indeed a benefactor, the understanding of the fruit arises through the principle of "otherwise-unaccountability" (*anyathānupapatti*). *Āpti* is the comprehension of the reality of the means for attaining the beneficial and avoiding the harmful by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); that which exists together with this is the *āpta*. And he is [the one who knows] the beneficial and the harmful...
Even though he has understood the reality of the means for attaining and abandoning [the states], he might at times fail to teach out of a lack of compassion.
Therefore it was said: "He is intent on the welfare of others. And these two—knowledge of reality and compassion—reside in another person (the teacher).
[Page 15]

Because of the impossibility of a result. For when the prompter is trustworthy (āpta), performs actions based on conviction, and acts for the benefit [of others], the understanding of a result follows from the fact that [the prompter’s action] would otherwise be inexplicable. But what is inexplicable in the case of verbal testimony? Since the mere act of prompting is possible even in the case of something contrary [to one's interest], just as in the case of wind and so forth.
If it is argued that this is not so because the scripture is directed toward the highest good of man (*puruṣa-śreyaḥ*), we say no; for there is a lack of evidence (*pramāṇa*).

Furthermore, prior to [its being recognized as] scripture, its status as scripture is not established. Moreover, if the operation of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth were the injunction itself, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of denoting the word’s own form. Otherwise, since the operation qualified by the word would not be cognized, the meaning too would be qualified simply by virtue of proximity (*sannidhāna*).
Because that [argument] follows as a consequence; because fitness (*yogyatva*) is not recognized in both cases. Therefore, *bhāvanā* is not the meaning of the injunction (*vidhi*).
From what is this understood? To this it is said: "the action accompanied by the suffix" (*sapratyayakriye*). The suffix (*pratyaya*) [indicates] the object that has been taught.

An action accompanied by conviction (*sapratyayā*) is one that exists together with corroboration through another means of knowledge (*mānāntara*). One whose instruction is of such a nature is called "one who possesses [such] instruction" (*sopadeśaka*);
[the term refers to] him. This is what is meant: whatever beneficial action he instructs someone to perform, that [action] leads to the person's engagement in it.

Since it is observed that one attains what is beneficial through the instruction of a teacher, both the knowledge of reality and compassion—which reside in the instructor—are indeed easy to acquire. Therefore, it is logical that the understanding of the result [of the teaching] arises from this prompter by virtue of the fact that the prompting could not otherwise be accounted for.
But as for the word [the Veda], what is unaccountable? If you say it is "prompting" (*pravartanā*), he says in response: "Prompting."

Because a treatise composed by an author who is either reliable or unreliable can be applicable even to what is contrary [to reality], as in the case of [treatises on] wind and so forth. He raises an objection: "If it is argued that this is not so for a scripture, since it is directed toward the welfare of man? For a scripture is called such because it instructs (śāsana) its students; and instruction consists in the attainment of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful through the exclusion of suspected or superimposed forms.
The meaning is that it makes known the reality of the means for avoidance, and from that very fact of being a treatise (*śāstra*), the human goal (*puruṣaśreyaḥ*) is understood.

He refutes this: "No, because there is a lack of valid evidence (*pramāṇa*). The sense is that before the result is understood, its status as a treatise is not established; and if its status as a treatise were dependent on the understanding of the result, it would lead to the fallacy of mutual dependence (*parasparāśraya*).

By this, the phrase "due to the impossibility of [producing] a result" has been explained. He explains the phrase "because of the mention of form": if the injunctive force (*vidhi*) were the operation of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, there would be the consequence of denoting the very nature of the optative suffix itself. Why? Because otherwise, if the nature of the optative suffix were not denoted, it would not be cognized; and consequently, since the specific operation [of the suffix] would not be understood, [the injunction would fail].

Because of the proximity of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, if the object were qualified by that [suffix], it would follow that the object also possesses the function of instigation (*pravartanā*), since there is no difference in their proximity. To this, he says: "If it is argued that because the object's fitness for instigation has not been ascertained, it does not have the function of instigation despite its proximity—in that case, [the author] replies: 'Fitness exists in both cases.'"
"Because it is fully known. For even the capacity of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth is not ascertained from any other source; this is the meaning.
He concludes the sense of the verse: "Therefore, the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) is not the denoted object in the form of an injunction (*vidhi*).

Now, it might be thought: "The denotation itself (*abhidhā*) is the productive urge (*bhāvanā*); the injunctive suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth have 'injunction' (*vidhi*) as their meaning. To this it is replied:

Because activity would result from every [meaning], or because [activity] would follow from any object whatsoever; because [the meaning] is understood through the sense of what is to be done (*kārya*); and because there is no reason for a restriction that would prevent [such over-extension]—the denotation itself is certainly not [the injunction].

The term "injunction" (*vidhi*) is supplied [from the previous context]. If denotation (*abhidhā*) were the injunction, then since that status would exist for all words in their respective denotata, it would follow that activity [toward those objects] would arise even from words such as "jar" (*ghaṭa*), because there is no distinction in this [denotation]. If, however, there is a difference [between words] based on the particularity of the denotatum, then that [particularity] alone is the cause of activity, as established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). But that which is not obtainable by other means—[is the object of the injunction].
If it is established that "the meaning of a word" [is the object], then it is incorrect for the denotation (*abhidhā*)—which is to be inferred from its effect—to be the meaning of the word.

Now, if it is thought: "The *bhāvanā* is not the denoted [meaning]; rather, the denotation itself is the word's operation toward the object, and this *bhāvanā*—the injunction (*vidhi*) expressed by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth—is the meaning. And of that [injunction], it is the meaning of the word...
The sense is that, for one whose real existence is established by the fruit of cognition, only the mere capacity to produce activity is to be inferred.
To this, it is said:

Because activity occurs toward all objects, because it would lead to an over-extension, because it follows from the effect, because it is not fixed, and because there is no cause for restriction, there is indeed no denotation at all.
The term "prescription" (*vidhi*) is supplied [from the context]. And that [prescription] is negated by the statement "it is not denotation.

He explains the reason for this thesis—that activity would otherwise result in over-extension everywhere—as follows: "If prescription were denotation, then for all words, in their respective denotable objects, there would be 'that state,' meaning the existence of the operation of denotation; thus, [this would apply] to jars and so forth."
There would be the undesirable consequence of activity arising even from words [other than those expressing injunction]. Why? Because there is no distinction in this denotation (*abhidhā*).

If it were argued that, although there is no distinction insofar as they are merely denotations of meaning, there will be a distinction in the denotation based on the distinction of the objects denoted;
indeed, such a distinction of the object denoted belongs to the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth, by which the denotation of the optative suffixes alone [is distinguished].

[The opponent argues: "It causes [the person] to act, but it is not the denotation of words such as 'jar' that does so. To this, he replies: "If there is a distinction based on the specific object denoted (*abhidheya-viśeṣa*), then that very distinction of the denotable object is the cause of activity, not the denotation itself. Why? Because activity occurs when the specific object denoted is understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*); for even when the denotation exists, [activity does not occur] in the absence of that [specific object] from words such as 'jar'."
The meaning is "due to the absence of activity.

By this, the phrase "or in the object" (*arthe vā*) has been explained. He explains the phrase "because it is understood from the effect": given the established principle that "the meaning of a word is not obtainable by any other means," the denotative power (*abhidhā*) is to be inferred from the effect characterized by the comprehension of the object.

Furthermore, if a designation were to depend upon another designation, it would result in an infinite regress. If it is argued that only the designation of the object depends [on something else], we say no;
for there is no restrictive cause [for such a dependence]. And this is because there is no [such dependence] here in the case of the designation of the object itself. For in this regard—

There is a reason: it is the denotation of the meaning alone that is required, not the denotation itself. Since "denotation" (abhidhā) is what is denoted (abhidhīyate), how can the activity of a person be connected to it? Therefore, denotation is not an injunction (*vidhi*).
Let it then be a difference in meaning; this also is not the case.
In a non-human (apauruṣeya) [scripture], the injunction (*preṣa*) and so forth, which are human attributes, are not possible.

Since they are obtained from another source, it is improper for them to be the meaning of the word. He explains this by the phrase "because of the impossibility" (*asthānāt*): if the denotation (*abhidhā*) requires a further denotation, then that denotation must itself be denoted as a denotation, and likewise its denotation as well, and so on.
An infinite regress [would result]. He raises an objection: "If it is argued that the denotation of the object (*arthābhidhā*) requires denotation (*abhidhā*), but denotation itself does not?
He refutes this: "No; because there is no restrictive cause (*niyāmaka-hetu*).
Furthermore, if the denotation of the object were to be denoted by that very same denotation, it would be denoted by another denotation.

Or [is it by another denotation]? If it were by another denotation, then the alternatives of simultaneity or succession would arise. Among these, the first alternative is not tenable, because it is rejected by the contradiction of something acting upon itself (*svātmani vṛttivirodha*). Nor is simultaneity possible, because a second fruit cannot logically exist within a single fruit. For there is no possibility of such a thing as "cooking" being cooked.
If it is argued that "cutting is cut" exists in some cases, just as "knowledge is known," we say no;

for that is untenable in the state of being a result (*phala*), and at the time of the production of another result, since that [action] would be an object of knowledge (*jñeya*), it would function as an object (*karman*), and thus there would be an absence of a result. Let it be, then, that there is a sequence: first, the meaning of its own [root] is [conveyed] by the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth.

If it is argued that the primary meaning (svārtha) is denoted [first], that is not so; for it is impossible for words, cognitions, and actions that have not been repeated to function with an interval between them.
By this very [argument], successive denotation is refuted. With this intention, he says:

"And of the denotation of meaning": the meaning is that there is also an absence of a cause for the denotation of meaning. By this, the phrase "and because of the absence of a cause for restriction" is explained. The word "ca" (and) indicates a conjunction of the reasons, such as the absence of the denotation [of meaning].
He states the absence of a cause for restriction: "For here there is no cause; it is the denotation of meaning itself that requires denotation, not [the denotation]..."
"It is denoted" (abhidhīyate). The sense is that even that which is obtainable through other means is accepted as the meaning of a word.

Furthermore, it is denoted by the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth; yet, the activity of discerning persons—who seek to attain the beneficial and avoid the harmful—is said to be "the denotation of its own meaning. What connection is there between these two? Indeed, it is not like saying, "The palace is white."
Those who are thirsty fetch fire. He concludes: Therefore, even the denotation [of the word] is not the injunction (*vidhi*).
Let it be, then, that the very distinct meaning of the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth is the injunction. This also is not the case. Why?
Because in that which is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*), the nature of an exhortation (*praiṣa*) and so forth is not possible.
Nor is mere activity, devoid of distinction and lacking an agent, [possible].

In common worldly usage, the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is an excellence of intention belonging to the speaker, characterized by commanding, requesting, or permitting. This is impossible in the case of Vedic sentences, which are not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*). If it is argued that it is possible because such intention is perceived [in the Veda], we say no; for that would entail the consequence that the Veda is of human origin. [The intention] belongs to the self of the Veda...
This is far too crude; for if there were no composition, there would be no comprehension of the intended meaning, whereas if there were composition, the defect of human authorship would follow.
Nor can mere instigation, being devoid of distinction and lacking an agent, exist.

If there is a difference in the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, then [the meaning] would be an injunction (*vidhi*); however, since its determination is dependent upon common worldly usage, and since that [injunction] is observed in the world as being characterized by commanding, requesting, or permitting, it would simply be that [worldly injunction].
Furthermore, because such an injunction is of human origin, it is impossible for it to exist in the non-human Vedic sentences; thus he says: "For in the world..."

The meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is an excellence of intention characterized by commanding, requesting, or permitting—an excellence that constitutes the nature of a preeminent person who is to be obeyed; it is a property of the agent. This [intention] is impossible in the case of Vedic sentences, which are not of human origin.
An objection is raised: since the capacity [of the optative] is understood from common worldly usage, when the optative is heard even in the Veda, there is the cognition of commanding and so forth.
If it is argued that [the Veda] has an origin, [we reply: no, for there is nothing that is impossible when it is actually perceived; this is the sense. He refutes this:

No, because it would follow that [the Veda] is of human origin (*pauruṣeya*). Even those Vedāntins who, while accepting the Veda as being without a personal author (*apauruṣeya*), have maintained that the Veda is the body of the Veda—the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*)—who, with respect to the divine, abides in all the Vedas and is distinct from all...

"From whom the Vedas do not turn away, whom all the Vedas do not know, whose body all the Vedas are, who controls all the Vedas from within—this is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal," according to the Śruti. To those [who hold this view], he replies:
"The intention of the Vedas is the Self"—this is far-fetched. For it is said that the body is the substratum of movement, the senses, and their objects.
Those who know this [state] maintain that the entire Veda cannot be the substratum for the movements and other functions of any individual soul.

Indeed, in this [Veda], there are no actions preceded by intelligence, as there are in the bodies of Devadatta and others. Furthermore, it is not the case that [the Veda] consists of parts of space delimited by the rims of wheels joined to axles, which are composed of earth, water, fire, and air, and are bound together by unseen merit (adṛṣṭa).

The status of being the substratum for the formless sense organs is not possible [for the body]. Nor is it logical that the mind alone, independent of the external senses, can serve as the instrument of experience.
By this, its status as the locus of objects is also refuted. Therefore, because it lacks the characteristics of a body, [the soul] is distinct from the body.

The claim that this is the intention of the Self whose body is the Veda is extremely far-fetched. Furthermore, when in the world, from sentences such as "Bring the cow," various intentions of the speaker— such as a command— are perceived, and not those of anyone else, then if the Inner Controller (Antaryāmī) were the author of the Veda, his intention could not be understood [from it], because he would be unrelated to it.
Because there is no transition [of meaning], and because if it were connected [to a person], the defects of being human-made would follow, this is untenable.

Furthermore, as for the view that [the Veda is not authoritative] because of the defect of having to postulate multiple capacities and because of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding injunctions (*praiṣa*) and so forth—

"Because it is expressible and because it is non-deviant, the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth in common worldly usage is merely 'instigation' (*pravartanā*); this is also logically consistent in the Veda. This too is not tenable, because a universal devoid of particulars is impossible, and because an operation is untenable in the absence of an agent. To begin with, particulars such as "command" (*praiṣa*) and so forth cannot exist in the Veda; nor can any other [particular] exist.

A certain distinction is being demonstrated. Or, if that distinction were demonstrated, the establishment of a general term for it would be useless at this juncture. Thus, this general property of instigation (*pravartanā-sāmānya*), from which all particular differences have been excluded, would be like the status of being a Brahmin (*brāhmaṇya*) when the distinctions of the Kaṭha and other sub-schools have been abandoned. And instigation is the activity of the one who instigates.

Without that [injunction], it does not shine forth clearly, because of the absence of a person (*puruṣa*). Furthermore, since the capacity of a word to instigate action has been denied, there is an absence of an instigator.
If it should be thought that the fruit (*phala*) is the instigator and its operation is the instigation (*pravartanā*), then for a person who desires the fruit—

Furthermore, as for the view that because it would involve the fault of postulating multiple capacities to express various specific intentions such as commanding and so forth, and because there is deviation [from these intentions], commands and the like are not what is expressed; rather, since it is non-deviant, the meaning of the optative (*liṅ*) in common usage is merely "incitement to action" (*pravartanāmātra*), and not specifically commands and so forth. And this [meaning] is applicable even in the impersonal Veda.

The sense is this: these various intentions, such as commands and the like, lead one to understand the person [who intends them] because they are invariably concomitant with that person, not merely the act of instigation (*pravartanā*). This is because the latter is not invariably concomitant with the former. He refutes this: "This too is not sound. Why? Because a universal devoid of particulars is impossible; for if there were no agent..."
And because of the impossibility of [such] activity.

He first explains the reason: "To begin with, specific elements such as commands (*praiṣa*) and so forth are not possible in the Veda, because that would contradict its authorlessness (*apauruṣeyatva*). Nor is any other specific element demonstrated. If such were demonstrated..."
Alternatively, establishing the designation of a "universal" at this juncture is useless, because only the particular (viśeṣa) functions as the motivator.

Thus, this universal of instigation, from which all distinctions have been discarded, would be like the state of being a Brāhmaṇa when the distinctions of Kaṭha and so forth are abandoned; the meaning is that it would be as non-existent as a flower in the sky.

He explains the second [point]: "And instigation (*pravartanā*) is the activity of an instigator; that [activity] does not shine forth without such an instigator. Now, one might object: "The person (*puruṣa*) will be the instigator.
To this he says: "Because of the non-existence of a person. Nor is it the word, as he says: "And because the status of being an instigator is denied of the word."

Below that: therefore, there is an absence of an instigator; due to that absence, there is also an absence of "instigation" (*pravartanā*), which is pervaded by it. If it should be thought that the fruit is the instigator, then its operation would be the desire for the object (*arthitā*), whose nature is pleasure (*prīti*).
Because activity occurs toward the means of achieving that [result], and because it would not otherwise occur. Nor is "incitement" (*pravartanā*) some specific kind of operation;

rather, it is simply any operation capable of producing activity, which constitutes the operation of the instigator (*prayojaka*). This is seen from such instances as "alms cause one to dwell" (*bhikṣā vāsayati*) and "the kārīṣa fire causes one to study" (*kārīṣo 'gnir adhyāpayati*). That [position] is incorrect.
A person’s desire and activity [arise] from this; on what basis is there a restriction?
