The fact that an action is a means to a result is to be determined by the action itself; when, then, is it the end to be accomplished?

If the desire for a fruit is the cause of activity, then that [cause] must be either the desire itself, its connection [with the agent], or the inherence of the desire [in the agent]. According to the rule, "In the case of primary derivatives, secondary derivatives, and compounds, the relation is expressed by the suffixes *tva* and *tal*," this [desire] is a property of the person; thus, the fruit is not the activity itself. Alternatively, it might be argued that the property which is the cause of activity toward the fruit is pleasure (*prīti*), acting through the mediation of the desire for that [fruit].

Is the operation toward the fruit (*phalavyāpāra*) the instigation (*pravartanā*)? That too resides only there [in the fruit], not in the action (*karman*). Or rather, is the instigation the operation toward the fruit? Why? Because a person desiring a fruit engages in the means of attaining that fruit; otherwise, it would not exist in the absence of an operation toward the fruit. For instigation is not some particular kind of operation.

Rather, the operation of the instigator (*prayojaka*) is merely an activity capable of inciting action; whereas this operation of the fruit—characterized either by the desire for it (*arthitā*) or by its nature as pleasure (*prītyātmatā*)—is incapable of inciting action. This is seen from such instances as "alms cause one to dwell" (*bhikṣā vāsayati*) and "the kārīṣa fire causes one to study" (*kārīṣo 'gnir adhyāpayati*), because [in these cases] the taking up of food and the removal of cold [are not themselves the instigating agents].
[The opponent says: "At the navel. He refutes that: "That is incorrect.
What is the basis for the restriction that a person's activity [must be] based on desire?
The fact that an action is a means to a result must be determined; when, then, is it the goal to be accomplished?"

If the desire for a result (*phalārthitā*) is the cause of engagement—whether that be the desire itself, its connection (*tadyoga*), or its inherence (*icchāsamavāya*)—then, according to the statement of the author of the *Vārttika*, "In the case of primary derivatives, secondary derivatives, and compounds, the relation is expressed by the suffixes *tva* and *tal*," it is a property of the person (*puruṣadharma*) alone and not a property of the result; thus, the result is not the active agent. Indeed, [the desire] does not inhere in anything else.

It cannot have another operation, because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). [The opponent] objects: "If it is argued that the property which is the cause of activity toward the fruit is through the presentation of a desire for that [fruit], and that the operation of the fruit is its nature as pleasure (*prītyātmatā*), which is the instigation (*pravartanā*), and that the fruit is defined by being desired, and since desire follows after pleasure, the fruit must consist of the nature of pleasure; [for] by means of the fruit, one brings about the desire for it through its quality as pleasure..."

It carries [the result], and desire produces effort; thus, by way of presenting desire, the state of being pleasure—which inheres in the result—becomes "instigation" (*pravartanā*) because it is an operation that causes engagement. He refutes this: even that state of being pleasure resides only in that very result. And it has already been stated that the result is not the object of engagement; for when the result is directly perceived...

"An action of the agent. And since activity occurs toward an action that is a means to a result, and since that [action] is of the nature of suffering and not of the nature of pleasure, he says: "not in the action" [p.

If it were to operate everywhere, it would do so because of the absence of any restrictive cause. Since it is the means to that [result], it operates only toward the action, not everywhere. If that is the case, then the cause of operation toward the action is its being the means to that [result], and not the form of the result itself; and since that [means-ness] inheres in the action, the action would be the instigator. If this is so, then [the cause is] its being the object to be accomplished.

The cause of activity is that [desire], and since it inheres in the fruit, there is no fault. For instance, because satisfaction and the like, which are intensely desired, are to be accomplished through a specific action, activity occurs toward that very [action]. But what is this "state of being to be accomplished" (*sādhyatā*)?

If it were the nature of the fruit, there would be the undesirable consequence of activity occurring everywhere. It is rather a specific state of the causal factor (*kāraka*). For that indeed belongs to the fruit.

The distinction of capacities is determined by their respective means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), just like color and other qualities; otherwise, they would lack the status of being causal factors (*kāraka*).

For instance, if it were argued that "the person will engage in action because of the operation consisting of the nature of pleasure inherent in the fruit," to this he replies: "If one engages due to the operation of the fruit, one would have to engage in everything. Why?

Because there is no distinction between that which is other than the fruit and the means to it, as well as other things, there is an absence of any cause for restriction. [The opponent] objects: "One engages only in action because it is the means to that [fruit], since not everything is a means to the fruit in every case. [The author] replies: "Precisely because of that"—namely, because engagement occurs only when something is a means to that [fruit]. Let it be so.

In that case, it is the state of being a means to that [result] which is the cause of activity with respect to the action, and not the form of the result itself. [Objection: Let it be so; what is the fault? To this he says: "And consequently, since it would reside in the action and not reside in the result, the action alone would be the motivator.
[The opponent] objects: "In that case, then, the fact of being achievable through that action is the cause of activity, and that [fact] resides in the result. Thus [he says]: "Not so."

[Objection: A fault [has been raised]. Was it not said that since that [desire] inheres in the fruit, how could it be the cause for engaging in another action? For that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

To this he replies: "For in this way, because the desired satisfaction and so forth are to be accomplished by means of a specific action, engagement occurs only in that specific action, not elsewhere."

This is what is meant: although this "state of being an end" (sādhyatā) inheres in the fruit, it is dependent upon the means for its definition; thus, while it takes the means as its object, it does not take that which is not a means. Therefore, by virtue of that very distinction, it impels one toward the means alone, and not everywhere. He refutes this [objection] with the words: "But what is this..."

What is this "sādhyatā" (the state of being an object to be accomplished)? If it were the nature of the fruit (*phala*), then, because that [fruit] would not depend upon a means for its own definition, one would not engage in the means. Or, if one were to so engage, one would do so everywhere, since there is no distinction in its being "other" [than the means]. He objects: It is a specific type of *kāraka* (factor). That particular capacity by which the objective *kāraka* is distinguished—that is, set apart from things such as a sky-flower—is [what constitutes *sādhyatā*].

Thus it has been stated. Now, one might ask: "Even so, how does it [the desire] function as an instigator toward the means? To this he says: "For that is a specific capacity (śaktibheda) of the fruit which is restricted to the means. The meaning is: therefore, one engages in the means. He provides an illustration: "Like color and so forth" (rūpādivat). Why is there a cognition of a specific capacity? To this he says: "Otherwise, if the capacity of the fruit..."
Otherwise, there would be no distinction; for this [action], which is well-known to both common people and investigators, would lack the status of being a causal factor (*kāraka*).

Those who know [the matter] hold that "a causal factor is that which possesses power. He distinguishes between the example and the thing illustrated: "For just as in the case of color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth...

Just as there is a restriction of the means (*sādhana*) in the apprehension of form and other objects due to their specific capacities (*śakti-viśeṣa*), so too should it be understood regarding effects (*phala*).

This is because [an effect] such as a sky-flower never arises [from a cause], and because satisfaction and the like arise from the mere action alone. But when is this differentiation of capacity designated as "that which is to be accomplished" (*sādhya*)? Not, first of all, at the time of the existence of the effect; for that would be redundant and would not serve as a cause for activity.

Indeed, there is no arising of that which has already arisen; for if it were so, the power (*śakti*) of the yoginī would be purposeless. Nor does anyone engage in the means of accomplishment when the result is already established. Furthermore, how could that which is non-existent at the time of its absence possess power, like a sky-flower?
Is it not the case, then, that only an existent effect arises?

Just as there is a restriction regarding the instruments such as the eye when perceiving objects due to the specific capacities of the causal factors (*karmakāraka*), so too should it be understood in the case of results (*phala*). Indeed, it is possible that there exists such an excellence of capacity in the result itself— which is the object of action— by which both that which is non-existent by nature, such as a sky-flower, and that which is existent by nature, such as a jar, are produced through their respective means.

He states that difference is established by way of distinction: because there is no production of things such as sky-flowers, and because results such as satisfaction arise from action alone. Having thus formulated this, he refutes it: "But when is this difference of potency to be established by the statement? Not, first of all, at the time of the existence of the result; why? Because it would be useless and because it would not be a cause for activity."

He explains the reason "because of futility": indeed, there is no production of that which has already been produced; therefore, the power [of a cause] associated with it would not be purposeful. He further explains "and because it is not a cause for activity": moreover, no discerning person engages in the means of achieving a result once the result is already established. Furthermore, how can that which is non-existent even at the time when the result is absent possess power?

Like a sky-flower. [The opponent] objects: "But surely an effect that already exists is produced? This is the underlying intention here: that which is non-existent is not produced, just like a hare's horn. If the effect were non-existent in the cause, it too would not be produced, because of its non-existence. Yet it is produced; therefore, it exists. For instance, while being produced...

The state of being an effect (*kriyamāṇatva*) is pervaded by being an agent of existence (*bhavanakartṛtā*); and that [agenthood], by excluding itself from what is non-existent, excludes its own pervaded [property], namely the state of being an effect, thereby establishing it as existing alone—thus the logical connection (*pratibandha*) is proven. Furthermore, even though there is no difference in their status as causal factors (*kārakatva*), why is it that cloth and the like consist only of threads and the like, and not of weavers and the like?

For there is no distinction whatsoever regarding that which is non-existent. Furthermore, the natures of the threads and so forth are perceived; therefore, cloths and the like exist within the threads and so forth. Moreover, if cloths and the like were non-existent within the threads and so forth, why do they arise from the threads and so forth specifically, and not from grass and other such materials? Or rather, why does the cloth arise from the threads alone?

Do mats and the like not arise? Therefore, there is indeed no distinction whatsoever regarding non-existence. This twofold restriction—that an effect exists or does not exist within its own cause—indicates [its existence] elsewhere.
Furthermore, because an impossible effect cannot arise from an incapable cause, as that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), the effect must arise only from a capable cause.
First, this must be said by addressing the proponent of the theory that the effect is non-existent (*asatkāryavādin*):
an effect must arise from what is capable; and that which is capable is that which possesses capacity; furthermore, capacity consists in the nature of a relation.
Just as conjunction, which depends on both [relata], does not exist in the absence of those two, so too the existence of the capacity must be admitted [to depend on its object];
moreover, that which is called a "cause" has its limits defined by its effect, and if that effect is absent, it cannot exist—
for whatever has its limits defined by something else does not exist in the absence of that thing, just as one who possesses earrings does not exist when the earrings are absent.

It does not exist in the absence of the earring. Therefore, because of the existence of the cause, the effect exists therein. The Sāṅkhyas have declared this fivefold "non-deviating" (avīta) proof for the existence of the effect in the cause (satkārya). He refutes this: first, this must be addressed by addressing the proponent of the theory that the effect is non-existent (asatkāryavādin).

This is the intended meaning: first of all, the state of being currently in the process of being produced (*kriyamāṇatva*) cannot serve as a valid means of proof here, because it is not a common property (*asādhāraṇatva*) and because it contradicts non-perception (*anupalabdhi*). For just as that which is non-existent can never be made existent, so too that which is already existent can never become existent; thus, the power (*śakti*), which is unchanging and infinite, is not within the scope of action. Furthermore, this...
This which has been taught by the Noble One—this spell, medicine, or sorcery—is a particular excellence (*atiśaya*) that is neither produced nor destroyed;

it is an obscuration (*vyavadhāna*) located at no great distance. For that very person, with those same sense faculties and so forth in their original state, it is sometimes perceptible and sometimes imperceptible;
whereby at one time there is its perception through direct observation (*pratyakṣa*), and at another time through inference (*anumāna*), and [at yet another time]...
The tradition of consciousness [states]: because these various modes are contradictory within that very state of non-distinction (*anatiśaya*). If one should think:

"It is not a state of non-distinction, for a distinction in worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) is perceived through the arising of one excellence (*atiśaya*) and the cessation of another excellence"; indeed, according to the Sāṅkhyas, there are three types of transformations of existence (*bhāvapariṇati*), beginning with *dharma*...

Nor [is there a difference] due to a distinction in states (*avasthā*), for they each have as their substratum (*adhikaraṇa*) the characteristics of subject (*dharmin*) and attribute (*dharma*) according to their own nature. For example: the single reality of gold is the subject; its transformations—such as the *svastika* and *rucaka* ornaments—are the attributes, which possess the nature of arising and passing away; and there is likewise the transformation of their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-pariṇāma*). To illustrate: when this goldsmith [fashions] a *svastika*...

Having destroyed the *rucaka* (necklace), one fashions a *svastika*; then, having abandoned the characteristic of the present, it attains the characteristic of the past. The *rucaka*, however, having abandoned the characteristic of the future, attains the state of the present.
Thus, the transformation of state (*avasthā-pariṇāma*) pertains to the characteristics. At every moment, things possess the nature of arising and ceasing, being ever-new.

From that [state], there arise the conditions of being newer, newer, old, older, oldest, and so forth; for even in the case of clothing and the like, which are preserved with great effort, one observes the state of being "oldest" at the edges. Thus, this threefold transformation is called *atiśaya* (excellence or intensity). Now, is this threefold *atiśaya* eternal (*sanātana*) or occasional (*kādācitka*) in its substrate (*dharmī*)?

If it were eternal, then the svastika and other forms, as well as the three times and states such as newness and oldness, would be perceived simultaneously in a single substratum, such as gold. But if they are merely occasional, how can there be the production of what was previously non-existent? If you argue that this fault does not apply because they exist in the form of a potentiality (*śakti*), we say no; for potentiality is...

Furthermore, since an effect cannot arise without an upādāna (material cause), and because there is no absolute distinction between them, regarding the upādeya (the derived product) and its substrate (*āśraya*):

is it a single reality or manifold? In that case, if it were a single entity, then with the birth [of the effect], there would be the cessation of non-birth; and with the non-cessation [of the substrate], there would be the non-cessation [of the effect].

How can perceptibility, non-perceptibility, utility in causal efficacy, and non-utility be logically possible in a single entity without alternation and while being mutually contradictory? Or, if there is multiplicity, even though the entity exists, since the excellence of its power is occasional, how is this not the arising of the non-existent? Or, if the excellence were always present, why was the previously mentioned [objection] not raised?
Is there not the consequence of a logical fault? If it is argued that there is no contradiction between the excellence (*atiśaya*) and its manifestation or non-manifestation, [we ask]:

are this manifestation and non-manifestation also eternal for the excellence, or not? In the case of their being eternal, the aforementioned contradiction remains exactly as it was. If they are occasional, how is it that there is no production of what was previously non-existent? Thus, [the capacity for future existence] (*bhavyatva*).

And this will be established later in the section defining the subject matter (*adhikāra-nirūpaṇa*). Furthermore, even if [the effect] is non-existent, the restriction of the effect is logically possible due to the restriction of the causal capacity. Otherwise, even in your own view, since the universe has the *pradhāna* as its material cause (*upādāna*), and since the *pradhāna* is pervasive (*anvayitva*) and thus uniform in nature everywhere, [the effect would be indistinguishable from] the nature of the material cause itself.

Because the entire range of effects to be grasped would exist everywhere, from everything, in all places, at all times, and in every way, there would be no restriction such as "this is not that," "this is not here," "this is not this," "this is not now," "this is not this very thing," or "this is not thus. This is because there would be no cause for the distinction of any particular form in any manner, at any time, or in any place; [this would apply] everywhere.

If you argue that even though all entities (*sattva*) are non-distinct, there is a restriction on manifestation due to the restriction of the capacity of the cause, then alas! What has been wronged by the theory of the arising of the non-existent (*asat*), such that there would not be a similar restriction in that case as well? For you, however, since everything consists of everything else (*sarvātmakatva*), and because a distinction in manifestation is logically untenable, the restriction is difficult to establish; this has already been stated at length.

By this, the proof of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*)—based on the fact that even when a weaver and other factors are present, the cloth is invariably composed of threads—is refuted. Furthermore, a capacity (*śakti*), although having the object of its power as its domain, resides in the possessor of that capacity; thus, even without the actual existence of the object of power, it is logically possible for it to exist, just as knowledge, although having the object of knowledge as its domain, resides in the knower even in the absence of the object of knowledge.

Furthermore, causality is a specific capacity (*śaktibheda*) of a cause with respect to its effect. And that [capacity] resides in the cause alone, not in both the cause and the effect. Moreover, the determination of this [capacity] is dependent upon the cognition of the effect, rather than being dependent upon the existence of the effect; thus, the fivefold *avīta* argument is not capable of proving the pre-existence of the effect (*satkārya*). Therefore, [the arguments regarding] the threads and so forth...

The proponents of the theory that the effect is non-existent (*asatkāryavādins*) have demonstrated their position by stating: "Causes produce an effect that was previously non-existent through their own operation, because they are causes, just like the causes of manifestation. Therefore, having addressed them with this argument, it must be stated: "Only an existent effect is produced."

Moreover, even those of our own school who share the same philosophical standpoint, such as the Svāyambhuvas, do not assert the production of an existent entity in its entirety, because they do not accept [the doctrine of] absolute non-duality (*ekānta*). Rather, they maintain that the effect is produced from the cause insofar as it exists in the form of the material cause (*upādāna*), but not as something already existing in the form of the effect itself. Thus he says: "Furthermore, there is no production of an effect without a material cause (*nirupādāna*)."

The arising of that which exists in the form of a material cause (*upādāna-rūpeṇa*) is what is meant [by "arising"]. However, if it were to exist in its entirety (*sarvātmanā*), such arising would be impossible and would be purposeless, just like the material cause itself.
That which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*) is not the material cause. How then is an object (*karman*) an agent (*kāraka*)? It is certainly not an agent.

Some maintain that [the object] is dependent upon the agent (*kāraka*). Alternatively, there is no fault because [the object] exists as either a product (*vikārya*) or something to be reached (*prāpya*). In that case, however, the threefold classification [of objects] would be lost. Let it be so; yet, it is impossible to determine the agency (*kārakatva*) of that which is non-existent. How then is the usage "he makes a pot" (*ghaṭaṃ karoti*) possible? It is because the material cause (*upādāna*) is indicated by the mention of the thing to be produced (*upādeya*). Or else, [it refers to] that which resides in the intellect (*buddhistha*).
Because there is no absolute difference [between cause and effect], the production of that which is to be produced (upādeya) is said to occur in the form of its material cause (upādāna).
An effect that has emerged from its material cause is "without a material cause" (nirupādāna), meaning it exists in a location distinct from the threads and other such causes.
This is what is being said: just as this [effect] is perceived in a location distinct from the weaver and so forth, it is not so [perceived] here.

This relationship of attribute and substrate (*dharmadharmibhāva*) between the threads and so forth cannot exist if there were absolute difference, as in the case of a cow and a horse; nor can it exist if there were absolute non-difference, as in the case of the very nature of the substrate itself. Therefore, some kind of difference and some kind of non-difference must be accepted. This is the meaning of the acceptance of non-absolutism (*anekānta*).
Now, one might ask: "Why is the production of that which already exists in the form of the effect (*upādeya*) not stated?
To this he says: "Because production is untenable if [the cause] exists in its entirety. Therefore, because production is untenable, he states another reason:
"And because of the futility of the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). Why? "Like the effect (*upādeya*). That is to say, it would be endowed with that [effect] even in the form of the effect.

This means "that which is to be accomplished. It is not the material cause (*upādāna*) that is worthy of being the object of accomplishment, because an instrument (*sādhana*) that does not produce a specific change in an object whose action has already been completed would overstep the very logic of being an instrument. Now, if it is argued that if production occurs from what is non-existent, then since that [non-existent thing] lacks existence, it cannot serve as a causal condition (*nimitta*) for an action; how then can it be a *karmakāraka* (the object-case factor)?

Thus he asks: "How then is there an object-kāraka? He refutes this according to the view of certain [teachers]: "Some say that the kāraka is not at all dependent on the object-kāraka. As they have said: "The object [is so called] because it arises from the kāraka. Since this contradicts the rule for designating the object (*karman*) within the section on *kārakas*, he disregards that and presents another position:

Alternatively, there is no fault because both the "object to be modified" (*vikārya*) and the "object to be attained" (*prāpya*) exist. He objects: "In that case, O foremost of grammarians, the threefold classification of the object (*karman*) would be lost, since that which is to be produced (*nirvartya*) is non-existent and thus cannot be an object. He replies: "Granted, but it is impossible to determine that what is non-existent can be a causal factor (*kāraka*); for that would contradict the venerable and learned Pāṇini."

The sense is that Kātyāyana is a proponent of an incorrect view. Now, if that which is produced (*nirvartya*) does not possess the status of an object (*karman*), then how is it that the instrumental usage of the accusative case occurs in "he makes a jar" (*ghaṭaṃ karoti*)? Therefore, the meaning is that due to the contradiction with common worldly usage, Pāṇini himself is a proponent of an incorrect view. He provides the resolution: "By the direct statement (*śruti*) regarding the jar to be acquired (*upādeya*)," that is, by the word "jar."

Up to this point: because the designation [of the clay] as the material cause (*upādāna*) is based on its being the instrumental cause for that purpose (the jar), and because the status of being an agent (*kāraka*) is established for the material cause by virtue of its existence, the employment of the accusative case is justified.
This is what is meant: the worldly usage is "he makes a jar" (*ghaṭaṃ karoti*), but not [in the sense of] its...

Primacy is also [applicable], since that [status] is seen in the world even in a figurative sense; as in the expression "the galleries cry out" (*mañcāḥ krośanti*), the status of being a *kāraka* (participant in action) is appropriate for that which is to be produced (*nirvartya*), because of its utility in the action. As it has been said:

When the individual object (*vyakti*) is the referent of the word, the status of being a *kāraka* for the action being produced— such as that of sound and so forth— is likewise unestablished [in reality] and is merely conceptualized through the form of cognition (*buddhi*).

By this, the mutual compatibility between the goal (sādhya) and the means (sādhana) is refuted. Let it be, then, that action (karma) is the motivator; its "incitement" (pravartanā) consists in being the means to what is desired, because it has the nature of being the cause of engagement. No; for that [action] is the object (viṣaya). Moreover—
The instigation (*pravartanā*) to be expressed by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and others is cognized;
it is not a property of the agent (*prayoktṛdharma*), just as the causative suffix (*ṇic*) does not have a fixed agent.

For the comprehension of the meaning of words arises from worldly usage. And in that context, the instigation [of action] has a fixed substratum and resides solely in the agent, as for example [in the case of the verb].

Therefore, it is determined here that [the status of being an object] is merely figurative, based on the authoritative traditional rule (smṛti): "That which is most desired by the agent among the factors of action (kāraka) is the object (karman); the second case-affix is used for the object. Thus, whatever possesses primacy is not contradicted by that traditional rule.

It is worldly; for that application which is worldly, there is no contradiction. Or, let it be primary, even so there is no contradiction, as he says: "Because of its utility in actions while residing in the intellect. When it is logical for [the object] to be the cause of action, the status of being a *kāraka* (participant in action) is appropriate for that which is to be produced (*nirvartya*). As it has been said:

When the individual object (*vyakti*) is the referent of the word, the status of being a *kāraka* (grammatical factor) for the action being produced— such as that of sound and so forth— is likewise established as being conceptually constructed (*prakalpita*) through the form of cognition (*buddhi*).
The meaning is that if the word-referent were the form (*ākṛti*), then because that [form] is eternal, its being produced would be untenable.

Therefore, the "state of being an object-to-be-accomplished" (*sādhyatā*) is not a distinction in the power residing in the fruit. By this alone—the mere refutation of the state of being an object-to-be-accomplished as a distinction in the power residing in the fruit—the relationship between the means and the end is established as a mutual compatibility regarding the accomplishment [of the result]; this is "the state of being an object-to-be-accomplished."
It should be understood that [the objection] is refuted; for even there, the question remains as to "when" due to the equality [of the two cases].

Let it be then that the action (*karman*) is the motivator. Its function, which causes motivation, consists in being the means to what is desired (*abhimata-sādhanatā*). Why? Because it has the nature of being the cause of engagement (*pravṛtti-hetu-rūpatvāt*). For indeed, in the case of an action that is a means to what is desired...

A person engages even in that which is of the nature of suffering. He refutes this as follows: No; because it is the object (*viṣaya*), the motivator (*pravartaka*) is the prompter (*prayojaka*) of the agent of the engagement, and that [object] must already be established. Therefore, if the action (*karman*) were established prior to the engagement—that is, prior to the mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*)—it could not be the object of that cultivation. The sky can never be its object of cultivation.

It must be so. If the object (*viṣaya*) were the action (*karman*), then since it is not yet established (*asiddhatvāt*), how could it be the instigator? This is the meaning. Furthermore—the incitement (*prarvatanā*) to be expressed by the optative suffixes (*liṅ* etc.
is a property of the agent (*prayoktṛdharma*), not of the causative suffix (*ṇic*), just as [the incitement] does not have a fixed agent.

For the comprehension of the capacity of words is established through worldly usage. In that context, it is understood that the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth is an instigation (*pravartanā*) that has a fixed substratum and resides solely in the agent who employs the word. However, the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is an instigation whose substratum is not fixed.

The meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth is understood [as the prompting]. However, the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) has an indefinite substratum. Moreover, the meaning of the optative suffix cannot be the same as the meaning of the causative suffix, because the determination of word-meanings follows worldly understanding. For one who holds this view, the human effort is a mere restatement (*anuvāda*), whereas the activity is that which follows upon the oblation (*homa*).

Because it is stated in the Śruti, [bhāvanā] consists of the operation of a conscious agent; otherwise, it is merely the activity of the self characterized by the departure from indifference, common to both motion and non-motion. Bhāvanā, which is synonymous with the word "injunction" (vidhi), is the meaning of the optative suffix (liṅ) when the distinction of time is not intended. However, although [the sense of] existence is present in the optative and other suffixes, the form of the injunction is not perceived due to the specific nature of the action.

The view is that [the meaning of the optative suffix] is that which is denoted by the optative (*liṅ*), because it is the cause for the non-occurrence [of an action] due to being bound, just as in the case of "if" (*yadi*) and so forth;
in response to that, it is said: "It is not one [single thing] that is bound, nor is it its specific qualification—if that were the case, let it be stated."
Granted that no action proceeds from this [desire] due to a lack of consideration for the difference in time.

When the form of the injunction is obstructed by a difference in time within the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth, there is an absence of the cognition of *bhāvanā* (productive activity); nor can the meaning of the optative suffix be [the object of that cognition] in the same way as the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*), because the determination of the word-meaning follows worldly understanding. This is easy to understand. The phrase "of whom, however, is the view" is connected with what follows. He asks: "What is that? and says:

This being the case, human effort (*puruṣaprayatna*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*), whereas the operation pertaining to the oblation (*homa*) and the fire-laying (*ādhāna*) is expressed by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*). This is because we observe such usage by the author of the *Bhāṣya* in various sections of the treatise (*śāstra*). Thus, [effort] consists of the operation of a conscious agent and is what is made known by the word "effort" (*prayatna*). Otherwise, if it were common to both movement (*spanda*) and non-movement (*aspanda*), it would result in the negation of indifference (*audāsīnya*).
Bhāvanā, which consists merely in the activity of the self as it is being perceived, is synonymous with *vidhi* (injunction) and is the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*).

Now, one might object: if *bhāvanā* alone is the injunction, then since *bhāvanā* exists in such cases as "he cooks," "he cooked," and "he will cook," it would follow that these have the same meaning as "he should cook" (*paced*). To this he replies: [the *bhāvanā*] is an impulsion (*pravṛtti*) in which the distinctions of time are not taken into account.

The meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is the causal productive operation (*bhāvanā*), which is the cause for that [action] and whose temporal distinctions are not touched upon; however, this is not the case for the meaning of the imperfect (*laṅ*) and other such suffixes. The point is that although the productive operation exists even in the case of the imperfect and so forth, because its form as an injunction is obstructed by a specific time—such as the present—it does not serve as a cause for activity, and thus it does not have the same meaning as the optative suffix and others, just as in the case of "if" (*yadi*) and so on.

"Like [the action] denoted by the optative suffix (*liṅ*). This refers to cases such as: "If the Soma sacrifice were to have the *Rathantara* as its *sāman*, and if the offering of that [Soma] should suffer damage," and so forth. To this, it is replied:
"One thing is not bound [to another], nor is it its qualification; if it were, let that be explained."
Granted that activity does not arise from this [inference] due to the non-apprehension of a difference in time.

For if *bhāvanā* (the productive operation) and the injunction (*vidhi*) were one and the same reality, then, when the form of the injunction is obstructed by a difference in tense within the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth,
there would be an absence of knowledge of the *bhāvanā*, because the injunction and the *bhāvanā* are non-different. [p.28] When unobstructed...

Because of the distinction [between the two]. For if it were unobstructed, there would be the consequence of a distinction [between them]. Indeed, it is not logical for one and the same thing to be both obstructed and unobstructed. Obstruction applies to the specific feature (*viśeṣa*), not to that which has the nature of an entity (*bhāva-rūpa*). This is because the presence or absence of activity follows the presence or absence of the specific feature. Therefore, that specific feature is indeed an injunction (*vidhi*); it is not the entity itself, nor the productive urge (*bhāvanā*).

Injunction (*vidhi*), instruction (*upadeśa*), and instigation (*preraṇā*) are one and the same. And this [injunction] is that which is to be illustrated. If it is argued that it is "that which is to be done" (*kartavyatā*), we say no;
for that very thing is what one desires to know.

Now, is it not the case that the distinction [of injunction] consists simply in the absence of any reference to a difference in time? What need is there for anything else? [For it is] of the nature of the present and so forth...

Because it is not something to be performed, even in its absence there is the cognition that it is to be performed. Let this distinction exist; however, it is not the cause for a person's engagement in action. Granted, one may cognize the *bhāvanā* as distinct from time; but whence comes the performance? For the mere apprehension of the nature of an object is not the cause of engagement. Indeed, [one does not engage simply upon hearing] "a jar."

Having understood the object, one then proceeds toward it to that very extent. If it is argued that "one proceeds by way of something to be accomplished" (*sādhyatayā*), then there would follow the consequence of a division [in the agent] due to the imposition of mutually contradictory properties—namely, being bound up with *bhāvanā* and not being bound up with it. He demonstrates the impossibility of the imposition of contradictory properties upon a single entity: indeed, it is neither logical nor possible for one and the same thing to be both bound up and not bound up.

[The opponent] objects: "The restriction applies to the specific feature (*viśeṣa*), not to that which has the nature of an entity (*bhāva*). For the word *bhāva* is derived from the root *bhū* with the causative suffix (*ṇic*) and the suffix *ac*; thus, it denotes 'productive activity' (*bhāvanā*). [The author] replies: "Because the presence or absence of engagement [in action] follows the presence or absence of the entity in its specific form. [The opponent concludes: "In that case, then, the injunction (*vidhi*) is that specific feature. Therefore, it is not an entity, nor is it productive activity (*bhāvanā*)."

Injunction (*vidhi*), instruction (*upadeśa*), and impulsion (*preraṇā*) are one and the same thing, and this is what must be demonstrated. An objection is raised: "If it is argued that the injunction is the 'state of being something to be done' (*kartavyatā*) regarding the productive urge (*bhāvanā*)? He refutes this: "No; because it is precisely that [urge] which one desires to know. The meaning is: it is true that the injunction is the state of being something to be done, but the question is being asked what kind of state that is. An objection is raised: "But surely [the injunction] is concerned with a difference in time..."

The very absence of [the ordinary] consideration (*marśa*) is the specific feature of the productive urge (*bhāvanā*), which is the injunction of what is to be done (*kartavyatā-vidhi*); so what need is there for any other specific feature?

Here he demonstrates the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*): because a productive urge in its present form and so forth is not something to be performed, whereas in its absence there is the cognition that it is to be performed, and because being-to-be-performed is dependent upon an injunction, [there is a distinction] due to the difference in time.

"It is now argued that the injunction (*vidhi*) is simply the consideration (*parāmarśa*) of the *bhāvanā* as something to be performed. He refutes this: Let this distinction exist; however, it is not the cause of a person's engagement (*pravṛtti*). And how can that which is not the cause of engagement be an injunction? [Objection:

But surely engagement arises precisely from the comprehension of what is to be accomplished (*anuṣṭheya*), and that comprehension occurs when there is no consideration of a difference in time regarding the *bhāvanā*."

To this he says: Granted that a person may understand meditation (*bhāvanā*) as being devoid of temporal distinctions; but from what cause [would there arise] the performance (*anuṣṭhāna*) [of it]? Now, was it not already stated that the very distinction consisting in the presence or absence of the understanding of what is to be performed—which follows upon the presence or absence of the non-consideration of temporal distinctions—is the cause of engagement? So why ask for a further reason?

To this he says: "For the mere cognition of the form of an object is not the cause of purposeful action (*pravṛtti*). Why? Because one does not, having cognized 'this is a jar,' act toward that very jar immediately upon hearing the word 'jar' without reflecting on the distinction between the [word's] meaning and time. Therefore, the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is inconclusive (*vyabhicārin*). He raises an objection: "One acts because [the object] is something to be accomplished (*sādhya*)."

[Page 29] What is this "state of being to be proven" (*sādhyatā*)? If it is the state of being unestablished (*asiddhatva*), then it would follow that a sky-flower is [to be proven]. Furthermore, it would entail the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that a pot does not exist even in the state of a lump of clay. Alternatively, if it is the state of being an object of causal factors (*kāraka*), then [it would apply] to the activity-inducing [action] which has been made an object by those [factors].

For what purpose would one engage [in action]? And from where does it follow that one must engage in this [action] for the sake of the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*)? If it is argued that one engages because of the understanding of its being fruitful (*phalavattā*), then from where does that [fruitfulness] come? If it is argued that it comes from the understanding of its being something to be performed (*anuṣṭheyatva*), no; for if the status of being something to be performed is already established, then the postulation of a fruit follows, and from that, the status of being something to be performed follows—thus there is the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*).

In this very way, the objection regarding the specific designation of meanings is refuted. For one who has not yet acted, the initial impulse—whether it be intention (*ākūta*), the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*), or determination (*adhyavasāya*)—is the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth.

Subsequent action, or effort, or the movement of the body and speech, is the meaning of the imperfect suffix (*laṅ*) and so forth; thus, the distinction [of meanings] is set aside. This is because there is no cause for such a distinction, since there is no activity resulting from the mere cognition of the person's form.

And because no other reason (*hetvantara*) is perceived: the past and the present obstruct that [obligation], but not the other time (the future), since there is no contradiction in its being to be performed in the future.
If this is argued, he refutes it by means of an alternative analysis: what is this "state of being to be accomplished" (*sādhyatā*)? First, it is not a reflection upon a difference in time...

It has been stated above that [the reason] is non-existent because it is erratic (*vyabhicāra*). This being the case, if [non-existence] were defined as being unestablished (*asiddhatva*) by means of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) and prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), then it would follow that one could act toward even a sky-flower, since "the jar does not exist" is equally provable in the state of a lump of clay and so forth. Alternatively, if [non-existence] were defined as being the object of causal factors (*kāraka*), then activity would occur only toward that which has been made an object by those factors.
For what purpose would he engage the means? For the function of an agent consists in setting the means into operation;

and if the means have already been set into their own operations, then the purpose of the instigator is fulfilled—this is the meaning. Furthermore, this discerning person, desiring the attainment of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful, must engage himself in the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) which is the goal to be accomplished.

From where [does this arise]? He raises an objection: "If it is argued that one engages [in action] because of the cognition of its possessing a fruit (phalavattā), he refutes it: "In your view, since that very [fruit] is an internal factor, how could it [be the motive] when the meaning of the verbal root is already occupied by the object to be brought about (bhāvya)? If it is argued that it is from the cognition of its being something to be performed (anuṣṭheyatva), [we reply: no; for the postulation of a fruit occurs once its status as something to be performed is established, and the performance occurs once the fruit has been postulated."
This involves mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). In this very way, there is an initial activity for that which has not yet been active. He analyzes that [activity] itself:

whether it be intention (*ākūta*), the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*), or determination (*adhyavasāya*), the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is effort preceded by those; whereas subsequent activity, or effort, or the movement of the body and speech is the meaning of the imperfect (*laṅ*) and other suffixes. Thus, the specific assertions of those who follow the tradition of the Teacher (the Grammarians) have been refuted.

Thus, he shows the reason for what has been extended by analogy [in the word] "evam" (thus): "because of the absence of its cause. The word "tat" (that) refers back to the aforementioned activity. Why is that? Because there is no activity resulting from the mere perception of the form of the person (*puruṣa*), nor because another cause, the goal to be accomplished, or the fruit is not perceived. Furthermore, let that very consideration of a difference in time be abandoned, which...

Cultivation (*bhāvanā*) destroys the state of being an object-to-be-accomplished (*sādhyatā*); this applies likewise to the past and the present, but not to the future, because no contradiction between the future and that cultivation has been established. Therefore, in such cases as "he will cook" (*pakṣyati*), the cultivation is understood as having its status as an object-to-be-accomplished unimpaired, which leads to the consequence that it possesses the nature of an injunction (*vidhi*). To this he says: "And that [cultivation] is obstructed by the past and the present."
The other time [the future] is not [excluded], because there is no contradiction in its being something to be performed later.
As for the argument— that the self’s connection with the action occurs through an action whose relationship [to the self] has not yet been established—

Just as in common worldly usage, "this is your duty today" implies an activity based on a specific occasion (*pratītyā pravṛttiḥ*), so too here, even when the suffix *liṅ* is present, there arises the contingency that it would convey a meaning not already apprehended by other means of knowledge for the hearer, thereby resulting in its status as an injunction (*vidhi*).

This is not so; for its expression [of the action] occurs only when no other cause (or occasion) has been reached, whereas in that case, it is precisely that which has already been reached by another cause [that is expressed].

Because the meaning is expressed by the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth as something yet to be, it is designated in that manner. Therefore, the utterances of those who know injunctions (*vidhi*) declare: "An injunction is the making known of what was unknown, the instigation of one who has not yet acted, and the connection between an action and its agent regarding something not [otherwise] obtained, through the prohibition of both types of [previously] obtained [alternatives]."
This is not sound, because:
activity does not arise from the knowledge of yoga in this world due to the perception of [another's] intentions; otherwise, it would be false. If that were so, why would he exert himself in vain?

As for the justification: activity occurs through the cognition of the self's connection with an action that has not yet been established as connected [to it], just as in common worldly usage one says, "Today this task is yours. For when a master says to a servant, "Caitra! Today your task is to go to the city," then indeed this Caitra [understands] his own...

Just as one proceeds toward going to a city after understanding the connection thereto— something not previously known from any other source through the command of a master— so too here, one who desires heaven proceeds toward sacrifice and such actions after understanding the connection between the desire for heaven and the performance of sacrifice, which was not previously known from any other source through the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth; thus, the meaning is that an injunction (*vidhi*) is precisely the relation of an action to an agent that has not [otherwise] been established.

An adherent of a particular school (ekadeśin), however, raises an objection: "In this justification as well, there would be the consequence [of it being] an injunction (vidhi) regarding a statement ending in the conditional suffix (liṅ), such as 'he will cook' (pakṣyati), because it causes the listener to understand a matter not previously apprehended by other means of knowledge.
The challenger (codaka) refutes this: "No; for that [suffix] applies when there is a connection between the action and its agent, provided no other cause [for its application] has occurred."

The expression of that [future time] by the optative (*liṅ*) and other suffixes is the expression of a relation; in that context, regarding the optative and so forth, the expression of the meaning—that is, the relation—is as a future state of something that has already been occasioned by another cause. However, the expression by the optative and others is an expression as something not yet occasioned by another cause. For when something is not yet attained, its attainment is of two kinds.

Both production (*utpatti*) and valid cognition (*pramiti*) are negated. In that regard, although there is no attainment in the form of valid cognition (*pramiti-rūpā prāpti*) in a verb ending in the *liṅ* suffix—which conveys a relationship not previously apprehended by other means of knowledge—there does exist attainment in the form of production (*utpatti-rūpā*), because it is that very [action] which is about to arise from another cause that is denoted therein. However, it is not so in the case of a verb ending in the *loṭ* suffix.

The meaning is that, since the connection with sacrifices and so forth cannot be established through any other means without human effort based on the comprehension of the sentence-meaning, therefore—because it is thus—the utterances of those who know injunction (*vidhi*) declare: "An injunction is the making known of what was unknown, the inciting of one who has not yet acted, and the connection between an action and its agent regarding something not already obtained, by way of prohibiting both types of [already] obtained [alternatives]. This is as follows:
He refutes this: This is not sound.

Because—Activity does not arise from the cognition of yoga in the world, since [activity] proceeds from the perception of [another's] intention. If it were otherwise, let it be false; why would he exert himself in vain?

Let it be granted that this person understands from the word his connection with the action, and determines that "it is so" when it is indeed so, and "it is not so" in the opposite case. But why does he proceed to act? For in the world, [one says] "this is yours today."

From the statement "action" (*karma*), the intention of the speaker is understood: that which conforms to a particular intention is fit to proceed, otherwise everything would proceed [indiscriminately]. [Objection: Here too, one will proceed in accordance with the word. [Reply:
There is no basis whatsoever for conforming to the word. [Objection: Is there not its validity (*prāmāṇya*)? And that is established once action has occurred.

Otherwise, there would be the consequence of its being false. How so? Because there is no connection between the past and the present. Furthermore, if the person does not act even regarding the future, that [knowledge] would not exist; thus, there is the consequence of falsity. If, then, its validity depends upon the activity of the person, let it be false as you wish; what is the purpose of this [person] being a means of valid cognition (*śabda-pramāṇa*) for him?

What is the effort involved in the instrument? And for him, a much greater exertion would thus fall upon him. Let this word indeed convey the connection of the self with action through the apprehension of all false cognitions; and let it determine that this is so when there is corroboration by another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) in its being such, but [determine otherwise] in the case of the opposite, when there is sublation by another means of knowledge.

"It is not so. But why does [the person] act? Is it not said that in common worldly usage, "This is your work"? To this he replies: In the world, however, when one hears the statement, "This is your work today," and having thereby understood the distinction in the speaker's intention, whoever conforms to that intention is entitled to act upon the comprehension of that intention. For at that time...

The meaning is that [the Vedic word] does not incite activity by making known the relationship between an action and its agent; rather, it is the specific intention of one who is to be obeyed—such as a command (*ājñā*) and so forth—that does so.

Why? Because otherwise, if the mere cognition of the relationship between an action and its agent were the cause of engagement, and not the cognition of the specific intention of one to be obeyed, then since such a cognition of the relationship would be common to all, it would follow for everyone...

[This is] because of the activity [of the agent]. He objects: "But here too, one will act in accordance with the word, just as in common worldly practice one acts in accordance with the intention. He refutes this: "There is no reason for acting in accordance with the word; for while a master, in accordance with his intention, indeed conforms his behavior to his servant, he bestows what is beneficial upon that servant."

Or rather, it does not bring about what is harmful. He anticipates [the objection]: "Surely there is validity; but how can it be the cause of activity? To this he says: "And that [validity] becomes established in relation to activity. Why? Because otherwise, in the absence of activity, there would be an absolute lack of connection between the agent and the action; therefore, for one who asserts that [connection], [the validity of the means of knowledge is established].

Because it would follow that the entire mass of the Vedas is false. He asks: "But how is there an absence of relationship in the absence of activity? The answer: Because past and present relationships, which are capable of being perceived, are not perceived, they do not exist. Furthermore, if a person does not engage in activity even with respect to a future relationship, then for him, [that relationship] across the three times...

[The opponent argues: "In the case of *viveka* (discrimination), there is an absolute non-existence like that of a sky-flower; therefore, since its object does not exist, that [cognition] would not have that [object], and thus its validity (*prāmāṇya*) would not exist. This results in the fallacy of its being false. He refutes this as follows: "In that case, validity [arises] from the activity of the person. Let it be so; what is the fault? To this he replies: "Therefore, at will..."

Let it be that the word is false; for what purpose is this man’s effort to treat the word as a means of valid cognition? For surely, for this discerning person, there is neither the attainment of benefit nor the avoidance of harm in treating it as a means of valid cognition. If [p.32]...

Because it is accepted as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Now, one might object: verbal cognition is not false knowledge, because there are two kinds of causes [for falsity] that are absent here. Even if there were no defect in the cause (*hetu-doṣa*), the sublater (*bādhaka*) is difficult to avoid; for we do not perceive the past or present relations that would otherwise fall within the range of perception. Furthermore, there is an absence of a cause for what is yet to come. [Objection: The authority of the word itself is the cause. [Reply: No.

Because its existence depends upon activity, there would be a mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*). [Objection: Since cognition possesses intrinsic validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*), there is no mutual dependence. [Reply: No; because that [intrinsic validity] is sublated by the absence of a cause for activity. Since a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that which delimits an object, it is not by itself a cause for activity. Validity exists only through the presence of a cause for activity.
[This is] because of the establishment [of the object].

But surely, since validity is intrinsic (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*), it will be postulated as the cause of activity; for when there is the establishment of what is cognized (*pramita-siddhi*), there is the determination of something else, and because of the non-determination of anything else, the status of being cognized (*pramitatā*) would be lost. What [is that other thing]? It is the result (*phala*). No.

In that case, the mere establishment of validity was intended, yet a great deal more than that has resulted as something to be accomplished, because all false cognitions would thereby be rendered authoritative. He objects: "But verbal cognition is not false, due to the absence of the two kinds of causes [for falsity]. Therefore, it is the very validity of the word that will impel the person's activity."

This is the meaning. He refutes [this]: even if there were no defect in the reason (*hetu*) due to its being non-human in origin (*apauruṣeya*), sublation (*bādha*) would nonetheless be difficult to avoid. Why? Because of the non-apprehension of two relations—one past and one present—which are within the range of perception and possess the specific nature of having all other causal conditions for their apprehension complete. As for the future [relation], it is not a reason...

Because [the effect] exists [only when the cause exists]; and in the absence of the cause, there is an absence of the effect. Otherwise, its occasional occurrence would be untenable—this is the sense. He objects: "There is a cause for the validity of the word, namely, the future relationship. He refutes this: "No; because that validity exists upon the activity [of the word], and since the establishment of activity depends upon validity, there is a mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*)."

[The opponent] objects: "Since the validity of cognition is intrinsic (*svataḥ*), validity is not the cause for purposeful activity; therefore, there is no circularity (*itaretarāśraya*). [The author] refutes this: "No. Because of the absence of a cause for activity, that validity—even though it is the natural rule (*autsargika*)—is set aside. [The opponent asks: "But surely validity itself is the cause for activity, being intrinsic..."

Because it implies that [validity] through the impossibility of its being otherwise, he says: "Because a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that which delimits [an object], and because it is not by itself the cause of activity. For validity is established precisely from the existence of a cause for activity.
This is the underlying intention: what indeed is this so-called "implication" (*ākṣepa*)? It is certainly not "making known," since that is not its cause.

Bodies are absolutely unreal, like flowers in the sky; since they cannot be established through verbal testimony (*śabda-prāmāṇya*) due to their lack of causal activity, they must be admitted to be productive of meaning by implication. And in that case, the aforementioned fault applies. [The opponent] objects: "But surely, because of intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*), it will be postulated as the cause of activity. Why? Because its status as a means of valid cognition is self-evident."

When that which is cognized by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is established, another factor that serves as its warrant is determined through the principle of "otherwise-unaccountability" (*anyathānupapatti*). He demonstrates this very "otherwise-unaccountability" of the cognized object: because otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the loss of its status as being cognized, due to the non-cognition of something else. What is this "other" that is the cause for purposeful action? The answer is: the result (*phala*).
[Page 33] Furthermore,

even if there were a result, one who desires it would not engage [in action], because engagement occurs without distinction regarding the connection to the action; and even if that [connection] were imagined, such engagement would still be untenable.

Is it not the case that only those such as "one who desires heaven" are heard in scripture as being connected with ritual action? True; however, this is not so in every instance, as in the cases of "One should sacrifice with the Viśvajit" and "One should offer the Agnihotra as long as one lives. For this very reason, in one case a desired result is postulated, while in the other the avoidance of misfortune is postulated. True; yet it is not exactly so.
Nor is there any scriptural justification for this; for it is said:

"Even for one who desires [the result], the action is not necessarily performed by command, nor is it necessarily occasioned [by the desire], due to laziness, obstacles, or the non-performance of what is prescribed."

Indeed, one who desires a result or possesses a [specific] sign, even with the purpose of avoiding misfortune, does not necessarily undergo a connection with the ritual action such that a connection with the action heard in scripture would be established, given the existence of the postulations of either a result or the avoidance of misfortune. For that which is the cause for establishing that necessary connection with the action must be demonstrated.

[The opponent] concedes: "But how is it that there is no activity for one who desires a result or fears an evil rebirth? [It is] due to laziness. This does not refute [our position], because even when a result exists, one who lacks desire does not engage in activity. [The opponent objects: "Granted, let there be no activity for one who lacks desire; however, one who *does* desire will engage in activity. To this he replies: "Because the connection with action is the same for both the desirer and the non-desirer."

Because of the activity [of the agent]. Even if that result were imagined, it would be untenable for an action to have a connection with an agent who acts without distinction [regarding that result]. For indeed, it is a known fact that what is unaccounted for (the unaccounted-for) postulates a means of accounting for it (the account), but not merely that which is unaccounted for without a means of accounting. And a result that lacks a means of accounting cannot serve as the basis for the action of an agent who acts without distinction.

The meaning is "of the relationship"—thus he objects: "But it is only those such as 'one who desires heaven' who are heard in scripture as being connected with the action, not merely the person in general. He refutes this: "True, but only in some cases, not in all—for example, 'One should sacrifice with the Viśvajit,' and 'One should offer the Agnihotra as long as one lives. The objector says: "Therefore, [the action] is desired by everyone."

In one case, the Viśvajit sacrifice, heaven is postulated as the fruit; in the other, the occasional (naimittika) rite, the purpose is the avoidance of misfortune (*apāya-parihāra*), not a [desirable] fruit, because one who desires such a fruit lacks the qualification for that rite, as will be explained under the section on "Capability for All" (*sarvaśakti*). He refutes this as follows: True; however, even so, there is no justification for what has been heard in the scripture. For instance:
Even for those who seek [the goal], action does not necessarily follow from the injunction, nor does it arise from the causal factors,
due to laziness, obstacles, or the failure to perform what has been prescribed.

Indeed, an agent who desires a result, or one who possesses a sign, or one whose purpose is the avoidance of misfortune, does not experience or attain a connection with an action by virtue of being enjoined, such that there would be the possibility of a connection with the action as heard [in scripture], given the existence of the two alternatives of postulating either a result or an avoidance. Why, then, would this not be the case? To this he says: "Because..."

Since that cause is necessarily connected with action, it is capable of establishing it—he asks: "But how is it that for one who desires a fruit in rites such as the Viśvajit, or for one who fears misfortune in occasional rites (*naimittika*), action is not necessarily performed?
In that case, there is the state of being desirous. This desire, being personally experienced (*pratyātmavedya*), cannot be denied due to the absence of action.

Likewise, there is non-engagement with obstacles such as death and the like. Furthermore, if engagement were mandatory, it would follow that there could be no non-performance of what is enjoined. Moreover—
The attainment [of results] from delusion and so forth is conceived through other causal signs;
therefore, a person would not wait for an instructive word.

For if the result (*phala*) were imagined as the cause of activity (*pravṛtti-hetu*), the connection with action would not have the word as its basis, but rather would be brought about by verbal [injunction]; thus, the impossibility of it being unattained through any other cause would be undermined. If it is argued that this is possible because it is not apprehended by any other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); we reply that the same consequence would apply even in the case of the *liṭ* (perfect) ending, as has already been stated. Furthermore, [this would apply] in cases such as delusion or chance.

When there is a possibility of a causal connection with an action, one should not assume its fruitfulness as an absolute certainty. If it is argued that the assumption of a fruit arises because the scripture teaches what is beneficial for man (*puruṣaśreya*), we say no; for [in this case] it would not be a scripture (*aśāstra*). The subsequent [objection] is that it is due to laziness. The questioner’s statement is: "In that case, there is no desire [for the fruit]. For it is impossible [to have the capacity] and yet to lack the desire for that [fruit].

The meaning is that there would be an absence of such activity. The reply is: desire, which is self-evident to each individual through internal mental perception (*pratyātmasaṃvedya*) due to its inherence in the mind, cannot be denied by an inference based on the absence of activity. This is because an inference does not arise when its object is sublated by mental perception. Likewise, there is no activity on the part of one who desires [an object] due to obstacles such as death.

Moreover, if activity were mandatory by necessity, it would follow that there could be no non-performance of what is enjoined; and thus, as has been stated, the scriptural injunction "not performing the enjoined rite" would be rendered devoid of scope. Furthermore, the occurrence [of activity] is established through other causes, such as delusion and the like.
Nor would a person, therefore, look toward a word as an instructor.

For if the fruit (phala) is postulated as the cause of engagement (pravṛtti-hetu), it follows that the connection with the action is not based on the word itself, but rather is brought about by the verbal fruit; thus, the impossibility of there being another cause [for the engagement] is untenable. If one should think: "Let the fruit be the cause by way of its being a producer (utpādakatā), but by way of its being a communicator (jñāpakatā)..."

He raises the objection: "The word will be the cause for a relationship that is not known from any other source," provided that there is justification because it has not been apprehended through any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). He refutes this: "It has already been stated that the consequence would be that even [words] ending in the optative suffix (*liṅ*) would possess injunctive force (*vidhitva*). Furthermore, since causes for the connection with action such as delusion or chance are possible...

It is not possible to conceive that an action invariably possesses a fruit, since activity is observed even out of delusion, as in the case of [taking] medicine and the like. Furthermore, the connection between an action and its agent—even when the action is something as mundane as the gathering of lotus petals in a playful manner with tender sprouts—is well-established in the world. He raises an objection regarding the scripture: *śāstrasya...*
If it is argued that there is an assumption of a result because [the Veda] does not prescribe what is beneficial for man, and because it excludes delusion, chance, and so forth?
He refutes this: No, because it is not a scripture (*aśāstra*). He demonstrates this: For a scripture is that which provides instruction (*upadeśaka*).

For this is the nature of scripture. Nor are words such as "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) the instructors of these [past and future objects]. For by these, one is not instructed in the form "do this"; rather, the connection between the one desiring heaven and the sacrifice is understood, just as the connection with a staff is understood from the hearing of the word "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*). And that [connection], whether past or present, is refuted by non-perception (*anupalabdhi*).
Thus, nothing remains for the future.

Moreover, in this way, a person would not act preceded by a means of valid cognition (*pratyaya*); he would merely await a connection with action whose cause is unexamined, like that described by a so-called expert in portents. And thus, the scriptural word would be useless, due to the absence of human effort (*puruṣakāra*).

Furthermore, there is this view: the meaning of the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth is an injunction (*vidhi*), which is not within the scope of other means of valid cognition, which has the word alone as its objective support, which is to be personally experienced as "I am enjoined," which is like pleasure and the like, and which is untouched by the three divisions of time.
Nor are words such as "one should sacrifice" (yajeta) the instructors of these [meanings], because by them one is not instructed in the form "do this";

rather, by words such as "one should sacrifice," the connection of the one desiring heaven (svargakāma) with the sacrifice is understood. The form "gamyate" is derived from the causative suffix (ṇic). Just as by the hearing of words such as "staff-bearer" (daṇḍin), even though they are not direct instructions, a connection with a staff and so forth is understood.

In the case of Devadatta and others, that [past or present cause] has been refuted by non-perception; thus, only a future [cause] remains. And since even factors such as delusion or chance are possible causes therein—just like the fruit—it is not the case that the postulation of a specific fruit is necessarily possible.

Moreover, in this way, a person does not act preceded by a conscious deliberation based on an instruction such as "Do this," but rather observes a connection with an action whose specific cause has not been determined, as if it were described by an expert in physiognomy (sāmudrika).
[Objection: Let him observe; what is the fault? To this he replies: "And thus there would be the futility of the verbal instruction. Why?

Because of the absence of human effort (*puruṣakāra*). For where one, having understood the meaning from a statement, proceeds and attains some desired object, there the statement has its purpose; for in the absence of that [understanding], there is no comprehension and thus no activity, and consequently the attainment of the desired object is impossible. However, when even after understanding the meaning from a statement, a person must still exert effort... [the statement lacks efficacy].

[If it were so], then the statement would be useless; such is the meaning. Now, he presents the view of the commentator (ṭīkākāra): "Even that perception which is not within the scope of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not without a basis in valid cognition; for it has the word alone as its objective support (*ālambana*), having the word alone as its objective support."
That whose locus is [the injunction] by way of being that which conveys it is described as such. But how, then, is this [injunction] conveyed by words?

To this he says: because immediately upon hearing a sentence containing an optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, there arises for the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), such as one desiring heaven, a self-evident awareness—"I am enjoined"—just like pleasure and the like. For just as, when there is heat...

Just as one who is distressed, immediately after being anointed with sandalwood paste, experiences a particular kind of pleasure that is cognizable by the mind alone even internally while his eyes are closed—a pleasure for which there is no other means of knowledge—in the same way, one experiences a "niyoga" (an imperative) immediately after hearing a sentence containing the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth; this is the meaning. He states the reason why it is not within the scope of other means of knowledge: "not touched by the three divisions of time."
To this it is replied:
The meaning of the sentence is indeed the meaning of the individual words, and that is not beyond the scope of other means of cognition.
An action cannot be without an agent, and that which is devoid of time is like a flower in the sky.

Indeed, that which is the meaning of a sentence (vākyārtha) or the meaning of a word (padārtha) must have verbal testimony (śabda) as its means of valid cognition. In this regard, since it is precisely the meaning of a word—qualified by the meanings of other words—that constitutes the meaning of a sentence, it would be untenable for it to be something that is not the meaning of a word. Even for one who maintains that the relation [between word-meanings] is the sentence-meaning, that specific relation is the sentence-meaning, and the relata are nothing other than the word-meanings; thus, it is not [the case that the sentence-meaning is non-verbal].

For other means of knowledge, such as perception and the rest, have existent things as their objects, and existence belongs to those things through their connection with different points of time; however, this *niyoga* (injunction) cannot be apprehended by any mode of being—whether past, future, or present—and thus, because it is something to be accomplished (*kārya*), it is not within the scope of other means of knowledge. Furthermore, it stands in opposition to what is already accomplished.

It is the apprehension of what is presently existing, not by way of being an antidote to the past and the future. Therefore, since that [apprehension] exists even in the case of inference and other means of knowledge whose objects are past and future, the reason (hetu) is not "partially unestablished" (bhāgāsiddha). This very meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth is the mandate (*niyoga*), the injunction (*vidhi*). And when the Vedic impulsion (*codanā*) has such a meaning, its validity follows from its independence.
Regarding the term "accomplishment" (*siddhi*):
it is said in reply— that the meaning of the sentence is indeed the meaning of the individual words, and that [meaning] is not beyond the scope of other [cognitions].
An action cannot be without an agent, and that which is devoid of time is like a flower in the sky.
Indeed, that *niyoga* (injunction), which has sound as its means of valid cognition, must be either the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*) or the meaning of the word (*padārtha*).

He refutes its being the meaning of the sentence if it is not the meaning of a word: in that regard, since in common worldly usage it is observed that the meaning of a sentence consists precisely in a single word-meaning qualified by the other word-meanings, its status as the sentence-meaning would be untenable if it were not the meaning of a word.

Even in the view of those who maintain that the meaning of a sentence is a relation (*sambandha*), the mere relation itself cannot be the sentence-meaning; for, since it does not serve as a basis for specific linguistic usage, it would be impossible for a listener of the sentence to engage in or desist from action toward anything based on it. Therefore, the sentence-meaning must be a specific instance of that relation. Nor can it be the mandate (*niyoga*).

It is a dual distinction, because it consists of the nature of non-connection. Furthermore, a connection, when being qualified, must itself be qualified by its relata; for since it is defined by its relata, no distinction can be established in its own essential form.
