And since these relata are, by rule, categories (*padārtha*), [the connection] is [qualified] only by a category that exists as a relatum.
It must be so, and not by means of a non-entity (*apadārtha*). Nor is the sentence-meaning merely the relation itself; thus he says:

"The relation alone, undifferentiated from the related word-meanings, is indeed just a word-meaning, being within the scope of words such as 'relation,' 'conjunction,' or 'interpenetration' (*anvaya-vyatiṣaṅga*); it is not, however, fit for qualified linguistic usage," as has been stated.

Therefore, even in the view of those who maintain that the meaning of a sentence consists in the relation (*sambandha*), it is not tenable for the *niyoga* (injunction) to be the meaning of the sentence if it is not the meaning of a word. This is because the meaning of a sentence is precisely the specific relation, even though it is not the meaning of a word. [p.37] Of that which has become a non-word-meaning...
The meaning of a sentence is the meaning of the words.
Let it then be the word-meaning? No, for that is not possible, since it is not within the scope of any other means of valid cognition;

because [the understanding of a sentence] depends upon the cognition of the relationship [between words]; and because that [cognition of the relationship] is preceded by the determination of the related terms.

And because that [injunction] is impossible without a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Is it not the case that verbal testimony (*śabda*) is a means of valid cognition? No; because of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*). For the apprehension of the relationship [between word and meaning] occurs only when the injunction has been cognized by means of the word, and only when that [relationship] exists does the cognition of it arise from the word. This is because the connection [of the word] is unknown [prior to the act of cognition].

The meaning is that it has been stated that because the word-base (prakṛti), the suffix (pratyaya), and [the word as a whole] are not individually expressive, it is untenable for the mandate (niyoga) to serve as their delimiting factor due to its lack of connection with them. He takes up the second alternative: "Let it be, then, the word-meaning (padārtha). He refutes this:
It is not so; for that which is not within the scope of any other means of valid cognition cannot be established as a reality, nor can its status as a "category" (padārtha) be justified.
Why? Because being a category depends upon the cognition of a relation. [The opponent might say: "Let there be dependence on the cognition of a relation;
what of it? To this he replies: "And that cognition of a relation is preceded by the determination of the relata."

[The opponent says: "Because [it is] so. Even if that were the case, what [follows]? He says: because the determination of that which is related to an effect is impossible without a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For determination is the fruit of a means of valid cognition; therefore, in the absence of that [means], it cannot exist, just as a sprout cannot exist in the absence of a seed—this is the meaning. [The opponent] objects: "But surely there is the word (*śabda*) as a means of valid cognition."
He refutes this: "No, because of mutual dependence. He demonstrates this: for when the injunction (*niyoga*) has been cognized by the word, then its connection [with that word] is grasped;
and when that grasp of the connection exists, there is the cognition of that injunction by means of the word.
As for the one who thinks: "Indeed, the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth possess such a pre-eminent capacity (*sāmarthyātiśaya*) by which [the injunction is understood] even when not grasped..."

The relationship, having a distinct object and being assisted by a few hearings, produces a cognition with a distinct object; for that [cognition] occurs immediately after those few hearings. Nor can it be otherwise, because words do not denote their own meanings unless their connection has been grasped by another [means of knowledge]. Mā.
It might be argued that for others [the word] does not have the purpose of producing direct realization, and thus its nature is likewise [ineffective].

He refutes this: because a word whose connection [with its meaning] is unknown through other means of knowledge—whether it be a verbal root (*prakṛti*) or an affix (*pratyaya*)—is not expressive. This is the underlying intention: just as upon first hearing [a word], when the relationship [between word and meaning] has not been grasped, even after hearing it hundreds of times...

Furthermore, since a cognition of an object distinct from that [already] heard does not arise from the optative suffix (*liṅ*) alone, and since the observation of linguistic usage arises as being inherently grounded in the observation of a relationship with a real entity, there is no sublation of the requirement for a relationship residing naturally in the word itself— by resorting to the postulation of an extraordinary capacity never before seen— so long as there is no occurrence of a powerful subverting factor.
It is appropriate [to say this],
because in the world there is a recognition of commands (*praiṣa*) and so forth; thus, the relationship is grasped with respect to that which resides therein, conditioned by those [factors].

Here he raises an objection: Since commands and the like are recognized in common worldly usage, the relationship [of the word] with its object is grasped through that [usage], which serves as its limiting condition (*upādhi*).

This is the underlying intention: First, it is understood from the sentences of teachers—such as "Boy, fetch the fuel! and so forth—that the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and other such markers denote an action to be accomplished (*kārya*). For indeed, immediately after hearing such a sentence, a person proceeds to act.

Observing a boy gathering fuel, an onlooker desiring to understand [the nature of action] determines as follows: "This activity of his is preceded by cognition, because it is an independent activity, like my own activity; and that which I have understood before acting is precisely what this [boy] has [understood], since he is not different from me. And I do not act merely upon the understanding of the action itself, nor merely upon the understanding of the result."

Nor is it because of the understanding that [the Veda] is a means to a fruit; rather, it is because of the understanding of its being a task (kāryatā). Indeed, ultimately, as long as a child has not understood even an action such as suckling at the breast to be a task, he does not engage in it. Nor is the state of being a means to the good (śreyaḥ-sādhanatā) identical to the state of being a task; for they are mutually distinct.

Because it would involve a contradiction regarding the locus of the characteristics of abiding in a necklace (*hāra-sthiti-lakṣaṇa-virodhādhāratvāt*). For there is no possibility that that which is the means (*sādhanatva*) toward a desired end could simultaneously be the object to be accomplished (*sādhyatva*) with respect to human effort (*kṛti*), i.e., exertion. However, some have perceived non-difference (*abheda*) in the sense that for action (*karman*) whose nature is affliction (*kleśātman*), its being an "effect" (*kāryatā*) consists in its being connected to the status of being a means to a fruit (*phala-sādhanatā-anvayinī*). Likewise...

Furthermore, there is no comprehension of something as a "task" (kāryatā) apart from its being a means to a desired end (phalasādhanatā). Therefore, even a young boy concludes that his own activity arises from the cognition of a task distinct from being a means to an end; and since this cognition arises in him immediately after the teacher's instruction, it must be [derived] from that.
Since the word’s denotative power is restricted solely to the *kārya* (the thing to be accomplished), and since that *kārya* is established as the denotable object only when it is related (*anvita*),

then in sentences such as "One desiring heaven should perform the Agnihotra," the person desiring heaven must be presented as the *niyojya* (the person to be impelled) by means of the term "one desiring heaven," in accordance with the conclusion reached in the sixth chapter [of the *Śābarabhāṣya*].

Thus it is established. And he who understands the task (*kārya*) is the one to be enjoined (*niyojya*). One who desires heaven (*svargakāma*) is distinguished by the desire for heaven as that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*). And he connects himself with that very task as the one to be enjoined, provided that [the task] is capable of being experienced as the means to that which is desired. Furthermore, an action (*kriyā*), being momentary, cannot exist at a later time.

The phrase "the cause of the fruit" does not connect with the person to be impelled (niyojya) by way of being an effect (*kāryatā*). Since only that which is an effect persisting until another time is capable of entering into such a connection, the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and others denote an effect that is distinct from action and is known solely through another means of knowledge (*māna*). And because it is not previously known through any other means of knowledge, it is called *apūrva* (the unprecedented), and it is [denoted] as an effect.

That which, being understood within oneself, impels a person [to act] is designated as *niyoga* (an injunction). Nor does it follow that, even though [the result] occurs immediately after the action, [the injunction] brings about heaven and so forth only immediately by depending on auxiliary factors such as place and time. Furthermore, there is no loss of the status of the sentence-meaning for the *apūrva* (the unseen potency), because its subordinate status (*guṇabhāva*) arises from its being the producer of the fruit; for its own...

For the sake of obtaining the qualities to be enjoined, it resorts to conformity with the result, just as one does for oneself; just as a master, performing an act for his own sake, benefits a slave born in the house, so too is this case. And this is not the case in the Veda alone.

In that case, the cognition of the relationship pertains to those [particulars] themselves, and not to the mandate (*niyoga*). Those limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) are not the word-meanings, because they are subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*). That which persists through them all as the instigator of action is the word-meaning, since it is never abandoned in any instance.

This is not sound. If the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) were established by other means of knowledge, then there could be no single recurring motivator for the linguistic usage among them, because the understanding of words arises solely from worldly usage, which—by following Vedic sentences—extends as far as the *apūrva*.
Nor is it the case that the denotation of multiple meanings by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and others is not perceived; for the student indeed says to the teacher: [“I understand the meaning”].

"Prompted" means set in motion, that is to say, made aware of the task to be done; for indeed, a conscious being cannot be incited to act otherwise. Since, as such, these [terms] like "command" (praiṣa) and so forth are understood in common worldly usage, and since activity is impossible without the comprehension of a task to be done, the apprehension of the relationship residing therein—and having grasped that very relationship—culminates in the Veda.

[Objection: But surely, in common worldly usage, injunctions (*praiṣa*) and so forth are also understood; how then can it be said that the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and others denote only the "thing to be done" (*kārya*)? To this, he says: "Because of that as a limiting adjunct" (*tadupādheḥ*). That is, because of the limiting adjuncts such as injunctions. What is meant is this:
these are merely limiting adjuncts, not the primary meanings of the words. And those alone are the limiting adjuncts which are incidental (*taṭastha*) to the observation of usage.
Grammarians establish the meaning of a word within a specific context by means of an adjunct (*upādhi*), just as "animal-ness" (*paśutva*) is the adjunct for that which is denoted by the word *hari*.

For instance, since animal-ness is merely incidental (*taṭastha*) and does not enter into the primary denotation, it serves to restrict the sense of "bearer" (*hartṛtva*)—which is the actual meaning of the word *hari*—to the animal alone. In the same way, verbal commands (*praiṣa*) and the like also do not enter into the primary denotation.

[The opponent argues: "They establish [the meaning] as a specific action (*kārya*), but not as the denotable object (*abhidheya*); therefore, because the apprehension of the relationship is possible, it follows that the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth denote an injunction (*niyoga*).
He refutes this: "In that case, since only those [meanings] such as *praiṣa* (command) and so forth are perceived, there can be no knowledge of the relationship [between word and meaning]."

[This refers to] the *niyoga* (the mandate) as something unprecedented (*apūrva*). Now, it was argued that those adjuncts (*upādhi*) are not the meanings of the word, because they are variable (*vyabhicāra*). For injunctions (*praiṣa*) and the like are not the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*), since it is not employed in the case of an invitation (*āmantraṇa*) which is equal [to an injunction]. Nor is it an invitation, since it is employed even when addressing a superior in the form of a request (*adhyeṣaṇa*). Nor is it a request, since it is employed even when sending someone who is inferior.

Because of its application; this is the deviation [from the literal meaning]. That which persists through them all as the motivator is the meaning of the word. Why? Because it is not abandoned in any instance. For in all cases—whether in commands (*praiṣa*) or the like—a single "to-be-done-ness" (*kartavyatā*) must be possible, since otherwise, as has been stated, independent activity would be untenable.

Therefore, the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and others, which express "what ought to be done" (*kartavyatā*),— due to their connection with the word *svargakāma* (one desiring heaven)— denote the *apūrva*, which is distinct from sacrifices and the like that perish immediately, and which is conducive to the attainment of heaven and so forth that serve as the goal for the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*). Thus, it is established that the *niyoga* (the mandate) is the meaning of the optative suffixes and the like, being beyond the scope of other means of knowledge.
He refutes that: this is not sound. If the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) were established by other means of knowledge, then there would be no single, recurring injunction (*niyoga*) among them.
Since they fall within the scope of other means of knowledge, the cognition of their relationship does not belong to that [injunction]. It is unknown...

Because it is impossible to comprehend the relationship with an object [in the case of other means of knowledge], only those [Vedic] words and their meanings [are authoritative], since their connection is already known, and not others. The *niyoga* (the injunction) is the motivator; that is to say, it is the *apūrva*. Therefore, because they fall within the scope of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), those [other things] are not [authoritative].

The knowledge of the relationship [of the word] is only with respect to the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), not with respect to that *niyoga* (the mandate) which is otherwise called the "unprecedented" (*apūrva*). Why? Because it is impossible to comprehend a relationship whose object is unknown.
[An objection: "Let there be knowledge of the relationship with respect to the adjuncts, and let there be none with respect to the *apūrva*; what does this matter? To this, he says:

Only those [words] have such meanings, because they possess a known connection with the *niyoga* (the mandate), and not others, due to their lack of awareness of such a connection with the *niyoga*. This is the underlying intention here: it is true that the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth denote "what is to be done" (*kartavyatā*), but "what is to be done" belongs only to the action (*kriyā*), not to the *apūrva* (the unseen potency), because the capacity of words is determined based on worldly usage.
And because that very [apūrva] is known through another means of knowledge within one's own self as being an object to be accomplished (*kārya*) and thus a cause for activity.

Now, if it is argued: "Since that apūrva is not within the scope of other means of knowledge, and since in common worldly usage the optative suffixes (*liṅ* etc. have their connection established only with respect to what is to be done (*kartavyatā-mātra*), they acquire a specific apūrva in the Veda through their connection with the word 'one who desires heaven' (*svargakāma-pada*)."

Granted that the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth is indeed this very "thing-to-be-done" (*kartavya*), but how is it established that this does not also apply to worldly action? Because it is improper for a single word to have multiple meanings. Furthermore, since the usage of the optative suffixes is justified even when referring to a worldly action that is to be performed, the "novel thing-to-be-done" (*apūrva-kartavyatā*) [is what must be intended].

Because of the state of being inseparable (nāntarīyakatva). For it is impossible for an action to be a means to that [result] unless the necessity of performing the action has been established; because there is no contradiction with worldly usage; and because, since the necessity of performing the *apūrva* is never observed to be inseparable from the worldly necessity of performing an action, the opposite case is impossible, and thus it is absolutely [unprecedented].

If it is argued that, through repeated practice, even a word used in its figurative sense may be considered expressive [of the primary meaning], thereby establishing the injunction (*niyoga*) for the expression of the *apūrva* (the unseen potency), then we ask: why is it improper to assume multiple meanings? If you say it is because of the burden of postulating multiple potencies (*aneka-śakti-kalpanā-gaurava*), then we reply: since the *apūrva* itself is manifold—residing in various principal rites and subsidiaries—is there not likewise a multiplicity [of meanings]? How, then, can there be a single meaning?

If it is argued that the optative suffix (*liṅ*) possesses a single power regarding the *apūrva*s—despite differences in their forms—because its basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*), namely being pervaded by human effort (*kṛtivyāpyatā*), is uniform everywhere, just as the word "one-year-old cow" (*ekahāyanī*) has a single power [regarding various individuals]? Alas!
What offense has been committed by the action (*kriyā*) itself, which is of the nature of what is to be done (*kartavyatārūpā*), such that this [single power] is not attributed to it?

The optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth are like a husband who accepts another power as a bribe. If it is argued that this is not a fault because there is a difference in what is to be done (*kartavyatā*) despite the identity of the word, we say no; for there is no such difference.
If one should think: "Even though there is an identity of the word 'what is to be done,' nevertheless, [the optative] intends toward an action (*kṛti*)," [we reply: no.

The "to-be-done-ness" (kartavyatā) of the unprecedented (apūrva) consists in the exertion of human effort directed toward that end; it is this very [to-be-done-ness] that constitutes the causal basis for the application of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth. Nor is such a "to-be-done-ness" applicable to the action itself, because, being of the nature of suffering, [one would not engage in it].

Because its status as a primary object is untenable, that [apūrva] has the nature of being something to be accomplished (*kartavyatā*), characterized by being pervaded by the activity of one who is engaged for the sake of rice-porridge and the like; however, since it is distinct [from the action], that *kartavyatā* cannot be the object of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth without another capacity (*śakti*).
This is not so, because there is no difference from the *kartavyatā* of the action itself. Indeed, one does not [act] with reference to the apūrva.

An action ought to be undertaken for the sake of a goal, for that [action] is human effort. And since that effort is underlain by desire (*icchā*), it must have that very thing as its objective. Whatever is the object of desire is also the object of that [effort], namely pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth, because desire is underlain by pleasure. Now, the *apūrva* (unseen merit) is not pleasure; how then could it be desired? If it were undesired, how could one act with it as the objective?

What is the motivation for action? It is because it is understood as such from the word [of scripture]. If it is argued that even that which is not pleasure and not desired is the primary object toward which action is directed, then does the word cause this to be understood? If so, would smoke not also exist where there is no fire? Or is consciousness of the nature of bliss, according to the scriptural text, "Consciousness is bliss"? No, because it contradicts other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

If it is argued that [this is not so], we say no; for here too, the same principle applies. This is because one accepts that the *apūrva* (unseen potency) pertaining to the *samit* and other [subsidiary acts]—though itself not directly to be performed—is to be regarded as something "to be done" (*kartavyatva*) by virtue of its being subordinate to the *adhikārāpūrva* (the primary unseen potency of the qualified person’s entitlement).

Since this *apūrva* is conducive to heaven and other results, even though it is not pleasure itself, it remains an object of desire; thus, how could there be any contradiction with other means of valid cognition (*māna*)?

If this is argued, we say no; for even in the case of an action (*kriyā*), the state of being a means to a desired end (*samīhitasādhanatā*) exists in that same way [as a property of the action]. Furthermore, it is untenable for the *apūrva* of occasional rites (*naimittika*) and prohibitions (*niṣedha*)—which lack a [visible] fruit—to possess that [property of being a means to a desired end]. Thus, there is no establishment of the *apūrva* for the *liṅ* and other suffixes in the case of the *apūrva* of occasional rites and prohibitions, [only] for one who possesses the occasion (*nimitta*) and for the agent of the prohibited action.
This is because there is no contradiction in the agent (*niyojya*), who is delimited by a specific qualification (*siddha-viśeṣaṇa*), understanding that the action is to be performed.
Furthermore, the coexistence of the primary rite and its subsidiaries is possible even through the mediation of the postulated *apūrva*, which is not itself the literal meaning of the word.
Moreover, why should the agent—who is characterized by the heaven to be attained—not understand the action itself as what is to be performed?

Because that [action] perishes very quickly, it lacks the capacity to be conducive to that [result]. For something is conducive to the production of another only when, being present, the other arises, and not when it is absent. If it is argued that "the otherworldly results such as heaven do indeed arise when the action exists, even though it has long since perished, because they are produced from it," then what about the *āgneya* and other sacrifices? In those cases too, would this be the case?

Is the status of being a means (*sādhanatva*) for the *apūrva* [result] not due to the eligibility (*adhikāra*), or is their status as a means merely figurative (*bhākta*)? For if that status were figurative, its connection with the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) would not be possible; indeed, a boy who has only figuratively been called "fire" is never employed for burning or cooking. Furthermore, you maintain that these [means] have a single nature as objects (*viṣayatva*) and a manifold nature as instruments (*karaṇatva*).
It is explained as follows: because those two consist of different modes of approach (*prasthāna*). For the object (*viṣaya*) is connected to the means of comprehension (*pratipatti*);

it is established according to how it is perceived. In that regard, once the *Āgneya* and other sacrifices have been uttered, they experience their status as objects exactly as they are understood from the single cognition [arising from the injunction] "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa. Thus, these [sacrifices] constitute a single [act].

The status of being the object (*viṣayatva*) with respect to the *apūrva* resulting from the injunction is the state of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*), and that [instrumentality] depends upon the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) [of the action], not upon its subsequent realization (*pratipatti*). And since the intrinsic nature of these [actions], such as the *Āgneya*, is understood to be distinct from one another from such texts as "The *Āgneya* [cake] on eight potsherds," their status as means (*sādhanatā*), which follows that [nature], is likewise distinct.

Furthermore, there is no such thing as being a means for one another when they are mutually independent, because the supreme *apūrva* is established through the performance of the ritual acts exactly as they are heard in scripture. Moreover, many such acts are prescribed for it; therefore, it cannot be accomplished by a single means alone.
This must be so. Furthermore, it is observed even in the world that a single action may be accomplished by multiple instruments;
for example: "The king proceeds at twilight, accompanied by a horse, a torch, and attendants with swords in their hands.
If it is argued that the instruments, such as the horse and the rest, are distinct because of the difference in their intermediate operations (*avāntaravyāpāra*), [we reply:]...

In this case as well, the intermediate operations (*avāntaravyāpāra*) are indeed the *utpattyapūrvas* (origination-apūrvas). And since these differ with each sacrifice, such as the Āgneya and others, the principle is the same. Consequently, there is no confusion of ritual properties (*dharma*) among the clarified butter (*ājya*), the vegetable offerings (*auṣadha*), and the milk offerings (*sāṃnāyya*). Even though [the rites] are prompted by the *paramāpūrva* (final apūrva), because the status of being a means (*sādhanabhāva*) differs according to the distinction between the intermediate operations and the origination-apūrvas, they are distinct means for the apūrva.

And because they have been so established; otherwise, if there were no distinction between them, there would be the undesirable consequence of confusion (*saṅkara*). Therefore, just as at the time of the production of the *adhikāra-apūrva*, the intermediate operations (*avāntaravyāpāra*) or potencies (*śakti*)—namely, the *utpatti-apūrvas*—belong to the *Āgneya* and other sacrifices even though they do not yet exist, since their status as means is understood through verbal testimony; likewise, [the intermediate operations belong] to that [action] whose status as a means toward the fruit is understood.

The intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*) or the capacity (*śakti*) of the ritual action will be the *apūrva*. If it is asked: "How can the capacity of one thing reside in another, or how can there be an intermediate operation in the absence of an agent possessing such an operation? [the answer is: This applies equally to the *āgneya* and other sacrifices, which are the means for the ultimate *apūrva*, in their intermediate operations or capacities, namely, the *utpattyapūrvas* (originative *apūrvas*).

Because the objection is equally applicable [to both views]. If it is argued that the *utpattyapūrvas* (origination-apūrvas)—which belong to other [substances], which do not coexist with the Āgneya and other sacrifices whose means and efficient force (*bhāvanā*) are understood from words independent [of other means of knowledge], and which are even non-simultaneous—are the operations or the capacities [of those sacrifices], then [we ask]:
is it on the basis of worldly usage that one says, "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa"?

An action (*kriyā*) is not understood as something to be accomplished (*kārya*) through its qualification by a goal such as heaven (*svarga*); nor is there any incompatibility in the suffix (*pratyaya*) with respect to its own qualifier in the form of that goal, such that— on account of incorporating that [qualifier]— an intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*) or capacity (*sāmarthya*) of the action would have to be postulated as the *apūrva*.

It is also false to claim that an action which is a means to the means of a result is not itself a means to that result; for it is precisely because it is directed toward the result that it serves as its means. This is just as the *āgneya* and other sacrifices, though directed toward the supreme *apūrva*, serve as the means to the *utpattyapūrva*; or as the act of plowing, though directed toward the acquisition of grain, serves as the means to breaking the earth and so forth.

[The question arises: Is it the status of being a means (*sādhanatva*)? Nor is it correct to say that the status of being a means toward the supreme *apūrva* belongs only to the *utpattyapūrvas* (origination-*apūrvas*) and not to the Āgneya and other sacrifices. For the expressions "by means of the Darśapūrṇamāsa" and "one should sacrifice" do not denote the *utpattyapūrvas*, but rather refer to the six [sacrifices] beginning with the Āgneya, which have already arisen [in the ritual sequence] through their connection with specific times.

Regarding the constituent parts that have not been restated [in the injunction], their respective originative sentences are not capable of establishing their causality toward their own originative *apūrva*s. Because these originative sentences are recited in proximity to the sentence of qualification (*adhikāra-vākya*), there arises a suspicion of the recognition of that same qualification-*apūrva*; consequently, they do not immediately lead to the cognition of a distinct *apūrva*.

Because it does not produce a cognition. As for the *apūrva* (unseen potency) belonging to the subsequent Agni and other sacrifices that have already arisen and been restated, is its establishment through another means of knowledge? No; because its independence is established by the fact that it is not the object of another means of knowledge.

Moreover, an injunction (*niyoga*) is the operation of an enjoiner; it cannot be established without an enjoiner. This is because it is impossible for objects, instruments, and results—which have already been apprehended and exist independently of one another—to constitute such an injunction.

To establish that [injunction], the "origination-apūrvas" (*utpattyapūrva*) are postulated; although these are denoted by the suffixes and possess the nature of a task (*kārya*), they do not belong to the [deities] such as Āgneya.

The subordinate means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) must attain the status of being their own instruments with respect to the principal [action]. For when the supreme *apūrva* is to be produced by those [subsidiaries] such as the *Āgneya* sacrifice, they are postulated as intermediate operations (*avāntaravyāpāra*). And since the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is established in that very way, it is impossible for them to possess primacy; for a connection with two principals in a single [action] is difficult to establish.

Therefore, just as for you [the opponent], the ultimate *apūrva* and its fruit are the object of a single volitional effort (*kṛti*) regarding the *utpattyapūrva*s— which serve as intermediate operations— of the *Āgneya* and other sacrifices, such that each one possesses the status of an instrument (*karaṇa*) toward that expanded end;
so too, for me, even though the action has the *apūrva* as its intermediate operation, it possesses the capacity to be conducive to heaven (*svarga*), and thus it is the goal to be accomplished.

Even one distinguished by the desire for heaven is indeed capable of understanding the necessity of performing an action. Nor is it an absolute rule that whoever desires a particular end understands only its means as something to be done, and not what is not a means; this will be demonstrated later. And it has been shown in the *Bhāvanāviveka* that the cognition of the necessity of an action pertains to that which is a means to what is desired by the agent.

It will be explained later that there would be no application [of the suffixes] to the object or to the result; therefore, the denotation of the *apūrva* (the unprecedented) by the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and others is not established through their connection with those desiring heaven and so forth.
Nor, in common worldly usage, does the *apūrva* follow immediately after a teacher’s command such as, "O boy, perform the twilight worship."

It is argued that, having observed purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*), and since that activity depends upon the comprehension of an end (*kārya*), and because the ritual act of twilight worship (*sandhyopāsana*) is inherently painful and thus cannot be such an end, the apprehension of the linguistic convention (*saṅgatigraha*) for the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth must pertain to an end other than that [worship], which is not known through any other means of knowledge (*māna*). This is incorrect, because it is the action (*kriyā*) itself that can logically be the thing to be done (*kartavyatā*). As for the claim that it is untenable due to its being painful—

If you say this, then it would be better to simply postulate that [the self] itself is the means for either the attainment of the beneficial or the avoidance of the harmful; for such a thing alone is perceived as the cause for activity toward the self. But even this is extremely flimsy. Therefore, because it is not the object of any other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and because it is not a [constituent] category (*padārtha*), it cannot possibly be the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*).
Thus it is established that the *niyoga* (the mandate) is something not previously known (*apūrva*).

However, if, out of a desire to maintain the status of the *niyoga* as a primary category (*padārtha*), one were to resort to its being an object of other means of knowledge (*mānāntara*)—even though this is undesirable—then, by virtue of being an object of another means of knowledge, the *codanā* (Vedic injunction) would lose its independence (*anapekṣatva*). To this, he says:

Now, is it established through another means of knowledge (*mānāntara*)? No; for the independence (*anapekṣatva*) of the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) is established by the fact that it does not have another means of knowledge as its object.

Furthermore, words such as "command" (*niyoga*), "incitement" (*pravartanā*), and "impulsion" (*preraṇā*) possess conventional meanings established in reference to the activity of an instigator (*niyoktṛ*); they convey that [activity]. And this [activity] is not possible without an instigator.
He says: "Because in the absence of a cause, the effect ceases. Furthermore, an injunction (*niyoga*) is the operation of an enjoiner (*niyoktṛ*);
it is not possible without an enjoiner. To the objection, "Then let there be an enjoiner," he replies: "And he does not exist" (p. 44).

Furthermore, its origin is impossible, because you accept that it is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*), and because sound has already been refuted previously. Since there is no reference to "doing" (*kurv iti*) therein, it cannot have anything else as its object. If it were [based] on the word, then the same consequence would apply even to a jar (*ghaṭa*) and so forth;
for the words "jar" and the like do not refer to any one of the [categories] such as "past" (*bhūta*). If [it were based] on the object, then [the consequence is] absolute...

"Existence [of the Veda] is like a sky-flower and the like, because absolute non-existence is characterized by such [absence of existence]. Furthermore, since eternal things are characterized by presentness, there is no deviation [from this rule]. If presentness consists in being the counter-correlate of something else, that [presentness] is not possible in the case of eternal things. Now, one might argue that the Person (Puruṣa) will be the instigator; to this he says: 'Because of the acceptance of its being authorless (apauruṣeyatva)...'"
Because of the absence of a person [to command] in the Veda. Let it be then that the word itself is the instigator; to this he replies:

"Because of the prior refutation of the word," by means of the passage beginning with "because it is a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇatvāt*). Furthermore, since other means of valid cognition have as their scope objects whose temporal status is subject to change, [the word] does not refer to them; because it does not refer to them, it does not refer to the three times.

Because there would be the undesirable consequence that *riṣyasi*, *akārṣīḥ*, and *karoṣi* would have identical meanings, [the object] would not be within the scope of anything else. If that were so, then by virtue of the word itself, there would be the undesirable consequence that even in the case of a jar (*ghaṭa*) and so forth, it would not be within the scope of other means of knowledge; for even the words "jar" and so on do not refer to any one among the past and other times. Indeed, in the cognition "jar," there is no reference to any one among the past and other times.

The application [of the terms] "the jar existed," "exists," and "will exist" is possible; the meaning is that when all three are considered together, there is no tautology, despite the apparent contradiction. Now, if it is argued that the reference to the three times is based on the actual state of things (*arthataḥ*) and not merely from words, he refutes this: [the jar] would be absolutely non-existent, like a sky-flower and the like. Just as sky-flowers and such did not exist...

If they were thus [non-existent], then even their causal necessity (*niyoga*) would not exist, for there would be no distinction between them [and other non-entities]. Indeed, there is no definition of absolute non-existence other than this. Therefore, he says "due to the exclusion from the three times," because this is the definition of absolute non-existence. For the existence of that which transcends time is determined by its delimitation within time.

The meaning is as follows: that which is pervaded, being excluded from time by its own limitation, is thereby excluded from existence itself—just as the property of being a *śiṃśapā* tree is excluded from a region of a mountain consisting of a single solid rock when the property of being a tree is excluded. [Objection: But surely atoms, space, and so forth exist as entities distinct from time, and yet they are not time.

"Since [existence] is thus delimited, there is no deviation [from the rule]; therefore, he says: 'And because eternal things are present, there is no deviation. The meaning is that for eternal things, which are conditioned by an act of existence (*astikriyā*) that is distinguished from the past and future and which necessarily excludes its own non-connection with them, their state of being present is perpetual."

He raises an objection: If being present (*vartamānatā*) consists in being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitā*) of others, then it does not exist in eternal things (*nitya*). For that which is indeed called "presentness" is something that arises by way of its cause having been suppressed, and which is itself suppressed by way of its own destructive cause through its state of having passed away (*atītatā*); such presentness is not possible in eternal things. Priorly...

The meaning is that because it is invariably concomitant with the non-existence of destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), it is contradictory to permanence. This aforementioned "presentness" is technical (*pāribhāṣika*) and not established by common worldly usage; for indeed, [it exists] even in that which is devoid of prior and subsequent non-existence (*prākpradhvaṃsābhāva*).
In that case, since even that which is unconnected with time would be an object of another means of knowledge (*māna*), the presentation of the distinction from time is redundant. [Objection:

Being graspable by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇagrāhyatā*) is the definition of existence (*sattva*); therefore, there is no absolute non-existence. [Reply: No; for even in the case of non-entities (*abhāva*) such as space (*ākāśa*) and so forth, ordinary people experience the natural perception of their presence, as in "there is space."
This is because we observe such usages as "there is space" (*kāśo'sti*). Nor is this usage merely figurative (*bhākta*), for there is no distinguishing factor [to justify it].

Indeed, no distinction is perceived between the statements "the self exists" (*ātmā'sti*) and "consciousness exists" (*vijñānamasti*). Furthermore, if one were to assume that one of these two is figurative despite their lack of distinction, it would follow that everything other than that [one] must also be figurative.

Even though this refutation is quite substantial, he states another defect: "In that case, even that which is not connected with time would be the object of another means of knowledge; thus, the presentation of the distinction of time regarding the mandate (niyoga) is futile.
By this, [he refutes] what they say: "For it is the operation of the causal factors (kāraka) that is delimited by the three times, not the entitlement (adhikāra)."

That too must be understood as refuted. Just as *adhikāra* (authorization), *niyoga* (injunction), and *kārya* (the task) are not of the nature of an operation (*vyāpāra*) and are not connected with the three times, so too are jars and other such things. For they are never non-operations, nor are they beyond the scope of other means of knowledge (*mānāntara*). Likewise, authorization (*adhikāra*), though not delimited by time, is [known] through other means of knowledge.

The presentation of the distinction of time would be useless, on the grounds that it might serve as the object [of the cognition]. But surely, existence is neither a relation with time, nor is it pervaded by it, for that would entail the consequence that time—which is not related to it—is non-existent. Nor is it a universal (sāmānya), because that is untenable in the absence of a prior reflective awareness, just as in the case of one who has seen a black-eyed cow [later] seeing a brindled cow.

There is no such reflective awareness (*tad-avamārśa*) regarding snow mountains and the like, nor regarding motes of dust and the like, nor regarding color and so forth, nor regarding upward motion and the like, nor regarding "cowness" (*gotva*) and the like; by this, it should be understood that "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) and other such categories are also refuted.
Therefore, even "Being" (*sattā*) is not a universal (*sāmānya*); rather, the definition of existence is simply being apprehensible by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇagrāhyatā*). And that—

Just as time, which is unconditioned by the three periods of time, exists, so too does the *niyoga* (the mandate), which is to be known through its application as established by the authority of the scripture; thus, it is not absolutely non-existent. However, things such as a sky-flower, which lack all possible status as objects of valid cognition even in the past, are indeed absolutely non-existent.

The opponent urges: "Being graspable by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the definition of existence; therefore, the mandate (*niyoga*) is not absolutely non-existent. He refutes this: "No, because even a non-entity (*abhāva*) is an object of knowledge (*prameya*). Indeed, being an object of knowledge is not existence itself, because existence is excluded [from non-entities] even while the property of being an object of knowledge persists in them.
For when something persists in another, yet that other is excluded from it..."

That [object] is indeed different from that [cognition], just as flowers are different from their threads; and "existent" and "non-existent" are objects of knowledge established in the world as mutually exclusive. As the authorities on valid cognition have said:
"The existent is that which is apprehended as 'existent,' exactly as it is."

And reality (*tattva*) is that which is non-erroneous (*aviparīta*). How is it that the unreal (*asat*), when apprehended as "it is non-existent," is reality as it truly is, non-erroneous? When it was established that the non-existence of thorns and the like is not an object of cognition (*prameya*), how then is it not [an object]?

[If you argue that] non-existence is an object of cognition (*prameya*), then it is well said [that it is so]; yet how can there be the linguistic usage "it exists" for that which is said to "not exist" while being cognized? It is because of the delimitation of the object (*viṣayāvacchedāt*). For a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) whose object is delimited, by making known that [specific] thing while not making known anything else, brings about the linguistic usage "it does not exist. How could a linguistic usage regarding one object [be produced] by another object?

Is it from a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) having a different object? This [means of valid cognition] does not have a different object, because its object is the delimitation of the object of that [other means of valid cognition], since that [delimitation] has a distinct object. To explain: this meaning "it does not exist" is not perceived as "this. Thus, existence and non-existence are experienced as mutually excluded, being eternally delimited by their respective natures of existence and non-existence.
The objector spoke with derision: "It is well-said that non-existence (*abhāva*) is an object of knowledge (*prameya*. He shows the seed of this derision:

"How can it be that something does not exist and yet is cognized? For this non-existence does not manifest like substances, qualities, and universals, which are mutually distinct and possess differences in their own nature (*svabhāva*)."

Moreover, it is experience itself—mutually exclusive, possessing distinct intrinsic natures, and consistent with the path of valid cognition—that constitutes the light of reality for the world; it is not merely a matter of human rumor. For such rumors could arise like the case of the yakṣa at Savaṭa. Therefore, the designation "it does not exist" is based solely on its not being perceived.

It has an object, yet it does not take non-existence as a concrete entity within its range. Thus, "the jar does not exist" means that it is not cognized. How is there a connection between this and the phrase "how is it cognized"? It is because of contradiction; such is the meaning. If this were so, how would the conventional usage regarding non-existence—such as the practice of stepping on the ground [only where] thorns and the like are absent—be possible?

If one asks: "What is the basis for the non-existence of things like jars, which consist of positive activity (*pravṛtti*), and for the unreality of things consisting of negation (*nivṛtti*)? He says: When it was established that "non-existence is not an object of knowledge (*prameya*) regarding thorns and the like," how then does the conventional usage "it does not exist" occur at that time? He provides the answer: "Due to the delimitation of the object (*viṣayāvacchedāt*) by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)."
[It refers to] those who apprehend the bare ground. He clarifies this very point: a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that has a delimited object apprehends the solitary ground;

that is to say, it does not apprehend a ground accompanied by a jar, a thorn, or other such things. By making known the ground while not making known anything else, it brings about the conventional usage that "the jar, the thorn, and so forth do not exist."

This can be clarified as follows: how can a linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) whose object is the absence of a jar or the like arise from a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) whose object is something else, such as the ground? This linguistic usage of absence is well-known to all people and cannot be denied, just like the linguistic usage of presence. Therefore, this [usage] must arise precisely from absence.

The meaning is that if the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding one thing were to arise from something else, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). He refutes this: "This [usage] does not have another thing as its object.
It does not have a distinct absence (*abhāva*) as its object, because such an absence is not perceived as having a concrete form (*vigraha*) like other positive entities.
If so, what is its object? To this he says: "It is the delimitation (*avaccheda*) of the object of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with respect to that linguistic usage of absence."

Because it is an object [of cognition]. Now, one might ask: if the delimitation by the object is also distinct from the positive entity that serves as the object, then why is this linguistic usage of "absence" not considered to have a different object? To this he says: "Because that [delimitation] is not a separate object. It is not so.

"The ground is cognized, but the jar is not; therefore, in that case, non-cognition is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This is unworldly. To this it is replied: we see you engaging in discourse without having properly defined your terms. Let your honor define this: [p.47] "The ground is cognized, but the jar is not; therefore, in that case, non-cognition is the means of valid cognition. This is unworldly. To this it is replied: we see you engaging in discourse without having properly defined your terms. Let your honor define this:

Regarding this worldly transaction characterized by engagement and withdrawal—which occurs when people think "it does not exist" in some respect—is this due to non-apprehension, or due to the apprehension of something else, or due to the apprehension of its absence? If it were due to non-apprehension, they would not seek to know the absence of what is desired, for they would simply withdraw from it because of that non-apprehension; [likewise] regarding what is undesired...

[The opponent argues: "Cognitions would proceed precisely from such determination (*pariccheda*). For practical activity (*vyavahāra*) is based solely on the non-determination of the object of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

[The author replies: No, because there is no distinction [between the two cases]. For the non-determination of that [object] and its other [the absence] is not distinguished. Indeed, what is called "determination" as a non-cognition is not something distinct from the existence of the ground; rather, it is the absence of a visible counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), such as a jar or a thorn.
In the case of "ka" and so forth, there is the apprehension of the bare ground alone; and that has as its object the solitary ground.

When a certain thing is desired to be seen, and when a certain counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is visible, the absence of that [desired thing] is said to exist, and it brings about the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding that absence.
Now, let it be granted that this linguistic usage of absence—namely, the designation "it does not exist"—has this as its object.
Thinking that [the opponent] might rely on an object distinct from the worldly entities, he says: "For instance, the meaning of 'it does not exist' is not this:

that the bare ground is perceived; rather, even the designation 'no jar' has as its object precisely the delimitation of the scope of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and is not without an object. And this delimitation of the scope of a means of valid cognition..."

It has been explained. Therefore, he says that the mockery is justified: "Consequently, to claim that there is both non-cognition and a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in that case is extraordinary (*alaukika*).
He begins to refute this as follows: "It is said: Your Honor’s discourse is unexamined."

We observe this. However, upon closer examination, this [explanation] for the conventional usage of "non-existence" is untenable; therefore, he urges one toward its investigation. Let your honor investigate this: regarding this conventional usage of worldly people characterized by engagement and withdrawal—such as "this does not exist somewhere"—is it due to a lack of cognition, or is it characterized by the absence of all descriptions?

Is it from the non-apprehension [of the desired], or from the apprehension of something else, or from the apprehension of its absence? Regarding these, he refutes the first alternative: if it were due to non-apprehension, people would not seek to know the absence of what is desired. Furthermore, they would desist simply because of non-apprehension, and they would act simply because of the non-apprehension of what is undesired. Even one who is seeking to know [the truth]...

Indeed, one would arrive at non-determination itself; for it is not admitted that there can be an absence of an object of cognition (prameyābhāva) apart from that which exceeds the body [of the means of knowledge]. And since that [non-determination] is already attained, those who possess discernment would have no desire to investigate absence.
[The opponent] objects: "Conventional practice is based solely on the non-determination of the object of a means of valid cognition; it is not [based on] non-determination..."

Only a mere semblance (*damātra*) is intended here; rather, the meaning is that of the perceptible counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*). He refutes this: No, because there is no distinction. He explains that very point: For the non-discrimination between "that" and "other than that" does not differ [in the two cases].

Indeed, whether there is perceptibility or imperceptibility, there is no difference in the non-discrimination of the two counter-correlates, which consists in a simple negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*).
No specific property can exist for that which is devoid of all designations; for if such a property were possible, its insubstantiality (tucchatva) would be untenable.
Furthermore, it is incorrect to say that engagement and withdrawal occur due to the cognition of another object;

for such a claim is false, because even when the counter-correlate (the object to be avoided) exists, those [engagements and withdrawals] would necessarily follow. Indeed, when both the jar and the thorn are being perceived, it is precisely their cognition that serves as the basis for those [actions].

[This concerns] engagement and withdrawal. Well then, [it follows that] there is a reversal [of these] due to the absence of that [knowledge], not due to the existence of some other entity, because the knowledge of what is a means to the desired or undesired still exists at that time and is present before one. He states another objection: "And engagement and withdrawal being not preceded by cognition is incorrect."

Indeed, a cognition or a cause that is as insubstantial as a flower in the sky—being void and undifferentiated—is impossible. Therefore, one who asserts that the engagement in or withdrawal from activity by a discerning person arises from such an undifferentiated state would, by another way of speaking, be asserting either the accidental nature of those two or their being devoid of a preceding cognition; for they are only occasional.
The meaning is that both your [proponent’s] engagement and withdrawal by means of discernment would be untenable.

Now, one might object: there are two kinds of cognition regarding the ground and so forth—namely, that which has a ground accompanied by something else as its object, and that which has a solitary ground as its object.

Furthermore, the latter is also twofold: that in which the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) is perceptible, and that in which it is imperceptible. And this perceptibility of it [the counter-correlative] is as follows:

The completeness of other conditions for perception and the specific nature [of the object] itself are required for apprehension; and that specific nature is said to be that in whose presence, while the other conditions for perception are present, its existence is experienced. And thus, it is precisely the cognition of the ground with respect to a perceptible counter-positive that serves as the means for establishing the linguistic usage of non-existence, and of which—

"Because of its insubstantiality (*tucchatva*), the application of qualifiers is possible; and for the sake of establishing that [insubstantiality], the desire to know subtle insects, thorns, and so forth is appropriate. To this he says: "If it is argued that they proceed from the cognition of another object, that is false. Why? Because even when the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), such as a jar, exists, that [cognition] would follow in respect to a floor or similar surface. [Otherwise,] there would be no cessation [of the cognition] in the form 'the jar is not here.'"

[The opponent argues: "There is no thorn," because it would follow that there would be activity [toward the thorn]. He raises an objection: "When the jar and the thorn are present and arising, activity and cessation are based precisely on those two; they are not based on the cognition of the ground. He refutes this: "In that case, alas, due to the absence of that [jar], the jar..."

Because of the absence of the two thorns, there is the reversal of the cognition of the means to the desired and the undesired, which consists in the cognition of the jar and the thorn. Now, why does the mere existence of the ground not itself become the cause for the reversal of the cognition of the means to the desired and the undesired? To this he says:
"Not because of the existence of another thing. It is not from the existence of the ground that the reversal of the cognition of the means to the desired and the undesired arises.

Why? Because even at that time—the moment of the cognition of what is a means to the desired or the undesired—the ground (bhūtala) continues to exist. This is what is meant: if there were a contradiction between the ground and the cognition of what is a means to the desired or the undesired, then the ground would perish because of it; however, there is no such contradiction between these two, for it [the ground] coexists with the continuous stream of that cognition.
Regarding the phrase "due to long-term persistence":
even a portion of ground that does not coexist with the cognition of a means to a desired end possesses the quality of being an obstacle to the error of that cognition.

He says "and before" [in the verse]: because of the existence of the ground. The meaning is that the ground, which is perceived before the cognition of the means to the desired or undesired (such as the cognition of a jar or a thorn) is absent, is not necessarily concomitant with that absence.
Here, the underlying intention is this: regarding this worldly linguistic usage of non-existence, such as "the jar does not exist," [it is established].

The absence [of a thorn] is characterized by cessation (*nivṛtti*), while the presence [of a thorn] is characterized by activity (*pravṛtti*). This [absence] cannot, for its part, be based on the perception of a ground-surface when there are visible objects such as a jar or a thorn, because it would follow that [the absence] would apply even when a jar or the like situated upon that [ground] is being perceived.
Nor is it invisible, since it is being perceived. [Objection: There is no such fault, because this [perception of absence] is based solely on the perception of the bare ground-surface.

If it is asked: "What, then, is its isolation (*kaivalya*)? If you say it is its own nature (*svarūpa*), we say no; for it exists even when one perceives a jar, a thorn, or other objects. If you say it is a property (*dharma*) of that [surface], then it follows that it is opposed to the existence of the jar and so forth, and thus, by means of another state (*bhūmikā*), it is established as the very absence (*abhāva*) of those things—this is precisely what we maintain. Now, even for those who maintain that non-existence is an object of valid cognition (*prameya*), there is the ground...
A cause for the cognition of the existence of the apprehension must be sought. As it has been said:

"Having apprehended the existence of the object and having remembered the counter-correlate. In that regard, first of all, the apprehension of the floor as conjoined [with the jar] cannot be the cause of that [cognition], because of the contradiction. Nor...
Indeed, it is possible that there is the apprehension of the ground as conjoined with a jar, yet at that same time there is the ascertainment of the absence of the jar;

nor is it the apprehension of the ground as possessing the absence of the jar, for that would entail the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*). For it is not tenable that the very thing itself should be its own cause. Therefore, when the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), such as a jar, is imperceptible, there is merely the apprehension of the ground.

Since it must be admitted even against one's will that the cause for the determination of the absence of a jar is the bare ground— which is distinct from the absence of the jar— itself serves as the basis for the conventional usage of "absence. What, then, is the use of an internalized "absence of the jar"?

This is incorrect, because we do not maintain that the mere apprehension of the existence of a real entity is the cause of the cognition of its absence; rather, it is held that this [apprehension] serves as the cause only when there is a non-apprehension of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) which is equally capable of being perceived. Thus he says: "and having remembered the counter-positive. By this, he indicates its state of not being apprehended.

It indicates [the following]: because memory is untenable regarding reality. Nor is it correct to say that the perception of the ground itself, as being in contact with a single cognition, is the non-perception of the jar;

for there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the non-perception of the jar even when one perceives the ground in contact with a jar that has never been perceived before, since at that time too the perception of the ground exists. And [this would imply] the non-perception of the jar...

Because it is non-different from that [object]. Now, is this non-apprehension (anupalambha) the cause for the cognition of absence when it is itself cognized, or even when it is not cognized? It cannot be the former, because that would lead to an infinite regress (anavasthā). For since that [non-apprehension] is of the nature of an absence of apprehension, it too must be established by another non-apprehension; and that other non-apprehension likewise [requires another], resulting in an infinite regress.

If, however, it were unperceived, existence would be the probans. And thus, when Maitra— who has perceived the ground of the square where Caitra was previously observed by means of a valid cognition, yet who, due to the absence of any desire to know [Caitra's] current state, does not perceive Caitra’s absence there— has recently arrived and is asked by someone else, "Maitra, was Caitra here before?"

Then, his curiosity aroused by that question, he ascertained at that very moment the prior non-existence of the visible Caitra and gave the answer: "O long-lived one, Caitra was here; he has now arrived."
That is not tenable; for by the perception occurring at that time, there is a sublation of its non-perception.

Nor can a prior non-perception instill in it a present cognition of absence. Indeed, one whose eyes are closed does not see a form now merely because of the former existence of the eyes. Therefore, [it is] one—

The perception of another object through its connection with cognition must be accepted as the very cause of the knowledge of non-existence. And since that [perception] itself, established by self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), is sufficient to accomplish the conventional usage of non-existence, there is no need for non-existence as a separate object of cognition (*prameya*).

To this it is replied: First of all, the mere perception of the ground without the perception of the jar is not the means for establishing the linguistic usage of non-existence. Nor has it been stated that the perception of the ground itself is the non-perception of that [jar].
Therefore, the non-perception of the counter-positive (pratiyogin) must be accepted as the requisite factor. And its non-existence cannot be established if it is not itself cognized.

It is a means for establishing worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), because it is impossible for the transaction of a discerning person to be devoid of prior cognition. However, it may be a means for the cognition of its own absence; for even that which is not itself known is seen to be a means for knowledge, like the eyes and other sense organs.
[Objection: In this case, you would be admitting that it is a means by its mere existence (*sattāmātra*). But that is untenable, because [a non-existent thing]...

It has been stated that [otherwise] there would be the undesirable consequence of the arising of a cognition of the non-existence of that [object] upon its non-perception. This is not so, because the non-existence of non-perception remains unestablished. Now, at the time of the question, "Was this Caitra here on the square?", Maitra—who is currently perceiving him—is himself one who perceives him; how then could he be [said to be] one who does not perceive him? True, he perceives Caitra, but not...
One remembers its prior existence there, just as one remembers the existence of a person at a crossroads. Nor is memory a non-perception;

therefore, the absence [of that object] is likewise a non-perception. Thus, just as the non-apprehension of something capable of being apprehended is the means for perceiving its absence, so too, even though it is not being apprehended now, Caitra’s prior existence at the crossroads [is established by memory].

In that case, at midday, because the object worthy of being remembered is not remembered, the absence of midday remembrance—being present—is indeed capable of producing the midday cognition whose object is a prior absence. Nor is it correct to maintain that only perceptual non-apprehension (*pratyakṣānupalabdhi*) is the means for the knowledge of absence; [for this would exclude] the appropriate means of valid cognition...

Because non-perception is the means of establishing that; for if it were not the means of establishing that, there would be the cessation of inference and the other [means of knowledge]. Furthermore, this applies to the presence of the sun in the sea, the existence of fish and such [in the sky], the status of dharma in the worship of *caityas* and the like, the fact that the *darvihoma* is a unique (*apūrva*) act, and the prevention of the view that the word "hearing" is produced by a continuous series of similar [sounds] merely through the arrival of sound-waves.

[This is] not [the case] because of non-existence; for just as with other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is logical that even a non-valid cognition such as memory possesses fitness (*yogyatva*) regarding its own object. Furthermore, since "perceptibility," which is characterized by the completeness of other causal conditions, is logically possible only when the cognition has the object as its cause, the absence of such [an object] results in the cessation of inference and so forth, thereby establishing the non-existence of the inferable and the like.

For it is not possible that there should be an absence or a linguistic usage regarding objects of cognition— such as those apprehended by inference and so forth— which share a single objective domain, when all other cognitions distinct from that [specific cognition] are present; for when that [completeness of conditions] exists, there arises a cognition of existence which is incompatible with non-existence.
Because [otherwise] practical activity would be impossible, and because even when the object is a cause, it is not possible for there to be a completeness of other conditions;

for the contact between the sense organ and the object is itself impossible if the object does not exist. Therefore, even in the absence of a mental impression (*saṃskāra*), its fitness to be remembered is established.
Nor is there a contradiction between perception and non-perception, since they establish existence and non-existence occurring at different times.
Because their objects are distinct.

It might be argued as follows: "If non-existence were established by mere existence [of the means], then since non-apprehension itself would likewise be perceptible, there would be no desire to investigate subtle insects, thorns, and so forth, for the sake of establishing knowledge of them. This is not so.

For that [non-perception] is for the sake of establishing perceptibility (*dṛśyatva*), since the true nature of that which is not sought to be known cannot be established; it is not, however, for the sake of knowing perceptibility itself. Or, even if the knowledge of perceptibility were the cause—just like the knowledge of the ground—what does that have to do with non-perception? For it is not the case that because light is a cause when it is being known, the eye must likewise function in that same way.

It must be understood that smoke, once perceived, is the cause of inferential knowledge; likewise, the mind must also be known as its cause. Therefore, since non-perception by way of existence (*sattayā*) is the cause of the cognition of absence, there is no infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Nor is there an admission of a "mere-ness" (*kaivalya*) distinct from the absence of the object of knowledge (*prameya*). This is because the perception of the courtyard floor [is the cause] for [the cognition of] Caitra’s...

Because when there is non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), that [non-existence] is its cause. Thus, this conventional usage regarding non-existence (*abhāvavyavahāra*) arises from causes other than the apprehension of the existence of the real entity (*vastu-sadbhāva-grahaṇa*), the recollection of its counter-correlate (*tat-pratiyogi-smaraṇa*), and the desire to know it (*tad-bubhutsā*). Just as, even when threads exist, a cloth sometimes appears only through the production of a specific conjunction (*saṃyoga-bheda*) distinct from those [threads]. This is so when the counter-correlate is perceptible (*dṛśya*).

If it is argued that the reason [for non-existence] is unestablished because the linguistic usage of "non-existence" necessarily occurs only when there is the apprehension of the existence of the object being remembered, we say no; for even when the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is being perceived but not remembered, the linguistic usage of its prior absence proceeds immediately after the question, "What was there? Let it be then that this applies when the counter-correlate is desired to be known and capable of being cognized.

The cognition of the existence of a thing is the means for establishing the conventional usage of its non-existence. Furthermore, when Caitra is being perceived, immediately after the question "Where was he?", there arises a desire to remember his prior existence at that place. When this desire exists, the memory of the courtyard floor as it was at the previous time is necessarily the cause for the engagement in the conventional usage of his non-existence.

It is not established as a reason; for even in this case, there is no rule of necessity. This is because, even when cognition and recollection are present, there is no cessation of the desire to remember (*susmūrṣā*) and the desire to experience (*anububhūṣā*) due to their being extremely dear [to the subject].

And thus, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasakti*) that the practical usage (*vyavahāra*) of the absence of an object would occur in each instance upon the experience or recollection of its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*).

If it is argued that there is no fault because of the qualification "in the case of non-recollection and non-experience," then you have effectively admitted that negation (*abhāva*) is a distinct cause [of knowledge]. If it is further argued that even so, since this [negation] consists in the absence of apprehension (*upalambha*), the absence of an object of cognition (*prameya-abhāva*) is not thereby established— the Teacher himself will state the answer to this immediately hereafter.

Now, it has been stated that non-existence (*abhāva*) is not experienced as anything possessing a physical form; therefore, is this linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) of "non-existence" without a basis, or does it lack a cause? It cannot be that it lacks a cause, for it occurs only occasionally.

Therefore, neither based on another valid cognition (*pramiti*) nor based on a non-valid cognition (*apramiti*) do we have "the desired does not exist" or "the undesired does not exist," which would lead to engagement or withdrawal; rather, they are based on the apprehension of absence (*abhāva*).
What has been determined as the object of the cognition "it does not exist"? Has it not already been stated? What offense has been committed by you regarding the object?

[Is it] by way of its being? For it has been stated that what transcends that [being] is called the "absence of a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇābhāva*) as its object. Nor is it the absence of a knowable thing (*jñeyābhāva*), because that would entail the impossibility of consciousness (*citkatva*). Furthermore, it has been said that there is no other cause for this. Nor is it non-existent, because it has been stated that this would lead to the denial of even the conventional usage of existence (*bhāvavyavahāra*). How, then, can that which is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) be experienced?

If it is asked, "What is its nature?"—it is not so; for that [nature] is perceived as consisting in the exclusion of existence (*sad-vyāvṛtti*), and no internal distinction is perceived in itself. If it is argued that its nature is "lack of intrinsic being" (*niḥsvabhāvatā*)—no; for that consequence would then apply to cognition, power, and so forth as well. For even in these, no difference is determined from their own side; rather, it is dependent upon the difference between the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) and the capacity (*śakti*).

If it is argued that its differentiation is to be established [by another means], we say no; for even here, its differentiation is established through the difference of its counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*).
Thus, everything is clear.
He concludes the subject at hand: "Therefore, it is neither based on another valid cognition (*pramiti*), nor is it based on invalid cognition (*apramiti*)."

Activity and cessation do not occur on the grounds that "the desired is not present" or "the undesired is not present"; rather, they are based on the comprehension of non-existence by way of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*). The establishment of non-existence does not follow merely from the impossibility of otherwise accounting for worldly practice; furthermore, just as there is the cognition "the jar exists," the cognition of its absence is likewise apprehended. And cognition is not without an objective basis (*nirālambana*).
This will be explained later. Intending to show that its objective support (*ālambana*) is nothing other than non-existence (*abhāva*), he asks:
"What object has been determined for the cognition of 'it does not exist'? Another says: "Has it not already been stated? The meaning is that this is not perceived here."

In that case, first of all, when the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is imperceptible, there can be no cognition of the existence of the object, for it has already been stated that even the non-cognition of the counter-positive is impossible. Therefore, one must speak of the absence of non-apprehension other than that [object]. And so, what wrong has been done here by the venerable absence of the object (*viṣayābhāva*), since that [object] is being cognized?
Having bypassed [the previous point], it is stated that the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) constitutes the object [of knowledge].
An objection is raised: since the specific individual differences are not perceived, the absence of the knowable (*jñeya*) cannot be an object of valid cognition (*prameya*). This is refuted:
let it be so, provided there is a distinction between the absence of cognition (*jñāna*) and the absence of the knowable; for even the absence of cognition is not [perceived] by its own nature.

It possesses distinctions, because even that distinction is defined in dependence upon the distinction of its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*). Thus, the cognition "Caitra is not" is to be understood through the effect characterized by the manifestation of that absence; it is not appropriate to explain it, as one might a bad poet's work, with great difficulty as having for its object merely the non-existence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāva*). Furthermore—
It is said [to exist] because of its distinct nature (*vaijātya*); yet, it is not that it does not exist in reality, for there exist both cognition and linguistic convention (*buddhi-vyavahāra*).

Rather, it is an object of knowledge (*prameya*). Let it be so; if there is such a specific cause, then in the absence of actual knowledge, there is the error of knowledge regarding linguistic conventions.
[Objection: "The delusion of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra-bhrama*) occurs with respect to existence, just as there is the delusion of darkness when light is not seen. [Response:
No, because this would entail the same error in states such as deep sleep; furthermore, a delusion is impossible regarding that which is not cognized, just as in the case of deep sleep and so forth."
In the absence of seeing Caitra, the cognition "Caitra is not present" is an error; in the absence of activity appropriate for Caitra, there is an error regarding activity.
He provides an illustration for this very point: it is like the error of darkness when light is not seen. Indeed, it is not that [darkness] exists...

Does "action" (kāra) exist in reality, or is it merely a conceptual construct? For it must be one of the [six] categories, such as substance and so forth, since the entire universe is subsumed under those alone.
