In that regard, if it were a substance, would it be one of the [nine] substances such as darkness, earth, and so on, or something else? It cannot be one of those. Among earth, water, and self, there are fourteen... [properties].

[Space and time] are not included among the qualities, nor among fire which has eleven qualities, nor among wind which has nine qualities, nor among the mind which has eight qualities, nor among ether which has six qualities, because the two imperishable entities, space and time, would otherwise lack inclusion [within these categories]. Alternatively, if they were included, it would follow that they possess those same number of qualities, and consequently, they would have to be eternal. Nor are they a separate substance.

If it is argued that darkness is a distinct substance because it is perceived as dark like the petal of a blue lotus, is large in extent, and cannot logically be a quality-less entity, we say no. This is because black color—which is invariably concomitant with and inherent in effects such as odor—is absent where those qualities are absent. Thus, [darkness] would be devoid of all qualities.

It is not a substance (*dravyatva*). Furthermore, the existence of qualities, actions, or universals (*sāmānya*) is impossible for that which lacks a substratum (*anāśraya*). Nor can earth and other substances serve as its substratum; for if they were its substratum, one would necessarily perceive its qualities and those [qualities] concomitant with them. Moreover, the perception of this darkness (*tamas*) is not logically tenable.
Because there is no perceiver [of it]. Nor does this darkness fall within the range of the sense organs;

for if that were so, it would follow that it could not be perceived when those senses are absent. Furthermore, even for one with eyes closed, there is the conceit, "I see darkness. It is quite crude to claim that darkness is the object of the olfactory and other senses. As for the mind—
Moreover, that which is restricted to an internal object is even further removed from external things such as sense organs or logical marks.

And an effect cannot arise in the absence of its cause, for if it were accidental, its occasional occurrence would be impossible. Therefore, there is no such thing as "darkness," nor is there any cognition thereof.
Furthermore, there is a common worldly conceit that "we perceive darkness as blue like a *tāmasa* tree," which occurs when light is not seen;
this is an error (*viplava*). The point is that, in the same way, the perception of non-existence and the linguistic usage thereof are nothing but errors.
He refutes this [view] with the words: "No; because it would entail an absurd consequence (*prasaṅga*) in states such as deep sleep. For if knowledge...

If error were to exist in the absence of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), it would follow by the same logic even in states such as deep sleep; for at that time there is neither cognition nor linguistic usage, since the state of deep sleep and so forth is characterized by the withdrawal of all consciousness. He states another reason: "And because error is impossible regarding what is not cognized, as in the case of deep sleep and so forth."
The perception of darkness, however, is the perception of the shadow of the earth;
for a delusion consisting of superimposition occurs only upon a perceived object, and not upon that which is non-existent, nor upon that which is unperceived.

It has been established in the *Vibhramaviveka* that there is neither a form of cognition nor a non-apprehension; this will also be indicated here. Furthermore, neither the absence of cognition nor the absence of linguistic convention has ever been observed before. Or, if such were observed, what would be the point of introducing error (*bhrama*) here? Therefore, the meaning is that since error is impossible regarding that which is not cognized, this [position] is untenable.

He states that the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*): "For this very reason, the perception of darkness is the perception of the shadow of the earth. This is the intended meaning (*abhisandhi*) here: first of all, darkness is cognized as being dark like a garland of *tamāla* flowers; and a delusion regarding cognition cannot occur in the absence of a prior cognition. Furthermore, there is no subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against this.

And that which is being cognized cannot be denied when it exists, for that would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga). Nor is it proper to deny darkness simply because no means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is perceived [to apprehend it], for that would entail the same consequence for the perception of color and so forth.
Indeed, the means of knowledge for that [perception]—such as the sense organs—is not itself perceived; rather, it is inferred from the perception of color and so forth.

If it is argued that its apprehension is through inference (*anumāna*), we say no; for the same objection applies here as well. But has it not been stated that this [non-apprehension] is within the range of the eyes and other sense organs? In that case, it would be better to admit a new means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)—one never before perceived—even though it is not previously known, because the effect of valid cognition (*pramiti*) is observed in darkness, which is the object of the direct perception of all people; but it cannot be derived from anything else.

Because it is not perceived, the reversal of an effect that was clearly observed is logical. Or, let the eye itself be its cause; yet, for one with closed eyes or one with a cataract (*paṭala*), that [cause] is not absent, but rather it is covered.
If it is asked, "How then could it function toward external darkness, as in the case of a jar or other objects, when it is covered?"—[the answer is: let it be so.

It proceeds. What is destroyed? For the eye, even when it covers the eyelid or the film—both of which are very close and act as occluders—perceives only that [object] which covers the shadow of the eyelid or the film, and not the eyelid or the film themselves. Stimulated by light, it is capable of grasping earth and other elements, but not their shadows.

If one were to go toward that which is contrary to it, [the object] would appear there because of the capacity of the [eye] alone; for since that [capacity] is inferred from the observation of its effect, even something subtle like a blade of grass or cotton, when situated near the eye and obstructing it, appears as something immensely large and boundless—so too does this [object]. And it is not the case that, for the blind, [this occurs] in the location of the eyeball itself, as is the case with other parts of the body.
The perception of its effect is possible; or rather, it has been stated that if such [an effect] exists, it is better to postulate another perceiver.

But what, then, is darkness among substances and so forth? Is it not indeed a substance, because it possesses the quality of blackness and because it possesses motion? For instance, only blackness is perceived as its color, just as in the case of water and fire.

Whiteness [is perceived]. Likewise, number, beginning with oneness, is also perceived; its dimension is fourfold, as is inferred from the atoms of darkness just as from the dyads of earth and other substances. Separateness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, and the impressions (saṃskāra)—these, along with the fivefold action, are observed through direct perception. As the venerable author of the Vārttika has said:
But surely, mere non-existence is not accepted by the elders as being darkness;
for in the Purāṇa, it is heard that "the blackness of shadow" is a quality of the earth element.
The meaning is that, because of the perception of another substance within the shadow—which possesses the quality of earth such as blackness—[the shadow is not darkness].
[Furthermore,] it follows the movements of the body near or far from lamps and the like;
it is large or small, and moving or stationary, according to whether the lamp and so forth are near or far.
"The shadow that follows the body does not exist by way of being a real substance (*vastu*) and so forth.

Nor is it any one of the elements such as earth; for first of all, there is no possibility of water or other [elements] being the entity of darkness, which is black in form, because water and fire are white, and likewise because wind and the others lack color (*arūpa*). Nor...
At present, this blackness of darkness arises from proximity to another, like that of the waters of the Yamunā;
for it is never perceived as possessing any other inherent nature when not influenced by another, just as the water of the Yamunā, when drawn up from its bed, is naturally clear and white.

Nor is it darkness consisting of earth, because of the absence of its qualities, such as odor and so forth. But was it not said that black color, which is likewise pervaded by odor and the rest, becomes non-existent when those qualities cease? Is it then the case that the touch of air, which is neither hot nor cold, is simply non-existent? No, for that touch, though pervaded by odor and the rest, is perceived in earth; and in air, too, [it is perceived].

[Objection: Because of their absence [in air], tactile sensation produced by heating (*pākaja*) is pervaded by odor and so forth; however, this tactile sensation [of wind] is not produced by heating, as it belongs to the nature of air (*vāyavīya*). [Reply: No, for the same logic applies here as well. Indeed, even the blackness of darkness is not produced by heating. Furthermore, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is identical in both cases. Moreover, the atoms of darkness (*tamaḥ-paramāṇu*) are of the nature of earth and the other [elements].

Just as atoms, through the sequence of dyads and so forth, originate a large composite whole of darkness—just as they do for an earthy substance—that [darkness] is visible because it possesses a specific color and consists of multiple substances or is large in dimension; thus, there is no difficulty in accounting for its production. Nor is its origination possible during the day, given the eternal opposition between darkness and light.

The particles of clay never fail to initiate a jar when struck by a hammer or similar object possessing touch and momentum as an obstacle, nor do they fail to sustain the jar once it has been initiated. For this very reason, they indeed begin [the production] even during the day in a mountain cave where light has been dispelled.

It might be argued as follows: "Tamas-constituted atoms do not initiate a composite whole (*avayavin*), because they lack touch, like the self (*ātman*), the mind (*manas*), and space (*vyoman*). Nor is the possession of color (*rūpavattva*) the determining factor for initiation; for we observe that even though the atoms of air (*pavana*) are devoid of color, they initiate substances possessing touch, whereas the self and the mind, being devoid of touch, lack that capacity."

Therefore, do atoms of darkness exist for you here, or not? If they do exist, how can there be an absence of that which possesses parts (the composite)? For the existence of atoms is characterized by the existence of those [parts]. Or, if atoms of darkness do not exist, why is there no "unestablished locus" (*āśrayāsiddhi*) for the reason? [If you argue: "There is no fault, because the reason—non-tangibility—is of a non-existent nature and thus has a non-existent locus."
If you say this, it is not so; for that which is void is not a cause, and a thing whose existence is merely superimposed through conceptual construction cannot be a prover.
Smoke that is merely superimposed upon mist never serves as a means of proving fire. This is the view of the proponent of valid cognition (*prāmāṇika*).

For the non-existence of something is impossible without a locus for its existence. If the atoms of darkness do not exist, then [the reason] becomes unestablished due to the non-establishment of its substratum; however, that which is itself unestablished does not possess the status of being a member of a proof even if it is established for another, because that which is not cognized by oneself is unfit to convey cognition to another. As it has been said:

Even in the case where that which is unestablished for the opponent is said to be established for oneself, a remedy may exist there; but what remedy can there be when it is unestablished even for oneself?

Furthermore, because that which is intangible does not initiate substances, a natural connection between the mind and [the body] cannot be established, since the limiting condition (upādhi) of purposelessness exists; for the production of all effects is caused by merit and demerit (dharma-adharma). Indeed, every class of effect, being a means to experience, is produced either directly or indirectly.

It might be argued that the mind, as a composite whole, could serve as the instrument of experience either by being the body or by being an object; however, this is not possible. For it cannot constitute a body because it lacks the status of being the locus of the sense organs, and it is not admitted that what is non-earthen can possess that status. Furthermore, its status as an object is untenable because it is not perceived. [The same applies to] the sense organ...

The existence of the mind is indeed atomic; however, since darkness—which possesses form—serves as a means of experience by way of being an object, there is no futility [in its existence]. Furthermore, for those things that are of supreme magnitude (the all-pervading), a larger dimension in the effect-substance is impossible due to the absence of conjunction as an inherent cause, and because no effect is observed to have a dimension greater than, or smaller than, that of its causes. Thus, it is not [possible for the soul to be] larger.

Furthermore, because of non-conjunction (*ayoga*) and because of the contradiction with its being of supreme magnitude (*paramamahattva*), it cannot be the originator of the substance in which it inheres;

this is the limiting condition (*upādhi*). Nor is a relation based on such a limiting condition a factor for inference. Otherwise, there would be no inference for a student who has repeatedly observed the coexistence [of the teacher and the lesson] upon seeing the teacher. Nor, in the case of one blind to blue, can it be established otherwise...
When direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), which obstructs the experience of [the object], is manifest, inference (*anumāna*) is unable to arise with respect to an object that has been sublated.

Let there not be the inference that "fire is not hot because it is a substance, like earth and so forth. Furthermore, it is observed that one substance can reside in another substance; for example, the case of gold and other metals produced in a mine, which are substances of fire residing in an earthly substrate.

There is support by a substance; otherwise, falling and so forth would not occur due to the absence of gravity. And just as light supported by noble gems such as the great sapphire (*mahānīla*) does not [fall], this is not like that; rather, it is currently held that it is light because of its whirling. For light—even that which ultimately resides in fireflies and the like—possesses some degree of color as its substratum.

Because darkness is pervaded by light, and because it is the opposite of that [light], therefore darkness, even as a distinct substance, will conform to earth and the other elements, and will perish upon the destruction of fire. Upon the disappearance of that [fire], it will arise again from earth and the others. This is so even in a case where, for one who has entered a room through a quadrangle, there is a rarefaction caused by the penetration of a few particles of light.
The perception of density in darkness is an error caused by the impairment of the sense faculties due to the influence of prolonged exposure to time.
However, upon the removal of that impairment, one perceives the objects situated within the inner chamber as they truly are, and observes only a slight shadow there.

And the perception of the absence of light is not the same [as the perception of darkness]. That [absence] is dense and conceals objects, rather than being thinned out by light. Nor is it correct to say that darkness is merely the absence of light, because for one who has neither remembered nor perceived light, the blueness [of darkness] would be inexplicable.

Furthermore, it would follow that the very possibility of darkness being perceived as an object would be untenable. Consequently, motion and other qualities residing therein, which are not otherwise apprehended, could not be explained away through any amount of forced interpretation. Therefore, since there is no subverting evidence, it is established that darkness is a distinct substance, the eleventh, proven by perception, and that it possesses nine qualities.
There is no perception of that which is not seen, nor is there a shadow when it has gone out of memory;
because of its form and the existence of the means [of perception], substance follows after another substance.
This is the summary verse.

Or rather, enough with this dispute with the Naiyāyikas; darkness is simply the absence of light. Nevertheless, he says—"and the perception of the absence of light"—to show that our desired conclusion is nonetheless established. Therefore, [the case] is not the same.

Regarding the phrase "by the illustrative instance" (*dārṣṭāntikena*): if being graspable by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) means a connection with that means of valid cognition, or if it means fitness for it, then since both of these exist eternally even in the case of non-existence (*abhāva*), it would follow that non-existence itself must be existent. If, on the other hand, [you mean] its existence as its own nature (*svarūpa-vartamānatā*), that does not exist in the case of non-existence. No; because we have already established that it is not a mere nothingness (*atucchatva*). And even so, it is not the case [that non-existence is existent].

The universal (*sāmānya*), which exists as differentiated according to each individual entity (*pratibhāva*), must be the object of the cognition and designation "existent, existent" (*sat-sat*), both of which apprehend an undifferentiated object. Or, if there were no difference [between the individuals], it would simply be a universal under another name. If it is argued that a universal lacks epistemic warrant (*aprāmāṇika*) without a prior reflective awareness (*pūrvābhimarśa*), we say no; for that argument cannot withstand analysis (*vikalpāsahatvāt*). Which...?
Is this prior perception intended by the Venerable One as the apprehension of all perceived forms, or rather as that of only some forms? In that regard, the first case is impossible in any instance.
For indeed, even one who has previously perceived mica (*śilābhra*) does not have such a [recognition] when seeing it again during the rains or in autumn.

There is a prior reflective awareness (*pūrvāvamarsa*). Since that too lacks such [an awareness], it would follow that it is something else. A partial reflective awareness is common here as well; for indeed, there is a persistence (*anugama*) of several forms in both the triad of atoms (*trasareṇu*) and the mote (*kareṇu*), despite their various distinct aggregations, by virtue of their being substances (*dravyatva*) and so forth. Therefore, just as there is no difference between the cognition and the designation of "existent" (*sat*), [so too is the case here].

Because it is impossible to establish the possession of qualities (*guṇavattva*) through a distinction for each individual quality, there exists that "Being" (*sattva*) which is the underlying thread (*anusyūta*) of substances,

qualities, actions, and universals— even though these are absolutely distinct— since they share the same cognition and designation as "existent. And that [Being], because of its lack of connection with the three times, is absolutely non-existent [in the sense of being devoid of temporal relation].
[This refers to] things such as a rabbit's horn; that [negation] by the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*) for which atoms, space, and so forth are absolutely existent;

that by the exclusion of absolute non-connection (*atyantāyogavyavaccheda*) for which cloth and so forth exist only at certain times; and that through whose connection substances, qualities, actions, and universals appear from their own experience by the exclusion of their own non-existence—this is the universal (*sāmānya*).
Or, let it be that [the injunction] is apprehended by a means of valid cognition; however, existence is said to be its state of being present.
There is an absence of an object for the injunction when there is the exclusion of the past and so forth in the verbal [cognition].
The state of having no other object-domain does not occur when another means of valid cognition arises.
If the injunction (*niyoga*) were not verbal, then the meaning of the sentence would be that "one who desires heaven is not enjoined, was not enjoined, nor will be enjoined"—
thus the qualification (*adhikāra*) would be well-defined. Now, if the negation of the past and so forth is not verbal, but rather its [the injunction's]...

If there is an ascertainment [of the object] through another means of knowledge (*māna*) due to its being empty [of that property], then it is not the case that [the object] has no other scope [than that means].

Since its suchness is ascertained by another means of knowledge, the distinction from what is cognized by verbal testimony lies therein. Just as in the case of a mountain perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), the difference in the cognition of its specific qualities is based on the greater or lesser degree of its various forms, such as its possession of fire. As for example:
The Teacher [says]: "When there is an abundance of the nature of the universal (sāmānya), reality shines forth from that;
when it is deficient, its distinctness (vilakṣaṇatva) manifests because of the non-emergence of that [universal]. Thus.
This has been made clear in the *Brahmasiddhi* for those who have exerted effort therein, and thus it is not elaborated upon here.

Nevertheless, it is stated by way of concession: let existence (*sattva*) be the state of being graspable by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); even so, that [existence] is merely the state of being present (*vartamānatā*).
Why? Because there is the cognition and linguistic usage of "non-existence" (*asat*) even with respect to the past and the future, which are indeed graspable by means of valid cognition.

Because of its being a substance (*dravyatva*). For existence (*sattva*) is said to be nothing other than presentness (*vartamānatā*). And thus, an injunction (*niyoga*) that is in reality unconditioned by time, even if it were graspable by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), would simply not exist; and it is established that if it did exist, it would not be within the scope of any other means of knowledge (*māna*).
Furthermore—
There is no object for an injunction when the verbal [cognition] excludes what has already occurred and so forth;
nor is there a lack of scope for other means of knowledge when they have arisen.
Furthermore, is its non-restriction by the three times (past, present, and future) communicated by means of a word, or by another means of knowledge?

If it were by a word, then it would be absolutely non-existent [as a real entity]. But if it is restricted by the three times through another means of knowledge, then because it would fall within the scope of that other means of knowledge, the intended meaning could not be brought about. Thus he says: "If the injunction (*niyoga*) is not verbal..."

If it were to communicate that "it was not, it is not, it will not be," then the meaning of the sentence would be: "one who desires heaven is neither enjoined, nor is being enjoined, nor will be enjoined"—thus the qualification (*adhikāra*) would be utterly undermined. Now, if the negation of the past and so forth is not verbal, then that word [denoting the agent] would lack its primary denotation (*audāsīnya*) with respect to those objects of negation, such as the past and so forth.
[It is] not from non-existence, but rather the determination [of it] is through another means of valid cognition (*mānāntara*), namely, a determination by way of its exclusion from the three times.

In that case, it is not the case that [the object] has no other sphere of perception. Why? Because its suchness and its exclusion from the three times are determined by another means of valid cognition.

[It is argued that it is known] through inference. No; for when the qualified object is not apprehended, the qualifier cannot be its object. Furthermore, even if suchness were understood from another source, there would be no injunction at all for one who desires heaven, since that [other source] would also be a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Or, to speak of the distinction from the elements (*bhūta*) and so forth regarding that which is not real is mere prattle. [Objection: But surely the elements and so forth are merely adventitious attributes (*upādhi*); and when an attribute ceases, there is neither the cessation nor the non-perception of the substratum possessing that attribute. [Reply: Let it be so in the case of other attributes;

however, in this case, such a definition itself constitutes absolute non-existence. Furthermore, upon the cessation of the attributes of "eternal" and "non-eternal," the attribute [itself] does not [persist].
[The cognition] arising from me [is as follows]: perception, at the moment of its initial occurrence, grasps only that form which is devoid of limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of difference;
therefore, there is no difference in the object [between perception and other means of knowledge]. Since that which is non-existent lacks form, it has the present as its object.

[The opponent] raises a valid objection regarding the reality of the matter: "Since the specific injunction (niyoga) is cognized through verbal testimony, its distinction from other means of knowledge consists in its exclusion from the three periods of time."
"But another means of knowledge does not operate toward the injunction. To this very point, he provides an illustration:

"Just as the specific property of a mountain's possession of fire [is known] through inference, yet that [inference], while having the possession of fire as its object, is not capable of making the mountain itself its object. He refutes this: "No; for when the qualified [subject] is not apprehended, the qualification..."

Because it is an object [of cognition]. For it is impossible that the mountain and so forth, as qualified [by fire], should not be determined, while its qualification—fire-possessingness—is nevertheless cognized. Nor is it tenable to say that one who has not perceived the mountain is capable of inferring its qualification; for at the time of inference, the perceptual knowledge of the mountain has already passed away.

And because recollection would be impossible due to [the mind's] limited capacity. For at that time, since the simultaneous arising of cognitions is impossible, the internal organ possesses the capacity for a succession of cognitions; otherwise, a continuous stream of cognitions regarding the same object would be impossible, as everything that ought to be done would be accomplished all at once, and it is impossible for a capable thing to delay its action. Furthermore, this applies to both perception and inference regarding the subject (*dharmin*).

Because its object is merely the form of the dharma, even though it coexists [with the person], it does not appear as something distinct. Furthermore, since its validity can be established through other means as well, there is no injunction for one who desires heaven; for that [other means] is also a source of valid knowledge, being free from the three times. Or, if it were [to be established by injunction alone], there would be the designation of a distinction such as "past" and so forth.

This is mere idle chatter, as it contradicts the authoritative means of knowledge. [The opponent] objects: "But surely the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) are qualifiers that exist as real entities, like earrings and so forth are to the ear; they are not, however, the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). What follows from this? To this he replies:
"And when the limiting adjunct has ceased, there is neither the cessation nor the non-perception of that which possesses the adjunct. Indeed, not..."

When the earring ceases, the ear ceases, or is no longer perceived. [The opponent] offers this rebuttal: "Let it be so in the case of other limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as earrings; however, in this case, 'absolute non-existence' is defined precisely by the distinction from the three periods of time.
Indeed, the absolute non-existence of things like a hare’s horn is nothing other than this. Therefore, regarding the three periods of time..."

Because of discrimination (*viveka*). Not only this, but there are other limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) as well, which, upon their cessation, cause the existence of the thing itself to cease; thus he says: "When the limiting adjuncts of eternality and non-eternality cease, that which possesses the adjunct cannot exist.

Furthermore, while in the case of verbal cognition there is no consideration of the three times, in perception—which arises immediately—the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*) [is perceived].

Since it grasps only the form of the object as distinct from the limiting condition of temporal difference through non-conceptualization (*an-avamarśāt*), there can be no difference in the object of verbal cognition compared to that perception.
Not from valid cognition (*pramiti*). In reality, when there is a distinction from the present and so forth, the state of being devoid of self (*nirātmakatva*) results from absolute non-cognition;
it is not due to a difference in objects that the word is independent of other means of knowledge. This is a double-edged sword (*ubhayataspāśā*). [Objection:

But surely the object to be accomplished (*kāryārtha*) is perceived in the injunction "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*); [Reply: No, because there is an absence of a means of knowledge for its future existence, as it is entirely...

Because it is not grasped in nine ways; and precisely because it is an effect, it does not persist into other times. Nor is it non-existent, because it is perceived. This has already been answered: if [the object] possesses a self, there is no real difference in time; if [the difference is claimed] from the perspective of cognition, there is no difference in the object itself—thus, there is selflessness (*nairātmya*). How, then, is there perception? Precisely for this reason, it is merely a mental appearance (*pratibhā*) or merely a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

The wise maintain that verbal cognition is [of this nature], and worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) is based upon intuition (*pratibhā*). Furthermore, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), when supported by intuition, constitute a factor of worldly transaction.
He raises an objection: "Since that which is not present lacks form, it must have the present as its object. He refutes this: "True."
In reality, it does not arise from a valid cognition (*pramiti*). He summarizes the point already stated:

In that regard, with respect to the injunction (*niyoga*), its being devoid of self-nature (*nirātmakatva*) in the distinction from what is actually present [in the world] is due to its absolute lack of being a valid cognition, and not because of a difference in object; thus, the word’s independence from other means of knowledge is like a rope caught at both ends.

He objects: "Is it not the case that when one says 'one should sacrifice' (yajeta), an object to be accomplished (kārya) is cognized? That [object] cannot be something yet to come (bhaviṣyat), because there is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for a future object, since it cannot be definitively ascertained and its true nature remains uncertain. [The author replies: "Let it not be something yet to come;
it might be present or past. To this he says: "Precisely because it is an effect (kāryatva), it does not conform to any other time [than the future]."

[Objection: "In that case, it would be like a flower in the sky. To this he says: "And it is not non-existent. Why? Because it is perceived. For it is not possible for that which is absolutely non-existent to become an object of perception. He provides the rebuttal: "The answer to this has already been stated. The response to this has essentially been given. He demonstrates that: "If it possessed a self-nature, it would not [exist] as a real entity in time..."

If it is argued that the distinction [of the injunction] is established through a means of valid cognition (*pramiti*), yet there is no difference in its object— namely, that it is known both through perception and through words such as "jar"—

then for one who desires that the injunction (*niyoga*) is not within the scope of other means of knowledge, its very nature would be undermined, because its existence is untenable without being free from temporal distinctions (*traikālya-sambheda*).

How, then, is there cognition of that which is absolutely non-existent? The answer is: for this very reason, because its object is non-existent, verbal cognition is merely a mental appearance (*pratibhā*) or merely a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); so say the wise. This very cognition of the non-existent receives different designations—either "mental appearance" or "conceptual construction"—according to the difference in philosophical views. This is what has been stated.

It exists; it is not merely that which is beyond the range of a cognition of absolute non-existence, but rather it is within the range of valid cognition (*pramiti*). [Objection: How can a cognition whose object is non-existent be a factor in linguistic and practical activity (*vyavahāra*)? For one who mistakes a firefly for fire does not burn or cook with it. To this he replies: "And linguistic and practical activity is based on appearance (*pratibhāna*). There is no such rule [that a cognition must correspond to reality].

Cognition of a non-existent object is not a factor in worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*). For doubt and error are likewise [not factors], since worldly transactions are not observed to arise from them. Intuition (*pratibhā*), however, is the cause of worldly transaction; this means that the existence or non-existence of the worldly transaction regarding a substance follows the existence or non-existence of that [intuition]. If this is so, then [it may be argued] that the status of being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) does not belong to [intuition] because it is not a means for accomplishing worldly transaction.

Since it might be argued that "it is indeed through intuition (*pratibhā*) that their establishment occurs," he says: "And the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), when assisted by intuition, constitute the basis for worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*). He will clarify this further below. The word *iti* marks the conclusion.
Moreover:
Thus, when there is doubt regarding the meaning of the Veda, the injunction (niyoga) does not constitute a task to be performed;
and the activity of one who has been enjoined is not bound solely by the injunction.

Indeed, that which is neither past nor present, nor known to be future—that is, whose single certainty is not ascertained—is the object of doubtful cognition (*saṃśaya-jñāna*). For example, when rain has not yet fallen and has not yet begun, its occurrence is brought to the path of cognition by the sight of the rising of extremely dark and dense clouds; yet, because deviation [from the expected result] is observed, its single certainty remains unascertained. This...
Alas, the meaning of the Veda has been brought to such a state by those possessed of great wisdom through their excessive exegesis!

Furthermore, the object [of the Vedic injunction] is that which is to be accomplished (*kārya*), not the mandate (*niyoga*). And that which is to be accomplished is the primary object of knowledge (*prameya*) of the Veda, because all other word-meanings are subordinate to it. It is precisely for the sake of establishing its independence—that it is not within the scope of other means of knowledge—by distinguishing it from time, that [the mandate is posited].
Moreover:
If the meaning of the Veda is thus questioned, the injunction (*niyoga*) does not constitute an action (*kāryatā*);
and the activity of one who is enjoined is not bound solely by the injunction.

Indeed, that which is neither past, nor present, nor future—that is, that whose single certainty is not determined—is the object of the cognition of doubt (*āśaṅkā*). For example, rain that has not yet fallen, being neither past nor currently occurring, enters the path of cognition through the power of frequently observing the rising of extremely dark and dense clouds; yet, because of the observation of deviation in some instances, it is not ascertained.

This is an absolute arrogance. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "And this state [of uncertainty] has been brought about regarding the meaning of the Veda by those possessed of wisdom through excessive interpretation. For a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must have certainty as its fruit. And this [interpretation], by producing doubt—which is essentially uncertain—regarding its own object, would be non-valid; such is the meaning.
Thus, it has been explained that such a doubt arises regarding the meaning of the Veda. He now explains that the *niyoga* (the mandate) is not itself the object to be accomplished (*kārya*):

"Furthermore, it is the object (*viṣaya*) that is to be accomplished, not the *niyoga*. For in the case of mandates such as commands (*ājñā*) where there is a commander such as a master, it is understood by the person being commanded (*niyojya*) that it is the object which is to be accomplished; and [this is true] even in the case of commands and so forth."

The meaning is "injunctions" (*niyoga*). What follows from this? He says: "And the *kārya* (the task to be accomplished) is the object of knowledge of the Veda, because of its conformity with worldly usage. [Objection: But since substances and other categories are also understood from those words, how can the *kārya* alone be the object of knowledge of the Veda? To this he replies: "Because other word-meanings are connected to it," that is, because they are connected to the *kārya*. This...

This is what is meant: every collection of words has action as its ultimate purpose, because linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*) occurs only with respect to that. Among these, some function as denoters [of the action], such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so on; others, however, denote their own meanings for the sake of that [action], such as "with curd" (*dadhnā*) and so on. Let this be so; but what follows from this in the present context? To this he says: "And thus, of that very..."

The distinction of time must be stated specifically regarding the *kārya* (the thing to be done), which is the meaning of the Veda, in order to establish that the *āmnāya* (scriptural tradition) is not dependent on other means of knowledge (*māna*), since it is beyond the scope of such means; however, this does not apply to the *niyoga* (the mandate), because as something that is not itself a *kārya*, it lacks the status of being the meaning of the Veda. Furthermore, the *kārya* is not devoid of time, for, as the object of the operation of causal factors (*kāraka*), it involves a reference to the three periods of time.
The meaning is "because of its possibility.
It must be stated: "But surely, the very injunction (niyoga) is the cognition of what is to be done (kāryatva). For they designate it thus:"
"One must carry out the teacher's command; the king's edict must be executed"—this is not so.
For it would entail the absurdity that the one who is commanded possesses the status of a commander. Indeed, the agent of a command is the commander.
Furthermore, from what source does the duty to perform the sacrifice arise for him through a command? For he is not commanded with respect to that [sacrifice].

That [obligation] must be performed by its very own nature; in that regard, there is no dependence on anything else, unlike the case of the object. Rather, the expression "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) would mean "one should cause [another] to sacrifice" (*yājayet*). And thus, one who desires heaven would have fulfilled the purpose of the scripture merely through another's performance of the injunction—well done indeed by your honor in accomplishing this! Furthermore, if the obligation were the thing to be performed, then [the relationship between] heaven and the sacrifice [would be lost].
The lack of mutual connection [between the two] follows from that [prior] sequence.
He raises an objection: "But surely, for ordinary people, the cognition of 'what is to be done' (kāryatva) applies only to an injunction (niyoga). Why?
Because they designate it thus: 'The teacher’s injunction must be performed,' or 'The king’s command must be carried out.'"

He refutes this: "This is not so. Why? Because if the *niyoga* (the mandate) were to be performed by the *niyojya* (the person to be enjoined), then it would follow that the *niyojya* is the *niyoktṛ* (the enjoiner).

Why? Because the agent of a *niyoga* is its enjoiner, just as a master or the like is the enjoiner of a command. Furthermore, according to your view, the duty (*kartavyatā*) of the sacrifice would arise from the *niyoga* directed toward it."

Regarding the mandate (*niyoga*): from what source does its obligatoriness arise? If it is argued that it arises "from the mandate," to that he replies: for this [Self] is not enjoined to that mandate, because there is no other mandate [to enjoin it], and because the relationship of object and subject is impossible with respect to itself;
for that [mandate] is based upon duality.

He raises an objection: that injunction (*niyoga*) itself must be what is to be accomplished (*kārya*). There is no dependence on anything else therein—not even dependence on another injunction—as there is in the case of the object (*viṣaya*). For just as the object is to be accomplished because it implies the necessity of the agent’s performance of the injunction toward that object, as it has been said:
As for the claim that "whatever is employed for the sake of accomplishing that [niyoga] is itself the object to be enjoined"—this is merely conventional usage within the system (*tantra*).
The meaning is that the *niyoga* itself does not have its status as something to be performed derived from anything else, because that is its very nature. He refutes this:
"Let it be so; however, the expression 'one should sacrifice' (*yajeta*) would then mean 'one should cause [another] to sacrifice' (*yājayet*)."

This is the intended meaning: It has already been established above that the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth is not an "injunction" (*niyoga*) understood as a task (*kārya*) concerning a previously non-existent entity (*apūrva*) directed toward a verbal action, which impels the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) toward itself;
rather, only [worldly] commands (*ājñā*) and the like remain. Thus, by the word *yajeta* ("one should sacrifice"), the optative suffix expresses an injunction (*niyoga*) as a task.

It would be stated that the meaning [of the Veda] consists of such things as commands (*ājñā*) regarding sacrifices, which are to be performed. And such [commands] are possible even in the impersonal (*apauruṣeya*) Veda. Furthermore, commands and the like cannot be carried out by an issuer of commands without the performance of the object [of the command].
Indeed, a king enjoining forced labor (*viṣṭi*) does not himself carry the palanquin while ordering others to carry it.

Consequently, one who desires heaven would have fulfilled the purpose of the scripture merely by performing the act of the sacrificial injunction; thus, you have accomplished something that is indeed easy to do.

Therefore, he says that the injunction (*niyoga*) is not what is to be performed: "And if the object of the injunction were itself the task to be performed, [there would be no relation] between heaven and the sacrifice."
There is no mutual connection. Why? Because of their connection with that; because both are connected with the injunction (*niyoga*) whose form is the effect.
This is due to the restriction between two things connected to a single injunction, like the red cow and the one-year-old heifer. True; it is not for the sake of another desire.

In the injunction regarding sacrifice (*yāga-niyoga*), the injunction for one who desires heaven does not apply elsewhere than to the sacrifice. However, the relationship between the end to be achieved (*sādhya*) and the means (*sādhana*) is untenable.

Now, it may be argued that an injunction (*niyoga*) is not capable of making known what is to be done (*kartavyatā*) without effecting a connection between the object (*viṣaya*) and the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*); for the very nature of an injunction is "it enjoins someone to something," such that "this must be done by him."

[Objection: A relationship is not possible without a relation of subordinate and principal; therefore, [the sacrifice] is not intended for the sake of the accomplishment of another, because heaven is not for the sake of anything else, and thus the sacrifice has that (heaven) as its purpose. [Response: Because when something is connected with what is desired, it is understood as being in syntactical connection for the sake of that [desired end].

Let the *niyoga* (injunction) establish the relationship between the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) and the object of the injunction; however, the connection with the specific qualification of the object and the person to be enjoined—
Why?

He objects: between heaven (svarga) and sacrifice (yāga), which are connected by a single application (viniyoga), there would be a fixed mutual relationship, just as between the red color (aruṇa) and the one-year-old cow (ekahāyanī). This is what is meant: the injunction (niyoga) does not override the application (viniyoga).

Because it exists as having that [sacrifice] as its object and because it does not contradict it, [the author] replies: "True; one who desires something else is not enjoined to the sacrifice. The injunction regarding the desire for heaven does not apply elsewhere than to the sacrifice. However, the relationship of means and end is improper [if taken literally].
Even though heaven and the sacrifice are both connected to a single injunction, it is understood that the connection is specifically between the desire for heaven and the sacrifice.
But this is not the case with heaven and sacrifice. The meaning is that an application which is not understood cannot be the object of an injunction.
He objects: "Surely an injunction, without effecting a relationship between the object and the person enjoined, cannot itself be an obligation."

"It is sufficient to understand it as such. Why? Because in the absence of that [connection], its form does not exist. It demonstrates the form characterized by the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of being an injunction (*niyoga*):
for the nature of an injunction consists in enjoining some person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), such as one who desires heaven, toward some object, such as a sacrifice;
this is because its nature is defined by means of both the object and the person to be enjoined. By these two..."

To demonstrate that it is to be defined, he states its essential nature as well: "It is to be defined by both [the agent and the object] through the form of being an effect, namely, 'this must be done by this [agent]'". Nor can the connection between heaven and the sacrifice be established even by that [form], through the medium of the person to be impelled (*niyojya*), without a relationship of subordinate and principal; thus, because it is not for the sake of another, heaven is not something extrinsic.

Since the sacrifice is not itself the desired end, its being "for that purpose" (tādarthya) means it is for the sake of heaven; therefore, the relationship of means and end between heaven and the sacrifice is established. [Objection: This [relationship] holds when there is "being for that purpose," but why is that so? To this he says:
because in a sentence connected with something desired, even that which is not itself desired is understood to be connected as a means to that desired end. He refutes [this]:

Let the *niyoga* (the mandate) establish the relationship between the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) and the object (*viṣaya*). But from where does the connection between the object and the qualifiers of the person to be enjoined arise? Let there be a rule of mutual syntactic connection (*parasparānvaya*) between two things that are related to the same *niyoga*, as in the case of "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) and the sacrifice (*yāga*). But what has this to do with heaven and the sacrifice? For heaven is not connected to the *niyoga* in the same way that the sacrifice is.
It is not connected [to the result], but rather it is a qualification of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*); this is the meaning.

If you argue that it is because of a specific connection [with the result], then there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even such things as "living" (*jīvana*) and so forth would be [connected to the result]. What follows from this? It would mean they are auxiliary elements (*aṅga*).

Alternatively, there is the question of whether the *nimitta* (the occasioning condition) is primary or subordinate. If it were subordinate, there would be the undesirable consequence (*atideśaprasaṅga*) of the *nimitta* being extended [to other cases].

If it were primary, there would be no distinction between the entitlements (*adhikāra*) for optional rites (*kāmya*) and occasional rites (*naimittika*), because both would be directed toward the accomplishment of a result; thus, the occasional rite would not be restricted to its specific performance. Consequently, in both cases, there would be either the inclusion of all auxiliary elements (*sarvāṅgopasaṃhāra*) or none at all.
Once its purpose has been fulfilled by providing the various persons to be enjoined (*niyojya*), life and so forth would have no connection with the object [of the injunction].

However, the relationship between the occasion (*nimitta*) and the occasional duty (*naimittika*) is established through implication (*ārtha*). And when that exists, because of the qualification (*adhikāra*) therein, the injunction "one who desires heaven should sacrifice" (*svargakāmo yajeta*) would likewise be of this same nature. But it will not be so, because [the desire for heaven] is merely a qualification of the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*).

Because it is desired. Nevertheless, there is no proof for its connection with the object [of the injunction]. He raises the objection that even something else might be what is to be accomplished: "If [it is argued] because of the connection with the qualified [agent]. Even if heaven is not directly connected with the mandate (*niyoga*), the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) who is qualified by it is connected with the mandate; thus, heaven also [is connected] by way of that [qualified agent].

"Connected with the mandate" (*niyoga*) means that, due to the connection with a single mandate, [the person] is connected even with the sacrifice. Thus, the meaning is that the relationship of the goal and the means (*sādhya-sādhanabhāva*) between these two is established. He refutes this: if even [factors] such as "living" (*jīvana*), which serve as the occasion (*nimitta*), were connected to the mandate by way of their connection to the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), then it would follow that they must also be connected to the sacrifice and so forth. The challenger asks:

What follows from this? The answer is: either the condition (nimitta) is a subsidiary element (aṅga) with respect to the sacrifice and so forth, which are the objects of the injunction (niyoga), or it possesses primacy (prādhānya).

In that regard, if it were a subsidiary, there would follow by extension (atideśa) in the modified rite (vikṛti) the same status as the *samit* and other such subsidiaries. However, primacy—characterized by being the goal (*sādhya*) in relation to the sacrifice—is simply not possible for an established condition such as "living" (*jīvana*).

It is stated in response to this objection: There would be no distinction between the entitlements for optional (*kāmya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites regarding their primary status. Why? Because both are directed toward the accomplishment of a task (*kāryaniṣṭhatvāt*). Consequently, the occasional rite would not be restricted to its specific performance (*prayoga*). [The opponent asks: "Let it not be so; what harm is there to us? To this, he replies: And thus, in both cases—the optional and the occasional—all the auxiliary parts (*sarvāṅga*)...

Is there a subsumption (*pasaṃhāra*) or not? The objector says: Since [the injunction] has already fulfilled its purpose by providing a distinct person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), there can be no connection with the objective (*viṣaya*) for [the condition such as] living (*jīvana*). For it does not become useless without a connection to an objective; rather, it possesses purposefulness by way of delimiting the person to be enjoined. This is the meaning. If living were to have fulfilled its purpose merely by providing a distinct person to be enjoined...

It cannot admit of any other relationship; alas, it would follow that it could not even possess the relationship of cause and effect (*nimitta-naimittika-bhāva*). Therefore, he says: for [factors] such as "living" (*jīvana*), which are intended solely to provide the distinction of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya-bheda*), the relationship of cause and effect is merely implied (*ārtha*). He demonstrates this implication: because there is entitlement (*adhikāra*) to that [rite] when that [condition] exists. He then refutes [the objection]:

"In that case, it would also be so in the instance: 'One desiring heaven should sacrifice. The meaning is that the desire, which qualifies the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), is connected as a causal condition (*nimitta*), and not as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*). The opponent says: 'The status of desire as a causal condition will not hold; for only that which is already established can function as a condition, whereas desire is precisely what is to be accomplished by the person to be enjoined.'"
Because it is a qualifier. Why is this [the self] itself that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*)? To this he says: "Because it is desired" (*kāmyatvāt*).

For whatever one desires is what is to be accomplished for that person; the point is that there is no lack of co-location (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) between desire and effort. He refutes this: even so, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the connection of desire with the object.

Because the status of being a qualifier is logically established, and because it is observed to be based on mere desire. Now, the understanding that one who possesses a desire has the entitlement (*adhikāra*) is appropriate only in regard to a means to that desired object, and not otherwise; for if it were otherwise, the act would not have been performed by the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*). It is performed by one who possesses the desire.
The action would be performed by the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*);

however, desire is not the cause of engagement (*pravṛtti*), but rather the cause of entitlement (*adhikāra*). Engagement is held to be caused by entitlement, not caused by the fruit, because that [fruit] is unknown prior to the entitlement.

[Objection: Since that which is to be accomplished (sādhya) requires a means of accomplishment (sādhana), the object (viṣaya) will be connected to this [niyoga] as its means by virtue of proximity. To this, he says: "Because even something to be accomplished by another can function as a qualifier. This is the intended meaning: by virtue of being expressed in the same word, the verbal root-meaning (bhāvārtha), which is the object of the niyoga itself, is [understood] as the cause.

Once accepted [as the goal], it cannot be experienced as having that same status elsewhere, because the coexistence of two things to be accomplished (*sādhya*) in a single locus is impossible, which would result in a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*). Furthermore, the status of heaven and the injunction (*niyoga*) as things to be accomplished does not fail to be established otherwise, such that an increase in the number of things to be accomplished would have to be postulated. This is because even heaven, though a thing to be accomplished by another [the injunction], serves as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*).

This is because the understanding that [the object] is to be accomplished through an injunction (*niyoga*) is logically consistent. Furthermore, this was stated while provisionally accepting that desire is something to be accomplished;
however, in ultimate reality, even its status as something to be accomplished is not perceived. Thus he says: "And because it is seen to be mere desire.
For being to be accomplished consists in being pervaded by effort, and not merely in being the intended object, nor even in being invariably concomitant with it.
It has been refuted. The point is that causes do not necessarily possess their effects, because of the possibility of deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
The opponent objects: "But surely, for one who possesses desire (*kāmin*), there is the comprehension of an entitlement (*adhikāra*), which is the comprehension of an injunction (*niyoga*);
this amounts to the self's cognition of its own independence with respect to the primary task—the means to [attain] heaven and so forth, which are the means to fulfill desire."

Thus, an injunction (*niyoga*) whose object is not the [specific] element (*dhātu*) is only possible when it is conducive to the production of that which is desired (*kāmya*). For otherwise, if it were not a means to the desired end, that action would not be enjoined by one who desires [the result] as a means to be performed; rather, it would be undertaken by any person whatsoever. This is because, once the injunction conducive to the fruit is understood, the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*) becomes intensified.

Having understood that the action is a means for the sake of the fruit of the injunction (*niyoga*), one would perform it. Therefore, by the very power of the cognition of such an injunction, it must necessarily be admitted that the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*) is a means to the desired object (*kāma*); this is the sense.
The reply: That which is performed by one who possesses desire (*kāmī*) would be performed by the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*). In that case, how can it be a means to the desired object?

To this he says: "But desire is not the cause of activity. For if desire were the cause of activity, then one who possesses desire would not engage in what is not a means [to that end]; thus, the object of activity would possess the status of being a means to it. However, the meaning is that desire itself is not the cause of activity. [Objection: Is this desire then entirely without a cause? And if so, its mention in the scripture would be useless. To this [he replies]:
He says: But the cause of entitlement (*adhikāra*) is [the purpose]; however, the cause for the comprehension of the mandate (*niyoga*) is by way of delimiting the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*).

From what, then, does activity (*pravṛtti*) arise? To this he says: Activity is held to be caused by entitlement, not caused by the fruit (*phala*). Why? Because prior to entitlement, that fruit is unknown. As for the comprehension of the mandate, however...

[66] But surely, it is one who possesses desire who has the qualification (*adhikāra*). And when there is no means for that desire, the qualification does not have desire as its cause; nor is it without a cause, nor does it have something else as its cause. It has desire as its cause. When this exists, one is qualified.
Because it is [the nature of] pride (*māna*).
Now, for one who is authorized in respect to what is not a means, the desire for the fruit is not the cause [of the mandate].

For it is the desire for the goal to be reached through a means that is the cause of the mandate (*niyoga*). Therefore, the mandate occurs once the relationship between the means and the goal has been established. No.

[Objection: Its accomplishment is due to the injunction (*niyoga*). This [injunction] is indeed understood through the injunction. [Response: No, because it is dependent [on something else]. For instance: if the meaning of the word is the injunction of a qualified person, how is that [person] known from the injunction? Or, if the injunction is caused by a specific result, that [result] does not exist prior to the injunction; therefore, [the injunction] must be established beforehand.

If the result is to be understood beforehand, then the understanding of the result is redundant; the meaning is that activity is established simply from the understanding of the injunction (*niyoga*).
He objects again: "But surely the qualification belongs to one who desires [the result], due to the connection with words such as 'one who desires heaven' (*svargakāma*)."

This is understood from the context; thus, the meaning is that desire (*kāma*) is the cause (*nimitta*) for the qualification (*adhikāra*). [The opponent asks: "Let it be so; what follows from that? [The author] replies: "And when there is no means (*upāya*) for the desired object, there is no injunction (*niyoga*) caused by desire. Nor is it without a cause; as he says: "Qualification consists in the form of a task (*kārya*). It is not without a cause, because that would entail the loss of its essential nature (*svarūpa-hāni*).

Nor is it caused by another motive; the sense is that [otherwise] the word "desire" (kāma) would be redundant. The answer is: it is caused by desire. Why? Because one is qualified [for the rite] only when this desire exists. The challenger states his own view: "But surely, for one who is qualified even in the absence of a means, there is a longing for the fruit."

For the comprehension of an injunction (*niyoga*) does not have that as its cause. Why? Because it is the desire for the goal (*upeya*) that is the cause for the comprehension of the injunction regarding the means (*upāya*). He refutes this: if the desire for the goal is the cause for the comprehension of the injunction even when there is no means, then the injunction would apply once the relationship between the means and the goal is already established. To the one who says "yes," he replies: "Not from the injunction."

[The word] *siddhiḥ* [means] "establishment. And thus, the sense is that it is accepted as established. The opponent says: "This very [injunction] is understood from the mandate (*niyoga*). The meaning is this: the cognition of the mandate does not precede the understanding of that [result]; rather, for the person to be enjoined who desires heaven, the understanding of the mandate regarding the sacrifice, being incomplete, [necessarily implies] the relationship of end and means between heaven and the sacrifice.

It implies the relationship between the means and the end (*upāyopeyabhāva*). Thus, that relationship is indeed established. [The opponent claims: "It is made known by necessity through another cause. He refutes this:
No, because it would entail the consequence of dependence (*sāpekṣatva*). He demonstrates this:
For instance, if the meaning of the word were the injunction (*niyoga*) of a qualified person, then that person who, by means of a method for attaining heaven...

If one understands "this is to be accomplished by me," then that *niyoga* (the mandate) is the meaning of the word. In that case, since this specific qualification must be understood by the person prior to the *niyoga*, how can that specific qualification be known from the *niyoga*? Or, if the *niyoga* is caused by a specific result—where the specific qualification is heaven’s being accomplished through sacrifice—is it caused by that?

He refutes the claim that *niyoga* (the mandate) is the meaning of the word: "That [mandate] cannot be expressed by the word as depending upon the existence of the sacrifice, since that [sacrifice] is not previously established or known; thus, there would follow the undesirable consequence of its dependence on another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*)."
Furthermore, if the object to be attained (*upeya*) itself were the cause of entitlement (*adhikāra*), there would be no entitlement in cases such as "as long as one lives" (*jīvan*);

moreover, this is untenable because there is no word that serves as the cause for the cognition of it being a causal condition (*nimitta*). Rather, when that [object] exists, it is called a "cause" only by implication (*arthāt*) because it qualifies the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) in relation to the mandate (*niyoga*). And if [it were so] that those such as "one desiring heaven" (*svargakāma*)...

If the result were something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), it would have to come into being; thus, since its existence would have to be previously established by another means of knowledge (*mānāntara*), the verbal expression [of the injunction] would depend upon that other means of knowledge, leading to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of dependence on another authority.
This is the underlying intention here: first of all, there can be no object of sacrifice (*yāga-viṣaya*) that is not already distinguished by the result to be accomplished, such as heaven (*svarga*).

The comprehension of the action as a task (kārya) is capable of implying that the sacrifice is a means toward heaven as the end to be accomplished; however, it is rather liable to be rejected because it would contradict the primacy of the mandate (niyoga). This is because [the sacrifice] enters [into the process] for the sake of establishing the person to be enjoined (niyojya), which is conducive to the fulfillment of the mandate that constitutes the primary element. Even though the fruit is what is desired to be performed, its status as the end to be accomplished does not belong to the task in the form of the mandate.
If it is argued that [the subordinate action] does not contradict the predominance [of the principal action] because its cognition is dependent upon that [principal],

but rather it subsists for the sake of that [principal] by being conducive to the predominance in the performance of the *niyoga*— just like the service rendered by a slave born in the house (*garbhadāsa*)— we say no.

For when there is a conjunction of what is intended to be performed and what is not intended to be performed, the non-intended is [subordinated] by the conscious activity directed toward the intended object.
Because it functions for the sake of that [end]. For it is impossible for something to be conducive to an end by being rendered subordinate to it.
If it is argued that its conduciveness arises from its being directed toward that end, we say no; for such conduciveness is impossible due to the contradiction with its very nature.
Indeed, fire placed down to provide relief to one suffering from heat never acts in a manner conducive to that [suffering]; nor does it bring about unhappiness.
It has been explained that the desire to produce something previously non-existent is the object of the means for achieving happiness (*asukha-sādhana*).

As for what was said regarding [the analogy] of the "born slave" (*garbhadāsa*), that is incorrect; for in that case, there are two distinct efforts inherent in two different conscious agents. Among these, the effort of the master is directed toward his own interest for the sake of benefiting the born slave.

[The agent] proceeds. Even a slave born in the house (*garbhadāsa*) proceeds for the sake of his master only when his own mental activity is directed toward securing his own maintenance and safety (*yogakṣema*). And this person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), who stands in the place of the slave born in the house, would engage in the performance of the injunction through desire.
Thus, his effort proceeds with desire as its object, just as the slave born in the house proceeds for the sake of the master while aiming at his own interest.

The injunction (niyoga) would pervade [the action] as if it were a master, but not as its primary element. Furthermore, there is no other conscious agent here who could be a master such that the injunction would have primacy with respect to his performance. Therefore, it is correct to conclude that the fact of the meaning of the verbal root being a means to the desired end is not obtainable through the implication of the injunction.

If one should think that it is impossible for desire (*kāma*) to be the motive for what is to be attained (*upeya*) because it is the motive for the injunction (*niyoga*), and thus [desire] must be the object to be attained with respect to the sacrifice (*yāga*), to this he says: "Furthermore, if the object to be attained itself were the cause of entitlement (*adhikāra-nimitta*), it would follow that there could be no entitlement in cases such as 'as long as one lives' (*jīvana-ādi*). Moreover, this was stated while accepting that desire is the cause of entitlement."

From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), however, this status of being a cause for the cognition of a motive is indeed untenable for desire, because words such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth—which are the causes for the cognition of a motive—are absent.
[The opponent] objects: "Let it not be that the word is the cause for the cognition of a motive; rather, let it be merely a qualification of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*)."

In that case, [the words] would be intent upon the *nimitta* (occasioning condition) rather than intent upon the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*). Consequently, since no qualification for entitlement (*adhikāra*) is perceived therein, there would be no performance [of the rite].
If it is argued that the entitlement is established by implication (*arthāt*), then the rejection of the position that the agent is a qualifier [of the injunction] is rendered futile.

For just as the qualification (*adhikāra*) is understood through desire with respect to the meaning of the verbal root which serves as the means (*upāya*), so too agency (*kartṛtva*) is not [understood] through desire unless it is a non-means; and for whom the means is the desired object, for him this is the ritual action (*karman*).

Thus, by implication, the establishment of qualification follows from the injunction that restricts the agent. Just as from the injunction of qualification, the restriction of the agent is established.

And when that [desire for heaven] exists, it is called the "occasion" (nimitta) by necessity and implication. He refutes this: if those such as "one desiring heaven" were intent upon the occasion, they would not then be intent upon the person entitled to perform the rite (*adhikārin*). The word "but" (*tu*) serves to set aside the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), because if the sentence were intent upon both, there would be the undesirable consequence of a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*). In that case, if it were intent upon the occasion, there would be no entitlement...

"There is no application [of the word] because it is already understood. Now, if it is argued that the understanding of the qualification (*adhikāra*)—namely, the person possessing the cause—is established from the meaning itself, even though the word expresses only the cause, because that is required; otherwise, due to the absence of performance, there would be a contradiction of the nature of the body [of the injunction]," [the author] refutes this: "In that case, it is useless for the sake of establishing the qualification."

Refutation of the view that [the qualification] is a qualifier of the agent: First of all, on the view that it is a qualifier of the agent, the agent himself must necessarily be adopted as a qualifier by virtue of being a constituent of the action; otherwise, just as in the case of the meditation on the mind of Sagara, because the desire for the fruit is common to all who undertake the practice, no specific agent would be obtained. Rather, it is like [the case of] a king...

The caste (*jāti*) of being a king, like purity and so forth, because it cannot be produced by effort, is not something to be undertaken (*anupādeya*); yet, it delimits the agent [of the action], as in: "One who desires sovereignty should sacrifice with the Rājasūya. For whomsoever that caste of kingship exists—even though it is not something to be undertaken—there is eligibility (*adhikāra*) for him by implication, but not for Brāhmaṇas or Vaiśyas. It is not the caste...

In the case of two separated lovers: thus, because the fruit is naturally beautiful by its very nature, the activity of desire and the desire itself may arise even though they are not something to be acquired by the person. Since that [desire] manifests, it is possible to distinguish the agent from other conscious beings by means of it, thereby differentiating him from those whose desires are dormant, attenuated, or interrupted; therefore, there is no absence of that which is to be excluded (*vyavacchedya*). Nor is it the case that...

Since, within the scope of the verbal suffix (*ākhyātapada*), the agent alone is presented first— either by the final action (*caramakriyā*) or by the number of the agent (*kartṛsaṅkhyā*)— and because the qualification of the entitled person (*adhikārin*) depends upon the knowledge of the performance of the ritual with all its auxiliary parts (*sāṅgaprayoga*), which itself is dependent upon the [prior] cognition of the effect (*kārya*), there is no immediate comprehension [of the qualified agent] even when there is a requirement for it; thus, it is not denoted first.
The "connection" will be explained further below.

Even so, from what source is the qualification of the agent established? To this he says: "Just as in your view the qualification is understood through desire with respect to the meaning of the verbal root which serves as the means, so too for us it is likewise."
Agency does not exist without a means, for the principle that "whoever desires something, he performs the action to achieve it" applies here as well.

[Objection: Even so, how is the attainment of a specific qualification (adhikāra) established? To this, he says: "And for whom there is a means to desire, for him this is the ritual act"—by implication, the establishment of our qualification follows from the rule that restricts agency.

Furthermore, in a sentence connected with a desired end, the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) is with the desired object, not with the mandate (*niyoga*); for if it were connected with both objects, there would be a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*).
But surely, an injunction (*niyoga*) does not sublate an application (*viniyoga*), because there is no contradiction; for that [injunction] is understood in accordance with the application.

In that case, the word-meanings, mutually connected, become the objects of the injunction. And connection does not occur without a relationship of subordinate and principal. Therefore, since it is desired [as the goal], heaven is the principal and the ritual action is subordinate.

When the ritual action (*karman*) is subordinate, the person desiring heaven (*svargakāma*) is enjoined; thus, the primacy of the injunction (*niyoga*) is not lost, and the connection between the ritual action and its fruit is established. Furthermore, the person to be enjoined does not engage in the desire for the fruit spontaneously; even one who seeks it [does not act] without a means (*upāya*).
Because [the knowledge of the means and the end] arises from the activity [itself]. Nor is there a cognition of the means and the end prior to the injunction (*niyoga*).

Indeed, for you, the establishment of the restriction on the agent does not result from the connection with the application (*viniyoga*), as it does for those who hold the injunction of qualification (*adhikāravidhi*). He states another objection:
in a sentence connected with a desired object, the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is with the desired end, not with the meaning of the injunction. Why then is it not connected with both?

Does it so become? To this he says: "Because there would be a split in the sentence if there were a connection for both purposes. And it was stated above that the analogy of the "born slave" (*garbhadāsa*) is not applicable.
Now he sets forth the view of the old Prābhākara: "But surely [the *liṅga*] does not sublate the application (*viniyoga*)."
Whence [arises] the mandate (*niyoga*)? From the absence of contradiction. He states that very point: "Because it is understood according to its application (*yathāviniyogam*).

In that context, the word-meanings, being mutually connected, become the objects of the mandate. And connection does not occur without a relationship of primary and subordinate; therein, because it is desired, heaven (*svarga*) is the primary, while the action (*karma*) is subordinate—that is, a quality (*guṇa*).

The suffix *tasi* is used in all case-sense relations (*sārvavibhaktika*). Thus, in this [interpretation], where heaven is the subordinate element of the object—meaning that in this heaven which is to be accomplished by sacrifice, the person desiring heaven (*svargakāma*) is enjoined—the primacy of the injunction (*niyoga*) is not lost, and the connection between the action and its fruit is established. This is easy to understand.

Now, it might be argued that when desire is subordinate to the sacrifice, the person is not to be enjoined [with respect to that desire], because his engagement occurs solely through desire, and because the status of being an injunction consists in inciting one who has not yet engaged. To this, he says:
"And a person is not to be enjoined regarding a desire simply because of spontaneous engagement. Why? Because even for one who desires [the object], there is no engagement if the means are lacking."

Even when there is a desire, activity [toward an impossible end] is impossible.
