For men indeed desire omniscience, yet they do not engage in it because this [state] cannot be attained as it lacks a means; thus, prior to the knowledge of the means, even heaven and other such desirable ends do not become objects of activity. Therefore, the mandate (niyoga) [must indicate] its own means.

The meaning is that one proceeds there by understanding it; that is, one who desires that [result] acts. Furthermore, there is no knowledge of the means and the end prior to the injunction, because the understanding of those arises from that very [injunction].

The connection between heaven and the sacrifice is accepted as being of the third kind (the *tārtīyī*); however, this [connection] belongs to the sphere of the *niyoga* (the injunction). Furthermore, it would follow that the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*) is not the object of the *niyoga*, which has already been refuted. Moreover, there would be a lack of qualification (*niradhikāratā*), because the absence of an object [of action] is a cause for the absence of qualification; otherwise, one would have to assume such qualification even in cases like the Viśvajit sacrifice, which leads to an undesirable conclusion. This is because there is a contradiction between being something to be enjoined (*vidheya*) and being the definition of the object [of the injunction].

[The injunction does not apply] by virtue of attainment or non-attainment; nor because of the connection as an agent, since prior to the application (niyoga), there is an absence of being a person to be enjoined (niyojyatva). Furthermore, it would follow that [the act] must necessarily be performed, because desire is not the governing factor. Even if it were the governing factor, desire itself would also necessarily [be present].
He refutes this without contradicting his own independent established doctrine: "Indeed, the application (viniyoga)..."

The connection between heaven and sacrifice is held by you to be based on the relationship of means and end (*upāyopeya*). Why? Because that connection, which is based on application (*viniyoga*), belongs to the third [book];

however, this [connection] is based on injunction (*naiyogika*). Thus, there is a contradiction with the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*), as it is the consensus of the commentator who, in the third chapter concerning the section on Bādari, does not accept a direct connection.
Moreover, for one who accepts that the *niyoga* (the mandate) has as its object both the means and the fruit, another undesirable consequence follows.

Thus he says: "The mere *bhāvārtha* (the sense of the verbal root) would have to be withdrawn [from being the object] as the object of the *niyoga*. Furthermore, when the fruit is the object of the *niyoga*, there would be an absence of an *adhikārin* (a qualified agent). Why? Because of the object (*viṣaya*).

Because it would be a cause for non-qualification (*anadhikāra*). Now, why should the object (*viṣaya*) not itself be the cause of qualification? To this he says: because in the case of the Viśvajit sacrifice and others, there is the consequence that such [a cause] is not postulated, since the object exists as the very cause of qualification.
Surely this is the purpose; however, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must be stated. To this it is replied:

because there is a contradiction between being that which is to be enjoined (*vidheya*) and being the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). For that which is to be enjoined is indeed the object of the mandate (*niyoga*), whereas the defining characteristic is the cause of qualification (*adhikāra*);
for by being characterized by that [result], a person is distinguished from those not characterized by it and thus becomes a participant in the qualification.

Now, why is there a contradiction between these two? To this he says: because the characteristic is already established and well-known through attainment and non-attainment; for that [characteristic] is not possible in what is not well-known. Furthermore, since that which is not yet attained is the object of an injunction by virtue of being something to be enjoined, it is not possible for it to be so when it is already attained. Moreover, if it were the object of application (*viniyoga*)...

[If] it were so [that the injunction were primary], then before the determination of the injunction regarding that [subject], the application (*viniyoga*) would have to be determined, as well as the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*). Indeed, one who has not yet understood the meaning of the verbal root is not capable of determining the injunction. And just as the application—characterized by the relationship between the sacrifice and the one desiring heaven—is determined prior to the injunction as its "subject" (*viṣaya*), [so too must the application and the verbal meaning be understood first].

That must be examined. Furthermore, prior to the comprehension of the mandate (*niyoga*), the one desiring heaven (*svargakāma*), while being connected with the action, is connected only as an agent (*kartṛ*); but subsequently, upon the cognition of the mandate, he becomes the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*). Thus, because the agent becomes the entitled person (*adhikārin*), there is once again a contradiction of the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*). Therefore, he says: "And because of the connection as an agent prior to the mandate... [and so forth].

Because there is an absence of anything to be conjoined [with the injunction]. And he states that this further undesirable consequence follows: from the cognition of the "to-be-done-ness" (kartavyatā) regarding an object delimited by a sacrifice; and because the nature of what is contradictory to "to-be-done-ness" is excluded, there would necessarily follow the consequence that heaven and so forth must be performed along with their means.

[It would have to be] an effect. Therefore, there is a connection with the *niyoga* (injunction) between two things that are not mutually connected. For if they were so connected, there would be a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*). Even the relationship of means and end (*sādhya-sādhana-bhāva*) based on a connection to a single *niyoga* has already been refuted.

But surely, it is understood from the *niyoga* (injunction) that "this is a benefit for him"; how then could this [benefit] be his *karma* (action)? What kind of benefit could there be for him other than one directed toward a desired object (*kāmya*)? If there were some other benefit, the word "seeker" (*arthin*) would be meaningless. If, then, the meaning of the *niyoga* is the relationship between the benefactor and the beneficiary, what follows from this? The status of [the Veda] as an instructor (*upadeśaka*) is lost.

Furthermore, because it is a restatement of an existing fact (*sthitavastvanuvāda*), there is a state of dependence. Therefore, the meaning of the injunction (*niyoga*)—"this must be done by him"—is not connected with heaven and the like, whose limits are conditioned by desire (*kāma*), and since desire is not necessarily present, how can there be a necessity to perform [the rite]? To this, he says: "Because desire is not the governing factor" (*kāmasyātantratvāt*). [The rite is] necessarily to be performed due to the injunction (*niyoga*).
Since that [desire] excludes its own contrary—the absence of itself—the necessity of performing the act is necessarily understood;

however, this necessity cannot be connected with the desire because of the contradiction between the eternal and the non-eternal. Thus, while the desire may be considered non-essential (atantrā) in accordance with the primary injunction (niyoga), it cannot be a case of a scribal error (pramādapāṭha). This is the meaning.

But if it must be accepted that they are mutually dependent (*tantratā*), then he says: even in the case of mutual dependence, the desire (*icchā*) must necessarily be performed, because the mandate (*niyoga*) has that as its object, just like the fruit and so forth. He concludes: therefore, there is an association with the mandate (*niyogānvaya*) between the sacrifice and the one desiring heaven, which are not mutually connected [prior to that]. And when there is such an association with it, they are not mutually dependent, as is the case with the fruit as well.

Because there would be a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*) due to two things being [simultaneously] objects to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Furthermore, the relationship of means and end (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*) has already been refuted even on the grounds that they are connected to a single injunction (*niyoga*), because the analogy of the "born slave" (*garbhadāsa*) is inapplicable here; this is the intended meaning.

Now, it may be argued: "Granted, let there be no connection of heaven with the sacrifice by way of its being an object to be accomplished as a qualification of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya-viśeṣaṇa*)."

But one might object: "By the force of the cognition of entitlement (*adhikāra*), its status as a means to heaven in relation to the ritual act will be established. To this he replies: "Surely, from the injunction (*niyoga*) expressed by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, it is understood that this ritual act is beneficial to this person; let it be understood. But what follows from this? He says: "And how [is it established] that the ritual act belongs to that entitled person (*adhikārin*)?"

It might be argued that action is not beneficial [to the self]. For it is only when the conscious being partakes in the benefit produced by action that it attains ownership over that action, and not otherwise; this is the meaning. Nevertheless, one might ask: what does this have to do with the benefit characterized as heaven? To this he says: "What kind of benefit could there be for this [self] other than the desired benefit?"
One might ask: "Is this alone the benefit in the world? To this he says:

if another benefit were postulated, the word *arthin* (the seeker) would have its meaning unintended. Thus, two faults would ensue: the abandonment of what is heard in scripture (*śrutahāni*) and the postulation of what is not heard (*aśrutakalpanā*). He refutes [this objection]: if, by means of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, it were meant that "this action is beneficial to this person,"...

It is understood that [the Veda] is established as authoritative; however, if the meaning of the injunctive suffix (*liṅ*) is the sense of an injunction consisting in the relationship between the beneficiary and the benefactor, then the opponent asks: "What follows from this? The answer is: its well-known status as an *upadeśaka* (an original source of instruction) is lost. Why?

Because it would be a restatement of an already existing fact (*sthitavastvanuvāda*). Consequently, its dependence on something else—which is the preeminent cause of non-authoritativeness—would follow.

[Otherwise, it would] entail an absurdity. He concludes: Therefore, the meaning of the injunction (*niyoga*) is "this must be done by this person," and not [the meaning of] "the cognition of its performance" for this person; because [the former] is never absent [from the injunction], whereas the latter is not. Furthermore, [it is not so] because there is no assistance [rendered] in the case of occasional rites (*naimittika*), prohibitions (*niṣedha*), or [those concerning] qualification (*adhikāra*).

Because it is based on dependence (*āśrayaṇāt*). Nor is the injunction (*niyoga*) restricted solely to an action for the sake of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*); for that very reason, it is absent in worldly cases such as the act of studying. Now, [it may be argued: heaven is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), not a mere indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*).
Let there be its connection with the injunction; however, the injunction itself does not establish the relationship with the sacrifice. In this way, such a person...

It is said, "one is enjoined," as in the case of the rule: "He whose house is burned by fire [should perform a sacrifice]. Now, one might ask: "Is this [injunction] merely an auxiliary for the sake of accomplishing a desired end? Why? Because there is the cognition of performance, because it does not contradict the existence of well-known instructional status, and because it is non-deviant (*avyabhicāra*). However, if the relationship between the beneficiary (*upakārya*) and the benefactor (*upakāraka*) were the primary meaning of the injunction (*niyoga*), there would be deviation.

Why? Because neither the prohibition of a contingent act (*naimittika*) nor its qualification (*adhikāra*) can rely upon [the production of] an *apūrva* as a benefit (*upakāra*). Nor is the production of an *apūrva* itself the benefit; for that *apūrva*, being neither pleasure nor a means for attaining the beneficial or avoiding the harmful, lacks the quality of being experienced as agreeable, and thus it cannot function as a benefit—this is the sense.

[Objection: Is it not observed in common worldly usage that an injunction (*niyoga*) pertains to an action that serves the purpose of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), as in the case of "one who has a fever should eat wholesome food" (*jvaritaḥ pathyamaśnīyāt*)? And since the Veda is based upon that [worldly usage], it is appropriate that in the Veda as well, an injunction regarding an action whose object is the injunction should pertain to an action that serves the purpose of the person to be enjoined. To this, he says: "And an injunction does not pertain to an action solely for the sake of the person to be enjoined. Why?

For this very reason, because there is indeed a deviation between the occasional injunction (*naimittika*) and the qualification for the prohibition (*niṣedhādhikāra*). Now, one might argue: "We shall assume that in the world, by the force of common experience, the occasional injunction and the qualification for the prohibition provide mutual assistance. To this, he says: "And in the world, in cases such as a request (*adhyeṣaṇā*), there is an absence of the action's being for the sake of the person to be impelled (*niyojya*). Furthermore, [this applies] regarding heaven.

He establishes that [heaven] is a qualification of the person to be impelled (*niyojya*) by virtue of its distinction as a secondary characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*) within the state of being the goal (*sādhyatā*): "But surely heaven is a primary qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*), not a secondary characteristic; how could it fail to enter into the action (*kārya*) itself?
If one asks this, [the response is: Why should it not be connected as the goal? If you say "no," then why would sacrifice not be its means (*sādhana*)? Therefore...

The meaning is that there is a mutual connection between heaven and the sacrifice. He refutes this: "Let it be that heaven is connected to the injunction (*niyoga*), as is the case with the quality of redness (*āruṇya*); but how is it so for the sacrifice? Is it not the case that the injunction itself, through its connection with heaven, establishes the relationship of heaven with its own object, namely the sacrifice? And thus, there is a connection between heaven and the sacrifice?"

Regarding the phrase "the relationship between the goal and the means," he offers this rebuttal: "And thus, the connection between the one desiring heaven and the sacrifice is indeed through the mandate (niyoga), but not directly between heaven and the sacrifice. For it is not by this much that their connection with the mandate is not postulated.
He then demonstrates its nature: "A person such as this—one desiring heaven—is [connected] to this sacrifice..."
Regarding the phrase "is enjoined": he provides an illustration for such a case, namely, "He whose house is burned by fire should sacrifice.

Just as the injunction regarding the sacrifice for one who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) and whose house has been burned does not convey that the sacrifice is the means (*sādhana*) for the burning of the house, so too the injunction for the sacrifice for one desiring heaven (*svargakāma*) does not convey that the sacrifice is the means for that qualification [of heaven].
The meaning is that it ought to make known the state of being a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*).
Would the attainment of the fruit result from the injunction (*niyoga*) regarding the verbal root-meaning (*bhāvārtha*)? It would, if such were the verbal root-meaning; however, this is not so.

This has been stated in the *Bhāvanāviveka*: "And in the case of that which is occasioned by a specific cause, there would be the contingency of [an independent] result. Furthermore, it has been explained in the *Bhāvanāviveka* how, according to this view, there is no connection between the ritual act (*karman*) and its fruit. "Therefore, since there is no relationship between heaven and the sacrifice, there is no cognition of a means for achieving a human goal (*puruṣārtha*)."

Discerning people desire to know the means for accomplishing the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*). Since the meaning of words is understood from common worldly usage, he does not raise the following objection: "But surely, because of the mandate (*niyoga*) regarding the verbal root-meaning as a subordinate condition (*upādhi*) for the attainment of the desired end, the fruit would be accomplished. This is what is intended: although the verbal root refers merely to the form of the action, such as cooking (*pāka*) or cutting (*cheda*), etc.

Because the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) are understood from the nouns (*pada*), whereas through the connection with the verb (*ākhyāta*), its meaning is perceived as a cumulative process consisting of prior and subsequent stages. And since this state [of action] does not exist without a single unifying factor (*upasaṅgrāhaka*), that unifying factor is its result. Thus, this verb is a single entity that persists from the beginning until the production of the result, comprising the prior and subsequent stages.

Or rather, [the word] "pacati" (he cooks) denotes that which delimits the essence of an entity— either a continuum of actions of the same kind or a collection of actions of the same kind— as being conducive to the production of another [result]. And likewise, in the case of the injunction "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*),

it refers to the sacrificial act (*yāga-karman*) whose nature consists in the relinquishment of one's own ownership over the substance, preceded by the recollection of Devadatta and the mental apprehension of that substance, directed toward the desired fruit.

When there is an expectation for a distinction in the fruit due to the mandate (*niyoga*), even heaven—which serves as a qualification for the person entitled to the rite—is connected [to the action] by virtue of being achievable through sacrifice. He refutes this: "It would be so if the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*) were of such a nature; however, it is not so," as has been stated regarding *bhāvanā*.
Regarding isolation (*viveka*): if such an action (*karman*) is the object of an injunction (*niyoga*), then it must be understood prior to that injunction.

Indeed, an agent (*niyojya*) who has not understood the scope [of the action] is not capable of understanding the injunction whose scope is that action. Nor can a sacrifice having heaven as its limit be known through any other means of knowledge prior to the comprehension of the injunction, in the same way that cooking is known to have cooked rice as its limit.
It is capable of being understood; yet its understanding does not arise from the injunction (*niyoga*), because that would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence (*parasparāśraya*):

the determination of the injunction depends upon its understanding, while the understanding of it depends upon that determination. Even though the form of the sacrifice is established by other means of knowledge, it is nevertheless not established as having the nature of an action (*bhāva*); and therefore, it cannot be the object of that [injunction].

Furthermore, if its status as an object were established merely by its form (*rūpa*) or by that alone, it would have no connection with heaven; this is the intended meaning. Moreover, there would be the undesirable consequence of having to postulate a fruit for a contingent rite (*naimittika*). This is because there is no distinction here [in the case of a contingent rite] from the case of a desired rite (*kāmya*), since the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*) functions as the means to the desired end. And it has been stated more than once that the *apūrva* is not within the scope of desire, as follows:

Furthermore, in this view, the connection between action and its fruit cannot be established even by another means; as it has been stated in the *Bhāvanāviveka*: "Now, let there be no connection; what harm is that to us? To this he replies: "Therefore, because there is no connection between heaven and sacrifice, knowledge is not a means for achieving the human goal (*puruṣārtha*). He then asks: "What follows from that? and replies: "And [it must be] a means for achieving the human goal."
Those possessed of discernment investigate this matter.

Thus, by means of this treatise, the status of the *niyoga* as something to be accomplished (*kāryatā*) has been refuted due to the consequence that heaven and sacrifice would be mutually unrelated. Furthermore, he refutes that very same point by another method: "And from common usage, the meaning of words [is understood]..."
The primacy of the injunction (*niyoga*) [is untenable], because there is no injunction once that [object] is established. Nor does the cognizer comprehend it;

for even when the object is established, there is no performance [of the act]. Indeed, when one says "bring the cow," what is intended by the speaker is not the establishment of the injunction itself.
Nevertheless, the establishment of the object [of knowledge] remains unproven.

In the world, the function of words is one thing; in the Veda, it is another. For in the world, the syntactical connection (*samanvaya*) of words is intent upon the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*), whereas in the Veda, it is intent upon the injunction (*niyoga*). This is yet another "pustule upon a boil. Indeed, if...

If it is argued that the capacity of words to convey a sequence focused on the speaker’s intention is understood from worldly usage, but not their capacity for anything else—since the capacity of words has no other source of proof apart from the speaker—and that this is so because there is no speaker, [we reply: it follows that this very sequence focused on the speaker’s intention would itself lead to the inference of that speaker, thereby resulting in the conclusion that [the Veda] is of human origin. Alternatively, there would be a lack of comprehension; or, even if comprehension occurs...
The understanding [of the meaning] would not be based on the word itself, but would be either conventional (*sāmayikī*) or born from an inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭajā*).
Therefore, your confusion—that the *niyoga* (injunction) is the thing to be accomplished—is merely born from a technical usage of the term.
Furthermore, the *niyoga* is not primary with respect to the agent’s activity, because it is understood [as such]. Why? Because [the activity] is for the sake of the accomplishment of that *niyoga*.

Because that [result] is accomplished for the instigator alone by virtue of the instigation. Nor does the person being directed (the *pratipattṛ*) understand that accomplishment of the connection through the instigator’s words as being pervaded by his own action. Why? Because when the object is already accomplished, the person being directed does not perform the act; for one who has brought a cow himself does not begin the act of bringing it when it has been brought by another.

Therefore, since there is agreement between the instigator and the person to be instigated regarding the accomplishment of an object, one determines that the status of being a means (sādhanatā) refers exclusively to the connected object, and not to the mandate (niyoga); this is the meaning. He objects: "The function of words in the world is one thing, and in the Veda it is another. He clarifies this very point:

For in the world, the connection between words and their meanings is intent upon the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*), whereas in the Veda it is intent upon injunction (*niyoga*). Therefore, the meaning is that in that [Vedic] context, the status of being a task (*kāryatā*) belongs to the injunction alone. He refutes this: "This is another boil upon a tumor. He explains it: "If indeed the capacity of words is understood from worldly usage as being intent upon the speaker's intention, then..."

The Veda does not have as its purport anything other than what is intended [by an author]. Why? Because there is no other means of knowledge [for it], and because the capacity of words is known through worldly usage; thus, no other means for understanding that [intention] is possible in the case of the Veda. He raises an objection:
"If it is argued that since there is no speaker, there can be no possibility of intention in the Veda? He refutes this: "This very..."

If it is argued that the sequence [of words] is subordinate to the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*) and thus would lead one to infer that intention, then human authorship (*pauruṣeyatva*) follows as a consequence. Thus, in this position, upon the boil characterized by contradiction with the world, there arises the eruption characterized by the consequence of human authorship.
Alternatively, if its lack of human authorship were more firmly established, then the "eruption" would be the absence of comprehension, because of the absence of any means for such comprehension.

Now, if it is argued that the cognition established by one's own experience, which arises immediately upon hearing the Vedic sentences, cannot be denied, to this he replies: "Or, even if such a comprehension occurs, it is not caused by the words [themselves], but is conventional; for when Vedic sentences are already self-established, the comprehension of meaning from their utterance is based on conventions created by persons. This is the meaning: if...

However, because there is no recollection of an author (sambandhu), the performance of a convention (saṅketa) is impossible; therefore, it must arise from the form of "inference based on general observation" (sāmānyatodṛṣṭa). For a sentence joined with words such as "cow" has been observed to be the cause for the cognition of a specific meaning, and since a Vedic sentence is likewise [composed of such words], it too is a communicator of meaning; thus, the cognition of meaning arises even from a Vedic sentence through inference based on general observation.
This is the meaning.
Furthermore, in the world, a mere injunction (*niyoga*) is not the cause of activity, because everyone does not act upon every injunction. [Rather, it is] one who is to be obeyed...

And because that [compliance] exists due to an injunction (*niyoga*). Obedience (*anuvidheyatva*) is the cause for the agent's engagement [in action] through another person's injunction. Furthermore, the cause for such compliance—namely, the attainment of what is beneficial or the avoidance of what is harmful—is established here by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Moreover, there is no one to issue an injunction even in the Veda; how then could there be anyone to whom one must be obedient? [Objection: But surely it is the Word (*śabda*). [Response: Granted, let it be the issuer of the injunction, but...

It must be followed [by the agent], because there is no other cause [for such activity]. For there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish that the attainment of what is beneficial and the avoidance of what is harmful are dependent upon words. If it is argued that this is due to an injunction (*niyoga*), we say no; for that injunction is itself an object of knowledge (*prameya*).

If it is then argued that it is the cognition of the injunction, we say no; for that cognition has the injunction as its object, and the injunction is distinct from those two [attainment and avoidance]. Nor can the injunction be implied by the meaning [of the sentence].

As for the worldly designation presented as evidence— that when there is a duty to perform an injunction, the command of a teacher must be carried out and the royal edict must be executed— that is refuted by being shown to be established otherwise;
therefore, this delusion of yours, that "the injunction (niyoga) is what is to be done," arises from a figurative usage.

Having explained the first half of the verse by stating that the word *niyoga* (an injunction) indicates, through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*), the purposeful action (*bhāvārtha*) which is its own denoted object, he now explains the second half of the verse: "Furthermore, in common worldly usage, the mere injunction is not the cause of activity.
Why? Because everyone does not act upon every injunction; rather, activity occurs only upon the injunction of one who is to be obeyed."

Therefore, obedience is the cause of activity for the one being enjoined, arising from the injunction of another; and the grounds for such obedience—such as the attainment of benefit or the avoidance of harm—are established by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). If it is argued that in the Veda as well there must be one to be obeyed, just as in the world, [the author] says: "And even in the Veda, though it is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*), no enjoiner is perceived."

But why, moreover, should this [Dharma] be followed? The meaning is: because Dharma is absolutely unestablished. He raises an objection: "Is it not the case that the Word (śabda) is the director and thus to be followed? [The author replies: The status of the Word as a director was already refuted previously by the passage beginning with "Because it is not a means of valid cognition" (pramāṇatvāt). Even granting for the sake of argument that it is a director, he says: "Let it be a director indeed."

But it is not to be followed, because there is no cause for following it. [The opponent objects: "Will not the attainment of what is beneficial and the avoidance of what is harmful be the cause for following it? To this he says: "For there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the attainment of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful that depends upon following the word. [The opponent] raises a doubt: "If there were following of the word, then for the person who follows it..."

If it is argued that the injunction (*niyoga*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the attainment of what is beneficial or the cessation of what is harmful, he refutes this: "No; because that injunction is itself an object of cognition (*prameya*). Indeed, that which is an object of cognition cannot be a means of valid cognition by virtue of its true nature.
He raises a further objection: "If the injunction is not a means of valid cognition because it is an object of cognition, then [is] the knowledge of the injunction..."

"In that case, let it be a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). He refutes this: "No; because it has an injunction (niyoga) as its object, and because that injunction is distinct from both the attainment of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful. If one should think: "Let there indeed be no injunction; [let it be a means of valid cognition] by virtue of being an object of knowledge (prameya) regarding the attainment of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful," [the author replies:]...
Since the cognition of the word as a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is untenable without the activity of a conscious agent,

and since such activity is impossible without the attainment of a goal or the avoidance of what is harmful, it will imply an activity whose purpose is the attainment of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful; and in relation to that [activity], even the object of knowledge (*prameya*) attains the status of a means of valid knowledge, for words denoting causal factors function only relatively.

To this he replies: "Nor is there an implication by the force of the sense. Why? Because we observe the injunctions of non-authoritative persons to be devoid of the attainment of the beneficial or the avoidance of the harmful, as for example: "This path is safe; may you go by this very way."

In the world, an injunction (*niyoga*) is centered on the connection between word-meanings; since that [connection] is the object of other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), worldly activity depends upon it and is based upon it. In the Veda, however, the injunction is centered on the injunction itself; therefore, there is no dependence on anything else. This has already been answered.
Furthermore, the mere injunction is not the cause of activity. In that case, the cognition of the injunction would be false.

And that is not tenable, because of the absence of two causes [for falsity]. We do not disregard the injunction (*niyoga*), by which it would be false; for even when that exists, a person proceeds to act, just as in the world one acts upon any injunction whatsoever. Indeed, it is not the case that there is no injunction there. It has already been stated that if [the Veda] were not intent on that [injunction], its status as a means of valid knowledge (*prāmāṇya*) would lack a basis.

But surely, activity arises from the comprehension that something ought to be done; and one who is enjoined understands, "This is my duty," because he perceives the injunction of an authoritative person. An unauthoritative person, having described a bad path as a good path, induces one to act upon it, just as one says, "This path is safe; may you go by this way. [The opponent] objects:

The *niyoga*—expressed by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and other such markers—is that which culminates in the connection of word-meanings and culminates in the coordination characterized as the means for attaining what is beneficial and avoiding what is harmful.
This is because, according to the etymology "that by which one is impelled," in common worldly usage, that relationship of means and end is the object of other means of knowledge;
and since it depends upon other means of knowledge, the relationship of means and end is based upon them.

In the world, activity is based on a connection with an object; and in the case of the speech of one who is not authoritative, there is no activity because the injunction is sublated by another means of knowledge. However, in the Veda, the syntactical relation of word-meanings rests upon an injunction that is not within the scope of other means of knowledge.
And once that is cognized, it serves as the cause for activity by conforming to the means for attaining the beneficial and avoiding the harmful.

It does not depend [on anything else], because its nature is to incite action; therefore, there is no dependence on another. For the word as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) does not require another means of cognition to bring about that understanding. Nor does the injunction (*niyoga*) require [another] regarding the fact that it is the means for attaining the beneficial or avoiding the harmful in a person's activity. He refutes this: "This has already been answered. [The case of] intention to speak..."

In the context of refuting the notion of "otherness," he says: "Furthermore, even if we grant that the *niyoga* (injunction) is intended to have the sole essence of instigation (*pravartanā*), we still do not accept that;
for whether it be worldly or non-worldly, it is simply called 'injunction,' yet it is not merely an injunction."
[The opponent states: "It is the cause of engagement. [The proponent] objects: "If it does not cause one to engage, then the cognition of the *niyoga* (injunction) is false.

And this is not tenable, because of the absence of the two causes [of falsity]. [The proponent] replies: "We do not disregard the *niyoga*, by which the Veda would become false. Even though that [the *niyoga*] exists, human engagement occurs for whatever reason, as in the world."

Because of the necessity [of interpretation]. For it is not that there is no injunction (*niyoga*) therein. Now, if it is argued that even a worldly [text] does not have that injunction as its primary purpose, but rather has application (*viniyoga*) as its primary purpose, he says: "In the absence of such a primary purpose—that is, if a worldly text were not primarily concerned with an injunction—the purport (*tātparya*) of a Vedic text, whose meaning is determined by worldly usage, would lack the status of being an injunction, and thus its authority would be unestablished."
Thus it has been said.

Now, one might object: "We do not say that *niyoga* is merely an injunction (*niyukti*), but rather that it is a state of being something to be done (*kartavyatā*). And this [state], which is independent and understood from the Veda as the cause for activity, prompts action. To this he replies: "Surely, activity arises from the comprehension of what is to be done (*kartavyatā*)."
[Page 77] Thus it is said:

he who, though not going [to the place], does not perform what ought to be performed, is like one who, despite possessing the capacity for attaining the beneficial and avoiding the harmful, fails to act; such a person is not restrained by punishments. This, therefore, is a case where the nature of the injunction (*niyoga*) has not been properly considered. Likewise...

Indeed, *niyoga* (the injunction) is merely the act of impelling, and since that is the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, the cognition derived from the word is "I am impelled to this. However, the comprehension of the "to-be-done-ness" (*kartavyatā*) arises because the one who enjoins is authoritative; for when there is an injunction by an authoritative person, one resolves, "This is to be done by me. But in other cases, there is merely an impulsion...

Because it is understood as a mere name. And it has been said: "The injunction (*niyoga*) has the state of being something to be done (*kartavyatā*) as its object; the injunction does not express the state of being something to be done. Furthermore, one who is enjoined understands, "This is my duty to do. However, he who, even while understanding what is to be performed, does not perform it, is like one who does not act despite the presence of the attainment of benefit or the avoidance of harm; he is not subject to punishment.
This is what is intended: optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and the like, whose capacities are inferred from effects characterized by the activity of consciousness, denote the cause of activity.

And since that cause—the cognition of something as "to be done" (*kartavyatā*) within oneself—is already known, they express that "to-be-done-ness. Thus, even after one has understood the "to-be-done-ness" from them, there are those who do not engage in activity.
"By means of punishments, one does not drive others away from the attainment of the beneficial or the avoidance of the harmful. He refutes this:

"This statement has a form of injunction (*niyoga*) that has not been properly examined. For instance, according to worldly usage, an injunction is merely an impulsion (*pravartanā*) characterized as a command and so forth; and that is the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and other such markers, but it is not the cause of activity (*pravṛtti-hetu*), namely, the state of being something to be done (*kartavyatā*)."

Even when that [object] is understood, because there is no understanding of its being something to be done (*kartavyatā*), there is no cognition of an injunction (*niyoga*) in that case through an unenforceable mandate; rather, there is the understanding of its being something to be done. For when that understanding exists, provided no contrary cognition intervenes, there is a necessary rule that activity will inevitably follow. Therefore, [the thought is]: "I am impelled."

The understanding [of the injunction] is the cause for activity arising from the word. However, the understanding of what ought to be done belongs specifically to the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), because he follows the direction of the enjoiner (*niyoktṛ*) through deliberation. Why? Because when there is an injunction that must be followed, there arises the determination: "This is to be done by me. In other cases, however, there is merely the cognition of an impulsion devoid of the determination that something ought to be done.
Right here he states that the teacher’s words, as interpreted by the ancient Prābhākara, are consistent: "And it has been said:

*niyoga* (the mandate) is the duty of the instigator (*niyoktṛ*), consisting of the impulsion (*pravartanā*) whose object is what is to be done (*kartavyatā*). The optative suffix (*liṅ*) denotes that [mandate], not the state of being what-is-to-be-done (*kartavyatva*), which is the duty of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*). It does not state that the object of the impulsion is the object of the mandate. Regarding the relationship between the object and the subject...
Because they are different.
However, the moderns [the Mīmāṃsakas] raise this objection, beginning by stating that "this objection applies to one who has not ascertained the operation of the *niyoga*," and then say:

"For the *niyoga* has as its object the state of being something to be done (*kartavyatā*), but it does not express the state of being something to be done itself. [This refers to] the state of being something to be done regarding the sacrifice.

That injunction (*niyoga*) for which the performance (*anuṣṭhāna*) is the object is "such" (*tathā*). For by that [performance], the injunction is accomplished; however, the injunction does not cause the knowledge of the performance of the sacrifice.
What is meant is this: the injunction itself is directly understood as that which is to be performed from the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth.

But since that which is the object of the sacrifice cannot reach its completion as something to be done without its performance, the understanding of its "to-be-done-ness" (kartavyatā) arises precisely from its being the object of that performance. First of all, this is not verbal; for by the word—

Because it expresses merely the act of commanding (*niyoga*), nor does it have an external object, since such an object is absent in all cases of command. Therefore, the elders do not respect this view either, as it is attractive only when left unexamined. Well then, let there be a commander of beings who is to be followed—one who has directly perceived the means to the welfare taught in the scriptures, who desires the good, and who is omniscient.
It implies [something else]. This very operation of "appropriation" (upādāna), which is another name for "implication" (ākṣepa), is what is postulated as belonging to the mandate (niyoga).

This is tenable only if the mandate exists in the form of an action whose essence is the "unprecedented force" (apūrva). And the non-existence of that [mandate] has been demonstrated with great precision. Let this matter rest for now.

The opponent objects: "In that case, the understanding of the 'to-be-done-ness' (kartavyatā) arises precisely because the mandate (niyoga) has that [the action] as its object; for the object is inseparable from the subject. The author refutes this: "This is not so, at least on account of the word itself. Why? Because the word denotes only the mandate. But was it not said that [the action] is inseparable [from the mandate]?"

Because of this [reason], he says there: "Nor is it the meaning. Why? Because it is absent in all injunctions regarding the cognition of what is to be done (*kartavyatā*). Indeed, it has been stated that even if one who is not subject to authority is enjoined a hundred times, even while understanding the injunction, he will not comprehend it as something to be done. He concludes: "Therefore, this too..."

Even the perception of what is currently being seen as beautiful is not esteemed by the elders. Thus, this is established: the *liṅ* and other such suffixes under dispute do not denote an action (*kārya*) that is previously unknown through other means of knowledge (*mānāntara*), because their conventional relationship (*saṅgati*) [to such an object] has not been grasped;
for whatever has not had its conventional relationship grasped does not denote that thing, just as the word "vājin" does not denote a camel.

"Of what? [The answer is: Because if something were denotative without its relationship having been grasped, there would be no cause for establishing a fixed order; thus, everything would potentially be denotative of everything, resulting in a lack of fixed order.
This state of not having had the relationship grasped is pervaded by the absence of a cause for establishing a fixed order;

therefore, since it is observed that this pervading condition is contradicted by the presence of a fixed order, the property of being denotative must be excluded from that which lacks a grasped relationship, and cannot be non-denotative.

Thus, the establishment of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is that [the Lord] remains as the very cause of this. Now, the opponent objects in another way: "In that case, let there be a directing agent (*niyoktā*) who governs living beings, for by the command of that Blessed One, one attains what is beneficial and avoids what is harmful, just as under the direction of a physician."

"They will proceed and they will cease. Why is this so? He says: "Because he has directly realized the means to the welfare taught in the scriptures (*ānuśravika-śreyas-sādhana*). [Objection: But even one who has directly realized the means to the welfare accessible through scripture might sometimes speak otherwise, or perhaps not speak at all. So how can he be followed? To this he says:

The Blessed One, desiring the welfare of others, has made universal compassion his own purpose; endowed with the excellence of dispassion, he is untouched even in the slightest degree by the afflictions such as passion, nor by the secondary afflictions such as intoxication and pride. Thus, beholding living beings sinking into the vast mire of the suffering of saṃsāra, [he acts for their sake].

"How indeed might I deliver them?"—if one were not pained by their suffering, how could one who knows the reality of the means for attaining the beneficial and avoiding the harmful, and who possesses proficiency in the instruments of action, teach otherwise? One would not so teach.

Or [one might ask]: "But from where does he have such a nature? To this he says: This omniscient one—who has abandoned the obscurations of passion and so forth and possesses knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna)—indeed perceives the universe directly and without exception, as if an amalaka fruit were in the palm of his hand.
Thus, being omniscient, he becomes one who has directly realized the means for attaining the highest good (śreyas), and he becomes one who desires the welfare [of others].
For one who desires to deliver the world from suffering, such an endeavor is impossible without omniscience; therefore, he applies himself toward that state.

Nor is it the case that an omniscient being does not exist. To explain: the conventional designation of his non-existence would have to arise either from the presence of a subverting means of valid cognition (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) or from the absence of a proving means of valid cognition (*sādhaka-pramāṇa*). First of all, there is no presence of a subverting means of valid cognition.
Indeed, perception cannot be its sublater, because it is impossible for the reality of mother-of-pearl to be its object in the same way that it is for superimposed silver;

for there is no possibility of the presentation of anything contradictory to it. Furthermore, since omniscience is entirely beyond the senses, no contradiction with anything perceived through direct perception is ever apprehended. Nor can inference be its sublater.

The subverting [reason] (*bādhaka*) is of two kinds, being either a means for establishing a positive injunction (*vidhi*) or a means for establishing a negation (*niṣedha*). Among these, a means for establishing a positive injunction—whether it be based on an essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*) or an effect (*kāryahetu*)—is not capable of proving a negation as its probandum (*sādhya*). This is because a means for establishing one thing cannot logically result in the establishment of another. However, that which has non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) as its logical mark (*liṅga*) may indeed be a means for establishing a negation. And that...

Other than by proving the non-perception of its own nature (*svabhāvānupalambha*), one might here attempt to prove the non-existence of an omniscient being either by establishing another object contradictory to omniscience, or by negating its cause or its pervader (*vyāpaka*). However, first of all, no contradiction has ever been observed between anything perceived and an omniscient being who is remote by nature (*svabhāvaviprakarṣin*). [Regarding] the contradictory...

Because contradiction is understood through the necessary concomitance with practice, or because when there is the cognition of a contradictory [state], there is no absolute negation of that [other state]. Furthermore, the causal relation established by perception and non-perception cannot be ascertained regarding an omniscient being who is remote in nature. For this very reason, the pervasion (vyāpakatva) of anything [by such a being] is also impossible.

The omniscient being is indeed difficult to ascertain. Nor does the operation of a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the contrary case serve as the basis for apprehending the absence of an omnipresent pervader (*vyāpaka*) of omniscience, as is the case with existence (*sattva*) regarding momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*). This is because such a proof is absent. Or, even if it were present, there can be no negation of that which is absolutely non-existent; for indeed, a sky-flower cannot possibly be the pervaded (*vyāpya*) of anything.
Or [it might be] pervasive. Yet, the cessation of one thing does not entail the cessation of another, because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). As they have said:
"How could the cessation of one thing result from the cessation of something else?"
"Should a mortal not possess horses, or even cattle? Furthermore,

qualities such as being an existent entity or being knowable— which are observed thousands of times as co-occurring with omniscience and are pervaded by it— do not refute the omniscience of this preeminent person under debate by establishing a contradictory property.

Now, [the reason] such as "being a sentient being" (sattva) and so forth is unestablished as being pervaded by [omniscience], because it is not the case that the cognition of pervasion is based merely on observation and non-observation. Otherwise, there would follow the inference: "Caitra is dark-complexioned because he is the son of Maitrī, like the sons of Maitrī who are currently observed to be dark. For in that case, the state of being her son would be in contradiction with the absence of darkness.

If it is argued that this is not an inference because its negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is doubtful due to the nature of existence (*bhāva*), we say no; for the same [objection] applies here as well. Indeed, there is no contradiction whatsoever between existence (*sattva*) and the like on the one hand and omniscience (*sarvavit-tva*) on the other, such that the latter would not [be established].

The negative concomitance (vyatireka) would be doubtful. For the cognition of contradiction is of two kinds: either non-coexistence, as in the case of shadow and sunlight, or mutual exclusion, as in the case of existence and non-existence. It is not the case that there is an absence of omniscience when its causes are complete—just as there is an absence of darkness when there is light—such that they could be non-coexistent. Since... [sahānavasthāna]... [text truncated]
There would be a contradiction with the nature of persistence. And thus it has been stated that, in the case of existence, there can be no absolute non-existence of omniscience.

Nor is the latter [alternative] tenable; for indeed, it is not the case that existence and so forth are abandoned by the presence of omniscience, nor is omniscience abandoned by existence and so forth.
Due to their nature as relata, entities enter the path of cognition like existence and non-existence; yet it has been stated that there is no pervasion of them by omniscience.
This might be the case: the very composition of this treatise would constitute a sublation of the vision of the reality of all things. Thus:
Indeed, instruction is the source of conceptual cognition (*vikalpavijñāna*), and since it has as its object that which is superimposed (*samāropita*), it is false;

thus, the cognition of a Tathāgata cannot be like that. Therefore, this instruction is the effect of a conceptual cognition whose object is superimposed and which is contrary to the cognition of reality regarding all objects to be negated; [it is established] by the perception of a contrary effect (*viruddhakāryopalabdhi*).
[The opponent argues: "The proof for the absence of omniscience in the Buddha and others [is as follows]: either there is no teaching, or the proof of that [omniscience] is futile;

or, if it is accepted that the injunctions for venerating shrines (*caitya-vandana*) and so forth do not issue from him merely due to his presence, then there would be a lack of confidence [in his authority].
This is not so, because conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is not incompatible with knowing all things. For conceptual construction is of two kinds: erroneous..."

It is preceded by error, or it is not so preceded. In this regard, for those like you, it is preceded by error; for the Venerable Omniscient One, it is not so preceded. Indeed, he is neither deluded nor possessed of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); rather, having fully understood the entire expanse of the reality of all things, his mind is governed by compassion, and he desires to instruct those who suffer. For that [instruction] would be impossible without speech.

Because that [conventional usage] is impossible without conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), even one who knows its lack of ultimate reality (*atāttvikatva*) employs it. Just as one who knows the reality of selflessness (*nairātmyatattva*) nevertheless employs conceptualization to negate the superimposed self, saying, "There is no self";
or just as the preeminent grammarian, though knowing words such as *gāvī* and others to be incorrect, uses them for the sake of ordinary people (*pṛthagjana*).

Even when employing [words] with the desire to cause understanding, one does not become a user of ungrammatical forms (*apaśabda*). This form of his is merely adventitious (*āhārya*) and not real; thus, for those who know the truth, there is no contradiction with the [grammatical] instruction. Nor is there any possession of passion (*rāga*) and so forth. For compassion (*kṛpā*) certainly does not fall within the category of passion. [Objection: But surely this is just passion, since it is the desire to remove the suffering of others. [Reply: Not so; for it is not simply desire...

Attachment is not merely [lustful] passion; rather, they call attachment that which is a stain upon the mind, an obscuration to the vision of the Self, and a delighting in unreal qualities. For indeed, in the absence of the perception of an eternal Self, no one would exert themselves while overwhelmed by thirst for their own interests.
Just as Caitra, beholding Maitra who is distinct from himself, [acts out of] thirst for his own happiness...

One who is overwhelmed by craving for one's own welfare does not strive for the happiness of others through friendliness (*maitrī*). Likewise, one who directly perceives consciousness-only (*vijñānamātra*) as the self—which is devoid of preceding and succeeding moments—does not engage in the activity of benefiting others through the performance of actions characterized by qualities opposite to that [self-perception].
Yet, being overwhelmed by craving for one's own welfare, he does indeed engage [in such activity]. Therefore, we understand that he certainly conceives: "I am this."
No; because that [result] is untenable and because it is unknown. For instance:
since there is no effect in the absence of a cause, there is no valid cognition (pramā) when the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is absent.
The external mind has as its object the dependent nature (paratantra), which consists of the eye and so forth as previously described.

Although the cessation of one's own perception does not necessarily entail the non-existence of things that are remote— since even one's own mental moments, though distinct from all other perceptions, are manifold due to their multiplicity— nevertheless, this innate vision of a self is the primary cause of passion and the like,
as expressed in the thoughts: "May I be happy," and "May I not suffer."

For one who is satisfied, the very cognition that "I am" is itself the innate vision of reality (*sahaja-tattvadarśana*). Furthermore, even the compassion of an omniscient being—which takes the form "I shall benefit others"—is not a constituent part of the vision of sentient beings (*sattvadarśana*), because this [compassion] does not result in the attainment of a fruit for oneself; rather, it has been stated that it is simply the desire to eliminate the suffering of others, regardless of one's own interest. Nor is it the case that all minds...

The moments (*kṣaṇa*), though arising through a competitive impulse (*ahamahamikā*)—each thinking "I shall benefit the other"—are merely components of the view of self (*ātmadarśana*). This is because the desire to benefit others can be established even without that [view of self], and because when there is the vision of reality (*tattvadarśana*), instruction is possible; for the benefit of others is desired even without it being directed toward oneself, since the fruit is characterized by its being required [by others].

Because the engagement with existing relationships does not undermine one's status as a discerning person (*prekṣāvat*), and because there is no contradiction between [the existence of] instruction and the knowledge of reality, the statement [of the opponent]—having a doubtful negative concomitance (*sandigdhavyatirekitva*)—is not a sublater of omniscience. Thus, neither is there the presence of a sublatory means of valid cognition (*bādhakapramāṇa*) that could establish the non-existence of [omniscience], nor is there an absence of a proving means of valid cognition (*sādhakapramāṇa*). Likewise...

Indeed, there must be either the absence of perception or the absence of all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, regarding the absence of perception, it must be either the absence for oneself or for everyone; and if it is for oneself, it must be either qualified by visibility or unqualified. First of all, the cessation of one's own perception of the self, when qualified by visibility, cannot establish the non-existence of an omniscient being. This is because its nature is...

Because it is not possible for reality to be remote [from us], because [the absence of perception] is well-known [only in certain cases], because there is deviation in the case of that which lacks qualification, and because the cessation of all perception is unestablished; for indeed, the cessation of all perception does not belong to those of limited vision, as it is unestablished. Furthermore, a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is neither a pervader (*vyāpaka*) nor a cause (*kāraṇa*) of the object of knowledge (*prameya*), such that [the object] would cease upon its cessation.

One would [thereby] desist. Therefore, neither is the non-existence of that established, nor is there even doubt regarding its existence; for its positive existence will be demonstrated by means of its proof. Consequently, it is correct to hold that engagement and desistance arise solely from the injunction of the preeminent person who is to be followed.
He refutes this as follows: No. Why? Because that which is to be enjoined—the omniscient one—is untenable;

and because of ignorance. Having felled the tree of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he purifies [the argument] accordingly: for instance, since there is no fruit in the absence of a cause, when the means of valid cognition exists, there is no [valid] knowledge.
The external mind has as its object the dependent nature (paratantra), which consists of the eye and so forth, as well as their respective objects.

Intending to explain this, he prepares the introductory stage: although the cessation of the perception of the self occurs for those things remote by the three kinds of remoteness—namely, remoteness of time, space, and nature—as is the case with Rāma, Sumeru, and atoms [p.

The cessation [of all means of knowledge] is unestablished. Furthermore, for one who does not perceive everything, the non-existence of an object cannot be established by the cessation of all means of knowledge; for there is no necessary rule that the cessation of the pervader entails the cessation of the pervaded. And this lack of pervasion exists because [the absence of means of knowledge] is not a cause [for the absence of the object], and because there is no necessary concomitance with that alone. Otherwise, it would follow that everyone would be omniscient.

And because there is no distinction [between objects]. Even though speech and the other [faculties] do not cease [their functions] due to the absence of contradiction, nevertheless, since the cessation of the effect is understood through the cessation of its cause, we infer by means of the non-occurrence of the means of knowledge that there is an absence of consciousness regarding all objects, which is the effect of those [faculties]. To explain: perception arising from the eyes and so forth does not pertain to all objects, for they have specific objects.
Because of necessity. For only certain things that are present and related [to the sense organ] are its objects, not all things.

And although the restriction [of perception] by way of form is difficult to define due to the cognition of various kinds of objects of knowledge, it is contradicted by the absence of [perceptions of] intensity, dullness, and so forth. The cessation of all perception is unproven for those like us who do not see everything.

Furthermore, the non-existence of an object is not established by the cessation of all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Why? Because there is no necessary rule that the cessation of the non-pervader (*avyāpaka*) entails the cessation of the non-pervaded (*avyāpya*). Why is it a non-pervader? He says: "It is a non-pervader because it is not a cause, because it is not a causal factor, and because there is no necessary connection (*pratibandha*) with it alone. This refers to the property of being a cause (*hetu-dharma*).

For a property of the subject (*sādhyadharma*) is pervasive (*vyāpaka*) with respect to that which is invariably concomitant with its measure (*mātrānubandha*), just as "treeness" is pervasive of "śiṃśapā-ness. However, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not invariably concomitant with the mere object of cognition (*prameyamātra*). Otherwise, if the means of valid cognition were invariably concomitant with the object of cognition, it would follow that everyone, such as ourselves, would be omniscient. If that were the case, there would be no distinction between us and others.

According to what you accept, omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) consists in possessing the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that is invariably concomitant with the entire range of objects of knowledge (*prameya*). And since this [possession of such means] belongs to people like us as well, it follows that there is no distinction [between us and an omniscient being]. Furthermore, although speech and the like do not preclude [the existence of] a wise person who knows the reality of all things, there is nonetheless no contradiction between speech and the like and [the state of] knowing all things, because [qualities such as] existence (*sattva*) and so forth coexist with speech. Thus...

There is also the cognition of the cessation of the effect through the cessation of the cause; for it is impossible that there be no fire (the bearer of smoke) and yet there be smoke. And since a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the instrument of valid knowledge (*pramā*), we infer the non-existence of the consciousness of all objects—which is its effect—through the impossibility of that means of valid cognition.

He demonstrates precisely the impossibility of [such] means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): namely, perception arising from the eyes and so forth is not possible with respect to all objects. Why? Because those [senses], such as the eyes, have a restriction regarding their objects.
He states the distinction of this restriction: only that which is present and connected is their object; for it is not merely the present that [is perceived].
That would have them as its object; for it would follow that even atoms and the like, which are remote by nature (*svabhāvaviprakṛṣṭa*), would also be its objects.

Therefore, it was said: "only certain composite substances (*avayavidravya*) and so forth. Even so, it would follow that things separated by time and remote in space would also be its objects; therefore, it was said: "connected" (*sambaddha*).

And regarding this restriction, he states that sensory cognition does not have all things as its object: "Nor do all objects possess excellence in terms of place, time, and intrinsic nature. Furthermore, regarding another restriction, he states that any objection is refuted simply by the fact that it is not accepted: "Even though there is a restriction based on form due to the perception of various kinds of objects of knowledge..."

Furthermore, because there is a determination of objects of various locations and dimensions, there is no restriction of connection by way of location, nor is there a restriction by way of dimension. However, it is now examined by way of time: if [the sense organ] functions by reaching [its object], then that which is not present [at the time of cognition]...

Because there is no contact [between the sense organ and the object]. Even if [the sense organ] functions without reaching [its object], it still depends upon the causal capacity (*sāmarthya*) of the object.
Furthermore, regarding the production of cognition, that which has not yet arisen and that which has already ceased are indefinable and lack causal capacity;

thus, [the existence of such an object] is difficult to establish. To explain: first of all, it is not the case that what is visible must possess color-form (*rūpa*), for even number (*saṃkhyā*) and other qualities, though lacking color-form, are nonetheless perceived by the eye.
Nor is it inherent in color (*rūpa*); for even time (*kāla*) and so forth, which are devoid of color and not inherent in color, are visible.

Thus, there is no restriction based on color. Nor is it the intensity (*pāṭava*) of color, sound, and so forth, as designated by the term "manifestation" (*udbhava*), nor the object's existence within bright light, that is the cause for the necessity of sensory perception.

He states that the following argument—that there is non-perception of unmanifest or weak forms, sounds, and so forth located in the eyes and other sense organs, as well as of jars and the like situated in darkness—is not tenable: "Furthermore, a fixed rule regarding perception and non-perception based on distinctions such as intensity and weakness is difficult to establish; for even with the varying degrees of acuity of the sense organs, there is non-perception of what is weak, weaker, and weakest. [This is illustrated by] the cat...

And because there is the perception of objects that are distant and lack light as their medium; nor are proximity of place and largeness the causes for the restriction of the perception of substances—as he says: "Because of the determination of objects of various places and dimensions, there is no restriction based on place.
It is not possible to maintain the restriction that "the eye is in contact with an object at this much distance, and not at that much," for such a rule does not hold.

Because we observe the perception of jars and other objects situated on the earth and so forth as being equal [in size], and because a restriction based on dimension is difficult to establish, given that objects are found to range from subtle, to subtler, to most subtle. The objection that an atom is imperceptible is not tenable; for that very thing which you consider to be a *tryaṇuka* (a triad of atoms), we designate as the *paramāṇu* (the ultimate atom).

Because its parts are not perceived, and because the grounds for postulating it are untenable; and because it is possible for the gross part that is actually seen to be composed of those very same subtle components. Furthermore, since even non-great qualities such as color and so forth are visible to the eye, the possession of the quality of magnitude (*mahiman*) is not the cause thereof. Or, if the inherence in the same object as that [magnitude] were the cause, [the same objection would apply].

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that the triad (tryaṇuka) could not be perceived; for in the absence of that [perceptibility], if both were causes depending upon one another, then both the triad and the quality (guṇa) etc., which possess only a single cause, would be imperceptible. If, however, they were causes independent of one another, then the possibility of a third category would be unavoidable. Or, let it be simply a matter of intrinsic nature (svabhāva).

Since the specific quality of being visible (*cākṣuṣatva*) is the sole cause [of perception], there is no logical justification for a restriction based on dimension (*parimāṇa*). Therefore, because there is no other way to define it, the restriction is defined in terms of time (*kāla*).
For instance: whether the sense organs function by reaching their objects (*prāpyakārīṇi*) or not, in either case, they [perceive] only the present.

He states that [the sense-faculties] have objects as their domain: since it follows that they act by reaching [their objects], an object that is non-existent—which does not abide as a locus for both [the faculty and the cognition]—cannot serve as a locus; therefore, due to the absence of contact, even if an object is not required as a locus to be reached when [the faculties] act without reaching, nevertheless, because the senses do not produce cognition in the absence of an object, there is a dependence upon the causal efficacy (*sāmarthya*) of the object.
Because, regarding the effect that is the arising of cognition, since the unarisen and the ceased are indefinable, the cause lacks efficacy. Furthermore,
even though there are various excellences, the eyes and other sense organs [perceive] only their own respective objects in terms of location, dimension, and number.

Or they might cause one to cognize something more [than what is present], but not that which is beyond the scope [of the senses], unborn, or past. This has been stated because [perception] consists in the apprehension of what is currently existing. To explain: in the case of direct perception, such as the cognition of color and so forth, it is dependent upon the eyes and other [senses];
precisely due to that restriction, a past enemy certainly does not now satisfy the Brahmins with food and drink, nor does he raise up a sacrificial post.

The great sign of the future Cakravartin Śaṅkha is fully accomplished. If it be said that the past and future do not indeed come within the range of the eyes of those with limited vision, yet those whose eyes are brightened by the pure collyrium of yoga will perceive at once the entire extent of the objects existing and yet to exist within the belly of the world; for [the power of yoga] is inconceivable.
The excellence of the capacity of the senses and the excellence of the power of yoga [are as follows].

For just as there is no restriction regarding the eyes and other senses in terms of location, size, or number, so too let there be none in terms of time; to this he says: when it is established that there is a restriction in terms of time, then...

Even for yogins who have attained extraordinary powers through means such as *siddhāñjana* (magical ointment), their eyes and other sense organs would only perceive their own respective objects—exceeding them in terms of location, magnitude, or number—but never that which is not an object, nor that which is unborn or undestroyed. This is what is meant: just as an effect cannot be without a cause, nor can it be merely occasional (*kādācitka*).

This is because it would contradict the definition of a cause; likewise, even that which has an indefinite cause [is not a cause]. Indeed, having an indefinite cause does not differ from having no cause at all. For the nature of a cause consists in the necessity of its existence prior to the effect; and this is untenable if the occasioning factor is indefinite. For never indeed will a barley seed, even if thoroughly prepared, [produce rice].

The reed-pen is conceived as the cause for the sprout; those of coarse vision regard the scorpion and other such things as having various distinct causes. However, those of keen insight, looking with focused attention, perceive even therein some specific difference in genus (*jātibheda*).
Therefore, just as other causes possess capacities restricted to their own respective effects, they produce excellence (*atiśaya*) only in that specific effect.

It is established that [the senses] do not function toward what is not to be done, nor toward the object of another [sense], just as the senses likewise do not function toward their own object when it is not present, nor toward the object of another.
In this very context, he applies a portion of the sūtra: "As it has been said, because [perception] is the apprehension of what is present..."
[Diti: "But surely, while the external sense-faculties may not function, the mind (*manas*) will still function. To this he says:

even mental perception does not apprehend everything, because the mind is not independent with respect to external objects. For the mind must operate only where it is already present, since it follows its own internal cognitions; and [it operates] in the case of internal objects such as pleasure and so forth.

That [cognition] is independent; that refers to the objects such as pleasure and so forth. Nor is it correct to say that pleasure and so forth are self-evident through the perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*), because they are distinct from consciousness (*vijñāna*). If it is argued that their reality consists in having a non-different cause from consciousness, we say no, because the state of being produced from a non-different cause is unproven. For there is indeed contact between the sense organ and the object.

Sandalwood is the cause of the consciousness [of pleasure], whereas that consciousness is the cause of pleasure; for even in its absence, one observes the arising of pleasure from consciousness alone in dreams. Furthermore, pleasure does not arise during the winter even when sandalwood paste is applied. This is the general direction of the argument. Therefore, mental pleasure and so forth cannot have an external object as their domain, because in that case... [the pleasure would not arise].
Because the mind is dependent upon the sense faculties and so forth, and because the sense faculties and so forth are not within its own range, it is necessarily so;

otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the non-existence of those who are blind and so forth. Thus, mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*) also exists, such as internal pleasure and the like.

[The mind] has an object [as its domain]. Because the external mind lacks independence; for it has been stated that if it were independent, there would follow the absurd consequence of the non-existence of the blind, the deaf, and so forth. If it is argued that there is no such non-existence of the blind and others because [the mind] requires the cooperation of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for its arising, [we reply that] in every respect, dependence is not removed, since it still has that [external object] as its domain. Otherwise, if it were assisted by other sense-faculties...
Even regarding the activity of the mind, that very absence of blindness and so forth [is required]. Nor is it the case that [the mind] has only objects of a similar class as its immediate antecedent;

why then is the external mind not independent? To this he says: because if the mind were independent with respect to color-form and so forth, it would follow that there would be no blind or deaf people. For indeed, the blind and others are not devoid of mind, since they possess memory and so on.

Because it would follow that [the mind] exists as a [permanent] entity. Furthermore, if the mind were to perceive forms and so forth independently of the eyes and other [senses], it would follow that no one would be blind or deaf. He clarifies this very point: "For instance, in the direct perception of forms and so forth, that mind is dependent upon the eyes and other [senses]; it is restricted precisely by that [dependence]. Otherwise, in the absence of such restriction, there would be an absence of blindness and so forth."

Regarding the phrase "as a consequence": he raises an objection that was previously stated—if there is no absence of blindness and so forth because [the mind] depends on the cooperation of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for its arising.
This is the meaning: it is certainly not the case that what is called "mind" (*manas*) is some other sense organ (*indriya*) like the eye and so forth.

We agree; however, we maintain that the preceding cognition alone is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the final cognition. For that very [preceding] cognition, by virtue of being a consciousness and because it is immediately contiguous (*avyavahita*), is called the "immediately preceding condition" (*samanantarapratyaya*).

In that regard, [the final cognition arises] through the cooperation of the immediately preceding condition consisting of the sensory cognition and the material cause consisting of the momentary object belonging to that same sense-faculty.

The cognition that arises immediately after the perception of a form, at the same time as the sensory consciousness produced by it, which has as its object the momentary instant that produced itself, and which is clear and vivid for one whose sensory activity has ceased—that is mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*).
