It is not born of the senses, because it exists even when their activity has ceased. Nor does it have an internal object, because it is produced from the momentary instant that is the object of the sensory consciousness.

Because it has as its object a different moment; nor is there an absence of the blind, the deaf, and so forth, for they lack the appropriation [of consciousness] due to the absence of cognition arising from sense faculties, which results from their being devoid of such faculties; nor is it non-perceptual, because it possesses a vivid appearance.

He refutes [the objection]: in no way does the dependence upon another sense organ cease for mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*) in its own production. Why? Because that which is to be grasped is the immediately succeeding moment of the object of the sensory cognition;

this is because it has as its object the object produced by the sense organ [which itself had as its object] the object produced by that [same] sense organ. Otherwise, it would not have as its object the object produced by the sense organ [which itself had as its object] the object produced by that [same] sense organ.

In the case of perception, when a visual consciousness arises from its object as a cooperative factor for a mental consciousness produced by another sense organ, that very same absence of blindness and so forth would necessarily follow. A cooperative factor is so called because it produces its own effect (svopādeya) together with the material cause (upādāna). If it were argued that [the cooperative factor] operates only upon an object of the same class...

"The immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) does not have an object of a different kind; therefore, this undesirable consequence does not arise. To this, he replies: "The immediately preceding condition does not have only an object of the same kind. Why? Because there is a transition to another class [of phenomena].

It is not a property of the sense-faculties (*indriya*), because there is no transition between different classes of beings (*jātyantara-saṃcāra*). Indeed, it is not a property of cognition (*jñāna*), because [cognition] does involve transition between different classes. It is not a property of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because it depends on forms and so forth that have not been conceptualized (*avitarkita*). Nor is it a property of the mental faculty (*mānasa*), because it is not observed in the case of pleasure and the like. Furthermore, let there be dependence on auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*) due to the restriction of objects.

Or rather, dependence [on another] is appropriate for memory because it is observed to be so; furthermore, regarding that which is grasped by a single sense-organ, there would be the undesirable consequence of perceiving other forms of the same genus. If one were to depend on a sub-genus, there would follow the occurrence of distinct streams [of consciousness], since there is no difference in genus between those occurring in that stream and those not in that stream. Therefore, within a single stream, at a given moment, [the preceding cognition possesses] the status of an immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

Because it would follow that [consciousness] exists as a substantial entity (*bhāva*). First of all, consciousness cannot exist without a material cause (*upādāna*); nor can it have an indefinite material cause.

This has already been stated: that having an indefinite cause is not distinct from being causeless. Therefore, in this case, since the existence and non-existence of the subsequent cognition follow the existence and non-existence of the preceding cognition, that very [preceding cognition] is the material cause.

This is correct. Consequently, the cognition of cold touch that arises immediately after the cognition of white must be accepted as having the cognition of white as its material cause (*upādāna*). Otherwise, there would be no transition from a continuum belonging to the class of "white-cognition" to a different class, namely "cold-cognition. This is the meaning.

He analyzes this as follows: This is certainly not a property of mere cognition (*jñāna-mātra*). Why? Because there is a transition to another genus (*jāty-antara-saṃcārāt*). It is not a property of the internal self (*pratyag-dharma*). Why? Because it depends upon an object whose form is free from conceptual construction (*avikalpita-rūpa-artha-apekṣaṇāt*).

For when there is the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of an object whose form is free from conceptual construction, and when a prior cognition regarding that object is possible, [it occurs] upon the recollection of words and so forth.
Or rather, the meaning is that there would be mere mental observation (*ālocana-mātra*). It is not a property of mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*). Why?
Because in the case of pleasure and so forth, no prior cognition of its object is observed.
Thus, in the manner already stated, even if it has a different moment as its object through dependence on a specific auxiliary cause (*sahakāri-viśeṣa*), [it remains mental perception].
Having established the dependence of the mind, he now determines that this dependence arises specifically through the objects of the senses by means of critical reflection:

"Furthermore, let there be dependence due to the restriction of objects, or perhaps it depends on auxiliary objects. Having thus reflected, he determines his own position: "Dependence is logical; for whatever is the object of a particular sense-organ [is dependent upon it]."

The meaning is that it is logical that the mind functions there (in the object) in dependence upon that sense faculty. Why? Because it is observed to be so in the case of recollection. Furthermore, one who asserts that the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*)—which has an object of a similar class—is the cause of mental perception, cannot claim that "similarity of class" is based on being apprehended by the same single sense faculty, for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

He says this: if it is admitted that [the universal] is perceivable by a single sense-organ, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of perceiving other colors as well; even the visual perception of yellow would produce a mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*) of blue, even when [the eye] is not in contact with it, because the fitness for being grasped by that sense-organ is indistinguishable in both cases. This is the meaning. However, if a subordinate genus (*avāntara-jāti*) were to be postulated...

And since this [object] is not a different kind of form (*rūpāntara*), there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in that regard; to this he replies: "For if one were to depend upon an intermediate genus (*avāntarajāti*), there would follow the cognition of distinct continua (*santāna*). A mental perception (*mānasa*) directed toward the specific characteristic of a single blue lotus existing within a single continuum of blue lotuses would also produce a clear [cognition] regarding the specific characteristic of a blue lotus existing in another continuum that is not in contact with the sense organ."
Why? Because there is no difference in their genus (*jāti*) due to the occurrence of those two—the blue color and the lotus—within a single continuum. He concludes:

Therefore, in the sensory cognition produced by the sense organ which has as its object a moment existing within a single continuum of a blue lotus, that sense organ serves as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

By saying this, one has effectively stated that [the mental consciousness] grasps the same objects as the eye and other [senses]. This is because, since there is no appearance of a distinction between moments and there is an appearance of non-difference, the [opponent's] denial of momentariness is rejected.
Thus, even if one does not wish it, by asserting that the mental [consciousness] arises from the object of the sensory cognition, it must grasp the objects of the eye and so forth.
It is stated that it is precisely the grasping [of the object] that is meant. And thus, its dependence on the sense-faculties (*indriya-pāratantrya*) is established.

Nor does this much alone imply that it will be the object of the eye and so forth, rather than the grasping of the object of the eye and so forth; therefore, he says: "Because of the manifestation of the distinction between moments. This is what is intended: regarding momentariness...
For if [the existence of] things were already established, that [non-existence] might indeed belong to them; however, this is not the case. To explain:

its proof would have to be either perception (*pratyakṣa*) or inference (*anumāna*), because there is no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This is because any existing means of valid cognition must be included within these two, and it is established that if it were not so included, its status as a valid means of knowledge would be untenable. Among these, it cannot first of all be perception.

The worldly [cognition] takes as its object the momentariness of things such as blue lotuses and so forth. But is it not the case that there is no real entity called "momentariness" distinct from the blue? For [a separate entity] would exist in that way only if there were a difference in causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), as in the case of white and other colors. However, there is no causal efficiency belonging to momentariness that is distinct from the causal efficiency accomplished by the blue, which constitutes its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).

It would have to exist as distinct [from blue]. If momentariness is indeed different from blue in reality by virtue of the same causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) that establishes blue—just as yellow and other colors are—it follows that it must be distinct.

If it is not distinct, then surely momentariness is grasped by the very perception that grasps blue, because of its non-difference from it. That is untenable, because it does not ascend to [the level of] experience; for experience is certainly not a matter of mere interpretation.

It is fit [to say] "it is blue," but not "it is momentary. Since stability (*sthemna*) is non-different from that [object], if it were within the scope of that [perception], it would follow that it too is of the same nature as that [momentary object]. However, if the difference of the momentary [from the stable] is established through another means of knowledge (*mānāntara*), then to claim that it is established by perception (*pratyakṣa*) is mere prattle; for perception does not produce a determinate cognition (*avasāya*) regarding that [momentary nature]. [Determinate] cognition—
For it is not accepted that perception, whose operation is not subsequently integrated, possesses validity with respect to its object of engagement.
This might be argued: the state of existing for only a single moment belongs to blue and other objects precisely as they are mounted upon experience.
For instance, perceptual cognition, being itself momentary, determines [its object] as delimited by its own very time. For example:

The perception of the form blue, while delimiting the blue, excludes its absence; and by excluding that absence, it also excludes yellow and other colors which are non-deviant from that absence. Likewise, while delimiting the blue as qualified by the time of its setting, it excludes the absence of its own temporal existence; and by excluding that absence, [it excludes] those things inseparable from that absence.

This [perception] excludes its existence at times prior to and subsequent to that [moment]. If that were not excluded, then yellow and other [colors] would likewise not be excluded; and in that case, those seeking the causal efficiency to be accomplished by blue would not act with necessity toward any specific object. Thus, the momentariness of entities is established by the very experience of them.

That is untenable, because perception has only the blue object as its domain. Indeed, it does not even take itself as its domain; its capacity to take itself as its object is even more remote. Even if self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) were admitted, that would merely mean the manifestation of the self as non-self; it would not, however, connect the self with itself or by itself to the blue, nor the self with the blue by means of itself.

Because mere observation (*ālocana*) does not have the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) as its object; even if that observation is uninterrupted at that time, it is not established that blue and other such objects exist for only a single moment. Observation...

Since even that [cognition] lasts for two or three moments, its existence for only a single moment is unproven; nor is it contradictory for a single entity to have a successive connection with multiple things, as will be demonstrated later. Thus, it is established that because the distinction between moments does not appear in perception, mental cognition does not have as its object that which is produced by the sense-faculties, but rather [the object of] the sense-faculty itself.
"It is simply the grasping of the object.
Now, one might ask: "Granted that the difference between moments does not appear, but from what [source] does their non-difference arise? To this he says:
"Because of the appearance of non-difference. This very venerable recognition—that "this is that same crystal"—will establish it.

[Regarding] the crystal: indeed, this [consciousness] cannot take as its object the stability of the crystal, characterized by its persistence through preceding and succeeding moments. For certainly, this is not a single cognition, due to the difference in causes, the difference in objects, and the contradiction in their intrinsic natures. To explain: "that" implies mediacy (*pārokṣya*), whereas "this" is direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*). It is not [one].

It is not possible even for Śakra to bring about the unification of these two, which are opposed in nature like fire and snow, for that would entail the absurd consequence of the three worlds becoming one. Furthermore, although there is no difference in their designation as "crystal," their respective objects are distinct due to the association with contradictory properties arising from differences in place and time. Nor is the prior... [saṃskāraḥ pūrvā]... [text fragment]

Since it has its origin in experience, [the cognition] is restricted to that which is its object; therefore, it is capable of making known its existence at the present time, even though that existence has not been previously experienced. Furthermore, the sense organs, which have only proximate objects as their domain, do not perceive the existence of that which was their object in the past, for that existence is not proximate. Nor is it possible for there to be non-difference in the effect despite a difference in the cause.

Because the difference or non-difference of those [two] depends upon the difference or non-difference of their causes; otherwise, it would follow that they are accidental. Furthermore, memory and perception, which operate solely within their own respective domains, do not conjoin the objects of one another.
Nor is there possible any other single cognition distinct from these two that is capable of effecting the conjunction of both objects.

This has already been stated in due order. Furthermore, this [recognition] lacks validity because, being conceptual in nature, it manifests as a non-entity and is no different from memory. Therefore, the claim that "recognition establishes the existence of things" is a mere wishful thinking.

To this it is replied: This single cognition is designated as "recognition. Now, was it not argued that this is not so because of a contradiction in its own nature? In that case, do you maintain that inferential cognition (*anumāna-vijñāna*) is also not a single unity?
For that too consists of both perception and non-perception, conceptualization and non-conceptualization, and superimposition and non-superimposition.

If it is argued that there is no contradiction regarding perception and so forth, because the nature of the object—which is established as non-different through one's own experience—is perceived in relation to the difference of those [external] objects of apprehension; we say no, for here too the case is the same. For this cognition does not take as its object a single crystal colored by both "thatness" and "thisness," such that it would perceive them as non-different.

It is either being experienced or has been experienced. Furthermore, even though an object is a single entity, its status as perceptible (*pratyakṣatā*) or non-perceptible (*parokṣatā*) will not be contradictory, depending on the distinction between the coloring factors (*anurañjaka*) such as "that-ness" (*tattā*) and "this-ness" (*idantā*). Moreover, the unity of consciousness is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because they occur simultaneously.

Because [the two are] distinct: it is not contradictory for a single entity to have a connection with a previous place and time—expressed as "that"—and a connection with a proximate place and time—expressed as "this. Therefore, it is logical that when the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of a ruby is determined, its absence is excluded;
for if that [absence] were not excluded, its own nature would not be determined, and thus its exclusion of its own non-existence [could not occur].

Because the nature of being a ruby (*padmarāga*) is its very essence; for as long as that [nature] is not excluded, it is impossible to delimit it. But why are other things, such as topazes (*puṣparāga*), excluded? If you say it is because they are invariably concomitant with the absence of that [ruby-nature], then from what does that [invariable concomitance] arise? It cannot be through perception, since at no time is there ever perceived an identity (*tādātmya*) between a topaz and a ruby.

If it is argued that [the relation] is due to the apprehension of power (*balambhāt*), then in a case where there is an apprehension of identity (*tādātmya*) with an existent thing, there is no necessary concomitance (*avinābhāva*) with its absence.

And there exists a direct perception—a cognition appearing as if immediate—that manifests a single essence of ruby (*padmarāga*) persisting through differences of place and time, such as "this is that very same ruby. Therefore, let there be [a relation] between that [essence] and space and time.

Or rather, it is the two relations themselves that are mutually non-identical with the ruby, but not the ruby as delimited by them. This is because the ruby is distinct from those two relations and from their conjunction. If it is asked: "If it is distinct from them, how can the relations belong to it?"—the answer is: "Simply by its own nature. This will be demonstrated more thoroughly in the *Saṃsargaparīkṣā*. Therefore, that [is]...

The identity between the ruby residing in the tooth and the experience illuminating it is established either through direct experience or through inference, arising from the non-difference of the result characterized by that illumination. Furthermore, when a clearer effect is established, a cause—even if not perceived—must be postulated; one should not, however, refrain from such a postulation out of fear of imagining something unperceived.
It is improper to deny the clarity of the effect, for that would entail the denial of the cognitions of form and so forth as well.

Therefore, in this case, although the sense organ alone is incapable, and although mere latent impression (*saṃskāra*) alone is [insufficient], the sense organ accompanied by the latent impression will produce the recognition; for the presence or absence of recognition conforms to the presence or absence of the latent impression.

For it is not the case that because a seed does not produce a sprout [at one time], it will likewise fail to produce one even when accompanied by soil and other factors. Therefore, let it be that a stable entity produces its effect once it has acquired an excellence (*atiśaya*) through the conjunction of auxiliary conditions (*sahakāri-pratyaya*); or let it be that there is a gradual approach (*upasarpaṇa*) due to the non-difference [of the entity] having attained such a state through a succession of conditions—in either case, [the objection remains].

Furthermore, it is possible for the eyes and other sense organs—when accompanied by mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), or when co-arising with the distinctions of the latent impressions of experience—to possess the capacity to produce recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*). If recognition were produced solely from the latent impressions of experience, the cognition "this" would be untenable; if it were produced solely by the sense organs, the cognition "that" would be impossible; and if it were produced without an object, there would be a difference in its manifestation depending on whether the object is present or absent.

[This is] because it is untenable [otherwise]. Nor is it the case that the sense organs are connected with past time; for even in the absence of such a direct connection, the manifestation of pastness is possible through the medium of the latent impression (saṃskāra) of a successive connection with them. And it is not correct to say that pastness is therefore not perceptible, because it is an object of cognition produced by the senses, being invariably concomitant with that [cognition].
And because perceptibility depends upon a connection with the sense organs, if it were instead dependent solely on that [connection],
then even those things such as odors and so forth— which are not objects of the consciousness produced by that [connection]— as well as the supreme self, the mind, and so on, would be imperceptible.

This is an undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*). Therefore, there is no absence of a cause, nor is there a difference in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) from which the difference in the effect would arise;

for when that [effect] is to be produced, the impressions (*saṃskāra*), the sense organs (*indriya*), and so forth, which invariably precede it, constitute a single causal complex in one instance. Thus it is established that the perception of non-difference, consisting of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), is one [entity] existing across multiple places and times.

It makes the ruby and other such objects appear as connected with various states. And this [cognition] is not based on memory, because it has the authority to follow the sequence of preceding and succeeding places, times, and states. Nor is its lack of validity due to its conceptual nature, because there is no contradiction between the validity of a manifestation that is capable of being associated with verbal expression and its having a superimposed object when [the object] is absent.

Because there is no sublation [of the cognition]. Nor is it merely a mental synthesis, such as when sacrificers who are distinct from one another employ the mere designation, "We have become one here in this sacrificial session (*satra*)," which occurs due to some limiting condition (*upādhi*) and does not constitute an actual apprehension of oneness.
In this case, however, even though there is a difference in the association of place, time, and state, they perceive the single essence of the ruby as having non-distinct place and time.
This is just as worldly investigators [understand it]. Thus, it is established that [the object] exists because of its appearance as non-different.
Now, one might argue: "Granted that there is an appearance of non-difference, this does not, however, entail the non-momentariness of entities and so forth;
for, since there is a subverting argument (*bādhaka*), [this appearance] has as its object a superimposition (*samāropita*). Indeed, there is a subverting argument: "Whatever exists is momentary."

Just like a jar or similar objects; and sound and so forth, which are the subject of dispute, are existent—this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*), because the object to be proven (*sādhya*) is necessarily concomitant with mere existence. But how is the necessary concomitance of momentariness—with its characteristic of abiding for only a duration of time devoid of prior and posterior parts—established here with mere existence? It is as follows:

For instance: existence (*sattā*), which is defined as the opposite of being devoid of all designations (*upākhyā*), does not exceed the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritā*). Indeed, there is no possibility of an entity that is incapable of any causal efficiency whatsoever.
To explain: is it the object of an omniscient cognition that is invariably connected with its own essential nature (*svarūpa*)? Or is it not an object [of such cognition]? If it is not an object...
That which is called "form" (rūpa) is not a real entity (bhāva), because the nature of a thing, which is pervaded by being the object of that [cognition], ceases when that [cognition] ceases.

Or, if it is indeed its object, how can it be without an objective support (anālambana)? If it has an objective support, how can it be without a causal cognition (apratyaya)? If it is a causal cognition, why is it not employed in purposeful action (arthakriyā)? For the very existence (sattā) of entities consists in their capacity for such purposeful action.
And that [existence] is pervaded by either succession or simultaneity, because there is an absence of a third possibility. To explain:
with respect to their various causal functions, existence and non-existence manifest as mutually exclusive alternatives; and thus, any other mode besides succession...

If something distinct from such sequential and non-sequential [perceptions]— which have been experienced and determined as being of these very natures— were admitted, then there would follow the consequence of a mutual confusion between those very sequential and non-sequential [phenomena] that are currently perceived;
thus, the perceived sequence would consist of non-sequence, and the non-sequence would consist of sequence, and it would be exactly so in accordance with [the nature of] experience.

Otherwise, the faults of existence and activity would follow. Thus, by excluding succession and non-succession—which are mutually exclusive—perception itself is rejected; nor does it tolerate any other mode that is a mixture of such succession and non-succession.

[The non-perception] of one [thing] is sufficient; and even that non-perception, though lacking the qualification of being "visible," is capable of establishing the linguistic usage of its absence because it consists in the negation of identity with what is being perceived. For the status of non-existence is established through mere non-perception without distinction for invisible things such as *piśācas* or monkeys, by virtue of their identity with the visible pillar.

However, in another mode that is distinct from both such succession and simultaneity, neither succession nor simultaneity is possible. If it is argued: "Let them not exist; let there be some other mode, distinct from what is designated as succession and non-succession (simultaneity), by resorting to which it will be employed in causal operations," we reply: does this [other mode] possess causal efficiency like those other modes?

Is it like a *piśāca* (a ghost)? If that were so, what harm would there be to us? However, those perceived causal efficacies (*arthakriyā*), whose bodies are embraced by two modes—namely, the mutually exclusive forms of succession and simultaneity as determined through experience—are not capable of arising from any other mode. Nor is even that [other mode] possible. To explain: in whatever case a particular mode is excluded...

Where there is a determination of one alternative through the exclusion of another, there the possibility of other alternatives exists. For example, the determination of the alternative "non-blue" occurs through the exclusion of the alternative "blue," as in the case of yellow. And likewise, there is a determination of one of the two alternatives—succession or simultaneity—through the exclusion of the other, which implies the existence of the alternative being excluded.

"When an object is made the focus of cognition, causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) exists everywhere; this is the perception of the contradictory (*viruddhopalabdhi*). For when two mutually exclusive possibilities are negated, one must be established;
since no other mode is possible, the causal efficiency of entities is pervaded by succession and simultaneity, and these two..."

Turning away from stability, these two [non-existence and non-momentariness] also exclude causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), just as the property of being a *śiṃśapā* excludes it from a single stone-made mountain.
To explain: causal efficiency cannot occur sequentially, for entities exist by their very own nature...

Since things are observed to be employed for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), whatever follows the presence and absence of an effect in its own presence and absence is capable of producing that effect; and since their form (*rūpa*) follows the presence and absence of the effect, that [form] alone is capable. And since that [form] exists in the first moment just as it does in the second and subsequent moments, [the entity is momentary].

If [the cause] were to produce the entire collection of effects generated in the second and subsequent moments during the very first moment, then because it would be capable [of doing so], there could be no delay;
thus, a non-momentary entity cannot possess successive operations.
One might argue: "Even though it is incapable [by itself], it acts successively due to the proximity of successive auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*)."

That is untenable, because it cannot withstand critical analysis (*vikalpā'sahatvāt*). Do these auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) provide some assistance (*upakāra*) to this [entity], or not? Even if they do provide it, is that assistance distinct from the entity or non-distinct? In that regard, if a distinct assistance is provided, then even though the nature of the entity exists and its production has not yet been obtained, since it is not perceived while this [assistance] exists, the assistance must belong only to that which is subject to origination (*utpattimat*).

Because the effect has already been produced, the entity that produces it would not be its cause. Nor is it tenable to say that the effect is generated by an auxiliary that provides assistance; for if that assistance were to generate another assistance, it would lead to an infinite regress. Precisely for this reason, [p.

It has been stated that because an effect is produced, there follows the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that the entity does not perform that action [itself]. If an imparted benefit were non-different [from the entity], then the entity itself would be what is being designated; yet, since that [entity] was already established prior [to the benefit], it could not be something to which a benefit is imparted. Alternatively, if the co-operating causes (sahakārin) do not provide a benefit, they would not be required by the entity, and thus the seed would produce the sprout at the very moment of its own arising.

Because for that which is independent, delay is impossible; or, if there were delay, it would not produce the effect even later. If one should think: "Even though they do not provide any assistance, they are auxiliary causes (sahakārin), because the entity produces the effect only when in association with them; and yet they are not disregarded, since the effect does not arise without them"—that is not so. For if [the entity] is a producer of the effect by its own nature...

Why does an entity (*bhāva*) not produce [its effect] immediately after those [causes]? Because its form (*rūpa*) exists even prior to them. Furthermore, if it produces [the effect] by means of a form that acts simultaneously [with the causes], then those [causes] alone would be the producers, not the entity. Or, if one thing were to produce another by means of a different form, it would follow that even a sky-lotus (*gagananalinam*)—by virtue of its existence—would fall within the scope of the conventional usage of "existent" (*sadvyavahāra*). Nor is both [possible].

It is correct to say that the presence or absence of causal efficiency follows from the presence or absence of an entity, because there is deviation [of causal efficiency] from each one taken individually; therefore, its birth is dependent upon both. For when the final cause exists—that is, when it has arisen—there is a rule of necessity regarding the arising of the effect, and thus there is no deviation. Nor [is this contradicted] by [the case of] its own cause... (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the logical argument concerning the relationship between the existence of a cause and the occurrence of an effect.)

It is not tenable to say that an entity has acquired a nature of producing its effect due to a delay consisting of several moments of time, and thus acts slowly by virtue of its very nature; for this cannot withstand logical analysis. Does its nature of acting slowly cease upon this brief delay, or does it not? If it ceases, how can that same entity [be said to have acted slowly]?
Is it ceased? Because its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) has ceased. Or, if it were not ceased, how could this be its intrinsic nature?

[It would not be], because of the association with contradictory properties (*viruddhadharma*), namely the forms of cessation and non-cessation. Alternatively, if it did not have that as its intrinsic nature, it would not linger;
consequently, it would follow that it has accomplished its purpose immediately after arising. If there were no cessation, then even after the lapse of some portion of time, [it would still persist].

It would produce the effect; for the nature [of the entity] characterized by delayed action remains in that same state. Thus, according to the sequence already stated, it is not possible for an entity to perform causal efficiency sequentially. Nor is it logically consistent for it to do so simultaneously.
Therefore, whatever effect is produced in the first moment by that non-momentary [entity] through its own self-nature—

One should accomplish all [effects] at the second and subsequent moments; for the self, which is capable of accomplishing those effects, is present during the second and subsequent moments. And thus, since it is impossible to accomplish what has already been accomplished, if there were a difference [between the selves], then that which is to be accomplished in the second and subsequent moments could not simultaneously perform its entire range of causal functions.

This is logical for that which is momentary. Thus, by this line of reasoning, it is established that for that which is non-momentary, causal efficiency cannot be conceived through either successive or simultaneous action. Since the pervader (causal efficiency) is absent in the counter-example of non-momentariness, existence—which is excluded from that [non-momentariness]—is pervaded by momentariness; thus, the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is proven.

It might be argued as follows: Is even a momentary entity (bhāva) by its very nature capable of producing causal efficiency (arthakriyā), or not? If it is not, then it is simply non-existent. If, however, it is by nature a producer, then what use has it for auxiliary causes (sahakārin)? Consequently, the seed should produce the sprout at the very moment of its arising. [Objection: But surely, once arisen, the momentary seed is capable and must indeed produce the sprout; why is this not so?

If its production from the preceding seed-moment occurs again, then, since all moments falling within that continuum are indistinguishable in their nature as seeds, they would all possess the capacity to produce a sprout; thus, a seed would produce a sprout immediately upon being born.

Not so. A subsequent moment of the seed—produced from a series of successive moments of earth, seed, wind, and so forth, which possess specific enhancements (atiśaya) arising from the conjunction of each preceding moment—is capable [of producing the sprout]. This efficient moment of the seed, coexisting with efficient moments of earth and the rest, produces the sprout independently. Nor is there any dependence on the coexisting earth and other factors for this [seed-moment], even though it exists simultaneously with them.
Without them, the production of the effect does not occur, because that which is produced by a single causal complex [the seed] is absent when they are absent.

Nor are the earth and other factors non-cooperative, since the sprout is generated precisely together with them. This is because there is no difference in their status, as they too possess the necessary regularity of occurring prior to the effect, and causality consists in nothing more than that.

Nor do they, even when independent of one another, initiate a different effect from each other, because only that [specific effect] is perceived from them, as their causal capacity is restricted to that alone. Nor is there non-action on the part of the others due to one having already performed its function, for it is impossible for something to be "done" in a joint action. Furthermore, those things which have attained mutual proximity through the power of their own causes are not conscious deliberators.
They might argue that this [effect] can be produced by even one among us, and thus, having been accomplished through mere proximity, they are able to withdraw.

However, it is not a difference in auxiliary causes (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*) that is the cause of a difference in the effect, but rather a difference in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*). For when that [difference in the complex] exists, a difference in the effect is observed. Since the causal complex here is non-different, a difference in the effect is impossible.

Furthermore, the mutual conjunction of earth and the other elements arises from conditions of approach; thus, because there is no contradiction with causal efficiency for that which is momentary, the reason is not "uncommon" (asādhāraṇa). Nor is the statement of the reason a non-essential member of the proof, since the probandum is established simply by the demonstration of pervasion (vyāpti) through examples such as sound, which are observed in the locus of the probandum (sādhyadharmin). Indeed, it is not the case that [the pervasion must be] universal...

The pervasion [of the reason] must be one that involves a reductive withdrawal (*saṃhāravatī*) and has as its object only that which is perceptible. For an opponent might suspect: "Since you have not excluded the existence of perceptible things on the grounds of their non-momentariness, existence (*sattva*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) and cannot prove momentariness. Therefore, whatever exists—whether perceptible or imperceptible—all that is momentary.

The pervasion (*vyāpti*) is indeed observable. [Objection: Even so, since the momentariness of sound and other such subjects under dispute is established by the very force of observation, the statement of the reason remains as useless as before in being a non-constituent of the proof. [Reply: Not so.
For even in the case of things like a rabbit’s horn which do not exist, it is observed that whatever is existent—whether perceptible or imperceptible—is all momentary. Just as...

The pervasion (*vyāpti*) that includes all cases is thus established. Yet, things such as the horns of a hare are not momentary. Therefore, even if the pervasion is established despite the absence of sound and other such subjects under dispute, momentariness is not thereby proven; consequently, existence (*sattva*) must necessarily be shown as the means for proving their momentariness.

The statement of the reason (*hetu*) is not a non-member of the proof (*asādhanāṅga*). Furthermore, do entities that are produced arise from their own causes as perishable or as imperishable? If they are perishable, they would cease immediately after their arising; thus, momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) is established. If, on the other hand, they are imperishable, they would never [perish].

They would perish. Indeed, that which is indestructible cannot possibly perish. Blue produced from its own cause never becomes yellow. Nor is it tenable to claim that their destruction has an origination dependent on another cause, because this cannot withstand logical analysis. For that destruction, if produced by another cause, must be either different from or non-different from the entity itself.

Or rather: it cannot be non-different [from the entity], because of the difference in its causes. But if it were different, then since the entity remains in its original state (*tādavasthya*), there would follow the consequence that it would be perceived as before. If it is argued that "therefore the entity is concealed," we say no; for concealment...

If there were a difference [between the non-existent and its cause], the existence [of the non-existent] would remain as it was; if there were no difference, the distinction of causes would be untenable. Therefore, since action is impossible for even a non-existent—which lacks all form and is merely conceptual—the expression "one makes a non-existent" is untenable, because a connection between the act of making and a non-existent devoid of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva) is impossible. This is due to the negative particle (nañ).
A concomitant relation does not produce an entity; and that which does not produce it is a non-agent, and as such lacks causality—therefore, there are no causes for destruction.
However, some [maintain] that this entity, possessing the property of existing for only a single moment, has arisen from its own cause.

In the second moment, it does not exist by itself; furthermore, it does not depend on a cause for this. Indeed, when blue arises established in its own nature from its own causes, it does not depend on a cause for its state as yellow or other colors, nor is it subject to such inquiry. Moreover, the destruction of produced entities is perceived as being inevitable; therefore, by that as well—
Momentariness can be inferred as follows:
for whatever is certain to occur, there is no dependence upon other causes, just as in the case of the metallic nature of forms and so forth.

Since the destruction of produced entities is certain to occur, the perception of a property pervaded by its opposite (viruddhavyāptopalabdhi) establishes that destruction does not depend on other causes.

It refutes [the opponent's position]. For "inevitability" (dhruvabhāvitva), by its pervasion with the absence of dependence on another cause—which is the opposite of the dependence on another cause being negated—establishes independence from other causes. And that [independence] excludes its own opposite, namely dependence on other causes. For example: whatever depends on other causes is not inevitable.

Likewise, it is with the dye and so forth in the cloth. Just as if entities were to require another cause for their destruction apart from their own causes, then—since there would be no means of proof for a rule regarding the presence of that [other cause]—not even a single produced thing would ever perish. Therefore, this destruction of momentary entities is necessarily inherent in them by virtue of their own causes.

This indicates the arising of things that do not persist for even a single moment. Thus, since entities themselves do not exist in the second moment, their momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) is established.
However, those whose intellects are deceived by the production of successive similar [moments] fail to perceive the mutual difference between these moments.
Anticipating the objection that those with limited vision, like the ignorant, determine "this very thing is a pillar" and so forth while perceiving it, he says:
"Because momentariness has been refuted.
This is the underlying intention: existence (*sattva*) is certainly not capable of proving momentariness, for [if] in momentariness...

Because a systematic determination is untenable due to its lack of commonality. To explain: it is accepted that moments reaching their final stage produce an effect. In this regard, being questioned, please explain: does a single effect arise from a single [moment], or from many? Likewise, does a single effect arise from many [moments], or many effects? It is not the case that...

Indeed, a cause is said to be "imitated" by another through a single effect when it possesses a necessary presence prior to the production of that effect, following the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) of the other. And many factors, such as the earth and the seed,
imitate [the sprout] through their own positive and negative concomitance, since they invariably exist together prior to its production.

But by way of the "crow-and-palm-fruit" maxim (*kākatālīya*), the prior existence of the moments of earth and so forth would not be subject to a fixed rule. Nor is it the case that only the sprout necessarily follows after the moment of the seed; for the moments of earth and the other elements likewise follow.

Because they exist in such a manner. Indeed, those [subsequent moments] are also necessarily determined to follow immediately after the seed-moment, just as the sprout [follows the seed]. Furthermore, there is no causal relationship other than the necessity of priority and posteriority (*paurvāparyaniyama*). Moreover, if each [moment] were not a cause, then the earth and other factors that coexist with the sprout would not be restricted to being its causes.

Therefore, a single thing does not arise from multiple [causes], as it has been said: "Nothing at all arises from a single [cause]. Nor does a plurality [of things] arise from a single [cause], because sprouts and other effects—which are multiple—are restricted to occurring immediately after earth, seed, fire, air, and water, which are themselves multiple. Furthermore, it is not tenable that a single sprout alone is produced from multiple [causes]; for [the causes] are distinct from the sprout.
For if earth and the other factors did not share a single common cause with it [the seed], there would follow the consequence that their coexistence with it would not be necessary;

yet the necessity of their coexistence is established because, like the sprout, they too are indistinguishable [in that regard]. Therefore, the production of the manifold from the manifold remains as the only remaining possibility.

In this regard, the following must be considered: Are the preceding moments the producers of the subsequent moments entirely independently of one another, or are they dependent? Now, it has already been stated that those moments which have reached their final stage produce effects independently of each other; so why this elaborate display of refuting what has not even been accepted?
In that case, if even the momentary seed-capacity that is capable of producing [the sprout] does not produce it [without them], then what is the use of auxiliary causes?

But was it not said that these [causes] are not conscious agents; rather, their proximity is restricted by their own specific conditions, and they cannot control the intervention [of obstacles]? Is even this farmer not a conscious agent, who, having taken the seed out of the granary, sows it?

For when the ground has been prepared, it is observed that the capacity to produce a sprout arises through a succession of emergent qualities produced by the earth and other factors coexisting with the seed; whereas a seed remaining in a granary does not exhibit such capacity even after a hundred years. If you argue that [the seed] sows [its potential] there, then is this momentary seed not capable of producing its own continuum alone?

If that is so, why would it not depend upon another continuum as a cooperative cause (*sahakārin*) in the production of its effect? But surely it does indeed depend [on others] for its own arising, though not for its own effect; and it is said that it is independent only with respect to the latter, not with respect to its own arising. But even regarding its arising, there exists its own preceding moment within its own continuum which is itself independent. And the same applies to its predecessor.

If the preceding [moment] alone, having fallen within its own continuum, were to remain independent and active in producing [the effect], then a farmer would achieve his purpose merely by placing a seed in a granary; there would be no need for this discerning person to perform the laborious task of farming, which is a source of suffering. If it should be thought that the effect here is of two kinds—one produced with excellence imparted by auxiliary causes (sahakārin)—and...

The first [type of effect] has the nature of producing a succession of specific qualities (*viśeṣa*), whereas the second is produced independently of a succession of excellence in auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*).

In that regard, the sprout’s birth depends on another [factor] once a specific excellence has been imparted to it; however, the initial excellence is produced without depending on a succession of excellences created by auxiliaries. And neither of these two kinds of effects belongs to the seed alone.

[96] It is logical that [the seed] is capable of arising from its own continuum alone; however, it is postulated that the act of cultivation consists in the fact that, while residing within its own continuum, it produces an occasional effect only by depending upon other continua such as soil and so forth. As for those other continua, they are occasional...

Those very auxiliary conditions (*sahakāri-pratyaya*) which [contribute] to the production of an effect are, just as in the case of a sprout, the causes for awakening the capacity of the seed; sometimes, those very causes for the conjunction of these factors such as earth and so forth become the causes for awakening that capacity. Likewise, they are the causes for awakening the capacity in the production of the initial excellence (*atiśaya*) of seeds.

Regarding the conditions of approach (*upasarpaṇapratyaya*): in no way can a seed that has not had its capacity for excellence infused by other continua produce a specific effect that occurs only occasionally. Furthermore, the causes for the awakening of this capacity are twofold: cooperative conditions (*sahakāripratyaya*) and conditions of approach.

That is untenable. For instance: let it be granted that the effect is twofold, and let it be granted that, because it occurs only occasionally, it depends upon another continuum. However, the meaning of this "dependence" must be stated. If you say it means "the awakening of the cause's own capacity," [we reply: surely there is no distinction between the capacity and its awakening, nor between the state of being capable and its manifestation.

It would have to be said that the production of a capable cognition occurs from a single [moment]. And thus, for its own production, it would depend upon causes and auxiliary conditions (*sahakāri-pratyaya*). True; however, the mere admission [of this dependence] is not being urged as a fault.
Now, is this moment capable of producing the sprout, or is it the first excellence? Is it independent, or does it arise from its own continuum alone?

[The seed-moment] is produced by its birth, which is the preceding seed-moment acting independently, and not by something born merely from its own continuum; for that [subsequent seed] also arises from the very same preceding aggregate. Now, among many seed-continuums produced from seeds within the same granary, why is it that only a certain seed produces, through a succession, a seed-moment that is conducive to the production of a sprout?

Other seed-moments that have fallen into a different continuum are not [capable of producing an effect]. Indeed, prior to the advent of the auxiliary condition (*upasarpaṇapratyaya*), there is no mutual distinction whatsoever among those seed-moments residing in either homogeneous or heterogeneous continua. Thus, prior to the advent of the auxiliary condition, those residing in that [specific] continuum do not produce [the effect], even indirectly, as something conducive to the production of a sprout.

The seed-moment: because they produce only the seed, there arises in some seed-moment—through the presence of a cooperative condition (*upasarpaṇapratyaya*)—the production of an initial excellence (*atiśaya*). Alas, in that case, even if it has arisen, it would surely produce [the sprout] even in the absence of that [excellence].
Nor is there a rule that this [seed] must necessarily coexist with a cooperative condition; for seeds existing within a granary belong to that same continuum.
Because even for moments that share the same acquisition and preservation (*yogakṣema*) as it, there is an absence of the coexistence of the conditions for their approach;

and because it is impossible to determine a causal relationship between one moment and another single moment, since positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*)—which have a universal as their object—is only applicable therein. Indeed, [causality] does not [arise] through a difference in causes; and thus, of those that are isolated...

Because deviation is possible, even one who is unwilling must admit that for the production of the first excellence or the production of the sprout, earth and the other factors produce it only when they are mutually dependent.
Furthermore, the seed reaching its final moment does not produce the sprout independently of earth, air, water, and fire.

It would produce them. Would it produce those others by the very same form through which it produces the sprout, or by another form? Not by that same form, for that would entail that even earth and the other factors possess the nature of the sprout. Indeed, there can be no cause...
In the case of difference, the effect ought to possess difference, because it would otherwise follow that the distinction between effects is accidental. As it has been said:

"This indeed is difference, or rather the cause of difference, namely, the superimposition of contradictory actions and the difference in causes. Nor can there be a difference in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), because that too is one; otherwise, there would be no rule governing their coexistence.

If it is argued that for these [other factors], that [seed] is a producer by way of another form; for instance, when the seed produces the sprout and so forth, it is the material cause (*upādāna*), because that [sprout] arises through its modification; whereas for the others, it is merely a cooperative condition (*sahakāri-pratyaya*); and as for those [others], their respective prior causes, such as the soil and so forth, are their material causes, because they arise through the modification of those—[we reply: But then, regarding the cooperative...
Regarding the "appropriation of the field" (*kṣetropādānatā*): is this a single reality or manifold? If it is one, how can it be a producer by means of different forms?

If it is manifold, are these two distinct from the seed or non-distinct? If they are distinct, how can the seed possess the quality of being a producer, since the sprout and so forth would arise from those two alone? Or, if they are non-distinct, how can the seed be manifold? [For] there would be no differentiation.
Because of identity (*tādātmya*). There is oneness between these two because of their identity as one.

If it were argued that when earth and so forth are to be produced, there is merely another form of the seed itself which serves as their material cause (*upādāna*), then the seed would not be the producer of earth and so forth independently of that [other form]. If it were independent of that, [the consequence would follow].

Because it is logically impossible for them to be distinct from the sprout; and you yourself have stated that things which provide no assistance are not required [as causes]; nor is assistance possible for a momentary entity other than its production, because that [production] is indivisible. Thus, since the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritā*) is pervaded by the necessity of dependence on either unity or plurality, and because there is an absence of a third mode, [the momentary cannot possess such efficiency].

Since the negation of one alternative is invariably concomitant with the affirmation of the other, and since both modes— oneness and manyness— which pervade momentariness are absent in the case of existence, existence has not been excluded by the aforementioned sequence; thus, [the reason] is an uncommon inconclusive (asādhāraṇānaikāntika) reason, like "possessing odor."

If one should think: "Even though they provide no assistance, auxiliary causes (sahakārin) are to be depended upon because their presence and absence are followed by the presence and absence of the effect, and because they perform the function of auxiliaries"—[we reply: "But surely, by this same logic, even a non-momentary entity (akṣaṇika), though providing no assistance, would have its positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) imitated by the successive effects of its auxiliaries."

[The opponent argues: "It will not depend on other factors, yet it will produce effects sequentially by virtue of the successive assembly of auxiliary causes. Thus, since the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) is unestablished, existence (*sattva*) is an inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika*) because its negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is doubtful for proving momentariness.
[The proponent replies: But surely this non-momentary entity produces the effect through its own nature (*svarūpa*). And that nature [remains] as it is in the third and subsequent moments, just as...

If it exists as "being" even in the second moment, then it would have to produce [the effect] then as well; or else, not producing it in the second moment, it would not produce it in the third moment and so on, because that which is stable remains in the same state. Or, if it does not remain in the same state, then that very [change] constitutes its momentariness.

To this it is replied: It is true that [the cause] produces the effect by its own nature, but not by that [nature] alone, because it is productive only when accompanied by its auxiliaries. Since the conjunction of those auxiliaries—which depends upon its own successive cognitions—occurs in the second moment, the conjunction of the auxiliaries, like the essential nature itself, is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

It conforms to that [cause] in the production of its effect. It is not correct to argue that because the effect is accomplished merely through the convergence of auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*), their own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) is redundant; for the effect arises from that [primary cause] only when it is accompanied by those [auxiliaries].

If it is argued that because the effect does not arise even when color (*rūpa*) is present [upon seeing], whereas it does arise when they are in conjunction, therefore only that [moisture] is the cause and not color as well—[we reply:
even though the lack of causality is equal in both cases, why is it that the sprout arises only when the color of the seed is present, and not from donkeys and so forth?
[It is because] only when the seed and other factors are present...

If it is argued that the cause is simply the coming together [of the factors] in their own nature (*svarūpa-samavadhāna*), then if that is the cause, why is the nature itself—which is contained therein—not also a cause? Or, if it is not a cause, how is it not equivalent to a donkey or other such irrelevant things? Nor can the inclusion of the nature be dismissed as being unavoidable, because the mere coming together occurs even without that [nature]. Indeed, the specific distinction [between the relevant and the irrelevant] is the nature itself.

Therefore, just as the determination of pervasion (*vyāpti*)— which depends upon both [the pervaded and the pervader]— is defined such that the existence of the pervader (*vyāpaka*) in the pervaded (*vyāpya*) is necessarily its presence there and not its absence, whereas the existence of the pervaded in the pervader is necessarily its presence there and not elsewhere; so too, although the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is determined by both [cause and effect], it is defined such that the cause exists only prior to the effect and not in its absence.

That an effect exists only when its cause exists and not when it is absent is determined in accordance with experience; for this is precisely how the causal relationship is understood by both worldly people and investigators. Furthermore, causality itself is not the nature or essence of "blue" and so forth as established by experience; rather, that [object] is delimited by its own inherent nature through that very essence.

It is employed in various such causal functions; however, its nature is not merely that which is produced by those [functions]. Let there be no multiplicity of natures [in a single entity] due to its performing multiple causal functions simultaneously, and let there be no dependence on external conditions for its determination either, because existence (*sattva*)—as mere "being"—is being determined as nothing other than "causality" itself. As for the case of causality being existence...

Although "being an effect" (kāryatva) is the very nature of an entity, in reality its definition is dependent upon a cause; likewise, "being a cause" (kāraṇatva) cannot be defined without an effect related to it. Thus, existence (sattva) could not be defined in its pure form. Consequently, [the argument] that destruction—whether depending on an adjunct or being pure—is like an effect in terms of having existence as its nature, would be contradicted. And so:

Even if an omniscient being exists, it is nonetheless established that an entity must be of a real nature (sadrūpa) in order to experience the status of being an objective condition (ālambana-pratyaya) for the cognition of that [omniscient being]. On the other hand, even if such a being does not exist, an entity—having acquired its own essential nature from its respective causes—is initially non-functional; yet, despite being capable, it will be employed in various purposeful actions (arthakriyā) through the proximity of their respective auxiliary conditions (sahakārin).

Nor can it be argued that [the seed] lacks capacity because its effect is not perceived at the outset; for if that were the case, it would follow—just as was stated—that even a donkey or similar entity could produce a sprout when in conjunction with earth and other factors. Now, one might object: how can the contradictory properties of being a producer and being a non-producer coexist in a single locus? Likewise, how can both the production of a sprout and the non-production of a sprout reside in the very same seed?

And why is the characteristic of being the producer of earth and so forth not contradictory? If it were contradictory, how could there be non-difference? If there were difference, nothing in the world would be one; and if nothing were one, even the manifold (aneka) would not exist. Thus has the true nature of entities been well-determined by your honor: that even when a diversity of effects is perceived simultaneously, there is no difference in the seed-nature of the producer.

If it is argued that there is non-difference [of the seed] from the sprout based on perception, we say no; for the same [objection] applies here as well. Indeed, even here, despite the difference in successive effects, the nature of the seed does not require one thing to be different from another. Nor is contradiction understood merely from the presence or absence of the use of the negative particle (*nañ*), because that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Furthermore, it is not the case that the seed possesses the capacity to produce [the effect] only at a specific time.

At that very moment, it lacks the capacity to produce [cognition]. Nor is its capacity to produce [cognition] its inherent nature (*svabhāva*); rather, the capacity to produce is contingent upon the seed.

Furthermore, since there is no perception of color and so forth when there is a defect in the mind or an absence of the eye and other [faculties], it is determined that [the object] is perceivable by both.
But how is it that [the object] is not cognizable by the mind alone? If you say, "Because it is apprehended in the second moment," we say no.

In that case, there is either the conjunction of the eye and other causal conditions, or a specific capacity (*sāmarthya*), or a distinct property (*dharmabheda*). And this conjunction depends upon the causal condition of the movement [of the object].
Nor is there non-difference between the property and the substratum (*dharmadharmi*), because the former is distinct from the latter. Even though they are distinct...

Furthermore, because it is obtained by depending upon that [substratum], and because it performs its function as a cooperative cause with it, there is a connection between them. Thus, since even for a non-momentary entity the performance of causal efficiency (arthakriyā) through either successive or simultaneous action is logically possible, existence (sattva) is inconclusive (anaikāntika) due to its doubtful negative concomitance (sandigdhavyatirekitva). Therefore, existence is not a valid constituent of the proof for the momentariness of entities.

Regarding the conceptualization that entities arise by their own nature as either perishable or imperishable, it is said in response: we do not recognize them as being either perishable or imperishable; rather, existing things arise from their own causes and perish due to other causes whose presence is dependent upon their own conditions.

Furthermore, destruction is non-different from that which is being destroyed, due to a difference in cause and a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). And this difference in intrinsic nature has been established in the "Examination of the Injunction" (*niyogaparīkṣā*). Now, even when this [destruction] has arisen with a distinct form, what has happened to the entity?
Nothing at all has happened. This venerable entity still exists. Let it be so, as its birth is dependent upon its own causes.

By the absence of that [nature], characterized by the lack of its own essential form, does not the possession of its own specific characteristic—which brings about a corresponding conventional usage—render all causal efficiency (arthakriyā) impossible? Nor does the necessity of destruction imply independence from other causes; for this is both unproven and inconclusive. For this [is as follows]:
Let your honor examine this: is the sequence of potsherds necessarily co-extensive with the sequence of the pot, or not?

If it is not, then even the destruction of the pot would not be a necessary occurrence. Indeed, those whose eyes are closed do not perceive the destruction of the pot except upon the arising of the moment of division. Thus, the necessity of destruction remains unproven.

Now, as for "necessarily occurring": even in that very same series of distinct moments which is necessarily occurring, the necessity of occurrence (*dhruvabhāvitva*)—which depends upon a hammer—is not invariably concomitant with independence; therefore, it cannot serve to negate dependence on other causes. Consequently, since the inference proving momentariness has been refuted, recognition remains uncontradicted.
It is established that you [the opponent] maintain this position.

Thus, because momentariness has been refuted, there exists no momentary entity produced from that same object at the time of sensory cognition which could become the domain of mental cognition; so it has been stated. Or, let it be granted for the sake of argument; nevertheless, this too—

It is perceptible by the eye, not merely within the domain of the mind. He states this because the presence or absence of that consciousness follows the presence or absence of both [the organ and the object]: "Furthermore, since those whose minds are turned away from other objects do not perceive color and so forth when there is a defect in the mind or when the mind is not directed [toward it]—such as the blind and others—and since they do perceive them when the eye and other organs are absent [but the mind is directed], the fact that it is perceivable by both is inferred."

"From what [source] does the state of being cognizable by the mind alone arise? He raises an objection: "If it is argued that because the capacity of the sense organs is exhausted in the very first moment, the fact that [the object] is cognized in the second moment allows one to infer its state of being cognizable by the mind alone? He refutes this: "No. Why?
Because the capacity of the eyes and other organs, whose capacity was determined in such moments or moments of a similar kind, has been completely exhausted."
Because there is no cause for it, these [faculties] do not possess efficacy in a single moment alone such that it would not exist in another moment;
for their efficacy would be exhausted due to the absence of a cause. Furthermore, this is because we observe a continuous flow of that cognition, as in the case of memory.
However, dependence is indeed well-known in the case of inference and the like, because cognition occurs only when there is an absence of a mark (*liṅga*) and so forth;

thus, the mind never functions independently with respect to anything external. Therefore, the internal [object] alone is the direct object, and only through direct operation upon that very [internal object] could it experience excellence, not with respect to what is not its object.

Thus he says: "And because we observe the continuous flow (*dhārāvāhikatva*) of that cognition. Now, an objection is raised: "In recollection (*smaraṇa*), the mind (*manas*) operates independently alone, since even those who are blind and so forth are observed to have recollections of form and other objects. To this he replies: "But in the case of recollection, the dependence of the mind is indeed evident, because its object is something already apprehended by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)."

The meaning is that the mind, accompanied by the mental impression (*bhāvanā*) deposited by an experience produced by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), is the cause of recollection, but not independently. Nor is it independent in cognitions such as inference; thus he says: "In the case of inference and so forth, the dependence of the mind is established because cognition occurs even in the absence of a logical mark (*liṅga*) and the like. Therefore, it is not [independent] anywhere.

The mind (*manas*) operates directly and independently within the interior of consciousness (*cidanāntare*). Therefore, pleasure and so forth are its direct objects—internal and unmediated—through a contact characterized by *saṃyuktasamavāya* (inherence in that which is conjoined), since the mind is independent. External objects, however, are not [its objects], because they lack such a direct connection, like the eyes and other senses, and because [the mind] is not dependent upon them. Thus, that mind [perceives] only therein.
It could not experience excellence through direct functioning with respect to that which is not its object, namely the external. Thus, it is established:

those eyes and other sense organs under dispute do not produce cognitions of past or future objects, because they produce their effects only when possessing the cooperation of an object; for whatever produces an effect only when possessing a cooperative cause does not produce that effect in the absence of that cause.

Just as a seed, when its auxiliary causes such as the earth—which produce the sprout—have passed away or are yet to come, is not capable of producing a sprout; nor is it unestablished that objects act as auxiliaries for the sense faculties, for if they did not so act in the production of consciousness, it would follow that even people like us would have direct perception of past and future objects. This is because [the capacity of the senses] is established through the power of perfected medicines, mantras, and asceticism.
It has been stated that although the intellects (dhīs) obscure the eyes and other sense organs, they do not transcend their own respective objects.
Nor is there a doubt regarding the negative concomitance (vyatireka). To explain: being an auxiliary cause (sahakāritva) is pervaded by the state of being dependent;

however, in the absence of that [auxiliary], the state of being independent—which is the opposite of dependence—is present in the production of the effect, as it is the opposite of the pervader (vyāpaka-viruddha).

Since it also excludes [the mind's] functioning as a cooperative cause through non-perception, the logical connection (*pratibandha*) is established. Thus, the mind under dispute does not function toward external objects independently of the eyes and other [senses], because its functioning is dependent upon them; for whatever functions in dependence on something else does not function toward that object independently of it, just as the eye, which depends on light, does not [function] with respect to form in the dark.
This is the perception of the contradictory. Nor is it tenable to say that the mind is not dependent on the external [objects] such as the eye;

for this would entail the consequence that there would be no such things as the blind or the deaf, as has been explained in detail. Now, one might object: "Granted that sensory perception and mental perception are not all-encompassing in their objects, yet there will be a perception consisting of cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*) which is so. For instance, by means of that which consists of hearing..."
Having apprehended the selflessness of all things and so forth through cognition, and having established their reality by means of reasoning, there arises—
through the culmination of the excellence of cultivation consisting of the repeated application of the mind— a direct perception born of that [process].

The Tathāgata will bring about an extremely clear mental focus upon the universe—beginning with the self and so forth—as its objective support, by means of a portion of his human nature, just as one perceives a lotus in the palm of the hand. Nor is such a cognition impossible, for it arises from the excellence of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*). To explain: [it would not arise] either due to the absence of cultivation, or due to the absence of its excellence, or due to the absence of its capacity.
It would not exist; for in the absence of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), the cultivation of the selflessness of all phenomena (*sarvadharmanairātmya*) would be impossible.

Indeed, it would not exist in this way if there were no such thing as suffering (*duḥkha*) in the world, or if that which exists were not desired to be abandoned, or if that which is desired to be abandoned could not be abandoned, or if its inability to be abandoned were due to its being eternal or due to the lack of means for it.

Either because of a lack of full comprehension, or because even if the means were not fully understood and even if suffering could be abandoned, the cultivation of selflessness (*nairātmya*) is not the means, or because of the possibility of other more efficient means. It is certainly not the case that there is no such thing as suffering in the world; for indeed, by way of transformation, affliction, and conditioning, all five aggregates (*pañca-skandhāḥ*) are without exception [suffering].

[These sufferings belong] to those wandering in saṃsāra. Nor are these undesired by oneself or others; for they are to be felt as disagreeable by a leader among men—whether one who is fixed in the enlightenment of a śrāvaka or one whose mind is dependent on natural compassion—who suffers in the suffering of others. Nor is their removal impossible, for an entity that is eternal cannot possibly exist.
Because he is devoid of all activity, he is like a lotus in the sky. Nor is it due to a lack of knowledge regarding the means;

for instance, the defects (*doṣa*) that produce suffering—such as passion, hatred, and so forth, as well as intoxication, pride, and the like—are themselves the producers [of suffering], yet by ceasing from their constituent parts, they bring about the cessation of that [suffering] as well, just as [the fever] arising from phlegm [subsides].

Fever ceases through the removal of phlegm (*kapha*). Furthermore, the afflictions (*doṣas*) arise from the perception of a permanent self and so forth; they are its components and exist inseparably from it, and thus they do not cease in the absence of that [self]. There is no cause for their cessation other than the direct realization of its opposite, because only that is antagonistic to them. For instance, wherever there is a conjunction with something contradictory to another...
In that case, there must necessarily be the cessation of its opposite, just as cold ceases upon the presence of its contradictory, fire.

And since the internalization of the selflessness of all phenomena—which is opposed to the perception of a stable self—is possible within the mind, this is a "perception of what is naturally contradictory" (*svabhāvaviruddhopalabdhi*). Consequently, there is also the absolute cessation of passion and other afflictions which have that [perception of a stable self] as their cause. For instance:

Those things which possess an extreme increase that is opposed by their own possible causes are subject to an absolute destruction; for example, hair that has reached an extreme increase due to *indralupta* (a disease causing hair loss). Passion (*rāga*) and the like possess an extreme increase that is opposed by their own possible causes;

this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). Furthermore, the selflessness of all phenomena (*sarvadharmanairātmya*) is the antidote to those [passions], and its direct realization is not [possible].

[It arises] from another source, namely the excellence of cultivation (*bhāvanā-prakarṣa*); yet that excellence of cultivation does not exist without cultivation itself. Furthermore, the excellence of cultivation is not capable [of producing] the cognition of the selflessness of all phenomena (*sarvadharmanairātmya-vijñāna*).
For instance, whatever mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) possesses a possible excellence of cultivation, its object of knowledge (*jñeya*) is that which is to be established by that cultivation.
