The clarity of form refers to the mental consciousness— in states such as those afflicted by desire according to one's wish— which has an object such as a beloved woman as its focal point and possesses a state of vividness produced by the intensification of meditative cultivation; and it is possible for the conceptualization of selflessness to reach such an intensification of cultivation.

Thus, this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*), because [clarity] is caused solely by the excellence of cultivation (*bhāvanāprakarṣa*). For whatever possesses the excellence of cultivation, its state of having a clear manifestation is necessarily established; therefore, since clarity of manifestation is invariably concomitant with the mere possibility of the excellence of cultivation, even if the excellence of cultivation were possible, if—

The clarity of the manifestation would not arise if it were dependent upon another cause; however, excellence is observed to be pervaded by independence. Therefore, since the excellence of cultivation—being excluded from the counter-example through the perception of what is incompatible with its pervader—is pervaded by clarity, there is no doubt regarding the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). Nor is it unestablished (*asiddha*).

Because the commencement of the intensification of cultivation occurs either through compassion or through the fear of suffering; and because, unlike jumping or the heating of water, there is no interruption in the intensification of the mind regarding the selflessness of all phenomena, whereby no dispute could possibly arise.
For whatever dharma has a stable basis, having arisen in a certain way within a certain [basis], it possesses the portion of that which was thus established.

For the sake of further progress, he does not require renewed effort; rather, he reaches ultimate perfection therein. Just as the purity of gold, produced through a continuous process of smelting and heating, attains a state of redness and essential excellence, so too, once the realization of the selflessness of all phenomena has arisen in one who possesses a stable basis, there occurs a potential for extreme cultivation that no longer requires further exertion for specific improvements.

The phrase "of persons" (*puṃsām*) constitutes a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*), since having a stable substratum establishes the existence of another world (*paraloka*). Is that which is not primary [the cause] distinct from the entity or non-distinct? In that regard, if it were non-distinct, there would be an absence of assistance; even when this [non-distinct cause] exists, the effect would not have arisen, because it is not perceived despite its presence. Furthermore, since the production of the effect occurs only through an auxiliary that possesses the capacity for origination, the entity could not exist [as a cause] if it were incapable. It is not so.

It is now argued that an auxiliary produces an effect [in the entity]. However, this leads to an infinite regress if one auxiliary were to produce another auxiliary. For the effect would arise from that very [subsequent auxiliary], resulting in the absurdity that the primary entity does not produce it—this has already been stated. Alternatively, if an undifferentiated auxiliary is imparted, then the entity itself must be what is imparted; yet that [entity] cannot be imparted, as it is already established beforehand.

[The opponent might argue: "In order to produce [the effect], [the seed] must depend on auxiliary causes. [To this we reply: If they provide no assistance, then it would not depend on them as auxiliary causes;

thus, the seed would produce the sprout and so forth at the very moment of its arising. Since that which is independent cannot delay [production], or if it were to delay, it would not produce [the effect] even later, because there is no difference [in its state]. If you think that even those things which provide no assistance can be auxiliary causes...

Because they possess a coexistence that performs the effect; nor are they not required, since without them the effect would be impossible. In that regard, if an entity were the producer of the effect by its own nature, then it would not be the case that the birth [of the effect] depends on both, because of the deviation from each one individually—namely, non-existence. This is the reason for the stated effect.

Because there is no deviation [from the rule], due to the necessary certainty of its arising; nor is it tenable to say that an entity, having arisen from its own cause with a nature that produces its effect after a delay of several moments of time, is therefore a "delayed producer" by virtue of its very nature, because such a position cannot withstand critical analysis.
For what is this "several moments of time"?

Does the nature of causing delay cease or not? If it ceases, how is it that the entity does not cease? Because its nature has ceased. If it does not cease, there is a sublation of this [entity], because its nature would be of a ceased form due to the association with a contradictory property. Or, if it were not of that nature, it would not delay; therefore, it would exist only immediately after its birth.

The entity would follow as being one that has already accomplished its purpose. If it does not cease [its activity], then even after the lapse of some portion of time, it would not produce the effect, because the nature of the entity, which causes delay, remains in the same state. As it has been said: "Not by succession...

The causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) of an entity is not possible, nor is it logically consistent with simultaneity; for whatever effect whatsoever was produced by that non-momentary nature in the first moment, all those effects would have to be produced again in the second and subsequent moments. However, for a momentary entity, causal efficiency is possible through both succession and simultaneity.

Thus: since existence is excluded from the counter-example of momentariness due to the absence of its pervader, it is pervaded by momentariness; therefore, the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is established.
It might be argued: even a momentary entity has the nature of producing purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). And this is not [the case] only here.
If there is an absence of the capacity to produce [the sprout], what use have these [factors] as auxiliaries? Thus, the seed should produce the sprout immediately upon its own arising. [Objection:
But surely the arisen moment of the seed, being capable, does indeed produce it. [Reply: From where, then, does its arising come?
[From] a previous moment of the seed. [Objection: In that case, since all [moments] falling within that continuum are indistinguishable in their nature as seeds, [they would all produce the sprout].

If it were merely the capacity to produce, then the seed, as soon as it has acquired birth, would produce the sprout. This is not so. Rather, another moment—born from a series of successive moments possessing a specific excellence produced by the prior conjunction of the earth, seed, wind, and other factors—and being capable, when assisted by capable moments of earth and the rest, produces the sprout independently.

It produces [the effect]. Nor is there the production of an effect by those [factors] such as earth and so forth—which are co-existent with [the seed]—even when they are independent of it, because in their absence, that [effect] is absent, being dependent solely upon the capacity of that [seed]. Furthermore, the non-cooperation of earth and the other factors is not established; thus, there is no fixed limit to the increase [of the effect], like the heating of water. In that case, by extreme heat, the waters which constitute its substratum [are destroyed].

Because of the instability of the basis for one who has desisted, nor does it possess an excellence established like jumping. This is because, upon the production of a newly acquired portion [of the jump], one must again depend on effort therein. For in that case, the previously established [state]—merely being an object of focus—is not sufficient to prevent further jumping; rather, it has perished. But the subsequent jumping depends on the previous...

It proceeds through the exertion of power, like jumping; however, that which has the nature of illuminating the selflessness of all phenomena flows by the very essence of the mind and thus does not require further effort. For this [wisdom], due to the attainment of ever-increasing superior distinctions produced by previous cultivation, arises in ultimate excellence because it has become the very nature of its basis. In this regard:

Jumping, however, characterized by excellence, is not the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) of the body; for even when the substratum [the body] exists, it requires further effort. Likewise, the heating of water is not the inherent nature of water, because it is subject to destruction. Or, the argument is stated by taking mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) as the subject:
for whatever mental cultivation is practiced with attention, continuity, and over a long period of time, all of that [is effective].

The fruit is a cognition in which the objective support appears as clearly as an *āmalaka* fruit in the palm of one's hand. For example, the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of a beloved woman by one afflicted with passion—possessing three specific characteristics—is the cause for the clear appearance of a cognition whose object is that woman.
Likewise, the cultivation of the selflessness of all things possesses three specific characteristics; this is thus a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

For this mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is clearly manifest; such a cultivation, even while following its own positive and negative concomitances, is seen among those afflicted by desire and the like to be independent of other causes. Therefore, if—even when this [cultivation] exists—the state of clear manifestation were not to arise for a consciousness that grasps the selflessness of all things, then [there would be no cause].
It would follow that this [cognition] would depend upon something else. And thus, the observed independence [of meditative cultivation] would be undermined;
for even a cognition consisting of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*) has as its object what was heard or inferred, since it is impossible for meditative cultivation to arise spontaneously.

[Verbal testimony] is dependent upon perception and inference. It is not a means of valid knowledge (*apramāṇa*) because it is contingent, following the correspondence or non-correspondence with reality of its source cognition.

[The phrase] "it would be contradicted" indicates that in the case of the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), there is observed a dependence characterized by a factor incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpaka-viruddha*). This is because [testimony] generates a clarity of cognition [derived from its source].

By the perception of what is incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*), mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is excluded; what remains is that which is necessarily connected to the production of vividness.

Thus, because the production of clarity follows a specific type of cultivation and not mere cultivation in general, this is a *svabhāvahetu* (essential reason). Furthermore, from such a cause, there is an inference of the capacity of the complete causal complex to produce its effect. And so it is said:

Since the fruit necessarily arises when that causal complex (sāmagrī) exists without obstruction, it is determined that the causal complex does not have as its object the possibility of a fruit occurring only occasionally; thus, because of this certainty, there is no contradiction in its being an inference (*anumāna*).
Nor is the reason (*hetu*) unestablished (*asiddha*), for a cultivation (*bhāvanā*) possessing the three qualifications is indeed possible regarding worldly suffering.

For those fixed in the enlightenment of the Śrāvakas who fear signs, as well as for the compassionate ones who, accepting all suffering beings as their very self, pacify the causes of all suffering and have thinned out internal defilements through the practice of the perfections such as generosity, there arises a non-erroneous cognition born from the excellence of such cultivation.

Because its object is a thing established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); and because it is non-conceptual due to its clarity; and because it has all things as its object, since it consists in the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of selflessness (*nairātmya*). Furthermore, there is no such thing called "selflessness" that exists separately from entities, which could become an object of perception even when those entities themselves are not within the range of perception. And that which is mounted upon conceptual construction is not vivid.

Cognition does not appear without conceptualization (*avikalpya*). Therefore, this clarity (*vaiśadya*) produced by cultivation (*bhāvanā*) could not exist as an essence of clear manifestation unless it were itself clear. Thus, the clarity regarding the selflessness of all things (*viśvanairātmya-vaiśadya*) is simply the clarity of everything (*viśva-vaiśadya*). This omniscience (*sārvajña*) arises precisely from the cultivation of the true nature of reality (*bhūtārtha-bhāvanā*), when it has been practiced with devotion, continuity, and for a long duration, in all its aspects.

Anticipating the objection that the absence of the cause is unestablished because the direct perception of all things is possible, [the author] says: even cognition consisting of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) has as its object that which has been heard or inferred. Why?
Because cultivation cannot occur without a cause. It is dependent upon scripture and inference; it is directly [perceptive] only with respect to its own specific object.

The connection with the preceding [statement] is: "it would experience excellence through its function, yet it would not have that as its object. And he says that even that [subsequent cognition] is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) characterized by excellence: "Furthermore, because it conforms to the subversion of the factual nature of the prior cognition, it is not a valid means of knowledge due to its dependence [on that prior cognition]."

This is the true meaning intended by the Teacher here: it is true that we do not deny that cultivation (*bhāvanā*)—which operates within the domain of what is heard or inferred—is a cause for clear cognition; however, that which has arisen with respect to a particular object is the very thing that becomes the domain of clear apprehension, and never does the excellence of the cultivation of color lead to the clarity of a cognition whose object is taste.
It is argued: "But surely we do not maintain that cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is the cause for the clarity of other objects;
rather, we maintain only that it is the cause for the clarity of the objects of scripture and inference. And the object of those is the selflessness (*nairātmya*) of all things.

It has been stated that the culmination of its cultivation clarifies the selflessness (*nairātmya*) of all things; for since that [clarification of selflessness] is impossible without the clarity of all things, it brings about the clarity of all things.
This is true as stated, but it is incorrect. For instance, [selflessness] is not within the scope of scripture (*āgama*) or inference (*anumāna*).

Regarding these distinct entities which are devoid of self-nature yet exist as ultimate realities: it is not the case that this [conceptual cognition], which apprehends merely the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), is capable of taking as its object the ultimate reality of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). Nor can meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) directed toward that [conceptual cognition] have the particular characteristic as its object—even though that characteristic is not directly grasped by it—on the grounds that the characteristic is the object of that [cognition] by virtue of being determined (*adhyavasita*) by it; thus, cultivation is also rooted in that [conceptual cognition].

If it is argued that [the conceptual cognition] has that [particular] as its object because it is the cause of the excellence and clarity of that [object], we say no. This is because even that which is determined by it lacks ultimate reality (*paramārthasattva*). To explain: both that which is apprehended through a mental after-effect (*anupāna*) and that which is determined are exclusions of others (*anyāpoha*), not real entities (*vastu*). For if they were to penetrate the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), it would be impossible for them to appear as representations capable of being associated with verbal expressions.

Let it be that the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of those two is not the object; however, there will arise for the mind—which is produced by the intensification of the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) originating from them—a vivid appearance, just as for one afflicted by passion there is a direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) of the particular characteristic of a beloved woman due to the intensification of the cultivation originating from the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of her. [As in the verse: "O you whose jar-like breasts are as firm as an elephant's frontal globes..."

"O lady with eyes as tremulous as a doe’s, with a creeper-like body as white as a campaka petal, O lake of loveliness, O beloved wife, grant me an embrace—the very root of your lovely sprout-like arms—and revive me!
I have fallen at your lotus-feet. This is established by the perception of both his speech and his physical gestures. It exists.

And since conceptual and non-conceptual cognitions have, in some way, the same object, there is no over-extension [of the definition]. True; experience is possible, but the possibility of its being a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) with respect to that object is not. This is because it does not arise from that [object], and because for that which is not of the nature of that [object], a rule of non-deviation from it is impossible. Furthermore, there is no identity between the object and the cognition, because the object is distinct from the cognition.

Moreover, even if there is no difference [between cognitions], because they are distinct from one another in their identity, it is impossible for one cognition to experience another cognition. If the unity of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of cognition is accepted, then that [cognition] must be practiced as the eternal, unitary, non-dual Brahman; thus, the acceptance of the practice of momentariness and selflessness is abandoned.

It would follow that [the cognition] would be attached to the water-offering (jalāñjali). Therefore, its non-deviation from the object is not due to identity (*tādātmya*), nor is it due to being its effect (*tatkāryatva*).
For this is indeed the effect of the excellence of mental cultivation (*bhāvanāprakarṣa*), not the effect of the object itself.
If it were argued that it is indirectly its effect, like inference—for instance, as [cognition arises] from the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of fire—

The particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of smoke arises first; from that, the experience of smoke; from that, the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of fire; and from that, the inference is produced.

Thus, through this succession, because it is connected to fire, it leads to the attainment of fire—which performs burning and cooking. Likewise, this [yogic perception] also, being born at the limit of the excellence of the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) produced by inference, is not non-deviant with respect to its object, because it is ultimately derived from the object through such a succession.

If you say it is a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), do you mean that for one who has established fire through inference and then meditates upon it, the clear consciousness (*vijñāna*) whose object is fire is a valid means of cognition? To one who says "yes," [the following applies] when ascending the mountain slope:

If there were a cognition of fire produced by the contact of the senses, it would necessarily follow that it must agree with the clear cognition produced by mental cultivation; yet, disagreement is frequently observed. Furthermore, if a deviation is possible even when a definition is applicable, that very definition is sublated; thus, even a cognition that appears clear is merely intuitive (prātibha).

That which is overcome by doubt is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*). The fact that the cultivation of such [meditation] has a real object is not the cause for the validity of the clear cognition arising therefrom, because of the possibility of error. And thus, just as for a wandering beggar the direct perception of a mass of wealth brought about by a succession of desires—beginning with the acquisition of a vessel of flour and culminating in the gain of its root—is [illusory], so too is the Tathāgata’s direct perception of all things as being without self (*nirātman*).

It follows that there is a direct realization of the object (*vastu-sākṣātkāra*). If it is argued that for a cognition residing in a mental continuum refined by the cultivation of all objective entities, the object serves as its objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and thus, because the cognition arises from that [object], there is a rule of non-deviation from it—[we reply:
the status of an object as an objective condition for consciousness is pervaded by dependence upon the sense faculty; and that [dependence]...
Therefore, by the perception of the incompatible (*viruddhopalabdhi*), its exclusion also negates the object's status as an objective support-condition (*ālambanapratyayatā*).

Indeed, a specific kind of fuel that is a cause of smoke does not produce smoke even by a thousand refinements (*saṃskāra*) without fire. Or, if it were to produce it, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the destruction of inference, because [that fuel] would then be the cause of all effects. And as for mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*)...

It is observed that even a cognition concerning a real object possesses the capacity to produce a clear consciousness only when it is independent of the external object, as in the case of a woman afflicted by passion; therefore, even a cognition of a real object is capable [of producing its effect] independently of it. Thus, it is impossible to establish that an external object serves as the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). Furthermore, it is more logical that for this [consciousness], only those very moments [of the cognition itself] should constitute the objective conditions.

Those [beings] who exist before him without any intervening space are thus the only ones perceivable by him; however, those who existed even earlier at that same time, as well as those yet to come in the future, are not so perceived, and therefore his knowledge does not have everything as its object. Furthermore, regarding the living beings included within the three realms who are currently being seen, when they undergo a transition to another birth, there exists a multitude of past and future karmic bonds.

The vision [of the Blessed One], whose nature consists of both the cause and the effect, apprehends even the past and the future as its objects by way of being a qualifier through its identity with that which is currently being seen. Nor does this consequence apply to the vision of those such as ourselves, because it is veiled by the impurities of passion and so forth; for the Blessed One’s [vision] has all the stains of the primary and secondary afflictions completely wiped away.
Consciousness, which is unobstructed on all sides, shining forth, and taking its own object as a condition, perceives its entire range in all its aspects;

and because it is somehow related to everything—either directly or indirectly—it would perceive objects distinguished by space, time, and nature exactly as they are. Yet, this cannot occur without the apprehension of everything.
It is established that his consciousness is unobstructed regarding all objects;

however, that is untenable because it cannot withstand scrutiny. For instance, if this quality of being distinguished by all [objects] belonging to the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) were intrinsic, it could not be one and the same across every objective condition.
Because it is logically impossible for a single entity to reside in many [places]. If they were multiple, then the statement that "all are both objects and conditions" would be the truth;

and since there would be no such connection, the cognition of them all would not be perceived everywhere as having a real object, but rather as a conceptual construction superimposing reality upon what is merely a mental fabrication. It is well said that [cognition] has as its domain only its own object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

[The cognition] is non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*) and produces a determinative ascertainment (*adhyavasāya*) regarding an object qualified by all things. Therefore, even though it is non-conceptual, its activity follows that ascertainment, and thus it has all things as its object. As it has been said: "Having determined..."

If it is argued that those of great intelligence perceive [all things] in every aspect in an instant, then from where does this power of an experience—which has only a few objects as its support—come, such that there is a determination of all things? If it is said that this is due to the removal of beginningless obstructions (*āvaraṇa*), then one would see them exactly as they are; however, this does not mean that [the cognition] is devoid of an object.

That is incorrect. It is logical that this [cognition] possesses skill in the construction of conceptualizations; for while impurities such as hair-tufts (keśa) etc. indeed obscure reality (*tattva*), they do not constitute an obstacle to the construction of conceptualizations. Therefore, because it arises merely from the intensity of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and lacks a rule of non-deviation from the object, even though it appears clearly, it is not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*) and is not direct perception (*apratyakṣa*), since it is overcome by doubt.
And this is the current point:

as for the claim that the manifestation of a real object is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of cognition, whereas its having an unreal object is adventitious (*āgantuka*), and therefore, in the absence of a subverting factor (*bādhaka*), it must indeed have a real object—that is incorrect. [For instance, consider] a vivid [cognition] whose object is fire that has been inferred and subsequently produced...

Because it would follow that the cognition of an existent entity (*bhavijñāna*) and so forth would possess validity; and since its object is seen to be sublated in some cases, invalidity here is the same [as in other cases], due to attachment elsewhere. Therefore, if in this context the fact that meditation is the cause of a vividly appearing cognition is being proven by means of a qualification, then it is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). Let it be so.

The Tathāgata possesses such true cognition; however, that cognition of his regarding reality is not a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because it lacks the status of a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇatvāt*).

Thus, due to the absence of the property in the subject (*apakṣadharmatā*), the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*); for there can be no object of inference (*anumeya*) when the subject is already well-known and its particularity is not sought to be known. Now, if it is argued that the state of being a cause of direct perceptual cognition belongs to meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) as established by direct perception for another person—

If it were so established, then the reason (*hetu*) would be contradictory (*viruddha*) because it is pervaded by the opposite of the probandum (*sādhyaviparyaya*). This is because even a cultivation (*bhāvanā*) possessing the three qualifications produces a cognition that is vivid and non-erroneous; furthermore, the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) would be devoid of the probandum. And when, despite being produced by the cultivation of a real object (*bhūtārtha*), this [cognition] lacks authority (*prāmāṇya*) because its object is unreal (*abhūtārtha*), then—
As it has been said:
"That which is free from affliction, which is the true nature of reality, cannot be subverted by errors,
even though the intellect lacks effort [to discern it], because the intellect has a natural bias toward that [true nature]."

That is untenable. For if cognition were based on reality (*bhūtārtha*), then when it has taken the side of that [reality], there could be no sublation by opposing views which are not based on reality.

However, this [cognition] is not based on reality; thus, even though its own nature has ceased to exist, it is subject to sublation—just like one's own [false] view. Therefore, there is merely an increase of the opposing view, and an absolute increase is not possible.

Just as when faults are eradicated by uprooting them, they will not arise again; for this very reason, even though its basis is unstable and it does not require further effort, an absolute finality is not possible for it, because—just like the view that things belong to a self—a contrary cognition can arise. And the possibility of such a contrary cognition exists because [the view] has an unreal object. But that is not the case, because [the truth] has been heard and inferred...

But direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is simply not possible [in this case], because those two [inference and verbal testimony] involve the apprehension of an object that is beyond the senses (*parokṣa*).
And as for direct perception—surely there is no restriction regarding the eyes and other [senses] even in terms of time; for [they can perceive] non-present silver and so forth.

Because of [the nature of] apprehension. For that is not the apprehension of mother-of-pearl and the like; since it is impossible for a cognition having one form to have another thing as its object, there would be a lack of confidence [in the cognition].

Because its object is the opposite of that [apprehended thing], and because it conforms to the real nature residing in that [object], verbal testimony and inference regarding its own object [are established].

Furthermore, validity is untenable because it would depend upon another cognition. Thus, it is established that the cognition produced at the culmination of the intensification of the meditation on a real object (*bhūtārtha-bhāvanā-prakarṣa-paryanta-ja*) is not non-perceptual, because it is a means of valid knowledge regarding its object; whatever is not a means of valid knowledge regarding its object is non-perceptual, such as the cognition of a woman in one afflicted by lust. And this [cognition in question] is not invalid, since it possesses extreme clarity.

Because it is produced by meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*). That cognition which, while possessing extreme clarity, is born from the excellence of meditative cultivation is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*); for example, the clear-cognition regarding fire that has been cultivated through inference. Thus, having the same cause is pervaded by having the same nature. As it has been said: "Entities that possess such-and-such a nature or do not possess such-and-such a nature are born from causes that possess such-and-such a nature or do not possess such-and-such a nature."
Therefore, the validity of this [cognition], being withdrawn, also withdraws its status as being born from the same causes [as perception].

Nor does this [verbal cognition] differ from perception in the case of an existing object when it reaches the culmination of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), when it is in contact with supersensible objects, when it possesses the clarity of fire inferred and then manifested, or even when it possesses the clarity of all things despite being devoid of self-nature (*nirātmaka*). Nor is the absence of obscurations such as passion (*rāga*) a distinguishing feature.

Indeed, these [impediments] do not obscure consciousness in the manner of a woolen blanket or similar objects; rather, one who is distracted by that [consciousness] and overwhelmed by various cravings for different objects is unable to cultivate it. Thus, their utility lies solely in the removal of the lack of respect for cultivation (*bhāvanā*). And here too, there exists a body-stump rendered sluggish by the numbness produced by extreme cold.

There may be an application of the mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) regarding the inferred presence of fire; thus, there is no difference in the logical reason (*hetu*), and the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is established.

Nor is there a fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) due to various states such as odor, taste, color, and touch—which arise from a single earth-atom as their inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) and have as their non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) a single conjunction with fire that depends on a single heat—despite these being distinct entities. For even though they are one [in their substratum], there is a diversity of capacity (*sāmarthya*) in the earth-element.

Of that atom; and its diversity is known from the observation of the diversity of effects. And that [diversity], being eternally inherent, is eternal and arises in the composite product of earth through the sequence of the causal capacities; thus it is explained.
We shall discuss the remainder at the time of explaining the text. Let this suffice for now.
Now, someone who is a mere scent of a Prābhākara, having established [the theory] and then seeking to uproot it, objects:
"But there is no restriction of the eyes and other senses even by way of time. Why? Because of the perception of non-present silver and so forth in the cognition 'this is silver. [Objection:
But how can the cognition 'this is silver,' which rests upon the mother-of-pearl present before one, [be said to grasp] that which is not proximate?"
To the question, "Is there the perception of silver at that place and time? he says: No, for that is not the perception of mother-of-pearl and the like. Why?

Because it is impossible for a cognition having one form to have a different object. If that were possible, there would be no restriction regarding objects, and thus all cognition would have everything as its object; consequently, omniscience would be established without effort.

The wish of the Tathāgata has thus borne fruit. Therefore, whatever form the consciousness takes, that alone is sought as its object. Furthermore, the mind has attained independence in dreams; yet dream-consciousness is not memory, because it does not possess the form of that [past object].
Because it has already been refuted. This is not substantial. For instance:
"The requirement for an external object is futile; the manifestation of another form is equally [unproven]. Indeed, even in a dream, the experience of a living being as present is clearly a memory."

The eyes and other sense organs reveal only the present object, such as a fragment of mother-of-pearl, because they depend upon it; otherwise, their proximity would be useless, since the cognition of silver would occur even in the absence of that object. Therefore, for the sake of restriction—namely, that "this has the form of silver"—that [silver] alone is its object, and not the mother-of-pearl.

Because there would be no cognition [of the object] and because there would be no basis for confidence. For if a cognition having one form were to have another thing as its object, then, since cognition would deviate from its own object, there would follow a lack of confidence in every instance; thus, a discerning person would neither engage in nor desist from anything anywhere. Therefore, this [cognition] must indeed have silver as its object. Nor is this...

The cognition "this is silver," although it is an apprehension of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), is actually a non-apprehension of non-coreferentiality due to the influence of a defect;
yet it is not a memory, because it is the locus of direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*). Nor is it non-existent, because it is established by self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).
Therefore, one must necessarily admit that either the eye or the mind is its cause, whose capacity has been activated.
It must be admitted that the eye or the mind does not take as its object even a non-present silver simply because that silver is not present;

thus, there is no restriction [on the objects of cognition] even with respect to time. This implies that the external mind is dependent on other factors, whereas in dreams, the mind has attained independence.

Therefore, in other external cases as well, [the mind] is indeed independent. If it were argued that even in a dream, the mind produces a memory capable of sustaining the impression (*bhāvanā*) of a prior experience, and thus it is not independent, to that he replies: "And dream-cognition is not memory. Why? Because it does not have that form. For the nature of memory is the non-forgetting of an experienced object.
Non-forgetfulness (*asaṃpramoṣa*) is the recollection of an experienced object by virtue of its having been experienced. Such is not the case with dream-cognition;
therefore, it is not memory. Nor is it visual, because of the absence of the operation of the eyes. Thus it is established that the mind is independent with respect to external objects.
He refutes this as follows: "This is not sound;
for in that case, the dependence on an object would be useless, and the manifestation of another form would be equally [unjustified]."
For even memory, though clear, is present as if occurring through a defect when it occurs in a dream.

Regarding what was stated—that the eye and other senses do not have the past as their object—it is replied: the eye and other senses indeed manifest an object that is present, such as a fragment of mother-of-pearl. Why? Because of the dependence upon it; that is, because of the dependence upon the mother-of-pearl and so forth. Otherwise, if there were no such dependence, the proximity of that object—the presence of the mother-of-pearl—would be useless.

Whence follows the consequence of its fruitlessness? To this he says: because the cognition of silver would occur even in the absence of that [mother-of-pearl], were it not dependent upon it. This is the intended meaning: the cognition of silver is not, like the eye and other [senses], a cause [of the object].
If the appearance as silver does not have the mother-of-pearl as its object, then even the appearance of the present cannot have the non-present as its domain;
for the fragment of mother-of-pearl requires that [appearance] alone, just as in the absence of the eye and other [senses], there is no perception of silver elsewhere when they are absent.

For otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that even in the case of silver-cognition, there would be an absence of [the cognition of] silver. Therefore, the cognition of silver depends upon the piece of mother-of-pearl precisely by way of being its object.
As for what was said—that [cognition] has another object while being unassociated with another form—to that he says: "If the manifestation of silver..."
Nor, then, does the appearance of the present have the mother-of-pearl as its object; rather, it does not have the non-present as its domain.

This is the intended meaning: if this cognition had the past silver as its object, it would apprehend the silver in that very state of being past; and in that case, those desiring to obtain it would not act toward it, because what is past cannot be attained. It is not so.

Indeed, having understood the past [silver] as such through the word, the beggar—though his own body is emaciated by hunger—proceeds to beg from Yudhiṣṭhira, who is most dear to the generous man. This is because, although the silver is past, it does not appear there as a defect;
and because of the perception of a form common to silver, which is grasped as "this is mother-of-pearl" in its present state. The cause for the non-discrimination between them is...

And because the specific universal of "mother-of-pearl-ness" does not manifest, there arises—due to the force of repeated practice in the non-determination of difference—an equivalence with the cognition of nearby, desired silver. Consequently, there occurs the grammatical co-referential designation (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) "this is silver," as well as the initiation of a practical activity identical to that of a correct cognition of nearby silver; yet it is merely mother-of-pearl.

If it is argued that the status of [the cognition] as a sublater is established because it removes the non-apprehension of difference—which is opposed to its own object—thereby negating the practical activity regarding silver previously occasioned by the prior cognition, we say no; for it is illogical that the mere non-apprehension of difference should initiate such practical activity. Indeed, it is the appearance of nearby silver that constitutes that practical activity.

The absence of a reason (rahetu) does not mean that it does not appear as such; rather, because it is similar to that [real object], it is also capable of giving rise to its conventional usage (*tadvyavahāra*).

If it is argued that "similarity to that" consists in the non-appearance of difference, then since this [present cognition] also possesses similarity to the cognition of past silver through its appearing as something not presently existing, there would also follow for it the engagement in the same conventional usage as that [past cognition].
Thus, for you, it follows that one possessing the cognition of silver would both engage with and withdraw from the piece of mother-of-pearl lying before them;

this results in two contradictory actions. [Objection: This undesirable consequence does not apply, because the very appearance of the object lying before one—when its difference from silver is not apprehended due to the cognition of silver—is the cause for a practical activity similar to that of the appearance of real, present silver.

If it is argued: "But why does this cognition—'this is silver, and that is white and shining'—not initiate practical activity (vyavahāra), given that it is equal to a correct cognition of nearby silver due to the non-apprehension of their difference? For just as there is equality with that [correct] cognition because of the non-determination of difference, so too is there equality with the cognition 'that is silver, and this is white and shining' because of the non-apprehension of difference."

Because there is no determination (*adhyavasāya*). Nor is there any distinction between two determinations such that one alone would bring about its own appropriate similarity and the other would not. Thus, this [objection] remains in the same state regarding these two contradictory actions.

There would be the undesirable consequence of [the senses] being identical [to consciousness]. Furthermore, the means for knowledge are not equivalent to the means for the empirical usage of a conscious agent, such that one could claim that the empirical usage of the final object arises solely from the cause of knowledge. This is because we observe that even the eyes and other sense organs—which have not yet arisen in their specific form, nor their effects, nor their relations—are nonetheless means for knowledge. However, in the case of the empirical usage of a conscious agent, there is an invariable rule that it is produced by cognition (*vijñāna*).

Because it is not subject to further questioning, this is established: the cognition of silver under dispute has as its object the thing currently perceived before one, because—even though that [silver] is not the object of the means [to obtain silver]—it invariably causes a person desiring that [silver] to act toward that very [perceived thing]. Whatever, while not being the object of the means [to obtain something], causes a person desiring that thing to act toward a particular locus, has that locus as its object.

Just as there is a cognition of real silver that is established for both parties; for this restriction of activity is pervaded by having a cause, and since that [cause] is excluded when the object is not that [silver], it excludes its own pervaded—namely, the restriction of activity—and establishes it only when that [silver] is the object. Thus, the logical connection (*pratibandha*) is established. Nor is this [restriction] [possible] when the object is not that [silver].

It must also arise from the mere non-apprehension of difference; for it has been stated that even the non-apprehension of non-difference leads to the undesirable consequence of the agent’s engagement in or withdrawal from activity, due to the occurrence of contradictory operations through the instigation of its own appropriate empirical usage.
Therefore, one must admit the apprehension of one thing as another. And in this way, its manifestation as being present is logically established.

And likewise, if the appearance of silver does not have mother-of-pearl as its object because it is something else, then the appearance of the present [silver] would also not have the non-present as its domain, since the state of being "something else" remains unchanged. If it were argued that the cognition appearing as present will have the non-present as its domain due to a defect in consciousness—

This is due to [the specific] capacity [of the cause]. Nor is it correct to say that the function of the defects (*doṣas*) consists merely in obstructing the causal efficiency (*kāryakāraṇasāmarthya*) and not in producing another effect, for a barley seed damaged by defects never serves to produce a rice sprout. [For example], by the power of defects such as *bhasmaka*, the digestive fire (*vahni*) in the stomach digests various kinds of food and drink.

[The opponent argues: "Because [the reason] is unperceived and because there is deviation (*vyabhicāra*). The state of being the essence of food that has been eaten and drunk is the effect of the fire within the stomach; since the state of being the *bhasmaka* [disorder] occurs through its obstruction, there is no deviation.
[The author replies: No, for here too the same [principle] applies. Even in the case of the sense faculties and so forth, their capacity to produce ultimate cognition is inherent (*svābhāvika*).
The defects (doṣas), by obstructing the capacity [of the senses] and providing the cause for erroneous cognition, do not deviate from their essential nature.

Nor is it logical to claim that what is not present cannot be an object simply because it does not appear [in its true form], since that would render conceptual construction (vikalpa) impossible. Is it being argued that the non-present silver is not an object *because* it is non-present, or rather...

"Is it also an object by way of being silver? Regarding this, we do not disagree with the first alternative. However, if the point to be proven (*sādhya*) is that it is not an object by way of being silver, then "not appearing as such" (*tattvena-anavabhāsanam*) is unestablished (*asiddha*) and cannot serve as a reason (*hetu*). Thus it was stated by the Teacher:
"In some way it does appear, yet it does not appear absolutely; therefore, it is not non-cognitive (*nāvedikā*). Therefore...

He says that even though [an object] does not exist in the present due to the influence of a defect (*doṣa*), it is indeed perceived as being present: "The state of being such [i.e., appearing as present] for a cognition whose object is non-existent due to a defect is the manifestation of the present; this is exactly the same as the manifestation of silver for another [cognition] whose object is a mother-of-pearl shell."

The same defect applies equally to the other case as well. Furthermore, there is the appearance of what is not present within what is present, but not the appearance of what is present within what is not present, because the proximity of the object must be effective. And [there is the cognition]: "This is not silver."

Because a negation is only possible for that which has been previously asserted. The cognition of one suffering from ophthalmia as having a mass of hair in the rays of light does not constitute a deviation [from the rule] that depends upon an object. Regarding dreams as well, is it the memory that possesses the appearance of the present, or is it the independence of the mind? It is logical that it is the memory that has the appearance of the present. Immediately...

Because there is a clear recollection of what was experienced during the day, neither deficient nor excessive, and because it is perceived as if it were present due to the influence of a defect, no independence of the mind [to perceive the past] is observed; nor is there an excess of capacity due to the defect.
Having thus stated their superficial similarity, he states the distinction of his own [position] regarding the present: "In the present..."
This appearance of silver in a fragment of mother-of-pearl is not an appearance of present silver in something that is not present;
rather, the meaning is that the cognition "this is silver" has as its object the thing standing before one, and not a past object.
Why? Because the proximity of the object must be fruitful. And for what reason [is it so]? Because there is a negation of that which was suspected, such as "this is not silver."

Because negation is possible. By pointing to the finger, the disputants negate the very fragment of mother-of-pearl as being silver; thus, it is understood that silver was previously projected there by a prior cognition. Nor is that projection due to the non-apprehension of a distinction, for the non-apprehension of a distinction remains as an obstacle even while one is alive. Therefore, [it is] contrary...

In that case, it is logical that [the cognition] entails that [object], and not otherwise. Furthermore, "presence before the eyes" (purovarttitva) is not entailed by this [cognition] with respect to the past, because it is impossible to negate that [past object] as being "this" (idantayā). Thus, it is clear that this cognition has only the object present before one as its domain.

Now, is it not the case that for one suffering from ophthalmia (*taimirika*), a cognition of hairs arises? Yet, in that instance, there is no presence of hairs, nor of anything else, by which that [cognition] could have an objective support (*ālambana*). Therefore, that cognition must be admitted to have as its objective support hairs that are not present. Consequently, the visual [cognition] is inconstant (*vyabhicārin*) with respect to its object.

To this [objection] beginning with "of those such as the jaundiced," he says: "The cognition of one suffering from ophthalmia (taimirika) which appears as a mass of hair occurs in relation to the rays of light; thus, there is no deviation [from the rule] that depends upon an external object.
As for what was said—that in the state of dreaming, the mind, having attained independence, [perceives] the external—[that is refuted].

Desiring to explain this, he reflects: "Does memory even in a dream manifest the present, or is there an independence of the mind therein? Having reflected, he asserts his own position: "It is logical that memory manifests the present. He states the reason: "Because of a clear memory, which is neither deficient nor excessive, of what was experienced on the immediately preceding day."
Because it perceives [objects] as if they were present, due to the affliction of defects; however, it is not logical that the mind possesses an unobserved independence regarding external objects.

Now, why does the defect itself not bestow such an excellence of capacity upon the mind, by which it might function independently with respect to the external? To this, he says: "And no excellence of capacity is observed through defect, by which the mind..."

Because that [dream] is the cause for removing the defect. As for the perception of true dreams, if it is argued that it is "unseen" because one perceives the present object as such [during the dream], but "seen" because one observes a correspondence with the objects described in the dream upon waking— no, that is not so.

Because there is an absence of correspondence with the narrative. Any correspondence with the narrative would be merely coincidental (*kākatālīya*). But how can the perception of what is yet to come as if it were present be true? Let it not be true; nevertheless, the mind possesses independence. That [perception] too is a recollection of that which was experienced in two ways. Otherwise, there would be no unseen [cause] for the mind.

Independent knowledge of reality would produce that [cognition] regarding external objects; however, it has been stated that error arises from the mind solely due to its latent dispositions (*saṃskāra*). Why is there no excess of capacity in the mind resulting from defects? To this he says: "Because the defect is the cause for removing that. The word "that" refers back to the capacity for generating cognition.

If one should think that dream-vision is indeed real— for example, just as one who has experienced being embraced by a beloved in a dream perceives it exactly so even upon waking— it is not correct to say that this is a memory appearing as a present experience, because such an appearance would be untenable in the absence of a sublater (*bādhaka*), and there is no such sublater.
[The opponent argues: "Because of the observation of correspondence [between the dream and reality], one must therefore admit the independence of the mind in this case. To that, he replies:

"But as for the vision of a true dream, if it is because of grasping a present object in that way, then that is not seen [to be the case]. Indeed, even this cognition is not correspondent. For instance, in a dream, this self has reached a state of wakefulness and perceives itself as being embraced by a beloved woman."

He perceived that he had been embraced; yet, even while seeing the embrace of his beloved with his lotus-eyes wide open, he understands, "I was asleep and have only now awakened. The meaning is: how could there be for him a correspondence between the object seen in a dream and reality?
He raises an objection: "If it is argued that the independence of the mind is observed because we see a correspondence with objects seen in a dream upon waking— for instance,

when in a dream a man wearing white garlands and garments says to a certain Brahmin, 'O Somaśarman, on the fifth day from now, early in the morning, the king will honor you with a choice village consisting mostly of fertile land'."

Regarding the phrase "you [are that]," the meaning is that on the fifth day at dawn, Somaśarman, having been thus honored, becomes one for whom the dream was true. He refutes this, saying: "No. Why? Because there is an absence of correspondence with the narrative.
For when awakened by the narrative, Somaśarman, even while remembering, does not [recognize] the narrator, the Brāhmaṇāyana.

One perceives that excellence of the narrative and considers it to have ascended into memory. Let it not be thought that because there is a correspondence with the narrative, the dream is real; therefore, he says: "But the correspondence with the narrative is merely accidental (*kākatālīya*), occurring by chance through fate; it does not validate the dream-cognition, for such [correspondence] belongs only to that kind of [cognition] which possesses its own specific causal conditions."
Because it is frequently observed that the Greek [philosophers] were inconsistent; for consistency depends upon destiny (fate). Now, one might object:

where there is the appearance of the past as if it were present, let that be governed by mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), since the mind has its origin in the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of prior experience. But where, however, the future itself appears as if it were present—as in a dream—from what does that arise?
How much less, then, can there be experience, and how much less the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) thereof, since the mind is dependent upon those?
To this he says: "But how can the perception of what is yet to be be real, as if it were present? The objector says: "Let it not be real."

Because its capacity must be postulated; for if it were a specific property (*dharma-viśeṣa*), it would follow that there is perception of things as they truly are. This is because its capacity with respect to its effect is not observed and must therefore be postulated. Furthermore, if dream-cognition is not memory, then it is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) either, because there is no external object to be grasped in that manner. Therefore, it is not independent regarding an external object.

The mind [is not external]. Because it is ungraspable in a dream; or, if it were graspable, there would be a grasping of what has been previously experienced, as that is how it is observed. One should not assume an excess of capacity for the unseen due to some defect; thus, in either case, the mind is not independent and external. By this, the perception of hair and so forth caused by ophthalmia is also refuted.
Granted that there might be independence of the mind, since the possibility of [an external] impression (*saṃskāra*) is non-existent;
the respondent reveals his own intention: "Even that is the recollection of something of that kind previously experienced elsewhere.
For nothing entirely unexperienced is ever perceived in a dream. How could even mutually contradictory things [be so perceived] at some place and at some time?"

Since there is the possibility of the delusion of simultaneous experience regarding objects perceived by consciousness, why then is memory resorted to in all cases with such effort? To this he says: "Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of postulating an unseen independence for the mind.
If it were argued that even in a dream, because the arising of pleasure born from union with a beloved is perceived...

[Objection: Its function consists in its active manifestation (*samudācāra*); therefore, it is that very mind, as distinguished by that [function], which will bring about the experience of the pleasant, so there is no need for a latent impression (*saṃskāra*). To this, he replies: "If it were a specific quality (*dharma-viśeṣa*), it would follow that there is perception of things as they truly are.
For it is understood from scripture (*āgama*) that a specific quality is the cause of perceiving things as they truly are; how then could it lead to false cognition?

Moreover, a worldly cause produces its own effect by depending on something uncommon; yet, no such independence of the mind is perceived. Therefore, it must be postulated that a specific quality (*dharma-viśeṣa*) alone is the cause, acting without assistance, and this is established through the means of inference known as *adṛṣṭa*. Thus he says: "The independence of the mind [belongs] to that specific quality."

Because it would entail the postulation of an unseen capacity (*adṛṣṭasāmarthya*) for the sake of the effect. Furthermore, if dream-cognition is not memory and is not a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) according to your view, then the mind must function toward that object independently. Or, if it is not even a means of valid knowledge, why?
Because an object appears in dream-cognition, yet when there is a sublation (*bādhaka*), that object is not apprehended as existing externally in that manner.

The reply is: In that case, the mind is not independent with respect to external objects, because such a [mind] is not perceived as a grasper during dreams. Or, if it were to grasp an object in the form of a thing devoid of any distinction of mode, then mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) alone would be the cause of waking and of memory.
And since that [cultivation] is impossible without a prior experience, there is the grasping of what was previously experienced. Thus, the corruption of established [objects] is proven.

Because the mind, which is dependent on latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), is observed to be the cause of external memory; however, one should not assume an additional capacity based on defects or the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*). Therefore, whether the external object is apprehended or not apprehended, the external mind is in both cases not independent. By this, [the same applies] to the cognition of dreams regarding the mind.
By way of demonstrating independence, it has been refuted that the cognition of hair and so forth arising from ophthalmia is mental;
for that cognition has particles of light as its objective support, being caused by the eye together with its defects.
As for what was said regarding "lack of confidence," that has been addressed elsewhere by the Teacher:
"The non-scholar, knowing the established position of the Mīmāṃsakas— that validity arises from cognition alone— rejects it on account of [perceived] deviation."
Since this has been refuted by the preceding series of arguments, it is not refuted here again. Nevertheless, the method of refutation is indicated here:
Is non-deviation itself validity, or is it the cause of validity, or its pervader? For...

Because deviation is observed in some cases, there would be a lack of confidence in cognition in general even when that deviation is absent. Validity is not simply the absence of deviation; for even in the case of smoke and the like, which are invariably concomitant with fire and so forth, there would be invalidity if, due to some cause, they fail to produce the cognition of fire. Deviation...

It is not tenable that even the eyes and other [senses], which are the causes of the cognitions of their respective objects such as blue and so forth, possess validity (*prāmāṇya*), because they lack the status of being the most effective means (*sādhakatamatva*) with respect to the act of valid cognition (*pramiti*). Otherwise, it would follow that even firewood and the like would not be instruments for cooking and similar acts. Nor is [the sense organ] the cause of validity; therefore...

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that the eyes and other sense organs—though they cause the cognition of blue and other objects—are not valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*), because they deviate from those specific objects. For while certain things such as smoke depend upon non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) for the generation of the cognition of fire and so forth, the eyes and other organs do not require it; this is due to the restriction of their own nature (*svabhāvaniyama*). By this, pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*) [is refuted].

It should be understood that the validity of non-deviation has already been refuted. If it is argued that non-deviation is required by cognition for its own function, we say no, because this cannot withstand analysis. Furthermore, if it were the case that a cognition endowed with non-deviation is a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and the absence of that [non-deviation] is the reality, then such a cognition, being of that nature, would be sufficient for its own function.
"Because false cognition lacks capacity in that regard"—this is not so, because the alternatives are untenable. To explain:

its effect is said to be either the manifestation of the object of knowledge (*vijñeya-avabhāsa*), or the initiation of conventional activity appropriate to its own domain. In that case, it is first of all impossible for there to be an unerring [manifestation] when the manifestation of the object arises depending merely upon the acquisition of its own nature.

There is no dependence on the movement of the sense organs. For we do not wait for this [cognition] to observe the non-deviation from its own object regarding the manifestation of the object within the cognition that has already arisen. Indeed, the very arising of the cognition is the activity in the manifestation of the object.
As it has been said: "Therefore, the very birth of the intellect with respect to the object is held to be its operation; and that alone is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)."
Regarding "form" (rūpa):

"Indeed, that [cognition] does not remain for even a moment, nor is it produced as having the nature of valid cognition, such that it might subsequently function in the apprehension of an object, like the sense organs and so forth. And thus [it is said].

Now, in the engagement of conventional practice appropriate to its own domain, cognition requires non-deviation (*avyabhicāritā*). For cognition does not initiate conventional practice merely by virtue of being "cognition," since that would entail such practice even from false cognition (*mithyājñāna*). Therefore, its capacity for consistency—its ability to bring about purposeful action (*arthakriyā*)—which distinguishes it from false cognition, is non-deviation.

The characteristic of validity (*cāritālakṣaṇa*) must be understood as a factor for the engagement of a discerning person; for indeed, without non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*), there can be no attainment of that object from it, because there is no deviation regarding one's own purpose, since another cognition does not arise from it.
Otherwise, there would be an over-extension [of the definition]. As it has been said:
"Since [the cognition] exists even when the object is absent, it possesses the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) even in the case of perception;
if its cause is the nature of the connection [between the object and the cognition], then both [perception and inference] are equal."

That direct perception (*pratyakṣa-jñāna*) is of two kinds: the valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) which prompts action by manifesting the accomplishment of purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*), and that which is its opposite when it has reached a state of habitual familiarity (*abhyāsadaśā*). In this regard, the validity of the latter must be accepted based on the cognition that manifests purposeful activity. As it has been said: "When there is comprehension of an object through a means of valid cognition, [its validity is established] by the efficacy of the resulting activity."

"Valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that which possesses an object. Likewise, valid cognition is non-contradictory knowledge, which is the stability of purposeful action (*arthakriyāsthiti*), meaning non-deception. This [is established] through the perception of another thing that is invariably concomitant with that [first] object, when one has reached a state of mastery. For example, the validity of a distant cognition of fire, whose validity was obscured by the doubt that it might be a cluster of fire-trees (*kiśuka*), [is confirmed] by smoke.

If it is argued that the ascertainment of validity arises from perception [itself], yet a cognition manifesting purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) cannot determine the validity of the initial operative cognition (*pravartaka-vijñāna*) unless its own validity has been grasped— and if its validity were already grasped, there would be the consequence of an infinite regress— [we reply]: no, because the validity of the cognition manifesting purposeful action is established in its own nature (*svarūpa*).

Because that which is yet to be led [to its goal] cannot function as a fruit, it lacks the capacity to instigate activity; thus, it does not conform to the definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), since the ascertainment of deviation is of no use [in that case]. Furthermore, because that very nature is established through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), it is beyond the reach of doubt.
As it has been said: "The cognition of its own nature is intrinsic. The authors of the treatises have also stated:

"Only a cognition whose nature is pleasure and so forth, which is of such a kind as to be capable of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), possesses the definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); it has its capacity for apprehension established intrinsically (*svataḥ*).
If it is argued that this is not so because of mutual dependence (*anyonyasaṃśraya*), we say no, because activity is of two kinds. In this regard, the following might be thought:

If it is argued that the determination of non-deviation of the mind arises from a cognition that manifests as purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), then from what does that [cognition] itself arise? If it is argued that it arises from a cognition that prompts the activity of discerning persons (*prekṣāvat*) because its non-deviation is certain, then a circular dependency (*anyonyāśraya*) results; for in this regard, there are two kinds of activity for discerning persons. Indeed, there are two types of activity here for discerning persons, and of these, the first—

The first [cognition] is for the purpose of examining the initiating consciousness (*pravarttaka-vijñāna*), while the second is for the purpose of attaining causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) from a consciousness that manifests as the means of accomplishment already examined, arising from a consciousness of the same class. For example, just as a farmer’s initial activity—consisting of sowing seeds in a prepared field situated in a basin—is for the purpose of examining the seed, he... [continues].

In that case, having understood the true nature of the seed from the production of the sprout, one initiates a second activity—characterized by sowing seeds of that same kind—in soil that has been prepared, with the desire to obtain a crop. Likewise, this [present] activity is also twofold; thus, there is no circularity (*anyonyasaṃśraya*). Nor is there any contradiction with the status of being a discerning person (*prekṣāvattva*), for [this is done] through the means of investigation.

For one who is about to act, there is no engagement with that which is not a means or with a doubtful means; or, even if one were to engage due to doubt regarding the means, there is still no impairment of one's status as a discerning person (*prekṣāvat*), because doubt concerning benefit is a factor for the engagement of a discerning person, whereas doubt concerning harm is a factor for desisting from action. However, for one who has reached the stage of mastery, the perceptual cognition brings about the fulfillment of purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*).

The determination of the validity of knowledge arises from inference due to its similarity to other cognitions. However, in the case of inference itself, because it is produced by the perception of an object that is inseparably connected [with the probandum] and because its deviation has been ruled out, its validity is determined intrinsically (*svataḥ*). Its own...
"It may be that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) requires a determination of non-deviation for the sake of initiating activity appropriate to its object-domain;

this, however, is incorrect. For it is difficult for a cognition manifesting purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) to possess a determinative certainty regarding its own object even when there is non-deviation from the object—how much more so, then, for a prior cognition to possess such capacity for attainment?"

If it is argued: "Since that [cognition] which possesses causal efficacy is established by self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), what is the purpose of investigating its non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*), and what is the point of its validity (*prāmāṇya*)?"—then what about this case: when in a dream, a lover has a cognition of a woman who is capable of performing the function appropriate to her, followed by a cognition of activity toward her, and subsequently a cognition of sexual union?
Regarding the statement that "pleasure" and "the emission of the final element" [are valid], let it be granted for now that the first cognition of the beloved woman possesses validity;

for there is no cognition elsewhere that does not manifest as purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). However, because that [cognition] exists immediately prior to waking, and because the form of the beloved woman—which was supposed to perform that function—is sublated upon waking, and because pleasure and the emission of the final element consist of nothing but the mind (*manomātra*), [they lack external reality].

If it is argued that this is not a fault because, even in the absence of an actual beloved woman acting as the source, [the cognition] arises from the mere knowledge of her, and because its persistence during the waking state is not contradictory; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of its cessation—just like the bitten lower lip or nail-marks produced by the physical reality of the beloved—[we reply: No, for in the present case, the cognition manifesting purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) is non-deviant (*avyabhicārin*).

Because there is no certainty regarding the capacity for purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), due to the absence of grasping [the object] through direct experience, the cognition that prompts activity lacks the certainty of validity characterized by the attainment of an object capable of purposeful action; thus, it is equivalent to dream-consciousness.
If it should be thought that the cognition manifesting purposeful action is intrinsically valid (*svataḥ pramāṇam*), [then consider] purposeful action...

Because it consists of certainty (*niścayātmakatva*). Nor does this [definition] over-apply (*prasaṅga*) to dreams and the like; for in those cases, there is non-validity due to the arising of a sublater (*bādhaka*) at another time, in another person, or in another state. This applies equally even to those cognitions that prompt action, except in cases where there is persistent attachment (*abhiniveśa*). Furthermore, "non-deviation" (*avyabhicāritva*) of a cognition consists in its correspondence with the object; and this is not...

Without the apprehension of that object, it is not possible to reach a conclusion. Indeed, one who has not apprehended fire cannot ascertain the non-deviation of smoke from it. Furthermore, momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) is not entirely unknown, since it is well-established in the scriptures of the astronomers (*jyotirvida*) as the state of existing for only a mere fraction of time devoid of prior and posterior parts;
thus, it is not the case that [momentariness] is absolutely unestablished for existence (*sattva*).

The non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) of that [fire] would not be possible to ascertain. Or, let it be as it may; there is no harm to us whatsoever. Furthermore, neither a non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*), nor a valid cognition whose validity has not been determined by another valid cognition, can serve as the means for grasping that [non-deviation], which is a necessary factor for grasping non-deviation. Indeed, fire, even when made an object by a non-valid cognition or by a valid cognition whose validity has not been apprehended, is not [necessarily] non-deviant with respect to smoke.
It is possible for there to be the apprehension of the concomitance (*cāra*). Therefore, without the apprehension of the concomitance, there is no apprehension of the object;
and without the apprehension of the object, there is no apprehension of the concomitance. Thus, there arises the fallacy of mutual dependence (*parasparāśraya*).

And so, by means of an inference based on similarity with that which has been observed to have efficacy, there is the apprehension of the non-deviation of one's own object in the case of perceptual cognitions that have reached the stage of mastery (*abhyāsadaśāpanna*).
It should be understood as refuted.

Furthermore, regarding the intrinsic validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*) of inference that was asserted in that system—since perception grasps its own object's non-deviation, and since inference arises based on that [perception] according to the stated sequence—the very emergence of inference is difficult to obtain; how much less so its validity?

[118] Whence, then, is its validity? And how could it be intrinsic? But has it not been stated that, if non-deviation is not apprehended, there can be no confidence for discerning people based on cognition alone? True, this has been stated; however, this must be explained: what is this "lack of confidence"?

Is it doubt (*saṃśaya*) or rather ignorance (*ajñāna*)? It cannot be ignorance, because cognition itself is of the nature of knowledge. Nor can it be doubt; for they maintain that doubt is a deliberation dependent upon the recollection of specific characteristics, having either three or five causes:
the perception of common properties, the perception of multiple properties, disagreement, and the states of perception and non-perception regarding specific characteristics.

Those experts declare that doubt is a deliberation characterized by a desire for knowledge (*apekṣā*). Furthermore, the recollection of a particularity is not possible when that particularity has not been previously apprehended. Nor can the apprehension of that [particularity]—which is itself of the nature of doubt—be the cause of recollection; for if recollection were already present, then [the apprehension] would exist because of it, and since recollection would arise from that [apprehension], there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). This remains true even if [recollection] is held to be produced from a mental impression (*saṃskāra*).

Because it would lead to an infinite regress; and because, when another alternative is possible, one does not resort to beginninglessness. Thus it is established that the ascertainment of non-deviation is not the cause for the ascertainment of a cognition’s own object, since the cognition depends upon that [ascertainment] for its own production. That which is required for the production of the nature of something is not the cause of that thing. For example, the cognition of the inferable object [is not the cause of the inferable object itself].

Regarding the cognition of the mark (*liṅga*): nor is the reason (*hetu*) unestablished. For it has been stated—that the cognition of its non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) is dependent upon the ascertainment of its own object. Indeed, the state of being a cause (*kāraṇatva*) is pervaded by existence prior to the effect;

thus, when [the reason] is excluded from the opposite case (*vipakṣa*) through the perception of the contradictory (*viruddhopalabdhi*), it also excludes the state of being a cause. This is the logical connection (*pratibandha*).

Success (*siddhi*) [is achieved]. Even the power to attain an object is nothing other than the manifestation of that object as such; for cognition does not physically bring an object into its own hand, but rather prompts the knower to act toward it. And this prompting of the knower toward that object is nothing other than the presentation of the true nature of the thing. Furthermore, the true nature of an object is nothing other than its own essential form (*svarūpa*).
