And this cognition experiences that very form of its object by its very nature; it does not, however, depend upon non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) and other such factors.

This is what is called the self-validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) of cognition with respect to its object. Furthermore, cognition does not experience the object as being otherwise than the form that is being experienced. In the case of the error of silver, if one were to grasp the object as being otherwise through that error, then for one seeking silver—

There is no [need for external validation] there, because there is no activity [of such a validating cognition] and because no sublation is possible. Consequently, the "otherwise-ness" (anyathātva) of a cognition is to be determined by another cognition;

since it depends on something else in that regard, it is said to be "extrinsic" (parataḥ). Furthermore, as for the fact that this cognition consists in the realization of reality, that too is understood from another cognition—whether mental or inferential—that grasps it.

It is said that [validity] is intrinsic (*svataḥ*). This is because the cognition apprehending its own nature does not depend on another cognition. Nor should one suspect its lack of validity based on the possibility of sublation (*bādhaka*); for such a suspicion is untenable regarding that which is incapable of being sublated. Indeed, there exist certain cognitions belonging to a person whose senses and mind are healthy, occurring in the midst of bright light—

Regarding those [cognitions] whose objects are the objects of valid knowledge (*prameya*), wherein not even the slightest sublation has ever been observed, how could there be a possibility of sublation? Even in such cases, one must be a discerning observer. If, despite pursuing the matter with effort, one does not bring about its sublation, then its validity remains established as general, uncontradicted, and independent. But if one were to see [such sublation],...
Therefore, that which is excluded should not be imagined elsewhere. As it has been said:
"In the world, a mental intuition born from fallacious signs and the like is non-determinate."
One whose consciousness is full in every respect is [truly] full; there is no one at all who is deficient.

Furthermore, it is observed that even when one has the intuition, "My brother will surely come tomorrow," the mind functions independently of external factors such as the eyes or signs; and since all things— whether existent or non-existent entities such as substances and so forth— are [cognized] as "everything is everything," the validity of cognition is established by its very nature as consciousness.
A cognition is set aside by the knowledge of a defect arising from a cause that brings about a change in the object's nature.
In this world, only two are censured: one who is free from suspicion and one who is excessively suspicious.
Thus, no further cognition beyond three or four is required;
for that much alone suffices, as it attains validity by itself.
"For he who, out of delusion, imagines even non-sublation to be a sublation will, being of a doubting nature in all worldly transactions, go to his destruction.
Nor is this merely a curse; for it has been said: "A suspicion of sublation is not appropriate regarding that which is incapable of being sublated."

If it is argued that [validity] is not intrinsic (*svataḥ*), but rather that because invalidity is known through sublation (*bādhaka*) and the presence of defects in the cause (*kāraṇadoṣa*), the ascertainment of validity depends upon the apprehension of their absence—this is not so. For when a single cause is postulated for the production of an effect, it is illogical to postulate multiple causes.
Furthermore, the apprehension of sublation and the defects in the cause serves as the cause for the ascertainment of invalidity.

Since the absence [of defects] is merely that which obstructs validity, and since validity is established by cognition alone in the absence of such [obstruction], that absence need not be depended upon. Furthermore, it [the absence of obstruction] is required only when there is a suspicion; and that suspicion occurs only regarding such objects as have been previously observed [to be defective], not everywhere. Thus, it is established that the validity of all means of knowledge is intrinsic (*svataḥ*).

Because it does not depend on anything other than that. Whatever depends on something else for its existence, that [quality] belongs to it by its very nature (*svata eva*). For example, the power to burn belongs to fire by its own nature. And this independence from anything else has been established by the preceding argument. For if that which depends on something else were not dependent upon its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), there would be the subverting consequence (*bādhaka*) that it would not be supported by it, since being unsupported by it is the opposite of being supported by it.
The negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not doubtful; thus it has been said: "Let it be understood that the validity of all means of knowledge is intrinsic (*svataḥ*);
for a capacity that does not exist intrinsically cannot be produced by anything else."
Therefore, it is established that there is no lack of confidence [in the means of valid cognition].
Now, he refutes the Naiyāyika position that the universe is an object of yogic knowledge:
"In the world, intuitive flash arising from fallacious signs and the like is not a certain cognition."
Everyone possesses complete discernment when it is full; when it is deficient, no one does.

Furthermore, it is indeed observed that in worldly intuition—such as when one thinks, "My brother will surely come tomorrow"—the mind functions independently of external factors like sense organs or inferential marks (*liṅga*). But is it not the case that in such instances, the actual nature of the brother...

Whether [the objects] such as primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and the person (*puruṣa*), or the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), are taken non-differently as the object of the mind by virtue of worldly means of valid cognition (*lokapramāṇa*), omniscience is established externally even in terms of independence. To this it is replied:
first, supramundane intuition (*pratibhāna*) is the subject of dispute; however, mundane [intuition] has as its domain the pleasant and the unpleasant.

Generally, that which arises from the appearance of signs such as the simultaneous onset of mental clarity or agitation is designated as *pratibhāna* (intuition) itself, and not as a definitive cognition (*niścaya*). Because it touches upon both alternatives and is [perceived as] equal [in weight], it is not of the nature of doubt (*saṃśaya*). It is simply intuition; it is not a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because its result is non-definitive.

Because it is a certainty that depends upon another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); likewise, because it depends on the class of inferential marks (*liṅga*) and so forth, let it be so even there [in the case of inference], since there was prior perception. But here, however, since it is impossible to perceive all entities—scattered across specific places, times, and states—even by way of their form, how can the mind have independence in this regard? Therefore:

He said: "Everything" or "all"—is this arranged in a form devoid of specific modes, or as possessing a distinction of modes? Since it is not now [arranged] by way of causal modes, the Naiyāyika states the categories accepted by himself and others through distinctions such as "existent and non-existent categories," "substance and so forth," "primordial nature and spirit," or "the five aggregates," and so on, according to worldly authority and by means of the mind.
That which has been made an object of cultivation becomes the object of supramundane direct perception characterized by vivid manifestation;

thus, omniscience is established through the independence of the mind. This is what is meant: having grasped [an object] either without or with its specific modes by means of mundane valid cognition, for one who cultivates it, the mind—its obscurations removed by that cultivation—[attains such clarity].
"The universe itself plunges [into cognition] independently.

To this it is replied: First, supramundane intuition (*pratibhāna*), being a subject of dispute regarding its very existence, cannot have its independence denied in its essential nature. However, as for mundane [intuition], which has as its objects the pleasant and the unpleasant...

It does not arise from an independent mind, because it generally originates from the appearance of signs characterized by the simultaneous occurrence of mental clarity, agitation, and so forth; and precisely because it arises from the appearance of such signs, it is non-ascertaining in nature. Accordingly, they designate it as "such an intuition" (*pratibhāna*) rather than an ascertainment (*niścaya*). This is due to its contact with both alternatives...
"And because it is equal [to both alternatives], it is not of the nature of doubt.

Now, if it is neither doubt nor certainty, then the true nature of that cognition must be stated; therefore, he says: 'It is simply intuition (*pratibhā*)'. For this cognition does not have as its object two contradictory alternatives appearing equally, such that [it would be a doubt]."
It is of the nature of doubt; nor does it ascertain even a cognition whose object is a single alternative, by which it might be a certainty.
Nor does it fail to manifest an object that is a single alternative, by which it would not be [a means of knowledge]. Therefore, it is established that it is merely intuition (*pratibhā*).

If it is argued that, although it is itself non-ascertaining in nature, it may still be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it generates ascertainment—just like the eye and other sense organs—then:

He says: It is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Why? Because its result is non-definitive (*aniścaya*). [Objection: But when a distinction in intuition (*pratibhā*) has arisen, and where a definitive certainty (*niścaya*) follows immediately thereafter, why is that distinct intuition, which results in certainty, not a means of valid cognition? To this he replies: Because the certainty depends upon another means of valid cognition. It is not, first of all, [the case] of intuition...

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that everything would produce certainty independently; for dependence on the inferential mark (*liṅga*) and so forth is required. Otherwise, the connection with external objects would belong to everyone, being established by the mind alone without depending on those [marks].

"It would exist in everything at all times. Because of a specific unseen force (*adṛṣṭaviśeṣa*), the mind (*manas*)—independent of the sense organs, marks, and so forth—would [perceive] even external objects; thus, there would be the consequence of the uselessness of the initiation of the eyes and other organs. For from that very same unseen force, when conditioned by a specific [impression], the accomplishment of all cognition would follow, making those [organs] useless as well. [This implies] an agent who is not an instrument, namely the Self (*ātman*), [possessing] the unseen force...

For it is precisely through specific [causes] that the activity of determination is accomplished. Indeed, even an unseen object does not bring about its realization without a means, since it requires the initiation of the body and so forth. Therefore, the mind’s operation toward these objects is not independent of the senses, marks, and so on;
for this very reason, mental perception regarding all objects does not arise from *dharma* born of yoga, because the accomplishment [of knowledge] depends upon the means of sensory contact.

And if it were dependent on that [cognition], its status as the cause [of the word's meaning] would be rendered redundant, because the capacity of the inferential marks (*liṅga*) and so forth is perceived in various instances precisely when they are independent of such [a cognition].
He concludes: "Thus, because of dependence on things of the nature of inferential marks and so forth, and because of dependence on fallacious inferential marks and so forth..."

Even in that case of worldly intuition (*pratibhāna*), the mind is dependent on something else; otherwise, if it were independent, then— since the mind alone would be the means for the appearance of its signs and so forth, and because the mind is eternally present— the connection of the mind with external objects would occur for every person at all times and regarding all objects, and thus everyone would be an omniscient seer at all times.

Due to a specific *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit), the mind is independent with respect to external objects, occurring only for someone at some time; thus, there is no over-extension [of the principle].
Regarding this, he says: "Due to a specific *adṛṣṭa*, the mind—independent of the sense organs, inferential marks, and so forth—occurs for someone regarding some external object.
[Otherwise] there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the futility of initiating the eyes and other senses. Why? Precisely because of that specific *adṛṣṭa* of the mind.

Since the cognition of all forms and other objects is established through the conditioned [internal organ], let alone the eyes and so forth; even that mind would be useless. Why? Because the activity of discerning form and the rest is accomplished solely by the Self—the agent who is devoid of instruments—through its own specific unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*).

If it should be argued that even an unseen factor (*adṛṣṭa*) does not accomplish an object without a means (*anupāya*), why? Because [the unseen factor] initiates the body and so forth. In that case, the external operation of the mind would not be independent of the senses, marks, and so on. Therefore, since an unseen factor that lacks a means is not a means of accomplishment, mental perception regarding all objects does not arise from the merit (*dharma*) born of yoga; as for that which...

The followers of Svāyambhuva call it "tāraka" (the deliverer). Why? Because it is the means for the contact between the sense organs and their objects, thereby establishing the direct perception (*pratyakṣatva*) of external objects.

If it were argued that it is not merely the conjunction of the sense organ and the object [that constitutes perception], then knowledge of qualities and so forth—which serve as the means for that [conjunction]—would not be direct perception.

This follows as a logical consequence (*prasaṅga*). Nor is it merely *samavāya* (inherence) with the sense organ; for if that were the case, the cognition of sound itself would result in being perceptual (*pratyakṣa*).

Rather, *saṃyuktasamavāya* (inherence in what is conjoined) and other such relations are also means to that [perception]. For this very reason, the venerable Akṣapāda stated, "produced by the contact of the sense organ with the object," so as to avoid contradiction with all cases. Just as in the apprehension of its qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth, there is *saṃyuktasamavāya*.

Or rather, here too, it is because we do not accept that there is a connection— either through conjunction or through the conjunction of what is conjoined— between the mind (manas) conditioned by the factors born of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) or the external sense-organ and that [object]. Otherwise, there would follow the absurd consequence of perceiving objects obstructed by walls and the like.

For even in the case of inference, there would be the undesirable consequence of it being perception; moreover, that [contact] is impossible in the case of things not yet born or those already passed away. For this very reason, there is no contact between the sense organ and the object when both are established [as present], because past and future objects do not exist even then, which would lead to the absurdity of perceiving obstructed objects. Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of inference and other means of knowledge becoming perception.

And because the mention of "contact" (*sannikarṣa*) would be purposeless. [Objection: But surely, since past and future objects are known as qualifiers of place and so forth, cognition has specific places and so forth as its objective support; therefore, contact between the eye or the mind and those [objects] is possible. And since they exist and are present, there is no obstruction for the sense organ regarding cognition that has not yet arisen or has already passed away.

He states by implication that conjunction and so forth will be accepted as the substrata for the sake of establishing the perception of those respective [objects] separated by intervals; for you do not accept that the conjunction of what is conjoined is a cause of perceptual cognition.
Not only is it unaccepted, it is also untenable because it would lead to over-extension (atiprasaṅga); therefore he says: "Otherwise..."
For it would follow that people such as ourselves would perceive objects obstructed by walls and other barriers.

Furthermore, it has been stated in the *Bauddhasarvajñaparīkṣā* that such a capacity does not exist for a mind refined by meditative absorption (*samādhi*) or for the eyes and other sense organs. Consequently, since it would follow that everyone would be omniscient—given that everything is indeed related to everyone in some way [through causal connection]—[the opponent's position is untenable].

[Objection: There is a connection [to perception]. Likewise, it would follow that inference also becomes perception. For it is by virtue of being produced from the contact of a sense organ with its object (*indriyārthasannikarṣa*) that perception is distinguished from inference. If inference were also like that, then it too would be perception.
To explain: as long as smoke and so forth are in contact with the eyes and other senses, and smoke and so forth are [in contact] with fire and so forth, by this—

In some way or another, there exists some kind of sense-object contact; thus, the inference arising from that would result in being [classified as] perception. Nor is it reasonable to claim that, in this case, the smoke and so forth alone are the cause independently of the currently present eye and other senses.

For when the capacity for contact—which has been established as the requisite factor in each respective instance—is possible, it is improper to postulate a capacity for the inferential mark (*liṅga*) and so forth.
Because [the definition] would lead to an over-extension (*atipatti*). Nor does omniscience follow from this alone; thus he says: "Because it is also impossible with respect to things unborn or past.
For this very reason, *saṃnikarṣa* (contact) is not the existence of the sense-organ and the object in a state of mutual suitability for the production of knowledge.

He analyzes the phrase "for this very reason" [as follows]: because past and future objects do not exist at that time when consciousness occurs, it would follow that there is perception of objects that are spatially remote; furthermore, it would result in inference and other means of knowledge being reduced to direct perception (pratyakṣa). He states another reason: and because it would follow that the mention of "contact" (saṃnikarṣa) is purposeless. For by the mere statement "produced from sense-organ and object," those two [contact and non-contact] would already be implied.

Because existence is established; for that which is non-existent cannot be a producer. He objects: "But surely [past and future things exist], because they are known as qualifiers of place and so forth—for instance, 'this earth has had many past kings' or 'it will have many future kings'—since such knowledge has as its objective support a place and so forth that would otherwise be contradictory [to the object's non-existence]."

Because of the pointing out by that very finger and because of the resulting activity toward that object, the status of being a direct perception (pratyakṣatā) is determined for the eye or the mind respectively by the qualifiers such as place and so forth; it does not belong to the causal state [of the sense organ], since contact is possible. Why is it possible?
To this he says: "Because those qualifiers, such as place and so forth, exist and are present, [the contact] is unimpeded."

Since there is no distinction in the fact that knowledge which has not yet arisen or has already passed away is produced by the contact of the sense organ with its object, even the non-manifestation [of the qualifier] is due to the production [of cognition] from the contact of the sense organ with the object to be qualified (*viśeṣya*). Furthermore, in the absence of the characteristics of inference and so forth, [perception] is that which is produced by the contact of the sense organ with its object.

The term "knowledge" (*jñāna*) does not denote the reality (*tattva*) in the case of inference and the like. If it refers to any object whatsoever, then there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of memory being considered perception (*pratyakṣa*). If, on the other hand, it refers to the cognition of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) such as place and so forth, let that be perception because of its direct contact with that [object] alone;

however, it is not the cognition of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). Since it is held that qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*) is perception, the qualifier is also [perceived] by implication (*ākṣepa*) from that.

If it is argued that [the cognition] is perceptual (*pratyakṣa*), we say no, because there is no sensory contact (*asannikarṣāt*). For even if something exists in the present, it does not become a qualified object (*viśiṣṭa*) if its qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is absent; otherwise, the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) would follow that everything would be so. How then is Devadatta’s son called Yajñadatta when his mother has passed away? What is the point here? It is not that he is qualified by her at that time.

"By that [definition], one would fall into [the error of] including linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) [within perception]. The point is this: if, then, that which is not present (*avartamāna*) is not a factor in linguistic usage, then Devadatta [who is absent] would also [not be perceived], because he too is an object of that [same process]. Now, even so, since mountains and the like—which are in sensory contact—are objects of inference, it would follow that inference itself is perception; to this he says: "The definition of inference and the rest is distinct."

Because of the capacity for leading [to a conclusion], and because the definitions of inference and so forth are absent, the definition of perception is "that which arises from the contact of a sense-organ with its object"; thus, the status of being perception does not apply to inference and the like, due to their lack of that definition. He refutes this by means of an alternative analysis: if, first of all, it is any object whatsoever, and there is no contact of the sense-organ with it...

Whatever cognition arises from the contact [of the senses] and so forth is perception; consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that memory is also perception. For memory, too, indeed arises from the contact of the mind with the self through the awakening of latent impressions (saṃskāra). Furthermore, there is no separate definition for it established by the Great Sage (the author of the Nyāyasūtra). Now, as for the object of knowledge (prameya), that alone is the "object" (artha) because it is what is being sought; and the self is not such [an object].
[The opponent] objects: "It is not that [the object] is being sought through memory; rather, it is the previously experienced place and so forth. [The author] refutes this:
"Let the cognition of the mere place and so forth be perceptual, because of its contact with that alone, but the cognition of the qualifier is not.
[The opponent] raises an objection: "Since the cognition of the qualified is perceptual, by implication, the qualifier is also perceptual."
[The opponent] asks: "Why? [The author] refutes it: "No; because that [object], being non-prescriptive (avidheya), lacks proximity (*asaṃnikarṣa*) just like its qualifier.

Why, then, is a present thing qualified by a non-proximate or past qualifier, even though its mere form (*rūpamātra*) is present? From what [reason]? Because it would follow that everything would be so; for there is no difference in their lack of proximity."

The opponent objects: "If that which is qualified by qualifiers such as place and so forth must be present, then how is it that Devadatta’s son is called Yajñadatta when his mother has already passed away? With a hidden intention, the author asks in order to resolve this:
"How is it so in this case? The opponent replies: "He was not qualified by her at that time; therefore, he is not [inherently] 'Devadatta’s son'."

For it is only that which exists as something distinguished that can conform to linguistic usage; for that which does not exist cannot be a constituent part of linguistic usage. The respondent says: "If, then, that which does not exist is not a constituent part of linguistic usage, then Devadatta [would also not be a constituent part], since he too has passed away."

It would not be a factor for linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) by way of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). If, however, linguistic usage occurs by means of a qualifier that existed in the past, then such [usage] is not prohibited even when there is a state of being qualified (*viśiṣṭatā*). Nor is such a qualifier an incidental characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*), because that which is different in form is not present. Indeed, the distinction between these two is caused solely by presence and absence. Therefore...

A qualified object is not present when its qualifier is not present. If the qualifier is the object of cognition and the universal (*jāti*) and other such factors are also objects of cognition, then it would follow that perception arises even without contact with an object; yet this is not the case, because that definition [of perception] is absent, since the sense organ requires an object.

Now, it might be argued that only the particular place (*deśaviśeṣa*) is the object of cognition (*prameya*), and not its qualifier; likewise, there is no absence of its defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), because of the contact with that which is being sought. If that were so, then meditative practitioners (*dhyāyin*) who perceive things as unarisen and so forth would not have knowledge based on the place and other such factors. Furthermore, if perceptual knowledge (*pratyakṣajñāna*) arises from contact with only one part of the object of cognition, then everyone would be a seer of everything (*sarvapratyakṣadarśī*).

Established by fear, it would not be a factor in that conventional usage. The respondent, having raised the objection, brings forward an equality: "Now, even if there were a distinction due to a past attribute, such a distinction is not prevented by the staff. Furthermore, this was stated even while conceding that such a thing could serve as an attribute; however, in reality:

This [name] such as "Devadatta" is not the qualifier; therefore, he says: "But it is an indicator (upalakṣaṇa)," meaning it belongs to the particular (svalakṣaṇa) which is distinct in form and possesses a shape. This is because of the non-proximity of the qualificand, that is, because the intended object does not possess that form. Now, even if there were no proximity, why would it not still be a qualifier?

Therefore, he says: "The distinction between these two, namely the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), is indeed caused by their proximity (*saṃnidhi*) or lack thereof, respectively. Why? Because a qualified object (*viśiṣṭa*) is not proximate when its qualifier is not proximate. Even if the thing itself is proximate in its own nature, for that object whose qualifier is not proximate, only its own nature is perceived; [the qualifier] is not."
Furthermore, it is established that there is also distinctness (*viśiṣṭatva*).

And if, for the sake of establishing the object as qualified (*viśiṣṭaprameyatā*), the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) itself must also be admitted as an object of cognition—since without it, the status of being a qualified object of cognition would be untenable—then categories such as "universal" (*jāti*) and so forth would also be objects of cognition; thus, [the cognition] would not arise from the contact with a real entity (*anarthasaṃnikarṣaja*).

Even that cognition would have to be considered perceptual; however, this is not possible because there is no sensory contact (*saṃnikarṣa*) with the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), which is what is being sought.

Why? Because it lacks the definition of perception. For its definition is: "that which arises from the contact of a sense organ with its object. Now, let us grant that the definition does not apply, [but suppose] it were [perceptual] merely through contact with the sense organ and the qualified object (*viśeṣya*).
Since it will be produced from that and will be directly perceived due to its clarity, he says: "Because the sense organ depends upon the object.

Regarding the production of the knowledge of reality, we have stated that the generation of the cognition of reality is necessarily dependent on the sense organs acting in conjunction with their objects.

He raises this objection regarding its origin: "Now, it might be argued that among those [objects], only the specific location is the object of cognition (*prameya*), not its qualifiers such as 'past' and so forth; and thus there is no lack of the definition of perception, because of the required sense-object contact. The reply is: "In that case, meditative practitioners (*dhyāyins*) would not be knowers of things that have not yet arisen and so on, by means of a cognition whose objective support (*ālambana*) is the location and other such factors. If he should think:

For the meditator whose mental functions have been refined by meditation, the entire universe would indeed become the object of yoga through contact with even a single part of the object of knowledge (*prameya*).
This is because it is possible for everything to function as a qualifier in some way toward that which is in contact with all the sense organs. This is inference (*anumāna*).

Even in the absence of a secondary indicative function (*lakṣaṇā*), there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the recollection of an object existing at the time of perception is itself a form of perception. In that case, the cause is the mental impression (*saṃskāra*), not the actual existence of the object; for [recollection] occurs even when the object is non-existent. This is equally true for the other [type of cognition]. Since the dharma born of yoga (*yogajadharma*) is the cause, there is indeed no proof for the involvement of an object there, whether it be present, absent, or concealed.

Because it is accepted that yogic perception arises everywhere—even regarding what is obstructed, what is present, and what is not present—the claim that its objective support consists of a present place and so forth only in the absence of a logical mark (*liṅga*) and the like would exclude the possibility of a convergence (*saṃplava*) [of means of knowledge]. Furthermore, by stating "it is inferred from the sūtra," one has fabricated a sūtra that was not actually in the sūtra; for it is sublated by inference and the other means of knowledge.

[The opponent might argue: "The present [cognition] will somehow perceive the non-present object, which is in contact with the sense organ, by way of being a qualifier of a portion of the object of knowledge (*prameya*). To this, he replies: "But if, through contact with a portion of the object of knowledge, there were to arise a perceptual cognition whose scope is the entire universe by virtue of its being somehow qualified [by that portion], then everyone would be a seer of everything, because every object is in contact with the sense organs [in some part]."

For it is possible for [the word] to function as a qualifier in some way; indeed, it has been stated that "yoga" (application) does not prevail elsewhere. Furthermore, when the definition of perception is established for a domain not excluded by the definition of inference—in the case of perceiving something similar to a cow, such as a gavaya, upon which a latent impression is awakened—the [cognition] of another similar object [occurs].
If there were recollection of an existing object such as a cow, it would follow that it is a case of perception;

for it is indeed possible that an existing cow or similar object could somehow function as a qualifier for a *gavaya* or other object in perception. Thus, he raises the objection: "In that recollection, the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is the cause, not the object. Why?"
[Objection: Since memory occurs even when the object is absent, provided there is a mental impression (*saṃskāra*). [Response: This is the same in the other case as well. Why?

Because the cause is the dharma born of yoga, which is independent of the existence of an object. He demonstrates this: for there is no proof that in that case, when yogis produce direct perception of all objects, there is an application of all objects [to the senses]. Why? Because [this would apply] only to what is proximate.
In the treatise, it is accepted that yogic perception arises in every possible manner—whether with respect to what is proximate or remote, present or non-present.
If it is argued that [the object] there is the support (ālambana) characterized by the past and so forth, as well as by a proximate present place and so on, then [we reply]: no.

Regarding the phrase "within the range of the senses," he says there: the claim that the cognition of a yogin, which grasps objects qualified by the past and so forth, has as its objective support a presently existing place and so on, has already been refuted above. Furthermore, by employing the suffix *-tas* in the expression "by means of a valid means of knowledge" (*pramāṇatas*) for the purpose of including all statements, and by clarifying that meaning later on, the venerable Pakṣila [has already addressed this].

The Master has shown that there is a convergence (*saṃplava*) of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), since the cognition of a single object of knowledge, such as the Self, occurs through one means, two means, or even many means; however, this would entail a contradiction [with his own position]. Therefore, he says: "By stating that perception [occurs] in the absence of the mark (*liṅga*) and so forth, the convergence of the means of valid cognition would be rejected; moreover, [this view] is imagined in defiance of the Sūtra."
Indeed, there exists no sūtra for the enunciation (*uddeśa*), definition (*lakṣaṇa*), or examination (*parīkṣā*) stating "the absence of gender and so forth.
If you argue that this is not contrary to the sūtra, then the explanation of the term *avyapadeśya* (non-verbalizable) for the purpose of excluding sound would be improper. [Sixfold...]

If one were to admit [direct] contact (*pratyakṣa-sannikarṣa*) and the mention of the sense-faculties (*indriya-grahaṇa*), then statements such as "for the purpose of excluding inference (*anumāna*) and so forth" would be contradicted.

Therefore, the mind (*manas*) is dependent upon the sense-faculties, logical marks (*liṅga*), and so on. Furthermore, if everything were complete [within the scope of worldly means], then the object of worldly means of knowledge (*laukika-pramāṇa*) and the one who operates with worldly means of knowledge would also possess complete knowledge; thus, there would be no supermundane knowledge (*lokottara-jñāna*).

This is the distinction [of our position] from what is accepted [by others]. If [you claim that] cognition is that which has a clear manifestation (*spaṣṭāvabhāsa*), then that [clarity] is of no use in that regard [i.e., for establishing validity]. If, on the other hand, [validity] is certainty (*niścaya*), then that [certainty] is equally present in the other [means of knowledge, namely inference]. If you argue: "One who perceives through direct perception (*pratyakṣadarśin*) does not entertain doubt regarding all objects; therefore, because the formulation of the definitions of inference and so forth would be sublated, [our view] does not deviate from the Sūtra," [we reply: No, it does not [avoid deviation from the Sūtra]. The Sūtra—
The meaning is that even what is obtained through the capacity for the sake of [the object's] benefit is indeed for that purpose alone, because it is rooted in that. He refutes this:

the explanation of the term *avyapadeśya* (non-verbal) for the purpose of excluding verbal knowledge is incorrect; for the author of the Bhāṣya described the term *avyapadeśya* precisely for the purpose of excluding verbal cognition (*śābdajñāna*). To illustrate: in a case where [an object] is being perceived by direct perception...

When a city-dweller says to a forest-dweller regarding an object possessing a mane and other features, "This is a horse," the forest-dweller understands that the word "horse" denotes that object through the operation of two means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). For instance,
by the mere fact that [the object] is denotable by the word "horse," the word [is understood] with respect to the particular object standing before him.

Because the instruction regarding the sense-faculties and their objects occurs with respect to that [object], and because the word functions there; and because this cognition, although produced by both [the sense-faculty and the word], is indeed verbal (*śābda*), since the word is the most effective means (*sādhakatama*) therein. For even when there is contact between the sense-faculty and the object, that [cognition] does not occur in the absence of the word. However, when that [word] is absent, if a person in the forest remembers a thing that was previously experienced—

One apprehends the convention that "the object possessing a mane and so forth is a horse," because such understanding occurs when the sentence is present. Therefore, the explanation of the term *avyapadeśya* (non-verbal) would be inappropriate for the purpose of excluding verbal cognition from that which arises from both [senses and words]. This is because the definition of perception is established as being restricted to cases where there is an absence of inferential marks (*liṅga*) and the like; thus, it excludes the dual [source].
Because, being verbal in nature, it lacks the possibility of being perceptual.

This is what is meant: that which is obtained through the force of what is stated in the sūtra is not that which destroys a constituent part of the sūtra, nor even that which is destructive; likewise, [this applies to] perception whose object consists merely of things scattered across space and time.

The definition of perception as "the acceptance of knowledge in the absence of signs (liṅga) and so forth," and the inclusion of the term "senses" for the purpose of excluding inference, and so on, would be contradicted. It should be understood that what is indicated by such phrases as "perception has that [external object] as its domain" is also contradicted. He concludes the present topic: therefore, the mind is dependent upon the senses, signs, and so forth, even when directed toward external objects.

And is all that within the scope of worldly valid cognition (*laukika-pramāṇa*) complete or incomplete? If it were all complete, then even in the domain of worldly valid cognition, he would possess complete knowledge; thus, there would be no distinction between him and one who is considered to possess supramundane knowledge (*lokottara-jñāna*).

He raises an objection: "If the distinction [between worldly and non-worldly knowledge] is that cognition has a clear manifestation (*spaṣṭāvabhāsa*). What is meant by this? Even though the object is complete, worldly knowledge appears indistinct, whereas non-worldly knowledge, produced through meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), possesses a clear manifestation; therefore, this is the distinction between them. He refutes this: "No. For in that case, when everything is grasped in its entirety, there is no..."

The absence of expectancy belongs to the former, not to the other. For if even that which is not perceived is measured by another means of knowledge as being complete, what else would it expect? Indeed, there is no expectancy for another means of knowledge, because such expectancy exists only for the sake of establishing the object of knowledge (*prameya*).

[Objection: There would be a further requirement for another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in order to establish the object of knowledge (*prameya*). [Response: No, because that [object] is established even by the former [means], and because there is no reason to require the establishment again of what has already been established. Furthermore, the existence of another means would merely result in a requirement for yet another means. If it is argued that a particular pleasure is produced from the perception arising from the former means of valid cognition, [we reply that this is not so].

The utility [of scripture] lies in its clear manifestation. Since it makes known an object already established by worldly means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it would be like grinding what has already been ground.
He raises an objection: "But [it provides] certainty? He refutes it: "That [certainty] belongs to the other, the worldly [cognition], as well."

It is equal in terms of being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). He raises an objection: since every form of valid knowledge culminates in perception (*pratyakṣa*), there is a state of complete satisfaction regarding all objects for the ordinary person who perceives the totality of things through other means of knowledge; however, there is no such satisfaction regarding everything that is imperceptible. For instance, a knower, having understood an object through scripture (*āgama*), [seeks to verify it] through inference (*anumāna*).

Having inferred it, one desires to know it; and having inferred it, one desires to see it through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Then, having perceived it directly, one reaches a state of being free from further expectation. This entire process constitutes the valid cognition (*pratyakṣapramiti*) of perceivers. [The author] refutes this: "If even that which is not directly perceived has been fully ascertained by another means of knowledge (*mānāntara*), what else could one expect? Indeed, this applies even where there is inference.

One desires to see [the object] through perception; surely, there was no complete comprehension of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) through inference therein, because if that were the case, the desire to see would be untenable. As the venerable Vārttikakāra-miśras have said:
"As long as the object of knowledge is unknown or doubtful, so long will it be desired to be known."
"But once [an object] has been cognized, the eagerness of the cognizers for further cognition is frustrated.
Now, if one asks why another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is not required, he says: "Indeed, there is no requirement for another means of knowledge.
Why? Because that requirement exists for the sake of establishing the object of knowledge (*prameya*). For one who seeks to attain the beneficial and avoid the harmful...

For they seek that means [of knowledge], and since its determination depends upon the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), they follow after the *pramāṇa*. If that [means] is established by some *pramāṇa*, then what is the use for them of following after further *pramāṇas*? Nevertheless, if they do follow after them, the meaning is that these [seekers] surely desire to know another object of knowledge (*prameya*) as well. Now, from that [object of knowledge]...

Even if that [knowledge] were established, because it perishes very quickly, he refutes the expectation of yet another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the sake of re-establishing that object of cognition: "No; because that [object] has already been established repeatedly even by the former [means], there is no possibility of an effort directed toward the scope of yogic knowledge (*yogajavijñāna*), which is to be accomplished through the exertion of a succession of many births. Why? Because once something is established by some [means], [there is no need for] another means of knowledge..."

And because there is an absence of a cause for the expectation of success through ritual means (*rātsiddhi*). For it is possible that a continuous stream of memory regarding this object arises by virtue of the awakening of a latent impression (*bhāvanā*) produced by the experience of that [object].
He raises an objection: "Because the intentions (*abhisandhi*) of cognizing subjects (*pramātṛ*) are diverse, there exists another means toward that [end]..."

If it is argued that the object of knowledge (*prameya*) is intended to be specified as a qualifier, he refutes this: "In that case, by distinguishing between what is already attained and what is not yet attained, there would be a desire for another means (*upāya*), not a desire for another object of knowledge. He raises an objection:

Another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) would be useless. Furthermore, because other means exist, one who has already perceived something through other [means] might still desire to know it; for there is an inconsistency (*vyabhicāra*), in that perception consists of certainty while inference consists of uncertainty. Therefore, the desire to know arises precisely from the fact that [the object] has not yet been ascertained. This is so even in the case of that which is inconsistent and lacks certainty.

Because it is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Perception is that which is capable of manifesting [an object] through sense-contact, whereas inference and the like are not. If it is argued that sense-contact requires movement and so forth as its instrument, rather than being the instrument of the valid cognition itself—since the valid cognition is already established and sense-contact serves as the cause for the manifestation of the cognized object—[we reply: since the subject under discussion, perception, has for its object that which is not currently in contact, there is no lack of expectancy [for further explanation].

The term "sufficient" (*alam*) applies without distinction to both mundane and supramundane cognizers. Since inference and other such means have only generalities as their objects, they do not ascertain the specific nature of an object restricted to its own particularity; thus, the mundane [cognition] is characterized by expectancy if it involves a specific pleasure. This is just as when a mother-in-law, having seen her son-in-law through one window, looks through another.
The meaning is that he perceives this [object] in the same way as before, due to a particular intensity of affection. He refutes this:
if it is easily accomplished, then since it is established by the previous means of knowledge (pramāṇa) itself through repeated observation, another means of knowledge is redundant.

Furthermore, even in the case of something extremely difficult to accomplish, because other means exist, one who desires to know it again—even though it has already been seen through direct perception (pratyakṣa)—[seeks to establish it] by other means such as inference (anumāna) and so forth.
The cognizer possesses diverse intentions; thus, it is not the case that every valid cognition is dependent upon perception.

Or, if one maintains that perception is paramount, then the specific distinction of perception from other means of knowledge must be stated. Now, it might be argued that perception is determinate in nature because of its clarity, whereas inference and the like are non-determinate due to their susceptibility to error.

[The opponent says: "Because of perception. This is untenable; for even inference and the other means of knowledge, when they possess the aforementioned characteristics, are free from deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Since deviation occurs only in the case of fallacious [cognitions], and this is equally true for perception as well, [the author], without stating this, offers another broad refutation: "In that case, expectancy arises precisely because [the object] has not been cognized. Why? Because of deviation..."

Because it wanders [among various objects], and for that very reason, that which is non-definitive in nature lacks the status of a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*). He raises an objection: perception is that which is capable of manifesting [an object]. Why? Because the object is brought into proximity through sense-contact; such [manifestation] is impossible in the absence of proximity. This, however, is not the case with inference and the like, because their domain consists of objects scattered across space and time.

He refutes this: In that case, contact (sannikarṣa) would be the means for [producing] movement and so forth, but not the instrument of valid cognition (pramāṇa), which is the means for valid knowledge (pramā).

Why? Because valid knowledge is already established through inference and other such means. Nor can it be said that valid knowledge itself is the cause of manifestation and so forth; for he says: because contact, when aided merely by an instrument of knowledge, is the cause of manifestation and so forth.
Furthermore, the perception under discussion has as its object merely those things scattered across space and time, and since it does not have as its domain objects that are not in immediate contact,
it is not sufficient for the cessation of all expectancy. Therefore, there is no distinction between the ordinary and the supramundane cognizers with respect to any act of cognition.

Again, he raises an objection: since inference and the like arise from a mark (liṅga) whose relationship has been grasped, and since the perception of a relationship is impossible in the case of a particular (viśeṣa), these means of knowledge have the universal (sāmānya) as their object; therefore, the infinite particulars restricted to each individual object [cannot be known by them].

[This applies] to the knower. Even for the supramundane [cognition], there is no lack of distinction [from the mundane], because it achieves contentment through the determination of time-form (*kālarūpa*). If, then, mundane means of knowledge have as their object things that are incomplete, the supramundane [cognition] consisting of cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*)—being dependent on that [mundane cognition]—is not capable of taking those [complete things] as its domain. However, independence belongs to the external mind.
This has already been explained [by us]. Therefore, the claim that "everything is an object of the mind" is mere idle chatter. Moreover:
That which appears as present is indeed false; it is not perception otherwise.
Neither succession nor simultaneity can be conceived, and no object of cognition can be established.

Other means of knowledge have as their domain objects that undergo transformation across the three times, whereas perception has the present as its object. In that regard, for one who perceives [the present] as having a present nature, it is false cognition, because everything is not of that nature [in the past or future]. However, for one who perceives it according to reality, it is not perception, because perception lacks the capacity to have past or future objects. Or else, by this [perception], it must necessarily...

A single definition must be stated for the various types of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); otherwise, there would be a state of expectancy on the part of the worldly cognizer due to the failure to determine that [perception] is not a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). However, for the supramundane [cognizer], there is no such expectancy because all aspects are completely determined and because there is no object that has not been cognized. Thus, there is no lack of distinction [between the two].

He refutes this: If, then, worldly valid cognition (*laukika-pramāṇa*) does not have an undivided reality as its object, then even that supramundane [cognition] consisting of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*) which you have established must be dependent upon it; and since such cultivation is itself dependent upon worldly valid cognition whose objects are divided, it cannot possibly take that undivided [reality] as its domain. Nor can [the supramundane cognition] have as its object the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) deposited by cultivation...
He says that the mind functions independently in the external world—but it has already been made known that the mind does not possess independence with respect to external objects.
This has also been established more thoroughly in the *Bauddhasarvajñaparīkṣā* (Examination of the Buddhist Omniscient One). He concludes the present topic:
therefore, the claim that "everything is an object of the mind" is mere idle chatter. Furthermore:
Existing only as a false appearance, it is not perception in any other sense;
for neither succession nor simultaneity can be conceived, nor can an object of cognition be defined.

Just as other means of knowledge, such as inference and the like, have as their objects things existing within the three times as they are conventionally understood by the world, whereas perception has only the present as its object; in that case, for an omniscient being who perceives everything through perception as being of a present nature, there would be false cognition. Why? Because everything—past, future, and present—is not [actually] of that [present] nature.

Because of [the object's] existence, there is an absence of presentness. However, for one who perceives according to reality—that is, one who perceives it as past and so forth—knowledge having that as its object would not be perception (*pratyakṣa*). This is because perception lacks the quality of having past or future objects;
indeed, being a perception is pervaded by having a present object. And having a present object is [absent] in the case of the past and the future.
The meaning is that when [the cognition] ceases from the object and from consciousness, it also causes its status as perception (*pratyakṣatva*) to cease;

however, this is not another interpretation of the phrase "perception is not otherwise. Alternatively, one must necessarily state a single definition for this manifold perception; otherwise, if a single definition were not stated, [there would be no way to establish] its...

If a single instance of perception that has not been subsumed [under other categories] were designated as a distinct means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) from inference and the rest, it would be based on a lack of conviction. Furthermore, if one were to accept perception alone as the sole means of valid cognition despite its lack of a defining characteristic [distinct from others], then—

Nor can it be accepted as a definition because it would entail the admission of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*), as there is no purpose for such a technical designation (*paribhāṣā*). Furthermore, since worldly people apply the term "perception" (*pratyakṣa*) to certain things even when their characteristics differ, that [definition] is false; it does not apply to supramundane perception. In this regard, being "born from the sense-organ" (*akṣaja*) is not the defining characteristic, because it overextends (*ativyāpti*) to the mind (*manas*). Therefore, [the definition must be] "that which arises from the contact of a sense-organ and an object"...

Its definition is "being produced from an object in close proximity" (*sannikṛṣṭārthajatva*). As it has been stated: "Because it arises through the power of the object, [perception] is that which is produced from the contact of the sense organ with the object (*indriyārthasannikarṣotpanna*), [and is characterized by] 'contact with what exists' (*satsaṃprayoga*). Since the mind (*manas*) is a sense organ, this definition pervades the cognitions of pleasure and so forth; furthermore, because it is produced by the power of the object, it excludes inference (*anumāna*) and the like. Nor does it apply to objects that are subtle, remote, or obstructed.

Since the capacity for the arising of knowledge [is required], the perception of all objects is not established. Whether it be the state of being free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍhatva*) or the acceptance of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*), it would have to be a cognition. For if things possessing distinct characteristics were also considered perception, it would follow that inference and the other means of knowledge would also be perception; thus, the meaning is that those others should not be accepted as separate means of valid cognition.

If it were argued that, although there is no difference in their being distinct entities, the term "object" (*artha*) has been conventionally defined (*paribhāṣita*) as denoting only substances, qualities, and actions, and not universals, particulars, or inherence; and likewise, that the word "perception" (*pratyakṣa*) has been conventionally defined as applying only to certain specific instances of cognition, and not to instances of inference and so forth—to this he replies: "Conventional definition" (*paribhāṣā*).

Because there would be no purpose; the meaning is that if one were to define that which lacks a purpose, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Furthermore, even regarding certain things with distinct characteristics, worldly people employ the word "perception" (*pratyakṣa*) as a denotative term for them alone. Indeed, these people are not to be questioned. Moreover, the claim that the single word *akṣa* applies to three different classes [of sense organs] is also false. Why?
In that which you consider to be supramundane (*lokottara*), because it is indeed supramundane, a mundane application of it is impossible.
Therefore, a single definition of perception (*pratyakṣa*) must be stated as established.
Now, it might be argued that being born from the sense-faculties (*akṣaja*) is the single defining characteristic of perceptions, and thus the knowledge of an omniscient one [is such].
Since [the definition] "arising from the sense-organ designated as the mind" does not exclude [cognitions such as inference], he says:
"In that case, being produced by a sense-organ (*akṣajatva*) is not the defining characteristic. Why? Because it is as follows: is there a sense-organ named "mind" or not?

If the mind were a sense-organ, then since inference and so forth would also be born of the mind alone, they too would result in being perception; thus, because of over-extension (*ativyāpti*), [that definition is untenable].

[This] is the definition. Alternatively, if [perception] were not dependent on the senses, it would follow that the cognition of pleasure and so forth—being produced by non-external sense organs—is not perception;

thus, the definition would be over-narrow (*avyāpti*). Therefore, all disputants must accept that the very definition of perception is "that which is born from the causal efficiency of the sense organ and the object."
Right here he demonstrates the consensus of all [authorities]: because the object arises by virtue of its own capacity as previously described;

and for the blind and others, it is impossible [to perceive], with the word "of the sense-organ" being understood as the remainder [of the compound]. Likewise, [perception] is produced from the contact of the sense-organ and the object, and thus [the definition] is "contact with what is existent. This being the case, there is no lack of pervasion (avyāpti). As for pleasure and so forth, [they are perceived] when the mind functions as a sense-organ.

There is no over-extension [of the definition] due to the pervasion of knowledge, because [perception] is distinguished from inference and other means by its being produced through the capacity of the object. Now, one might ask: even so, why is a cognition whose objects are all things not considered perception? To this he says: "And there is no capacity for subtle, remote, or obstructed objects to produce a cognition"; therefore, there is no perception of all objects.

[Objection: It follows that there would be [the fault of over-extension]. [Response: If you say it is the definition of perception, what is this "conceptualization" (kalpanā)? If it is a cognition appearing as a word, then auditory [cognition]...
If it is argued that knowledge is not direct perception because its appearance is capable of association with verbal expression,

[the opponent] objects: "If it is said that 'being free from conceptual construction' (*kalpanāpoḍha*) is the definition of direct perception, then this indeed excludes direct perception from inference and other forms of cognition which are conceptual in nature, and establishes it for pleasure and the like."

The meaning is that perceptuality belongs to those [cognitions] which are established through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) by virtue of having a known form, and from which conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) has been excluded; and it includes the cognition of the Omniscient One as being entirely free from conceptual construction.
He refutes this by analyzing it according to its possible variations: "What is this conceptual construction, from whose exclusion..."
How is perceptuality [of conceptual cognition] avoided?

If the cognition of the form of a word—an auditory cognition having sound as its object that appears clearly—were to result in being non-perceptual; or if conceptual construction (kalpanā) is defined as a cognition whose appearance is capable of association with a verbal expression (abhilāpa).

This is the meaning: conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) is that cognition which has an appearance (*ākāra*) capable of being associated with verbal expression. This is what is meant: only that [object] becomes associated with verbal expression upon which this verbal expression has established a convention; and only that is such [an object] as conforms to place, time, and state.

It shines forth; yet, the persistence (*anugati*) of a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) existing as a real entity is not possible. Nor can universals (*jāti*) and the like exist as real entities, because they cannot withstand critical analysis. For this very reason, the particulars (*bhedāḥ*) possessing those [universals] are also not ultimately real, since the state of possessing them (*tadvattā*) is untenable in their absence. Therefore, it is either its own appearance (*svābhāsam*) or it is false (*alīkam*).

Or rather, they perceive the external object such that one conceptualization of a cow is exactly like another conceptualization of a cow. Furthermore, the difference from the object of another conceptualization whose own object it is, is not grasped either by that [first] conceptualization itself nor by another conceptualization. Thus, due to the non-apprehension of difference, the object of a conceptualization is one. Because of that oneness of the object, there is also oneness of the conceptualizations. Due to that single conceptualization...

Furthermore, due to the capacity for creative manifestation (*nirmāṇa*), even the experiences themselves possess unity. Thus, there is a unity even among individual manifestations that are not the causes of one another, as it has been said:
"Because it is the cause of a single reflective awareness (*ekapratyavamarśa*), cognition is non-differentiated."
"Because they share the status of being the cause of a single cognition, there is non-difference even among individuals.
And that superimposed form has the nature of exclusion from others (*anyavyāvṛtti*); because it is common to both existence and non-existence;
because it brings about a semblance (*sādṛśya*) among things that are utterly dissimilar; and because it is not an external resemblance. Likewise:
Indeed, whatever form is common to both existence and non-existence is necessarily grounded in the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*), such as corporeality (*mūrtatva*) and so forth.

And since the object of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) such as "cow" and so on is likewise common to both existence and non-existence—because it serves as the locus for conceptualizations such as "the cow exists" and "the cow does not exist"—this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). For this [form], namely "cowness" (*gotva*) and so on, is indeed common to both existence and non-existence, because it is the basis for such conceptualizations. [Otherwise,] if it were not common...

Because that is untenable due to contradiction and tautology; likewise, even when there is self-awareness of a common form (*sāmānyākāra*), there is no perception of a similarity between things that are absolutely dissimilar. Now, if it is argued that there is a connection of one thing with another thing...

The perception of a universal form is [considered] direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because no other entity corresponding to that universal is admitted. It brings about [the cognition] as being restricted solely to the exclusion of others (*tadanyavyāvṛtti*), just as the state of "not being a camel" applies to pigs, buffaloes, elephants, and so forth, which are extremely dissimilar. And likewise, [it applies] to individual cows such as Śābaleya and others, which are themselves extremely dissimilar.

The nature of the universal "cowness" (*gotva*) among the characteristics is the logical reason (*hetu*). Likewise, whether it be the appearance in cognition, the non-entity (*aloka*), or that which is external, such similarity—whether from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) or as an absolutely non-existent form—is conceived solely as being produced by the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), and not otherwise. For this very reason, the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) regarding cowness is directed toward either the appearance in cognition or the unreal [universal].

An existing entity such as a horse, though its difference is not perceived due to similarity, is superimposed as external precisely as that which is excluded from the objects of conceptualization; thus, it is not the case that its nature as the exclusion of others does not manifest. Nor is it the case that the non-cow is not determined, because the cow is determined through the determination of its nature as the exclusion of the non-cow, and the determination of the non-cow is dependent upon the determination of the cow.

It is not correct to say that there is a mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*), because one of the two is established from the other. Whether it be the form of a cow, the aspect of cognition, or something unreal, its differentiation from others does not depend on a definition based upon those others; otherwise, the same fault would apply even to a real universal (*sāmānya*). Therefore:

Alternatively, it is the form of cognition (*jñānākāra*), or that which is false (*alīka*) yet determined as external, which—due to the existence of linguistic convention—becomes capable of association with words; and the cognition of those who are proficient [in language] regarding that object is conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). [The author] refutes the conceptual construction of those who maintain the theory of the form of cognition: "Even when there is self-awareness of the universal form, it is not perception."

This is what is intended: since sensation is impossible for anything other than cognition, the proponents of *sākāravāda* (those who maintain that cognition has a form) have established that the universal, which consists in the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), is the form of cognition. Furthermore, it will be demonstrated that it is not possible for that [external object] to be either the apprehended (*grāhya*) or the determined (*adhyavaseya*) object of a conceptual construction; thus, [cognition] is not without an objective support (*nirālambana*).

In this context, regarding the term "knowledge": by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), even though the generality of the form of knowledge is self-cognized, it would be non-perceptual because it is subject to conceptualization; how much more so, then, its externality, which is in every way ungraspable and undeterminable, since it falls entirely within the domain of conceptual construction.

Now, he raises a doubt regarding the view of those who maintain that cognition is formless (*nirākārajñānavādin*): "If a person, in the case of mother-of-pearl or the like situated before them, rejects the conceptual construction (*vijñānakalpanā*) that 'this is silver' with respect to another object such as silver, that cognition which has a general form (*sāmānyākārā pratītiḥ*) is that by which the universal (*sāmānya*) is made manifest (*ākriyate*), that is, revealed."
How could that [cognition] be perceptual through its own realization? Because no other entity possessing a universal form is admitted. As it has been said:
"In that [cognition], whatever appears as an external object, as if one and distinct from others..."
"It is as if it were excluded from reality due to the failure of examination.
133] Now, as for the application of verbal expression, that might be so for one who is unskilled in verbal expression.

Now, if perception (*pratyakṣa*) is defined as the cognition of mere form (*rūpa*) free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*), yet involving the superimposition (*āropa*) of what is non-material (*arūpa*), then the knowledge of yogins or others regarding things not yet born or already passed away would not be perception; for the form appearing in that cognition does not exist in those [past or future] objects. If it were to exist, it would follow that they are present (*pratyutpannatva*).
He raises an objection: "Now, [it might be argued that] there is a connection with denotation. He refutes the conceptualization regarding the denoted object:

"The cognition of a person who has not mastered language—which consists of an appearance capable of being associated with verbal expression and which is devoid of connection with words—would thus be perception. But this is not accepted. He raises another objection: "Now, a—"

The superimposition (*āropa*) of a false form (*rūpa*) as being external is conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). As it was stated by the Bhadanta: "That form which is delineated by a conceptualizing cognition as being distinct from other things—that cognition is not external. And this conceptual construction is common to both the learned and the unlearned. Therefore, perception (*pratyakṣa*) is the awareness of mere form (*rūpamātra*) from which that [conceptualization] has been excluded.

And thus, the aforementioned fault does not follow. [The author] refutes this: "In that case, then, the cognition of a yogin or anyone else regarding things that are unborn or have passed away would not be perception. Why? Because the form appearing in the cognition does not exist in those things that are unborn or have passed away. Why does it not exist? To this he says: "Or, if it did exist, [it would be] because of its being present."

[Otherwise there would be] the consequence [of over-extension]. This is the intended meaning: indeed, even if conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) manifest what is unreal (*alīka*), it is not possible for them to have a common object (*samānaviṣayatva*).

For the unreal is non-different (*abheda*) in each individual conceptual construction. Now, was it not stated that even though the unreal things are distinct, whatever one [conceptual construction] manifests...?

The conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) imagines one falsehood, and another [conceptual construction] imagines a similar one; thus, due to the non-apprehension of their difference, there is the determination of a difference between these false things.

This has been well said, but this must be examined: does that common nature (*tattirohitaṃ svarūpam*) belong to those whose essence is false, which, though appearing, does not manifest among them, or does it not exist at all? It cannot be the former, for it cannot belong to things that are non-existent (*avastusat*).

For those things whose form is dependent solely upon conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), it is impossible for a form to exist that is not presented by that construction; because if it were not conceptually constructed, it would be a real entity (*vastusat*), and thus its nature as a false appearance (*alīkarūpa*) would be untenable. Therefore, it should be understood that what does not appear [to cognition] does not exist. Furthermore, their non-existence alone is ultimate (*pāramārthika*), whereas their existence is merely conceptual.

[The object] would merely fall [into error]. Now, since there is a determination of non-difference based on the non-apprehension of difference among the objects of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), one must accept that their object is something entirely different. For whatever is a word must be capable of association [with its referent]; however, because individual conceptual constructions are distinct and false—just like unique particulars (*svalakṣaṇa*)—they cannot be the basis for linguistic convention, and thus lack the capacity for association with verbal expression.

Because it is impossible for [the universal] to be within the scope of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Nor is non-difference (*abheda*) possible. Indeed, how could unity be established for that whose existence depends solely on conceptual construction, given its difference from that [conceptual content]? For that [universal], when the [conceptual content] exists, it exists as if it were that; when that is born, it is born as if it were that; and when that perishes, it perishes. Thus, how would it not be differentiated by the differentiation of that [content]? If there were differentiation, it would be impossible [to maintain its unity].

Because it lacks the capacity for association with verbal expression due to its nature as a mental appearance (*mayatā*), it is false; yet, because it is not an external object like a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), it is not the object of conceptual construction. Thus, for the cognition, there is neither the form of the self, nor falsity, nor externality, nor is it a particular characteristic.

This is not the object [of a single cognition], because all things, being incapable of having a convention established for them, are unfit for association with verbal expression. Nor is it correct to say that there is a non-difference among certain unreal things by virtue of their consisting in the exclusion of the non-cow (*agovyāvṛtti*), because if they possessed that nature, it would follow that they could not be apprehended due to the fault of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). As the venerable author of the *Vārttika* has said in this regard:
"And if the established cow were excluded by the exclusion of 'cow,' then that [exclusion] would consist in the cessation of the cow;

in that case, one must speak of the cow itself, for it is otherness that is being negated. But if the cow is not established, there is no non-cow; and in its absence, how can there be a cow? Thus [it is said].

Moreover, this exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*), even if constructed by conceptual thought (*kalpanā*), cannot be common to many things while possessing differentiation according to their differences. For this very reason, even the positive form of "cowness" (*gotva*) is conceptually constructed;

for it is indeed excluded from everything of a different class, [derived] from the ultimately real particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) which is excluded from both those of the same class and those of a different class.

Even that which is distinct is apprehended as non-distinct; as it has been said: "Because it depends upon how one is intent, and because it is desired according to reality. Yet even that [apprehension] does not constitute the locus of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
For it is untenable for this form of cognition—whether unreal or otherwise—to be conceptually constructed as distinct in every individual instance of conceptualization.

If one should think: "Just as a non-existent form manifests as having the nature of existence, so too that which is devoid of unity appears as a unity. And it does not follow from this that there is a real difference [between them], because such a difference is untenable even in a conceptualized entity, since its basis is a real thing (*vastu*); therefore, this 'cowness' and so forth is neither different nor non-different, but rather *saṃbhinna* (intermingled)."

It appears as something external; and thus, its capacity for association with verbal expression is established. Now, is that which is the object of one conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) the very same as the object of another conceptual construction? If you say "yes," [we reply] no, because that too has its body dependent upon conceptualization. For this indeed is what it means for a constructed entity to be dependent upon conceptualization.

This refers to what is called the conformity to the distinctions and non-distinctions of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). For if it were not dependent upon that [conceptual construction], its status as being conceptually constructed would be untenable, leading to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that it is unreal (*alīka*), as has already been stated. And regarding the point that "for the unreal, there is neither reality nor unreality": we raise this objection in respect to the state in which everything is being perceived; however, it is impossible for something to persist through distinct conceptual constructions.

It is impossible to apprehend it as such, because it is not logically possible for it to be subordinate to that [perception]. For if one were to assume [such a thing], its nature could not possibly exist without another manifestation.
This might be argued: "Conceptual construction itself has arisen from its own causes in such a way that its own object..."

The [concept] "the one consciousness" appears as if it were excluded from certain things. But is such a thing not itself the object of another conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)? If it is not, then it is not capable of being associated with verbal expression (*abhilāpa-saṃsarga*), because that which has never been previously perceived cannot be the subject of a linguistic convention (*saṃketa*).

On the other hand, if it is the object of another conceptual construction, then—as has already been stated—it is untenable for [consciousness] to be dependent upon that [other concept]. Furthermore...
