Furthermore, it is impossible for there to be manifestation of things such as "cowness" (*gotva*) that are absolutely non-existent and do not possess any distinct nature (*svabhāva-bheda*). Even in the case of a sky-lotus, a man’s horn, and the like, there is no absolute non-existence; for while their relation (*saṃsarga*) is indeed non-existent, the relata themselves—the sky, the lotus, and so forth—exist here and there. This is because [only] the relation itself is absent.

And because it exists in some cases, and because it can somehow be established even there; for since it conforms to a superimposed form, it would result in being a conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) with respect to those things that are absolutely non-existent. For that which is not present...

The superimposition (ādhyāropa) of cognition upon something else occurs through the imitation of form (rūpānukāra). But surely, if there were no substratum (adhiṣṭhāna), there could be no superimposition;

therefore, the apprehension of a thing as having a form other than its own is conceptual construction (kalpanā). [Objection: In that case, the cognition of hair and so forth by one suffering from ophthalmia would be without a substratum. [Reply:

No, for the distinctions of relations (saṃsarga-bheda) are defined in dependence upon the distinctions of the related things (saṃsargin) which possess the nature of existence (sad-rūpa); thus, they appear with mutually exclusive forms.

Because [it] arises from that. Here, however, for universals such as "cowness" (*gotva*), which are defined in dependence upon the cognition of the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), the particular is [the basis], because the individual instances of that cognition are absolutely distinct. Since, even when there is difference, there is no appearance of non-difference, and since a single causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is untenable; and because [if one were to accept otherwise], it would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of having to rely on the exclusion of others (*atadvyāvṛtti*) later on.

Because it is a conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). Furthermore, an imagined *gotva* (cowness), whether in a positive form or as the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*), lacks the capacity for association with verbal expression. [Objection: Even if a universal (*sāmānya*) existing in the ultimate sense (*paramārthasat*) were denoted, its commonality across both existence and non-existence would not be established. For the individuals that serve as its substrata, or those indicated by it, are scattered across different places and times.

For by that [universal], the word-meaning can be established as common to both existence and non-existence. Nor is there absolute heterogeneity among individuals, such that one would have to resort to their exclusion from others alone as their commonality; for it is logical that a universal, being an existing entity, is determined as the substratum and possesses a common property (*sāmāna-dharma*). And this refutes the objection against that [position].

This will be explained in the *Saṃsargaparīkṣā*. Thus it is established that there is no fitness for association with verbal expression in either the form of cognition or in its false external object, because no convention can be made regarding them by means of verbal expression. Whatever cannot have a convention made for it by means of verbal expression is not fit for association with it, just as, for example, the self is not associated with the forms of pleasure and so forth. As it has been said:
"For the self of pleasure and so forth is incapable of being associated with linguistic conventions, as it does not share in anything else;
therefore, their self-awareness is not accompanied by verbal expression.
Indeed, the capacity for association with verbal expression is pervaded by the state of being capable of having a linguistic convention; otherwise, there would be an over-extension.

[This is] because of attachment (*saṅga*). Since that [nature of being an object] ceases along with the false externality that takes the form of cognition, it also causes the cessation of the fitness for association with verbal expression; thus, the logical connection (*pratibandha*) is established. Although this is a more well-known refutation, the Teacher has presented the establishment of the subject at hand as a refutation by not explicitly stating it.

[Objection: Is it not the case that conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) conforms to a superimposed form? And since the cognition of a yogi regarding the past and the future is not like that [superimposition], it is not a conceptual construction. To this, he says: because it conforms to a superimposed form, the status of being a conceptual construction would follow for the cognition of what has not yet arisen and what has already passed. [Objection: But is it not precisely the conformity to a superimposed form that constitutes this [conceptual construction]?

To this he says: "Siddham" [is established]. For there is no superimposition (*adhyāropa*) of knowledge other than the imitation of a non-existent form. Nor is this [form] existent; for it has been said: "Or, if it were existent, it would follow that it is present. He objects: But surely there can be a superimposition without a substratum (*anadhiṣṭhāna*). As it has been stated regarding the object of superimposition and the superimposition itself: [text fragment].

Or [it may be] the cognition "this is a delusion of silver. What follows from this? To this he says: Therefore, conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) is the apprehension of a real entity (*vastu*), which is a unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) existing in ultimate reality, in another form, namely, in the form of a universal (*sāmānya*). And thus, the direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) of a yogin regarding what is unborn or what has passed away is not conceptual construction; for in that case, there is no universal in what is unborn or what has passed away.

"It shines as having the nature of form. To this, a partisan of a particular school (ekadeśin) offers a rebuttal: "In that case, the visual perception of one suffering from ophthalmia (*taimira*) would be without a substratum (*niradhiṣṭhāna*). Or, if some substratum is asserted for it, then the cognition 'sky-flower' would be non-conceptual (*akalpanā*)."

It would be perception (*pratyakṣa*). Furthermore, with respect to a universal (*sāmānya*), the cognition of the form of the universal is not of the nature of a superimposition (*anāropa*), just as in self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*). Now, if [you argue that] conceptualization (*kalpanā*) is merely the construction of a form, then in the case of past, unborn, and other [objects], cognition is not based on conceptualization. Alternatively, if conceptualization regarding an object is the cognition of a universal form, then that [cognition] is perception; however, with respect to the universal...

Because it is erroneous, whose perception of hair and so forth would it follow to be? Having raised an objection, he refutes it: "Now, if it is said that in that case there is some substrate such as a portion of light," he states the ultimate refutation: "But [it would be like] a sky-flower."
Since knowledge is non-conceptual, it would be direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). For in that case, no substratum whatsoever is possible.

Indeed, for the Buddhists, there is nothing called "space" other than the absence of material form. And an absence, characterized by the lack of all descriptive attributes, cannot be the substratum of anything. Furthermore, in the case of a universal, [the cognition] has the form of a universal.

Cognition would be perception (*pratyakṣa*). But [an objection is raised]: since this [cognition] determines either a false form of knowledge or an external object, it is merely a superimposition (*samāropa*); so why is it not a conceptual construction (*kalpanā*)? To this he says: because, as in self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*), it does not have the nature of a superimposition with respect to that universal (*sāmānya*). For just as conceptual cognition (*vikalpavijñāna*), although directed toward the object of conceptualization, [is not a conceptual construction in that regard].

If it is argued that conceptualization (*kalpanā*) consists precisely in determining a universal, which is either unreal or a form of cognition, as being external— yet this does not occur in the mere [self-]awareness itself,
and that there is never any awareness of the mere form of that universal apart from superimposition (*āropa*)—
then, is there ever even an awareness of the nature of consciousness itself, setting aside that which is to be conceptualized?

It must be postulated that, because they exist at the same time, the cognition of that [external object] is identical even when there is a cognition of a universal that is superimposed upon the external object. Therefore, the meaning is that it would follow as a consequence that perception is merely conceptual with respect to the form of the universal, just as it is in the case of self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*).

He raises an objection: "Now, even the conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) of the mere form of a universal (*sāmānya*) and so forth, which do not exist in reality, is indeed a conceptual construction. And this being the case, it does not follow that [the cognition] of one's own sun is a conceptual construction, because the nature of the conceptualizing consciousness (*vikalpavijñāna*) itself exists. He refutes this: "[The cognition] of the past, the unborn, and so forth, is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*)."
Because the form appearing therein does not exist [ultimately], just like [the universal] *jāti* and so forth.

He raises an objection: "Now, a cognition whose form is a universal (*sāmānyākāra*) is a conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) with respect to a real entity (*vastu*), because it consists of a superimposition (*samāropa*);
therefore, it is not perception (*pratyakṣa*). If it is argued that 'let it not be so with respect to a real entity, but it may be so with respect to a universal,' to that he replies:"

But with respect to the universal (*sāmānya*), [the cognition] is erroneous. Indeed, this universal is non-existent because it cannot withstand analysis. Therefore, the cognition whose object is that [universal] is an illusion (*vibhrama*) due to having a non-existent thing as its referent. For Dignāga, who set forth the definition of perception as "free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*) and characterized by "exclusion of others" (*anyanirdeśya*), the definition of perception was not merely being free from conceptual construction; rather, it was that very [cognition]...
Kīrti considered that the definition of perception (*pratyakṣa*) must be accompanied by non-erroneousness (*abhrāntatva*). As he said:

"What, then, is this erroneousness? If it is the state of having an unreal object (*asadarthatā*), then this would apply equally to the cognition of an omniscient being; or if it is absolute non-existence..."

[Objection: Then the cognition of those suffering from ophthalmia (*taimirika*), dreams, and so forth would be direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). [Response: If non-erroneousness (*abhrāntatva*) consists in conformity with causal efficacy (*arthakriyā-saṃvāditva*), such that pleasure and pain, or the attainment and avoidance of objects, are based on the object itself—then for a sensation incapable of being either grasped or abandoned, [the definition] is "free from conceptual construction and non-erroneous. By including this qualification of "non-erroneous," [the definition is restricted] to that which has a real basis (*sad-adhiṣṭhāna*).

The erroneous nature of the cognition of hair-tufts and the like has been explained by its being non-perceptual (*apratyakṣatā*). Having raised this point, he refutes it through an analysis: "What, then, is this erroneous nature? If it consists in having an unreal object (*asadarthatā*), then this would apply equally to the cognition of an omniscient being, because that which is yet to be born and that which has already passed away are both non-existent. If, on the other hand, it consists in having an absolutely unreal object, then cognitions such as those of one suffering from ophthalmia or dreams would result in being perceptual (*pratyakṣa*)."

Because that object is not absolutely non-existent. Now, if non-delusion is defined as correspondence with causal efficiency—as it has been said: "Valid cognition is non-discrepant knowledge; non-discrepancy is the stability of causal efficiency"—then he refutes this by analyzing it: if [the two] are based on the object—that is, based on the objects of the cognitions—corresponding respectively to the attainment of pleasure and pain...

The "avoidance" [of error] is held to consist in the correspondence with purposeful action (*arthakriyā-saṃvāditva*); consequently, there would follow the undesirable consequence that cognitions whose objects are unfit for adoption or rejection—such as the cognition of the moon, stars, and so forth—are erroneous. If, on the other hand, correspondence is defined as the production of successive cognitions regarding a single object, then this [correspondence] exists even for the cognition whose objects are the moon, stars, and so forth.

If it is argued that "of consciousness" [refers to] that which is non-erroneous and direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and thus there is no deviation, [the author] refutes this: for you, the claim that a momentary object of consciousness is such [non-erroneous] would entail the error of [applying it to] a consciousness whose objects are lightning and the like, which perish even more rapidly. For in those cases, there is no subsequent [consciousness] regarding a single object.
The possibility of the arising of knowledge:

if one should think that the capacity to reach the object already indicated is itself the state of being a "reacher" (*prāpaka*), which is non-contradiction; and that the capacity to reach is itself the state of being a "prompter" (*pravartaka*), while the state of being a prompter is simply the state of being an indicator (*upadarśaka*). For [otherwise], there would be no purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).
Apart from the presentation of a capable object, no other mode of causing consciousness to arise or of bringing it about is possible for cognition.

Nor can the moon and stars, which are restricted by place, time, and form, possess such efficacy for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) and for their own appropriate functions as that which is presented by the cognition; nor would such [efficacy] not be attained if [the object] were not spatially remote.

"Or [the cognition] of lightning and so forth is not [non-erroneous] because of time"—this is incorrect, because it cannot withstand analysis. Does "correspondence" (saṃvāda) mean the attainment of the mere object, or the attainment of the object exactly as it was presented? The former alternative is not tenable;

for since the attainment of the mere object is possible even from a mere cognition, there would be the consequence that such a mere cognition would be non-erroneous simply by virtue of that correspondence.

Nor is the latter [position] tenable. For the appearance of something discrete and gross, which is necessarily established as non-erroneous due to its being a perception, cannot be logically accounted for in either of those two cases—namely, in the case of consciousness with forms (*sākāra-vijñāna*) or consciousness without forms (*nirākāra-vijñāna*). Indeed, that which is called "grossness" cannot exist as an ultimate reality, whether in consciousness or in the external object; for it would involve a conjunction with various contradictory properties in both instances.
Because it has been refuted. As it has been said:

"Therefore, there is no gross appearance either in the object or in the cognition, because that [grossness] is denied in the case of a single [atom]; since it is impossible in one, it is not possible even in many."
[Otherwise, there would be the consequence of error. Now, if it is the cessation of successive cognitions, then momentary consciousness possesses that nature.
Therefore, the perception of identity in what is not of that nature is an error. And thus, the cognition of the Omniscient One is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanā*).

The definition of perception as "that which is free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*) does not apply [to memory], because here the cognition proceeds in the form of an experience (*anubhava*);
thus, it certainly conforms to the definition. As it has been stated: "Even mental [cognition] is perception when it proceeds in the form of an experience.

Now, what is this "having the form of an experience"? If it means "having the nature of consciousness" (*bodhātmakatā*), then all cognition is such. Or if it means [the form of a specific] individual...

If it were merely a manifestation of light, then even when first encountered, the discernment of indistinct yellow and so forth—due to factors such as distance—would not constitute perception (*pratyakṣa*). On the other hand, if it were a cognition that is neither distant nor obscured, it would follow that the cognition of a universal (*sāmānya*) would also be perception.
Furthermore, in the system of formless consciousness (*nirākāra-vijñāna*), there are no multiple material atoms (*rūpa-paramāṇu*) arising in immediate succession.

They are capable of ascending into a single cognition and possess a gross appearance. As it has been said: "Grossness is not a property that exists [independently] of appearing; rather, a property existing at the time of appearing is what constitutes an appearing property. And it is not the case that these are not atoms of form (*rūpa-paramāṇu*), nor that they do not arise without interval, nor that they do not ascend into a single cognition. Nor...

And why is it not reasonable to say that [the cognition] is erroneous because it does not shine with such a designation of grossness? Because continuity is impossible; for if the intermediate spaces are not perceived, the apprehension of those [trees] would result in error, just like the cognition of a single dense forest in the case of trees that are utterly separated. It is not that those are not trees, nor is it that they do not appear in a single cognition.

They say: "And being without interval is equivalent to non-arising. Indeed, form-atoms do not arise without intervals like trees, because they are interspersed with heterogeneous odor-, taste-, and touch-atoms. Furthermore, if such [perceptions] were non-erroneous, then the perceptions of two moons, a whirling firebrand, moving trees, and so forth, would also be non-erroneous."

[Otherwise] there would be the undesirable consequence of [the definition] applying to you as well. Therefore, the Teacher [Dharmakīrti], considering that this non-erroneousness strikes back at you yourselves, has left it aside.
He concludes: "Therefore, by process of elimination, the cognition of identity in what is not that thing is an error.
[The opponent asks: "Granted that this is the definition of error, even so, what harm is done to us? To this he says: "And thus, error..."
If the two conceptual constructions were identical by way of being superimpositions, then the cognition of the Omniscient One would not be free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*).

This is because there would be a superimposition of the nature of form upon the past and future, which lack that nature; and if those [past and future objects] were not cognized, it would be impossible for [the cognition] to be perception, as it would follow that it is not a direct realization (*asākṣātkāra*). Nor is it non-erroneous, precisely because of the superimposition of a form that does not exist; thus, it is not perception.
It follows the definition.

He raises another objection regarding the definition of perception: "If perception functions with the form of direct experience (*anubhava*), then the omniscient one's knowledge, which has past and future things as its objects, certainly does follow that definition. As it has been said, even mental [cognition] is direct experience.
"Arising in the form of [the object]... Having thus formulated this, he refutes it: "What is this 'having the form of experience'?

If it is the nature of being consciousness (*bodhātmakatā*), then since all cognition is of that nature—being essentially consciousness—it would follow that everything is perception. Alternatively, if it is the appearance of another individual [object], then even though the indeterminate (*nirvikalpaka*) [cognition] arises first, it is [not perceived] due to defects such as distance."

"Direct perception would not be the discernment of manifest yellow and so forth. Now, if there is an engagement in the form of the experience of cognition regarding that which is neither distant nor obscured, then this applies even to the discernment of the unmanifest, provided it is neither distant nor obscured.

If it should be thought that the activity of experience consists in the manifestation of a present object situated in proximity, and that such is the vision of yogins and Tathāgatas regarding all objects—that is incorrect. For the previously mentioned fault has not been avoided.
Moreover, because they perceive what is not as it is in such a state, their vision of the present is merely false cognition, like the vision of one suffering from ophthalmia.

But perception does not become otherwise; it is characterized by being produced through the capacity of the sense organ and its object. Otherwise, for what reason would the vision of hair and such things, produced by a disorder such as cataracts (*timira*), not be confounded [with valid perception]? All perception indeed has the appearance of something not present [at the same time], because of the temporal difference between the object and the cognition due to their relationship as cause and effect. What then is this?

He further refutes [the opponent's position] by stating that if the object were at a great distance or concealed, it would follow that its cognition could not occur; for being at a distance or being concealed are properties of real entities (*vastu-dharma*). Since the universal (*sāmānya*) of that [object] is not a real entity, it can neither be at a distance nor be concealed. Consequently, the cognition of it must be perceptual (*pratyakṣa*).
If one should think: "The activity of the mode of experience indeed manifests what is proximate and present;

and the universal (sāmānya) is neither false, nor proximate, nor present. Yet such a [universal] is seen by yogins who have ascended to several stages, as well as by Tathāgatas who have reached the ten stages, with respect to all objects."

He refutes [the opponent's view]: that is incorrect. Why? Because the previous fault has not been avoided. Even though the universal (sāmānya), being unreal, is non-proximate and non-existent, nevertheless, since it appears in such a manner, its apprehension would result in being perception (pratyakṣa) due to the operation of the form of experience; this is the meaning of the statement that the previous fault recurs. Regarding this very point, the verse [states]:

With the first half [of the verse], he states another refutation: "Moreover, because such a thing is seen to exist in the present, as well as in the past and the future. He explains its being "such": the present is indeed false cognition, like the vision of one suffering from ophthalmia (*taimirika*). Why, then, is it not perception (*pratyakṣa*)? To this he says: "But perception does not become otherwise."

Why? Because the definition of perception is that which is produced by the capacity of the sense-organ and its object; specifically, perception is the cognition (*vijñāna*) arising from the capacity of both that [object] and the sense-organ—this is its definition. The meaning is that the activity in the form of experience (*anubhava*), as you intend it, is not the definition. Why, then, is this not [the case]?

What is the definition [of perception]? To this he says: otherwise, for what reason would the vision of hair and so forth produced by an affliction such as ophthalmia (*timira*) not be included within the category of perception?

For those who maintain that the definition of perception is "functioning in the form of an experience" (*anubhavākārapravṛttitva*), the cognition of one suffering from ophthalmia is not intended to be considered perception; such is the meaning.

Now, the proponent of the theory that cognition possesses a form (sākārajñānavādin) objects: "Let every perception indeed have the appearance of something not present; let it not cease to be perception simply because of that. Thus, this apprehension of something otherwise does not entail its being non-perceptual. Why is it that all cognition has the appearance of something not present? To this he says:
Because there is a temporal distinction between the object and its cognition due to their relationship as cause and effect, the correspondence of the items in this context is not accepted.
However, the proponent of the critique, harboring a hidden intention, asks: "What then is this blue and so forth, which exists in a proximate space and time?
What is it that appears? It is the form of cognition (*jñānākāra*). For at this time, there is no one who perceives even a single part of the whole [external object] directly through perception.

Since all practical activity (*vyavahāra*) regarding an object is observed to occur solely through the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of the feeling of the form of cognition, there is no loss of the perception of the object itself. How can there be a determination of one thing when there is a cognition of another? [This is possible] because of the deep-rootedness of the chronic epilepsy characterized by the persistent attachment to grasping an external object, which has been beginningless.

[This refers] to ignorance. In that case, may there be well-being for omniscience! It would be better to have a great deal of the epilepsy of ignorance; rather, it is preferable to have a lesser degree of ignorance, namely, the state of seeing only one part. Furthermore, even by way of technical definition, perception would pertain only to a single part; for it is only the state of being an object of apprehension (*grāhyatva*)—that is, the state of being a cause capable of imparting its form to the cognition—that [is perceived], and not everything.

Because that [object] lacks causality due to its non-proximity in terms of either space or time; otherwise, would it not follow that everyone would possess the quality of being all-seeing? The challenger says: "It is the form of the cognition. The questioner reveals his own intention with a touch of irony:
"For indeed, there exists no one at present who perceives directly even a single part of the object's form."

The one who perceives all objects directly has rightly established this: there is no loss of the perception of the object, because worldly transaction occurs through the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of the cognition of the object within the form of knowledge. For the objects of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are of two kinds: the apprehended (*grāhya*) and the determined (*adhyavaseya*). Among these, its own form is the apprehended; however, its externality is what is determined. As it has been said:

Activity occurs through the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of an object within one's own manifestation, even though that manifestation is not an external object. For in this system, apprehension cannot be established in any other manner. Therefore, all cognition consists precisely in the determination of the form of the cognition itself as being external.
And yet, it is not for this reason that [cognition] is erroneous; indeed, one who perceives by means of the mind’s function of grasping does not thereby become mistaken.

If one perceives otherwise at some times, or if one proceeds by means other than the appropriate means despite being directed toward the object, one is deluded (*bhrānta*). However, since neither of these two conditions exists in the Omniscient One, how could He be deluded?

[The opponent] objects: "How can there be a determination (*adhyavasāya*) of the perception of an external object (*bāhyavedana*) when there is only the perception of one's own form (*svākāravedana*)?"

The opponent says: "Because it is firmly established, [the grasping of objects] is due to ignorance (*avidyā*), characterized by a delusion consisting of an attachment to grasping objects that has been beginningless.

He refutes this with derision: "In that case, blessings upon your omniscience! It would be better to have a lesser degree of ignorance—that is, being a seer of only one part—rather than a profusion of ignorance characterized by delusion. For even one's own form, though it be not an object [of external reality],..."

Even by way of determination (*adhyavasāya*), [cognition] is non-erroneous because there is no other means [of apprehension]. Nor can this erroneous nature, which is established by logic (*nyāyasiddha*), be denied for fear of the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that all perception would be erroneous; for what is established by a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) cannot be denied when its purpose is obstructed. This is the intended meaning. Furthermore, the refutation of the agent of determination will be shown later.

Regarding the statement that "knowledge is not without an object": moreover, even by way of technical convention (*paribhāṣā*), perception would apply only to a single part [of the object]. He states the convention: "The state of being an object (*grāhyatva*) is precisely the state of being a cause capable of imparting its form to the knowledge. This is as stated in the Sautrāntika system.

If it is asked how that which exists at a different time can be apprehended, they [the proponents of this view] know its "apprehensibility" (grāhyatā) to be simply its state of being a cause (hetutva), at the moment it imparts its form to the cognition.
And this apprehensibility is technical (pāribhāṣika), being non-ordinary; and by means of it, only a single part [of the object] is [apprehended].

It is not the case, however, that everything is directly perceived. Why? Because it would follow that everything lacks a cause. Why is that? Because it would lead to an absurd consequence (*prasaṅga*). Alternatively, is cognition only of the form of the present, or is it also of the form of the past and the future?

In the former case, it is false because everything is not as it appears; in the latter case, it is not perception because it functions through the conceptualization of forms such as the "not-yet-come" (future) and so forth. Alternatively, everything would have to be known at the time of cognition either in its present state or in its actual state. In the first instance, there is falsity; in the second, not everything is perceived, because that which exists in another state is not being perceived.

Moreover, it is not possible to comprehend everything sequentially because of its infinity; for [everything] lacks both a prior and a posterior limit, whether in terms of space or time, due to its non-proximity. Therefore, those things which are remote in space or time are what are to be cultivated, but not so everything—this is the meaning. Now, why is that which is non-proximate not a cause?

To this he says: otherwise, if proximity were not required for causality, it would follow that everyone, including ourselves, would possess omniscience. Furthermore, the capacity of yoga has already been refuted here, just as in the first half [of the verse].
There is another interpretation of this: or rather, [the cognition] has a present form, that is, a form belonging to the present time.
Regarding the entire expansion of objects existing in the three times, consciousness may take on the forms of the past and the future as well.

In the former case, because everything would not exist in that manner [in the present], the consciousness of the omniscient one would be false. In the latter case, however, it would not be direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because it is understood through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) regarding the forms of the past, future, and so forth. [For direct perception is] devoid of conceptual construction.

Because of its nature as reality (*tattva*). First of all, it is not the case that the past and future are objects of non-conceptual cognition merely by way of their form (*rūpamātra*), since their mere form is no different from that of the present. For even the present does not appear in non-conceptual cognition as qualified by "presentness," but rather merely by way of its form. Therefore, [the object] is not qualified by pastness and so forth.

This must be understood regarding the two [types of] mental construction (*kalpanā*). For the very nature of conceptual constructions is indeed the apprehension of things through the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*), precisely because they are capable of being associated with verbal expression. It is not, however, the appearance of both word and object within a single cognition, since that is possible even in non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) perception. Therefore, [the cognition] qualified by the past and so forth...
It is thus established that knowledge having a [past or future] object is not perception, because it is conceptual.

As for the one who thinks: "Let perception have only the present as its object; nevertheless, it would still have all things as its objects, because even the past and the future are present by virtue of their being past and future," in order to refute this very [view]:
He states another explanation: "Or else, everything would be known at the time of cognition either in its present state or as it exists [at that time].

The meaning is: whatever is in a certain state, it is known as such. In the former case, there is falsity, because that which is in one state is apprehended otherwise. In the latter case, not everything would be perceptible. Why? Because other states are not perceived.

This is what is meant: that which is past, present, or future at the time of its cognition must be perceived exactly as it is. Furthermore, at the time of its own cognition, it was past or future, and was then present;
likewise, at the time of its own cognition, being present, it was future and will later become past. Thus, at a time inferior to its own...

Since the future states of existence— namely, the present and the past— would belong to that which has already passed, if one were to grasp an object as possessing distinct temporal states like those occurring at the time of its own cognition, then another state would remain ungrasped within it; thus, one would not be omniscient.
There is no finality regarding the production of that which is to be known; it does not occur simultaneously, precisely because of its infinity.

For if the limit [of objects] is not determined, there is no distinction between the comprehension of the whole and the comprehension of a single part. [Objection: Even without determining the limit, one understands everything simultaneously by way of its form (rūpa). [Reply: This is not sound. For if the limit is not determined, everything has not been determined.

Or it may be a single part [of the whole], because neither of the two is excluded. When there is a collection of many substances, the cognition of the whole arises precisely from the determination of its magnitude (*iyattā*); and that [determination] is possible only with respect to what is limited, not with respect to what is unlimited. Furthermore, the apprehension of the object of knowledge depends upon the form (*ākāra*) of the cognition; and for those forms residing in a single cognition that exist simultaneously—
He explains the latter half [of the verse]: "Moreover, it is not possible to comprehend everything through a sequential process.

Why? Because of its infinity. He demonstrates this very point: "For there is no finality for an object of knowledge that arises and is devoid of prior and posterior limits; even in the case of an eternal thing such as an atom (*paramāṇu*), there is no fixed end."

The meaning is: if even for form (*rūpa*) there is no such limit—how much more so for that which has an indefinite nature, like its arising? It is not simultaneous. Why? Precisely because of the aforementioned infinity; for if there were a determination of a limit, then the word "all" (*sarva*) would denote totality, and totality would entail a state of being without remainder, which [in this case] has not been determined.

The meaning is that not everything has been ascertained. Now, why is it that the ascertainment of "everything" depends upon the ascertainment of its "extent"? To this he says: because if its extent is not ascertained, there is no distinction between the comprehension of a part and the comprehension of the whole.
This is what is meant: for in common worldly experience, when many things are understood only partially, there is no comprehension of the whole.

Speakers say what is well-known: "We know only a portion of these things, not the whole. If everything were merely form (rūpa), then because there would be no distinction between those two cases, it would follow that there is no difference between the cognition of the whole and the cognition of a part.
The opponent objects: "But surely, even without determining the specific measure (*iyattā*) of things by way of their form, one cognizes everything simultaneously.

And since everything is indeed indeterminate (*aniyata*), how can it be possible to determine an unlimited form? Thus, the object of cognition (*prameya*) is at fault regarding its measure. That which is indeterminate cannot, however, have a cognition as its object that corresponds exactly to the object of cognition."

The meaning is that validity is untenable whether there is a determination of the limit [of objects] or no determination of the limit. He refutes this: "This is not sound. For if the limit is not determined, neither is everything determined nor is even a single part determined. Why?
Because if the limited form of one part is not apprehended, there is no exclusion [of the rest]. [If one part is not excluded,] the other...

And because one or the other is apprehended through the exclusion [of the opposite]. Having shown the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), he states the positive concomitance (*anvaya*): "In the case of inherence in many substances, the apprehension of 'all' occurs precisely from the determination of the limit of quantity. He says "inherence in many substances" because neither "all-ness" nor "being in one place" is possible in a single substance, nor in many things that are not mutually connected. That...

The state of being "without remainder" (*aniḥśeṣatā*) is possible regarding that which is limited, not regarding that which is unlimited; therefore, it is established that because [the object] is infinite, there is no state of being without remainder. And thus, it does not produce the manifestation of everything. Since the apprehension of "everything" is itself the apprehension of simultaneity, that too is absent. Furthermore, there is no simultaneous apprehension of the infinite whole, as in the system of the Sautrāntikas.

Furthermore, the apprehension of the object of knowledge depends upon the form of the cognition. And there cannot be an infinity of forms existing simultaneously within a single cognition; why? Because all of them would necessarily be present.

There is no end [to them], because all are present. For those that are unborn, those that have passed away, and those that are presently occurring—provided they are not separated by space or time—are infinite when considered together with the past, because there is no delimitation from the prior limit (*pūrvakoṭi*), and even if there were a delimitation, it would be only beyond [the future]. However, as many as are presently occurring are delimited by both limits.

If there are only as many [cognitions] as there are [objects] that have arisen, how can there be infinity? Therefore, there is no single cognition possessing infinite forms, nor are there multiple simultaneous cognitions. Furthermore, what is this "all" that one who knows it is called "all-knowing"? It cannot be the objects taken individually, nor even a certain number of them combined with others and governed by some commonality. No.
And such a state is possible among infinite things. If it is argued that "everything is primarily infinite," we say no;

for otherwise, why would there not be infinity even for those things that are presently existing? To this he says: "For those things that have not yet arisen, those that have passed away, and those that are presently existing, are infinite because their space and time are uninterrupted. [Objection: But surely the self of individual entities is not [infinite]?
Since the state of being delimited by space and time is also excluded, he says: "Mutually requiring one another" means being combined;

not only the three [present ones], but rather the past ones as well, which are infinite. Now, if all those preceding her are delimited by the past by means of a single moment of time, how can the past be infinite? To this he says: "the prior time."

Because the limit is not delimited, even if it were delimited, it would be so only by what follows; moreover, this mode does not exist for the forms that ascend to the cognitions of one or many, such that their infinity would necessarily follow. He says:
"But those that have arisen, delimited by both limits, are exactly as many as have arisen; how, then, could there be infinity?"
He summarizes: Therefore, there is neither a single cognition with infinite aspects, nor simultaneous cognitions that are infinite, because in both cases both alternatives are excluded.
He explains the meaning of the second half of the verse—that the object of knowledge (*prameya*) is not defined—by asking: "And what is this 'all'?"

Regarding the one who knows "all" (sarvavid): it is not the case that objects are [meant] individually, for the word "all" is not applied to individual things that are independent of others. Nor does it refer to unrelated things accompanied by others; otherwise, the word "all" might be applied even to a single son of Devadatta by taking some other person into account. Rather, it refers to a certain number of things brought under control by some common characteristic.

As in the cases "all Brāhmaṇas" or "all cows. Let it be so; what is the fault? To this he says: "In this manner, such a state [of being 'all'] is not possible with respect to infinite things. He raises an objection: "If it is argued that 'all' refers primarily to the infinite itself. For instance, in the absence of a specific context (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth...

The meaning is this: how can this word *sarva*, which functions without restriction, apply to infinite things? Therefore, its primary referent must be the infinite itself. He refutes [this objection]: even though the past and future possess infinity, those things belonging to one end of time (the past) are not "all" because they are limited by even that single [past] moment. [Likewise for the future. Pūrva-apa...
Furthermore, because all things consist of present entities that are uninterrupted and endowed with the nature of being present;

moreover, if "all-ness" (sarvatva) is indeed infinite, its determination is impossible. To explain: have all individual instances been determined or not? If they have been determined, then there are only that many and not an infinite number. If they have not been determined—

Their infinity consists in this very lack of determination; thus he says: "And how is it that non-determination is infinite? Because everything is determined. The point is that what is not being determined cannot be an object of knowledge (*prameya*).
Because those that possess temporal limits are not all-encompassing due to their non-universality, whereas those uninterrupted by prior or posterior [moments] are universal.

Furthermore, if there were universality, such a restriction [to "all"] would be impossible; for if all manifest things were restricted, they would be only that many and not infinite. Indeed, their infinity exists only when there is no such restriction.

And since that [object] is not determined as being infinite, how can there be its determination? If it is argued that all objects are delimited by the three times, we say no; for there is an absence of such delimitation in them, as they do not differ in their spatial location. Therefore, since there is no mode of existence other than succession and simultaneity, and since cognition is pervaded by those two, cognition is impossible when those two are absent. Furthermore, it is impossible because of the absence of any object of knowledge (*prameya*).

Furthermore, because inference and the other means of knowledge are preceded by perception, they too lack causality with respect to everything. Since there is no apprehension of a relation—either directly or indirectly—through perception, there can be no inference. For this very reason, there can be no verbal testimony (śabda), because the meaning of a sentence consists in a word-meaning as qualified by another word-meaning. Nor can there be presumptive testimony (arthāpatti), in the absence of that [relation].
"Because it is impossible for there to be a perception of [objects] being newly produced. It is not analogy (*upamāna*), because its object is similarity (*sādṛśya*).

He objects: 'In that case, all objects are delimited by the three times. We say that "all-ness" (*sarvatā*) is indeed infinitude; however, it is delimited by the distinction in the determination of objects as past and so forth, which is obtained through a single time by virtue of limiting conditions (*upādhi*)."

The meaning is that [the reason] is "all" because of the absence of non-existence [in them]. He refutes this: no, because there is no delimitation (*avaccheda*) among them; for since the reason is not specified as being in only one part, the comprehension of "all" is untenable. Indeed, these [moments] are not grasped by a single [cognition] as being "just this many," but rather as "this much. And as long as this single, eternal time remains undelimited by the apprehension of the defects, [the cognition of all does not occur].

"How can it be that even when delimited by speech, it is [only] this much? The meaning is that its past, future, and present states, even when combined, are not infinite either. Demonstrating the latter half of the verse as proof, he concludes:
"Therefore, because there is no mode of being that exceeds succession and simultaneity, cognition is pervaded by those two."

If that [perception] is untenable, then [omniscience] is untenable. Furthermore, due to the absence of objects of knowledge (*prameya*), the object of knowledge cannot be determined. It should be understood that omniscience is refuted precisely by this failure to determine the object of knowledge, and not merely on the basis of the capacity for universal apprehension. Now, one might argue: "Granted, he may not know everything through perception, but he will know it through inference and other means. To this, he says: "Perception is the prerequisite... (*pratyakṣapūrva*).
And because [the relation] has been established, inference and the other means of knowledge also possess validity as instruments of knowledge with respect to the whole [of reality].

He demonstrates individually that the means of knowledge are preceded by perception: the cause is the apprehension, through perception either directly or indirectly, of the relation characterized by the rule of being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*); and of that [relation], in the whole...

Inference does not [apply here], nor does verbal testimony (śabda), for that very reason, because it arises from the apprehension of a relationship [between word and object] through perception. Now, one might argue:
"Let it be that everything whose relationship has not been grasped is not the meaning of a word; however, the meaning of a sentence (vākyārtha) will still exist. To this he replies:

because the meaning of a sentence is simply the meaning of the words themselves as qualified by the other word-meanings [with which they are connected]. This has already been established in the examination of the *niyoga* (the mandatory injunction).

Nor is it presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). Why? Because it is impossible to perceive anything that, being absent in its entirety, is otherwise unaccountable or inconceivable. Nor is it analogy (*upamāna*), because analogy consists in the comparison of a perceived object—such as a cow—which has ascended into memory, with a presently perceived object such as a *gavaya*; and since everything [in its entirety] is never perceived anywhere, there can be no object of similarity.
And because everything has the nature of being dissimilar [to itself]. Nor is there an absence of that [non-existence] due to the absence of its object of cognition (*prameya*),
for it has non-existence as its object, just as it is for perception and the other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Succession and simultaneity are not possible, nor can an object of cognition be established. Thus, first of all, there is a lack of logical consistency. This applies to cognition as well:
for those who do not see everything, the knowledge of another is not within the range of the senses;
therefore, the effect of an omniscient being's cognition cannot be established.

First of all, even if it exists, a subsequent cognition is not perceptible to those who do not perceive supersensible objects; for this very reason, it is not inferable either, because its effect is unestablished in the absence of that [cognition]. Now, one might argue that there must be a limit to the degrees of excellence (atiśaya) because everything is an object [of cognition]. But this is untenable, since everything exists in both a real and an unreal form. This would apply equally to perception and to other means of knowledge as well.
Succession and simultaneity are neither conceivable nor possible for the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, the object of cognition (*prameya*) cannot be established.
Thus, first, the wood has been cleared away by the fire of non-occurrence (*anupapatti-pramāṇa*). Now, knowledge (*jñāna*) itself is also being examined.
To explain:
The cognition of all that is invisible is not within the range of the senses;
therefore, it cannot be established as the effect of the knowledge of an omniscient being.
For someone like us, who does not perceive supersensuous objects, even the existence of all subsequent cognitions cannot be known through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Now, one might object: just as, from observing effects such as smiling and crying in a newborn infant, joy, sorrow, and other states—which are themselves imperceptible—as well as the experiences of a previous life, are inferred; so too [should it be with] that which is characterized by instruction and the like.
One might infer that there exists a cognition whose object is everything because of the observation of its effects; therefore, he says:

"And for this very reason, precisely because it is absolutely imperceptible, it is not something to be inferred. Now, it was argued that it is to be inferred from the observation of its effects; to this he replies:
"Because, as long as that omniscient cognition is not established, its effects cannot be established by perception. One who has never perceived smoke [cannot infer fire]."

One understands smoke to be the effect of that [fire]. However, there is a distinction: whereas laughter, weeping, and so forth are recognized within oneself as being effects of grief and the like—which are themselves apprehended through mental perception—[the case of] instruction by Manu and others, or by Caraka and others, arises either from the Veda, or from the understanding of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) produced by activity originating from another instruction. It is not [otherwise].

Furthermore, there is no beginning to the instructions of the physician Caraka; indeed, even in a thousand human lifetimes, no one is capable of establishing through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) the [effects of] all medicinal herbs and their combinations independently of traditional scripture (*āgama*).

As for the instruction regarding the worship of shrines (*caityavandana*) and so forth, it is faultless [to conclude] that it arises from delusion or deception. As for those [arguments] stated by others...
The reasons for this have already been refuted below, so nothing remains hidden here.

Now, he introduces the following argument to refute the omniscience favored by the followers of the *Svāyambhuva* [Purāṇa]: "But surely, the attainment of the ultimate limit of degrees of magnitude is observed, as in the case of the *kuvala*, *āmalaka*, and *bilva* fruits."
That [knowledge] which possesses excellence reaches its ultimate limit in space (*ākāśa*). Since space is perceived as the supreme among all things of great dimension,
and knowledge is likewise possessed of excellence, it therefore reaches its ultimate limit in some [substratum].
Regarding the phrase "pervading all objects," it is said:
If the ultimate limit (*kāṣṭhā*) is intended as the boundary, then let it be so, since nothing beyond it is possible;
yet there is no lack of consistency [in its being infinite] with respect to produced substances and qualities such as weight (*garima*) and the like.

If that which beyond which there is nothing is the ultimate limit (*kāṣṭhā*), let it be attained; yet by that attainment, the status of having all things as its object is not established. Rather, there would be the status of having the greatest number of objects. Just as a terrestrial globe, compared to other terrestrial objects, occupies a much larger space in the ether but does not possess omnipresence (*sarvavyāpitā*). Now, if [it is argued that] from which...

But this is not tenable, because there is a deviation [from the rule] in the case of effect-substances (*kāryadravya*). For even jars and the like, despite their excellence, do not surpass what is impossible to surpass in terms of magnitude (*parimāṇa*), because it would follow that there would be no room for anything else, since everything would be pervaded by a single [magnitude]. Nor is it correct to say that this is a property of qualities (*guṇadharma*), because [it would then apply to] heaviness (*garima*) and so forth residing in those [substances].

This cognition is observed to possess degrees of excellence; it is logical that this very cognition reaches its culmination through its pervasion of one, two, or many objects and so forth. And this is its attainment of the ultimate limit:
namely, the state of abiding in the absence of that [object] once everything that is to be known has been known. As the venerable Patañjali said:

In this regard, [the opponent claims] that the cognition of the Omniscient One is unsurpassed. To this, the following reply is given: It is said—Granted, the "limit" (*kāṣṭhā*) may be the boundary, since nothing superior to it is possible; yet, there is no logical necessity (*anekānta*) because of produced substances and qualities such as heaviness (*garima*) and the like.

Having conceptualized this "limit" (*kāṣṭhā*), he refutes it: if that which beyond which nothing exists is the limit, let there be the attainment of it; however, the establishment of omniscience does not follow from that. We do not dispute the point that every cognition, having its specific nature acquired from its own causes, does not transcend the boundaries of its own object-domain. No.

The meaning is this: by this much alone, the cognition of all objects is established. However, for those who are wise and proficient in the six means of valid knowledge (*ṣatpramāṇī*), there may be a preponderance of objects within their cognition—just as in the case of an earthen globe that serves as the substratum for the entire world of living beings, which possesses a much greater expanse of space relative to other earthen things such as boulders and rocks.

It is pervasiveness, but not all-pervasiveness. He anticipates another objection: "Now, that beyond which nothing further can be conceived is the ultimate limit (*kāṣṭhā*), just as the dimension of the ether is its supreme magnitude and the sphericality of atoms is their limit; for there is nothing beyond these two."
Something greater or smaller comes into being. He refutes that [position]: there is a deviation [from the rule] in the case of effect-substances (*kāryadravya*).

He demonstrates this: for even though jars, pots, water-jars, and so forth possess excellence, they do not, by way of their dimension (*parimāṇa*), surpass another [dimension] whose form and location are impossible to conceive. Why? Because it would follow that there would be no room for anything else.

Since everything would be pervaded by a single substance possessing touch and having the magnitude of space, there would be no room for other substances possessing touch. [Objection: Because of the qualification "provided it is a quality" (*guṇatve sati*), there is no deviation with respect to effect-substances (*kāryadravya*).
[Page 147]

Because such a state is impossible; for there is no commencement of a single effect by all [entities] possessing gravity. Furthermore, the attainment of nearness or distance results from a specific effort, as seen in humans, wind, deer, lions, and birds. Nor is there an unsurpassable excellence (*atiśaya*) in that [gravity], because space is infinite. For some, however, it is unsurpassable.

Because there would be the consequence of falling even for those things already attained. For effort would be unsurpassed only upon reaching a destination where no further space remains to be traversed; since that [space] is infinite, how could his effort be unsurpassed? Therefore, there is a deviation [from the rule] due to effort itself, or due to its specific qualities, or due to the qualities of the intellect. This [unsurpassed nature] does not belong to merit (*dharma*), which has sovereignty as its fruit.
The limit [of dharma] is the same, because it produces sovereignty. This is because the sovereignty of Īśvara cannot be the fruit of dharma;

for if it were, there would be the consequence of multiple sovereignties due to the non-restraint of afflictions, karma, its maturation, and latent dispositions, which would result in the contradiction of sovereignty.
Furthermore—

To this he replies: "Nor is it correct to say that this is a property of the qualities (*guṇadharma*). Why? Because it is impossible for heaviness (*gurutva*) and other such properties residing in substances that are their effects to reach that ultimate limit (*kāṣṭhā*) of state. For if heaviness were to observe two states, it would be by all those possessing the quality of heaviness combining together to produce a single, supreme quality of heaviness."
An effect is initiated; however, this is not possible, as he says: because there is no initiation of a single effect by all [causes] that possess gravity.
Now, if it is argued that there is no deviation [from the rule] due to the qualification "being a quality" (guṇatva) while being uncommon (asādhāraṇya), he replies:
"And from a specific effort, there is the reaching of near and distant [objects] by humans, wind, deer, lions, and birds. Nor...

The excellence (*atiśaya*) of that particularity reaches a state of culmination that is inconceivable. Why? Because space, which is to be traversed, is infinite; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of falling for certain [beings] whose effort is unsurpassed. For when all regions to be traversed have been reached, effort—which is the cause of motion—becomes unsurpassed because it has attained its goal (*prāpaṇīya*).

It might be argued that because of its infinity, how could there be any lack of excellence for this [dharma]? Therefore, the point is that the fallacy of deviation remains as before, whether by means of the specific quality of effort (*prayatna*) or the quality of intellect (*buddhi*). If it were said that knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty indeed arise from dharma that is neither white nor black, [the response follows].

In that regard, one might argue that there is a deviation [from the rule] because the knowledge produced by that [dharma] is unsurpassed, just as detachment (*vairāgya*) and sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) are produced by specific types of dharma; to this he replies: "There is no such limit for dharma that results in sovereignty, and thus dharma is designated as such because it produces sovereignty and the like. But why is there no such limit for dharma that is neither white nor black?

Regarding the point "in wood," he says: because [if it were so], the sovereignty of God would result in being merely the fruit of merit (*dharma*). However, the non-white and non-black (*aśuklākṛṣṇa*) merits belong to the yogins only in relation to their derivative sovereignty (*bhākta aiśvarya*), and not to the unsurpassed [sovereignty]. That [unsurpassed sovereignty] indeed belongs only to the Blessed Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) in its primary sense. Furthermore, that knowledge is not likewise a mere quality (*dharma*) of Him. Therefore, this reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*).
Furthermore, the example is devoid of the probans. Why, then, would the sovereignty of the Supreme Lord not be produced by merit (*dharma*)?
[p.148] If the sky, which cannot possibly exist in any other state, were not limited...
Furthermore, because of their infinity, reality is not characterized by any finite measure.

Therefore, he says: "Because of not being touched by afflictions, actions, their results, or latent dispositions. As the venerable Patañjali has stated here: "Īśvara is a particular Puruṣa who is untouched by afflictions, actions, their results, and latent dispositions.
Ignorance, egoism, attachment, aversion, and the will to live are the afflictions (*kleśas*). Wholesome and unwholesome deeds are the actions (*karmas*).

The results of that [karma] are birth, lifespan, and experience. They are called "residues" (*āśaya*) because they lie dormant; they consist of the latent impressions of karma, as their objects are merit and demerit. Nevertheless, one might suspect that this Blessed One is not distinct from liberated souls or those who have attained dissolution into primordial nature (*prakṛtilaya*) or isolation (*vaidehya*), since they too are untouched by afflictions and the like; therefore, it is said that he is a "particular soul" (*puruṣaviśeṣa*).

Indeed, for those liberated souls (muktātman), there exists a prior limit of bondage; and for those such as Sanatkumāra, who are liberated-in-body (videha) or absorbed-into-primal-matter (prakṛtilaya), there exists a subsequent limit. However, this very distinction belongs to that Blessed One (the Lord) compared to them, because here [in his case], the afflictions (kleśa) and so forth are merely optional (vaikalpika). Therefore, what [need is there to speak of] his sovereignty produced by a specific quality (dharma)? This is the meaning.

But to one who, out of obstinacy, disregards the word of the elders and maintains that even the sovereignty of the Supreme Lord is produced by merit (*dharma*), he says: "Because it would follow that there are multiple Lords, and because the sovereignty of all [others] would be impaired.
This is the meaning: if lordship were produced by merit, then whoever possesses that merit would be a Lord, and there would be many.
If they possess that [power], then by virtue of it, many lords would result. In that case, the sovereignty of all would be either equal to or less than the sovereignty of one.

And if there is inferiority, then whatever is superior would truly be the lordship; thus, the sovereignty of the others would be merely figurative. And that [figurative status] is possible because it is inherent, since inherent nature is not subject to fluctuation.

Now, if [their lordship] were born of their nature (*dharma*), would they rule by acting together—like an assembly (*pariṣad*)—due to the lack of fixed order even when there is equality, or would each rule individually? In the first case, like an assembly, no one would be a Lord (*īśvara*), because lordship is exercised collectively.
In the latter case, since lordship has been accomplished by one alone, what could the other do to be a Lord? For "lordship" (*īśanā*) does not consist in mere existence.

If [the Lord] were an agent, independent [beings] could not possibly possess a single intention. Consequently, when there are conflicting intentions, no effect whatsoever can arise; or, if an effect were to arise, the world would be perceived simultaneously as possessing mutually contradictory natures. Furthermore, the claim that sovereignty is produced by karma is also contrary to scripture.

"Because there is no sequential limit even for that which is born of Dharma. Furthermore, regarding what was stated—that the attainment of the ultimate limit is perceived among measurements—he refutes this by means of an alternative analysis: "Moreover, if space were limited, its supreme state would not be impossible."
Furthermore, because of their infinity, reality is not characterized by a finite measure for them.

If space were limited, why could something greater than that not be conceived? This possibility is to be inferred from the observation of increasingly superior dimensions in things such as the *kuvala*, the *āmalaka*, and the *bilva*. One might suspect that even beyond this much sky there will be something of greater dimension; however, because space is infinite, such a thing is impossible.

If it is argued that this is because of infinity (*anantatva*), what is this "infinity"? It is being undelimited (*aparicchinna*). But is this not simply the absence of measurement (*parimāṇa*)? In that case, this much is the measurement. And such an attainment of the ultimate limit (*kāṣṭhāprāpti*) belongs to Īśvara.
By speaking of ignorance regarding knowledge, he reveals his own ignorance; this is like the rising of a vampire during a rite for peace.

Therefore, omniscience follows precisely from being the agent of all effects; for potters and other agents are those who are cognizant of the material cause, the instruments, the recipient, and the purpose. And God is the agent of all effects.

[He is] one who knows the material cause and so forth of all effects; and thus, he is omniscient. Are these [beings] knowers of every single instrument of their own effect, or knowers of only a few instruments? First, it is not to be accepted that they possess every single instrument. Wishing to dispel this doubt, the objector asks: "What is this infinity? [The respondent] says: "The objector..."

He says: "Infinite" (anantya) is simply the state of being undelimited; there is nothing else called "infinity" other than this. The reply is: But surely this is merely the absence of measurement (parimāṇa), resorted to through a different mode of expression. He clarifies that very point: "In that case, 'this much' is the measurement, while its opposite is the absence thereof. Let it be so, then.

If it is argued that the Lord’s knowledge is infinite like space and that this itself constitutes its attainment of the ultimate limit (*kāṣṭhāprāpti*), so what is the use of our grasping its magnitude?
To this he replies: by asserting such an attainment of the ultimate limit for the Lord’s knowledge, one reveals the Lord’s ignorance;
for [the Lord] would then be lacking complete knowledge of his own very own cognition. Or, if [he did possess such complete knowledge], then...

How can there be infinity for this [knowledge], since in the case of totality, it is excluded by the determination of a finite measure (iyattā), which is invariably concomitant with limitation? Thus, in this attempt to establish the omniscience of God through the infinity of His knowledge during the performance of rites for peace (śāntikarma),
one merely invokes a vampire (vetālodaya) characterized by the very ignorance of the reality that God possesses.

Now the Naiyāyikas offer a rebuttal: "In that case, omniscience follows precisely from being the agent of all effects. An agent who is perceived as the creator of all effects, such as bodies, the earth, and so forth, is perceived as necessarily including omniscience within himself, just as a lamp is perceived as including its light and rays, by virtue of its own means of proof."
This is the meaning. Now, one might ask: "Granted that there is agency, but why is there omniscience? To this he says:

"For potters and other such agents are those who possess knowledge of the material cause (*upādāna*), the instruments (*upakaraṇa*), the recipient (*saṃpradāna*), and the purpose (*prayojana*). Here, the material cause consists of the four classes of atoms; the instruments are merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) inherent in all individual souls (*kṣetrajña*)."

The recipients are the *kṣetrajñas* (knowers of the field), toward whom this Blessed One directs [his activity] by means of their own actions. The purpose is the experience of pleasure and pain by the *kṣetrajñas*. As for the material cause (*upādāna*) and so forth, which are the objects of the potter’s and other agents’ operations, they are indeed well known.
This is what is meant: those who are the agents of something are aware of its material cause and so forth, as in the case of potters and others. This applies to all [agents].
And [they hold that] God is the agent of effects, one who is cognizant of the material causes and so forth of all effects; thus, He is omniscient.
Having thus presented this dependent system of tenets along with its illustrations, he begins to refute it: "What are these..."

Potters and others are knowers of the complete set of implements required for their own work, yet they are not knowers of even a few of the implements [required for the creation of the world], because of their ignorance of the unseen (adṛṣṭa). Nor are they knowers of the specific recipient or the specific purpose [of the creation].

Since it is possible for that [agency] to belong to many individuals, the proof of omniscience does not follow from the knowledge of those [specific] things alone. Furthermore, children, the insane, and others do not possess knowledge of the purposes and so forth of all effects. If agency is what is to be proven, how can it be established—without a probans—that it includes omniscience?
Is it not already established that things possessing arrangement and so forth must be preceded by an intelligent agent?

No; for they do not know all the instruments and other requirements. Why? Because they lack knowledge of the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), which is the efficient cause of all things that have an origin. Nor do they know the specific recipient or the particular purpose [of the creation]. Of that...

For there exists a multiplicity of recipients, such as Devadatta and others, and a multiplicity of purposes, such as the holding of honey, water, and so forth; thus, even though these are manifold, they are possible. Now, if it is argued that the knowledge of the potter and others consists only of the instruments and so on, and not of the knowledge of all instruments and so on, then by that very same example, the Lord’s knowledge would also consist only of those instruments and so on; and if it is only the knowledge of those [instruments], then [the conclusion follows].

The attainment of omniscience [is thus established]. For if that were not the case, he would be merely a possessor of limited knowledge. Nor is it the case that even with knowledge of only that much, God is like a child or the like; as he says: "Children, madmen, and others do not know the purpose and so forth of their own actions, for we observe their engagement in those actions despite being devoid of intention. Not...

Furthermore, there is no restrictive reason why potters and the like serve as examples [of intelligent agents] while children and the like do not. If that agency is what is to be proven, how can it be established—without a probans—that it includes omniscience? To this, the opponent objects: "But it is already established. Why? Because things possessing structure and so forth are preceded by an intelligent being..."
Because [it is] due to being composed of parts. Indeed, there are three types of entities in the world:
those whose conscious creator is well-known, such as palaces, watchtowers, gate-towers, and archways; those whose opposite is well-known, such as atoms, space, and so forth;
and those whose creator is doubtful, such as grass, trees, the earth, mountains, and so forth. Among these—

Those things under dispute have an intelligent agent as their maker, because they are effects or because they have non-intelligent material causes; for whatever is an effect or has a non-intelligent material cause is preceded by an intelligent agent, just like a palace or similar structures; and such are the body, the world, and so forth; therefore, these too are preceded by an intelligent being. This is intended to indicate the two aforementioned reasons.

The mention of "possessing an arrangement and so forth" [is for this reason]: otherwise, because the reason would not pervade qualities (*guṇa*) and actions (*karman*), there would be the consequence of its being unestablished in one part (*ekadeśāsiddhatva*). Nor is the fact that earth and the other elements are effects unestablished; for that is established—just like a garment and the like—by their having action while possessing magnitude, or by their having parts. If one should think [that the probandum is] merely "having an intelligent agent" (*buddhimattvamātra*):

This is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), for even our opponents admit that the class of effects is born of karma, and since karma has consciousness as its cause, the world has that [consciousness] as its cause. However, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the reason by the state of being preceded by an omniscient being has never been observed.
Furthermore, the example is devoid of the probandum (*sādhyahīna*), because potters and the like are not omniscient. Moreover, the reason is contradictory (*viruddha*).

For it is observed that in the case of jars and the like, the property of having an origin, or the property of having a non-conscious material cause, is pervaded precisely by the state of being preceded by one who is not omniscient. Moreover, the object of the proof is not merely the state of being preceded by an intelligent agent; rather, it is that specific [quality].
It is not tenable that the fact of being preceded by an omniscient being is established from that [inference], even though it is not its object. For instance:
if this particularity is not pervaded by the probans (*sādhana*), how can it be established by it? If it is established, how can it not be its object?
And if it is its object, how is it that it does not touch upon the defects residing in its own locus? This is incorrect, because it is a generality (*sāmānya*).

Even when there is pervasion by the universal (*sāmānya*), it is only the universal as qualified by its specific instance that is inferred in the subject (*pakṣadharmin*) by virtue of the property of being a feature of the subject; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the total abolition of all inference. For instance, even the inference of fire does not have the mere universal of fire as its object, because that has already been established [prior to the inference]; nor does it have that [universal] as qualified [by a particular instance].

The mountain cannot be the locus of "fire-ness" (vahnitva), because since that universal [fire-ness] lacks a relation to the mountain, it cannot logically be a particular instance of it. Otherwise, just as individual cows such as Śābaleya are related to "cowness" through inherence (samavāya), the mountain would also absurdly follow as being fire itself due to its inherence in "fire-ness. If it is argued that there exists a relation between the mountain and "fire-ness" by way of "inherence in what is conjoined" (saṃyukta-samavāya)—[the answer follows].

In that case, since it is not possible to apprehend [the object] without first apprehending the specific fire conjoined with the mountain, there is also an inference of that specific fire. Thus, the previously mentioned fault does not follow.
This same point should be shown regarding the inference of the sense organ as well; for even there, it is not the case that the sense organ...

A certain action possessing an instrument has been perceived. Indeed, actions such as cutting are not accomplished by means of the sense organs, because axes and the like are not sense organs. Nor is it possible for actions characterized by the discernment of color and so forth to have axes and the like as their instruments. Therefore, even though the universal property of "action-ness" (kriyātva) exists [in these cases],...

Just as, although [the property of] being dependent on an instrument in general is not pervaded [by the specific nature of the sense organs], the specific instrument characterized as a sense organ is established by virtue of its presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*),

so too here: although "having an origin" and "having a non-conscious material cause" are pervaded by an agent in general who knows the material cause (*upādāna*), the instruments (*upakaraṇa*), the recipient (*saṃpradāna*), and the purpose (*prayojana*), nevertheless, by the force of their presence in the subject— namely, those things under dispute— their specific [nature as such an agent] is established.

[The argument for] proof [is as follows]: otherwise, even the universal (sāmānya), which is intended to be pervasive, would remain unproven, because that which is devoid of particulars is impossible, and no other particular can be logically established. Furthermore, for one who is not omniscient—and thus lacks knowledge of the distinctions between unseen forces (adṛṣṭa) and so forth—the status of being a presiding agent (adhiṣṭhātṛ) is impossible. Therefore, although [the world] possesses a creator who is an observer...

Nevertheless, because the specific [property] of that [subject] is obtained through the force of its being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), inference has a particular as its object. Nor does the aforementioned fault follow; for the application of the charge of "over-extension" (*utkarṣa*) or "under-extension" (*apakarṣa*) based on the variation of properties between the probandum and the example is common to all inferences, and thus constitutes a rejection of the validity of inference in general.
