Because it is the cause [of that cognition]. Thus it is established that those things under dispute have an intelligent agent as their maker. Here, the proof expressed by the word [“because”] is dependent on the establishment of what is desired [to be proven], because its object—namely, the material cause and so forth—is dependent on that [establishment].
Whatever has its object, such as the material cause and so forth, dependent on something, that proof is dependent on the establishment of that thing; just as smoke [proves fire].

The fact that fire and other such things have as their objects their material causes and so forth—which depend upon the establishment of specific locations—is established by depending on Him [the Lord]. Nor is there ignorance regarding these [causes] on His part due to a lack of causes for knowledge of the merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) inherent in all individual souls (*kṣetrajña*);
for the knowledge, volition, and effort inherent in those [souls] are eternal. Furthermore, there is no contradiction whatsoever between the intellect (*buddhi*) and its eternity.

If it is argued that there is a contradiction because a non-eternal cognition is perceived here and there, then it would follow as a consequence that even the atoms of water and so forth do not possess color and other qualities, since only the effects of the earthy elements— namely color and the rest— are perceived.
And here [in this case], they are not produced because color and other qualities are observed in snow, hail, and so forth;

furthermore, since those qualities residing in an effect-substance arise through the sequence of the qualities of the cause, even the qualities of water possess color and so on. If it is argued that the color and other qualities residing in that [water] are eternal because it is always a cause, [we reply: here too, by virtue of being an effect and having an insentient material cause...

Or, because it is established that [the Lord] is eternal due to His being the constant cause of the inference of knowledge of all objects, He is likewise capable of presiding over merit and demerit inherent in other persons, owing to their connection.

For conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and inherence (*samavāya*) are not the only types of connection; the inherence in that which is conjoined with what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasaṃyogisamavāya*) is also such a relation.
Or rather: atoms are indeed impelled by the Lord; by those [atoms] alone, the individual souls (kṣetrajña) [are impelled], as are the merit and demerit inherent in them.
Or else, there is inherence in what is conjoined (saṃyuktasamavāya), because of the Lord’s conjunction with the individual souls. This is established through inference:
the Lord is conjoined with the individual souls, because He is conjoined with corporeal substances; for whatever is conjoined with corporeal substances is conjoined with the individual souls.

For example, like a jar and so forth. And that [disjunction] of his is unproduced, because of the absence of those causes of conjunction—conjunctions arising from the action of one or both [of the two things]. The "activity" (*pravṛtti*) of merit and demerit is simply their orientation toward the commencement of an effect.
And that [activity], like place, time, and so forth, also depends upon the impulse of the Lord (*īśvara*). Nor should it be said that merit and demerit [or atoms] [are the cause].

How can the Lord impel with effort those who are not supported by their own *dharma*? For it is observed that one skilled in the science of poisons can impel a fragment of poison even when it is not supported by its own *dharma*. Furthermore, once the eternality of the knowledge, will, and effort residing in Him is established, what is the use of His assuming a body? From those alone [the three attributes] are the atoms, the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), and so forth [impelled].

Because the production of effects characterized by the body, earth, and so forth is logically possible through [the Lord’s] activity; nor should it be said that the Lord is not the creator of the earth and other things because of a lack of purpose, or that the Lord’s cognition is impermanent because it is a cognition. For if the subject—the Lord and his cognition—is unestablished, the reason suffers from the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*). Once that [subject] is established...

Or rather, since the existence of the Creator, who possesses eternal knowledge, is established by inference itself—which apprehends the subject (dharmin)—an inference that contradicts that [eternity] cannot establish its own validity by taking that [Creator] as its locus. Therefore, what is the point of this effort to prove the superiority of an inference that apprehends the non-eternality of God’s knowledge on the grounds that it has a particular (viśeṣa) as its object? Its very root is undermined.

The axe has already been refuted. Furthermore, there is an inconsistency [in your argument] because the status of the senses and the mind as instruments for the production of cognition is not perceived;
and because insentient milk proceeds spontaneously as the cause for the growth of a calf;
and because we observe the growth of forest trees even without effort. Thus, your reason is inconclusive.

Now, because all of those [entities] are subjects of dispute, they are placed within the category of the "thesis" (pakṣa). Nor is there the existence of a rabbit’s horn, because that is contradicted by its non-perception. It is not possible for the Blessed One to contradict it on the grounds of its being unfit for direct perception; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the destruction of all inference. As for the horn, however—

This is a mere pretense; for it is like the horns existing on a rabbit's head or those belonging to a cow and so forth— something that, while appearing fit for perception, is refuted by non-apprehension and thus unfit to be established as a proof.

Nor is there a deviation [of the reason] by the subject (*pakṣa*), because that would be too easy to find everywhere, resulting in the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the destruction of all inference. Alternatively, the negative-only (*vyatirekin*) reason should be employed by taking "everything that has an origin" as the subject. And it is formulated as follows: "Everything other than eternal things is preceded by an omniscient being, because it possesses an origin and has non-conscious matter as its material cause."

Or else: whatever is not preceded by an omniscient being is either not produced or has an insentient material cause, such as atoms and so forth. And this [world] is not like that; therefore, it is preceded by an omniscient being. Since "being preceded by an omniscient being" is unestablished for the opponent, the mere fact of being an effect (*kāryamātra*) is stated as the subject of the thesis. Furthermore, if it were not presided over by a conscious agent...

Those [causes] would perform their own respective functions; consequently, they would produce effects at any place whatsoever without being restricted by specific locations. Thus, an effect characterized by production restricted to particular places and times would not be observed. If it is argued that the effect is not produced by the causes individually, but rather through the coming together of the causes, this is true; however, it is precisely this mutual conjunction of the causes [that is required].

Why? If it is argued that this is due to a specific unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) whose maturation occurs only occasionally, then how could this [unseen force], being itself insentient, bring about the necessary causes in their proper proximity? Indeed, sticks and other such tools situated here and there do not, by means of a specific unseen force alone and without the effort of a potter, mutually come into proximity with one another. Nor...

Or rather, they [the causes] have power over the production of the effect. Therefore, since the arising of an effect is pervaded by the conjunction of its causes, and since that [conjunction] is impossible in the absence of a preceding intelligent being, the pervader (the conjunction) being excluded from the counter-example (the vipakṣa) where the effect arises, it is pervaded by "possessing an intelligent perceiver. Thus, the invariable concomitance (pratibandha) is established. Not so.
It is correct to say that this divine knowledge is not perceptual because it does not arise from the contact of the sense organs with their objects;
for that is the definition of worldly perception. Indeed, its defining characteristic must be understood as the direct intuition of all objects.
And on this point, there is a scriptural authority:
"Under the command of this Imperishable, O Gārgī,
heaven and earth stand held apart;
it is the one God who generated heaven and earth."
And there is this traditional teaching:
"This creature is ignorant and not the master of its own pleasure and pain;
impelled by the Lord, it goes either to heaven or indeed to hell."
Furthermore, the knowledge of Īśvara does not arise in dependence upon a body or sense organs; for there is a scriptural passage [Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.19]:

"Handless and footless, yet swift and a grasper; he sees without eyes, he hears without ears; he knows the universe, yet there is no knower of him; they call him the Great Supreme Person," and so forth. Therefore, by inference...
"By these two arguments, the Lord's status as creator and his omniscience are established.

He refutes this: "This is a mere pretense (vārtta). The underlying intention here is as follows: It is not at all possible to establish a specific presiding agent over those [effects] merely by virtue of their being properties of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), based on the observation of effects characterized by innumerable stationary things and so forth occurring simultaneously, [which would require an agent] whose scope encompasses everything."

It is not possible for God, who possesses eternal pure consciousness and the six attributes, to be established as the creator; for by this much alone, the universe does not come into being as an effect.
Indeed, even a potter, though he knows the material cause and other factors, never produces a jar when he neither desires to make one nor has the desire to do so.

One who does not exert effort due to laziness regarding those means of acquisition and so forth is incapable of undertaking the production of a jar. Therefore, the material cause of an effect must arise from the conjunction of knowledge, the desire to act, and effort; it cannot come from knowledge alone.
Let it not be that smoke—which arises from the burning of moist fuel—should instead arise from mere moist fuel, or that the cognition of an ordinary person should arise from fire alone.
If it is argued that the Lord’s cognition, being unique and entirely without assistance, is sufficient for all effects in the universe; then, alas!

what is the use of this cognition itself? If you say that an excellence of its own nature will serve as its assistant in each respective effect, and thus no effect arises from a single cause without assistance—then, surely, those very excellences belong to that [cognition] itself.
If it is argued that merit and demerit reside in the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*) and that atoms exist as its auxiliaries, what is the use of knowledge?

If you say that knowledge is required because those [atoms] do not act when they are unknown, then why do they not act while remaining unknown? If you say it is because they are not perceived in the same way as the means for making a jar and so forth, then—

One must also admit that there is knowledge, a desire to act (*cikīrṣā*), and effort (*prayatna*) [in this case as well]; and therein, knowledge would be employed toward a specific desire to act, and that particular effort would be the cause of the distinction in effort. Thus, since the arising of direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) has its cause solely in a specific cause of effort, how could it be possible without that? For indeed, rice is not produced merely by throwing parched grain and blowing, without fire.
It is established.

If one should think that both the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) and effort (*prayatna*) indeed exist in the Blessed Lord (*bhagavat īśvara*), then are these two eternal or non-eternal? If they are eternal, then what is the use of the Lord’s knowledge, since the desire to act [would already be present]?

Because they are useless for the production of effort, since both [the self and the internal organ] are eternal and thus do not depend upon anything for their own production. Furthermore, knowledge, like effort, is not a direct factor in the production of the effect. For it is by means of different efforts that one presides over the material cause and so forth; at that time, there is no utility whatsoever for knowledge or for the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*).

Since a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) that does not produce any further distinction once its function has been fulfilled violates the very principle of being a means, the omniscience of God is as good as having its throat throttled by water. Alternatively, if [the two] are non-eternal, then their cause of production must be stated.
But surely eternal cognition itself is the root cause of their production; what need is there for anything else?

For what reason? Oh, what a lapse! That he has even resolved to assert that [cognition] arises from mere knowledge alone, without the desire and effort which are the non-inherent causes of the specific conjunction between the self and the mind. If that were so, he might as well produce cream even from rice that contains no starch.

If it is argued that there certainly exist conjunctions of this [Self] with the minds of liberated souls, and therefore, aided by those, it simultaneously produces a series of volitions (*cikīrṣā*) and efforts (*prayatna*) for the sake of generating their effects—[we reply: But do those minds and their conjunctions produce volition and effort while being uncontrolled (*anadhiṣṭhita*), or while being controlled (*adhiṣṭhita*)? If [they do so while being...]
Therefore, there would be a deviation [from the rule] because of those very [atoms], since they are not presided over. Furthermore, presiding is indeed impossible without effort (*prayatna*).

Presiding over them occurs through another effort born from another desire to act (*cikīrṣā*). If it is argued that the stream of desire to act and effort is beginningless? [We reply: Just as this Lord, having generated the desire to withdraw [the world], [acts] toward the individual souls (*kṣetrajña*).
[155] Although everything possessing arrangement and so forth has an intelligent cause,
how can there be a single cause for the well-known [instances of] arrangement and so forth?
When the collection of merit and demerit has its activity obstructed and the world has reached a state of atomic dissolution,

the [Supreme Being] remains inactive for some time; then, when He desires to act or exerts effort, since there exists neither a prior desire to act nor a prior effort that could serve as the cause for the desire to act and effort about to be produced, from what [source] would they arise?

Is it the substratum of the minds or of their conjunctions? For if they were not so supported, effort (*prayatna*) and desire-to-act (*cikīrṣā*) would not arise from those minds and their conjunctions. Or, if they were to arise [without such support], how would the two reasons—being an effect (*kāryatva*) and having an insentient material cause (*acetanopādānatva*)—not deviate from their logical concomitance? Furthermore, the Lord’s knowledge is not merely like the light of the sun.

It is also untenable to claim that consciousness, being merely indeterminate and merely an effort, becomes directed toward various objects through the conditioning of the distinctions of those respective states;

for this would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). For there can be no conditioning by those respective states while consciousness is not yet directed toward those objects, nor can there be such directionality without the conditioning by those states; because an effect consisting of such conditioning cannot arise in the absence of a substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) upon which it is conditioned, and that [substrate]...
"Because it does not arise [from that]. Furthermore, the refutation of the position that cognition is non-eternal will be explained later.

How can such a distinction, which cannot withstand scrutiny, be subsumed under the subject possessing the property to be proven (*sādhyadharmin*) even by the force of the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*)? For that which is itself untenable is not capable of establishing another. What?

In that case, how can there be a cognition of a universal established by inference in the absence of a particular? Must it necessarily have a cognition? Surely, that which is established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must be accounted for, provided that its inferential justification is possible; however, as for that which is simply not possible, let there be nothing but its non-occurrence. Is it not a contradiction to say that something established by a means of valid cognition is impossible?

[This is] established. If that is so, then let there simply be a refutation of the establishment of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the sake of non-contradiction; however, there can be no logical justification (*upapatti*) for that which is itself illogical (*anupapanna*). What, then, is this refutation of the proof? It is not a refutation of the proof; rather, it is [the fault] of that proponent who, in order to avoid specific distinctions such as "with or without a companion," "eternal" or "non-eternal," [is attempting to prove] a sky-flower.
One employs a proof for the general property of being preceded by an intelligent agent as it exists in things such as the earth, which is otherwise incapable of being proven.

Yet, no such specific instance is possible upon which that general property of being preceded by an intelligent agent could be established in relation to the earth and so forth. Nor does this entail the undesirable consequence of the abolition of all inference, because [inference] has as its object a specific instance that is indeed possible.
Of these inferences:
for it is not impossible that there exists a specific fire on a mountain slope, or that a fiery constituent of the eye, possessing unmanifest color and touch, is the means for the perception of form;
because causes possessing the capacities for variegated color and shape are perceived here and there. Therefore, just as someone at night...
Just as a person who wields a sword against the sky is restrained [from his action], but neither the sword nor the sky is thereby affected;

likewise, the property of being an effect (*kāryatva*) or having an insentient material cause (*acetanopādānatva*), when aided by reasoning, has as its object only the conjunction of the *kṣetrajña* (the individual soul) with atoms and so forth—conjunctions which have reached maturity through the influence of unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*)—and not the omniscient Lord (*īśvara*). This is what has been stated.
"This is a mere report.
As for that which has been refuted by the elders, it is disregarded due to its extreme notoriety; therefore, he states another refutation:
"Even if everything possessing an arrangement and so forth has an intelligent cause," [the following applies].
How can there be a single cause for the arrangement and so forth that are well-known [to be diverse]?

[Page 156] Regarding this, the elders raised an objection: "Is 'merely having an origin' (utpattimattva) alone made the reason here, or rather a specific quality thereof, by the perception of which the cognition that something has been produced arises even for one who does not observe the actual act of production? This is what is being said.

Indeed, those things which possess origination and whose presence and absence are observed by means of valid cognition to follow the presence and absence of an intelligent agent—such as palaces, watchtowers, gate-towers, and archways—are preceded by an intelligent creator who provides non-intelligent material causes;

however, this is not the case for bodies, the world, and so forth. For it is certainly not the case that the presence and absence of those [latter] follows the presence and absence of an intelligent agent.
If it is argued that no such rule has ever been observed, yet because things like jars, which possess origination,

are observed to have such [origination], while things like space, which lack origination, are not so observed, and since the state of possessing origination is non-different even in the case of bodies and worlds,

they must likewise [possess a creator]— then what of this? Has it been observed that a jar, which is a modification of clay, is the work of a human being, such that [by analogy] the head of Śakra [should be the creator of the world]?

It must also have that [clay] as its cause. Nor does its being a modification of clay or its configuration differ, for we observe the production of human forms even from such modifications of clay. If it is argued that, despite having such a nature, it is not the effect of that [clay] because no positive or negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with it is observed, we say: no, for the same logic applies here as well.

For even in this case, let it be granted that everything which follows the presence and absence of an intelligent agent—such as a palace and the like—is preceded by one; however, this cannot apply even to the world and such things, because they do not follow the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of that [intelligent agent]. Now, as for this particular smoke which [indicates] fire...

The presence and absence of a thing is observed to follow upon the presence and absence of another; let all such [correlation] be preceded by fire, but how can fire be inferred from [the smoke] located on a mountain slope on that basis? For even if the object is a universal (*sāmānya*), the determination of the causal relationship is the same in this case as well.
In that case, since walls and such things—which are the products of human effort—are observed [in the world], should the head of Śakra also be considered likewise?
If you argue that this is not so because there is a certain distinction between the head of Śakra and things like walls, [we reply:
then that same distinction must exist between palaces and such things on the one hand, and the body and the universe on the other; thus, there is no difference. No.

This very smoke, which conforms to the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with fire, possesses a specific nature distinct from the smoke on the mountain; for this reason alone, there is no inference of fire from mere white substances such as lilies or pigeons.

This is because it is the universal (*sāmānya*) of "smokeness" itself that effects the distinction between those [white substances] and [actual] smoke. Nor is there a convergence of the causal factors (*hetu-samavadhāna*).

It is impossible [for this to occur] without consciousness, because its production—characterized by occasional occurrence and arising in specific places and times—is accounted for solely by the ripening of the unseen (adṛṣṭa). Consequently, the restriction of the effect is established; for an effect cannot arise indeterminately from causes that possess capacities restricted to specific modes. Otherwise, if the agent were conscious...
This undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) is likewise unavoidable, because that [earth and so forth] too must be a motivator in accordance with the capacity of its own causes.
Nor can it be argued that material causes such as jars do not function without a conscious being; for if that were so, then causes such as the earth would likewise not function.
For just as the material causes of a jar do not function without the effort of an embodied being, [so it would follow for the earth].
[Page 157] Even though trees, mountains, oceans, and so forth differ from the arrangement of things like palaces which are seen to be preceded by deliberate observation,

they are nonetheless [classified as such] due to the commonality of being mere arrangements; this being the case, [the term "arrangement"] applies to its own referent by virtue of its distinct denotation.

Alternatively, since the creation of the world is seen to result in suffering, even if the absence of a motive is refuted by [the argument] of favoring others, the establishment of a mere sentient being might still follow; however, from where would its unity come? For indeed, even when preceded by a single intelligent agent, the causes such as earth and so forth do not require the effort of an embodied being for their own activity, just as in the case of pots, chariots, and the like.

They will not even require an effort consisting of mere consciousness; rather, they will proceed solely from the conjunction with the *kṣetrajña* (the individual soul) when its *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit) has reached maturity.
Therefore, what is the use of postulating such a conscious agent? Consequently, the specific form of "having an origin" (*utpattimattva*) is unestablished (*asiddha*).
As for the mere fact of having an origin in the case of earth and so forth, it is irrelevant (*aprayojaka*), as it depends upon a pervasion (*vyāpti*) conditioned by specific qualifications.

Because there is an absence of an essential connection (*svābhāvikapratibandha*) by virtue of [the cause] being mere vitality; and because only a reason possessing an essential connection constitutes a limb of inference. Otherwise, there would follow the absurdity that even the sight of a teacher and so forth could serve as an inferential mark for a pupil and so forth.
Furthermore, the activity of discerning persons (*prekṣāvat*) is pervaded by having a purpose. And [there is no such purpose] for a discerning Lord.

We do not perceive any purpose in the creation of the world; for one who has attained all that belongs to living beings, there is nothing further to be attained, and ultimately, even the pleasure achievable through play has already been obtained. Nor does He act for the sake of others out of compassion, because that would entail the creation of a world consisting entirely of happiness, whereas the actual creation is predominantly full of suffering.
Nor is it tenable that the diversity of emanations belongs to one who has *dharma* and *adharma* as his companions;

for it is impossible for a compassionate being to preside over *adharma*, which is not a cause for the suffering of the world. Furthermore, there would follow the consequence of a logical fallacy (inconsistency) regarding the cause producing its effect if it were not presided over [by an intelligent agent]. Nor does the experience of suffering lead to the arising of dispassion (*vairāgya*).

It is not reasonable to say that [the Lord], desiring the welfare of others, presides over their demerit (adharma) as a means to liberation through the door [of experience]. For since the production of suffering is dependent upon the Lord, if He turns away from it, that suffering will not arise; thus, liberation characterized by absolute release from it is effectively attained as a result. Nor is this [exercise of power] purposeless.

It is not logical that he [the Lord] creates even these [worlds] solely from his own nature, because that would contradict his being a rational agent (*prekṣāvattva*). Consequently, there would be no confidence in the scriptures composed by him; having thus shown indifference toward that position, he states another refutation:
"Even though there is a difference in the arrangement of trees, mountains, and so forth among others, [such things as] palaces, which are preceded by deliberate design, are observed..."

The connection with the opponent is as follows: "Even if the establishment of consciousness [in the elements] were to occur merely because of the commonality of their structural arrangement, such as that of the oceans and so forth; even so, since they are distinct entities and lack either a purpose for themselves or the favoring of another, why do they not favor others? To this, he says: "Because we observe that creation is followed by suffering. This refers to the purpose.

Even if the existence of pure consciousness were established by the refutation of material elements (*bhāva*), one might ask: "From where does that Lord's oneness derive, given that we observe such things as pots and chariots to have multiple makers? To this, he says: "For pots, chariots, and the like, are not preceded by a single intelligent agent."
[The opponents reply:

"All [things] are preceded by Īśvara. If it is argued that this is so because of [the presence of] a specific arrangement, [we respond that] that is yet to be proven, since such an arrangement is invariably concomitant with mere sentience, given that we observe it to be so in some cases. If it is argued that it must be so elsewhere as well, [then you must provide] an example.

[The reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to the two things to be proven (*sādhya*). If everything were to be proven, there would be an absence of an example (*dṛṣṭānta*). Furthermore, if there were two agents for a jar and so forth, then the world and the like would also have [two agents], leading to the consequence of a Lord of the Lord (*īśvareśvara*), which results in an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). For this very reason, the second inference is not valid. In that case, let there be no single inference either; even so, the infinite regress remains equal. Now, if...

Pots and other such things do not have two presiding agents; rather, everything has a single presiding agent. Thus, the establishment of omniscience [is not achieved]. He raises an objection: "If it is argued that because the entire collection of effects has God as its creator, they likewise have a single creator, then since the fact that the entire collection of effects is preceded by God is what remains to be proven (*sādhya*), how can that very point be employed as the means of proof (*sādhana*)?"

The meaning is "because. Again, he raises an objection: since the arrangement [of parts] is invariably concomitant with being preceded by an intelligent agent, and because this is observed in certain cases such as jars, chariots, and so forth, it follows that the same must be the case elsewhere, such as in the earth and other things; thus, its being preceded by God is established. And if it is argued that, consequently, there is a single creator, he refutes this with the following example: "dṛṣṭānta" (the example).

The reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to the two probanda (*sādhya*). For in the example, such as a jar, there is a single agent like a potter, whereas in the subject (*pakṣa*), such as the earth and so forth, the agent is Īśvara; thus, due to this deviation (*vyabhicāra*), neither "having an origin" nor "having an insentient material cause" can prove that the body, the world, and so forth have a conscious being as their agent. This is because the example possesses multiple agents.
The meaning is: "because [the two] things to be proven are observed.

However, if everything were to be proven as having God as its antecedent cause, then, because jars and other such things would be included within the subject (*pakṣa*) by virtue of having God as their antecedent cause, there would be no corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*). Thus he says: "If everything were to be the thing to be proven, there would be an absence of a corroborative instance."

Furthermore, a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) as a logical reason is not possible; the point is that because the production of effects restricted by place, time, and so forth can be accounted for solely through the occasional ripening of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), the absence of deviation in the negative concomitance cannot be established.
This has been demonstrated below.

Furthermore, even if God were the creator of jars and the like, the potter and others who are directly perceived would also be creators; thus, since jars and such things have two creators, the world and its like must likewise have two creators by that same analogy.
This leads to an infinite regress, as it would imply a second God for God himself.

This is what is meant: just as in the case of a jar or similar object whose maker, such as a potter, is directly perceived, and whose production is accounted for by that alone, one cannot postulate another conscious being, namely God, to preside over that potter as its maker;
likewise, one could not postulate another God to preside over that [first] God. Thus, there would be an infinite regress. For this very reason:

The opponent objects: "Precisely because it would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā-prasaṅga*), there can be no inference for a second God; therefore, there is no duality of agents. The author replies: "In that case, let there not even be an inference for a single [God]. Why?

Because the same infinite regress applies equally even in the case of inferring a single [God]. [This is so] because [the creation of the world] occurs solely through the conjunction of the *kṣetrajña* (the individual soul) with a destiny (*adṛṣṭa*) whose maturation has been attained.

The meaning is that even if one assumes a single Lord as the cause for the production of effects characterized by earth and so forth, the infinite regress (anavasthā) remains exactly the same. He raises an objection: "Now, jars and the like do not have two presiding agents; rather, all of them have individual potters and so forth as their presiding agents. Consequently, there is no inference of another Lord, nor is there an infinite regress. He refutes this: "No."
In this world, parts such as those of a chariot are seen to have been fashioned by various craftsmen, yet they generally function as mutual benefactors and beneficiaries;
and thus, it is observed that things like chariot parts are preceded by a single craftsman. Therefore, the world as well must be preceded by a single creator.
This [argument] is fallacious, because we observe even that which is preceded by various craftsmen.
An effect is not inferred when it is rejected by the absence of a cause;
nor is the mere presence of a conscious agent the cause, for such a view is untenable.

For in the absence of the latent impressions of karma (*karmāśaya*), neither its connection with a body and sense organs nor its intellect or sovereignty is possible; thus, the acceptance of such [a being] contradicts the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This is because an effect cannot arise in the absence of a cause. Or, if it were possible, its inference would not be from its specific configuration (*saṃniveśa*). Alternatively, if it were preceded by the latent impressions of karma, then knowledge of that [being] would have to come from another source.

The proof of omniscience: For if there were a single creator of all effects, then, since ignorance would be impossible for such a being, he would necessarily be omniscient. On the other hand, if each individual effect is produced by a distinct creator, then whoever produces a particular thing knows only its specific causes and is not omniscient; this is the meaning.

Furthermore, someone might argue: "Whatever is established as existing through a relationship of mutual assistance and assistance-giver is seen to have a single agent, just as the parts of a chariot are seen to be preceded by a single carpenter; and such is the case with bodies and worlds."
To the objection that here too there exists some kind of mutual relationship of benefactor and beneficiary, he says:
"In this world, even the parts of a chariot and so forth, though fashioned by various craftsmen, are generally seen to be mutually beneficial;
the entire world is observed to be mutually beneficial and beneficiary—so what of such a thing?"
Is it observed that a chariot and such things are preceded by a single carpenter? Therefore, the world also must be preceded by a single creator; and thus, the creator of the world is omniscient.
[The author] refutes this: this is inconclusive. Why? Because there is also the possibility of being preceded by multiple carpenters.
Because it is observed:
an effect is not inferred from the absence of a cause;
nor is the cause mere consciousness, for such a view is untenable.

Because it is accepted that the Lord is untouched by afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, its fruition (*vipāka*), or latent dispositions (*āśaya*). For, in the absence of latent dispositions of karma, neither His connection with a body, senses, and so forth, nor His intellect or sovereignty is possible; thus, that acceptance contradicts valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). He states the contradiction with valid means of knowledge: "Because in the absence of a cause, an effect is impossible. Indeed, there is none.

The meaning is this: there is no fire, yet smoke exists; and since bodies and the like—which are the causes for the accumulation of karma—cannot exist in its absence, [the inference fails]. Or, even if the logical possibility were granted, since the production of an effect cannot occur in the absence of a cause, there can be no inference of an intelligent agent from the arrangement [of the world], even according to your own position. This is because [the effect] would arise even without a cause.
Because of the production of an effect. As for anyone who, out of audacity, would admit that even in the case of God there is a reference to the accumulation of karma—[p.

160] would it not then follow that His inference [of God] is based on the very fact that in the absence of a cause there is an absence of an effect? Otherwise, even a refutation would not be possible.

It might be so; or rather, a distinction must be stated as to why there is refutation and not proof. It is said in reply: for by perception, arrangements that are dissimilar and not preceded by conscious intention would be shown to have no such [intentional] cause. Yet, the intellect is not thus to be inferred, because the inference proceeds from observed similarity. Furthermore, even when there is equality [of logical status], refutation occurs merely through the presence of a necessary connection (*pratibandha*).
The proof is as follows: a proof, indeed, establishes the probandum only when its counter-arguments have been refuted. Nor is mere consciousness sufficient;
he says this in response to that: if [the body] were preceded by a store of karma (*karmāśaya*), then the knowledge of that [karma] would have to come from elsewhere.

For that very store of karma by which his body and other organs are to be produced must first be known and presided over [by a conscious agent], since the eyes and other senses [cannot do so] on their own.

It should be understood that [the body] is not sufficient for its own production; nor can it be produced by a body and so forth born from itself, because that would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).

Nor can it be produced by another body belonging to a previous life, because at the time of birth, that [previous body] has already ceased to exist. Furthermore, other [schools] do not admit the existence of another God (*īśvara*); or, if such a God were admitted, the same difficulty would be unavoidable even in that case.

The consequence [is as follows]. He objects: "But surely, for this very reason—that in the absence of a cause there is an absence of the effect—there is an inference of that intelligent cause of the body, the world, and so forth. Otherwise, if the effect were to exist even in the absence of a cause, then the refutation [of the opponent's position]—that the effect is not inferred because it is precluded by the absence of a cause—would not be possible."

Or rather, such a distinction must be stated, whereby it is a refutation and not a proof. For both the proponent of the proof and the proponent of the refutation are engaged in asserting that "in the absence of a cause, there is no effect. So why is one of them alone questioned by this [objection]? As the elders say: "That fault which applies to both sides does not belong to either one."
[The opponent] is not to be challenged.

[The author] refutes [the objection] by demonstrating a distinction within his own position: It is said in reply: For the configurations of the earth and so forth, which are distinct from direct perception and are not preceded by conscious intent (*apratyaya-pūrvaka*), would either lack a cause or have a cause that lacks conscious intent. Now, if...

Just as the configurations of palaces and the like are perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) to be distinct from the configurations of the earth and so forth, so too is the intellect (*buddhi*) perceived through inference (*anumāna*) to be distinct from non-worldly [configurations].
To this he says: "And the intellect is not to be inferred in this manner. Why? Because inference proceeds by way of similarity to what is observed (*dṛṣṭasālakṣaṇyena*). This is what was stated:

It is so: perception, arising independently of the observation of things produced by the senses, is indeed capable of taking as its object the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of an object—even one never before seen and even one distinct from the three worlds. Inference, however, because it depends upon conceptual construction (*vyutpatti*), and because such construction is dependent upon prior observation, can take as its object only that which possesses a previously observed common characteristic, but not [the specific characteristic].

It is of a different nature, for its relationship with a logical mark (*liṅga*) has not been perceived. Therefore, when cognition is inferred here, it should be inferred according to what is observed. And that [cognition] is non-eternal, caused by the conjunction of the body, the self, and the mind, and is a perceiver of non-universal objects in the case of people like us; thus it must be inferred as being of that very kind. Consequently, [the attributes of] eternality and omniscience—

Regarding the term "divya-ābhāti" (divine manifestation): there is no such over-extension (*prasaṅga*) in the case of inferences concerning fire and the like. For indeed, in those cases, a fire situated on a mountain slope—which is distinct from the fire observed in a kitchen (*mahānasa*) and so forth—is not what is being inferred. Nor is there a difference of location [that would prevent the inference].

*Prekṣā* consists of the deliberation and determination regarding the purpose of the arrangement and the reason for its disposition. And that [deliberation] is not possible in this case, because there is an absence of both a self-interest and an interest in others. Now, one might object: "Let there be no omniscient creator; however, let one who knows *dharma* be the subject. For it has already been stated that the restriction of the objects of the eyes and other senses is not determined by their physical form alone.

Regarding the restriction by time: when there is present existence, then it is not contradictory for the eyes and other senses to have an object characterized by excellence (*atiśaya*). And regarding absolute non-existence, it has been stated that there is absolute non-reality, like a sky-flower;
this is sufficient to establish the distinction [between the two], because they are different. How, then, is the inference of the sense organs from the perception of color and so forth?

For there is no similarity with instruments such as a staff in that case, because the sense organs, which are the instruments for the determination of color-form and so forth, are not within the scope of inference. Indeed, this presumption (arthāpatti) arising from the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the determination of color-form and so forth has the sense organs as its object; and since it is independent of the observation of a relation, it does not involve a perceived similarity.

[The opponent] observes this. However, there is no such presumption (*arthāpatti*) regarding the fact that [the world] is preceded by an intelligent agent, because nothing is observed for which this would be the only possible explanation. Furthermore, it has been stated more than once that the body, the universe, and so forth, arise from the conjunction of the *kṣetrajña* (the individual soul) with atoms, mediated by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*). Thus, there is indeed a distinction between the proof and the refutation.

Moreover, even if there were no distinction, the mere caviller (*vaitaṇḍika*) could not be refuted—he who, while lacking the establishment of his own position, merely attacks the position of another—as he himself has stated: "Furthermore, when [the two positions] are equal, the refutation consists in a mere counter-argument; thus the proof is also countered by an opposing argument. But the proof, having its opposing argument dispelled, is the means for establishing the probandum."
It abides in that [state], and not merely due to an obstruction by its opposite.

Having thus explained the first half of the verse, he explains the second half: "And it is not mere cognition (*buddhi*) that is the cause of the arrangement; rather, it consists of the investigation and determination regarding the purpose and the application of the disposition."

That is to say, it is a specific kind of discerning intelligence (*prekṣābuddhiviśeṣa*). [The opponent objects: "In that case, let discernment itself belong to the Blessed Lord, the Supreme Being. To this he replies:
"And that is not possible, because there is an absence of both his own interest and the interest of others; and that absence has already been demonstrated above.
Now the opponent objects from another perspective: "Well then, let there be no omniscient director."

Through direct perception, let the Knower of Dharma be accepted, as it has been said: "He who makes known the reality of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, along with the means [thereto], is accepted as a valid authority; but not one who knows everything."
Of what use to us is his knowledge of the number of insects?
Let him see far, or let him not; he sees, however, that which is desired—the truth.
"If the one who sees from afar were the authority, then we would worship vultures," and so forth.
Now, one might ask: "Since this Dharma lacks any specific form (rūpa), how can it be preceded by direct perception? To this he says:
"For it has been stated that no restriction of objects is observed for the eyes and other [senses] when they possess a form. But has this not also been stated?

In this context, "dharma" has the meaning of "that which is to be performed," because objects such as sacrifice (yāga) are accepted as being dharma by virtue of their being that which is to be accomplished.

If it is argued that [dharma] is imperceptible because it is something yet to be produced, then let it be so for that which is unproduced; however, even when produced, is it not dharma by its very nature?

But that [capacity] is supersensuous (atīndriya) by virtue of being a means to the ultimate good (śreyas). What, then, is this "being a means to the ultimate good"? If it is simply potency (śakti), and that is supersensuous, it has been stated in this regard that the restriction of the senses to their respective objects is not well-established either by way of their dimension or otherwise. Or else, it is because of its non-existence at that time, since it occurs at a later time.

[It must be] for the sake of the better; otherwise, there would be a loss of its status as *dharma*. Since the means to the better (*śreyaḥ-sādhana*) is present, the eye and other [senses] have only the present time as their object. And since *dharma* is not present, he says: "But regarding the restriction by time, when *dharma* is present, then the object of the eye and so forth possesses excellence (*atiśaya*)."
The existence [of the injunction] is not contradictory. If it were argued that this [injunction] never exists in the present, to that he says:
"And if there were absolute non-existence in the present, then there would be absolute non-reality, like a sky-flower," as has been stated.
Now, one might object: the injunction "Do! is a property (dharma), and this is not present; yet [the form] "you do" is no different [from the injunction].
[This follows] from the context. However, since that which is in a present state is not an injunction (*niyoga*), it is not *dharma*;

therefore, he says: "In that case, the meaning 'do it' is *dharma*. Why? Because sacrifice and the like, which are the objects of the injunction, are accepted as being *dharma*, and it is precisely therein that the status of being *dharma* is well-established. [The opponent] objects: "Because it is something to be produced and is not present, it too is imperceptible (*apratyakṣa*)."

[The opponent] refutes [this]: "Let it be so for that which has already arisen. He then raises a further objection: "Even though sacrifice and the like have arisen, they are not *dharma* by their own nature; rather, they are *dharma* as the means to the attainment of the highest good (*śreyas*), and in that capacity, they are beyond the senses (*atīndriya*). To refute this, he offers a dilemma: "But what is this 'being a means to the highest good'? If it is a potency (*śakti*), and that is beyond the senses..."
Yet [the opponent] objects: it has been stated here that there is no restriction of the sense organs by way of their size, and rather, the restriction of their objects has been established.
Now, if "being a means to the good" (*śreyaḥ-sādhanatvam*) refers to the connection of the means with the good, this is because of the statement of the author of the *Vārttika*:
"In the case of primary derivatives (*kṛt*), secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), and compounds, the relation is expressed by the suffixes *tva* and *tal*. And as for this relation...

He raises an objection: "The determination [of a relation] depends upon two related entities; it cannot be determined without a related entity. Therefore, since the *śreyaḥ* (the ultimate good) does not exist at that time but occurs at a later time, how could its connection with sacrifices and the like be perceived through direct perception? [The author replies: "Because it is non-existent at that time, namely, at the moment of the sacrifice and so forth. To the question "How is it non-existent?", he says "at a later time" (*kālāntara*).
[Objection: Because the welfare of the next world, such as heaven and so forth, occurs at a later time. [Reply: Let it be that welfare occurs at a later time;

however, the excellence (*atiśaya*) which is the means (*sādhana*) for that [welfare] and which inheres in the sacrifice (*yāga*) and so forth, exists at that same time—that is, the time of the sacrifice and so forth.
Indeed, a relationship of substrate and superstratum (*ādhārādheya-bhāva*) is not possible between two things existing at different times. If such a relationship were possible...

Why is that very reality so? To this he says: "Otherwise, because there would be no inherence of excellence, sacrifices and the like would lack the status of being means to the highest good (*śreyas*), and thus their nature as *dharma* would be lost. Therefore, whether it occurs at that time or another, since the state of being a means to the highest good exists [in the present], *dharma*—in the form of a means to the highest good—is not beyond the scope of the senses.

[It is] not that dharma is not an object of the senses. But surely, prior to its performance, knowledge of dharma is desired by those who perform it; and thus, being something yet to come, it would not be an object of the senses. We do not say that dharma is perceptible to the presiding deities (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*), but rather—

[This refers to] the teacher who possesses excellence. And that excellence may be innate, like the vastness of space, or it may be produced by other instructions and dependent upon action; thus there is no fault.
It is said:

They say that the capacity of an action, which perishes in a single moment, has a duration unequal [to its result] for the sake of a fruit that ripens after a long time; this is not perceived by direct perception.
It acquires an increase through the dissolution of past karma; it undergoes different states brought about by its preceding and succeeding parts.

This is what is meant: let the word "means to the good" (*śreyas-sādhana*) indeed be expressive of a relationship, but the word "dharma" (*dharma*) itself does not denote only that which is a means to the good. For there is no dispute among worldly people and investigators regarding its [the word "dharma's"] application...

[The opponent] says: "And since sacrifice and the like are the means for that [result] by virtue of their excellence, they alone are the locus of the term 'dharma. And those who possess it are present; thus, those who possess it are perceptible. He objects: "But surely, prior to performance, knowledge of dharma is desired by the performers; therefore, that knowledge..."

Because [the Veda] is a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to its performance (*anuṣṭhāna*). And thus, it is not an object for those whose senses are directed toward the future. He refutes this: we do not say that Dharma is perceptible to performers such as ourselves; rather, it is perceptible to a teacher who possesses extraordinary excellence (*atiśaya*).

For he indeed perceives through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) that sacrifices and the like, when performed by another, are means to the highest good (*śreyas-sādhana*). But from what source does he [obtain] this [knowledge]?

"What is this excellence? To this he says: "And that excellence of his is either innate, like the vastness of space; or born from another instruction, being dependent on action—such as when someone, having understood the eight-limbed yoga through the instruction of a reliable teacher, ascends to each respective stage of yoga upon the ripening of its practice, [resulting in] *saṃprajñāta* [samādhi]."
This excellence arises solely from the power of *samādhi*, because its capacity is inconceivable.

As it has been said: "Who indeed, other than through the power of yoga, could drink the ocean like Agastya, or create the Daṇḍaka forest like him? Thus, this twofold excellence consists of that which is conditioned by the means (*upāya-pratyaya*) and that which is conditioned by the goal (*upeya-pratyaya*).
"It is taught by the masters of yoga (yogācāryas)"; therefore, there is no fault.
Thus, having been thus countered, he refutes the opponent: it is said:
"The capacity of an action that perishes in a moment does not exist at the same time [as its result]."

They say that [the result] does not perceive that [action] because it bears fruit after a long time. He explains this as follows: because action perishes very quickly, it is lost while being dissolved; thus, there is no immediate succession of action for it, so what need be said of its simultaneity? He says: [it is obtained through a latent impression].

[Page 164] A certain excellence (*atiśaya*) residing in the agent— which, though transcending even immediate succession (*ānantarya*), undergoes a transformation (*pariṇati*) brought about by time and other factors— is said to be the means (*sādhana*) for the fruit of an action that occurs after a long interval. That [excellence], however, is not...

Existing at the time of the action—even though existing at its own [present] time—it does not perceive [the action] through direct perception as being connected to the action, because the action has already passed away. As it has been said:
"by which [means] it [is perceived] at that time in the form of the means to the fruit."
"It does not exist" [is said because]: at the time of the action (*karman*), it has not yet come into being, and at that time, the action is absent.

How, then, can the action be an instrument (*sādhana*) when it inheres in something other than itself? Because it is produced by that [action]. For there is no rule that an instrument must inhere only in its own [substratum]; rather, it is to be inferred from its effect, wherever it is capable of producing that effect.

In that very [substratum], its capacity is appropriate because it is deposited there. Nor is this merely figurative; for the action possesses a distinct state previously established through its constituent parts, such as the preparatory rites (*pūrvāṅga*), the subsequent parts (*parāṅga*), the placing of the fire (*agnyanvādhāna*), and the satiation of the Brahman priest (*brahmaṇatarpaṇa*).
Even by this much, this is not a mere "excellence" (*atiśaya*); rather, it is [the result] obtained in dependence upon conditions such as place, time, and state.

This is a difference in transformation. While this aforementioned sequence of causes bypasses the immediate action, what indeed is this excellence of action that [occurs] at the same time? Now, since an effect without a substratum is untenable, one might ask:
what is the substratum of this excellence which has the nature of arising? To this he says: "In the agent, the eternal self."
Is that [apūrva] located in the agent, belonging only to the agent, and not rather to the action? [Objection: Since the action itself is enjoined for the sake of the fruit, let it accomplish that;

what is the use of an apūrva hidden within it? To this he says: "The elders declare that the means of accomplishing a fruit that occurs after a long time is [the apūrva]. For an action that has perished long ago cannot, without having produced a specific excellence (atiśaya), [be the cause] of a fruit occurring after a long time."
The meaning is that it is capable of producing a result. [Objection: Let this be so; what does it have to do with the present topic? To this he says:

"Therefore, this [cause] does not exist at the time of the action. [Objection: Then is it never existing at all? In that case, the consequence would be that it is like a sky-lotus. To this he says: "Even though it exists at its own time. [Objection: Let it not be so.

At the time of the action, why is the action not present at that very time? To this he says: because of its extremely rapid perishability, the action has already passed away by that time. Therefore, since the action and its excellence (atiśaya) do not exist at the same time, and since that which possesses the excellence is absolutely non-existent [at the moment of perception], perception—which is restricted to a present object—cannot have that [action] as its object.

He says that [the self] cannot be perceived as being connected with action: "At that time, it does not exist in the form of a means to a result, by which [perception would occur]. He clarifies this very point: at the time of the action, that excellence (atiśaya) characterized by the aforementioned temporal sequence is yet to come into being, and at that time, the action itself is absent.

[The opponent] challenges: "In that case, how can the action (*karman*) be the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), given that its *apūrva* inheres in something else? [The author] answers: "Because it is produced by that [action]. For there is no rule that a means of accomplishment must inhere in itself alone. [The opponent objects: "Even so, since it inheres in the self (*ātman*), why does it not belong to the self alone? To this he says:

That *apūrva* is to be inferred from the action (*kārya*), and it is logical that it resides precisely where it is capable of producing that action. This is the meaning: if its nature were understood as independent of anything else, then it would belong to whatever is perceived as being in close proximity to it, such as the whiteness of a jar; but this is not the case. Rather, when an action is enjoined toward a result by way of being an instrument (*karaṇa*), [the *apūrva* belongs to that action].

[The opponent replies: It is a positive entity (*bhāva*), because it is established in the same way in the case of wood and so forth. [The proponent asks: But do they not consider that it does not exist? Because there is a lack of valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Nor is presumptive testimony based on what was heard (*śrutārthāpatti*) a valid means of cognition, since the authority of the injunction (*codanā*) applies only to the connection with the fruit.
Because of its destruction. For at that time, since it is unestablished, it must attain establishment through either scriptural injunction (*codanā*) or presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*);

thus, it would have *arthāpatti* as its cause. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of having to resort to *arthāpatti* for the sake of establishing the connection between action and its fruit.
Once that [connection] is established, what else could be required to postulate that [destruction]? For it is not independent. Even if there were dependence—

If, upon the cognition of the connection between the sacrifice and its fruit, another factor were required, how could there be such a cognition in the absence of that [factor]? Since this [factor] is postulated for the sake of making that [connection] possible, it is understood at the time of comprehension as being connected precisely with the ritual action (*karman*). For something connected with one thing cannot bring about the connection of the ritual action with the fruit. Even if it were perceived in such a way, if the ritual action—

"If it were connected with another [meaning], it would lose its very own nature; therefore, it belongs to the *karman* (the object) alone. Now, one might object: "Granted that there is first a cognition of a connection with the *karman*, its actual, real connection with that [object] must be stated. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of that cognition being false. To this, he says: "Because it is brought about (*āhita*) by that *karman*. Regarding that *karman*:

The potency (*śakti*). Another interpretation: Why is that *apūrva* postulated as inhering in something other [than the action], rather than as inhering in the action itself? To this he says: "That which is to be inferred from the effect is properly located only where it is capable of producing that effect."

Indeed, an action that perishes very quickly cannot serve as a basis for a future result once it has perished; therefore, [the capacity] must reside in an eternal self. If it were merely inherent in the self, one might object that it would be the power of the self alone and not of the action; to this he says: "Because it is deposited by that [action], it is the power of that [self] alone. Nor is this [usage] merely figurative.

The status of being an instrument (*sādhanabhāva*) belongs to the action (*karman*), as it is established in the same way for firewood and other such things. Indeed, even for firewood and the like, there is no direct instrumentality toward the manifestation [of cooking]; rather, it belongs to the specific transformation of the accumulation of conjunctions with fire, which depends upon heat. Nevertheless, in the expression "they cook with firewood" (*kāṣṭhaiḥ pacanti*), the instrumentality of the firewood is indeed primary, even though the fire—which is inherent in the rice—is also present.
The conjunction [of the sacrifice with its result] is preceded by that [apūrva]; the same applies to sacrifices and so forth. This has already been established in the *Niyogaparīkṣā*.
Now, the "beloved of the gods" (the Mīmāṃsakas) maintain that such an apūrva does not exist. Why? Because of the lack of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

[Objection: "Because [the relationship] exists. And since the presumption based on what is heard (*śrutārthāpatti*) is itself the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) here, how can there be an absence of a means of valid cognition?

To this, he says: "And the presumption based on what is heard is not a means of valid cognition. Why? Because the connection between the action and its fruit would destroy the authority of the Vedic injunction (*codanā*). For that [connection] is unestablished at that time, since the postulation of the *apūrva* [is required]."

The connection between the action and its fruit is established through the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) only when there is the postulation of the *apūrva* (unseen potency), because [the connection] exists only when that [potency] exists; thus, it would be caused by presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) and have presumptive testimony as its means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Otherwise, since the connection between the action and its fruit would be established from the word independently [of such a potency], there would be the undesirable consequence of [resorting to] presumptive testimony for no reason at all. [To this, the following] reply is given: "Once [the connection] is established..."

If the connection between action and its fruit exists, why should that cognition require some other inexplicable entity (*apūrva*)—in the absence of which it would be untenable—to postulate such an *apūrva*? For a cognition that is not otherwise untenable is not capable of prompting a conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) without further dependence.

If it is argued that the very cognition of the connection between sacrifice and its fruit is itself untenable, and thus requires something else to be made tenable, [we reply: what is that other thing which is itself untenable?

The meaning of a sentence is not something whose constituent word-meanings are unknown, for if it were to depend upon another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), its independence would be contradicted. Furthermore, the heard sentence would be untenable because of that dependence, as in the case of the Viśvajit sacrifice.

Because there is no explicit mention [of the apūrva] that would require such an ellipsis—as in the case of the word *yajeta*—the meaning [of the apūrva] is either unestablished, or else it would require the assumption of a supplementary portion (*vākyaśeṣa*) as in the previous case. Furthermore, there is no logical necessity [for such an assumption]. Since the sentence "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*svargakāmo yajeta*) is complete in itself, and since a supplementary portion is otherwise unnecessary, the consequence would follow that the *apūrva* is produced prior to the sacrifice, [as if one were to say] "having performed the *apūrva* by means of the sacrifice. [But this is not the case. "Having performed the *apūrva* by means of the sacrifice"—[this is what must be understood].

There would be a double enunciation of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice), and the aforementioned defect would persist. If [the apūrva] is untenable even when it is heard in the subsequent [passage], then the same alternative [of the previous position] applies. It is incorrect to say that because it is untenable in its own nature, one must postulate an apūrva for the sake of establishing what is heard in scripture.

To this, he says: even if there is a requirement, if another entity were expected for its own production upon the cognition of the connection between the sacrifice and the fruit, [it would be untenable].

That is untenable; for how can there be a cognition of the establishment of the connection between that [agent] and the fruit of his action if that distinct entity is not apprehended? Since a sentence-meaning cannot exist when its constituent word-meanings are not apprehended, if it were to depend on another means of knowledge (pramāṇa) rather than on the distinct entity itself, then its independence (anapekṣatva) would be contradicted. Furthermore, what is this "inexplicability" (anupapatti) even?
Does [the incongruity] belong to the sentence or to its meaning? Thus he raises the alternative. Moreover, the heard sentence is untenable because it is dependent.
Why is it dependent? To this he says: as in the case of "One should sacrifice with the Viśvajit," something must be supplied by ellipsis (*adhyāhārya*).

Because of the insertion [of a word], the term *svargakāmada* (granting heaven to one who desires it) is either something whose part of a sentence must be supplied (*adhyāhārya*), or it is figuratively called "to be supplied" because it possesses a supply within the whole sentence; since that [term] is not explicitly stated, there is a state of expectancy (*sāpekṣatva*). Thus he states the second position: "Or the meaning is untenable. Having thus formulated the alternatives, he refutes them:

In the previous case, there would have to be a postulation of a supplementary portion of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*). For it is a worldly convention that an incomplete sentence cannot be completed by a meaning of a different kind, but rather only by a word itself. This was stated on the assumption that this sentence is indeed untenable; however, in reality, there is no such untenability. Why? Because [the connection] with the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices...

Since the comprehension of the sentence-meaning is completed through the expression of their own individual meanings by the words "one desiring heaven should sacrifice," that which is postulated by the elders as a supplementary part of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*)—namely, "having performed the *apūrva*"—is also untenable; thus he says:

"And because a supplementary part of the sentence is untenable, [the phrase] 'having performed the *apūrva*' is itself non-*apūrva*. For [the injunction] "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" is indeed...
From this sentence, the following meaning is understood: "One who desires heaven should sacrifice after having performed some unprecedented [efficacy] (*apūrva*).

If that were the case, it would follow that the *apūrva* is produced prior to the sacrifice. Furthermore, if the word "by means of the sacrifice" (*yāgena*) were connected even to the act of producing the *apūrva*, then it would likewise have to be connected to the fruit; thus, there would be a double utterance of the root *yaj* (sacrifice), which constitutes the aforementioned fault.

It cannot be that the very same sacrifice by which the *apūrva* is produced subsequently produces the fruit as well, because it is impossible for an action to function after having ceased its operation. Therefore, it must be by means of another sacrifice; and in that case, there arises the previously mentioned defect: the contingency that the *apūrva* would be produced even before the sacrifice serves as the means to the fruit. Furthermore, if [the *apūrva*] were not postulated on account of what is heard in the scripture...
The meaning of the sentence is precisely the aforementioned conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), because it shares the same defects as that.

Therefore, even here, one must postulate a different object solely on the basis of its verbal nature; for if, having abandoned the actual reality, [one were to proceed] by means of another intrinsic nature...

If it were maintained that there is no logical possibility [of the result] through any other intrinsic nature, then the statement of the elders—that "the postulation of the *apūrva* (unseen potency) is for the sake of establishing what is heard in scripture"—would be incorrect. This multitude of refutations devised by those dear to the gods (the Mīmāṃsakas) is to be countered by the crest-jewels of the gods (the Buddhists) themselves; thus, even the Teacher (Dharmakīrti) did not take it up.

In that regard, who are "we" and who are "you," such that there could be [the notions] "mine" and "yours"? In this matter, the power of the intellect is utterly exhausted. Furthermore, if the Vedas were of human origin, then because they were composed by an omniscient being, those who follow them might indeed attain understanding from them; however, they do not possess human authorship. Is it not the case that a mere sentence is produced by a person?

This is a statement of dependence. For instance, even those [recitations] such as the *pada* and *krama*, which are human compositions, are seen to possess the same nature as those [Vedic texts] through their difficulty of pronunciation, their connection with specific sequences of phonemes, or their function in bringing about objects such as the fetching of water;
this is observed even in various Buddhist and other scriptures where human authorship is admitted. And whatever is of a non-different nature from something else...

That [Vedic word-arrangement] does not have a cause different from that [worldly word-arrangement], just as another *kalama* sprout—which possesses a non-different nature from one *kalama* sprout—has the same cause; likewise, Vedic word-arrangements are of a non-different nature from worldly word-sequences. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). For, due to having a different cause, there would be a nature different from its own, which is contradictory to itself.

Since the absence of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāvatva) is excluded by the perception of what is contradictory to its own nature—which is pervaded [by the absence of intrinsic nature]—it is pervaded by the non-difference from the cause; thus, the necessary connection (pratibandha) is established.
To this, it is replied: Is it merely the fact that Vedic sentences were composed by a person that is being proven, or rather...

Is it rather the state of being composed by an independent person (*svatantra-puruṣa*)? In the former case, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). For indeed, even we do not assert that sentences which are non-different from words—delimited by a specific sequence (*ānupūrvī-viśeṣa*)—are non-human (*apauruṣeya*), despite the eternity of phonemes (*varṇa*). To explain: because phonemes are eternal and all-pervading (*vibhu*), they are not [differentiated] by location.

Alternatively, if a sequential order is not possible in terms of time, then that [order] must be said to depend upon manifestation (*abhivyakti*). And since that manifestation has its source in human effort (*puruṣaprayatna*), how could words such as "cow" (*go*) and Vedic sentences—which have their limits defined by such distinctions—be considered of human origin? Or rather, let it be that they are composed by independent persons, like the sentences of the Niṣādas and others.

It is indeed appropriate [to argue] that the venerable Prācetas, the primordial poet, is independent, and likewise that there is some other [author], such as Īśvara, for the Vedic sentences as well; however, this is not so, because [the reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). This is because [the Vedas] lack the quality of being composed by an independent person such as Prācetas.

It might be argued as follows: we do not seek to prove that the Vedic sentences were composed by an independent person, but rather that they have an independent person as their antecedent. And since even in the compositions of persons such as ourselves—such as the arrangement of words like "mā niṣāda" and so forth—there exists, through tradition, the independence of the ancient poet (the Veda), there is no lack of pervasion (*anaikānta*).

That is untenable; for even if the non-difference of Vedic word-arrangements from worldly ones were established merely by their being composed by a person due to the identity of their cause, the independence of a person regarding the Vedas— which is not perceived and serves no purpose— [would still remain unproven].

Since conceptual construction is untenable, there is no contradiction whatsoever in the fact that having a similar configuration [of the image] is absolutely dependent upon the Person (puruṣa). For, while it excludes absolute dependence—which is its opposite—there is no logical ground for the conceptual construction of a person who lacks independence, because such a construction is untenable. And regarding this similarity of configuration in the person...
There is no contradiction with absolute dependence such that [the state of being free from it] would exclude absolute dependence as its opposite and thereby pervade human independence. Therefore,
just as among the sons of Maitra, even though they share the same mother, some alone exhibit a dark complexion caused by the consumption of specific foods and drinks throughout their various births;

It is not the case that for all [sons], the inference of dark complexion based on being his son is valid; likewise, since the production of speech arises from striking [the vocal organs] with efforts of a distinct nature, it is logical that its diversity or non-diversity follows the diversity or non-diversity of those [causes]. However, it does not permit one to treat it as dependent upon the person [who utters it]. Thus, because its negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is doubtful, it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

This is a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*). For one who lacks an understanding of how things appear and fails to comprehend them as they are, yet honors appearances as they seem and would treat them as valid means of knowledge—
considering that the statements in the *Mahābhārata* and other such texts were composed by independent persons— the Vedic statements, being likewise [mere] sentences...

If it is argued that [the Vedas] are of such a nature because they are [authorless], he should be told: "The study of the Veda under dispute is preceded by a prior study of the Veda, because it is a study of the Veda, like our own study of the Veda. This inference does not apply to the *Mahābhārata* and similar works;
for in their case, the inference is sublated by the very firm traditional remembrance (*smaraṇa*) of authors such as Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana. Thus, the [argument for authorlessness] must be set aside.

Because [the Veda] is eternal and unoriginated; whereas in the case of the Veda, since a firm memory of an author is impossible, it is logical to state that what is designated by names such as "Kāṭhaka" is a "recitation. Thus, an inference whose object is unsublated arises without obstruction. Furthermore, your inference has no power to sublate its object, because [your inference] is based on a relationship perceived through general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*).
For a general rule is indeed weaker than a specific rule. Thus it has been said:
"That which possesses well-known constituent parts, or that which is established in a specific context, is stronger than a general inference based on its constituent parts."

It might be argued as follows: Since the communication of meaning by words arises in dependence upon human convention, some person, for the sake of worldly practical intercourse, established the relationship between words and their meanings and thereby composed the Veda. Furthermore, words do not possess an inherent power (*svābhāvikī śakti*) toward the communication of meaning; rather, [this capacity] is [produced] by convention.

Now, it is being argued that [the capacity] is manifested by convention (*saṅketa*).
