For if, even when a convention exists, some sound (*dhvani*) did not manifest some object, then the inherent denotative power (*vācakatva*) of a certain sound—whose capacity is manifested by convention—would be possible; but this is not the case. Without convention, the form of an object is not conveyed by sound.

Because [the relationship] is established; for when there is a convention (*saṅketa*), it is observed that the cognition of all objects arises even from every [word]. Therefore, that [position] is incorrect. For even without a convention, since the usage of elders has been observed from time immemorial, the comprehension of meaning from words whose capacity is manifested is logically possible. Furthermore, because the presumption (*arthāpatti*) [of a relationship] is exhausted once the relationship is postulated, and moreover—
It is not correct to say that the very act of observing legal proceedings constitutes a restriction; for indeed, this specific meaning is not expressed by this word.
Instruction (upadeśa) is the exhortation of one who has not yet set out toward an action whose purpose is for the sake of the person to be enjoined;
it is well-known [to apply] to teachers, physicians, and so forth, and it is not unfit even in the case of what is obligatory (nitya).

Although commands and requests are inappropriate in the Veda, instruction is appropriate; and that too, like those two, is known in the world as a fourth [type of speech] consisting of instigation (*preraṇā*). For instance, while a command or a request has the form "this is to be understood," [instruction] rather consists in activity or cessation immediately following the utterance of the word.

It is the appearance of joy and so forth. And that [appearance] serves as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the word's causality therein, by way of inferring the manifestation of a specific object which is the basis for one's own subsequent activity and so on. Furthermore, those who are undergoing the process of linguistic acquisition do not at that time perceive either the convention (*saṅketa*) or the maker of that convention. And here, in the absence of both the convention and its maker, to whom [would the word refer]?

The perception of the object as distinct from consciousness is logically untenable; therefore, one concludes that the word itself must inherently be the cause of the cognition of the distinction between objects. Furthermore, since words such as "cow" and so forth function with respect to horses and the like, and words such as "Devadatta" and so forth function with respect to various individuals, depending upon convention (*saṅketa*), it follows that even in the case of "cowness" and other universals, words such as "cow" are dependent upon convention.

It is possible to infer [the existence of such usage]: because there is no contradiction in the occurrence of words in their own meanings—given that they are causes for the cognition of meanings through an innate capacity manifested by a beginningless succession of the linguistic usage of elders—and because this occurs in the absence of any convention (saṅketa).
However, against one who honors what is merely observed, it is indeed possible to counter-argue as follows: "The persons under dispute..."

The cognition of "cowness" and so forth arising from words such as "cow" is independent of convention, because it is a cognition of cowness and so forth from words such as "cow," just like [the cognitions] of people such as ourselves; this has been elaborated by the elders, so only a mere indication has been provided here. Let the wise forgive this slight departure from the formal text, and I shall now conclude.
Thus ends the first section.
He introduces the established conclusion (siddhānta): It is said:
An injunction (upadeśa) is a command that has not yet been undertaken, whose action is for the sake of the person to be enjoined;
it is well-known [to apply] to teachers, physicians, and so forth, and it is not possible even in the case of what is obligatory (nitya).

Regarding what was previously stated—that "in that which is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*), commands and the like, being human attributes, are not possible"—we certainly grant this if by those [terms] you mean prohibitions against *ājñā* (command), *abhyarthanā* (request), and *anujñā* (permission). However, we do not tolerate the prohibition of *upadeśa* (instruction); thus he says: "Even if command, request, and permission are untenable in the Veda because of its non-human origin..."

Because there is no conscious instigator (*niyoktṛ*), [the Veda] cannot be an injunction; however, it is appropriate that it be an instruction (*upadeśa*), since that is possible even for what is not of human origin.
For he will state that this [instruction] does not have the function of instigating, by which it would have a conscious agent as its author.
Nor is it the case that it is not worldly or that it does not consist of instigation, such that it would not be an injunction; thus he says: "That too..."

In that very same way, the fourth [type of speech], consisting of instigation (*preraṇā*), is recognized in the world as being like a command (*ājñā*). Now, one might ask: "If it consists of instigation, how does it differ from commands and the rest? And if it differs from them, how can it consist of instigation? To this he says: "For instance: a command (*ājñā*) and a request (*abhyarthanā*) both have as their object an action whose fruit is disregarded by the person being enjoined (*niyojya*), while the purpose lies solely with the enjoiner (*niyoktṛ*)."

[The agent] takes as his sphere of action that karma which disregards the fruit for the sake of the instigator (*niyoktr*) and is directed toward the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*). Instruction (*upadeśa*), however, is for the sake of the person to be enjoined.
Although permission (*anujñā*) is likewise in some cases, it is not instruction because its object is a person who has already begun to act. The person to be enjoined...

The wise describe *upadeśa* (instruction) as the setting in motion of what has not yet been set in motion within the sphere of purposeful action. For there is no cognition of *upadeśa* in such [secular] commands as "Drive the cow," "Teach the boy," or "Do as you please. Nor is there a cognition of *ājñā* (command) and the like in such [advisory statements] as "One should practice begging" or "One who has a fever should eat wholesome food. Furthermore, this [instruction] predominantly occurs in human compositions for the sake of desire and wealth.

In the treatises and other such works, [the injunction] is recognized in the world through commands and the like; likewise, in the words of cowherds and others intent on describing a path, they say, "One should go by this way. For an injunction does not have the nature of a command regarding an object that is not to be enjoined;
rather, the instruction of action has as its scope that which is for the purpose of being enjoined. Therefore, by this very fact, the instruction is an action whose purpose is to enjoin.
The meaning of the verse has been explained.

This is what is meant: commands (*ājñā*), requests (*abhyarthanā*), and instructions (*upadeśa*) are identical in their nature as instigations (*preraṇātmatayā*), insofar as they bring about engagement in an action by making that action their object; among these, [the first two] have their object through command and request.

An action being performed for the sake of an injunction whose purpose and the agent to be enjoined are disregarded serves the purpose of the one who commands or the one who entreats. However, an action within the scope of an instruction (upadeśa) disregards the purpose of the instructor and exists solely for the sake of the matter to be instructed; this is the distinction between instruction and [the acts of] commanding or entreating, and it possesses the nature of instigation for the sake of the person to be enjoined.

The construction of the words is as follows: that instruction for which the action is for the sake of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), and not for the sake of the enjoiner, is described as such.
Now, one might object: if the instruction of an action is for the sake of the person to be enjoined, then alas, even an authorization (*anujñā*) would result in being an "instruction" (*upadeśa*).
For that too is, in some cases, an action for the sake of the person to be enjoined. To this he says: "But although authorization is thus in some cases, nevertheless..."

Because it concerns a person already engaged in action, it is not an *upadeśa* (instruction). Even though its agent is distinct from the object of the action, it is indeed an *anujñā* (permission). For instance, there is the mention in some [texts] of a master granting permission to a servant who, desiring to do what is beneficial for his master, acts impulsively out of a desire for that master's welfare. By this, it is explained that [this is] an impulsion toward what has not yet been undertaken (*aprasthita-codanā*). [The term] "not yet undertaken" (*aprasthita*)...

The construction of the words is as follows: "the instigation (*prasthāpanā*) of that man who has not yet acted is *codanā*. Why is such an instruction well-known in the world? To this he says: "The wise declare that instruction (*upadeśa*) is the instigation of one who has not yet acted toward an action whose object is the purpose of the person to be directed (*niyojya-artha-karma-gocara*). Nor is it mere narration; even comprehension [of the meaning] is distinct from commands (*ājñā*) and the like.

He states that [instruction] has a specific object: for indeed, when there is a command such as "Bring the cow," a request such as "Teach the boy," or a permission such as "Do as you wish," there is no cognition of instruction (*upadeśa*). Nor is there a cognition of command and so forth in such cases as "One who is feverish should beg for alms" or "One who is feverish should eat wholesome food. Furthermore, this instruction is not understood in any way whatsoever in those instances.

He says that it is because [the truth] is understood everywhere by means of many modes: "And indeed, in the case of human compositions such as treatises on pleasure and wealth, an understanding unvitiated by commands and the like is recognized in the world. For authors of treatises are worldly persons endowed with both innate and acquired excellence of intellect, not merely those whose words are spoken with inferior intelligence."

He states that joy (*pīti*) is more well-known through the example: "In the words of cowherds and others intent on describing a path, such as 'Go by this way,' why is this not one of the others, such as a command (*ājñā*)? To this he says: 'For not...

The authorization of one who has not yet begun [to act] is the *bhyarthanānujñānam*. For this very reason, it is called "instruction" (*upadeśa*). Since it is perceived as distinct from commands (*ājñā*) and the like, the knowledge of that [authorization] is "instruction"; thus, it is shown by the word "instruction" as being distinct from those. Let it be distinct from those; but what, then, is it? Has it not been stated that "instruction" refers to a specific kind of word?
[Objection: If that were so, there would be the undesirable consequence of activity even for one who is unlearned [in the scriptures]. It is said in reply:
"That which teaches the specific means for the pure human goal—that human goal which is desired by a person at a particular time through a particular [means]."
The word *śabda* is said to be distinguished by its excellence because it makes known that which was previously unknown regarding the means to the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*).

Otherwise, since every word is distinct from other words, there would be no distinction [between them]. Therefore, for one who is inferior, who does not know, and who has not yet engaged in the action for his own sake, there is the request for and permission to act. Precisely for this reason, it is [called] *gopāla*.

For this very reason, since commands (*ājñā*) and the like—which would otherwise be applicable—are prohibited, and since there is no possibility [of such application] elsewhere than in narrative accounts (*upākhyāna*) and the like, the understanding [of the term *vacas*] remains restricted to the remaining case; thus he says: "For this very reason, instruction (*upadeśa*) is possible even in that which is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*)," as has been shown by the author of the Sūtras. Therefore, [the term *vacas*] is distinguished from commands and the rest.

Because it has attained the status of being recognized as such, "instruction" (upadeśa) is defined as knowledge; therefore, instruction is shown to be distinct from commands and the like. Granted that it is distinct from those, what then is its defining characteristic? The meaning is: what is the denotation of this [term] that serves to exclude both similar and dissimilar classes?

But was it not already stated by the author of the Bhāṣya, in saying "instruction is the utterance of the qualified [word]," that a specific quality belonging to the form of the word was intended? And since that [quality] resides in the perceptible word, it would follow that even a first-time listener should act upon it; to this he says: "If this were so, then even one who is unacquainted [with the convention] would act."

This is a logical consequence (*prasaṅga*). The meaning is that [the scripture] does not depend upon the acquisition of knowledge through perception (*pratyakṣa*). It is said: "That which declares the means for the attainment of the pure human goal (*puruṣārtha*)—that human goal which is desired by a person, at whatever time, and by whichever man."
The distinction residing in the word is not the cause [of its excellence] because it inheres in the echo;

rather, the word is said to be distinguished by a distinction residing in the meaning. He explains this distinction residing in the meaning as follows: the word is said to be distinguished by its excellence because it makes known a means to human goals that was previously unknown. Otherwise, every [word] would be so.

The statement that "a word is distinguished from other words" would be without qualification; therefore, by granting that [the word] is not understood, [the author] excludes [this possibility]. Furthermore, since the status of a word as an instruction depends upon a specific meaning, and since there can be no cognition of that [meaning] by a person who has not grasped the relationship [between word and object], he says that for this reason also, there is a dependence upon linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*): "Therefore, it is not unknown."

The activity of a person who hears a matter for the first time arises from instruction (*upadeśa*). Now, instruction is indeed an injunction (*vidhi*), and that is a word which expresses a distinct meaning; thus, in some places it speaks of the "utterance of the word," while in other places it speaks of the "meaning," because [the word] forms a single syntactical unit with the statement of the injunction (*vidhyuddeśa*). In yet other places, it calls it "speech" (*vacana*) or "impulsion" (*codanā*).

[Page 172] There is no activity on the part of one who has not understood the meaning. This [statement] is for the sake of illustration. Therefore, the knowledge of the object, the word, the denotation, the utterance, and so forth, is expressed by the term "instruction" (*upadeśa*) through the grammatical derivation based on the relationship of object, agent, and instrument, just as in the case of "commanding" (*preṣaṇa*) and the like.

For even by them, objects and so forth are indicated according to their intended meaning. If it is argued that the object (*artha*) is therefore the motivator, [we reply]: True, but the word (*śabda*) is also [the motivator], because it brings about the cognition of that object. How then is there the instruction regarding the auxiliary factors (*aṅga*)? For an object is required as a human goal (*puruṣārtha*); otherwise, even things like a village would not be such [a goal]. And it is precisely when it is required that it is taught.

[This is] the favor of the means of accomplishment (*sādhanānugraha*). Now, it may be argued that instigation (*pravartanā*) is understood from the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and other such markers. But this is contradicted by the statement: "Speech is the instigator of action. Furthermore, [the definition of scripture is given as]: "In some cases, knowledge is scripture; it is the cognition of an object not present [to the senses] arising from the cognition of a word. And the author of the *Vārttika* says that they speak of the "productive urge of denotation" (*abhidhābhāvanā*), referring to it as "denotation" (*abhidhā*).

Therefore, he says: "And this is for the sake of illustration, namely that 'injunction' (vidhi) is a specific kind of word. Consequently, the knowledge of meaning, words, denotation, pronunciation, and so forth, is expressed by the term "instruction" (upadeśa)—which functions as a means [of accomplishment] through the roles of object, agent, and instrument—as appropriate.
The meaning is that in those various sections of the treatise, the terms *codanā*, *vidhi*, and *śāstra* are themselves simply terms for "instruction."
Right here he states a worldly illustration: "like the word *preṣaṇa* (sending) and so forth. To the question "How is this an illustration?", he says:

"For even by those words such as *preṣaṇa*, which are means for performing actions, meanings and so forth are indicated according to the speaker's intention. If superiority [is claimed] on the grounds that it denotes a distinct meaning, then, by distinguishing between what is already established and what is not yet established, it is the meaning itself [that is superior]."

If it is argued that "the word is not the motivator," then the author of the treatise would fall into a contradiction with his own statement that "Dharma is a matter characterized by Vedic injunction" (*codanā-lakṣaṇa*).
To this he says: "In that case, the object (*artha*) is the motivator.
He replies: "True; the word is also a motivator, because it brings about the cognition of that [object]. This is the intended meaning (*abhisandhi*).
The fact that something is a directly sought-after means is not itself the cause of activity, because such a state does not exist prior to the activity;

rather, it prompts activity through its own cognition. In that regard, [the word] is produced by the word itself. Just as the object is an instigator of activity because it possesses the nature of being the referent (*yathārtha*), so too is the word an instigator because it generates that [cognition]; thus, there is no distinction between them. And consequently, there is no contradiction.
By this, the first half of the verse has been explained. Here, in the phrase "of the human goal" (*puruṣārthasya*), the person (*puruṣa*) is intended as the one to be enjoined (*niyojya*);

by "pure" (*śuddhasya*), the meaning is that it refers only to the purpose of the one to be enjoined, and not to the purpose of the enjoiner. Now, if an instruction (*upadeśa*) is a word that expresses the means to a human goal, how then can there be an instruction regarding the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*)? For surely the auxiliaries [are not ends].

[The opponent claims that these] are means for achieving the goals of man (*puruṣārtha*), rather than being for the sake of the ritual (*kratvartha*). [The author] refutes this: For in this context, the "goal of man" is that which is required; no thing is established as a goal of man by its very nature (*jāti*). Otherwise, even things such as a village would not be so [a goal]. If it is argued that even those [like a village] are sometimes and in some way desired, despite not being pleasure in themselves—then [the response follows].

In that case, the status of being for the sake of man (*puruṣārthatva*) is based on genus (*jāti*). As the proponent of Nyāya has said: "This purpose of living beings is incalculable, because the varieties of living beings are incalculable. Nor is it the case that there is no expectation of men toward the function of the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) simply by virtue of genus; as he says: "And the assistance to the means of attaining the highest good (*śreyas*), which is itself a means [to that end], is required and is taught."
Because, in the absence of favor, the highest good (*śreyaḥ*) is not produced due to a deficiency in the means;
thus, "instruction is an impulsion directed toward an action for the sake of the person to be enjoined" (*niyojyārthakarmā prasthitacodanā*). This is not contradicted. For it is as follows:
Since a person is not motivated by the mere means itself toward actions, there is no other motivator [than the desire for the result];
and they declare that the property which is the cause of engagement is "incitement" (pravartanā).
For *pravartanā* is a certain excellence (*atiśaya*) of being capable of impelling, which is designated as "activity" (*vyāpāra*).

And that [excellence] is simply the fact that [the means] is the required means (*apekṣitopāyatā*) for actions. For one does not engage in them without first apprehending that they possess such a nature.
Here, an objection is raised: "But surely it is from the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth that *pravartanā* is understood; otherwise..."

For one who has heard [the statement], activity would be impossible; it is not, however, the status of being a means to a human goal [that causes activity]. Indeed, the cognition of an already existing fact (*bhūtārtha*) is not the cause of activity. And this [statement]—"An instruction is an impelling of one who has not yet set out toward an action that serves the purpose of the person to be enjoined"—is self-contradictory.

For if they say that the action which serves the purpose of the person to be enjoined is the object [of the injunction], how can this be an "impelling of one who has not yet set out"? This is the contradiction.
The intention is that this [objection] is not refuted; for by avoiding only this specific contradiction, everything is not thereby avoided. Why?
Because it is as follows:
"For a person, there is no other motivator toward actions than the fact that they are a desired means."

For the actions of body and speech of discerning persons are preceded by effort, and that effort is preceded by desire (*rāga*). Furthermore, desire—which is associated with pleasure—cannot exist in relation to suffering or to that which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant, because of aversion toward the former and indifference toward the latter. Moreover, it is the common experience of the world that action is suffering. If that [action] were not even a means to pleasure, those seeking pleasure would not engage in it.

Furthermore, these means are not capable of directing one toward happiness directly; thus, it would follow that the activity of a discerning person would be purposeless. Therefore, it is the very fact of being a means to happiness that prompts one toward actions that are in essence suffering, by way of presenting an offering of desire.
And it has been stated that one presents this desire, which is the cause of engagement, through one’s own cognition. If...
Furthermore, the word would not convey the state of being a means to pleasure, nor would it impel a person toward action. Now, one might object:
"Even so, only the fact of being a means to what is desired is conveyed by the word; how then does the cognition of an impulsion (pravartanā) arise from this?
To this, he says:
And they declare that the phenomenon which is the cause of engagement is "setting-in-motion."
He explains this: "An excellence (*atiśaya*) of some entity (*bhāva*), capable of producing activity and designated as 'operation' (*vyāpāra*), is instigation (*pravarttanā*).

This is the meaning: we do not declare that operation is exclusively physical motion (*parispanda*), such that we would be subject to the objection that the state of being a means to a desired end—which is non-motion by nature—is not itself instigation; rather,"

A "functional property" (*bhāvadharma*) is simply some entity that is conducive to the accomplishment of a desired goal; it is the referent of the term "activity" (*vyāpāra*). For example, in the case of the self (*ātman*) which is engaged in producing cognition and so forth, its conjunction with the mind (*manaḥ-saṃyoga*) is precisely such a functional property. Similarly, in this context as well, whether it be motion (*spanda*) or something else, a functional property of an entity that is conducive to the production of activity is a specific operation called "instigation" (*pravartanā*). It is not...

And he says that this is both the word and the cultivation of it (*tadbhāvanā*): "And that [cultivation] is simply the fact that actions possess the status of being required means (*apekṣitopāyatā*). Why?
Because even that activity which arises from commands and the like possesses, in some way or another, the quality of having a required basis as its means."
[It is] by depending [on that very cognition], for otherwise there would be no such thing. But surely, activity proceeds from the cognition "this is to be done. How so?

For no one engages in actions toward something without apprehending it as a means to a desired end (*apekṣitopāyatva*). But surely, even toward what is not a means to a desired end, discerning people act at the command of a king; how then can it be a means to a desired end?

Is that alone the cause of activity? To this he says: even that activity which arises from commands and the like also depends, in some way, upon a basis that is required [by the agent]. Although commands and so forth have as their object the action of the commander, nevertheless, the accomplishment of that object also possesses, in some sense, the character of being a basis required by the one who is directed. For instance:
Satisfied by the fulfillment of that [purpose], the commander bestows upon him what is desired or does not inflict what is harmful.

It is with reference to this expectation that the servant’s activity proceeds. Why is this so? He says: because otherwise, in the absence of relying on that [commander], there would be no activity; for indeed, one does not engage in an action for which someone is neither a source of benefit nor of harm.

One strives through avoidance and application; thus, one conforms to that command. Yet, it is not on this account that instruction (upadeśa) is indistinguishable from commands and the like. For those [commands and the like] proceed with the aim of enjoining a specific purpose as their primary object, whereas the purpose of the person to be enjoined (niyojya-artha) is incidental to instruction, which is the reverse of that. Therefore, the understanding of the instigation (pravartanā) derived from the optative suffixes (liṅ) and so forth is both logically established and [otherwise] unestablished.
Regarding the term "refutation" (*parāhati*):

on this point, some who pride themselves on their traditional learning (*āmnāya*) say: "Surely, activity proceeds from the cognition that 'this must be done. This is the underlying intention: these [cognitions] indeed have their operations inferred from the observation of effects."

The optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth [indicate this]. Furthermore, among the elders, an activity characterized by engagement is observed immediately following the hearing of the optative suffixes and so forth.

And that [activity] is preceded by cognition, because it is an independent engagement, just like our own engagement. And the inferred cognition ranges within the object of the cognition that is the cause of our own engagement, because it is a cognition that is the cause of engagement, just like our own [cognition].

"Like the cognition that is the cause of activity. And regarding its object, having ourselves opened our eyes and set aside the [mere] lump of flesh, while reflecting upon it, we—by excluding the operation of words, the intention of the person, and the fact of being a means to what is desired by him—comprehend only the state of being something to be done (*kartavyatā*). For instance, even in the case of suckling at the breast and so forth...

We do not engage in action merely because a means has been desired; rather, we act with the thought, "This must be done. For even regarding the past, present, and future as described by those skilled in the *sāmudra* (astrology/omens), one engages in action in the form of a duty, thinking, "This will happen to you. And since one engages in action toward that [future object] once it is understood as being of the nature of a duty, it is the state of being a duty (*kartavyatā*) alone that is the cause of engagement; this is what is expressed by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth.

The activity that immediately follows hearing [the word] brings about the very expression of "that which is to be done" (kartavyatā) by the optative suffixes (liṅ) and so forth. Thus, because their relationship [to the meaning] is known, the optative suffixes and others express that same [obligation] even in the Veda. However, this much is the difference:
worldly speech depends on other means of knowledge for its activity, and is preceded by the cognition of being a required means [of attaining a desired end].

The cognition of what is to be done (*kartavyatā*) arises by internalizing the status of that [cognition] as a valid means of knowledge, which is required for the understanding that an action whose nature is suffering must be performed. However, since the Veda, being of non-human origin, does not require another means of knowledge regarding its own meaning, it is independent.

For would he not fail to act if he proceeded in such a manner? For who could give an answer to one who, having perceived gold, says it is clay? But what is this meaning of "it ought to be done"? Nothing at all; it is intuition (*pratibhā*). And what is this? It is wisdom (*prajñā*) conducive to the comprehension of an action delimited by specific means.

For if it were the object of the activity of intuition (*pratibhā*), there would be a cognition of the action itself; and that [cognition] is the cause of engagement. Furthermore, the cognition of what ought to be done (*kartavyatā*) is the cause of engagement independently of the comprehension of the means (*upāyatva*). Thus, when that [ought-to-be-done-ness] is understood from the Veda, it requires an authorized agent (*adhikārin*) who is the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), and not a goal (*sādhya*) for that very [action].

Because of that very nature. And where the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) is qualified by something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), there the cognition is of that which is to be accomplished, as in "one desiring heaven should sacrifice. But where he is characterized by a causal condition (*nimitta*), such as "as long as one lives," or where he is the agent of a prohibited action, such as "one should not eat *kalañja*," in those cases, the authoritative scripture (*āmnāya*) alone is the source.

Having cast aside all suspicion of defects, [the Veda]— whether its subject matter be the meaning of a positive term or the meaning of a negative particle— enjoins engagement or withdrawal by making known an action that is independent of the understanding of it as a means to achieve what is beneficial or avoid what is harmful; so why would it require being a means to an end?
Now, one might object that even if something is stated a hundred times as "it ought to be done," it will not lead to action unless it is understood as a means toward a desired end;

therefore, he says: for how could one who understands it in such a way not proceed to act? First of all, the word, having its conventional relationship known, makes known the state of being something to be done (*kartavyatā*). Likewise, [there is] the occasional prohibition (*naimittika-niṣedha*)...

It cannot be said that this [negation], being cognized through the two negative particles (*nañ*), is impossible. Nor is it correct to claim that because the status of being a required means ceases upon cessation [of the action], the negation itself must also cease; for that [status] is not the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for that [negation].
Furthermore, when one means of valid cognition has ceased, that very thing which is cognized by another means of valid cognition ought not to be negated. No.
For it is not the case that because a substance is not perceived by the eye in total darkness, it must therefore be established by the sense of touch;

nor should a discerning person fail to perform a subsequent rite (*naimittika*) simply because its cause (*nimitta*) is absent. An inference is indeed possible: "Because it does not produce happiness and is not a means for attaining the beneficial or avoiding the harmful, it is like the examination of a crow's teeth."

Because its object is sublated by the understanding of what is to be done (*kartavyatā*) born from the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*). As it has been said: "For who could give an answer to one who, having perceived gold, says 'it is clay'? Therefore, the understanding of what is to be done derived from the independent sacred tradition necessarily implies its performance; otherwise, its very reality would be untenable. Of that...
Because it is invariably concomitant with that [desire]. Therefore, it is well said: "For how could one who understands it in such a way not engage [in action]?
Now, if the state of being something to be done (*kartavyatā*) is not the fact of being a means to achieve what is beneficial, then its true nature must be stated; yet no such thing exists.
Bearing this intention in mind, the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntin*) asks: "But what is this meaning of 'it is to be done' (*kartavyam*)?"

In that context, one who holds a portion of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣaikadeśin*) says: "Nothing at all. [The opponent objects: "But in this case, the cognition of an obligation (*kartavyatā*) whose object is non-existent would be invalid (*apramāṇa*). And that which is invalid cannot serve for practical activity (*vyavahāra*). To this he replies: "It is intuition (*pratibhā*). [The opponent asks:
"But surely intuition is a cognition produced from an inconclusive logical mark (*anaikāntika-liṅga*), consisting of a determination of an object despite its deviation (*vyabhicāra*)."

Invalid cognition (*apramāṇa*) is not a factor for linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*), for doubt (*saṃśaya*) and error (*viparyaya*) are likewise [excluded]. Indeed, one does not engage in action—thinking "this must be done by this person in this manner"—regarding an object even when it is understood through perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth, if the distinction of intuitive insight (*pratibhā*) has not arisen. For in that case:

The completion of the function of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For the world, whose eye is intuition (*pratibhā*), strives toward its duties (*itikartavyatā*); such is the view of those who possess intuition.
And since a cognition that is not of the nature of certainty cannot be a factor in worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), the author, holding this intention, asks:
"What, then, is this? The reply of the *ekadeśin* (the partisan of a specific school) is: "It is the comprehension of an action delimited by a specific means..."
"Kūlā" means "prajñā" (wisdom). For those who have described *pratibhā* as a cognition that is non-determinative in nature are not truly insightful;

for that [state] is indeed doubt (*saṃśaya*). We, however, hold that it is the cooperative factor (*sahakārī*) required for the agent when performing the task characterized by the execution of an action, through the comprehension of that action which is delimited by the goal (*sādhya*), the means (*sādhana*), and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*).

Thus we have studied wisdom and inspired intuition (*prajñā* and *pratibhā*). If that is so, then since its object is indeed action (*kriyā*), it is not without an object; therefore, he says: "For if intuition were to have action as its object, there would be a cognition of action, and that [cognition] has as its domain an action delimited by the three times—as in 'he cooks,' 'he will cook,' or 'he cooked. This..."

Furthermore, wisdom (*prajñā*) manifests as if it were a marvelous reality, unconditioned by any one of the past, future, or present. However, its object is not ultimately real (*paramārthasat*), because it is devoid of the three times, like a flower in the sky.
Indeed, the designation "present" cannot mean "I shall do," for that would entail the consequence of it being indistinguishable from "I am doing. Nor can it be the future.
"I shall do it," "I did it"—these [cognitions] are not valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because their object is non-existent;

they are not doubt (*saṃśaya*) because they are determinations of a single alternative; nor are they error (*viparyaya*) because they are observed as a form of practical activity (*vyavahāra*) for everyone in all circumstances. For this very reason, the Teachers call this mental modification a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), defined as that which follows upon verbal knowledge and is devoid of a real object.
They say it is a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

Now, it was asked: "How can intuition (*pratibhā*), being a non-valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*), initiate practical activity (*vyavahāra*)? To this he says: "And that [intuition] is the cause of engagement. Why is it that this non-valid means of knowledge is not a constituent part of practical activity? [Because] doubt and error [are not so].

For it is thus. The intention is that *pratibhā* (intuition), however, is distinct from those two and initiates worldly activity (*vyavahāra*). Is it then the cause of activity merely by being thought of? No, for activity and its absence follow the presence and absence of that [intuition], as evidenced by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). In this regard, he first states the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*): "For it is not the case that one acts simply because of the thought, 'This must be done by me in this way,' without..."

The differentiation of intuition (*pratibhā*) proceeds even regarding an object already apprehended through perception. Now, one might ask: since the results of perception and the other means of knowledge are simply avoidance, acquisition, or indifference, what is the purpose of intuition? To this he says: "For therein lies the completion of the function of the means of knowledge.
The function of the means of knowledge, characterized by avoidance and so forth, is completed only when there is that differentiation of intuition, and not otherwise. Therefore...

It has been stated that the means of knowledge, such as perception, which are engaged in activities like avoidance and so forth—even though they depend upon intuition (*pratibhā*) as their primary cause, just as firewood depends on fire for cooking—are not without a cause. Now he states the positive concomitance (*anvaya*): "For the world, having intuition as its eye, exerts itself toward duties (*itikartavyatā*)," meaning toward the performance of bodily and vocal actions.

The meaning is that the world is characterized by the means of manifestation (*pratibhā*), insofar as it strives and exerts effort toward actions, thinking "this is to be done. By this, the conformity toward the apprehension of action within manifestations has been demonstrated. Now, one might object: "This is a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), and that [conceptual construction] is verbal...

What, then, is its cause? It is sound (*śabda*). For those who are proficient in it, there is either a direct cultivation [of the meaning] or, for children and others whose linguistic usage is not based on well-known words, there is the beginningless cultivation of sound. Otherwise, the initial arrangement of the organs of articulation and so forth would be impossible. As it has been said:
The initial arrangement of the instruments, the upward movement of the vital breath,
and the striking of the locations do not occur without the cultivation of sound.

Those who know [the nature of] cognition say that it follows after knowledge. However, intuition (*pratibhā*) does not follow after verbal knowledge; for if it did, there would be the undesirable consequence that it would not arise in children and others due to the absence of such knowledge, and thus they would fail to act. Therefore, another cause must be stated, yet no such thing exists.
With this intention, he asks: "What, then, is its cause? The answer is: "The word (*śabda*). In that regard, those who...

To that extent, even for children and others who lack proficiency in linguistic usage based on unfamiliar words—whether through direct experience or by means of mental cultivation—their intuition (*pratibhā*) is established.
Now, one might object: how can this intuition arise in the absence of prior experience, given that it depends upon repeated practice (*abhyāsa*), attention (*ādara*), and cognition (*pratyaya*)?

Even experience [of meaning] does not arise without the cognition of words whose relationship [to that meaning] is already known. In this present life, such experience cannot exist for infants and others; as for experience from a previous birth, it is destroyed by death, which severs all latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), and thus it cannot produce a present intuition (*pratibhā*). Or, even if it were produced, those who are blind from birth, deaf, and so forth, would not possess the experience of that [meaning] in this life.
Lest it be argued that they might describe even forms, sounds, and so forth as if they were experienced in another birth, [the author] says:

"The beginningless cultivation of words must necessarily be accepted. Why? Because otherwise, the initial arrangement of the organs of articulation and so forth would be impossible. As has been stated by those who know intuitive insight (*pratibhā*):
The initial arrangement of the instruments, the upward movement of the vital breath,
and the striking of the points of articulation do not occur without the cultivation of sound.
As soon as he is born, this infant licks with his tongue the honey and clarified butter offered into his mouth by his father;
this is the first arrangement of the instruments [of action]. Furthermore, he impels the vital breaths upward, whereby it is said that "he breathes.
Moreover, by means of the impelled air, he strikes against the locations such as the heart, from which various sounds arise.
It is evident. All this is a manifestation of the latent impressions (*bhāvanā*) of words from a previous existence. Here is the formal argument (*prayoga*):
such activity on the part of infants is preceded by the cognition that it ought to be done, because it is an independent activity of a conscious being;
whatever is an independent activity of a conscious being is preceded by the cognition that it ought to be done, just as in the case of ourselves and others.

Likewise, the cognition of what is to be done (*kartavyatā*), which is the subject of dispute, has its source in verbal testimony (*śabdayoni*), because it has the form of "what is to be done. Whatever has such a form is all sourced in verbal testimony, just as is the case for people like us. And that verbal testimony, though not perceived directly, functions as the instrument (*karaṇa*) by way of the mental impression (*bhāvanā*), according to the logic of a *adhikaraṇasiddhānta* (a conclusion established by implication).

It does not follow [that there is such a fault]. Furthermore, cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is to be inferred from the observation of its effects; since it is established only as far as the observation of the effect extends, there is no consequence of blind-born or deaf individuals being able to explain forms and other objects experienced in a previous life.

Furthermore, even for word-meanings that are perceived as discrete, how could they be synthesized? [The author] says that there exists a *pratibhā* (intuition) which is the source of verbal *bhāvanā* even for those who are proficient; it arises as a manifestation of a previously acquired capacity that has not been discarded by critical inquiry, and it brings about a connection [between meanings] as if that previously acquired capacity were being re-awakened. Thus he says: "Even for those whose perceptions are discrete... (*vicchinnaprati...*)

Furthermore, regarding even those objects that have already been perceived, the question arises as to how and why they are synthesized. The conceptualization of inquiry, having recalled its prior capacity, brings about a connection (*upaśleṣa*) as it arises within the manifestation of that previously recalled capacity.
This is the meaning: for those whose bodies are scorched by heat, upon the mere sight of a cool lake, they proceed to plunge into the waters.
They do not reflect internally: "The water found in this visible lake is capable of removing heat;

since it possesses the quality of coldness, whatever water is cold is capable of dispelling heat—just like the water of the Gaṅgā—and we are scorched by heat, so let us plunge here to allay it. Nor do they [reflect] thus.

Without mutual contact, there can be no "to-be-done-ness" (kartavyatā); nor, in the absence of this, can there be the activity of an independent conscious agent. Furthermore, there is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for such contact manifesting as a collective operation. Therefore, it must be accepted that the verbal productive force (śabdabhāvanā), whose form is not consciously perceived, is the cause of the intuition (pratibhā) that "this is to be done in this manner by this [agent]. Nor should it be argued thus:

Whether it arises from a previous birth or from this very life, let that which appears in a particular instance be the seed for the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of that very thing; what is the use of words? For a cultivation born of inferential experience has as its object an already existing reality (*bhūtārtha*), and thus cannot be the cause of a cognition in the form of "this ought to be done" (*kartavyatākāra*). And here, there is no connection with anything devoid of the form of "this ought to be done."

Because the measure (mātra) is perceived. Here, the phrase "the deficiency of inquiry as to what and how it is connected" indicates the absence of those factors that serve as the seeds of inference: the observation of the nature of the subject (dharmin), doubt regarding its properties, the desire to know, the consideration of the thesis, the reason, the reflection on the property of the reason, and non-sublation by other means of valid cognition. The phrase "whose prior capacity has not been reflected upon" refers to the recollection of pervasion (vyāpti).
He states the [opponent's] position: "Even one who has grasped the pervasion (vyāpti) is not able to infer if he does not remember it. [The opponent objects:

"But if there is no recollection of the prior capacity, why would one proceed to plunge into a cool lake when suffering from heat, rather than embracing a mass of blazing flames? He refutes this: "Because of the prior experience... (samāviṣṭapūrva).

Because it is a manifestation of a prior capacity (*śakti*), this is not an inference which would depend upon a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of that prior capacity; rather, arising from its own cause in the form of a prior capacity, it functions in some cases and not in others. Now, if intuition (*pratibhā*) is a manifestation of a prior capacity, then its object is that very prior capacity, and thus it is not without an object.

He refutes this with the word "as if" (*iva*); it is not that [the power] itself [is non-existent]. For instance, intuition (*pratibhā*), which manifests as something to be done (*kartavyatā*), also takes the prior power as its object by way of delimiting it; and since the "to-be-done-ness" is not ultimately real, the power—by virtue of being mounted upon intuition through that delimitation—is also non-existent in reality. However, its existence is [only] in terms of its own nature (*svarūpeṇa*).
Because it does not ascend to the level of the *prayojaka* (the instigator) of intuition (*pratibhā*). This very kind of intuition brings about the connection (*upaśleṣa*) of entities.
Why? Because its purpose is that; for it has activity as its aim. [Objection:
"Granted that the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) has activity as its aim; but how does it bring about connection? To this he says: "Not..."

Because that [usage] would be absent in the absence of such connection (*anupaśleṣa*). Conventional usage, which is based on the comprehension of a qualified meaning, establishes itself as uninterrupted. Since it exists for that purpose, it would be absent in the absence of connection. And even by the wise, when the means of knowledge are difficult to discern...

In the case of birds, when there are distinctions based on specific variations in tone, their initial engagement with the sound-impression (*śabdabhāvanā*) results in an intuition (*pratibhā*) that follows the operation of the present sound; this intuition is the cause of their activity, not a cognition of a means [to an end], because there is an absence of both instruction and repeated observation. Furthermore, the acquisition of specific food by those of that species occurs through a primary cognition [of it] as a means to pleasure, even though such a means was previously unknown to them.

There would be no basis [for activity]. The meaning is that the engagement in activities such as swimming by those of various castes whose differences in intuition are manifested, or the engagement consisting of passion and so forth by those of a single caste who do not know the means, could not arise from mere objects of cognition that are eternally established. Furthermore, even for the wise, by means of the instruments of valid knowledge...

Even for birds of dull intellect, that which is difficult for others to accomplish is easy; for even in the absence of a present operation of words, through the power of a particular intuition (*pratibhā*) born from the following of the latent impressions (*bhāvanā*) of previous sounds, it is easily achieved.

Thus, he demonstrates the superior capacity of intuition even over the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): "And regarding the means of knowledge that are difficult to discern, even by the wise, [it is known] through specific tones..."

In the case of various substrates, it is *pratibhā*—which follows from the prior mental impression (*bhāvanā*) of words—that, having its operation mediated by distant sounds, serves as the basis for activity.
Now, one might object: "Is it not simply the knowledge of the means (*upāyajñāna*), which constitutes the valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), that is the basis for our activity? Why [posit *pratibhā*]?"
[If it is asked: "By what means [is this known]? To this he says: "The knowledge of the means (*upāyajñāna*) is not the cause for the commencement [of activity]. Why?

Because the knowledge of the means is the cause [only] due to the absence of instruction and repeated observation; therefore, when these two causes cease, the knowledge of the means ceases, just as smoke ceases when the fire (the source of smoke) ceases. Now, regarding the construction of nests by sparrows, there is a distinction in their voices...
And regarding the transformation in spring, he says that the repeated observation [of the male cuckoos] should be superimposed as the seed of their knowledge of means:
"The acquisition of specific food by those like us is what we must attend to"—that is to say, it is a flash of intuition (*pratibhā*).
This is because for those of that same species—meaning those belonging to that same genus—who have just been born, there is an absence of repeated observation.
It could not be based on the first cognition, since [the means for producing pleasure] would already be known; by the mention of "first," the absence of repeated observation is indicated.
Now, because rebirth is beginningless, there is again the assumption of various bodies, both similar and dissimilar in kind.

Otherwise, for one who has acquired a specific accumulation of impressions (*bhāvanā*) determined by a particular birth, there would be the undesirable consequence of the simultaneous arising of all intuitive flashes (*pratibhā*) even within a single birth, because the cause is present; therefore, he says: "of the various distinctions of intuition manifested through the differences of birth. This is what is meant: that birth which is acquired through a certain latent deposit of karma (*karmāśaya*), that [birth]...

It manifests only that cultivation (bhāvanā) appropriate to that birth, not that appropriate to another birth, because the latter would be useless there. The differentiation of manifested cultivation, producing a differentiation of intuition (pratibhā), manifests it. Once [the intuition] has arisen, there occurs the engagement in activities such as swimming and so forth, based on cognition; this is observed even among those who have not learned the means and are born just at that moment. Thus, the wheel [of existence turns].
There would be no activity consisting of passion and hatred among parrots and the like, nor among pigeons, cranes, and so forth— beings of a single species who, being born [in that state],
have not yet known the means for pleasure and pain. Furthermore, there would be no hateful activity among snakes, mongooses, and others who are eternally opposed to one another.
The engagement with things that are disagreeable arises from aversion. Therefore, it is not merely the perception of a desired means that is the cause of engagement;
rather, the elders demonstrate this by showing [the opposite], as they have said:
That [cognition], when unexamined, produces as it were a close contact with objects;
having assumed, as it were, all forms, it exists as the objective domain.
Whether produced by the direct word or by following the meditative cultivation (bhāvanā),
no one can overstep that [cultivation] regarding the manner of performance (itikartavyatā).
All the world follows it as a valid means of knowledge;
even the worldly transactions of animals proceed by its power.

A proponent of one side of the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣaikadeśin) summarizes the present topic: "Therefore, it is not the status of being a desired means that is the cause of activity, but rather the mental image (pratibhā). And the elders have shown this, as they said:
"Unexamined, it brings about, as it were, a close connection among objects."

It has been explained that when not investigated, one wonders "what" and "how" it is being connected, which constitutes a deficiency in investigation. And this [cognition] does not have a distinct object; thus he says:
"Having attained, as it were, a universal form (sārvarūpya), it exists as an object."
It brings about the sudden conjunction of things whose cognitions were previously separate, such as the waters of a lake and heat;

it appears as if those things have attained a state of universal form (*sārvarūpya*), yet they have not actually attained it, because the objective existence (*vastusattā*) of those things superimposed upon it cannot withstand critical inquiry.
Therefore, it is only the intuition (*pratibhā*) itself that exists as the object by having attained that form; there is no object distinct from it.

There is such an object. Furthermore, this has been explained as arising even in the case of many objects whose cognition is interrupted, when there is a manifestation of the previously integrated power [of memory]. Nor is this [manifestation] accidental, nor is it the case that, although it is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is not a factor in linguistic and practical activity (*vyavahāra*). Thus he says:
Whether produced by the direct word or through the sequence of the meditative cultivation (bhāvanā),
no one can overstep that [injunction] regarding what is to be done (itikartavyatā).
And although it has become immeasurable, it is [the means] for worldly transactions because it is internal to them and because it is non-erroneous due to its lack of an external object.
Not only for discerning humans, but also— for others:
The entire world follows it as a means of valid cognition;
even the practical activities of animals proceed by its power.
To demonstrate the extreme renown of that collection of examples, he says: "Otherwise, how could the male cuckoo transform its vocalization in the spring? [p.181]
How could living beings and others be taught how to construct nests and the like?
And in activities such as feeding, mating, and swimming,
which are established by their species and lineage, he was the director of the beasts and birds.
It is said:
Knowledge is not without an objective support when it is connected with the means of action;
for even regarding this remote universal, there arises a cognition of the means [of its realization] through words such as "that."

Is this intuition (pratibhā) indeed possessed of an object, or not? If it is possessed of an object, then that very object must be understood as the cause of [worldly] activity, and nothing other than that [object] can be the means to what is desired. How else could the male cuckoo transform its own natural disposition in the spring?
How could living beings and others be taught how to construct nests and the like?
In activities such as taking food, feeling pleasure or aversion, and swimming— actions well-established by their species and lineage— who is the instigator for beasts and birds?
In this regard, the proponent of the final view (siddhāntin) refutes the partial proponent (pūrvapakṣaikadeśin) immediately following him, saying: "It is replied:
cognition is not without an objective basis when it is connected with the means of action."
When this universal is remote, there arises a cognition of the means [of its apprehension] similar to that of the word "yat."

Although it has been stated that intuition (*pratibhā*) is without an object, this might nevertheless be merely an accepted tenet and not ontologically real; thus, with the desire to state a refutation, the following alternative is considered: Is that intuition indeed possessed of an objective support (*ālambana*), or not? Regarding this, he states the first position: "If it is possessed of an objective support, then that very [support]..."
Or rather, it is the *bodhya* (the object to be realized) that is the cause of engagement, not the *pratibhā* (intuition). [Objection: Even with this much, how is your desired conclusion established?

To this he says: "And that [intuition] is not other than the state of being the means to the desired [end]. This will be demonstrated more thoroughly below. And thus, the desired conclusion is established.

The opponent resorts to the second alternative: "But surely it is not possible for consciousness to have a sentence as its object, because it cannot withstand critical analysis. Is that object of the sentence apprehended by a formless consciousness or by one with a form?
It cannot be the former, because the definition of an object would be untenable. For instance, if [the object] exists..."

If "object" (*viṣaya*) refers to all things because existence in its mere essence (*sattāmātra*) is common to all, then it would follow that everyone is omniscient. If, on the other hand, being an object consists in being a producer [of cognition], and this applies only to a certain thing for a certain perceiver with respect to a certain cognition, then there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); nevertheless, since the eyes and so forth are also producers [of cognition], they too would be objects.

Otherwise, it would follow that [the object] possesses the status of being an object (*viṣayatva*) at the very moment of consciousness; and since its producer has already passed away by that time, there would be no simultaneous occurrence of cause and effect due to their momentariness. Consequently, it would follow that there is an absence of knowledge regarding the present state [of the object]. Such is the collection of these [objections].

Or, if [the cognition] has the present as its object due to a restriction, then there would be the undesirable consequence that the eyes and other [senses], which also enter into that same causal complex and exist at the time of the cognition, would be perceived.
This might be argued: "The cognition, having acquired a specific capacity from its own causes, apprehends only a certain object..."
It illuminates the present, but not everything; for that indeed is its greatness, and thus it is not an object of the eyes and other senses.
As it has been said: "The grasping of an object is the property of consciousness. In this regard, the following must be considered:
does this difference in capacity of consciousness, which arises dependent upon its own causes, have the external object as its domain? Or is it the object itself?

If you ask: "What is this [knowledge] for him? Is it something to be produced (*nirvartya*), like a lump of dough for the act of kneading; or something to be modified (*vikārya*), like rice-grains for the act of threshing; or something to be purified (*saṃskārya*), like the mortar and so forth for the act of sprinkling water;

or something to be attained (*prāpya*), like milk for the act of milking? What is the point of this unwarranted superimposition? For when the object is already attained, knowledge [is simply the realization of it].

We say that it is capable. But what is this "attainment" (*prāpti*)? If you argue that it is a property of the object (*artha-dharma*) consisting of valid cognition (*pramiti*), which pertains only to a particular cognizer—just as a number such as duality pertains to one who possesses the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*)—and that it perishes upon the destruction of that cognition, just as duality and so forth perish from the destruction of the enumerative cognition; [we reply: first of all, duality and so forth are not [perceived] by one whose eyes are opened...
We do not perceive the cognition of that property [in the same way]. Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of non-cognition regarding the past and the future;
for it is impossible that a subject (dharmin) and its property (dharma) be non-present while the property itself is present.
If it is argued that the manifestation of the object is not something other than consciousness, but rather that very manifestation is consciousness itself.

The illumination of consciousness is consciousness itself. If it is asked how the illumination of one thing can belong to another, the answer is: because of a difference in their intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*). For form and the other [sensory objects], arising from their own respective conditions, are not illuminators of themselves or of others; whereas knowledge, having its birth obtained through its own conditions, has as its ultimate reality the illumination of both itself and others.

If it were seen in its own form at first without that object, and only later became connected with it—like a pure axe whose birth depends on its own causes and which is later used for cutting—then one might be subject to such an objection; however, since it [the cognition] arises only together with the object, it does not deserve such questioning. For an axe, being made of iron by its very nature due to its own causes, requires nothing else nor is it questioned regarding that fact. This is because it is its inherent nature.

Furthermore, its illumination of another object is its "result" (phala), which is in some sense conceived as distinct through the exclusion of non-illumination; and its capacity for illuminating both itself and others is its "means of valid cognition" (pramāṇa), which is in some sense conceived as distinct through the exclusion of incapacity.
Thus, this capacity is not without an object.
To this we reply: what, then, is the meaning of "consciousness whose ultimate nature is the illumination of both self and other"?

If it means that its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is illumination, then this is already established [for us]. But if it means that its intrinsic nature is a mutual relationship, then what is this relationship among them?

If you say the relationship is that of object and subject (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*), then [we ask] regarding that [relationship], because of its inherence (*samavāya*) in both the object and the cognition...

Multiplicity would follow from its occurrence in many [objects]; and thus those [objects] themselves would be the reality. Furthermore, it has already been largely explained how this [consciousness] could have past and future objects as its referents. But if it rests solely upon consciousness itself, how [could this be]?

What would be the connection with the object? Therefore, by one who describes consciousness as having the ultimate nature of illuminating both itself and others, the identity of consciousness with blue and other objects is necessarily admitted. And thus, since it is impossible for an object to be defined in relation to a formless consciousness, the object must be that which possesses a form.

Furthermore, if the manifestation of the object were nothing other than the manifestation of consciousness itself, then the distinction between objects would have to be established by a distinction within that [consciousness]. Since consciousness is formless (nirākāra) and thus lacks any internal differentiation, there would be no way to distinguish "this is the cognition of blue" from "this is the cognition of yellow. Consequently, those seeking specific causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*) would not be able to act toward their respective objects.

However, when consciousness possesses a distinction of aspects (*ākāra*), its similarity to the blue object (*nīlasārūpya*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it is the cause for establishing [the cognition],

whereas its nature as self-awareness (*saṃvidrūpatā*) is the result (*phala*) because it is that which is established in respect to the blue object. Although similarity and consciousness are one and the same reality, nevertheless, there is an apprehension of their forms as being respectively restricted to the exclusion of the one or the other.

Through its own natures and conceptual constructions, it attains the state of being the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*), wherein difference is superimposed upon what is actually free from difference. As it has been said:

"It is not logical that the mere existence of a cognition constitutes the awareness of an object, because since that existence is indistinguishable in all cases, it would lead to the undesirable consequence of non-distinction [between cognitions].

Rather, it is by entering into similarity (*sārūpya*) with the object that the cognition brings about the object as possessing its own form. And this is due to both similarity with the object and arising from it.

There is no such consequence [of over-extension] regarding the sense organs and so forth, because they do not possess the status of being objects. Furthermore, the cognition of an object is simply the experience of the form imparted by that object;
and since the forms of cognition exist in the present, their presentness is also logically established. As it has been said:
"If it is asked how that which belongs to a different time can be the apprehended, they understand 'apprehended-ness' [to be the presence of the form]."
"It is logical that its very nature as a cause is capable of imparting its form to the cognition.
Nevertheless, it may still be said that "there is the cognition of an object. Therefore, the Sautrāntikas maintained that the object is the domain of a cognition possessing a form.

This, however, is untenable. To explain: it is established either through experience or through inference that cognition possesses an aspect (*sākāra*) and has an object as its domain. First of all, experience does not terminate in its own aspect alone while simultaneously perceiving something else, such as blue;
for the manifestation is "blue," and not "in blue. Nor is it [the case that] being distinct...
It has been stated that [the object] ought to be such.
This may be so: for the objects of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are of two kinds—the apprehended (*grāhya*) and the determined (*adhyavaseya*).

For example, in the case of perception (*pratyakṣa*), the apprehended is a single moment, while the determined—and thus the object of purposive action (*pravṛtti-viṣaya*)—is the continuum (*santāna*).

Otherwise, a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would fail to incite one who seeks purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). For the capacity to incite and the capacity to lead [to the goal] consist in the presentation of the object of activity (*pravṛttiviṣaya*). Now, the very moment of the object being grasped (*grāhyakṣaṇa*) cannot be the object of activity, because at that time it has already passed away. However, the continuum (*santāna*) might be such an object; yet, since that [continuum] is not what is grasped, it must be that which is determined (*adhyavaseya*).
This must be accepted. Likewise, for conceptual inference as well, the apprehended object (*grāhya*) is the universal in the form of the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*).

However, the determined object (*adhyavaseya*) is the objective referent of purposeful activity (*pravṛttiviṣaya*), which is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākṣama*). For the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of these two depends upon the objective referent of purposeful activity. As it has been said:

For one who acts after having determined an object by means of these two [cognitions] is not deceived regarding purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). Thus, the external object, though ungraspable, is the "object" (*viṣaya*) by virtue of being determinable; in that regard, conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is determination because it does not fully comprehend the object of determination. Among those, inference, due to its conceptual nature, [is determination].

If it is argued that [the cognition] has two objects because it generates a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), then surely, since even a conceptual construction has its own internal form as its object, how can it determine an external object? If one should think that the object of conceptual constructions is not even their own internal form...
But this applies to cognition. For that which is conceptualized as the object of conceptualization belongs to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), yet its own nature (*svarūpa*) is not conceptualized.

This is because, being excluded from everything else, it lacks the capacity for association with verbal expression (*abhilāpa-saṃsarga-yogyatva*), and because it appears with vivid clarity (*viśada-pratibhāsatva*). Therefore, non-conceptual cognitions, while appearing as themselves, conceptualize their own manifestation as something external.

Those seeking their own practical ends engage in various activities here and there; because [cognition] arises from external objects through a causal lineage, and because it is connected to them and leads to their attainment, it does not deceive the world. As it has been said: "Activity occurs by determining an object within one's own internal appearance, even though that appearance is not the actual object. He asks: how is it defined that it determines an object within its own appearance as being the object? It is defined by the etymology: *anarthe svabhāsam artham adhyavasyati* (it determines an object within its own appearance, even though that appearance is not the actual object).

This is incorrect. Now, when it is said that "they superimpose the object," does this mean that the experience of the conceptual construction's own nature is itself the superimposition, or is the experience of its own nature a separate operation?

It cannot be the first alternative, because identity between the experience and the superimposition is impossible—just as it is between fluidity and hardness—given that they consist respectively of conceptual and non-conceptual forms. If it were a separate operation, there would be a sequence.

Or [there is] simultaneity. First of all, there is no succession. Since it is impossible for a momentary consciousness to have a successive operation, and since even for those who maintain that things are non-momentary, it is impossible for cognition and action to operate after having ceased, a successive operation is not possible. If it is argued that experience and superimposition are simultaneous, let them be simultaneous.

Time-ness (*kālatva*) is to be known only as abiding within its own nature (*ātmabhāva*), because when another nature is perceived, the perception of its own essential form (*svarūpa*) is logically untenable. Thus, in the cognition of the self, the object experienced in the forms of the grasped and the grasper is superimposed. However, while the self is not being cognized, it is not superimposed; nor is the object being superimposed directly perceivable (*pratyakṣavedya*). And that—

Superimposition (*samāropa*) is simply the apprehension of an object that either exists or does not exist. And it has already been stated that the apprehension of anything other than cognition itself is impossible. If it is argued that superimposition of the external consists in the non-apprehension of the difference between one’s own appearance and the external object, and that activity toward the external arises from this, [we ask]: does this [non-apprehension] occur while the external object is being apprehended, or not? It cannot be while it is being apprehended.

For it has been stated that the apprehension of that [universal] is not possible. However, if it is not apprehended, there would be no restriction on purposeful activity due to the non-apprehension of difference, because other things would also be unapprehended at that time, leading to the undesirable consequence of activity occurring elsewhere as well. Therefore, it is established neither by perception nor by inference. That too—

It has already been stated that an external object cannot be grasped or determined as if it were directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*). Nor does there exist any reason—whether identical with that [object], its effect, or otherwise—that serves as a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) to such an external object. But surely this [reason] exists:
whatever occurs only occasionally (*kādācitka*) when something else is present must all depend upon a cause other than that [present condition], just like a broken tradition (*vicchinnāgama*).

Cognitions appearing as speech depend upon another mental continuum. Thus, those [cognitions] under dispute—even while the continuum of the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) exists—are all six types of active cognitions (*pravṛttivijñāna*); this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). And that which is distinct from the continuum of the storehouse-consciousness is the object, which arises only occasionally due to the condition of the maturation of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

If it is argued that [the effect] arises at some time because of this [maturity], we reply: indeed, for the *ālayavijñānas* falling within a single continuum, a "latent impression" (*vāsanā*) is the capacity to produce various corresponding active cognitions (*pravṛttivijñāna*). The "maturation" (*paripāka*) of that [impression] is its orientation toward the production of its own effect, and the "condition" (*pratyaya*) for that [maturation] is the preceding moment existing within its own continuum. This is because the dependence upon another continuum is not admitted.
[Page 185] No;

for in that case, all moments falling within the continuum of the *ālayavijñāna* would be causes of maturation, or else none at all, because there would be no distinction. Whatever moment of the *ālayavijñāna* continuum is intended as a cause of maturation—

Thus, there is no distinction, as all [moments] are likewise non-fallen. If it is argued that because of the difference between moments there is a difference in capacity, and because that [capacity] is occasional, the effect is occasional—then, in that case, a single moment alone would possess both the capacity to produce a cognition of blue and the capacity to produce its awakening, whereas another moment would not have those. Or, if they do exist [in the other], how [is this explained]?

Is there a difference in capacity due to the difference in moments? [If so,] then all [moments] existing within the continuum of the *ālayavijñāna* would be equally capable; and since the efficient cause (*samartha-hetu*) is present, the non-production of the effect is untenable. Furthermore, if [the effect] were dependent solely upon its own continuum, then the occasional nature (*kādācitkatva*) of that which is to be negated would be contradicted by its permanent nature (*sadātana*). And by the perception of that [permanent nature], the occasional nature is sublated.

The proof of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is established by the fact that pride (*māna*) is restricted to depending on another cause. Furthermore, the proponents of Consciousness-Only (*vijñānavādin*) do not accept that all active cognitions (*pravṛttivijñāna*) have another mental continuum as their cause; rather, they accept this only for certain cognitions that appear as scriptural words. Moreover, if [pride] were caused by another continuum—

Because that [cause] is also always present, its occurrence could not be occasional. Indeed, for a very dense continuum, spatial remoteness—which might account for occasionality—is impossible; for in the Vijñānavāda, there is no separate location, since cognitions are immaterial and lack spatial extension. Nor can it be due to temporal remoteness.

Since the appearance of a previously non-existent entity is not admitted, the claim that there exists an inference establishing an external object is untenable. Even if [cognition] arises solely from its own continuum, the occasional nature of cognition can still be accounted for;
thus, because the reason's exclusion from the opposite case is doubtful, it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). This remains so even if an external cause is admitted.

If it is argued: "How is it that at one time there is the cognition of blue and at another time the cognition of yellow? Even though the proximity of external blue is absent, there will be a difference in capacity based on its own causes; for the members of the continuum (santānin) possess the causes for momentary differences, and these indeed differ with each effect according to the presence or absence of [external objects] within the continuum. To this, [the author replies]: "Now..."
When yellow is present, why does the cognition of blue and so forth not arise, or why does the cognition of yellow arise?
