If you say it is due to capacity (*sāmarthya*) and lack of capacity (*asāmarthya*) in the other [cognition], then from what does this difference in capacity arise?
If you say it is due to a difference in its own causes (*svahetubheda*), then in that case, for momentary entities (*kṣaṇa*) as well, [the difference] is based on a difference in their own causes.

There will be a difference in capacity (*śakti*). For continua (*santāna*)—which are the causes of the difference between moments—do indeed differ with each effect. Furthermore, there exists no single entity called a "continuum" that acts as a producer such that, due to its non-difference, the moments would not differ. Now, it was argued that the difference or non-difference of capacities does not follow from the difference or non-difference of moments, because [the moments themselves] are different...
Through the perception of what capacity? Otherwise, only the preceding moment would produce the cognition of blue, and not other moments;

thus, other cognitions with the form of blue would not arise, if distinct things did not possess a single capacity. But surely, even for those belonging to the continuum of blue, which are mutually distinct, there is no single [capacity] for blue?
Regarding the capacity [of a cause] such as a jar: even when another blue object is in proximity, the cognition of blue does not arise.

If it is argued that although there is a difference in the members of the continuum (*santānin*), the capacity remains undifferentiated, then what wrong has been committed by the difference between moments (*kṣaṇa*), such that [the cognition] does not occur even when that [momentary difference] exists? Alternatively, if there is indeed a difference in capacity due to the difference in the members of the continuum, and thus a difference in the effect, then it is not the case that...
[186] However, knowledge that is without an object is simply untenable.
In what respect would a cognition having the form of blue, and another cognition also having the form of blue, be able to be that very same thing? That...

This is equally true for us, despite the difference in our positions, because of our adherence to other [doctrines]. Furthermore, if an object were defined by both its similarity to the cognition and its being produced from it, then the eye, light, and the mental impression (saṃskāra) would also— respectively through their contact with the restriction toward the apprehension of form,
through their being the producer of the knowledge of that [restriction], and through their similarity to it— be apprehended as blue, just like the color blue itself.

Alternatively, if [the object] were the object of cognition due to extreme similarity, then the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) of the cognition of blue—which is even more similar to it than the blue object itself—would also result in being the object of that cognition of blue. If it is argued that the status of being an object arises from the determination (*adhyavasāya*) despite the presence of both [causality and] similarity, and that this [determination] occurs only with respect to the object and not elsewhere; we say no, because the answer to this has already been stated. This has been explained.
This is as follows: "Just as an external object is not within the scope of determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*).

By this sequence of arguments, the reason characterized by "being an object of cognition" (*vedyatva*) is established for the Vijñānavādins. And it proceeds in this way as a formal syllogism: That which is cognized by a particular cognition is not distinct from that cognition, just as the form of a cognition [is not distinct from the cognition itself].

This is the perception of a property pervaded by the contradictory [of the negandum]: blue and so forth are indeed perceived. For non-difference is indeed the contradictory of the difference that is to be negated; and it has been explained above that perceptibility is pervaded by that [non-difference], because it is impossible for something distinct—whether cognized as having a form or being formless—to be apprehended by consciousness. Therefore, this consists in the perception of perceptibility, which is pervaded by the contradictory [of the negandum], namely non-difference.
Since non-apprehension alone is the proof for the absence of difference, it is established that cognitions have no external object as their support.

And therefore, this is the case: there is a rule of simultaneous apprehension between cognition and its object. For instance: whatever is invariably apprehended simultaneously with something else is not distinct from that thing, just as a second moon is not distinct from one moon.

The cognition that there is a necessary concomitance (*niyata-sahopalambhana*) with the object is a perception of what is incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpaka-viruddhopalabdhi*). For non-difference (*abheda*) is pervaded by the necessity of simultaneous apprehension; indeed, distinct blue and yellow are not necessarily apprehended together.
This rule, being incompatible with that [distinction], excludes its opposite—non-necessity—and thereby also excludes distinction, which is pervaded by that non-necessity.

[The opponent] objects: "The non-existence of difference is established through the perception of what is incompatible with the pervader [of difference]. As it has been said: 'Because of the rule of simultaneous apprehension, there is no difference between the blue and its cognition. How then does the cognition of difference arise for the object from the cognizer, who is of the nature of consciousness, such as 'this is blue'? [The answer is: It is sublated by the inference based on the rule of simultaneous apprehension and the fact of being a powerful object of cognition."
It is indeed an error. As it has been said: "And difference is seen by erroneous cognitions, like the [double] moon.

Furthermore, whatever is a cognition, all that is without an external object of support, just like a dream-cognition; and the cognition under dispute is a cognition—this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). That consciousness is without an object of support in the interim...
And she [the opponent] objects that it is likewise [unfounded]. To this he says: "But knowledge without an object is simply untenable.
The underlying intention here is as follows: This cannot serve as a valid means of proof (*pramāṇa*) for the state of being without an object.
For instance, is the reality of the perceived object such as blue—which is established through experience—intended as the reason, or rather that of something else? In that regard:

If, therefore, that which is established by experience—the gross, non-substrate-of-ego, non-black, and so forth, differentiated as blue and so on—is experienced as an object of cognition, then its nature as internal consciousness cannot be proven. As the Teacher said [p.

"The connection with an external object is perceived through direct perception. Now, as for another [position]: its status as an object of cognition (*vedyatva*) is unestablished. And if it were of the nature of the form of cognition (*jñānākāra*), there would be no harm at all. If it should be argued that it is not the mere fact of being experienced (*anubhūtatva*) that serves as the reason, but rather the fact of being determined as experienced (*anubhūtāvasitatva*); and that determination (*avasāya*) by its very nature rests upon the exclusion of others (*ekavyāvṛtti*).

A conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*) that penetrates the form (*rūpa*) does not, in the slightest degree, comprehend any other exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). Let it not be the case here that all conceptual cognitions of words such as "cow" and so forth are synonymous with the verbal expression of existence (*sad-abhilāpa*). Furthermore, the distinctions among exclusions follow the distinctions among the objects to be excluded (*vyāvartya*). Therefore, in this context, the conceptual cognition that penetrates the state of being knowable produced by the exclusion of the unknowable (*avedya-vyāvṛtti*) is not non-external (*abāhya*).

There is no contradiction in the claim that "externality" is being investigated as something constituted by exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*); for whatever degree of cognizability of blue and so forth has been experienced and determined even by a commoner with dusty feet or a plowman, that is sufficient to refute [the notion of] externality.

That is incorrect; for we do not bring about a contradiction merely because [something] is not the object of a single determinative cognition (*avasāya*), but rather because of that [specific] externality which—

Furthermore, the grossness of blue and other objects, as determined by experience, is incompatible with those two [theories]. To explain: if blue were of the nature of cognition, its grossness—consisting in its pervasion of multiple directions and locations—and its spatial discontinuity and externality would not be possible. Indeed, it is not merely the simultaneous apprehension and non-apprehension of a single thing that constitutes a contradiction, such that [these properties] would exist within the locus of consciousness.

There would be no contradiction merely because of the perception of a gross object such as blue; rather, it would also be due to its occupying that same location or not occupying it. To explain: even for two things situated in different locations, there is a state of existence through mutual exclusion, and their being in different locations is due to the causal capacities of cognitions appearing as distinct. In that regard, [the cognition] is distinct from the blue situated in the eastern part...

It appears through direct perception; however, it is not determined by a certainty that conforms to experience as being mutually identical, because it is not determined in that way and is rather determined as being distinct from one another. And whatever is being seen is determined by a certainty conforming to experience exactly as it is, provided there is no sublation. Furthermore, if [it were] in the eastern direction...

An object situated in one direction would not be perceived at all, for there would be no observation of its existence in a different direction; yet such observation does occur. Therefore, a form situated in another direction is not perceived as being in the other direction. This being so, just as when blue is perceived, the absence of yellow is excluded because yellow is not seen, so too, in the case of determining a form in the eastern direction, that which is other than it—such as yellow—is likewise excluded.

The form of the eastern direction is "unseen"; thus, when that form of the eastern direction is delimited, its absence is excluded. Otherwise, that very nature would not be delimited. And just as there is the absence of that [form], those situated in other spatial divisions—possessing the absence of the eastern direction—must be excluded from their own nature, just as things possessing the absence of blue are excluded by the delimitation of blue.

Thus, it is established that between [the two] occupying the same location and not occupying the same location, there exists a contradiction characterized by mutual exclusion, as in the case of yellow and other colors.
Wherever such a contradiction between two positive entities exists, there is a non-difference of locus, as in the case of blue and yellow.
And since such a contradiction exists in the case of a perceived gross blue object, this is an "observation of what is incompatible with the pervader" (*vyāpaka-viruddhopalabdhi*).

Indeed, difference must be negated, for it is pervaded by the absence of contradiction, whereas contradiction is its opposite. Therefore, as much as is said to be "not blue," so much is said to be "blue and gross. Nor is it logical that [the object] consists of multiple cognitions, because unity is incompatible with multiplicity. Nor [is it logical] that there are multiple cognitions...

This is the correct principle: for if each individual cognition were restricted solely to its own manifestation, there would be the undesirable consequence that the experience of a gross appearance could not occur in multiple cognitions. Nor can it be argued that this is a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arising from the impressions (*vāsanā*) produced by the experience of various forms.

Therefore, it must possess a gross form consisting of a synthesis of the forms of those experiences. For if that [cognition] were also unitary, its appearing as such [a gross object] would be untenable, just like the experience itself. Alternatively, if it were manifold, it would follow that there could be no appearance of grossness;

furthermore, because it would be an object of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), its clarity of appearance would be untenable. As it has been said: "For one who is bound by conceptual construction, there is no clear object."

Regarding the phrase "it appears": the grossness [of the object] has not been experienced [by the sense-faculties], such that, with that as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), there could be a vivid appearance in the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Therefore, since grossness is untenable both in the external object and in consciousness, this [appearance of grossness] must be accepted as non-existent. Furthermore, that [consciousness] is not possible, because the identity of the existent and the non-existent is untenable. By this, [the notion of] "this" as something distinct...
The meaning has been explained. Therefore, even if one does not wish it, the fact that cognitions are objects of the mind must be admitted.

And thus, being an object of cognition (*vedyatva*) is not pervaded by non-difference; consequently, the "perception of a contradictory pervader" (*viruddhavyāpakopalabdhi*) is unestablished and cannot refute difference by means of establishing non-difference. Now, it may be argued that the establishment of a fact does not result from a mere counter-argument against another.

And it has been stated that consciousness—whether with form (*sākāra*) or without form (*anākāra*)—is incapable of being the self-nature of feeling. Now, is this gross experience (*sthūlānubhava*) something that must simply be established [as non-existent], or is it that it does not exist at all? It is certainly not that it does not exist, for it is experienced just like the color blue (*nīla*). If that [gross experience] were denied, it would follow that the experience of the color blue must also be denied, as both would be equally without foundation.

And likewise, from what could its difference [from other cognitions] arise? If it does exist, then it cannot be unestablished; nor can it be a form of cognition itself. What, then, is its establishment? For this very reason, the cognition that manifests a non-self (anātman) cannot be subject to doubt, as its distinct nature is established by its own causes through the absence of counter-examples. Indeed, experience...

It requires an illustration [to show] that there might not be a non-experience of unique qualities such as odor in earth and so forth. If it is asked, "What, then, is this relation's connection with the relata?"—then what is the connection of a relation elsewhere with its two relata? It is by its very nature (*rūpa*) that it is so; thus, it does not require another relation. Never indeed...

This [connection] is defined as being without the two related entities; yet, when those two exist, they do not become related entities [merely by virtue of it], and therefore the connection between related entities is not ultimately real.

If it is argued that the connection is simply the two related entities arising in such a manner, [we reply: surely even the experience of something gross does not occur without the gross object itself.
It is being examined: and since that [subtle form] exists, the gross is not unexperienced;

thus, by its very nature, even that [gross] has as its ultimate reality the manifestation of the gross, just like a relation. Or rather, the two [the subtle and the gross], having arisen in such a way, are ultimately real as if they were related entities through a relation.
This is the justification. If this is so, it would result in the conclusion that mere experience itself does not grasp an object distinct from itself.

[Objection: No, for even when there is the experience of blue and so forth, it is not determined apart from the blue and so forth; nor is it the case that while that [experience] exists, the blue and so forth have not been experienced. Thus, just like the experience of a gross object, the experience of the non-self such as blue occurs by its very nature and not through another relation—this is the truth. [Reply: This is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because it is possible for that which is not of the nature of that [object] to be an object of cognition (*vedyatva*).

[The reason] "being an object of cognition" [is also inconclusive]. Likewise, the rule of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambha-niyama*) is also inconclusive. For such a difference in nature (*svabhāva-bheda*) of consciousness depends upon its own causes, by virtue of which there is this single apprehension of both self and non-self. And it has already been stated that nature is not within the scope of inquiry. By this very [argument], the status of being a cognition (*pratyayatva*) is also refuted, as in the case of cognitions such as dreams.

Furthermore, because external objects are superimposed [upon cognition], the example lacks the property to be proven (sādhyavikala). Consequently, the logical reason (hetu) is contradictory (viruddha).

Furthermore, the simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambha*) is unestablished (*asiddha*). For there is no such rule that the very apprehension of blue is the same as the apprehension of its cognition; indeed, this is not within the scope of experience. To explain:
a perceiver with wide-open eyes, seeing "this is blue," does not at that very moment see the experience of it as well.

For the experiencer is inclined toward the blue [object] and not toward the experience; as the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of that which is being experienced, it also delimits the experience itself. Indeed, it is not the case that "the experience is experienced" when the experience does not appear. For there is no possibility that while the staff is not grasped, the person with the staff is grasped. Therefore, even when the experience is grasped as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), [it is so] while being experienced...

If it is argued that the rule of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambhaniyama*) is established because the experiencer is inclined toward [the object], this is not so. For it is not the case that one experiences "I am experiencing blue," but rather simply "blue. If the manifestation of the experience were non-existent, objects would not manifest;
for their manifestation is dependent upon that [experience]. Indeed, an experience of blue that has not dissolved into the object is not capable of illuminating it.

For there is no manifestation of an object other than the experience itself; that which is not manifesting, even though it is grasped through the power of the sense organs and so forth, is in reality nothing but the experience whose ultimate nature is the illumination of the other, and its manifestation is that very [experience]. And thus, if it were to remain hidden, then because its own nature would be hidden, it would not cause the objects to appear either; consequently, there would be neither experience nor objects.

[If this were so,] total blindness would have come upon the entire world; therefore, it must be admitted that the manifestation of objects depends upon the light of experience (anubhava). Furthermore, in a single object, a clear and an unclear appearance are simultaneously perceived by cognizers. Nor is this clarity and so forth a property of the object itself, for it is impossible for contradictory properties such as clarity to coexist in a single thing at once.

Because of the impossibility of [multiple] forms [coexisting in one cognition], the distinction between cognitions is established; thus, it is a property of consciousness. And so, that knowledge is proven by experience.
Therefore, when self-awareness is established through experience itself, whoever—due to the influence of habitual adherence to their own philosophical tenets—[denies it...]

Delusion leads one astray; therefore, an inference is presented in response to it: whatever has its manifestation dependent upon the manifestation of something else, that manifests only when that [other thing] is manifesting—just as the person with a staff (daṇḍin) manifests only when the manifestation of the staff is dependent upon the manifestation of the staff.

And since the object to be cognized, such as color-form (rūpa), has its manifestation dependent upon the manifestation of the cognition, this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). Nor is it...

The dependence of the manifestation of color and other qualities upon the manifestation of a cognition is unestablished; for it has been said: "If it were not dependent on that [cognition], the entire world would necessarily fall into total blindness. Nor is there a contradiction regarding the operation [of a cognition] within itself in self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*), because there is no operation of cognition other than its own nature. For how could there be the relationship of agent and object within itself?

[Otherwise] it would be contradictory. However, they declare that self-awareness (*ātmasaṃvedana*) is precisely the manifestation of consciousness itself, whose nature is independent of anything else for its illumination.
And a thing is not contradicted by its own nature. Therefore, since self-awareness is established, the rule of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambhaniyama*) is established.

That is untenable, because the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*). For blue and other objects do not have their manifestation dependent upon the manifestation of the experience; rather, they have their manifestation dependent upon the experience itself. If this were so, then there would be an inconclusive argument (*anaikāntika*) due to the eyes and other sense organs. What, then, is the dependence of blue and other objects upon the experience? Indeed, what does even the manifestation of the experience depend upon? If [it depends on nothing else]...

There is no statement here that is either redundant or excessive. [The opponent claims: "It depends on the manifestation of experience. If you say "manifestation," then surely it has been stated that that very manifestation is dependent upon it (the object), and that is untenable; for it does not depend upon itself, because there is a distinction...

If it is argued that because the state of being [an object] depends upon consciousness, the very experience itself—being the manifestation of the experience—is the manifestation of blue as related to both oneself and another;
and thus, since the manifestation of blue is dependent upon the manifestation of the experience, [the object is known through the experience];
then, in that case, it would have to be said that the relation to blue depends upon self-luminosity (*svaprakāśa*). In that regard, this much...

It must be said: let it be self-luminous; but from what [source] does its connection with blue arise? If you say "from its own nature" (*svabhāva*), then enough with self-luminosity, since that connection is established by nature alone. However, this is the distinction:
for you, that connection with it is imagined (*kalpitā*); for me, however, it is ultimate (*pāramārthikī*), which indeed is the manifestation of the object of knowledge (*jñeya*).

The teachers declare that this is either "knownness" (*jñātatā*) or "objectness" (*karmatā*). Now, if it is objectness, that is a property of the object; how then can this property of the object exist in the case of things past and so forth? This is not a property of the object, but rather "knownness" is simply a specific relation between the knower—the self—and the object of knowledge. And that, being a property of the knower, is delimited by the object being known with respect to that which is to be known.

The state of being a quality (*guṇabhāva*) of the self—like pleasure and the like—is perceivable by mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*) arising from an immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) independent of a desire to know (*pramitsā*);

although it inheres in one [of the two relata], it is possible as a relation that depends on both for its determination, just like a capacity (*śakti*). But surely this is nothing other than experience (*anubhava*) itself? For indeed, even that [experience] is restricted to a specific object of cognition (*vijñeya-viśeṣa*).
A specific property of the person, which conforms to worldly usage, is described [as "cognition"]. This is true; however, this is not the actual relation itself.

For that [property] is an operation (*vyāpāra*) of the self. Its fruit, however, is the relation characterized by the self's orientation toward the object of knowledge. But how is the cognition of that experience [established]? It is indeed from this very fruit, characterized as the relation.

As for the statement, "But when [the object] is known, one understands it through inference," if it is argued that because a result occurs only occasionally due to a specific conjunction of the self (*ātman*), there is no inference from experience, then must the self now become a subordinate factor (*guṇabhūta*) toward the object, thinking, "A specific conjunction of the self has arisen"? For action indeed establishes the relationship of subordinate and principal.

[The relation] brings about [the cognition] of entities, because it is observed in such cases as the cooking of Caitra’s rice and so forth. Now, if the relation is based on the imposition of an action (*kriyā*), how can it be apprehended when the action is not perceived?
If the action is already perceived, then its perception does not arise from the relation which is the result [of that action]. This is not so; for the action—

For there is no relation without a verbal root (*dhātu*); yet, it is not the case that the cognition of that [relation] does not occur without the cognition of the action, since the cognition of the relation occurs even with respect to an action that is itself not being cognized. Just as the sacrifice (*yajati*) is inferred from the relationship between the substance and the deity understood from the word "Āgneya," so too, from the knowledge of what has arisen, one [cognizes] oneself as subordinate to the object by means of the mind alone.

Having suddenly apprehended that cause, one infers the act of cognition (*saṃvedana-kriyā*), because that [apprehension] cannot be accounted for by the mere conjunction of the self and the mind. As it has been said: "First that [object] is grasped, and afterwards the cognition [is inferred] on account of its state of being known (*jñātatā*).
Furthermore, clarity (*sphuṭatva*) is merely a particularity of the object's knowability, not a particularity of the cognition itself. For instance, [in the case of] a universal (*sāmānya*)...

The cognizability of the particular and its possessor is clarity (*sphuṭatā*); its opposite is lack of clarity (*asphuṭatā*), because, as in the case of "the tree is far away," it is characterized by the effect of the manifestation of the object of cognition.

Furthermore, since there is no possibility of linguistic derivation in the absence of an object, activity would occur without depending upon it. People do not perceive [the tree] as "an aśoka" or "a sahakāra"; rather, approaching it, they perceive the sweet nectar being drunk by swarms of bees motionless with joy, its fresh sprouts trembling in the Malaya breeze.

A cluster of *kadamba* flowers at the foot of a red *aśoka* tree. Therefore, it is established that this distinction lies in the state of being known (*jñeyatā*), not in the act of knowing (*jñāna*); thus, cognitions are directed outward (*parāñcaḥ*) and not inward (*pratyak*). The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: those cognitions under dispute are known only by another cognition, because they are cognitions; whatever is so [is known by another cognition].

All those cognitions would have to be known by another cognition, just as [an object] is not known by that very same cognition; for if there were an appearance of what does not exist, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Therefore, one must admit that only that which is being known has an appearance. And in that case, regarding the self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) of consciousness, it would result in a contradiction, wherein that very same thing would be both its own object (*karman*) and its own action (*kriyā*). As it has been said:
"Just as the tip of a finger cannot touch itself by itself,

so too knowledge, being a part of itself, cannot know itself. Thus, since the state of being an object of cognition is pervaded by non-contradiction, [the existence of] self-cognition is established through the observation of contradiction in its opposite.
The pervasion is established because [consciousness], when turning away from being an object of cognition, is necessarily pervaded by being cognizable through another cognition.
In this same manner, properties such as knowability (*prameyatva*), quality-ness (*guṇatva*), and existence (*sattva*) may also be employed as reasons for being cognizable through another cognition.
Thus, it is proven that consciousness is not self-cognizing.

Furthermore, the rule of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambhaniyama*) is unestablished. Moreover, since cognition—which is inferred from the diversity of its results—is non-dual, it is not capable of producing a diversity of results; thus, even in the absence of the appearance of blue and so forth, the determination of each specific object (*pratikarma-vyavasthā*) is established by its own nature through differentiation. Therefore, in the absence of any sublation, experience itself, which grasps its own self, is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of the external world.

No other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) need be pursued here; for when an elephant is seen, wise people do not infer its presence by its trumpeting. An examination of the object of cognition (*prameya*) has been set aside for fear of prolixity. Thus, by this sequence of arguments, the intention of the Teacher—who maintains that it is simply untenable for cognition to be without an objective support (*nirālambana*)—has been stated.

He states another refutation: "Because it is characterized by the effect of manifesting the object of cognition (*jñeya*). The manifestation of the object of cognition is the state of being an object of cognition; by means of that, consciousness—which is otherwise entirely beyond the senses—must be inferred. It has already been stated that there is no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for that [consciousness]. However, if [consciousness] were without an objective support (*nirālambana*), the manifestation of the object of cognition would not exist at all; so by what could consciousness be inferred?

That of which "lack of objective support" (*nirālambanatva*) would be proven—by this, the contradiction between the subject (*dharmin*) and the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) has been shown. Thus, the meaning is that the reason (*hetu*) suffers from the fallacy of having an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhatva*). Furthermore, a word whose relationship [to its object] is well-established may produce a mental image (*pratibhā*); however, the establishment of the word’s relationship is with the object, not with consciousness as its effect, because [the relationship] belongs to the former.
Because of infinity and because of deviation; and because the universal, which is the object of intuition (*pratibhā*), is not an effect, it cannot be the activity of an agent.
[p.192] Is it not the case that action associated with the causal factors (*kāraka*) is indeed accepted as the objective support (*ālambana*)? No; for that [action] is subject to cessation.

Even in the case of verbal cognition (*vacana-janmanī*), because it is similar to [direct] manifestation (*prakhyā*), there would be the undesirable consequence of non-engagement [with action], since there is a difference in intuition (*pratibhā*) regarding words endowed with the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth.

Now, is it not the case that there exists no word that neither prompts engagement nor causes withdrawal? [It does exist], for otherwise it would be purposeless (*vaiyarthyāt*). [The word expresses] "that which is to be done" (*kartavyatā*).

For the operation of speech necessarily culminates in something to be accomplished (*kārya*). How then are the Vedāntas and worldly statements, which merely describe what already exists? Because they differ in their nature as things to be accomplished; that is, because they have as their objects the comprehension of engagement (*pravṛtti*) or desistance (*nivṛtti*).
Indeed, every thing to be accomplished possesses a distinction. In the Vedāntas, for instance, there is the duty of comprehending the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*).
In this world, the finality of a sentence consists in the understanding that "this [object], such as a jar and so forth, is to be apprehended here";

for it does not depend on prior linguistic usage regarding its own effect. Furthermore, if one accepts that there is no objective referent (*nirālambanatva*), then no object exists; since linguistic usage would thus be impossible, activity would have to occur even without depending on such usage. Yet, such [activity] does not occur; thus he says:
And because of the absence of an object, if linguistic derivation were impossible, there would be an engagement [of the mind] independent of that [derivation].

Someone says: "Surely it is accepted that action associated with causal factors (*kāraka*) is indeed the objective support (*ālambana*); nevertheless, the status of being the means (*upāyatā*) as intended by you is not established. He refutes this: "No, for [the cognition] 'one cooks with wood'..."
In this regard, even though it is a statement that does not incite action, since the manifestation (*prakhyā*) is the same, there would be activity;

or else, if there were no activity, then because there is no difference from the intuition (*pratibhā*) arising even from a sentence containing an optative suffix (*liṅ*) such as "one should cook with wood," the consequence would be a lack of activity [in all cases].
The opponent, however, unable to tolerate the claim that it arises from a statement that does not incite action, says: "But surely it is not non-inciting..."
Nor does there exist any speech that causes one to desist. Why? Because it would be purposeless.

For wise people utter speech for the sake of communicating with others. And that alone is to be communicated by another which possesses a purpose. However, the mere description of what has already come into being is not like that. Therefore, speech is nothing other than that which incites to action or causes one to desist.
The meaning is that there is a goal [to be reached].

Now, an objection is raised: "Is it not observed in both the world and the Veda that there are descriptions of what has already come to be—for instance, 'This portion of earth contains treasure,' or 'In the beginning, my dear, this was indeed Being'? To this he replies: "For every [injunction] culminates in something to be done."

The operation of speech [is directed toward action]. If this is so, how then are the Vedāntas, which describe existing things (*bhūta-anvākhyāyin*), and the many worldly utterances? The answer is: because of the difference in what is to be done (*kartavyatā-bheda*). This is because they have as their object the comprehension of engagement (*pravṛtti*) and withdrawal (*nivṛtti*). He clarifies this very point: for every thing to be done possesses differentiation. That very [point]...

He states the distinction: first, in the Vedāntas, there is the necessity of the realization of the Self. For in the injunction "the Self is to be known," realization is prescribed with respect to the Self, and the Vedāntas have that as their ultimate purpose. Even in common worldly usage, the conclusion of a statement is such as, "this treasure and so forth is to be realized here. He refutes this: this is not sound. Herein [is the reason]...
It must be considered that the Upaniṣads have as their primary purpose the duty of realizing the Self. Indeed, there are three types of realization possible:
that consisting of hearing (*śrutamayī*), that consisting of reflection (*cintāmayī*), and that which is characterized by direct intuition (*sākṣātkāravatī*). Among these, [p.193]...

This is not sound. Since comprehension arises from the word, the word has no further operation regarding that [comprehension], just as in the case of the cognition of the connection between an action and its fruit. Furthermore, if the certainty [of truth] also arises from the word, it has already been produced; if it arises from something else, then [the word] possesses authority. Nor does the word have "purposefulness" (arthaparatā) because the injunction to study one's own Veda (svādhyāyādhyayana-vidhi) has a visible purpose, just like ritual actions.

This is because of the maxim that "the meaning of a sentence is not distinct [from its constituent parts]," otherwise it would follow that only a sentence containing an injunction could possess an intended meaning. Nor is an injunction sought for the sake of making knowledge a human goal (*puruṣārtha*). Regarding the knowledge consisting of hearing (*śrutamayi*), which is the manifestation of the object of knowledge through cognition, he says: since comprehension arises from the word, there is no further operation regarding that [comprehension]. It is not [an injunction] regarding what has been heard...

[The result] is to be accomplished in me. From the word, what is to be accomplished is understood; the purpose of the injunction (*vidhi*) is activity at a subsequent time, and not the mere understanding from the word itself, because that would entail the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*). This is the sense. Just as in the case of the cognition of the connection between an action and its fruit—just as an injunctive statement regarding an action does not require another injunction for the cognition of the connection between the action and its fruit—so too [is it here].

The meaning is that even one who has sat down [in meditation] does not attain self-realization. He raises an objection: "Certainty regarding the Self [is achieved]. He refutes this by considering the fruit of the injunction:

if [certainty] arises from the word itself, then [the word is independent]; but if it arises from another source, namely another means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*), then the word lacks authority because it is dependent upon that other source. Alternatively, if [certainty arises] without an injunction, then the Vedāntas would have as their sole purport the nature of the word itself.

It might be argued that [the injunction] exists because of the primacy of its own form (*svarūpa*). However, when it is enjoined by the Vedāntas that "the Self is to be known," then since it would be impossible to effect the knowledge of the Self through those [Vedāntas] if their meaning were not intended to be expressed, one must conclude that the injunction intends that meaning. To this he replies: "Even the fact that [the text] has a purposeful meaning is not the function of the injunction. Why? Because [the study of the Veda] already has a visible purpose, namely, the mastery of one's own recitation (*svādhyāya*)."

[This applies] to the injunction for Vedic study (*adhyayana-vidhi*), just as it does to the injunctions for ritual acts (*karma-vidhi*) regarding the Upaniṣads. This is because of the maxim that "the meaning of a sentence is not distinct [in its purpose]. For the visible purpose of the injunction for Vedic study is indeed the comprehension of a meaningful object. If, however, its purpose were merely the acquisition of syllables (*akṣara-grahaṇa*), it would result in having an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatā*). Just as in the case of the injunctions for ritual acts, [the comprehension of meaning occurs] even without another separate injunction.

Thus, the fact that the Vedāntas have meaning as their primary purpose is simply the general rule (*autsargika*). However, if the injunction for Vedic study (*svādhyāya-vidhi*) were not intended to have a visible purpose, or if the general rule that words have meaning as their primary purpose did not apply, then only those texts accompanied by an injunction would have their meaning intended;

otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that only that which is accompanied by an injunction could have its meaning intended. This is what he says: "Otherwise... [and] "If it were argued that in the absence of an injunction..."

For indeed, only the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha) is that which is to be brought about by the productive operation (bhāvanā), because it is expressed within the same word [as the bhāvanā]. If there were an injunction (vidhi), then even if it were not expressed in the same word, the human goal (puruṣārtha) consisting of non-return (apunarāvṛtti)—though found in an explanatory passage (arthavāda)—would be obtained by means of that [injunction];
thus, an injunction is sought. To this, he says: "And an injunction is not sought for the sake of being a human goal."

Why? Because knowledge has as its fruit the manifestation of the object of knowledge (*jñeya*). And since that [manifestation] is inseparable from it, it is attained even without an injunction (*vidhi*). To this objection—that non-return (*apunarāvṛtti*) is the fruit, for the scriptural statement "he does not return again" is heard, and that cannot be understood without an injunction—the author replies: "ending with the fruit... (*phalānta*).

Because [the state of] non-return is not accepted [as something to be produced]. For liberation is defined as non-return; and it will be stated that this is not something to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Furthermore, if the Vedāntas were intent upon an injunction for realization, there would follow the consequence that they lack authority regarding the actual existence of the nature of Brahman. For that [nature], being eternal, is not an object even of an injunction, such that it would require an injunction.

For an injunction has practice as its domain, and it depends upon the reality of the self as the object of that practice. And thus, because it is a fruit, because no other fruit is admitted, and because an injunction is subordinate to action, there is no [injunction regarding] the existence of the nature of a real entity.

Because [the injunction] is not intended to be expressed, the performance [of the action] would be understood merely for the sake of attaining that [result], and there would be no realization of the reality of the Self (ātmatattva). Therefore, the injunction heard in such cases is not intended to be expressed, because [the action] is already established as a constant requirement.
But surely, how can there be authority for that which is devoid of an injunction, being a mere restatement (anuvāda) and thus incomplete?

Now, what is this nature of being a restatement (*anuvādatā*)? Is it the state of having an object already apprehended by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or is it the state of having an existent object (*bhūtārthatā*)?

If it were the state of having an object already apprehended by another means of valid cognition, then even that which is devoid of an injunction, and even that which is not of such a [injunctive] nature, would not be a restatement if it were non-human in origin (*apauruṣeya*).

If, on the other hand, it were the state of having an existent object, how could there be dependence [on another means of knowledge]? For in the case of worldly speech, [dependence exists] because [the object] has been apprehended by another means of valid cognition.

Since real objects are within the range of perception, dependence is observed in cases such as the drinking of medicinal herbs; and if it is argued that injunctions also serve as a means of valid knowledge regarding the Self, we say no. This is because comprehension is possible even through superimposition, without recourse to the true nature of the Self. And thus, since the Vedāntas lack the quality of being subservient to [injunctions], their status as the source of the knowledge of Brahman is well-established.
He says this [objection] would be refuted: because an injunction is intent upon action, the actual existence of the thing itself is not intended to be expressed;

therefore, its performance would be understood as being for the sake of attaining that [result], and not for the realization of the nature of the Self. [Objection: But there is a scriptural text stating "the Self is to be known," and this is certainly not an error. For the traditional authority is equal [in both cases], and there is syntactical unity with that [text].
Therefore, he refutes [the objection] under the guise of a conclusion:

"Hence, an injunction heard in such cases—which are unworthy of being enjoined—is not intended to be prescriptive, because it is already eternally established. For the realization of the nature of Brahman is indeed accomplished through the Vedāntas even without an injunction."
For it is impossible that one who has understood the connection of forms and knows the logic of words and the Vedāntas should fail to comprehend the meaning;

since this is already established, an injunction heard in such contexts is not intended to be significant. Nor can it be a case of negligence, because it is logically consistent even as a restatement (anuvāda). [Objection: Let there be no injunction for comprehension as a result; however, the injunction is for the sake of establishing authority (prāmāṇya) itself.

[The opponent] objects: "Otherwise, that [status] would be impossible; for how can there be authority for that which is devoid of an injunction, being merely a restatement (anuvāda) and thus inherently expectant [of something else], since authority is defined by independence? Otherwise, it would follow that even Smṛti would possess authority. He then analyzes this: "Now, what is this state of being a restatement?"

Does it mean "having an object already apprehended by another means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇāntarādhigatārthatā*), or rather "having an existent object" (*bhūtārthatā*)? He refutes [the first]: If it means "having an object already apprehended by another means of valid cognition," then even a statement devoid of an injunction (*vidhiśūnya*) that possesses an existent object—that is, one whose object has been made the subject of another means of valid cognition—would not be a restatement (*anuvāda*) if it were non-human in origin (*apauruṣeya*). For a restatement is a subsequent utterance preceded by [prior] knowledge; however, in the case of what is non-human in origin...

Since there is no knower or agent, it is not preceded by knowledge; thus, it is not a restatement (*anuvāda*). The phrase "by virtue of being dependent" is to be supplied [to the previous argument]. For human speech, being produced after one has apprehended an object through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), would be dependent on that other cognition; however, non-human (Vedic) speech is not like this—this is the meaning. Adopting the second position, he says: "If it is a statement of an existing fact (*bhūtārtha*), what causes its dependence?"
The meaning is that there is no necessary connection between being a statement of an existing fact (*bhūtārthatva*) and being dependent on other means of knowledge (*sāpekṣatva*).

An objection is raised: if it is observed that worldly statements concerning existing facts are dependent because their objects are already apprehended by other means of knowledge, then Vedic statements concerning existing facts must likewise be dependent. To this, the reply is given:

In the case of worldly procedures such as the drinking of medicinal herbs and so forth, that [Vedic injunction] would require them; thus, it would depend upon a non-Vedic injunction. And what are those [procedures]? It would likewise depend upon that which possesses such an injunction. Now, if it does not depend on them because it is authorless (*apauruṣeya*), then its authorlessness—

Even if it were measured, it would be purposeless. Now, if the dependence on other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) pertains to a statement of an existing fact (*bhūtārtha*), it does not apply to an injunction (*vidhi*). For if that [dependence] were possible regarding the meaning of an injunction, it would follow that even worldly [statements] would be independent of such [other means].
Since the application (*viniyoga*) depends upon human intellect as its authority, its dependence on that [intellect] results in dependence on that very [human intellect] in those cases.
Regarding the statement that [the Veda] is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*): it is not only independent of other cognitions, but also not an object of other means of knowledge (*māna*).
Thus, it is "independent of the cause that is the non-human word," because the reason for its independence is not the impossibility of other means of knowledge;
rather, being of human origin (*pauruṣeyatā*) is the cause of dependence. This applies even to worldly speech which is focused on an injunction (*niyoga*).

Because it is dependent [on other means], there is no possibility of it being a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Thus, if perception and inference are mutually dependent due to such dependence, then if the Vedic injunction, because it is authorless (*apauruṣeya*), does not depend on them, then its authorlessness would be equally useless in the case of other Vedic statements concerning established facts (*bhūtārtha*). Alternatively, if it is argued that the Vedic statement concerning an established fact is dependent because another means of valid cognition is possible, [then the same applies to the injunction].

[The opponent argues: It is because of the injunction (*vidhi*). Why? Because that [injunction] is impossible in the sense of an injunction; because no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is possible. [The author replies: As a consequence, even an ordinary worldly injunction regarding medicine and the like would entail independence from such [cognition]. If you think that words have, by their very nature, the purpose of an injunction (*niyoga*), or that their meaning consists in their own intrinsic purpose—that is not so; for substances, qualities, and actions have their own intrinsic purposes as their meanings.

Verbal expressions are not capable of effecting their own meaning solely by way of an injunction; thus, they depend upon application (*viniyoga*). This very connection of these [words] with the injunction occurs while they do not abandon their relation to action and its factors (*kriyā-kāraka-saṃsarga*); such is the established position regarding Vedic texts. Since the general rule (*utsarga*) remains unrefuted and persists in that state, therefore, in the case of what is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*), there is an injunction (*niyoga*).

Because the two types of injunction (*viniyoga*) are not preceded by cognition, the word [of scripture] is independent. However, worldly people compose statements either by perceiving an object through another means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) or by superimposing upon it something perceived elsewhere; for example: "One who has a fever should eat wholesome food," or "One seeking liberation should meditate on selflessness. And an injunction is not another means of valid knowledge.

Alternatively, [the word] may have superimposition as its object, because it is not perceived otherwise. However, application (*viniyoga*)—whether it falls within the scope of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or within the scope of superimposition—is possible as its object. And since intention follows from perception, and verbal composition follows from intention, one must set aside the general rule that [words] have application as their primary meaning, and instead [accept] application as the intended meaning through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

[The opponent] objects that [the Veda] depends on human agency and is, in fact, dependent—because the application (*viniyoga*) originates from human intellect, it possesses dependence therein. However, in the case of what is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*), even that application (*viniyoga*)—not merely the injunction (*niyoga*)—is independent of any other cognition. And the fact that [application] originates from human intellect applies to the application in the speech of a trustworthy person (*āptavākya*).

It should be understood that [the object] is to be known as such, and in the case of an unauthoritative statement, it is to be understood as something superimposed. He refutes this: even an objective fact (*bhūtarūpo'rthaḥ*) that is the domain of another means of knowledge (*mānāntara*) is independent of the cause that is an impersonal statement (*apauruṣeyavacana*), just like an injunction (*niyoga*). For the reason for being impersonal is independence, not the impossibility of other means of knowledge; whereas being personal (*pauruṣeyatā*) is the cause for dependence.
Right here he demonstrates positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*): "Because even worldly speech, though centered on an injunction (*niyoga*), is dependent [on something else].
This is the meaning: if worldly speech were not centered on an injunction, then Vedic speech would likewise not be so.

Because it arises from an object and is dependent [on other factors], there is a loss of its status as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, a statement is dependent because its activity is preceded by the desire to express what has been perceived through another means of knowledge, or because it possesses an injunction (*vidhi*) and is otherwise. Since the Vedic word is not like that—being both [independent]—it is free from dependence; thus, this is well-established. Consequently, even for the sake of its being a means of valid cognition, there is no intention to express an injunction.

It may be so, because a word whose relationship [to its meaning] is already known in common worldly usage possesses the power to convey meaning even in the Veda. However, if that which has not had its relationship grasped were to possess the power to convey meaning, it would follow as an undesirable consequence (*prasajyeta*) that even a person hearing it for the first time would have a cognition of the meaning. Therefore, although in the final doctrine (*rāddhānta*) of others, human speech does not have the mandate (*niyoga*) as its primary focus, but rather has the application (*viniyoga*) as its primary focus, nevertheless, having established this...
It should be understood that this has been stated as being grounded in *niyoga*.

The possibility of other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is not the cause for dependence; for even when such [other means] exist, the Vedic application (*viniyoga*) remains independent. On this very point, he states another incidental argument: "And likewise, in the case of dependence on perception..."

Because the two types of inference have mutually dependent objects, their status as valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is lost due to this mutual dependence. He summarizes this: "Therefore, human speech—whether it contains a positive injunction or otherwise—is dependent because its activity is preceded by the desire to express what has been perceived through another means of knowledge. But because it is not so, both kinds of Vedic speech are independent; thus, [the position] is well-founded."
He concludes the subject at hand: "Therefore, even for the sake of establishing its status as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), there is no intention to express an injunction (*vidhi*).

Someone says: "It is true that [the Veda] is independent because it is not of human origin; however, that very independence is established by the fact that its subject matter is beyond the scope of other means of knowledge. Indeed, people do not compose speech to communicate an object without first having apprehended that object in their intellect."

[These are] worldly [matters]. Furthermore, an object that is not within the scope of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) cannot be inscribed in the intellect. Moreover, the tendency of words toward injunctive force (*niyoga*) is a general rule, and this cannot be denied unless there is a sublation. And since in the Veda (*āmnāya*), injunctive force is not within the scope of other means of valid cognition but is cognizable solely through verbal testimony, it follows that [the Veda] has that as its purpose.
The Veda possesses the quality of being authorless (*apauruṣeyatā*). For if it were of human origin, its primary status as having "injunction" (*niyoga*) as its meaning would be lost.
Therefore, even arguments such as its being a "sentence" (*vākyatva*) cannot prove the authorship of the Veda, as their scope is sublated by scripture (*āgama*).
Consequently, the Veda is independent (*anapekṣatā*). Furthermore, this principle does not apply to cases such as "one suffering from fever should eat wholesome food," and so forth.

Since the fact of being authored by a person (pauruṣeyatva) is clearly perceived, even the primary sense of "niyoga" (an injunction) is set aside; for, through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā), it is rendered subservient to "viniyoga" (application). If, however, the Veda were to have an objective referent (bhūtārthatā), then because it would be capable of being verified by other means of knowledge, its status as being authored by a person would be unavoidable; thus, one must exert effort to avoid such an objective referent.
It is argued that the Veda’s orientation toward action is being established;
however, that is untenable. This desire would be fulfilled if such an injunction were within the scope of the Veda, but it has been demonstrated in the *Niyogaparīkṣā* that this is not possible.

Moreover, even this person of the Upaniṣads is not within the scope of other means of valid cognition; how then can the human origin of the Upaniṣads themselves not be unavoidable? If it is argued that because another such established entity has been observed to be within the scope of other means of valid cognition, this [Upaniṣadic person] must also have that as its object by virtue of being established—then, in that case, for that which consists of action...

[Page 197] But surely, this knowledge whose object is the reality of the Self is enjoined as something entirely distinct from that which arises from verbal testimony. For the nature of Brahman is not something to be fully comprehended through verbal cognition. For verbal testimony, characterized by sentences, is the means of valid knowledge; [whereas] the meaning of words...

Furthermore, its object consists of a relational synthesis, whereas the reality of the Self (ātmatattva) is that in which the entire manifold of difference has completely subsided; how, then, could this [reality] be within its range? Therefore, a distinct kind of knowledge—one whose nature is the manifestation of the non-dual reality (advaitatattva) and in which all delineations of limitation have dissolved—is enjoined as different from verbal cognition.

This is not correct. Indeed, a portion of the fruit is not within the scope of an injunction. Furthermore, the manifestation of the reality of the Self as free from phenomenal proliferation (*niṣprapañca*) is itself the fruit; nothing other than that is desired. If it is argued that this is "liberation" (*mokṣa*), we reply that it is non-different from that [fruit]. For the manifestation of the reality of the Self as possessed of phenomenal proliferation (*saprapañca*) is transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), whereas the manifestation of the Self as free from phenomenal proliferation is liberation.

Since the effect (*kārya*) is the object of another means of knowledge, the mandate (*niyoga*) must also have that as its referent by virtue of being an effect; consequently, it would be difficult to avoid the conclusion that the Veda, which has that as its referent, is of human origin. Alternatively, if its nature were not the object of another means of knowledge, then the same would apply to the Self taught in the Upaniṣads; thus, everything is equal, except for one's own dogmatic attachment. Let this matter rest.

Thus far, it has been stated that practice consisting of hearing (*śrutamayī pratipatti*) is not to be enjoined. Now, one might object: "Granted that this [practice] is not enjoined, let it be enjoined as that which possesses direct realization (*sākṣātkāravatī*). To this, he replies: "But surely this is something entirely different..."

From the cognition arising from words, knowledge whose object is the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*) is enjoined. Why, then, does the word not have the reality of the Self as its object? To this he says: "The nature of Brahman is not something to be fully comprehended through verbal cognition," for the word, characterized by a sentence (*vākya*), is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), since a mere word is not a means of valid knowledge. Even so, what [is the case]? To this he says:

And its object consists of the relation between word-meanings; yet that relation, because it depends upon multiple meanings being related, is itself vitiated by plurality even though it is a single entity. Furthermore, the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*) is not of such a nature; as he says—the reality of the Self is that in which the entire manifold of difference has subsided. Therefore, how could [the Vedic word] be its object? He concludes: "Therefore, [it applies] to that in which all limitations have dissolved..."

It is argued that a cognition consisting of the manifestation of the non-dual reality (*advaitatattva*), which is distinct from verbal knowledge, is enjoined. He refutes this: "This is a mere fancy. Indeed, the portion that constitutes the fruit (*phalāṃśa*) is not within the scope of an injunction, as the Great Sage [Jaimini] has said: 'The desire for that [fruit] is indicated by the purpose; and the manifestation of the non-proliferated reality of the Self (*niṣprapañcātmatattva*) is itself the fruit.'"

The term "niṣprapañca" (free from conceptual proliferation) indicates the state of having all suffering completely vanished. For conceptual proliferation is indeed suffering; thus, the grasping of reality points toward its nature as bliss. This is shown by the abundance of scriptural passages regarding bliss as the very fruit [of realization].
Nothing else is sought after beyond that, because of the vanishing of suffering and the attainment of the nature of bliss.

An objection is raised: [If you say] it is liberation, for it is heard in scripture that "he does not return again. The author refutes this: No; because there is no distinction from the manifestation of the reality of the Self as devoid of phenomenal proliferation (*niṣprapañca*). He demonstrates this very lack of distinction: For transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) is indeed the manifestation of the Self with phenomenal proliferation (*saprapañca*); [liberation is] the manifestation of the Self devoid of phenomenal proliferation...

Liberation is light. Since liberation has a nature that is the opposite of *saṃsāra*, *saṃsāra* is also briefly described in order to explain its nature. Furthermore, it is not an object of worldly activity because it is already established; thus he says: "Abiding in one's own self.

For liberation is indeed abiding in one's own Self; otherwise, because it would be a product, it would not be liberation. And the cause of bondage is the manifold world of karma and so forth, which is ignorance (*avidyā*); its destruction is knowledge (*vidyā*) alone. Furthermore, if Brahman were in no way whatsoever an object of verbal cognition, how could an injunction to know it be understood? For knowledge [arises] from its object.

There is the requirement for definition (*nirūpaṇa*), and it is an established entity that defines it; furthermore, the establishment of that [definition] would have to occur in the absence of any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

If that [definition] were also not an object [of cognition], then because it is unestablished, there would be no apprehension of the specific cognition, and consequently no apprehension of the injunction (*vidhi*). On the other hand, if it is somehow an object, then there is no independence from verbal cognition (*śābdajñāna*). Moreover, [the Veda] is intent upon the necessity of performance (*kartavyatā*).

It has been stated that such a nature of the word cannot be the meaning of the scripture (*āgama*), nor can it be the object (*artha*). For comprehension is possible even through superimposition (*adhyāropa*). Therefore, the true nature of reality (*vastutattva*) is not revealed by means of entering into an injunction (*niyoga*). Indeed, it should be understood that the state of liberation (*mokṣāvasthā*) favored by others is not being rejected by this; for the reasons for rejecting that [state] are Brahman...
These have been explained in detail in the *Siddhi*. However, if there is no abiding in one's own self, but rather liberation as conceived by others, he says:

"Otherwise, because it would be an effect, there would be no liberation. Now, why does the destruction of ignorance not occur? To this he says: Ignorance is the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) consisting of karma and so forth; it is nothing else. What follows from that? That...

And that which cuts off [ignorance] is knowledge alone. Since the manifestation of the reality of the Self—which is free from conceptual proliferation—is the reality of the Self itself, and that alone is liberation, it is not an object for purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*). Regarding this very point, he states another objection: "If Brahman is not an object of verbal cognition in any way whatsoever, how can an injunction to know it be understood? Why is it not possible?"
What is the practice? To this he says: "The determination of knowledge is by means of its object. The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of a reason.
[Objection: Let it be determined by the object; what is the harm? To this he says: "And the established object determines the knowledge;
let that [object] also be established—what is the loss? To this he says: "And the establishment of that [object] is through another means of valid cognition..."

It must be accepted as an entity because of the word [denoting it]. If that [word] also lacks an object, then, due to its non-establishment, there is a non-establishment of the object; consequently, there is no comprehension of the specific cognition, and thus no comprehension of the injunction (*vidhi*).
[The opponent] objects: "But how could it have that as its object? Even if its own nature (*svarūpa*) is not within the range of the word..."

The meaning is that even so, there is the status of being an object because of its determination by way of the dissolution of the proliferation of distinctions (*bhedaprapañca*). He refutes this: "In that case, it would not be the case that [Brahman] is not determined by verbal cognition. He applies here as well the objection stated against the first position: "And because the statement has as its purpose the necessity of a realization, the 'suchness' (the specific nature) expressed as 'it must be realized as being thus' is not the meaning of the scripture."

It has been stated that "it may be so," for the meaning of a word is that which the word aims at. If [the injunction] aims at the necessity of performance (*kartavyatā*), it does not aim at the act of comprehension (*pratipatti*); this is the meaning. It might be argued as follows: since the necessity of performance is the object of comprehension, and since comprehension has the thing to be communicated as its object, the necessity of performance itself will imply both the act of comprehension and its object; and therefore—

Because the ascertainment of the reality of that which is to be understood [is required], he says: "Nor is the object the object. Why? Because understanding is possible even through superimposition (*adhyāropa*). The meaning is this: while the necessity of performing an act of understanding implies that which is to be understood, it does not imply its actual reality as such, since that which is to be understood can be established even by way of superimposition. This is the point of the refutation.

In that regard, the authority of verbal testimony is established through its independence. Therefore, it is inconsistent to claim that the sacred tradition (āmnāya) is incapable of conveying even such things as the past and so forth, which are devoid of connection to a [future] result, since it is capable of doing so by virtue of its independent authority. This would be the case if [the Veda] were restricted solely to the form of what is to be accomplished (kārya).

How then is the meaning of the Veda—namely the mantras, the explanatory passages (arthavādas), and the Upaniṣads—established? Because it is the injunction (codanā) alone that makes known objects such as the past and so forth. How so? By making known an object as something to be accomplished (kārya), it also makes known the past and so forth.

He concludes: therefore, the true nature of reality is not revealed by entering into a mandatory injunction (*niyoga*). For in that case, the word has no authority regarding the reality of the thing itself.

He concludes: thus, even when the meaning is an existing state of affairs (*bhūtārtha*), since its authority is established through independence [from other means of knowledge], there is a connection with what is to be done (*kārya*).
"The Veda is capable of making known objects such as the past and so forth, even though it is devoid of its own [direct] form.

He states that the commentator's (nibandhanakṛt) explanation of the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "For the injunction" (*codanā hi*) is inconsistent: "This is inconsistent. He then presents the commentator's explanation, which refers back to everything by means of a pronoun: "If [the Veda] has the nature of an action (*kārya*)," and so on.

If it is asked, "In that case, how is it that the mantras and arthavādas, along with the Upaniṣads, express things as they actually exist (bhūtārtha)?"—anticipating this doubt, [the author] introduces the statement, "For the Vedic injunction (codanā) indeed... He explains its meaning: because the Vedic injunction alone makes known objects such as existing entities (bhūtādi). If an object such as an existing entity is not [the domain] of the injunction, then the Vedic meaning would not consist of something to be accomplished (kāryarūpa); nor is it [the case that it is not].
Anticipating this objection, he asks: "How so? The answer is: "By making known the *kārya* (the thing to be done), it also makes known the past and so forth.
For words are of two kinds: those that denote the *kārya*, such as the optative (*liṅ*) and others; and those that denote the past and so forth, such as the imperfect (*laṅ*) and others.
Among these, the optative and its like are intent upon the *kārya* precisely because they denote the *kārya*. As for the imperfect and its like...

Because they are intent upon the effects such as the primary elements (*bhūta*), they denote [those elements] as being indeed associated with that [purpose]. Consequently, since their purport (*tātparya*) also lies in the effect, it is established that they have the effect as their purpose. And thus, even those words denoting the primary elements and so forth possess independence (*nirapekṣatva*).
As it has been said: "There is no other sense-organ whatsoever... This has also been explained: "And this [object] is not within the range of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)."

By the words "mithyā" and so forth, this is what is meant: [the Veda] is not understood through another means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*) by way of a form connected to an effect. This, however, is inconsistent; for even if it has as its object an already existing thing (*bhūtārtha*), its status as a valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇya*) is established by its independence (*anapekṣatva*). It might be argued: the relationship between word and meaning is to be understood from the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*), and that usage consists of purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*).

Furthermore, for discerning persons, activity is preceded by the comprehension of something to be accomplished (*kārya*); therefore, all words acquire their linguistic competency (*vyutpatti*) either directly with respect to the *kārya* itself or through association with it as their own meaning. Thus, we maintain that the meaning of the Veda consists solely in the form of the *kārya*, and not merely on account of its being a source of valid knowledge (*prāmāṇya*). This has also been stated: because the acquisition of linguistic competency is possible even otherwise. To explain:

Indramitra, having learned of the birth of a son—the cause of joy for Devadatta—arrived at Devadatta’s residence from the very house of Devadatta along with a messenger. After first presenting a gift of scented cloth, immediately upon the messenger’s words, “By good fortune, Devadatta, you prosper; a son has been born to you,” his cheeks bristled with horripilation and his eyes blossomed wide.
Having observed Devadatta’s face, which is like a great lotus with an exceedingly radiant pair of eyes, one infers that joy has arisen in him;
and the cause of that joy is the knowledge of the birth of a son, since no other cause is perceived at that time. [p.200] This is due to the utterance of words.

Others, however, maintain that it is the production of a continuous stream of verbal knowledge [that constitutes the result], because that has as its fruit a pure and lucid cognition in which all delineations of difference have been withdrawn. Even in this case, there is no comprehension of the nature of the Self; and since the excellence of knowledge is well known to be dependent upon practice, it does not constitute the purpose of Vedic injunction. Therefore, regarding matters whose objects are perceptible—

There are specific injunctions regarding ritual actions (*karmasu viśeṣavidhayaḥ*). However, the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*) is understood from the Upaniṣadic statement independently of other injunctions.

Enough with this protracted debate with the teachers. Furthermore, one understands that the word serves as the cause for that [realization] because of its existence immediately following [the instruction]; nor is it [the cause] for one who is incapable.

He understands the capacity [of the word]. Suspecting another cause that would produce joy in such a situation, and suspecting even his own Brahminhood due to the suspicion that he might be his mother's lover, they are not entitled to perform the rites appropriate for Brahmins;
thus, enough with their laborious study of Mīmāṃsā! Moreover, [this applies to those who are] like unrefined wood...

In the case of a statement such as "Devadatta cooks rice in a pot with wood-sticks," even though it is a description of a present action, the word-meaning and the meaning of the case-inflection already established lead one to perceive that wood is the instrument (*karaṇa*) for the act of cooking; thus, one understands that the nominal stem *kāṣṭha* (wood) has that [instrumentality] as its meaning. Therefore, it is established that the speech under dispute has as its object a meaning that is not connected to a [future] result.
Because it generates valid cognition: whatever generates valid cognition regarding a certain object has that as its domain, just as the eye and other senses have form and so forth as their objects.

Now, wishing to refute the position consisting of reflection (*cintāmayī pratipatti*), he introduces it: "Others, however, maintain that there is an injunction for the continuous production of verbal knowledge (*śābdajñāna*). And it is not the case that this [knowledge] is not enjoined simply because it is of the nature of a result."
Rather, it is the means for the fruit—the direct realization of the reality of the Self—and therefore it must be enjoined; thus he says:

"Because its fruit is pure and clear knowledge in which all delineations of difference have been withdrawn. Purity (*viśuddhi*) consists in the exclusion of doubt and the like; clarity (*viśadatā*) consists in direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*). In this regard, he first attributes the previously mentioned defect [to the opponent's position]:

In this case as well, there is no realization of the nature of the Self, because the Vedāntas are intent upon the injunction for meditative practice (*pratipatti-vidhi*). Since the clarity of consciousness regarding the object to be cultivated is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), and thus being already attained, it follows that the stream of knowledge identical to the verbal cognition—which is another name for *bhāvanā*—is not something to be enjoined. Thus he says: "The manifestation of knowledge..."
Furthermore, since the sagehood [of the ṛṣis] is renowned as being based on practice (*abhyāsa*), it is not logical that it should have the nature of a Vedic injunction (*codanā*).

Now, one might object: sentences such as "Therefore, having become calm, self-controlled, and concentrated, one should see the Self in the very Self" do indeed enjoin the vision of the Self as being endowed with qualities such as tranquility; and this would not be possible if it were not something to be enjoined.

Since qualities can be enjoined only for one who has taken the view of a self as their basis, the view of a self must also be enjoined in order to enjoin qualities such as tranquility (*śāntatā*). To this he says: "Therefore, just as there are specific injunctions regarding rituals whose purposes are perceptible, the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*) in the Upanishads is understood from a sentence that does not depend on any other injunction. This is the underlying intention here.

For injunctions regarding qualities depend upon the accomplishment of the primary action, but they do not themselves constitute that injunction. Just as, when the acquisition of wealth is already established by natural inclination (*rāga*),
