the acceptance of gifts and so forth are restricted for Brāhmaṇas and others, so too here, for one who desires to directly realize the reality of the Self— which consists of eternal bliss and is free from all connection with suffering— positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) [are required].

Or rather, let it be granted that the comprehension of the true nature of the self occurs by way of an injunction regarding the duty of practice; for it has been stated that the majority of worldly statements are merely descriptive accounts of existing facts.

But has it not been stated here that [the scripture] is useless? This [charge of futility] applies equally even to an injunction for practice (*pratipatti-vidhi*), because the cognition of an already existing fact (*bhūtārtha*) does not differ [from the cognition produced by such an injunction]. If you argue that it is precisely the cognition of the self as it truly is (*aviparītātma-pratipatti*) [that is intended], then that is equally present even at the conclusion of a narrative of an existing fact. Therefore, let it be that all speech culminates in prompting activity (*pravṛtti-paryavasāyitva*); even an existing fact [is taught] for that purpose.

It is said [that one acts] elsewhere or right there for that reason; otherwise, there would be no purpose. No, for even the cessation of curiosity is a purpose. To explain: questions regarding things that are neither to be abandoned nor acquired, and which concern distant regions, kings, or legendary deeds, are observed among those possessed of curiosity. And the knowledge of those things is intended solely for the cessation of curiosity.

For one who has understood the means of meditation and is engaged in the meditation on the Self, there is the injunction regarding [qualities] such as tranquility (*śāntatva*). Therefore, since none of the three types of practical engagement (*pratipatti*) are fit for injunction, it has been established that the Vedāntas are devoted solely to the exposition of the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*). All of this is easily understood by those who have exerted effort in the *Brahmasiddhi*.
That it must be so has not been established by us here.

Now, [the author] speaks while for the sake of argument: "Enough with this dispute with the teachers. The respect [accorded to them] is merely figurative, due to their equality with the Arhats who have attained the unsurpassed state. Let it be that the duty of practice is performed by means of the injunction (niyoga) for the sake of realizing the reality of the Self.

It has been stated that worldly statements are for the most part narratives of past events (*bhūtānvākhyāna*). Nevertheless, the reason—that there is equality even in the case of a statement that does not incite action because it is equally well-known—is established; this is the meaning. Now, one might object: "A statement is not non-inciting, since futility (*vaiyarthyam*) has been mentioned here. He refutes this: "This [futility] is equal even in the case of an injunction of comprehension (*pratipattividhi*). Why?"

Because there is no difference from the comprehension of the real object (*bhūtārtha*). If the real object is not to be expressed because of a lack of purpose, then the comprehension having that as its object must also not be enjoined. For there is no fruit other than the pervasion of that which is to be comprehended by this [comprehension]; such is the meaning. Alternatively, the purpose of the injunction for comprehension is simply the comprehension of the self as it truly is (*aviparītātmapratipatti*).

It has already been stated that this meaning does not hold under the view that [the Veda] prescribes practical action (*pratipatti-vidhi*). Having provisionally accepted that position, he states another rebuttal: "That practical action remains the same even when it culminates in the narration of what has already come to be (*bhūtākhyāna*).
Again, he objects: "In that case, let it be that all speech culminates exclusively in engagement (*pravṛtti*) and desistance (*nivṛtti*)."
An object that has already come into being is also expressed; by means of this, one may act toward something else or toward that very same thing, for otherwise there would be no purpose.

This is the underlying intention here: every word is uttered by discerning persons for the sake of another, and that other person understands only that object which they intend to understand—be it something to be abandoned, something to be accepted, or something to be disregarded.

Because [if it were otherwise], the status of being a rational agent would be contradicted in the act of communication. This is especially true in the case of the Vedic corpus, which, through the injunction for the study of one's own recitation (*svādhyāyādhyayana-vidhi*), has attained the status of being subordinate to human goals. Therefore, let the word function as a cause for the cognition of an existing state of affairs (*bhūtārtha*);
however, the word’s purpose lies in inciting activity (*pravṛtti*) or cessation (*nivṛtti*). He refutes this: "Not out of curiosity..."

Because cessation (*nivṛtti*) is also a purposeful object. He demonstrates this very point: "For instance, words concerning that which is not to be abandoned, nor to be acquired, nor distant—such as descriptions of forests and the like in the *Mahābhārata* and other works—are devoid of both engagement and cessation, and result in the mere description of what has occurred."

Forms alone are the causes of pleasure; and the descriptions of activities for the sake of generating pleasure are neither for the purpose of engaging nor desisting the listener—enough of this digression.
Just as for infants, birds, and the like, a remote sound becomes a cause [of action] through the influence of latent impressions (*bhāvanā*).
Why is it not accepted that there is likewise a corresponding knowledge of means (*upāyajñāna*) by way of engagement and withdrawal?

Furthermore, specific universals (*jāti*) and other factors serve as the awakeners of the cultivation of the knowledge of means, just as they do for the cultivation of verbal disposition (*śabdabhāvanā*).
Questions concerning regions, royal designations, conduct, and so forth are observed among those who are curious; [these lead to] the cessation of curiosity.

Furthermore, the words of those who possess such knowledge, as well as descriptions of forests and the like in the *Mahābhārata* and other works—which are devoid of any injunction to act (*pravṛtti*) or abstain from action (*nivṛtti*)—serve merely as causes for pleasure by their very form, culminating in the description of past events. And pleasant narratives are intended for the production of pleasure, not for the sake of inciting the listener to act or desist; so enough of this digression. This is the underlying intention here: that wise people...
Words do not convey a meaning solely as an object of engagement (*pravṛtti*) or withdrawal (*nivṛtti*), but rather as something possessing a purpose (*prayojanavat*).

And this purposiveness is fulfilled in some cases by engagement and withdrawal occurring at a time subsequent to the cognition of the nature of the object, while in other cases it is fulfilled by the mere cognition of the nature of the object itself. As it has been said: "Because even the cessation of curiosity is a purpose. Thus...

It is not tenable to claim that the Upaniṣads do not have the purpose of [enjoining] engagement or withdrawal, on the grounds that the nature of Brahman—which is free from evil and whose knowledge is derived from the Upaniṣads—is itself the human goal, and thus there is no contradiction with the injunction for Vedic study (*svādhyāya-vidhi*). Therefore, it is established that [the object of comparison] which is connected to the means of action is "equal" (*samā*) in another respect; hence, it is not the support (*ālambana*) of the mental intuition (*pratibhā*), nor is it without a support.
This is not so; by process of elimination, it has as its object the state of being a means to one's welfare (*hitopāyatā*).

As for what was stated—that because of the specific tones and the specific substrata, and because infants, birds, and others follow the existence of preceding sounds, their intuition (*pratibhā*) is the cause of activity through the operation of remote sounds rather than through knowledge of a means—[that is refuted].

To this he replies: Just as for infants, birds, and the like, a remote sound serves as the cause for intuition (*pratibhā*) through the influence of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), why is it not accepted that such knowledge of the means (*upāyajñāna*) itself—by way of the influence of mental cultivation—is the basis for engagement and desistance? What is the need for a remote word, since it is the knowledge of the means alone that functions as the cause of engagement?
This is because it is established by one's own direct experience; how this is so will be explained further below. If it should be thought:

"If cultivation produced by the knowledge of the means is the cause of activity, then why does activity not occur even in a person who has previously experienced the birth of a bird [through such cultivation]? To this he says: "And due to the specific nature of the species (*jāti-viśeṣa*), etc."

The awakening factors for the cultivation of the knowledge of means are like those for the cultivation of verbal intention (*śabdabhāvanā*). Now, why is it that the cultivation of verbal intention is not likewise [awakened]? If you argue that it is due to a specific genus (*jāti*) or unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), the meaning is that this applies equally to the cultivation of the knowledge of means as well.
[Page 203] But surely, since the object of intuition (*pratibhā*) is not established by way of its own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*), it must be defined solely through the form of verbal cognition;
yet no present word exists. Therefore, mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) must be resorted to as its basis. This is not sound.

For non-origination is said to apply to the mental image (*pratibhā*) because its objective support (*ālambana*) does not exist as a present entity, or because it is a single essence resulting from a collection of multiple objects. This same [non-origination] applies equally to the word (*śabda*) as well; for that too, being a collection of past phonemes (*varṇa*), does not exist as a single unity. This is because it has been stated that there is an absence of perception of difference and a perception of non-difference.

Here, an objection is raised: "Surely, since the specific action—which is the means for achieving the desired goal and which constitutes the objective support of the intuition—is not established in its own nature, it cannot be that objective support. Furthermore, you yourself have stated that there can be no cognition without an objective support;
therefore, [the intuition] must be defined solely by the form of the verbal cognition. Moreover, this is not the case for newborn infants, birds, and the like."

The word exists; therefore, the *apūrva* (unprecedented) verbal *bhāvanā* must necessarily be resorted to. He refutes this: "This is not sound, because the alternatives are untenable. Therein, he first sets forth the alternatives: "Is the non-actualization [of the object] asserted on account of its being non-present, or on account of the synthesis of multiple objects, or on account of the unity of nature of the mental image (*pratibhā*)? [If it is the latter,] it has a present object..."

Indeed, the knowledge of means (*upāyajñāna*) does not function [with respect to the future], because its object has already come into being; therefore, it must be admitted that its object is the future. And thus, there is the non-establishment of the reality of the object of intuition (*pratibhā*). Alternatively, since the object of intuition consists of the synthesis of word-meanings (*padārtha-saṃsarga*), and since such a synthesis as a single entity is impossible, it must consist of multiple meanings whose actions and factors of action (*kriyā-kāraka*) are mutually distinct.

Because it is a mere collection (*samāhāra*). Furthermore, that which consists of multiple natures cannot be one, for that would entail the absurd consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even multiple things are one. And thus, there is no conjunction (*saṃsarga*). If there is multiplicity, then there are only the conjuncts; and thus, as before, there is no conjunction—the meaning is that the result is absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*). He states that both of these [objections] apply equally to the opponent’s position: "In the case of the word (*śabda*) as well, this [is the same]."

It is equal [to the objection]. For that [cognition] as well, being composed of a collection of phonemes (*varṇa*), does not exist as a single entity. Anticipating the objection that "the word-sound (*śabda*) accepted by others is the *sphoṭa*, which is distinct from the phonemes and is unitary;
therefore, it is appropriate as the objective support (*ālambana*) of the intuition," [the author] sets forth the arguments intended to refute the *sphoṭa*.

He cites the words of the Bhāṣya as if they were established facts: "Because of the absence of the perception of difference and because of the perception of non-difference," so it was stated by the author of the Bhāṣya. "Difference" (*bheda*) refers to the *sphoṭa*, which is said to be distinct from the phonemes (*varṇa*). [The phrase means] "due to the absence of the perception of that," i.e., due to the absence of the perception of difference. It is never the case that, even in the fourth cognition such as "cow" (*gauḥ*), there is an experience of a sequence of differences, as there is in the case of the phonemes.

"In a cognition that penetrates three phonemes joined together (*praśliṣṭa-varṇa*), something else appears distinct from the phonemes. If it is argued that—even though the phonemes [remain the same] in the case of *jarā* and *rāja*—there is a difference in the cognition of the meaning, and therefore there must be a denoter other than the phonemes, and that is the *sphoṭa*, to this he replies:
"And because no difference is perceived. The term *bheda* means those things which are differentiated; *abheda* means non-differentiation. Of those [phonemes],..."

Because of perception. This is what is meant: it is not the case that, in the two cognitions of "jarā" and "rāja," there appear two denoters distinct from the phonemes (varṇas) and mutually different; rather, those very same phonemes appear as having different sequential orders due to the differences in the latent impressions (saṃskāra) deposited by experience, and they will produce the difference in the cognition of the sphoṭa. This must necessarily be admitted...

Since this is something that ought to be done, even for those who maintain that words are partless, the distinction between mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) has been indicated here merely by way of direction; thus, the opinion of the Teacher has been briefly pointed out by us who do not follow it.

[Objection: In cases of this kind, you have indeed accepted that the cognition of an undifferentiated entity consists of a single word-essence; for in the case of non-entities—such as conjunction (*saṃsarga*), a collection (*samūha*), or absolute non-existence (*atyantāsadbhāva*)—or even in the case of related entities that are themselves manifold, the appearance of a single entity is not possible without the mediation of a single word-essence, whether by way of its proximity, its transformation (*pariṇāma*), or its manifestation (*vivarta*). [Reply: No, because it is established otherwise.
Again, the opponent objects from another perspective:

"Indeed, the wise have arrived at the very same kind of non-dual reality as being of the nature of a single word, namely *buddhi*. For instance, in the case of related entities such as action and its factors (*kriyākāraka*), quality and its possessor (*guṇaguṇin*), or purpose and its object (*prayojanaprayojin*), or in the case of collections such as the *śiṃśapā*, *aśoka*, and *kiṃśuka* trees, there is a relation or a collection."

A single entity that is a real thing (vastubhūta) appears, or rather, non-entities such as a hare’s horn or a fire-brand circle (ālātacakra) appear; yet, in the case of such things, the single cognition and the cognition of a real thing both rely solely upon a single, partless essence consisting of the word. Now, why are conjunction (saṃsarga) and the like, or those possessing them, not the objective support (ālambana) of this single cognition and cognition of a real thing?

To this he says: For indeed, among non-entities such as conjunction (*saṃsarga*), aggregates (*samūha*), or absolutely non-existent things (*atyantāsadbhūta*), or among various distinct entities, the appearance of a single entity is not possible. This is because conjunction and the like cannot possibly exist as ultimate realities (*paramārthasat*). To demonstrate this, there is the following reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅgasādhana*): whatever subsists in many [loci] is manifold, just as palm fruits contained in separate vessels.

Furthermore, the fact that [the universal] subsists in many instances (*anekavṛtti*) is accepted by the opponent; thus, this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). Since there is an absence of multiplicity, there is an absence of subsistence in many instances; this is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*), which is the contrapositive of the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Nor should it be argued that the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is doubtful because there is no contradiction between unity and subsistence in many instances, for such a lack of contradiction is unestablished. Thus:

For indeed, existence is pervaded by the absence of its contradictory; and here, that which is contradictory to it—the contradictory—is perceived through the perception of the contradiction of the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*), thereby negating actual unity. Thus, due to the absence of unity, there is no relation for those very things that are related.
For when one related thing is being delimited, the absence of that [other] is excluded.

And other related entities (saṃsargin) possess that absence; thus they too are excluded. Otherwise, this related entity would not be determinable. Likewise, when the nature of the relation within its connection to that [entity] is being determined, the absence of the nature of that related entity must be excluded. And those other related entities possess that absence.

Those things which possess the nature of a relation must also be excluded. If they were not excluded, it would result in a contradiction: that very same thing would be both that nature and not that nature. This is the superimposition of contradictory properties characterized by being in that location and not being in that location. Thus it is said: "The nature [of a thing] is delimited by its association with a single [entity] restricted to specific place, time, and state..."

Because there is no internal separation, a single entity that possesses multiple occurrences would possess the specific qualities of those locations and so forth; thus, there would be a conjunction with another.

Now, if when one related object is perceived, the relation residing therein were also perceived—since it exists in other related objects by that very same nature—then those others too ought to be perceived. Yet they are not perceived. Thus [it is concluded].
Even the relation itself would not be apprehended; thus, there is this contradiction characterized by both apprehension and non-apprehension.

Furthermore, does the relation, subsisting in various related entities, subsist part by part or in its entirety? It cannot subsist part by part, because [the relation] is partless. Or, if it were to have parts, it would lead to an infinite regress. Nor can it subsist in its entirety, because [it could not then exist] in another relation.

Because that would entail the consequence of their non-existence, and there is no other alternative; for the relation between one of those two when the other is negated is the definition of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), wherein the action is primary and the factors of action (*kāraka*) are subordinate, and the relations have unequal degrees of predominance.
Because it is not invariably concomitant [with its parts]. Therefore, neither the composite whole (*saṃsarga*) nor the collection (*samūha*) exists as ultimate reality (*paramārthasat*).

By this, one should understand that the "whole" (*avayavin*), "generality" (*sāmānya*), and so forth are likewise refuted. The intention is that the non-existence of things such as a rabbit’s horn is even more well-established.
And this mode of sublation, such as through conjunction and so forth, does not exist in the case of a partless word; thus he says: "Without one [of the following]:

proximity, transformation, or manifestation of the nature of the Word-sound. Proximity (*pratyāsa*) means superimposition (*adhyāsa*). For example, in the case of a large crystal gem which is actually clear and white, but whose whiteness is obscured by the pouring of lac-dye.

Due to its extreme subtlety, the substance characterized as lac is not perceived; thus, the cognition that "the crystal gem is red" through the superimposition (āropa) of the qualities of lac is *adhyāsa*. Similarly, among various word-meanings whose distinctions have been obscured, one's true unity—which is of the nature of the *sphoṭa*—is superimposed, resulting in the notion that "the sentence-meaning is a single entity consisting of a relation. And regarding the members of a collection, such as *kiṃśuka* flowers...

Furthermore, when distinctions have been set aside among various things, the cognition of unity arises by superimposing a real unity upon the word "forest" or "collection. Similarly, in the case of non-existent things such as a hare's horn, there is a cognition through the superimposition of existence belonging to the word "hare's horn" and so forth; this is the meaning of the term *pratyāsatti* (proximity). Transformation (*pariṇāma*) is also like this: just as a single essence of gold...
Just as gold transforms into various forms such as bracelets, crowns, earrings, and rings, so too does the essence of sound (śabdatattva) manifest in the form of diverse objects.

And in this view, the distinctions—which are in some way different from the essence of words—possess ultimate reality. This position is presented merely for the sake of its manifestation; however, it is actually a *vivarta* (illusory appearance).

Just as a single face, appearing in various jewels, swords, mirrors, and so forth— which are all real objects— shines forth assuming their respective reflections with diverse colors, dimensions, and locations, yet there do not exist in reality multiple faces with different colors, dimensions, and locations; even so, by virtue of the influence of the substrate of beginningless ignorance (*avidyā-vāsanā*), the single reality of the Word (*pada-tattva*) appears as manifold.

It manifests as the nature of the word-meanings, but word-meanings do not exist in ultimate reality as entities distinct from it. These—namely, *pratyaya* (implication), *pariṇāma* (transformation), and *vivarta* (illusory manifestation)—are to be understood according to different philosophical views.
He refutes this: No, because [the meaning] is established otherwise. He states that very point: first of all, the sentence-meaning is a relation (*saṃsarga*).

The definition [of difference] is that which has action as its subordinate element, the agent as its subordinate element, and the action as its primary element, and which relates to things whose primary status is not equal. Herein lies the underlying intention:

as for what was stated—that plurality arises because [a property] occurs in many [substrata]—that is incorrect, because since the occurrence in many substrata can coexist even with unity, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is doubtful; thus, the logical connection (*pratibandha*) with plurality is unestablished. It is not [the case that plurality follows from multiple occurrences].

Furthermore, for a single entity existing in various locations, there arises a contradiction characterized by occupying that location and not occupying that location; yet this is possible because they occur simultaneously.
This is logical: when an entity is being delimited, its absence is excluded, because entities consist in the exclusion of their own absence;
for if that were not excluded, the delimitation of the entity would be impossible. Thus, existence...

Because the exclusion of its absence consists in the nature of delimitation (*pariccheda*). Now, why is another relation excluded? If you say, "Because it possesses that absence," then from what does that [absence] follow? From the fact that it does not appear as identical (*tādātmya*) with it through perception; otherwise, like one related thing, another relation would also be manifested. As he said regarding its delimitation...

[Page 206] The proposition excludes that which is other than those [entities]. Therefore, it is precisely those things whose nature consists in mutual non-existence that are never perceived as intermingled by direct perception. Furthermore, this "conjunction" (saṃsarga) is manifold.
Being non-different from the associated [factors], it does not encounter contradiction through perception.
It might be argued: "This association is indeed a buyer who pays no price, since it neither deposits its form into cognitions nor yet wishes to accept perceptibility. That is incorrect.

Because by establishing that even blue and other objects are cognizable by a formless consciousness (*nirākāra-vijñāna*), there would follow the absurd consequence that they are non-existent, as one would be buying them at a price not paid for their value. Furthermore, that which possesses relations is not capable of knowing the relation itself;
nor is this [relation] non-different from the relata, because it is the locus of contradictory properties. Indeed, while these relata are mutually distinct...

That which persists while others persist, yet ceases when they cease, must be identical with them; for otherwise, it would follow that the three worlds are one. Therefore, let there be a contradiction between its being in that place and its absence from it;
however, there can be no contradiction between its being in that place and its not being in that place. For contradiction is not understood merely from the use of the negative particle (*nañ*). Mā...
"Having a son" and "being sonless"—this diversity exists even for a single son.

This might be the case: by the very same nature through which the relation subsists in one related object, does it subsist in another related object as well, or rather by a different nature? It cannot be by a different nature.

Because if there were a difference in the produced [effect] by way of its own nature, it would follow that there is a difference in the entities themselves. And if it were by that very same [nature], it would follow that the associated factors are absolutely non-different.

To this, it must be said: Now, by which nature does form produce another form as its effect—is it by that same nature [as it produces] its own objective consciousness, or by a different nature? This is exactly the same [dilemma]. If it should be argued:

Neither essence (*svabhāva*) nor capacity (*sāmarthya*) exceeds the form (*rūpa*); rather, that very [form], whose birth depends upon its own conditions, being perceived by direct perception as a single entity that produces both [effects] while possessing differentiation, cannot admit of division. Nor does the non-difference of the cause necessitate the non-difference of the effect, because they are distinct. So then, is there not one [entity] among various things that are conjoined?
A relation is perceived through direct perception as belonging to things that are not related by nature, whereby they would become non-different from it due to their non-difference from it.

If you argue that the causal relation is merely dependent origination and not something real (bhāvika) residing in both [cause and effect], and therefore the non-difference of the effect does not follow even when the other cause is non-different; well then, how can there be a relation with those things that are related?

Since even for this [color], there is no further connection with anything else, there is no non-difference among the related things despite the non-difference of that [color], because they are distinct.

If it is asked, "How can that which is a lack of relation be a relation for those very things?"—then [we reply]: if there were no relation, why would cognition arise only upon perceiving color within the consciousness of color, and not also with respect to taste and so forth? It is because of the difference in their intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*).

If [it is argued that there is contradiction], that is equal here as well. Therefore, since contradiction is not established, and because the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is doubtful, the fact of residing in many is not a valid means of proving plurality. Furthermore, a contradiction characterized by apprehension and non-apprehension is not possible in the case of a composite whole (*saṃsarga*), because that [whole], whose definition depends upon the apprehension of all its constituent correlates (*saṃsargin*), is apprehended precisely when they are apprehended.

Even a collection cannot exist without a single unifying cause for the existence of those things that constitute the collection; in that regard, the single manifestation serves as its limiting condition (*upādhi*). Even such things as a hare’s horn, when conceptualized in the form of an object perceived in other classes of entities, [function in this manner].

Or, if that [universal] were grasped, it would be grasped in its entirety; thus, the alternative of partiality—characterized by completeness (*sākalya*) or deficiency (*vaikalya*)—has no place here. For completeness and deficiency can belong to a plurality of things that are inherent in their effects, but they are not possible in a non-different reality.
Therefore, we can only say that inherence exists in its own nature among the related entities, but we cannot further [assert]...

Regarding the phrase "by way of both the whole and the parts": by this, the composite aggregate (*samūha*) has been explained, and certain reasons for refuting the whole (*avayavin*) and the universal (*sāmānya*) have been rejected; however, not all such reasons are addressed here for fear of prolixity.
Thus, in this manner, the perceptual relation between a quality and its possessor, or between a genus and its bearer, is a single relation that resides in both relata.

The relationship between action and its factors (*kriyākāraka*), or between substance and its parts (*avayavāvayavin*), is established by experience; it does not deserve to be rejected as long as there is no subverting evidence (*bādhaka*). As for the definition of sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*)—such as "Devadatta cooks rice in a pot"—although the two correlates (*pratisaṃsargin*) differ, nevertheless, because the factors of action exist for the sake of the action, that action is primary.

Because the sentence-meaning is a single entity, its primary constituent—the relation—is also said to be one. Furthermore, even though the sentence has as its purpose an action colored by various *kārakas*, since the mere individual word-meanings are obtained from other sources, the sentence-meaning is the relation itself, determined by the distinction between what is already obtained and what is not. This is what was stated: "the action is primary, with the *kārakas* being subordinate. Where, then, [is this not the case]?
Two actions are perceived, as in the case of "the hero among heroes, relying on the strength of his own arms, conquers":

how then can there be unity of meaning for the sentence? To this he says: *atulyapradhānasaṃsargī*. That which has an unequal primary [action] as its correlate is so described. This is what is meant: it is not merely the action that [is the factor].

Furthermore, the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*) is indeed the primary element. For one who desires victory and is a preeminent hero, the action based on the strength of his own arm is not the sentence-meaning because it is subordinate; rather, the act of victory itself is so [the sentence-meaning] due to its primacy.
He establishes the nature of a collection (*samūha*): even a collection does not exist without a single constituent member that serves as the cause for the cognition of that [collection].

Indeed, the *kiṃśuka* trees and others, which occupy the same place and time, are designated as a "collection" (*samūha*) or a "forest" (*vana*). Therefore, that [designation] also does not exist without a single place and time belonging to the members of the collection, which serves as the cause for the state of being a collection. In that regard, among the members of the collection, there is that limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), namely the limiting adjunct of a single place and time.

The meaning is that "illumination" (*prakāśa*) has a single object as its content. Even things such as a hare’s horn, when conceptualized and superimposed in the form of an object—a horn—observed in other classes of beings such as cows, appear as having the nature of a real entity. Therefore, since [the appearance] is established even otherwise, the appearance of a single cognition regarding relations and the like does not constitute [proof of] oneness.

The conceptualization of proximity to the nature of the word is logical. Furthermore, otherwise, if one were to postulate non-difference among distinct things based on their proximity to a single word-nature, then even in multiple locations conveyed by a single sentence, there would be unity. For example, from the single sentence "The white one runs," two meanings are understood: that it is a dog (*kauleyaka*) that is running, and that it is something white that is moving.
"It goes swiftly from here"— the meaning is that these two meanings, which are understood through a single sentence, should appear as if they were non-different due to their close proximity.
[Words] manifest as having the nature of their objects; otherwise, there would be no unity of sentence (*ekavākyatā*) in that which is understood from a single sentence.

Nor is there a difference of words therein, because there is no difference in form. If it is argued that "the difference [of words] arises from the difference of meaning," how could what is perceived in one way be otherwise?
If it is argued that "[the difference of words follows] from the inference of a difference of meaning," then the difference and non-difference of meaning must first be apprehended.
Since the difference or non-difference of words occurs only subsequently, the appearance of oneness among objects is not caused by the proximity of words.

Furthermore, there would be no distinction between a collection and a single word. Moreover, for one who is unaware of the word "collection," that appearance does not arise from afar. [Objection: But even here, there is a difference of words for each individual object. To this he replies: "And there is no difference of words therein; why?"

Because there is no difference in form (*rūpa*). For we do not perceive any differentiator of the sentence's own nature (*vākya-svarūpa*) in its being washed or its being understood. He objects: "If it is argued that there is a difference because of a difference in meaning (*artha-bheda*. The reply: "How otherwise could that which is perceived as one be otherwise manifold? He objects again: "If it is argued that it is due to the inference of a difference in meaning. Just as [it is] for a knower...
Even though [the sound] is perceived as stable by means of perception or inference, it is nonetheless determined to be subject to extremely rapid destruction;
likewise, even though a sentence is understood through perception to be a single unity, it is determined to be manifold due to the difference in its meanings. He refutes this:
"In that case, the difference or non-difference of the meaning would be apprehended first, and only afterwards the difference or non-difference of the word; thus, the cognition of the word..."

The appearance of unity among objects is due to the mark of similarity (*sādṛśyanimitta*). Indeed, an object whose internal differences have not been grasped appears as non-different because of the superimposition of non-difference residing in the word. For once the nature of mother-of-pearl is perceived, the superimposition of silver never occurs.

If the difference between objects were previously grasped independently of the difference or non-difference of words, then it would not be possible for the non-difference of the object to reside in the word.
The meaning is "superimposition" (*samāropa*). He states another defect: "There would be no distinction between a collection and a single word.

If, through the superimposition of oneness onto a word, diverse objects are understood as one, then just as in the case of "one space," the oneness of that which is non-different is understood as being non-contingent (*anaupādhika*), so too in the case of "a collection," it would not be understood as depending upon limiting conditions (*upādhi*).

Furthermore, if there were dependence upon a substrate (*upādhi*), even the notion that "space is one" would not be understood in its pure form; thus, the consequence of non-distinction (*aviśeṣa*) follows.

In some readings, it is stated: "there is no distinction between the word for a collection and the word for a single entity. Its meaning is as follows: just as in the case of "a collection of many *dhava* trees and so forth," a unity based on the single word appears, so too in the case of "trees" (*vṛkṣāḥ*), [unity would likewise appear].

Oneness would appear [in that case], but this is not so. Furthermore, if oneness were produced by the proximity of words, then one who has not learned the specific word [for it] would not perceive the object as one through its form alone; thus he says: "And for one who does not know the collective word for it, the appearance of that [oneness] would not be far off. Moreover, [it is said]: "In the case of non-existence, there is no word."

Through the cognition of the word "non-existence" (abhāva) as a positive entity (bhāva), there is a loss of the intended meaning. For if there is a superimposition of a word, the word "non-existence" itself must be superimposed and cognized; yet that [word] is a positive entity (bhāva).

Thus, there is indeed a loss of the intended meaning, for the sense would be "not a word" while it is actually "a word. These same defects should also be applied to the theories of illusory transformation (vivarta) and material transformation (pariṇāma).

He states that this is an even greater defect regarding both transformation (*pariṇāma*) and illusory manifestation (*vivarta*): "But in the case of manifestation and transformation, because everything is one, there can be no intermediate unity that could serve as the basis for the word 'one'. For those who maintain the superimposition of words that are mutually distinct, an intermediate unity such as "cow" or "horse" would indeed be possible.

Furthermore, for those who assert that an object is either an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) or a transformation (*pariṇāma*) of the undivided *śabdabrahman*, this [fault] would apply in all cases.

Moreover, in the case of the expression "the word is non-existent" (*abhāve śabdaḥ*), since there is the cognition of a positive word (*bhāva-śabda*), the intended meaning is lost. This applies to the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivarta*).

Since everything that is a transformation (*pariṇāma*) is one, intermediate unity cannot be the referent of the word "one. Furthermore, there would be no distinction between reality (*vastu*) and unreality (*avastu*). If it is argued that even though the linguistic transformation (*śabdavivarta*) is equal [in all cases], this distinction is based on something else—that is not so; it is indeed based on the linguistic transformation. For in the case of a hare's horn, a fire-brand circle (*alātacakra*), and the like, there is no determination of a real objective form.

And since this has already been extensively refuted in many ways by our own colleagues, enough with this digression. Therefore, being the means to what is desired is the cause for the agent’s engagement.
Now, one might object: "One engages because of the understanding that something ought to be done; let that [obligatoriness] itself be the cause. But what, then, is this [obligatoriness]?

It is simply that which ought to be done (*kartavyatā*). By what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is this understood? It is not perceived directly by the senses. The meaning is: since there is no distinction from the *śabdabrahman* (the Word-Brahman), how could there be any internal unity among word-meanings or sentence-meanings? Furthermore, the distinction between the real and the unreal would not exist; for in this view, there is no such object of knowledge (*prameya*).

The meaning is that whatever is either an evolution (*pariṇāma*) or an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) of the Word-Brahman (*śabda-brahman*), all such things are indeed existent; thus, there is no object of cognition (*prameya*) that is non-existent. Here, an objection is raised: "Even though the illusory manifestation of the word is equal [in nature], this distinction is based on the variety of impressions (*vāsanā*) from beginningless ignorance (*anādy-avidyā*). The reply is: "No, it is not based on the illusory manifestation of the word."
This is the intended meaning: that which is established by experience cannot be said to be based on beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyā*) when there is no subverting evidence (*bādhaka*).

For if it were so, the same consequence would apply even to the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*). Moreover, since [the world] is a transformation (*vivarta*) of that [Word-Brahman], it is impossible for it to have the nature of negation (*niṣedhātmatva*). Therefore, it is logical that [the world] is indeed ultimately real (*pāramārthika*). As it has been said:

The proponent of logic (nyāyavādī) maintains that what is apprehended as "existent" is reality (tattva), being such as it is and non-erroneous. Now, let it be granted that there is a real distinction between existence and non-existence; however, from where does the mutual distinction among various absences arise, given that their specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) have not been apprehended? To this, he says: [there is a distinction] in the case of things such as a rabbit's horn or a fire-brand circle (alātacakra), which possess the form of an entity...

"Ascertainment" (*nirūpaṇā*); "division" (*vibhāga*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. Although there is no difference in intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) among non-entities such as a rabbit's horn or a fire-brand circle, nevertheless, because the ascertainment of entities depends upon their delimiting conditions (*avacchedaka*), and because there is a difference in the intrinsic nature of those [delimiting] entities, the meaning is that there is also a mutual division among non-entities by virtue of those [entities] as their limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). This is the effort toward the refutation of the nature of the *sphoṭa*.

He states the reason regarding the nature [of the object]: "In this matter, much has indeed already been exerted by our own colleagues, beginning with the authors of the Bhāṣya and the Vārttika"; therefore, enough of this digression.
He concludes the subject at hand: "Therefore, being the means to what is desired is the cause of the agent's activity. Thus.

Once the partial proponent of the prima facie view has been refuted, the supreme proponent of the prima facie view now says: "Surely one proceeds to action because of the cognition of what is to be done (*kartavyatā*); let that very thing be [the object of the injunction]. He refutes this: "But what is this 'to-be-done-ness'? It cannot be a cognition without an objective basis, nor is it intended by you [proponents of the prima facie view] to be the state of being a means to the highest good (*śreyas-sādhanatā*). This is the sense. The response of the proponent of the prima facie view is as follows:

It is precisely the state of being an obligation (*kartavyatā*). Whatever appearance a cognition has, that is its objective support (*ālambana*); and since the comprehension of an obligation is itself an "appearance as an obligation," the meaning is that the state of being an obligation alone is its objective support. The proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntin*) asks: by what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is it comprehended? For the comprehension of an obligation is the effect of a means of valid cognition; in the absence of a cause, namely a means of valid cognition, [it cannot arise].

The meaning is that it ought to exist. He himself states this in a single continuous passage: "It is not perceived by the senses. [Objection: But surely it is not perceived by the others because it is imperceptible (*amūrtatva*). [Reply: True; [it is not perceived] by those [senses] other than the auditory organ. [Objection: But even sound, in relation to consciousness...

It depends upon the accomplishment of the capacity [of the word]. But surely this must be by necessity, since that [capacity] is possible even in the case of a word. [Objection: Would this not result in a circular argument? [Reply: No, because the mental disposition (*bhāvanā*) toward the word is beginningless. Indeed, a word, being remote, does not directly manifest the intuition of what is to be done (*kartavyatā*); rather, it does so through the mediation of the mental disposition. In that regard:

The cognition of a presently occurring word is not difficult to achieve through the realization of the process of verbal cultivation (*bhāvanā*) regarding a remote object, which is inferred by the arising of activity in another person toward what is to be done. And it has been said:
"Whether produced directly by the word or by means of the subsequent cultivation (*bhāvanā*)."
No one can overstep that which constitutes the manner of action.
The sense organs do not function [in this regard]; why, then, should the sphere of inference and the other means of knowledge not be made the object of "what is to be done" (*kartavyatā*)?

To this he says: "Because it is preceded by that, it is not by the others. For inference and the rest are preceded by perception, since they are its effects; therefore, they do not function when perception is absent—this is the meaning. The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) says: True, it is not something beyond verbal testimony (*śabda*).

It is understood [as such]. However, by the word "to be performed" (kartavyatā), it will be understood as that which is to be accomplished; this is the meaning. The proponent of the established conclusion (siddhāntin) says: But even the word, because it depends upon consciousness and depends upon the knowledge of the relationship [between word and meaning], is not perceived by one hearing it for the first time; thus, it requires the establishment of the other, namely, the establishment of the "to-be-performed" status by the other [means of knowledge]. The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) replies: But surely, by necessity, [it is known] from another means of valid cognition alone.
It requires the establishment of the meaning. Why? Because even when [the meaning] is established through the word, that possibility exists, since the knowledge of the relationship is possible.

The proponent (siddhāntin) says: "But then there would be a mutual dependence (itaretarāśraya): if the meaning is established through the word, there is knowledge of the relationship; and if there is knowledge of the relationship, the meaning is established through the word. The opponent (pūrvapakṣin) replies: "Because it is beginningless (anāditva)."

Regarding the cultivation of the word (*śabdabhāvanā*): just as in the case of a sprout from a seed and a seed from a sprout, although the types (*jāti*) of seed and sprout are mutually dependent, their distinction is established due to the difference between individual instances (*vyakti*). For it is not the case that the very same seed-instance from which a particular sprout-instance arises is itself produced from that same sprout-instance; rather, [the seed arises] from another instance belonging to that same class (*tajjātīya*).

Of another; and this [present] birth of hers is held to be from that other. Therefore, where there is mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*), there is no relationship of producer and produced (*janyajanakabhāva*); and where that relationship exists, there is no mutual dependence. Likewise here as well, through the cessation of the activity of words, the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) belonging to a previous life [is established]; and of that [cultivation], in this present birth—

The operation of a word occurs when its relationship [to the object] is known upon the comprehension of what is to be done (*kartavyatā*); from that, there follows the comprehension of what is to be done through the presently occurring word; and from that, the productive urge (*bhāvanā*). Thus, this cycle—consisting of the operation of the word, the comprehension of what is to be done, and the productive urge—revolves incessantly; therefore, there is no fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*).

Now, what is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*)? To this he says: Indeed, a word does not manifest the appearance of "what is to be done" (*kartavyatā*) directly, because it is remote; rather, it does so by way of meditative cultivation.
And this being the case, even though the nature of "what is to be done" is cognizable solely through the word, its realization is not difficult to achieve; thus he says:

In that regard, since the accomplishment of the means for distant cultivation is established, there is the cognition— that is, the knowledge— of a presently occurring, manifest word, which is not difficult [to attain] through the inference of a conviction induced by the production of activity in another, based on one’s own knowledge regarding the necessity of action as its cause. And it has been said:

"Whether produced by the direct word itself or through the accompaniment of the mental impression (*bhāvanā*), no one can overstep that which constitutes the 'manner of performance' (*itikartavyatā*).

Activity arises solely from the comprehension of what ought to be done (*kartavyatā*), not from the fact that something is a means to a desired end (*īpsitopāyatā*). For otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of non-activity even regarding obligatory rites (*nitya*). Alternatively, if they were means to a desired end, their obligatory nature (*nityatva*) would be contradicted.
It is replied:

The usage of words preceded by [the cognition of] prior [words], which does not depend upon [further] etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*), would be the specific cause; but what is the seed for the hearing of the meaning? Furthermore, what is this "word-potentiality" (*śabdabhāvanā*)? Is it the seed of the knowledge of a word that has the word as its object, or is it the word itself?

It is the seed for the knowledge of the meaning expressed by the word. If it were the object of the word itself, there would be an inconsistency with those very words from a previous birth whose impressions and memories have not perished; furthermore, linguistic proficiency (*vyutpatti*) would not be required in that case. If it is "that which is expressed by the word," even so, if the former [case] holds true, the same objection remains. Now, suppose this [latter case] is indeed the one. What is the distinction?

The reason must be stated: why it is this very exposition of meaning that is effective among those who are equal in their proficiency regarding the conditions, their practice, and their respect for the subject matter of the relationship between words and meanings. Furthermore, this [efficacy] must necessarily be accepted by the proponents of the Veda, and not merely as a means of proving a desired conclusion, because [the latter] is not all-pervasive; thus he says: "Activity proceeds from the mere understanding of what ought to be done; it does not proceed from a desire for a result."
[Otherwise,] there would be the undesirable consequence of [the injunction] not applying even to eternal things. Now, why is it that an eternal thing cannot be a means to what is desired?
To this he says: "Or, if an eternal thing were a means to what is desired, it would follow that it is non-eternal.

This is because, by virtue of being something to be desired, it would be dependent upon human will, and thus its status as something that must necessarily be performed would be untenable. He refutes this as follows:
It is said:
"The usage of previous words and the independence from etymological derivation may serve as specific reasons; but what is the seed for [the understanding of] meaning in the Veda?"

It was stated [previously] that [the injunction functions] "by means of following through with cultivation" (*bhāvanā*). In that regard, he analyzes this cultivation: what, then, is this "cultivation of the word"?

Is it a seed for the knowledge of the denotative power of the word—that is, having the word as its object and being qualified by the property of denotation—or is it a seed for the knowledge of the object expressed by the word? Or is it the instrument (*karaṇa*) which is the seed for the mere knowledge of what is to be done (*kartavyatā*)?

Because the meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and the consciousness (*vijñāna*) stand in a cause-and-effect relationship, they must have the same object. Regarding this, he speaks with reference to the first alternative: "If [the object] were sound, there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) from those very sounds belonging to a previous birth whose memory-impressions (*smṛti-saṃskāra*) have not perished. The meaning is that the impression which generates memory is not [a residual force] such as momentum (*vega*), and so forth. And that...

Furthermore, the etymological derivation that "a word is remembered as a denoter" would not be required; consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that even a person hearing a word for the first time would have a cognition of its meaning. This is what was stated: "There would be usage by means of previous words and no dependence upon etymological derivation. He raises another alternative: "If [the cognition] has as its object the meaning denoted by the word, let it be so; nevertheless..."

If it is argued that there is also a mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) whose object is the denotative word, then the same objection applies to that [cultivation] as well when it exists. Alternatively, if it is claimed that the mental cultivation has only the object as its domain and not the preceding word as its domain—the reply is: a specific reason must be stated for why, among the word, the object, and their relationship—which are equal in terms of the clarity of cognition, repetition, and attention—it is only the object that possesses the mental cultivation.

The seed consists of the intensity of the cognition and so forth, but not of the word or its connection [with the object]. There are three causes for cultivation (*bhāvanā*), taken either collectively or individually. For instance, in the case of things experienced only once, cultivation arises from the intensity of the cognition.

Thus, neither death nor suffering, nor the intervention of another birth, can destroy the seeds of mental impression (*bhāvanā*) associated with words regarding their objects. And if there were a persistence of these impressions even toward those [objects],
then those born deaf in another life would perceive the various kinds of forms and sounds experienced in that previous life, just as they do for things experienced in the present life.
They might say: "Furthermore, due to the continuity of memory from previous practice, a newborn infant experiences joy, fear, and grief;

however, this is a persistence of certain mental predispositions (*bhāvanā*) and not of all of them. This is because the infant's conduct is like that of one who has attained proficiency [in a skill]. Just as even for a dull-witted person, repeated exposure to suffering caused by the words of a wicked person cultivates a mental predisposition."

Just as there is the study of scriptures for one who is dull-witted, so too does cultivation (*bhāvanā*) arise from respect for the conviction, even when it is experienced only once or faintly. For example, in the Devahrada lake at Mahācaitrī, something like a bubble may arise; the seeing of the golden lotus and other such signs—whether occurring individually or collectively—are to be understood [as the means]. All three of these are indeed mental impressions (*saṃskāra*).

Since the cause [of the impression] is the same for the word, the object, and their relationship, how can it be that the refinement (*saṃskāra*) belongs to the object alone and not to the relationship between the word and the object? To this it has been said: "What is the specific reason, the seed, for [the impression] being in the case of the object but not in the case of the hearing? If one should think that, just as with the object, a cultivation (*bhāvanā*) indeed arises for both the word and its relationship, yet that [cultivation] is [destroyed] by death or by suffering—

Because memory is not produced when destroyed by dwelling in the womb, birth, or the establishment of a [new] species, he says: "Death, suffering, or the intervention of another birth [obstructs] the seeds of mental impressions (*bhāvanā*) regarding words and their relations with objects. The phrase "a specific cause must be stated" is to be supplied [to complete the sense]. The seeds consist of the forms of mental impressions.

The meaning is "from memory. The point is that if there were no restriction on the cause, a restriction on the effect would be impossible, as that would lead to the undesirable consequence of its being accidental (*āka-smikatva*). However, if someone, out of audacity, should accept that "in the case of the relations between words and their meanings, mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) follows along," he is addressed: "And even in those cases, if mental cultivation followed without distinction..."
Those born blind and deaf might describe various kinds of forms and sounds experienced in other births as if they were experienced in that very life.
To this, he objects: "Even so, due to the persistence of memories from previous practice, there is joy and fear in one who is born..."
Due to the occurrence of sorrow, there is a following of some meditative cultivations (*bhāvanā*) and not of all. This is the meaning:

birth is the connection with a specific class of unprecedented body, sense-faculties, cognitions, and sensations; one who performs that [birth] is "born. When there is a longing for a desired object and its attainment, there is the experience of pleasure, which is joy; [when it is] undesired...

When the means for attaining sense objects are present, the inability to abandon them constitutes fear. When there is an engagement with desired objects, the longing for that desired object which is impossible to attain is grief. Thus, the apprehension and experience of these—joy, fear, and grief—arise from the connection with the memory of what was previously practiced in a former birth. In a previous life...

Because of the continuity of memory regarding a practiced object: practice (*abhyāsa*) is the production of multiple cognitions having either a single object or a single form; that action is "practiced," as in the expressions "Devadatta has practiced this" or "rice has been practiced [cultivated]. When the grasping [of the object] has ceased, the cognition whose object is the subsequent connection with that [object] is memory (*smṛti*).

That by which one is bound is a "bond" (*anubandha*); the bond of memory is *bhāvanā* (mental impression). Therefore, due to the cause of the bond of memory practiced in a previous life, a newborn infant—even in the absence of contact with the objects of the senses—experiences joy, fear, and grief.
Let it be so;
however, because it depends upon a prior establishment, there is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for that [establishment].
The operation of the inferential mark (liṅga) and the statement (vākya) occurs with respect to what is established in a general sense, [not in its specific detail].

First of all, cognition arising from a logical mark (*liṅga*) and so forth is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding that [Brahman], because it depends on a prior established proof due to its origin in empirical consciousness. Nor is it [valid] for that which arises from meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), because it depends on a cognition of its own cause. Nor is it [valid] for that which arises from a logical mark or a sentence;
for while those two establish a general form, they cannot produce the comprehension of a sentence-meaning consisting of an unestablished category, since they only penetrate what is already qualified.

There is a persistence of certain mental impressions (*bhāvanā*) belonging to previous births, and there was previously a connection with another body. If it is argued that the manifestation of joy and so forth is unproven, we say no; for this is inferred from the presence of smiling, crying, and so on. To explain: the state of infancy possesses a self endowed with joy and so forth, because it is characterized by smiling, crying, and so on.

Just like the state of youth; likewise, the state of childhood possesses a self endowed with memory, because it possesses a self endowed with joy and so forth, just like the state of youth. Similarly, the state of childhood possesses a self endowed with mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), because it possesses a self endowed with memory, just like the state of youth.
And thus, the state of childhood possesses a self that has experienced previously experienced objects, [because it possesses a self endowed with mental impressions...]

Just as the state of youth possesses a self because it is associated with experience, so too the state of childhood at the time of experiencing must possess a self associated with the body, because it possesses a self that experiences, just like the state of youth; thus, by this reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*), the existence of the next world is also indicated. Therefore, in this way, there is a continuity of certain mental impressions (*bhāvanā*), but not of all of them.

Why? Because an infant does not engage in linguistic usage in the same manner as one who is proficient. For the latent impression (*bhāvanā*), which is inferred from the observation of an effect, persists only so long as the observation of that effect continues; this is the meaning.

Thus, having refuted the objection raised by the proponent of a partial doctrine (*siddhāntaikadeśin*), the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*) [addresses] the ultimate established doctrine (*paramasiddhāntin*).
He states the refutation: "Let it be so;
however, because it depends upon a prior establishment, there is no means of knowledge whatsoever regarding that [prior state].
The operation of the inferential mark (liṅga) and the sentence occurs with respect to what is established in a general sense, not with respect to the specific [state]."

He explains this: "In that case, knowledge arising from an indicative mark (*liṅga*) and so forth is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); neither is a word or a suffix a means of valid cognition regarding the duty to be performed. For what reason? Because such knowledge of the duty to be performed does not arise from indicative marks and so forth when they are heard for the first time; since it originates from consciousness, it depends upon a prior establishment by another means of cognition.

Nor is it born of cultivation (*bhāvanāja*), because it would depend upon a cognition of its cause; for whatever form a consciousness is to be produced by cultivation, it depends upon an experience of that very same form as its own cause from another means of knowledge (*mānāntara*). And it has already been stated that such [an experience] does not exist. [Objection: But surely the inferential mark (*liṅga*) and the sentence will apprehend the state of being something to be done (*kartavyatā*); these two are the means of valid cognition...
Nor [is it] born from a logical mark (*liṅga*) or a sentence (*vākya*), because they do not have as their object a meaning not already understood, and otherwise their validity would be untenable;
therefore, he says: "Nor [is it] born from a logical mark or a sentence. He states the reason: because those two [the mark and the sentence] establish only a general form.

[For] that which makes known the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*) is that which has grasped the relation by way of apprehending a specific [object]; and the relation [is grasped] when [the mark] pervades the subject (*pakṣa*) while being connected with its own probandum (*sādhya*).

The restriction is as follows: when the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) residing in the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmī*) has not been apprehended, a restriction of the reason (*hetu*) with respect to that [property] is impossible.

Consequently, since there is a dependence upon a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the establishment of the universal form [of the reason], in the absence of such [cognition], there is a lack of validity.
Just as it is in this life, so too in previous and even earlier lives that [causal relation] would have to be presupposed; however, there is no evidence for this.
In that case, would this [notion of the self] be merely a conceptual construction based on beginningless verbal impressions? And that has already been refuted above.
It is capable of being proven. Furthermore, there is no "property of the subject" (pakṣadharmatā) when proving the existence of a previously non-existent entity. To explain:

when existence is to be proven, the reason (hetu) must be stated as either a property of an existent thing or a property of a non-existent thing, since no other alternative exists. Regarding this, even the outsiders (Bāhyas) say:
"A property of existence does not exist in what is unestablished; that which depends on both [existence and non-existence] is inconclusive;
and a property contradictory to existence—how can its presence be established?
Therefore, inference concerns an object qualified by fire as it is known in its general form.

It apprehends the mountain and so forth; or rather, it apprehends that very mountain and such, which is well-known as the locus of the probans (sādhana) by virtue of its form being common to both the presence and absence of fire, as qualified by fire. By this, it is indicated that the operation of inference proceeds only when there is the cognition of the two types of relations in the form of "property-of-the-subject" (pakṣadharmatā), and not otherwise. Thus [the] sentence...

Even [the cognition] which apprehends an object whose action is generally established as qualified by another object—which is itself a factor (*kāraka*) and established in its general form—apprehends that very object; thus, it is said that these two have a qualified entity as their object, and not an object consisting of the existence of a thing never before perceived. Why is the sentence of such a kind? He says: "unestablished" (*aprasiddha*).

Because the cognition of the meaning of a sentence cannot be accounted for through the cognition of word-meanings alone, the meaning of a sentence is precisely the word-meaning itself as qualified by the meanings of the other words;

furthermore, that which has not had its relationship [with other words] grasped cannot be a word-meaning. Therefore, since there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the duty (*kartavyatā*) based on the well-known nature of universals, the indicative mark (*liṅga*) and the sentence (*vākya*) possess authority only with respect to that [duty] as something qualified.
[This is] the state of being.

Now, it was asked: "How does the cycle of the experience and mental impression (*bhāvanā*) regarding the necessity for the application of words revolve incessantly? What need is there here for another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*? To this, he says: "And as it is in this birth, so it was in the previous one, and in the one before that."

It is said that [the Veda] is dependent [on something else], which implies a lack of independent authority (*pramāṇa*). The underlying intention here is as follows: if it were established that a child acts spontaneously based on an understanding of what ought to be done produced by impressions (*bhāvanā*) from a previous birth, then the charge of beginninglessness (*anāditā*) could be avoided;
however, that very thing is not established. For instance, an impression produced by an experience regarding a certain object results in a memory regarding that very same object.

It does not, however, apply to other matters either, for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Nor is the general state of being "to-be-done" (*kartavyatā-sāmānya*) the cause for engaging in a specific action. Furthermore, a sense of "to-be-done-ness" that was previously understood as pertaining to a particular action cannot—when remembered by a child—induce engagement in a different action simply because it pertained to that same action. Nor [does it induce engagement] in another action.
It is recorded [in tradition]: indeed, one who has perceived a palace in Pāṭaliputra does not, when remembering it at Śilāhrada, become deluded.
Therefore, regarding the comprehension of the duty to perform actions such as suckling the breast, another cause for the mental impression (*bhāvanā*) must be stated;
yet no means of valid cognition exists to show that this occurs either in this life or in all previous lives. [This applies to] the state of being a desired means...
A child also infers that [the mother] belongs to that same class, based on the established recognition of the suckling of the breast and so forth. In that case,
if even the object were unestablished, this would be a mere conceptual construction (vikalpa) based upon beginningless linguistic predispositions (vāsanā).
Moreover:

"The worldly understanding is that what is a means to the agent's desired end is 'to be done' (kartavya), whereas its opposite is 'not to be done' (akartavya); therefore, [the status of being dharma or adharma] depends upon that [understanding]."

Indeed, that causal condition which follows after a particular object is its objective domain (*viṣaya*), just as whiteness is the domain of the cognition of white. For ordinary people, the cognitions of "this is to be done" and "this is not to be done" follow respectively from the state of being a required means and its opposite. Therefore, it is understood that these two [cognitions] have those two [states] as their respective objects.

And that has already been answered previously: that there is no cognition without an object. Therefore, by process of elimination, the basis (*ālambana*) for the cognition of what is to be done (*kartavyatā*) is simply the means desired by the agent as the cause of engagement.
Furthermore, he states that by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) as well, that alone is the basis:

For it is the worldly understanding that "what is beneficial to the agent is to be done," whereas regarding its opposite, the understanding is "it is not to be done. Therefore, [the Veda] has that as its object.

[Objection: But how can the two cognitions of "what ought to be done" (*kartavyatva*) and "what ought not to be done" (*akartavyatva*), which have as their objects respectively being pervaded by an effort (*kṛti*) and its opposite, be capable of having as their objects the state of being a means to what is desired and its opposite? Nor is there an identity between being a means (*sādhanatā*) and being what ought to be done (*kartavyatā*), because they are mutually contradictory in nature—like fire and snow—due to the distinction between the established and the to-be-established. To this, he says: "That which indeed..."

The object which a cognition follows is its objective domain, just as white is the domain of the cognition of "white. For worldly people, the cognitions "this is to be done" and "this is not to be done" have as their causes the fact that something is a desired means and its opposite.
Therefore, those two [cognitions] consist in the state of being a desired means and its opposite, regarding what is to be done and what is not to be done.
It is understood from positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that these two are the objects of the [injunction]. This is the underlying intention here:

it is true that "being to-be-done" (*kartavyatā*) consists merely in being achievable through effort (*kṛti-sādhyatā*); however, that alone is not the cause [of activity], because it would follow that even the desired result (*samīhita*), since it is also "to-be-done," would be a cause [of activity]. Indeed, the result itself is not the object of engagement under the notion that "the result is to-be-done"; rather, it is its means.

It might be argued that the duty to perform one thing does not impel one toward another, because that would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga). If it is claimed that there is no such over-extension because [the second thing] serves as a means (sādhana), then—by distinguishing between what is already attained and what is not—it follows that the cause of activity is indeed the status of being a means;
however, the Teacher himself will later demonstrate that this is not merely that status, but rather that it is "an efficient means toward what is desired by the agent" (karturiṣṭābhyupāya).

Therefore, from the statement "of the agent," it follows that for the teacher, the cause of activity is the state of being a means to a desired end (*samīhitasādhanatā*) which is inherent in the same object as the state of being a duty (*kartavyatā*); this is intended as the objective support (*ālambana*) for the cognition of duty. Furthermore, we shall demonstrate that there is no contradiction whatsoever in these two—[the desire and the duty]—having a common locus despite occurring at different times. Nor is [the cause of activity] merely the state of being a duty...

The fact that something is a means to achieve what is desired (*samīhitasādhanatā*) falls within the scope of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), but it is not the cause of engagement (*pravṛtti*). Rather, it is the state of being "that which ought to be done" (*kartavyatā*) alone which is the cause of that engagement.

This [state of being "to be done"] is understood in some cases through its being a means to the desired end, and in other cases directly from the word [of scripture]. Therefore, it is correct to maintain that even in the case of impermanent things, when the state of being "to be done" is understood—even in the absence of its being a means to the desired end—that [state] is the cause of engagement.
Therefore, even "to-be-done-ness" (kartavyatā) is nothing other than being the means to what is desired by the agent. As it has been stated by him:
"It is said that 'to-be-done-ness' alone is the cause of engagement. Furthermore, let it be included within the scope of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).

Nevertheless, there certainly exists some means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by whose absence the object of cognition (*prameya*) is excluded; for example, the state of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) is the means of valid cognition for the impermanence of entities. And yet, by its absence, impermanence is excluded, for it is simply not possible for an entity to be both unproduced and impermanent. Likewise here as well, "being an effect" (*kāryatā*) consists in being pervaded by volitional effort (*kṛti*), and volitional effort is...

Human effort is that which has desire, aversion, and the instinct for life as its source; it does not exist when its own source ceases, just as smoke does not exist when fire ceases. Nor is it impossible [for such effort] regarding the means or non-means of attaining the beneficial or avoiding the harmful, as in the case of occasional rites (*naimittika*), prohibitions (*niṣedha*), or original injunctions (*apūrva*); for aversion and the instinct for life are simply not to be entertained [as sources of effort in those contexts].

And because it has as its object that which is to be performed (vidheya). Now, this is an inference; and since the Veda—which enjoins the performance of what was previously unknown—possesses independent authority by virtue of being eternal, this inference cannot arise, as its object would be sublated.
For those who know [the logic of] inference maintain that "having an unsublated object" is included in the causal complex of inference, just like "residing in the subject" (pakṣadharmatā).

In that case, must those who live for exactly a thousand years be the qualified participants in a sacrificial session (*sattra*) lasting a thousand years? This *sattra* is prescribed as something to be accomplished over a thousand years. If it is argued that, because such people living for a thousand years are impossible, the word "year" (*saṃvatsara*) is used in its secondary sense to refer to days, we say no; for the impossibility [of such people] is unproven.

For indeed, from the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) itself—which is independent of other means of knowledge—there will arise men with a lifespan of a thousand years, as it prescribes a sacrificial session (*sattra*) lasting a thousand years. It might be argued that this is impossible because of the following inference: "The persons under dispute do not have a lifespan of a thousand years, because they are human beings, like ourselves and others. But surely, an inference that is sublated by scripture does not arise.

As for what was said— that "it is true that an operative scripture sublates inference"— but the very operation of that scripture is preceded by the determination of the fitness for the connection of the word-meanings as recalled; and at the time of that determination, the inference, having operated upon a subject already sublated, is blocked because the connection of the thousands of years of the Sattra-sacrifice is unfit, [leaving only] the year...
