If it is argued that [the word] causes the subordinate function (*jaghanyavṛtti*) to apply [to the primary meaning], we say no; for the same [objection] applies here as well. Indeed, when there is something to be disregarded, the two—namely, the prohibition of a contingent occasion (*naimittika-niṣedha*) and the apūrva—cannot be construed as being primarily related to the effort (*prayatna*). Nor is it logical to claim that the connection between two things denoted by a single word does not depend upon semantic fitness (*yogyatā*) at the time of determining the meaning of the word.

Because there is no determination of the connection [of the agent] with another [action] for those two who lack eligibility, the connection of that which is denoted by a single word [the optative suffix] is untenable. If it is argued that in the case of the *kāmya* (optional rite) there is a valid connection of the action with the agent because it is conducive to the fulfillment of a desire, what follows for the cases of the occasional (*naimittika*) and prohibitory (*niṣedha*) injunctions? In those cases, since there is recognition of the same word [the optative suffix] and no mention of a desire, there is only the necessity of performing the *apūrva* (unseen potency).

If it is argued that [the injunction] is understood [as the primary meaning], then even one who does not wish to must necessarily admit the inclusion of the "state of being something to be done" (*kartavyatā*), just as there must be an *adhikārī* (the person entitled to act), or as there is the agent of the prohibited action when it is accompanied by a specific occasion (*nimitta*). And thus, the state of being something to be done does not consist in the mere *niyoga* (the mandate). For if both the occasional (*naimittika*) and the prohibitory (*niṣedha-adhikāra*) mandates consisted merely in that [the mandate alone], then the state of being something to be done would [be reduced to that].

Just as there is no object of injunction in the case of a loss, it is established that "to-be-done-ness" (kartavyatā) consists in being a means desired by the agent, while its opposite is "not-to-be-done-ness" (akartavyatā). He concludes this as follows: "Therefore, 'to-be-done-ness' is also nothing other than this.

"The fruit of what is to be performed is happiness. But how, then, can there be permanence or the status of being "to be performed" in the case of obligatory rites (*nitya*)? And how can there be a performance of the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) according to one's capacity? For instance, if the son and so forth were the desired object, then the permanence of the means would be destroyed, because that desire is impermanent; in that case, the expression "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīvam*) would be meaningless.

Nor is it purposeful as a qualification of the qualified person (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*), because the result is already established [by other means]. Now, if it is thought that for everyone, at all times, every desired fruit—the removal of accumulated evil—will come to pass, then indeed there would be eternality; but this would be by virtue of the fruit, not from the word itself. For thus it is with respect to the fruit:

Because it is eternally desired, its necessity is real by virtue of that desire; however, the word is merely an indicator for the cognition of the means that is eternally desired. In that regard, if there were no operation of the word, then—just as in the case of *kṛcchra* and other penances—there would be no requirement to perform all the constituent parts (*aṅga*), since otherwise the result would not be achieved. For [the obligation] is verbal in nature, being eternal.

[This concerns] the state of having a means that is conducive to equanimity. On this very point, he cites the text of the *Bhāṣya*: "It has been said that the fruit of what is to be done (*kartavya*) is happiness.
Here, he raises an objection: if "to-be-done-ness" (*kartavyatā*) consists solely in being a means for achieving what is desired by the agent, how [is it so]?

In that case, would there be eternality or the state of being something to be performed (*kartavyatā*) in obligatory rites (*nitya*)? For it is not the case that this [obligatory rite] is eternally a means to achieve what is desired; such is the sense. In some readings, the text says: "How then could there be non-eternality or the state of being something to be performed even in the obligatory?
and that is indeed easy to understand. Furthermore, if it were a means to achieve what is desired, then there would be a performance of the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) according to one's capacity.

The phrase "how so? is drawn forward [from the previous context]. The meaning is that in the absence of that [desire], there is no permanence. Now, one might ask: what is the contradiction between being a means to a desired end and impermanence? To this he says: "For instance. If, first of all, a son or the like is desired, then the permanence of the goal (*upeya*) would be frustrated. Why? Because that desire itself is impermanent. Let it be so.

"What is the fault in impermanence? To this he says: Since that [action] is impermanent, the phrase "as long as one lives" (yāvajjīvam) is meaningless; nor is it meaningful as a qualification of the qualified person (adhikāriviśeṣaṇa). Since the purpose is already established, the futility of the word "as long as" (yāvat) remains certain. Even the mere duration of life cannot serve as a qualification of the qualified person, because there is nothing [else] to be excluded.

Because [the result] would exist [even without the performance of the rite]. For there is no possibility of entitlement for one who is not living; therefore, since the purpose is already accomplished [by the mere existence of the result], the [injunction] would be meaningless—this is the sense.

Now, if it is thought: "The result, which is always desired by all, will come about as the destruction of accumulated evil (duṣkṛta); and thus, because it is a means to what is eternally desired, its status as a *nitya* (obligatory) rite will be established," [we reply: this is refuted...
He explains: This would indeed be the case regarding eternality; however, it is by virtue of the result, not from the word itself. He clarifies this:
For instance, because the result is eternally desired, its necessary performance is real by virtue of that [desire].
The word, however, is exhausted merely by providing the cognition of the means to what is desired. [Objection: But we have no need for eternality.
And since that [efficacy] is obtained even through the result, what is the use of the word? To this he says:

"In that case, if there were no operation of the word, there would follow the necessity of including all auxiliary parts (aṅgas) for the sake of removing defects in the permanence [of the rite], just as in the case of the *kṛcchra* and other penances. Why? Because otherwise, if they were not included, there would be an absence of fruit for all the auxiliary parts, just as in the case of a penance [performed without its parts]. Nor does this [apply] even to the word."

[Page 218] "And always with all its constituent parts" is appropriate because of the impossibility of anything else; for otherwise, since the injunction regarding the constituent parts would be non-optional (*avikalpyatva*), it would follow that one should perform it whenever possible, as in the case of the *Viśvajit* sacrifice and others. For it is not the case for everyone...

In the Viśvajit sacrifice, those who are lame and others are qualified [to perform it] because the means for the desired end is present. A secondary (anuṣaṅgika) desire is not the motive, as there is no evidence for it; for even the assumption based on presumptive reasoning (arthāpatti) is refuted by the fact that non-performance leads to sin (pratyavāya).

Furthermore, it is more appropriate to assume that [the result] follows precisely from the Vedic injunction and its supplementary portions (vākyaśeṣa), and because that meaning is understood again from the Smṛti texts.

He states that there is a logical consequence regarding eternality: for if eternality were inherent in the verbal injunction itself, then because it would be impossible for it to be "always complete in its constituent parts," the requirement expressed by the word [itself] as something necessarily to be performed could not be fulfilled unless all the parts were assembled;
thus, the phrase "as far as one is able" becomes necessary. Alternatively, why would it not be possible even on the basis of actual eternality?

Thus he says: otherwise, if [the Vedic injunction] were truly eternal, then because the traditional teaching of its constituent parts would be eternally unimpaired, it would be perceived as being always present, like the Viśvajit sacrifice and others.
He explains the illustration: for [the Viśvajit] is not [perceived as always present], even though it is a means to the desired goal for everyone.
The lame and others are qualified [to perform sacrifices]. The phrase "the lame and others" indicates an irreparable deficiency of limbs.

This is the underlying intention here: the scriptural enumeration of the auxiliary requirements (*aṅga-āmnāya*) can be established as eternal only through its scriptural nature, not through its actual reality; for while the enumeration of auxiliaries is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), that which is to be known (*prameya*) is dependent upon the means of valid cognition.

Because of its established status. [Objection: Is it not the case that the scripture stating "one should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices as long as one lives" is intended to establish the obligatory nature of the rite due to its lifelong connection? Therefore, the obligatory nature will be derived from the verbal testimony (śābdī), and from that scripture intended for that purpose, the incidental destruction of evil (duritakṣaya)—which is always desired by all people—will follow as a secondary result.

To the objection that a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is being stated by you, he replies: "It is not intended as a secondary implication (*anuṣaṅgika*), because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for it.

Indeed, the supplementary portion of the lifelong injunction (*yāvajjīvavākyaśeṣa*) is not studied as "one who desires the destruction of previously incurred evil deeds. Nor is there presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). Why? Because even through the sin of non-performance (*pratyavāya*), [the evil deeds] are exhausted.
Now, since both alternatives are thus possible, which one is more appropriate to assume? To this he says:

because, based on both the Smṛti and the supplementary portion of the Vedic text (*vākyaśeṣa*), it is more logical to assume the commission of a transgression (*pratyavāya*) for the non-performance of that [act], rather than assuming anything else. In this regard, the Smṛti is the passage beginning with "One who does not perform the prescribed act," and so forth. The supplementary portion of the Vedic text is also... [he who...]

"If one who is a performer of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices should omit either the new-moon day or the full-moon day, he falls from the heavenly world. Thus it is said. For in this regard, there arises a doubt: regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, which are connected to "as long as one lives," should the destruction of previously acquired demerit be postulated, or rather, the incurrence of sin through non-performance?
The conclusion is that there is sin (pratyavāya) in non-performance, based on the completion of the sentence with "yo ha vai" and from Smṛti;

moreover, this is understood even from worldly Smṛti. For instance, in the world, certain things are enjoined as necessarily to be done and others are prohibited, such as [the case of] horses and the like belonging to a king brought from another village.

Ordinary people understand that the performance of rites such as the *nīrājanā* (lustration) or the offering of a finger-ring (*bhujagāṅgulidāna*) and so forth, and the non-performance thereof, results in spiritual demerit (*pratyavāya*). Thus, this is established by the firmness of beginningless worldly tradition (*smṛti*).

Furthermore, just as it is logical that there is demerit (*pratyavāya*) from the performance of what is prohibited—that which must necessarily not be done—it is likewise logical that there is demerit from the non-performance of what must necessarily be done; for in both cases, the application of a mandatory injunction (*niyoga*) is established. Since one engages with desired means out of a desire for them, whereas one engages with prohibited acts out of fear of demerit, the nature of engagement in the latter case is not the same as that in the former.

[This is] for the sake of compassion. Furthermore, because [the obligatory rites] lack the characteristics of being a means to what is eternally desired, being eternal, having a fruit, and being performable according to one's capacity, it is postulated that there is a transgression (pratyavāya) in their non-performance. Therefore, those which are not means to what is eternally desired are not obligatory (nitya). And the engagement in them [occurs] because of the postulation of a transgression in their non-performance; moreover, because action is of the nature of suffering, [there is engagement] through its incidental connection.

He states that "mastery" (vyutpatti) refers to the conceptualization of the removal of previously acquired evil, based on the seed of imagining a transgression (pratyavāya) arising from the non-performance of what must necessarily be done; for, from the Smṛti,

one understands that its purpose is such that just as there is a transgression in performing that which is prohibited and not to be done, so too there is a transgression in not performing that which is enjoined and must necessarily be done.
This is correct. And there is no doubt here such that a determination must be made through supplementary statements (*vākyaśeṣa*) and so forth; for he says:

"Because the application of the injunction (*niyoga*) is thus established, the necessity of the injunction—the state of being something that must be done—is established precisely by the postulation of demerit (*pratyavāya*) upon its non-performance. Why? Because [the action] is a desired means due to the fear of demerit arising from non-performance.
He states that activity is necessarily so: the sense is that activity occurs through desire for the means to what is desired, and desire itself is necessarily present.
Now, one might object: it is not merely being a means to what is desired, but rather being a means to what is eternally desired;
therefore, there is a rule of necessity regarding activity because of its cause. To this he says: "And thus, of whatever kind..."

Such activity does not lead to prosperity. To explain: even regarding things that are intensely desired, seekers may at times become indifferent toward the means for attaining them due to laziness; however, it is universally known that this is not the case when one fails to act against that which causes transgression (*pratyavāya*). He points out the contradiction in the opposing view: "the eternality of the means to what is eternally desired."

And what is the consistency between [the claims of] having a fruit (*phalavattva*), being performable according to one's capacity (*yathāśaktyanuṣṭheyatva*), and being eternally required (*nityatva*)? Indeed, this is contradictory:

namely, that it has a fruit, is performable according to capacity, and is eternally required. For instance, the eternity of the means consists in the possession of all its eternal auxiliary parts (*aṅga*); yet that [eternity] would be compromised by the deficiency of some parts through the principle of being performable according to capacity.

It is contradictory. Likewise, its status as a constant object of desire by virtue of being fruitful is contradicted. For instance: upon the attainment of what is desired, the desire ceases; if it does not cease, then surely it is not desired. And if the desire has ceased, it is not a constant object of desire. Thus, there is this contradiction arising from the incompatibility between being fruitful and being an object of desire.
Therefore, for the sake of maintaining the eternality understood from scripture, it is more appropriate to postulate that a transgression (pratyavāya) occurs upon non-performance.

He concludes: "Therefore, obligatory rites (*nitya-karmāṇi*) are not [performed] as means to what is eternally desired; rather, engagement in them is due to the fact that there is a transgression in their non-performance. Now, one might object: in some obligatory rites, the destruction of previously acquired demerit (*durita*) is also a result.

To this he says: "And because action is of the nature of suffering, there is an activity [toward liberation] due to the destruction of sin—which is an incidental consequence of that action and is opposed to its result. That [liberation] is not the scriptural fruit [of action];

for when an action, which by its very nature consists of suffering, is enjoined, the destruction of sin occurs as an incidental effect (ānuṣaṅgika), since sin is opposed to suffering, just like the transformation of the sacrificial oblation."
The meaning is "having performed.

[p.220] This is because of the destruction of the *pāpmans* (impurities) which are opposed to the result of the action, and because meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is that which is to be accomplished.

Because the expression "agnihotram" is intended as a designation, it can also occur in a modified form; thus, there is no contradiction in its being designated with the instrumental case. This [objection] is untenable. For it is said: "It is constant, for that which is the means to the eternal goal is constant, according to the Vedic revelation 'as long as one lives'."
Therefore, one should perform the ancillaries according to one's capacity, or else not all of them at all; otherwise, it is not so.

In that case, even though it is a means to what is desired, there is no contradiction with its being eternal, because it is conceived as something to be accomplished that is eternally desired—the removal of evil (duḥkha). For while one may occasionally be indifferent toward pleasure or its causes, one who is always repelled by suffering and its causes has a constant desire for their cessation; and this [cessation] is indeed beneficial.

If permanent rites (*nitya-karman*) do not serve as means to achieve a desired end, but rather those very rites are enjoined as things that must be performed, then the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) expressing their instrumentality—as in the phrase "by means of the Darśapūrṇamāsa"—would be untenable. Anticipating this objection, he says: "And because the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) is what is to be accomplished. This is the meaning: although the sacrifice (*yajña*) does not [directly] lead toward the desired end...

Regarding the status of being a means (*sādhanatā*): although the prior non-existence of transgression (*pratyavāya-prāgabhāva*) is not what is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), nevertheless, it is the productive urge itself (*bhāvanā*) that will be the object to be accomplished. Although the sacrifice (*yajña*) cannot function as an instrument (*karaṇa*) with respect to that [urge] because it is the object (*karman*) to be pervaded by the productive urge, nevertheless, just as in the case of the result, that which is pervaded by the productive urge functions as an instrument by way of delimiting the means, so too is it here.
"It will come to be.

He states another resolution: because it serves the purpose of a designation—as in the expression "the *agnihotra* [sacrifice]"—it is possible even when modified, and thus there is no contradiction with the use of the instrumental case.
This is the meaning: just as one says, "One desiring heaven should perform the *agnihotra*," [so too here].

"In this way, 'agnihotram' [is used] with the accusative case in the sense of the instrumental; likewise, in 'darśapūrṇamāsābhyām', the instrumental will function in the sense of the accusative. [The opponent says: "Because it serves the purpose of indication (nirdeśa). [That is to say: "Indication" (nirdeśa) means that which is indicated;
since its purpose is the object (karma-rūpa-artha), there is a transformation of the instrumental case—this is the meaning. [The author] refutes this: "This is trivial (vārtam)."
For it is thus:

since the scripture states that [the means to the eternal goal] must be practiced eternally for as long as one lives, the auxiliary rites (aṅgas) should therefore be performed according to one's capacity, or else not at all; otherwise, they would not be complete.

First of all, there is no contradiction with its eternality in its being a means to a desired end, because it is precisely that which is eternally desired which is postulated as the object to be accomplished; thus, the removal of evil is distinct from sacrifices such as the Viśvajit. To ensure the necessity of engagement, he says:
"There may be indifference toward pleasure or its cause at some time due to laziness and the like, but [indifference] toward pain and its causes exists at all times."

For one who regards [the removal of suffering] as his goal, there is always a desire for its cessation. Now, it might be argued that at the moment of desiring one's own welfare, such [desire for the cessation of suffering] does not exist;

however, for one who seeks [that welfare], there is indeed an exertion toward the destruction of obstacles. Therefore, [the cessation of suffering] is based on what is desired, [and thus] the removal of evil [is achieved].

Destruction [of sin] is always intended. Since the fruits of obligatory (*nitya*) rites are eternal—being understood from the scriptural expression "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīvam*)—there is no contradiction with their obligatory nature. For that [intention for destruction] would be frustrated if the goal were non-eternal. Furthermore, the performance according to one's capacity is possible because of that very obligatoriness; it is impossible to perform an obligatory rite constantly without its constituent parts (*ahīnāṅga*). Nor is this...

The eternality [of the ritual] is real; for those who maintain the existence of a fruit do not recite the word "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīva*) nor do they study the word for a specific fruit. Rather, having understood the eternality from the scriptural hearing (*śruti*) of "as long as one lives," they sometimes infer, through presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*), both a distinction in the fruit and a distinction in the performance. This is because when the goal is non-eternal, the performance must possess all its constituent parts (*paripūrṇāṅga*).

The notion of obligatory duty (*nitya-kartavyatā*) as understood from the word "as long as life lasts" (*yāvaj-jīva*) is untenable. For the term "as long as life lasts" does not apply to an obligatory duty that is at once a desired means and consists of a complete set of constituent parts (*paripūrṇāṅga-sādhana*). Furthermore, a distinct fruit imagined [for such rites] on account of their being obligatory does not sublate that very [obligatory nature]. How then is it a means to what is eternally desired?

Why has its eternality been stated? It is because there is no obstruction to that very [eternality] which is understood through verbal testimony; it is stated by means of the capacity of the word itself, through application according to one's ability, and through the method of *tantra*. For this very reason, another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) must be sought for these two. How [is it eternal] at all times? To this he says: "And even for one desiring what is beneficial, when the obstacles to that desired [result] are destroyed... [and so forth].

That by which one is bound is "durita" (evil); there is indeed a desire for its destruction. Therefore, there is no contradiction between [the obligatory nature of] being a means to what is eternally desired and the possession of a fruit; thus he says: "Therefore, the destruction of evil, which is the cause of what is desired, is always sought after. Precisely because the fruits of the obligatory rites (*nitya-karmāṇi*) are eternal, the word 'as long as life lasts' (*yāvajjīvam*) [is used]."

Because [the action] has passed away, there is no contradiction with its eternality. The meaning is that what is postulated because something else is otherwise inexplicable cannot itself be sublated by that very thing. Nor does its very nature contradict the eternality of the action; he shows this by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*): "If the goal were non-eternal, that [eternality] would be frustrated. This is intended as eternal. According to one's capacity...

He states the non-contradiction regarding the necessity of performance: "And the combination [of subsidiaries] according to one's capacity follows precisely from their obligatory nature (*nityatva*). Why? Because it is impossible for a subsidiary (*aṅga*) to be performed constantly [without exception]. Nor is this obligatory nature real (*vāstavam*), such that it would establish the object of knowledge (*prameya*) as always requiring all subsidiaries; rather, it is merely verbal. Why? For those who speak of the fruit [of the rite] do not [mean it applies] as long as one lives..."

They do not recite the word "va," or they study it as merely a word denoting a specific fruit; for, since the word conveys eternality, they would not otherwise postulate such a fruit. Rather, because the eternality is understood from the scriptural injunction "as long as one lives" (yāvajjīva), they infer from that very source, through presumptive testimony (arthāpatti), both the distinction of fruits and the distinction of performances. He demonstrates this presumptive testimony: when the goal is non-eternal...

Furthermore, when the application [of the rite] has all its constituent parts complete, it is untenable for the lifelong verbal expression to convey an obligatory duty; for the word "lifelong" (yāvajjīva), which consists of a means for achieving a desired end, cannot be construed with an obligatory duty that requires the performance of every single constituent part. Moreover, the distinction of a fruit that is merely postulated on account of its obligatoriness does not sublate that very [obligation], but rather [confirms] it.

Because it acquires its own nature through cognition, it persists by having a nature that conforms to that [cognition]. If eternality is indeed cognizable only through verbal testimony (*śabda*), how then is it said that "eternality" [is established] because it is the means to what is eternally desired?

He provides the answer: "of that which is cognized through verbal testimony alone"—namely, the eternality of the ritual action (*karman*) as understood from the verbal testimony "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīvam*).

There would be no contradiction, because that [dharma] is described as a means for what is eternally desired precisely through its capacity as a word-meaning, by means of practice according to one's ability and through the principle of *tantra* (simultaneous application).

And how is this eternality (*nityatva*) of the action established? If it is argued that it consists in being a means for accomplishing what is eternally desired, [then it follows] from the performance of it as a duty (*nitya-anuṣṭhāna*), because there is sin (*pratyavāya*) in its non-performance; thus, the eternality arises from the word itself. This is not so. If its obligatoriness (*kartavyatā*) is established by the word alone, for what purpose is the assumption of sin in its non-performance? Since activity is already established by the word alone. Nor...

It has been stated that the word is the cause of engagement by way of being a *kāraka* (instrumental factor). However, if it were merely a *jñāpaka* (informative indicator), there would be the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of [the fault of] making known the transgression (*pratyavāya*) even when the act is not performed; therefore, he says something further: "Precisely from that"—namely, because the result desired as a constant (*nitya*) is postulated here by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) qualified by the scriptural injunction of "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīva*)—"therefore, for both types of rites, the optional (*kāmya*) and the constant (*nitya*), [there is] desire..."

Our intended position— that the performance of the ritual system (*tantra*) is established as common because no distinction is perceived due to the lack of a specific commencement— is not achieved [by your view]. However,
for certain followers of Mīmāṃsā, when a rite for a specific desire (*kāmya*) is performed, [the initiation] proceeds from the mandate (*niyoga*) rather than from the desire itself.

Because of its greater strength, they consider the performance of obligatory rites (*nitya*) to be established incidentally (*prāsaṅgikī*) by virtue of being performed at a particular time, place, and by a particular agent. This, however, is incorrect. For if natural activity based on desire were stronger than activity based on an injunction (*niyoga*), then, according to your own view, those who turn away from fresh afflictions and the expenditure of wealth would [never perform] the obligatory rites.

Even if there were an injunction regarding occasional rites (*naimittika*), people would not engage in them; likewise, they would not refrain from prohibited acts such as violence. Consequently, the injunctions pertaining to obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and prohibited (*niṣedha*) matters would effectively be rendered null and void. This might be argued: "Desire alone is weak compared to an injunction, but when supported by an injunction..."

The stronger [obligation] would not be for the sake of a secondary benefit (*anugraha*). For in the case of obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites, once one has engaged through the injunction (*vidhi*), there is no utility whatsoever for desire (*kāmanā*) regarding what must be done. Nor is there utility for the injunction at that time in the case of optional (*kāmya*) rites which have a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*).
Therefore, when an optional rite is being performed, the obligatory rite does not become incidental (*prāsaṅgikatva*). Consequently, by adhering to our position—

"The dependence itself is what is delightful"—this is a reading found in some versions, rather than "not from that alone. Its meaning is as follows: the conception of its obligatory nature (*nityatva*) does not arise because it is a means for what is eternally desired or because of its performance according to one's capacity; rather, both of these [qualities] follow from its very being heard [in scripture] as obligatory.

"Otherwise" means that it would be according to the actual state of affairs. Furthermore, the fact that those two [rites] are the means for what is eternally desired must be sought through another means of knowledge (*mānāntara*) regarding their performance according to one's capacity. If, however, even when postulating a result that is eternally desired in order to establish the obligatory nature (*nityatva*) as understood from the scriptural injunction "as long as one lives," the obligatoriness remains real but not based on the verbal testimony [of the scripture], [then...]

To this, he says: "How can this be the real eternality of the ritual act (*karman*), if it is merely the state of being a means for accomplishing what is eternally desired"? He replies: "This is equal even for the other [the obligatory rite] because of its constant performance. He further states: "The performance of the other is also equal because of the sin incurred by non-performance. If one were to assume that [eternality] based on the primacy of the verbal injunction (*śabda-pūrvakatva*), it must be accepted as such.

In the case of *māṇā* (the daily recitation), there is no eternality of the injunction for both [the opponent and our own school], namely for the other [the opponent] and for ourselves. The opponent says: "In our view, the obligatory performance is not due to the sin of non-performance (*pratyavāya*), but rather from the verbal injunction itself. He refutes this: "This is not so. If the necessity of performance arises from the verbal injunction alone, what is the purpose of postulating a sin of non-performance? For the engagement in action is already established by the verbal injunction alone."

One might object: "But surely the word itself will cause one to act by its very nature, and let there be no sin for failing to act. Anticipating this, he says: "And it has been stated that the word is not a cause for activity by way of being a producer (*kāraka*); and if it were a communicator (*jñāpaka*), then in the case of non-performance...

Or rather, it would be truly so that [the scripture] causes one to perform it. Therefore, for those whose nature as injunctions is not fixed, there are such various manifestations. However, in the case of the Kṛcchra and Viśvajit [sacrifices], even though they are always means for accomplishing everything desired by everyone, because the words "of everything" and "at all times" are absent, there is the performance of all auxiliary parts (*aṅga*). Now, if there is efficacy in producing a result...

It is not possible [to perform the rite] according to one's capacity alone, because that would result in the absence of the fruit due to deficiency (*vaiguṇya*). What is this deficiency? It is the loss of the purpose of the injunction (*codanārthatva*). In that case, there is no deficiency, because even when the lifelong rite is performed with its limbs according to one's capacity, it still fulfills the purpose of the injunction. Or, if it did not fulfill the purpose of the injunction, then even if the capacity were fruitless, the inclusion of all limbs would be necessary; otherwise, it would not fulfill the purpose of the injunction.

And because there is no cessation [of activity]. At that time, since there is no goal to be accomplished (sādhya) apart from the action itself, there is no requirement for auxiliary parts (aṅga). It would follow that there is no status as an auxiliary part at all, because the ritual act (karman) is already known as the means [to the result]. If it is argued that the action, too, having its nature known in the form of something to be performed (vidheya), requires the auxiliaries for the accomplishment of the purpose of the injunction (codanārtha), then there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of having to employ all the auxiliaries. Or rather—

For those who state that the meaning of well-known words is their capacity (*śakti*), this capacity is the auxiliary factor; thus, according to the scriptural injunction regarding lifelong [observance], the capacity is the meaning of the *codanā*. For one who asserts the result, that [capacity] is not barred by force. Furthermore, what is this form of the *codanā*?
If it were to enjoin the obligatory performance through the communication of a transgression (*pratyavāya*), then the obligatoriness would be merely factual (*vāstavam*). He concludes:
Therefore, for those whose nature as injunctions is not fixed, such various manifestations arise.

As for what was stated regarding the Viśvajit sacrifice and others, he points out the dissimilarity there: although the Kṛcchra and the Viśvajit are always means for accomplishing the desired ends of everyone, because the word "of all" (sarvasya) and "at all times" (sarvadā) are absent [in their case], they lack all auxiliary parts (*aṅga*).

The formal argument: [The opponent] objects: "If there were a fruit [of action], it would not be possible for it to follow strictly from one's capacity, because of the consequence that the fruit would be absent due to the cause of deficiency. For the fruit must arise from the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*); and a means of accomplishment, which requires the completeness of its constituent parts (*aṅga*), cannot be established as such when there is a deficiency of parts. [The author] replies: "What is this?"

[Objection: There is a deficiency [of the rite]. [Response: If it is argued that there would be a loss of its status as being for the sake of the injunction (*codanārthatva*), he says: "In that case, there is no deficiency. Why?

Because even when performed according to one's capacity and endowed with the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) in the lifelong rite (*yāvajjīvika*), it remains for the sake of the injunction. The meaning is that this is the power of the word "lifelong" (*yāvajjīva*): that even a means of accomplishment lacking some few auxiliaries is capable of producing the fruit.

If this were not so, the same undesirable consequence would apply to the opponent's view as well; thus he says: "Or, even if there is no purpose for the injunction and the capacity [of the action] is fruitless, there must still be a performance of all the constituent parts (aṅgas). Why? Because, disregarding the word 'as long as one lives' (yāvajjīva), due to the connection with the phrase 'whenever [he desires],' the injunction aims at the performance of the rite together with its parts—even if it is fruitless—and because the purpose of the injunction is not accomplished if even a single part is deficient."

If it were argued that, because there is no goal to be accomplished (sādhya) apart from the action itself, there is no requirement for auxiliary factors (aṅga), and that the word "as long as life lasts" (yāvajjīva) is intended to indicate the absence of such a goal; [the author] refutes this: "In that case, it is more logical that the ritual act (karman) is indeed not an auxiliary factor. Why? Because its means are already known. He raises an objection: "But even an action, insofar as it is of the nature of an injunction, has an unknown essence."

If it is argued that [the primary act] requires its constituent parts (*aṅga*) for the fulfillment of the purpose of the injunction (*codanā*), [the response is as follows]: although the nature of the action is worldly and achievable by worldly means, nevertheless, because it is non-worldly (*alaukika*) in the form accessible through the injunction, and because the injunction’s purpose consists of the action together with its parts, the performance of the parts is likewise appropriate. He refutes this: "all parts... [and so on].

There is the risk of [the doctrine's] collapse. Anticipating this objection, he states their equality: "If it is argued that for verbal roots expressing an action, capacity (*śakti*) is a cooperative factor, then by the same logic, capacity would also belong to the injunction (*codanā*) based on the scriptural text regarding 'as long as one lives. Even for one who asserts a result [of the injunction], that [capacity] does not [apply]."

That which is designated as the *darśapūrṇamāsa* is understood from its originative injunction (*utpattivākya*); thus, there is an absence of [injunctions] that are not originative. Furthermore, nothing else [is the object], because it is the means to the highest good (*śreyas*). As it has been said: "For their status as a means to the highest good is always understood from the Veda," and "The teaching regarding them is that 'this is the means for attaining that. Nor is it...

The status of being a cause for transgression (*pratyavāya*) in the case of an instrument [of action] is precluded because it is impossible for that which is non-existent to be a cause; this has already been refuted by the staff [in the discussion on the nature of injunctions]. Furthermore, what is this "form" (*rūpa*) that constitutes the meaning of the Vedic injunction? For the essential nature of the ritual act (*karma-svarūpa*) consists in the renunciation of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) directed toward a deity, and since that is apprehended through other means of knowledge (*māna*), it does not constitute the meaning of the injunction in that regard.
The meaning is that [the nature of the action] is known through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Now, let it be granted that the essential form of the ritual act is cognizable through other means of knowledge; however, as for its having the *puroḍāśa* cake prepared on eight potsherds (*kapāla*) as its substance and Agni as its deity—this [is known] from the [scriptural injunction]: "The *āgneya* [offering] consists of eight potsherds."

[The opponent argues: "It is impossible to understand [the ritual] from anything other than its originative injunction (*utpattivākya*). Furthermore, once a ritual action has been understood through its various qualifications by means of the originative injunction, no other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is capable of adding or subtracting anything from it; for if such were done, there would follow the consequence of having to grasp the very nature of that [action] anew, since it would not have been known from any other source. Bearing this intention in mind, he raises the objection: "If [it is argued that] the Darśapūrṇamāsa..."

[The opponent] refutes [this view]: [If it were so,] since [the details] are understood from the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*), there would follow the non-existence of those things that are not part of the originative injunction. For only that much of a subsidiary element—such as the substance, the deity, and so forth—which is understood from the originative injunction cannot be abandoned; because if that were abandoned, it would entail the abandonment of the very nature of the ritual action (*karmasvarūpa*). Let there be no total rejection; [but] other [elements...]

Furthermore, there would follow the consequence of the non-existence of those auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) which are connected to the production of the rite— namely, the *sannipatyopakārakas* such as threshing (*avaghāta*), and the *ārādupakārakas* such as the *prayāja* offerings—

which are "non-productive" (*anautpattika*) in the sense that they are not connected to the production of the primary rites such as the *Āgneya*. Indeed, upon their abandonment, the essential nature of the rite (*karmasvarūpa*), as understood from the independent originative injunction (*utpattivākya*), would be lost.

It exists. Moreover, nothing else is [the means], because that alone is the means to the highest good (*śreyas*). As it has been said: "For their status as means to the highest good is eternally understood from the Veda," and "The teaching regarding them is that 'this is the means for attaining that.

Furthermore, as for what was stated—that the necessity of performing the ritual action is understood from the optative suffix (*liṅ*) due to its connection with the phrase "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīvam*)—[that too is addressed].

Furthermore, people understand that a certain action must necessarily be performed because an offense (*pratyavāya*) occurs if it is not done; for the kind of activity prompted by fear is not the same as that prompted by greed. Therefore, we shall postulate only the offense caused by its non-performance as the result, and not a fruit characterized by the destruction of previously acquired demerit (*durita*). This is so because there are many scriptural passages such as, "One who does not perform the enjoined rite... and so forth.
The statements of the authors of the Dharmaśāstras and the supplementary portions of their texts—which declare that "he who knows this will attain [the goal]"—are therefore addressed as follows:

nor is non-performance a cause of sin (pratyavāya). This is because it is logically impossible for a non-existent thing to be a cause. The meaning is this: while it is true that non-performance is removed by performance, why must it be removed? Because it is the cause of sin.

If it is argued that [it arises] from you (the agent), that is incorrect. Why? Because it is logically impossible for a non-existent thing to be a cause. Furthermore, a negative entity (*prāgabhāva*) in the form of the absence of transgression cannot be produced by an instrument (*karaṇa*) which is a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*). Now, one might object: "In the case of the non-performance of a mandatory rite (*nitya*), at that time there are indeed other various actions—ultimately even such things as the blinking of an eye."
They produce a transgression; however, even though those [auxiliaries] exist, they do not produce it in the case of the obligatory rite (nityakriyā).
Thus, since the status of being something to be accomplished (sādhyatva) is equal, there is no logical inconsistency regarding the fore-sacrifices (prayāja) and other such elements.

For that which is useless either in its own nature or toward the result is not an auxiliary (*aṅga*). Furthermore, there is no such usage [of the term "auxiliary"] for such a thing. Nor can it be argued: "Since action is inherently painful, why should one's engagement [in it] not be postulated as resulting from the incidental destruction of sin, even if it were non-scriptural (*aśāstrīya*)? It is not possible to so postulate. To explain: [the text says] "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīvam*).
"One should sacrifice" (juhuyāt) prompts a person toward a mental disposition (bhāvanā) colored by the act of offering; this is "incitement" (pravarttanā).

And this [incitement] is, through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), nothing other than the state of being a required means for the object of engagement, or, as "deterrence" (nivarttanā), the state of being a means to an undesirable end for the object of desisting. Therefore, it belongs precisely to that [object] toward which it incites and from which it causes one to desist.

It establishes that [the action] is a means to welfare and not a means to non-welfare; it does not, however, venture to convey that an action performed at another's time of sacrifice is a cause of sin, for when a direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) is possible,
it is improper to resort to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

As for what was said— that activity arising from fear is certain, whereas that arising from greed is not— that is true. For even when the tenfold activities of speech, mind, and body are avoided by a discerning person because they are prohibited, if they should nonetheless occur day and night due to fate, sin is incurred, resulting in various kinds of unbearable suffering.
Those who fear the seed of suffering will certainly exert themselves toward whatever is perceived as a means to achieve their desired end, even if that end is [merely] the cessation of pain.
Nor is it logical to claim that the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is sometimes "being a means to a desired object" and sometimes "being a means to an unconsidered desired object.

For if there were a single essence [in all cases], the diversity of meanings would not be possible, as it would lead to the consequence of a lack of systematic order (*avyavasthā*). It is not [the case].

And there is no contradiction with the Smṛti. Even though [the obligatory rites] are means for achieving what is desired, when they are not performed, the sins [accumulated] remain undestroyed; these will be destroyed by other expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*), so there is no logical inconsistency.

Furthermore, a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*), which is required when doubt arises, serves as the cause for determination. This applies when [the rite] is understood as a required means (*apekṣitopāyatva*).

Since there is no doubt that the destruction of previously incurred evil and the absence of transgression (pratyavāya) result from the performance [of rites], the obligatory (nitya) acts have no requirement for supplementary statements (vākyaśeṣa);
thus, the supplementary statement is merely an explanatory praise (arthavāda). Enough with this elaboration.
Furthermore, in this view, since the status of being an object to be accomplished (sādhyatva) is equal for both the Prayāja offerings and the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices...

Furthermore, since the third case-ending can also be explained in the sense of the second case, or because the *prayāja* offerings and so forth can somehow be established as instruments (*karaṇa*) within the process of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), their status as subsidiaries (*aṅga*) would be untenable due to the absence of a means of proof (*pramāṇa*) for their application. For they define "context" (*prakaraṇa*) as the statement of that which is to be performed when it stands in need of the manner of performance (*itikartavyatā*). Such [a context] does not exist here in the case of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*).

Since the two permanent sacrifices (*nitya*) are fruitless, and since the *prayāja* and other subsidiaries do not require the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices as long as those two are not yet to be performed, why would the *prayāja*s and others require the *darśapūrṇamāsa*s?
Thus, context (*prakaraṇa*) cannot be the means of application (*viniyojaka*). Nor is there any purpose for these [subsidiaries] apart from the context.

If another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is either asserted or recognized [for the auxiliary], then subsidiarity (*aṅgatā*) is not tenable in the absence of a function as its door (*dvāra*), because subsidiarity is pervaded by that [function] and thus ceases when it ceases. Thus he says: "Indeed, that which is useless with respect to either the essential nature (*svarūpa*) or the function (*kārya*) is not an auxiliary."

It is like climbing onto a heated stone and so forth. Furthermore, if it were produced by evil, human effort would be rendered useless; or, if it were not produced by that [effort], there would be no destruction of it. However, there is no fault in its ripening through a scriptural means.

If, then, even when there is a fruit, there is no inclusion of all the constituent parts (*aṅga*) in the case of a rite performed for a specific desire (*kāmya*), it would be the same in that case as well. If you argue that because of the scriptural injunction "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīva*), it must be so in the other case [the obligatory rite], then let it be the same here as well because of the scriptural injunction "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*). Just as it is impossible to perform [the rite] for the duration of one's life without omitting some parts, so too it is impossible for every person desiring heaven to perform it with all its parts at every time and in every way.

In that case, there can be a restriction [of the application] to only those [auxiliaries] which one is capable of performing; thus, whoever is capable of as many [as he can], he shall perform that many.

For, due to the conflict with the injunctions regarding the auxiliaries (*aṅga*), the scriptural text concerning "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*)—which refers to anyone who seeks [the result]—does not require a specific restriction.

However, when there is a dependence on capability and no conflict with the injunctions for the auxiliaries, it does not serve as a reason for requiring a specific restriction, just as in the case of obligatory rites (*nitya*).

[Objection: Let it be granted that there is no lack of application; however, the application itself through context (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth—which is synonymous with "implication" (*ākṣepa*) by the injunction (*vidhi*)—will establish the status of being a subsidiary (*aṅgatva*) for the *prayāja* offerings and the like, just as it does for gender, number, and so on. To this, he says:
because there is an absence even of such an application—"of such a kind" means even though [the *prayājas*] are equal to the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices in being things to be accomplished (*sādhya*).

For one who is already enjoined, the undertaking (*upādāna*) of an action is not possible through further application (*prayukti*), because undertaking follows from the specific injunction (*viniyoga*).

For this very reason, such rules as "one should not look at the rising sun" or "gold must be worn," being devoid of a specific injunction and not being implied by a ritual injunction (*kratu-vidhi*), do not serve the purpose of the ritual (*kratvartha*). Nor [is it the case that they are not *kratvartha*] simply because the action involves suffering.
If [the suffering] were not prescribed by scripture, its occurrence would result from the incidental destruction of sin, like climbing onto a heated stone and so forth.

Furthermore, if that suffering arising from the performance of obligatory rites (*nityakriyā*) were caused by previously accumulated sin, then the injunction [for those rites] would be purposeless; for since the obligatory rites arise solely from the ripening of sins from previous lives, human effort (*puruṣakāra*) would be rendered futile.

Or, if it were not caused by that [action], there would be no destruction [of the sin], because sin is opposed to its own fruit. Now, one might object: "If evil is destroyed by a rite not performed [for that purpose], then how, even in your view, will it be destroyed by obligatory (nitya) karma? To this he says: "But there is no fault in ripening [the sin] by means prescribed in the scriptures, just as in the case of expiations (prāyaścitta); for 'ripening' (pācana) means the production of a result."

The state of being present [in the ritual], its absolute cessation, and its digestion (vipācana) constitute the meaning of "prolonged duration" (*cirabhāva*). This matter is accessible through the scriptures and does not admit of objection;
the point is that practices such as climbing a heated stone slab do not fall within the scope of scriptural authority or logical reasoning.
Now, he raises an objection: "If, then, even when there is a fruit, there is no performance of all the constituent parts (*sarvāṅga*), then this would apply to optional rites (*kāmya*) as well."

It might be so. The *codaka* (the rule of transfer) itself raises an objection and refutes it: "If it is argued that because of the scriptural injunction 'as long as one lives' (*yāvajjīva*), there is no requirement to include all auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) in other obligatory rites (*nitya*), then let it be the same here as well, because of the injunction 'one desiring heaven' (*svargakāma*). He states this in a single passage: "Just as it is impossible to perform the lifelong rite without omitting its parts, so too it is impossible for every person desiring heaven to perform it in its entirety, just as in the case of the obligatory rite."

When one is able to perform as many [auxiliaries] as possible, then there is the inclusion of that many; likewise, in the case of optional rites (*kāmya*) as well, whoever is able to perform as many will include that many.
This might be argued: because the auxiliaries are enjoined as permanent (*nitya*), and because such a restriction would be untenable, it does not apply to the seeker of results (*arthin*).

The justification for the injunction is based on the mere [desire]. However, the scriptural mention of the seeker (*arthin*) is also justified by taking it to refer to one capable of performing all the constituent parts (*sarvāṅga*). For it is not the case that he does not desire heaven; therefore, in the case of optional rites (*kāmya*), it is proper to say "whoever desires this [specific result].
Thus [it is stated on p. 227].

Now, it might be thought that in order not to obstruct the scriptural injunction for one desiring heaven (*svargakāma-śruti*), the injunctions regarding the subsidiaries (*aṅga-vidhi*)—which apply without distinction—would indeed be obstructed by the restriction according to one's capacity (*yathāśakti*). But this is the same even in the case of the obligatory (*nitya*) rite; for the scriptural injunction "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīva-śruti*) has no other possible application.

In that case, the scriptural injunction for one desiring such [a result] is perfectly consistent even with respect to one capable of performing all the subsidiaries. Because there is no contradiction therein, [the principle of] *kāṃsya* [does not apply].

According to the principle of the *bhojinī* (the eater), the operation of the principal [act] conforms to that [of the subsidiary]. It is true that a contradiction—characterized by the contraction of the scope of the scriptural injunction for one who desires heaven (*svargakāma*)—has been shown without conflict. In that case, when there is a conflict between the subordinate and the principal, conformity to the principal is preferable.

As it is said: "Indeed, due to a conflict with the injunctions for the subsidiaries, the scriptural injunction for one who desires heaven, although its scope extends to all seekers, follows the specific [restriction]."

It is obstructed. However, when there is consideration of capacity (*śakti*) and no contradiction with the injunctions regarding the subsidiaries (*aṅga*), there is no reason for that [capacity] to favor a specific [limited] application, as it does in the case of obligatory rites (*nitya*). This is the meaning: when a contradiction exists with the injunctions for the subsidiaries, the scriptural statement "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*), which applies without distinction, must be interpreted as having a restricted scope; but in the case of obligatory rites, as in the rule "whosoever is able to perform as many [as he can]," there is consideration of capacity.

It is logical that there should be a restriction of the scriptural injunction regarding one who desires heaven (*svargakāma*), which has been set forth, so as not to conflict with the injunctions concerning the auxiliary rites (*aṅga-vidhi*). Now, it might be argued: "The conflict characterized by the restriction of the scope is indeed equal for both the injunctions of the auxiliaries and the scriptural injunction regarding one who desires heaven;
however, since the injunctions of the auxiliaries are numerous, it is better that the single scriptural injunction regarding one who desires heaven be restricted in accordance with them."

He raises an objection: "Now, it might be thought that if there is no contradiction with the scriptural injunction for one who desires heaven (*svargakāma*), then the injunctions regarding the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) would not be restricted, since they apply generally, unlike the restriction according to one's capacity. He refutes this: "The same applies even to the obligatory (*nitya*) rite.
The sense is that there too, there is only a single scriptural injunction for "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīva*), whereas the injunctions regarding the subsidiaries are many. This might be so.

If, in the case of a permanent rite (*nitya*), one were not to rely on the consideration of capacity regarding how many and which auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) are required at any given time, then the scriptural injunction "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīva*) would be completely contradicted. For it is impossible that one could sacrifice "as long as one lives" while including every single auxiliary part;

however, it is possible that one who desires heaven (*svargakāma*) might sacrifice while including all the auxiliary parts. Indeed, the inclusion of all auxiliary parts [is not possible for a *nitya*].

He says that for one who is capable and desires heaven, the term "desirer of heaven" (*svargakāma*) is not non-expressive, because the injunction "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīva*) has no other recourse. In that case, the scriptural mention of "desiring such [a result]" (*evamkāma*) is indeed appropriate even for one who is capable of performing all the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*). Now, one might object: even if the desirer of heaven is capable, how can that term have an unrestricted application?

Anticipating the objection, "Is [the primary injunction] restricted by the subsidiary injunctions? he says: "In that case, because there is no contradiction, the operation of the subsidiary injunctions follows the primary one according to the 'Kāṃsyabhojin' maxim. This is the meaning: for the word *kāmin* (one who has a desire), even when being restricted by the qualification of desire—which functions differently for each person—would be contradicted if it were restricted in a way that conflicted with the subsidiary injunctions.

According to the maxim of the one who eats from a bronze vessel (*kāṃsyabhojinnyāya*). For example, suppose a teacher is the principal figure and always eats from various specific vessels, while a disciple, being subordinate, eats only from a bronze vessel. In that case, since it is necessary to employ a single vessel for the sake of simplicity in practice, if some other vessel were employed out of deference to the method of the principal figure, the disciple’s meal would not [be properly served].

It would be so. However, when a bronze vessel (*kāṃsyapātra*) is used, there is no contradiction with the teacher’s meal consisting of eating from an indefinite vessel. Therefore, since there is no contradiction, even the principal [rule] is indeed restricted in accordance with the subordinate [rule]; thus, "in accordance with that" means the operation of the rule for the principal act (*aṅgin*) without contradicting the rules for the subsidiaries (*aṅga*). He refutes this as follows: "True, there is no contradiction..."

However, it has been shown that there is a contradiction characterized by the restriction of the scope of the scriptural injunction for one who desires heaven (*svargakāma-śruti*). Therefore, this is not a case for the application of the "eating from a bronze vessel" maxim (*kāṃsyapātra-bhojinī-nyāya*). To explain: in that case, even though the teacher eats from an indefinite variety of vessels, he does not—[p.

It is like the worldly practice. For example, when one says, "Feed the Brahmins with various kinds of food and utensils," the assignment of the utensils is according to one's capacity; thus, the number of Brahmins is determined in accordance with the available utensils. In the same way, the subsidiary injunctions (*aṅgavidhi*) do not require absolute completeness. Therefore, even in the case of optional rites (*kāmya*), let it be simply "as much as one is able to perform," and not "whatever [one can do] whenever [one wishes]."

"One might be able [to do so]," they say, because there is no distinction [between the cases]. This is not sound. For it would entail a discrepancy in the single injunction of performance (*prayogavidhi*), as one would then have to eat from all the vessels at once—which would contradict a disciple who eats from a fixed vessel—and the scriptural statement regarding desire (*kāmaśruti*), which functions solely by establishing a connection with desire, presents itself to any seeker whatsoever, whether capable or incapable, only once.
"Being paid when the capable suitor is present, how could she not be restrained by the rules regarding the limbs?
[The opponent objects: "Granted that there is a conflict, nevertheless, because they are more numerous, those pertaining to the limbs will be stronger and will set aside [the primary rule].
Anticipating this, he says: "In that case, when there is a conflict between the subsidiary and the principal, compliance with the principal is better, as in the world."

For when there is equality in every respect, numerical abundance is indeed the cause of greater strength; here, however, even a single scriptural injunction regarding desire (*kāma-śruti*), by virtue of its predominance, is certainly capable of regulating the subsidiary injunctions (*aṅga-vidhi*) despite their greater number due to their lack of predominance.
He explains the illustration "as in the world" (*lokavat*): "Just as [one says], 'Feed the Brahmins with this [food] individually'..."

"By means of various implements and food"— just as there is a restriction for a Brāhmaṇa based on his capacity and the arrangement of the implements provided, so too, when the injunctions regarding the subsidiaries are not restricted by the desire-based scriptural statement (kāmaśruti), then the rule is established that whichever person is capable of providing as many subsidiaries as he can,
he performs the primary rite equipped with that many. In that case:

The primary injunction sometimes requires certain subsidiaries and sometimes does not; thus, the requirement for subsidiary injunctions is not absolute. For example, when an understanding of an option arises—derived from the force of both a prescription and a prohibition—such as "one should shave the hair and beard, or not," the primary injunction would not necessarily require the subsidiary act of shaving at all. What then?

He says that even if one were to consider it thus, it is established that all these injunctions for optional rites (*kāma-vidhi*) are auxiliary (*aṅga*) [to the permanent ones]: "And thus, the injunctions for auxiliaries also do not have absolute dependence. And so, there would be no disparity between all the permanent (*nitya*) and optional (*kāmya*) injunctions; he says: "Therefore, even regarding optional rites, let it be simply 'as far as one is able,' and not 'he who...'"

"According as one may be able," because there is no distinction [in the capacity]. He refutes this: "This is not sound, because it would result in a discrepancy in the single injunction for performance.
This is the meaning: indeed, this scriptural injunction regarding desire (*kāma-śruti*), having been set in motion once, concerns every person who possesses the desire; if it were to apply to all...

Specifically, if one were to admit those who desire [the fruit], such as the blind and others with deficient limbs, then this injunction of performance—conditioned by the desire for heaven—would prescribe the gazing at the clarified butter (*ājyāvekṣaṇa*) toward a desirer of heaven who possesses eyes, yet that same injunction would not prescribe it toward a desirer of heaven who is blind; thus, a discrepancy (*vairūpya*) would result. For [it is impossible] that the blind and so forth...

The words are mentioned together with the word "seeker" (arthin), by which there might be a fixed determination. Now, it is not the case that the injunction of performance operates upon each [word] individually, such that there would be a discrepancy in its form; rather, through the connection to a single result, it brings about a state of single operation for one agent regarding both the purposes and the connections to the assistance of multiple primary acts. And thus...
The injunction of performance does not bring about the subsidiaries; rather, having observed that the subsidiaries are already established, it brings them together.

This is because there would otherwise follow the absurdity of postulating a separate performance for each, and because there is no usage of isolated word-meanings, as well as because there is no contradiction in the specific scriptural hearing.

That very injunction of performance (prayogavidhi) would not enjoin the performance of that very subsidiary (aṅga), but rather would merely prescribe it; furthermore, there would be the fault of conceptual complexity (kalpanāgaurava), because the performance differs according to the difference in capacity. And [the injunction] brings about the single performance of one word together with another word; that is to say, just as the subsidiaries obtained through direct statement (śruti) and so forth follow that...

Just as [the subsidiaries] are subsumed by the injunctive statement (*prayogavacana*) itself, so too, since the capacity of verbal roots expressing their meaning acts in conjunction [with other factors], the capacity of the agent is also a means of bringing about [the performance];

therefore, following the capacity of the agent who desires heaven while being blind, one will perform the collection of subsidiaries with the exception of only the "beholding of the clarified butter" (*ājyāvekṣaṇa*). [The word] *cakṣu*...

But what contradiction is there in [the mantra] being accompanied by that [word "cakṣuṣmantam"]? If one were to apply it only toward one who possesses eyes and not toward others, then there would indeed be a contradiction characterized by the inconsistency of the injunction for performance; anticipating this objection, he says:
"because it would entail the contingency of postulating multiple applications. Let there be no such inconsistency characterized by contradiction; [the mantra is] capable...

The meaning is that the statement of the performance (*prayogavacana*) indeed encounters a diversity of performance (*prayogavairūpya*)—consisting of various modes of application brought about by the adoption or avoidance of respective auxiliary elements through the establishment of the connection with capable objectives—which results in a conceptual complexity (*kalpanāgaurava*).
Now, one might object: even a conceptual complexity that is based on authoritative means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*) does not constitute a fault; and such exists here.

The authority for the scriptural injunction "one who desires heaven" consists in its non-restriction to a specific case, as it functions generally; for if there were uniformity [of application], a contradiction would arise in restricting the usage. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Because there is no usage of words in isolation, and because there is no contradiction with the specific scriptural statement. This is the meaning: discerning people utter words for the sake of communication, and that...

And thus, the meaning that is intended to be conveyed by them is precisely that which others desire to know; and it is only that which constitutes a factor of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) that others seek to understand. Furthermore, there is no linguistic usage whatsoever that can be accomplished by an unqualified object-entity alone.
Therefore, although only the mere object-entity is understood from the word, since that mere entity is not a factor of linguistic usage, the process does not terminate there.

When one word-meaning, requiring a specific qualifier, is brought into proximity by another word that is capable of it, that other word-meaning is certainly accepted as its delimitation in usage; however, it does not act as a negator [of the primary meaning]. Otherwise, because there would be no cognition of the sentence-meaning, the world would become utterly mute, with every word suspected of being severed from its function. Therefore, in this context, for one who desires heaven (*svargakāma*)—

Scripture as well, while concluding its own primary meaning in accordance with worldly usage, does not suffer any restriction when a particular qualification is presented by a suitable subsequent word or sentence; for it is not the case that [the qualification] is not obtained when a seeker is found who possesses the specific capacity to perform all the constituent parts [of the rite].

Since its own meaning (svārtha) is also [a means of knowledge] because it has as its essence that which is delimited by the connection with words expressing desire, it is unauthoritative; thus, the complexity of postulation (kalpanā-gaurava) is a fault.
It was stated that this would result in a dissimilarity in the injunction of a single performance (ekaprayoga-vidhi); he clarifies this: "For in this way, that very same..."
The rule of application (*prayogavidhi*) prescribes the performance of that very subsidiary (*aṅga*) itself; it does not [prescribe] something else.

He clarifies this by stating that it would otherwise lead to the contingency of assuming many things: "And there would be a burden of assumptions (*kalpanāgaurava*), because the performance differs according to the difference in the capacity of the subsidiaries."

Since the focus on a specific [condition] in the context of a relationship is universal, there is never any assumption of what is illogical. If it is argued that this should likewise apply even to the eternal,
such that one would live only when capable, and that the phrase "as long as" is untenable— [we reply that this applies] to cases where the causes are not fixed.

How so? Furthermore, there would be the consequence of the oblation being performed continuously. If it is argued that this is not the case because of the adherence to the specific mention of particular times, then—alas!—the scriptural injunction "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīva*), even while following the injunctions regarding the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*), must connect with capability; thus, by following the injunctions regarding the auxiliaries, it would mean "whenever [the capacity exists]."
Now, it may be thought: even while living, one is entitled only to a rite that possesses its constituent parts (*sāṅga*), not to one devoid of parts;

for there is no usage of a mere injunction or a mere individual element, and thus what was stated—that there is no contradiction with the specific scriptural hearing—is clarified: since the fact that a word refers to a specific [meaning] when connected with another word is universal, it is never unreasonable.

Regarding the term "conceptual construction" (*kalpanā*): Now, if it is argued that when a word is connected with another word, its capacity for denoting a specific [object] is not contradictory—and thus the word *svargakāma* (desiring heaven) has a qualified scope, resulting in the connection "whoever [desires heaven], whenever [the rite is performed]"—then, alas, by the same logic of capacity, even "living" (*jīvana*) would be delimited, and one would have to admit the connection "whoever [lives], whenever [the rite is performed]" even in the case of a compulsory (*nitya*) rite. To this, he says: "Even in the case of the compulsory... (*nitye 'pi*).

"In that case, let it be exactly so: 'as long as one is able to live'. [The opponent] objects: "If it is argued that the phrase 'as long as' (yāvat) is untenable," the underlying intention (*abhisandhi*) is as follows: Since the desire for heaven (*svargakāmanā*) is introduced with respect to each individual conscious agent, there is no contradiction; for even when only one person is capable, the scriptural injunction (*śruti*) regarding the "desirer of heaven" retains its relevant meaning (*samavetārtha*).

But here, since the word *yāvat* (as long as) has the sense of pervading the entire duration of life, while the word *yadā* (when) restricts [the action] to a single portion of time, there is an inconsistency due to this contradiction of pervasion, similar to the contradiction between "it exists" and "it does not exist. He provides the rebuttal:
"How so, in the case of occasional rites (*naimittika*) with indefinite causes? This is not an absolute rule, for it does not apply to occasional rites that are not connected with the word *yāvat*.

The meaning is that the connection "when one is able" (*yadā śaknuyāt*) is not appropriate in the context of baths during eclipses of the planets and so forth. Now, he raises an objection regarding the connection with the word "at present" (*idānīm*): even if there were the connection "when one is able," it would lead to the consequence of performing the *homa* continuously; furthermore, the term "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīvam*) [would apply] to the duration of life.

The phrase "for the purpose of pervading a delimited time" means that as long as one lives, one must offer oblations by this [fire]; for if the restriction of morning and evening were not required, the entire worldly activity of drinking and eating would cease without interruption.
Now, if it is argued that this is not so because of the adherence to the inclusion of specific times, he says in response: "Alas, the inclusion of specific times..."

Even though the scriptural injunction regarding "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīva*) conforms to the injunctions for all the subsidiary parts (*aṅga*), it connects with the relationship [of performance] based on capability;

thus, in accordance with the injunctions for the subsidiary parts, the term "when" (*yadā*) would apply. This is the meaning: just as, by the force of the injunctions for the times of evening and morning, the phrase "as long as" is restricted to life as delimited by those very times of evening and morning, so too [is it restricted] by the injunctions for all the subsidiary parts.
By implication, through syntactical unity with that [injunction], life itself— as delimited by the time when there is the capacity for the performance of all auxiliary parts—

is what will be connected [to the rite] by the phrase "as long as. Consequently, even in the case of a compulsory (nitya) rite, the connection is established just as in the case of an optional (kāmya) one, by means of the phrase "whenever one is able."

Now, if it is thought that even while living one is entitled only to the performance of a rite with its constituent parts (*sāṅga*), and not to a prescription devoid of its parts, because it is understood that only such a rite with its parts functions as the instrument; [the author], raising the objection—"But even so, what is the difference between the obligatory (*nitya*) and the optional (*kāmya*)?"—says: "However, for one who is entitled, the performance [of the obligatory] lasts as long as the entitlement, and the parts..."

However, the application (*prayoga*) of that which is the subject under discussion does not cease merely because of the requirements of the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*), but continues as long as the qualification (*adhikāra*) persists; for that [application] is dependent upon the qualification according to what is possible. Nor does this entail an over-extension (*prasaṅga*) even to optional rites (*kāmya*), because desires are directed toward the result (*kārya*).

Furthermore, because the entitlement (*adhikāra*) is rooted in the performance of the ritual, and because the occasional rite (*naimittika*) depends upon the means for its accomplishment, it ceases upon the obstruction of those means. This is the intended meaning: although, by the force of syntactical unity with the injunctions for the auxiliary parts (*aṅga-vidhi*), the entitlement of a living person capable of performing the entire set of auxiliaries is understood from the injunction, nevertheless, [this applies only] to one who possesses the capacity.

Suppose a person, having reflected and set out to act, subsequently becomes unable due to some negligence to perform a few constituent parts, yet remains capable of performing all the others. In that case, should he—merely because he is incapable regarding those few parts—desist from the performance altogether? Or rather, even where he is incapable, does his entitlement (adhikāra) still persist along with those very parts he cannot perform?

Should one perform [the rite] by the force of what is understood? Or rather, should one employ the principal act (pradhāna) accompanied by the collection of other limbs, excluding those few limbs that are impossible to perform? It is according to what is possible, because that [performance] depends upon qualification (adhikāra).
