This is the meaning: even though there is a cognition of qualification, since it is impossible to perform what cannot be done, and because qualification would otherwise be lost entirely if one were to desist from everything, [one must act as far as possible].

Because of the contradiction [with scripture], there is the risk of overstepping the qualification (*adhikāra*); therefore, the final position is accepted. Indeed, this injunction regarding performance (*prayogavidhi*) relies upon the performance of the primary rite accompanied by those other auxiliary elements that are not impossible to perform, in accordance with the qualification. Now, one might object: "But isn't all of this the same even in the case of rites for specific desires (*kāmya*)? Anticipating this, he says: "And there is no such application [of this rule] even in the case of a *kāmya* rite."

Because the qualification for rites performed for a desired end (*kāmya*) culminates in the result, and because the occasional rite (*naimittika*) culminates in the performance itself; this is the intended meaning.

For in the case of a rite for a desired end—such as "one desiring heaven should sacrifice"—the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) is characterized by the heaven to be achieved, and he understands that very task to be the duty which is favorable to his own qualification, since it is precisely that which is to be achieved that serves as the qualification.

But if the action were not conducive to that [end], then one who desires heaven would not be the *niyojya* (the person to be impelled) with respect to it; moreover, an action (*kārya*) defined by an effort (*kṛti*) cannot be determined when that effort is not being cognized. For one does not perceive a qualified object without having first perceived its qualifier. Indeed, an action is called "primary" (*pradhāna*) when it is pervaded by an effort; and its primacy consists in being the objective of that effort.

The activity of *kṛti* (volitional effort). And in such sentences, *kṛti* must be understood as the operation of a conscious agent, which is precisely what is denoted by the term "effort" (*prayatna*). For it is the conscious person who is the one to be enjoined (*niyojya*), and he undertakes that task alone in which he perceives himself as being directed. He cannot perceive himself as being directed toward something that is pervaded by the operation of another. And effort—
Like a cognition, it cannot be defined without an object, and its object is generally the meaning of a verbal root (*bhāvārtha*).

This is because an effort directed toward that [root-meaning] alone proceeds with the aim of producing an unseen result (*apūrva*), which is denoted by the verbal suffix. Indeed, even in the world, the effort of a cook cannot proceed with the aim of preparing rice (*odana*) unless its object is the verbal root-meaning in the form of the act of cooking (*pāka*).

Furthermore, since an effect cannot be determined without an effort (*kṛti*), and since effort is not perceived without the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*), the meaning of the verbal root becomes the object (*viṣaya*) of the effect by way of effort; this is because it is bound to that [effort]. This is derived from the etymology of the word *viṣaya* from the root *ṣiñ* (to bind). Thus, the effect, which is the means to the desired end, attains the status of being the object.

Since one who proceeds toward the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*) cannot reach the goal without a means, it is precisely by placing the state of being a means (*upāyatā*) foremost that the status of being an object (*viṣayatā*) is understood for the *bhāvārtha* in the case of rites performed for a desired end (*kāmya*). And this state of being a means is accomplished through the performance of all its constituent parts (*aṅga*).

Furthermore, since the status of being a means (*sādhana*) is understood only so far as each constituent part (*aṅga*), the accomplishment of the task occurs only through the inclusion of all the parts. Indeed, it is not otherwise; for the status of being a constituent part belongs to all of them when combined. If that status were attributed to each individually, there would arise the contingency of various options based on the eightfold defects [of ritual performance]. In that case, even if an adventitious part is omitted, the entire set of constituents [would remain deficient].

Because the means of production—the instrument—is unattained, it lacks the status of a means; consequently, since the qualification of the agent is not perceived, one does not perform an optional (*kāmya*) rite with deficient limbs by its force, but rather strives for the inclusion of all components. However, a capable person may desist from the performance at some point. But this mode does not apply to the obligatory (*nitya*) rite.

It is possible. For in that case, the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) is not qualified by the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*), such that he would not understand the task—which is a means—as something to be done (*kārya*).

Therefore, the person to be enjoined, delimited by a cause established from elsewhere, first understands the task as having the mere meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*) as its object, through the mediation of the act of doing (*kṛti*). But once he has understood the task as having an object...
Since the effect has its nature conditioned by the *kṛti* (the volitional effort), and since *kṛti*— being an action— is inseparable from an instrument (*karaṇa*),

that which requires an instrument for the sake of the effect attains the status of an instrument with respect to the verbal root-meaning (*bhāvārtha*) when it becomes the object [of that effort] due to its proximity.
Nor is it the case that once the *kṛti* has ceased, the verbal root-meaning cannot be the instrument for that very same *kṛti*.
It must be said: because in the world it is perceived that there is an absence of effort (*kṛti*) toward that specific *apūrva* which is delimited by that [action],
just as the axe, although pervaded by the agent's action characterized by raising and lowering,
becomes an instrument (*sādhana*) precisely with respect to that [action], since the raising and lowering directed toward the axe possess the nature of cutting.

Because [the action] is obtained [from the verbal root]. For people do not designate "cutting" as occurring when there is merely the raising and lowering [of an axe] based on a clod of earth, provided that a state of duality has not been produced. Therefore, although the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*) is pervaded by the action, since the action proceeds for the sake of the *apūrva* (the unseen potency), the meaning of the verbal root is not the object (*karman*) with respect to that [action]; rather, the *apūrva* is the primary object, because the action is performed with it as its goal.

Because it has already commenced. Thus, even though [the sacrifice] is eternal, since the verbal root-meaning (bhāvārtha) which serves as the object is understood to be performed subsequently, one who is capable of performing the principal rite along with its subsidiaries—having understood that they constitute the means—is already engaged. If, due to some cause, he is unable to perform even a portion [of it], nevertheless, because the qualification (adhikāra) has been cognized, the verbal root-meaning remains as a concomitant of that cognition.

One cannot cease from the means of understanding the subject matter [of the Veda], but rather one continues to perform the ritual application (prayoga), albeit with some deficiency in its constituent parts.
This state of being fixed upon the ritual application is presented as the opposite of being fixed upon the task to be accomplished (kāryaniṣṭhatva).
If the qualification based on desire (kāmādhikāra) were fixed upon the task to be accomplished, what would follow? To this he says:

Since the result depends upon the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), and since it is understood that every constituent part (*aṅga*) constitutes a means of accomplishment, the result is achieved only through the performance of all the parts; therefore, there is no application of the principle of *prasaṅga* (incidental performance) in the case of optional rites (*kāmya*). Now, one might object: "In both cases—the optional and the occasional (*naimittika*)—the entitlement (*adhikāra*) itself must be performed. For it is from the injunctive suffix (*vidhi-pratyaya*) that the mandate (*niyoga*) as the task to be accomplished is understood, and that alone is the primary [object]."
Because that [injunction] must be performed, and because its performance is impossible without [the agent’s] execution; because such execution is impossible without the person possessing agency;
because agency is not established without the qualified persons (adhikārin) having ownership over the ritual act;
and because qualification is not possible for the self without its being subject to the mandate (niyoga), which is the primary action to be accomplished.
Since the injunction cannot reach its conclusion without an agent who perceives the state of being stable, such an agent is required.
And since he cannot be understood as unqualified, there arises an expectancy for his qualification; in some cases, this qualification is indeed established as something already accomplished.
The entitlement (*adhikāra*) itself must indeed be established. True; in one case it extends to the occasion (*nimitta*), while in the other it extends to the result (*phala*).

Among these, when it extends to the occasion, for one who possesses the occasion and is entitled but does not perform [the rite], there is a transgression of the entitlement; thus the performance occurs according to what is possible. However, when it extends to the result, if there is a deficiency in the auxiliary members (*aṅga*), the result is not realized.

The desire for the fruit (*phalakāmitā*), which is the cause of qualification (*adhikārahetu*), ceases; thus, due to the absence of qualification, one does not undertake the life-stage duties (*jīvanādi*) nor heaven and so forth, which in some cases have the status of an end (*sādhyabhāva*) brought about by desire and other factors. Furthermore, the fact that the qualification is the end to be accomplished (*sādhyatā*) does not undermine the fact that the mandate (*niyoga*) itself is the end to be accomplished, for the mandate is what is to be accomplished.

Because the state of being an object to be accomplished (*sādhyatva*) is a qualification of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), and because of the maxim that "an injunction does not sublate the occasioning cause" (*nimitta*), the meaning is as follows: in both cases—the obligatory (*nitya*) and the optional (*kāmya*)—the injunction itself is what must be performed, since it has the effect (*kārya*) as its ultimate focus; thus, there is no difference between them.
He explains: It is true that in one case it extends to the cause (*nimitta*), while in the other it extends to the fruit (*phala*). This is the meaning:

because the scope [of the injunction] extends to the cause, and because the cause itself is not something to be accomplished (*asādhya*), one does not understand the task as having another means (*upāya*) characterized by that cause; rather, it has only the objective of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*) as its domain. And in that state, with respect to each...

Since the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*) is understood as being invariably concomitant with the result, it exists solely as that which colors or qualifies the result, and not as a means to it. Consequently, the qualification (*adhikāra*) occasioned by the result has as its object only the *bhāvārtha* itself, and not the *bhāvārtha* as a means. Therefore, because the understanding of the qualification arises from the very form of the *bhāvārtha*, it consists of that alone.

And because the status of being a cause culminates in the cause itself, it is said to be "culminating in the cause" (*nimittaparyanta*). However, in the context of desire (*kāma*), since the primary task is understood to be the means to that desire, it is said to be "culminating in the fruit" (*phalaparyanta*). If this is so, what is established thereby? To this he says: "In that case, regarding the one culminating in the cause, for the possessor of the cause, all the subsidiary parts (*aṅga*)..."

For one who is capable of performing the rite in its entirety but, by fate, is unable to perform some part of it, the *niyoga* (the mandate) remains focused solely on the essential meaning (*bhāvārtha*).

Since that mandate does not lapse due to the omission of a minor part, the person who is authorized (*adhikṛta*) does not transgress his qualification even if he does not carry out the performance of the entire ritual; thus, the performance should be carried out according to what is possible.

However, when the qualification for the result reaches its culmination, if there is a deficiency in the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*), there is no status as a means (*sādhana*), because only that which possesses all its auxiliaries has the nature of a means.
Since the result does not arise from what is not a means, or else, if it were to arise, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), the desire for the result ceases.
Now, one might object: "Is it not impossible to say that the desire for the result—which is personally experienced by each individual—does not cease even when the auxiliaries are lost?"

Anticipating the objection that this must be stated, he says: "The cause of entitlement (*adhikāra-hetu*). This is the meaning: indeed, the desire for the fruit, by means of the aforementioned path, brings about the status of being the object of entitlement for the verbal root-meaning (*bhāvārtha*) which serves as the instrument;

thus, it is the cause of entitlement. And that [desire], when there is a deficiency in the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*), because the verbal root-meaning alone lacks the status of being a means, results in the absence of an object [of action].

It is said that because the qualification of the subject (*viṣayin*) has also ceased—even though [the desire for results] exists—it does not exist as a cause for qualification; thus, the desire for the fruit (*phalakāmitā*) ceases. Therefore, due to the absence of qualification, there is no fault of overstepping the qualification, and so there is no performance [of the rite] in an arbitrary manner.

[Page 234] The term "defect" (doṣa) implies that the performance is not merely arbitrary. Thus, there is no lack of continuous performance, nor is there a failure to apply [the practice] to objects already secured according to one's capacity; this applies to obligatory rites (nitya), but not to optional ones (kāmya)—in this way, everything is consistent.
This is not correct. My friend, please explain this: is the entitlement (*adhikāra*) dependent upon one's capacity?

Indeed, if the entitlement does not cease even when there is a deficiency in the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) in the case of occasional rites (*naimittika*), because it remains directed toward the mere verbal action (*bhāvārtha*) itself; then, in the case of the injunction "one should perform the *Agnihotra* as long as one lives," [the entitlement would apply] to both the evening and morning times.

Fearing that—since the qualification for the rite does not depart even in its absence due to the rite being an obligatory duty (nitya)—one might fail to offer the oblation even at the midday and other prescribed times, thereby resulting in the undesirable consequence of a continuous stream of offerings, he says: "This being the case, there is no consequence of offering oblations incessantly. The underlying intention here is as follows: although in the case of occasional rites (naimittika), the primary meaning of the verbal root [denotes the action] first...

Although the object (*viṣaya*) is indeed merely the verbal root, nevertheless, since the action (*kārya*) is qualified by its purpose (*kṛti*), there arises a requirement for an instrument (*karaṇa*);

thus, the meaning of the verbal root subsequently becomes the instrument. And when that which has acquired the status of an instrument requires auxiliary elements (*aṅga*), the auxiliaries present themselves.

Therefore, it is understood that only that which possesses innate capacity (*svābhāvikasāmarthya*) toward the performance of the rite together with its auxiliaries subsequently acquires the qualification (*adhikāra*).

There is no eligibility for the ritual as prescribed for those who possess defects such as blindness that cannot be remedied by medicine; for those who lack the required constituent parts [of the sacrifice]; for those who do not belong to a lineage of three ṛṣis when the rite requires one of three ṛṣis; for those who do not maintain the sacred fires when the rite requires the Āhavanīya and other fires; and for men who perform it at midday when it is prescribed for the morning or evening times.
This is because they lack the inherent capacity for the performance of ritual acts (*karmopasaṃhāra*). However, for those who possess innate capacity—

such as the poor or those with correctable deafness and so forth— there is indeed eligibility (*adhikāra*) for the ritual acts that achieve wealth or the means of hearing and so forth, even while they remain poor or deaf.

Thus, in the case of those obligatory rites (*nitya*), there occurs a transgression of one's entitlement (*adhikārātikrama*) if they are not performed; however, this is not the case for optional rites (*kāmya*). Even when natural capacity exists, if there is a deficiency in the auxiliary factors (*aṅga-vaikalya*) due to a temporary incapacity that could otherwise be remedied, the status of being a means (*sādhanatva*) is lost. Consequently, the entitlement—which has as its object the ritual action (*bhāvārtha*) serving as the means—ceases to exist. But [one might object]: [The text continues: "But..."

Even if, regarding the qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*), the object of the injunction were merely the essential meaning (*bhāvārtha*) itself, nevertheless, since even that [essential meaning] arises dependent upon the instrument (*karaṇa*) by virtue of being an effect (*kāryatva*), if there is a non-performance of the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) due to a remediable incapacity (*asāmarthya*), then because of the deficiency of those [subsidiaries], the [principal action] would not arise. How then could there be no loss of the entitlement (*adhikāra*)? There is indeed a loss of it, as long as its scope (*viṣaya*) remains unfulfilled.
Because the object of the ritual— the meaning of the action— is recognized as persisting even when some parts are deficient,

and because one’s own inherent capacity to perform all the constituent parts has not departed, the entitlement [to the rite] does not cease. Rather, observing at that time a temporary capacity to perform only certain parts, one should regard the rite as achievable only to the extent that its constituent parts can be fully assembled.
It makes [the capacity] understood. For it is impossible that there be comprehension of the qualification (*adhikāra*) and yet no performance [of the rite].

Therefore, by the force of the comprehension of the qualification, at that stage, the primary action depends upon its own effect—the assistance provided by the subsidiaries being combined according to one's capacity—since otherwise it would be inexplicable. This [action], due to the deficiency of subsidiaries, is secondary (*gauṇa*).

This is called the meaning of the treatise (*śāstrārtha*). However, the general rule is that the performance consists precisely in the assistance rendered by the instrument through the accomplishment of the entire collection of subsidiaries (*aṅga*), and the application (*prayoga*) occurs according to one's qualification (*adhikāra*). Or rather, is the qualification dependent upon the Vedic revelation (*śruti*), while for one who is qualified...?

What is the application according to one's capacity? In the former [view], just as in a ritual associated with a specific time, those living at that time are authorized, because others lack the capacity to perform that specific ritual; otherwise, even at other times, there would be a transgression of the authorization for one who does not perform it. In the latter [view], however, the capacity for the auxiliary parts does not constitute the authorization.

Regarding the qualification for the permanent [obligation], the primary meaning of the scripture is the performance of all its constituent parts (*sarvāṅga-upasaṃhāra*). Therefore, it is well said that there is no performance at all times, nor during those times occupied by other purposes. Nor, for that very same *homa*, is there performance during times occupied by eating and so forth; just as the "continuous *homa*" (*satata-homa*) does not constantly depend on times such as evening and so forth, what then?

The support of a time that is not inconsistent with the purpose [is required], otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the absence of continuity; for it is indeed known that "it must be offered continuously," and that it does not depend on times such as evening and so forth. Likewise, in this case of the *homa*, because of the injunction regarding times such as evening, and because that [injunction] cannot necessarily be combined with times such as midday, therefore the *homa* is not performed continuously.
That the performance of obligatory rites may be adapted according to one's capacity, whereas this is not the case for optional rites, is entirely consistent.
To refute the view of those who hold a partial position, he raises an objection: "This is not consistent. You must explain this:
does the entitlement depend on one's capacity and the performance proceed according to that entitlement, or rather [is it] by virtue of the scriptural injunction?"
"Is the qualification dependent [on all subsidiaries], while the application for the qualified person is according to one's capacity? This is the meaning:

by virtue of the instruction regarding the subsidiaries (*aṅga*), even though not explicitly stated, the inherent capacity to combine all subsidiaries becomes a qualification of the person, because it is not something to be directly undertaken (*anupādeyatvāt*).
Thus, this qualification is dependent on that [capacity]. And the performance (*prayoga*) is according to the qualification; such is one view.

The alternative view is that eligibility depends solely on the scriptural injunction regarding "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīva*) and does not depend on the capacity to perform all auxiliary rites (*aṅga*), because such capacity is not mentioned in the scripture. Regarding this, he refutes the first alternative—that eligibility depends on capacity—by establishing it through two examples and then criticizing it: "Just as in a rite associated with a specific time [such as the new moon], even if it is performed 'as long as one lives'..."

In injunctions such as "One should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa," since someone other than one who lives at that specific time lacks the capacity to perform the ritual as qualified by that time, [the restriction] must necessarily be accepted; otherwise, even on other occasions such as the fifth day, there would be a transgression of the qualification for one who does not perform it.
It may be so. Just as in the case of the Rājasūya sacrifice, the qualification is restricted because it is impossible for anyone other than a king to achieve the status of a king;

for never could a Brāhmaṇa or a Vaiśya be capable of achieving the status of a king for himself, whereby they might be entitled to perform the Rājasūya, which has a king as its performer. Likewise, since the entitlement depends upon the specific mention of the constituent parts [of the ritual], it requires that capacity.

"An excellent livelihood is the cause of eligibility. [The opponent] says: "Let it be so; even then, what is the fault? To this he replies: "Why? In the first alternative (kalpa), there would be an overstepping of eligibility for one such as that who is incapable of performing the auxiliary rites (aṅga-upasaṃhāra).
He refutes the second alternative—that eligibility depends upon the Vedic text (śruti)—by stating: 'But in the latter case, there is no capacity for the auxiliaries.'"

The phrase "it qualifies the qualification" leads to the consequence of [the ritual] being continuous. This is the meaning: for when the qualification depends on the Vedic injunction (*śruti*), since only living is mentioned in the text, that alone would be the qualification of the performer;

consequently, there would be the consequence of the necessity of performing the *homa* and other rites continuously. Furthermore, in the case of optional rites (*kāmya*), if one fails to perform them due to the omission of auxiliary parts (*aṅga*), there would be a loss of qualification.

There would be a sequential order [of eligibility]. Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of the lame and others being entitled [to perform sacrifices], for they are not devoid of the desire for heaven, nor are they devoid of life.

To say that it "qualifies" [the eligibility] would entail the consequence of [eligibility being restricted to] continuity alone. We do not say that the capacity for the subsidiaries (aṅga-śakti) qualifies the eligibility; rather, we say that eligibility itself is dependent upon the capacity for the subsidiaries. Thus, even if a certain such subsidiary is impossible, the performance does not cease. Furthermore, it has been stated that due to deficiency (vaiguṇya), the very cause for eligibility regarding the fruit does not exist.

What is this "impossibility" (*asambhava*)? It is the incapacity to bring about the synthesis [of the subsidiaries]. In that case, it cannot be a qualification of the subject (*adhikṛta*), because that [incapacity] belongs to it [the subject]. Alternatively, if there is no synthesis, it is simply a lack of being a subsidiary (*anaṅgatva*). Is impossibility merely occasional incapacity? No; it is not by that [occasional incapacity] that [the subject is excluded] here. In this regard, a certain partisan (*ekadeśin*), harboring a hidden intention, first adopts the first position and says: "We do not say that the power of the subsidiary..."
He specifies the qualification [of the agent]: is the qualification indeed dependent solely on the capacity for the auxiliary parts (aṅga)?

If so, why is a contingent rite (naimittika) performed even when there is a deficiency in the auxiliaries? Anticipating this objection, he says: for even if some auxiliary part is impossible for a particular qualified person of that kind, the performance does not cease; thus, capacity constitutes the qualification.

The meaning is that even at that time, the qualifying attributes— the mere sense of the action and the subject matter of the entitlement— exist in the case of occasional rites (*naimittika*). However, in the case of a rite performed for a specific desire (*kāmya*), if it is performed with deficient limbs, there is a transgression of the entitlement for one who is capable.

Anticipating the objection that [this] would follow as a logical consequence (*prasajyeta*), he says: "And because of deficiency (*vaiguṇya*), there is no cause for entitlement (*adhikāra*) regarding the fruit.

This is the meaning: when there is deficiency, the state of having no fruit—that is to say, the status of being a means (*karaṇatva*)—is absent in the case of a rite performed for a specific desire (*kāmya*).

Since the verbal root-meaning (*bhāvārtha*) which has become the instrument possesses the status of being the object (*viṣayatva*), and in the case of deficiency it is not an instrument, there is an absence of the status of being the object.

It has been stated that the phrase "the dissolution of the understanding of the qualification" does not mean a transgression of the qualification in the case of non-performance, because the optional rite (kāmya) culminates in an action. Having raised this point, he refutes it by means of an alternative: "What is this impossibility?

If it is the incapacity to perform those subsidiaries, then one is not qualified [for the main rite], because that [incapacity] is a qualification of that [main rite]. This is the meaning: if a subsidiary..."

The inability to perform the subsidiary rites (*aṅga*) is described as their "impossibility" (*asambhava") by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra"), because [the latter] is the cause of the former. In that case, since the capacity [to perform them]—which is a qualification of the eligible performer (*adhikārin*)—is impossible, why would one who is not so qualified perform the occasional rite (*naimittika*) while omitting the subsidiary parts? Alternatively, if the non-performance [of the subsidiaries] means they are simply not subsidiary parts at all; or, if even though capable, one does not perform them.
If it is said that the absence of a certain auxiliary (aṅga) is merely its non-performance, then that [non-performance] is certainly not a true auxiliary;
for it is impossible that a wise and capable person would perform the principal act while omitting some auxiliary.
Thus, this is a rope with a noose at both ends.
Now, one who holds a partial view (ekadeśin) reveals his own intention: "Occasional incapacity does not constitute an impossibility;

therefore, there is no exclusion from eligibility [on that account], just as there is none in the case of a deficiency of auxiliary factors (aṅga) that cannot be remedied by means of a substance. This is the underlying point here: men are indeed established in two categories in this world—some are incapable, and some have their [spiritual] power obscured.

They are [divided into] those who possess the capacity and those who do not. Among them, those who are indeed incapable—such as the blind, the lame, and so forth, as well as the *śūdras* and others—have no qualification at all, because the capacity, which is a qualifying attribute of one who is eligible, is absent in them. As for those who are capable, [regardless of] some [disability]...

The exclusion [of certain persons] is due to their incapacity, like the deficiency of a ritual component that cannot be remedied by a substance. This is true; however, it is not as absolute as in the case of a Śūdra. Rather, when the cause of eligibility is absent, eligibility does not cease entirely—just as when the desire for the fruit has vanished. For those whose capacity is overcome by obstacles, there remains the existence of that capacity which constitutes the specific qualification of the eligible person. What [then]?

What is the cause for the disappearance of its capacity? Indeed, one whose capacity has been overcome does not become incapable. Nor should it be said that because capacity is to be determined by its effect, it is unproven when the effect is absent; for when something previously perceived as having capacity produces an effect, and subsequently fails to produce one and then produces it again, is there a destruction of its capacity?

Regarding the question of whether [the manifestation] consists of the production of the capacity (*sāmarthya*) or rather its concealment and appearance, the latter hypothesis is superior due to parsimony (*lāghava*), not the former; for in that case, there would be the consequence of excessive complexity (*gaurava*) in postulating a property in the form of a capacity. Consequently, since the capacity—which is a qualification of the subject (*adhikṛta-viśeṣaṇa*)—is already present, [the capacity exists] at the commencement of the application.

And since he is indeed duly authorized, he should undertake and complete the occasional rite (*naimittika*) according to his capacity. Regarding this very point, he provides an illustration: "like the deficiency of a limb that cannot be restored with a substitute material.
He refutes that [objection]: "True, it is not absolutely like that of a *śūdra*, but rather because the cause for his entitlement has not ceased."

The objection does not cease. This is the intended meaning here: let your honor explain this—does this capacity, which is said to be a qualification of the subject under discussion, belong to the direct hearing of the capacity itself, or rather by the force of the instruction regarding the subsidiaries (*aṅga*)? In that regard, the first alternative is indeed refuted by non-perception (*anupalabdhi*).

In the second [view], however, by virtue of the capacity for instruction regarding the constituent parts (*aṅga*), and because the determination of qualification (*adhikāra*) follows the specific application (*viniyoga*), this injunction of qualification (*adhikāravidhi*), implying the performance of the primary act together with its subsidiaries, implies an agent, since that performance would be impossible without one. Nor can incapacity possess agency, for agency belongs to a specific type of factor (*kāraka*), and it is power (*śakti*) that constitutes such a state.
And because it is a *kāraka* (grammatical factor). For a *kāraka* is the cause (*nimitta*) of action;

and it will be explained later that what is called a "cause" is that in whose presence the effect (*naimittika*) necessarily comes to be. Action does not necessarily occur merely when the essential nature of a substance (*dravya-svarūpa*) is present. Therefore, there must be the determination of a *kāraka* as being endowed with power (*śaktimat*). Just as...

The substance alone is not the agent, nor even that which possesses power; for even when power is present, action does not arise if that power is suppressed. Therefore, it is most reasonable to hold that agency and the status of being a causal factor (kārakatva) belong only to that which possesses manifest power and is accompanied by auxiliary conditions. Furthermore, there can be no agency without entitlement (adhikāra), nor can there be one who is subject to an injunction (niyojya).

Without [the presence of] a mantra, there is no entitlement (*adhikāra*). Therefore, that [self], having manifested its capacity, reaches the state of being subject to an injunction (*niyojyatā*) by way of agency (*kartṛtā*);

being something not to be taken up [as an object of action], it experiences the status of being a qualification of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya-viśeṣaṇatā*). Just as one who is incapable, even if his capacity is suppressed, is neither subject to an injunction nor entitled, so it has been said: "But he has no entitlement."

The claim that "the entitlement does not cease even when the causality [of the capacity] has vanished" is incorrect. It is not the mere capacity—though it exists—that continues the entitlement if it is useless for performance; rather, it is that specific capacity characterized by its manifestation which serves as the cause for performance. Since that alone is the cause of entitlement, if it has vanished, the entitlement necessarily ceases as well. Thus, for whom would [the entitlement persist]?

The meaning is that even when one has the capacity to withdraw all the constituent parts of consciousness, if one does not employ them during the state of concealment (*tirobhāva*), there is a transgression of the qualification for occasional rites (*naimittika-adhikāra*).
Furthermore, regarding the *jāteṣṭi* sacrifice, according to your own position on the "combined qualification" (*saṃvalita-adhikāra*) theory, it applies to one who possesses a birth.

[This applies] to those who possess desire. Otherwise, since the father—who is qualified, capable, desirous of heaven, and occasionally desirous of sense-organs and so forth as a result of his son’s birth—possesses the qualification [for the rite], the verbal root-meaning (*bhāvārtha*), like other optional rites (*kāmya*), would become the object of the action; consequently, if it were restricted solely to that [the son], its status as an optional rite would be untenable, and the same would apply to the occasional rite (*naimittika*) which has become the object of the action.
Since there is no contradiction even if the object is the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*), the impossibility of performing the ritual according to one's capacity may be set aside for now.

Now, it might be argued that the comprehension of the qualification (*adhikāra*) is useful prior to engagement because it is the cause of engagement, but not once engagement has already arisen; for a potter who has already produced a pot does not proceed to make another pot.

One who is qualified is one who possesses the capacity for both the primary and auxiliary rites arising therefrom; yet, if due to some oversight he does not perceive his own capacity regarding a portion of the auxiliaries, even then, being unqualified [in that respect], he ought not to desist. Therefore, it is said:
"Just as when the desire for the fruit has vanished for a seeker. This is the underlying intention here: for there exists something...

Even an instrumental cause (nimittakāraṇa), when it ceases after having produced its effect, causes that effect to cease as well. For example, the cognition of relative number (apekṣābuddhi), which is the instrumental cause of the number two, ceases after having produced duality, and thereby causes duality to cease too.
This is generally the course of events for inherence (samavāya) with respect to its inherent causes (samavāyikāraṇa). Therefore, here too—

Even one who has begun an action with the desire for heaven, if that desire ceases, is no longer qualified; yet, out of fear of being censured by the learned, he completes the rite even though he is no longer entitled to it. Similarly, one who possesses the occasion [for a rite] but whose capacity is obscured is not present and is not qualified; thus, by not performing it, he would not transgress his qualification. However, the completion of the rite—even in the case of a desire-based (kāmya) act—is due to the fear of censure by the learned.
"It is the same" does not mean that it is sufficient for there to be no contradiction with the occasional (naimittika) rite.

For if, when one who is capable has begun [an action], the cessation of that activity due to a subsequent loss of capability resulted in a lapse of entitlement (adhikārātikrānti), then such a lapse would undesirably follow even in the case of an occasional rite performed for a specific desire (kāmya); thus he says: "Otherwise, for one who is entitled..."

For one who is capable and desires heaven, if there should occasionally be a deficiency in a subsidiary element (*aṅga*) resulting in the non-production of the fruit, there would be a transgression of the qualification (*adhikāra*). However, as for those who say: "Even with the deficiency of a single subsidiary element, because the performance (*prayoga*) is still recognized, there is no loss of qualification for one who has set out [to perform it]; indeed, a bull does not cease to be a bull simply because its horn is broken"—in response to them:
The reply is that this is the same even in the case of optional rites (*kāmya*). Furthermore, setting aside that point because it is more well-known, he states another objection:

"And for one who does not perform [the rite] at the unobtained time, there would be a lapse of entitlement (*adhikārātikrānti*). This is connected [to the previous argument]. The meaning is that for one who does not perform the application of the *iṣṭi* sacrifice on the fifth day—which is the unobtained time—there would be a lapse of entitlement.

Now, it might be argued: why does one who fails to perform [the rite] when the time has arrived thus overstep their entitlement? For there is no authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) to suggest that the occasional duty (*naimittika*) must be performed immediately after the occasion (*nimitta*) arises; rather, it is understood that the occasion must simply exist. Indeed, this has been established by investigating the scriptures through Mīmāṃsā.
Regarding the *Jāteṣṭi* sacrifice: it is thus heard in scripture, "One should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara when a son is born.

In this regard, there is a doubt: should the offering be performed immediately after the birth of the son, or after the *jātakarman* (birth-rite) has been completed? What is the prima facie view? That it should be performed immediately after the birth of the son. Why? Because of the scriptural mention of "born" (*jāta*) as the occasioning cause (*nimitta*).
Even when the fruit does not arise due to a deficiency in capacity, there would be a transgression of the obligation for one who fails to perform it at the unattained time.

Now, even one who is entitled [to perform the rites] may, like a father whose son has been born, complete the period of impurity (*kālaśauca*) and yet not overstep his entitlement by performing [the rite] at that time; for the immediate sequence of the occasion (*nimitta-anantarya*) is not the literal meaning of the word. Even when the time has arrived, if there is a conflict with another subsidiary element (*aṅga*), the non-performance [of the primary rite] would result in a contradiction. To this, it is replied: "When the birth-rite (*jātakarman*) has been performed."

Why? Because, when there is this expectancy for a result (*bhāvya*) in the efficient-force (*bhāvanā*) of the *iṣṭi* sacrifice, many qualities—such as brilliance, possession of sense organs, and so forth—which are heard in the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) as residing in the son, are indeed capable of being connected with the efficient-force here.

Therefore, it is precisely those [qualities] that are assumed to be the fruit, according to the principle of the *Rātrisatra* sacrifice. And if [the result were to accrue] to the boy immediately upon birth...

If this sacrifice were to be performed [immediately after birth], then because the rite of giving breast milk is prohibited for one whose *jātakarman* has not yet been performed, and because the performance of the sacrifice would entail a delay in time, there would be the risk of the child’s death; thus, the sacrifice for the purpose of enjoining its specific qualities would be rendered useless.
Therefore, it was determined that it is not for "one just born."
Likewise, this other matter is now considered. It has been understood that [the rite] is not performed until the *jātakarman* has been completed.
Now, this is being doubted: should it be offered immediately after the *jātakarman*, or rather after ten nights have passed?
For fear of the child’s death, the immediate sequence following birth was bypassed; however, once the *jātakarman* has been performed...

Since the cause for the rite, namely the birth of a son, is present, and because there is no reason for a specific sequence [of other intervening rites], it follows that the *jātakarman* (birth-rite) should be performed immediately after [the birth]. To this we reply: since purity (*śauca*) is also a causal factor for eligibility in performing a rite—according to the rule "a rite must be performed by one who is pure"—and since the immediate succession [of the birth-rite] has already been established by the *jātakarman* itself, [the subsequent rites] occur when that [purity] merely exists.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that because it takes the state of the *nimitta* (the causal occasion) as its objective support, this sacrifice occurs even after ten nights have passed; thus, it is performed once the ten-night period has elapsed.
This is reconsidered further: does this *iṣṭi* take place immediately after the ten nights, or at a time such as the new moon (*amāvāsyā*)?

"Waiting for what? In this regard, since there is an absolute interval [between the cause and its effect], the causal status of the occasion (*nimitta*) as heard in scripture would be entirely contradicted; thus, when it is argued that [the rite] must occur immediately after the ten nights have passed, it is replied:
"It is waiting for the time. Because the occasion is delimited by that [time], the causal status [of the occasion] never ceases once the ten nights have elapsed.

The existence [of the qualification] delimited by the time of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices does not cease once a son is born; that is, one who has a son transcends the state of being "one whose son is yet to be born.

Thus, according to the logic of the *jāteṣṭi* (the sacrifice on the birth of a son), since immediate succession to the occasion (*nimittānantarya*) is not directly expressed by the words, one who does not perform the sacrifice even when the fifth case-ending is used does not fall outside the scope of the entitlement (*adhikāra*). Therefore, he says: "Now, as one who is entitled and has a son, [he performs it] during the period of impurity and at the proper time."

Just as one who has fathered a son, having concluded the period of ritual impurity (*śauca*) on account of that birth, does not let his entitlement lapse by performing the *Jāteṣṭi* sacrifice after ten nights on either the new moon or the full moon day; likewise, one who possesses life, having concluded the time for the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*Darśapūrṇamāsa*) on account of the occasion of being alive, does not let his entitlement lapse by performing them [at that time].

Because the immediate succession of the causal signs (*nimitta*) is not the meaning of the word. To this, the reply is: when there is the fulfillment of the time, one who acts while depending on the fulfillment of other auxiliary factors (*aṅga*) would be so; the meaning is that he would not overstep his entitlement (*adhikāra*).

If one were to act while depending upon prosperity, it would be so; however, if living itself, as delimited by the time that constitutes a subsidiary factor (*aṅga*), is the cause of qualification (*adhikāra*), then this applies equally to other subsidiaries as well. Furthermore, why would one who is qualified as possessing all complete subsidiaries perform [the rite] with a deficiency of subsidiaries? If it is argued that this is because such a thing is impossible, we say no, for there is a confusion regarding three possible alternatives. To explain:

Alternatively, because the mandate (niyoga) depends upon the completion of the ritual action (*karmaparyanta*), it is not applied until the qualification (*adhikāra*) is fulfilled; or else, by virtue of that qualification, in accordance with the possible instruction of additional subsidiaries (*adhikāṅga*). When such a possibility exists, even a subsidiary element like time (*kāla*) attains the status of a subsidiary by delimiting the occasion (*nimitta*); it does not do so without delimiting it.

He says that when the occasion (nimitte) is present, there is a withdrawal of time, but not a withdrawal of the auxiliary factors (aṅga). [Objection: In this case, living while delimited by the time that has become an auxiliary factor is the cause for entitlement (adhikārahetuḥ). [Response: This is the same even regarding other auxiliaries. Granted, let it be that the auxiliaries are not directly delimiters of the occasion; however, the determination [of their status] is attained through the force of the instruction regarding the auxiliaries.

The intention is that since the capacity to bring together all the constituent parts (*aṅga*) has arisen, it is able to delimit the causal sign (*nimitta*); thus, there is equality with respect to time for the other constituent parts.
Having in this way established the consequence that performance would occur even in the absence of the prescribed time, just as it would in the absence of the other constituent parts—
Now, refuting even that which was stated—that there is recognition of the performance (*prayoga*) despite some deficiency in its constituent parts (*aṅga*)—he says:
"Furthermore, why would one who is authorized as possessing all complete parts perform [the rite] with deficient parts? This matter is accessible through injunction (*vidhi*);
no other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) applies here. And by the injunction, the performance is prescribed as accompanied by the entire collection of constituent parts."

The meaning is this: although it has been taught there that one must abandon the limbs (aṅga) and the husks (tuṣa), the fact that these constitute the actual application (prayoga) of that [rite] was not taught by the injunction (vidhi). Therefore, for a person, this is merely a matter of personal intuition (pratibhā) and is not authoritative (prāmāṇika).
Here, an objection is raised: "If you say it is because of impossibility (asambhava). In order to refute this doubt, [the author] explains the meaning of the word "impossibility."

He raises an objection: No; because it is overwhelmed by three types of conceptual constructions (*kalpanā*). Indeed, three conceptual constructions are at play here. "Overwhelmed" means being subject to them. First, he shows a conceptual construction consistent with his own position along with a single textual passage: For instance, because the injunction (*niyoga*) depends upon a sequence that extends to the limit [of the fruit], there is no qualification (*adhikāra*)...

There is no application [of the injunction] for the sake of cessation. Since the status of being a subsidiary (*śeṣabhāva*) is understood through the specific application (*viniyoga*) and the material cause (*upādāna*), and since the injunction (*niyoga*)—which, while requiring that sequence expressed by words during the comprehension of the ritual acts, is not itself a constituent part (*anaṅga*)—is lifelong (*yāvajjīvika*) regarding its own production, it cannot come into being if the subsidiaries are omitted. Thus, the meaning of the word "impossibility" (*asaṃbhava*) is the total absence of performance in every respect.

He states the interpretation consistent with the injunction (*codaka*): "Or by virtue of the qualification (*adhikāra*), according to what is possible. This is the meaning: although this person is qualified even for the complete set of subsidiaries (*aṅga*), nevertheless, by the force of the cognition of that qualification, he completes the rite even with deficient subsidiaries when proceeding toward it. In cases where there is an incapacity to perform a subsidiary, there is the performance of the complete set of subsidiaries.

"Because of the performance [of the ritual]. This is impossible. He states a third hypothesis: "Or, because of the adherence to the instruction regarding additional limbs, there is the possibility of such a person when it is possible to perform the ritual with all its limbs. That which is possible is said to be the limb in comparison to those limbs that can be performed at that time. When one is able to bring together the ritual with all its limbs, then its performance is possible.

In that case, because both [the father and the son] are benefited and because the word *ānantarya* (immediacy) does not constitute the literal meaning of the injunction, it is appropriate to use the term *yadā* (when), as in the case of the *Jāteṣṭi* (the sacrifice performed upon the birth of a son). Alternatively, there is no performance [of the rite] due to the delimitation of the qualification by the capacity of the subsidiaries (*aṅga-śakti*), just as in the case of time. Furthermore, the injunction is not one and the same for those [subsidiaries] alone.

[The injunction] is both productive (*prayojaka*) and non-productive (*aprayojaka*). Furthermore, for what purpose does one engage in a rite with deficient limbs? We reply: for the fulfillment of the qualification (*adhikāra-nirvṛtti*). Is the fulfillment of the qualification independent of the limbs, like the fulfillment of the fruit [of the sacrifice]? If it were so, then there would be no status as a "limb" at all. If, however, it is dependent [on the limbs], then it must be accomplished by the limbs according to one's capacity; thus, in the case of deficiency—

In this regard, he first establishes the aforementioned alternative interpretation: "In that case, because both [the injunction and the qualification] are favored and because immediate sequence is not the literal meaning of the word, it is proper to say 'when' (yadā), as in the case of the Jāteṣṭi. This is the meaning: because the understanding of the qualification (*adhikāra*) and the instruction regarding the additional subsidiary (*adhika-aṅga*) are both favored, it is proper to say "when. Now, if this were so, [there would be no] immediate sequence of the occasion...

Anticipating the objection that the status of being a *nimitta* (occasioning cause) is precluded because [the occasion] is not mentioned in the text, he says: "Because immediate sequence (*ānantarya*) is not the meaning of the word, as in the case of the *Jātaputreṣṭi*. This has already been explained and is correct. Now, an objection is raised: "If the performance of the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) is according to what is possible, then there would be no distinction between optional (*kāmya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites. However, this applies only if there is the capacity to include all the auxiliary parts.

Since it is not something to be adopted [as a primary element], like time (*kāla*), it serves as a delimiting factor for the qualification (*adhikāra*); therefore, when there is a deficiency in the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*), the action does not exist, just as it would in the absence of the [proper] time. Furthermore, the absence of deficiency (*avaiguṇya*) is not possible for anyone throughout their entire life. Consequently, the meaning that "it must be performed as a combination of all auxiliary parts throughout one's life" is impossible due to contradiction. Therefore...

He states that because the meaning [of the injunction] is impossible to fulfill, the scripture lacks authority—like the instruction to adorn oneself with the crest-jewel of Takṣaka as a means to remove fever—and thus there is never its performance: "And due to the limitation of qualification by the power of the constituent parts, as in the case of time, there is non-performance. Now, one might ask: since the instruction applies for as long as one lives, why would even a defective performance [be considered invalid]?

Anticipating the objection, "Is this not improper? he says: "And it is not the case that a single injunction can be both the motivator and the non-motivator of those very same [auxiliaries]. For if that were so, it would result in the contradiction of a single injunction itself both implying and excluding those very auxiliaries. Therefore, the impossibility of performance is indeed absolute."
The opponent has stated: "This very arrow of your own strikes you"—the meaning is that this consequence has arrived.

Thus, as long as the entire collection of subsidiaries, which is the primary focus of the context, is understood as being to be employed, only that much should be employed. And it has been stated that a deficient performance is not considered spontaneous (*prātibha*). Now, [regarding]...
He also demonstrates the pointlessness of an incomplete performance: "Furthermore, for what purpose would one engage in that which lacks its constituent parts?

For the activity of discerning persons is pervaded by purposiveness; in the absence of purposiveness, such activity does not occur, just as the state of being a *śiṃśapā* tree does not exist in the absence of being a tree. This is the meaning.
On this point, one who holds a partial view states the purpose: "We say it is for the sake of the non-termination of the qualification (*adhikāra*). This is what is meant:
that toward which one proceeds is the *prayojana* (purpose), according to the etymology "that by which one is impelled" (*prayujyate 'nena*).

And the world proceeds with a task (*kārya*) as its objective; furthermore, the task is the qualification (*adhikāra*). Therefore, even in the case of a deficient limb [of the ritual], [the purpose remains].

"One engages in action for the sake of accomplishing the task. He refutes this as follows: "Is the accomplishment of the entitlement independent of the auxiliaries, like the production of the fruit? Anticipating the objection—"Let the accomplishment of the entitlement not depend on the auxiliaries; what is the harm?"—he says: "If that were so, then there would be a total lack of auxiliary status, since the assistance to the instrument would exist even without the auxiliaries."

[The ritual] would be a futile effort. Now, if it is argued that it is to be accomplished by the limbs according to one's capacity, this does not suffice to establish a distinction in the result. Furthermore, since the production of the fruit follows from the qualification [to perform the rite], in that case, [the rite must be performed] as endowed with the limbs according to one's capacity.

For one who is qualified [only] in such a manner, the accomplishment of the entitlement (*adhikāra*) serves as if it were caused by that very qualification. Now, if he is not qualified in such a manner, there would be no accomplishment of the entitlement either; the point is that for one qualified in a complete set of limbs (*aṅga*), the performance of the task of one with deficient limbs is impossible. If it is argued that [the rite] is dependent [on the performer], then it must be accomplished through the limbs exactly as they are prescribed; thus, in the case of deficiency, it is in vain.

[An] action would [be required]. He raises an objection: "Now, [the action] is to be accomplished by the limbs according to one's capacity. He refutes it: "The state of being restricted to the result is not sufficient for a distinction. This is what is meant: when there is restriction to the result, even in the case of an optional (kāmya) rite, because the verbal root-meaning (bhāvārtha) has become a subordinate instrument (upakaraṇa), the benefit produced by the entire collection of auxiliary parts (aṅga-grāma) [is also included within its scope].

Since the status of being an instrument belongs to the meaning of the verbal root (bhāvārtha), and since that [instrumentality] is untenable when even a single constituent part is missing—resulting in the absence of an object for the action—the qualification [for performance] collapses.

However, in the case of occasional rites (naimittika), because the mere meaning of the verbal root constitutes the object of the action, the qualification does not collapse even when there is a deficiency, as the status of being an object remains possible. Thus, the distinction between optional (kāmya) and occasional rites is not tenable.

If there is entitlement to a rite that is to be accomplished through its constituent parts according to one's capacity, then surely entitlement arises even from the principal act when it is deficient in its parts; for a performance lacking parts is untenable as a performance at all.
If it is a performance, how can it be without an object? If it has an object, how can there be no entitlement?
And if there is no entitlement, how can there be a distinction between optional (*kāmya*) and obligatory (*nitya*) rites? Thus [it is argued].

If it should be argued that, because in a contingent rite (*naimittika*) the mere meaning of the verbal root constitutes the object [of the injunction], the entitlement (*adhikāra*) remains intact even when there is a deficiency in the subsidiaries; and that for the sake of its own realization, the entitlement necessitates its own cause as produced by the subsidiaries according to one's capacity—just as in the case of a conflict among subsidiaries, it necessitates the assistance provided by those subsidiaries that are not actually sublated—this is incorrect. [The reason is: entitlement...
Because of their dissolution. For it is not merely the presence of the object that is required for the establishment of qualification;

rather, the specific qualifications of the qualified person are also required. And it has been stated that one who possesses the manifested capacity of all limbs and organs does not have the qualification when the capacity of those limbs is suppressed; thus, the discussion is concluded.

Having thus questioned the activity of the person, he states a further inquiry regarding the arising of qualification: "Moreover, it is established in your own view that the accomplishment of the fruit follows from qualification even in the case of optional (kāmya) action. Anticipating the objection, "Let it be so;
what is the harm? he says: "In that case, for one who is qualified [to perform] an action endowed with its constituent parts according to his capacity, such..."

O King, just as the fruit is accomplished through the completion of one's entitlement (*adhikāra*) by means of performing the constituent parts according to one's capacity—even if they are incomplete—the same applies here.

To illustrate this very point, he says: "like a cause" (*nimittam iva*). Just as a cause, even if its components are deficient, brings about the effect to be produced (*naimittika*) by way of completing the entitlement, and is thus established through its causal nature, so too is the fruit; such is the meaning.

Now, if there were no entitlement (*adhikāra*) for one who is deficient in such limbs in the case of a rite performed for a specific desire (*kāmya*), then likewise, in the case of an occasional rite (*naimittika*), there would also be no cessation of entitlement when the limbs are incomplete. This is because, for one who is entitled to perform a rite with all its limbs complete, performing it with deficient limbs is like performing an entirely different ritual action. Just as one who is entitled to the *Agnihotra* [does not perform] the worship of a shrine (*caityavandana*).

The meaning is that one who performs [the rite] fulfills the qualification; thus, one who is qualified for that [rite] together with its subsidiaries, by performing it deficient in its subsidiaries, does not fulfill the qualification.
This might be so: one who is qualified for the Agnihotra, while worshipping a caitya, does not fulfill the qualification.

Because the oblation (*homa*), which constitutes the instrument for the sphere of entitlement (*adhikāra*), is not performed; when they offer the sacrifice, even though it is devoid of its subsequent subsidiaries (*uttarāṅga*),
the distinction between subsidiary and principal (*aṅgapradhāna-bheda*) is likewise unhelpful here, just as in the performance of a different ritual action within the application of the entitlement.

Because there is no difference [between them] insofar as they are both objects of the injunction for performance; and because, if there were a difference, it would follow that [the subsidiary] lacks the status of being an auxiliary (*anaṅgatva*). Furthermore, since the relationship of auxiliary and principal (*aṅgapradhānabhāva*) cannot be determined [otherwise], the very fulfillment of the objective implies the status of being an instrument (*karaṇabhāva*) for such a *homa* through its connection with the qualification (*adhikāra*). Thus, [it establishes] the qualification.

He accomplishes [the result]; this is the distinction between the subsidiary (aṅga) and the principal (pradhāna): that in the absence of the principal there is no entitlement (adhikāra), whereas in the case of the absence of subsidiaries, the principal still comes to be. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Even the distinction between subsidiary and principal is irrelevant here. Why? He says: because there is no difference [between them] insofar as they both fall within the scope of the injunction regarding entitlement (adhikāravidhi). Although...

Since the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*) alone is the object of the *niyoga* because it is connected with the performance (*pratipatti*), even so, because the *niyoga* is the motivator (*prayojaka*) for both the subsidiary parts and the principal rite together, it is logical that there is no difference between the subsidiaries and the principal rite insofar as they constitute the object of the *niyoga*. If, however, out of fear of this [consequence], one were not to maintain that the *adhikāra-niyoga* is the motivator for the subsidiaries, then there would be a distinction.

Furthermore, if it were accepted that the definition of being an object [of injunction] consists in being something to be employed (*prayojyatva*) while the definition of not being an object consists in the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) not being things to be employed, then the consequence would follow that they are not subsidiaries at all. For that which, in the absence of which this entitlement (*adhikāra*)—which is by nature a task—does not arise, implies those very factors because their occurrence is inseparable from its own realization; it does not imply what is otherwise.

The meaning is that, in that case, the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) would also not arise by means of those [injunctions], and consequently, the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) would follow that they are not subsidiaries.

Furthermore, in the view of this proponent of a partial position (*ekadeśin*), the relationship is that [the subsidiary] is "not helpful" because the status of being a subsidiary (*aṅga*) and a primary (*pradhāna*) has not been properly determined. This is the underlying intention (*ākūta*) here: the meaning of the suffix is the *apūrva* in the form of an action to be accomplished (*kārya*). And the action to be accomplished...

Regarding human effort (*puruṣaprayatna*), that which is the primary objective is understood in the same way in sentences such as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices" as it is in the *samit* and other such injunctions; for it is impossible for the *samit* and others— which have other tasks as their objects— to serve as means toward the qualification (*adhikāra*), and [this applies] to the task (*kārya*) as well.

For, according to the principle that "that which is for another purpose cannot be the very task [itself] regarding objects such as the fuel-sticks (*samidh*)," there would be no relationship of subsidiary (*aṅga*) and principal (*pradhāna*) because the qualification (*adhikāra*) lacks the state of being for the sake of that task.

It might be argued: "Not everything that is an effect (*kārya*) is for the sake of something else; rather, it is that which is to be performed (*anuṣṭheya*). That is said to be 'to be performed' when a person understands an independent task as 'this is my duty. And the supreme *apūrva* is never perceived as being pervaded by human effort (*kṛti*), because it is not directed toward anything else, nor toward any other primary [purpose]."

Because it is understood from the beginning. [Objection: Is it not the case that the fruit is understood as something desired, rather than being grasped as a qualification of the *niyojya* (the person to be impelled) by means of the word "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*), since the *kārya* (the task to be done), which is first cognized, does not reach completion without a *niyojya* and thus requires a specific *niyojya*?
[Reply: That word is not intended to establish the fruit; rather, it is precisely that *kārya*, understood independently, [which is primary].

Since that which is qualified by the goal of heaven does not arise without producing heaven, it attains the status of being a means to heaven; thus, when there is no other effect to be accomplished, the cognition of the fruit occurs independently, and the cognition of the action does not occur only after the cognition of the fruit. For if it were dependent [on the fruit], the supreme *apūrva* would have to be performed. But that very [action]—

The optative suffix (*liṅ*), denoting a purpose that is independent [of other purposes], expresses the supreme *apūrva* as being connected with both the threshing and so forth—which are themselves the purposes due to their proximity and recitation—and the *samit*-offerings and so forth—which are the things to be employed.

It has been stated that even if there is an injunction (*codanā*), since its purpose is not accomplished, it would result in a futile effort. And what is this "qualification" (*adhikāra*) whose fulfillment [is required]? If it is the mandate (*niyoga*), then there is no fulfillment of that.

This very thing is designated as the "grasping by the grasper" (*grāhakagrahaṇa*). Thus, in the case of those [actions] mentioned in proximity to a mandatory injunction involving qualification (*adhikāravidhi*), [the same applies].

In the injunctions regarding the *samit* and other [subsidiary rites], since their objects are embraced by that [primary injunction], and because there is a subsequent recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of the effect characterized as the *apūrva*, the cognition of a distinct effect does not arise immediately. However, subsequently, since the *samit* and others—

being of the nature of actions— are transitory and cannot coexist with one another, they [function] like the act of sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and so forth as means for achieving the substance that brings about the *apūrva*.

Since the *samit* and other [subsidiary] sacrifices— which do not enter into the sphere of the *apūrva* through the medium of the *saṃskāra* (refinatory acts) and so forth— are apprehended by the supreme *apūrva*, their intermediate *apūrva* as an effect is postulated for those whose purpose (*idamarthya*) is more well-established. Even though the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) denoting the *samit* and others expresses that which resides in the *samit* etc., it is nevertheless expressed as an "effect" (*kārya*) because it is dependent upon the supreme *apūrva*.

[Objection: But surely, since it is not to be performed, the status of being a subordinate member (*aṅga*) is established even for the *samit* and other [rites], which have as their object a task to be accomplished.

To this it is replied: In the sentences concerning the qualification (*adhikāra*), these [words] such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*) possess a recognized capacity to denote an independent task; they are not able to denote a task directed toward something else in the sentences concerning the *samit* and others. If...

Is it that these are restatements (*anuvāda*) of the *apūrva* belonging to the primary injunction (*adhikāra*), like the *parama-vahantī* and other such cases, or do they intend to denote a different *apūrva*? This remains a question regarding the word itself; however, it is not logical for the primary status of the action—which is denoted by the injunctive suffix (*liṅ*) and the like, and which is itself the principal element—to be abandoned. Now, it was argued that these [subsidiary acts], such as the *samidh* and others, are indeed recited within the context of the primary injunction...

Those [actions] which, by the very fact of being denoted through that same injunctive rule (*adhikāravidhi*), have their purpose established [as subserving the sacrifice], cannot possibly become objects of an independent operation (*svaniṣṭhakārya*), because that would contradict their purpose of subserving the primary *apūrva*. Nor are they like [the acts of] threshing (*avahanti*) and so forth, which enter into the scope of the primary *apūrva*; consequently, they are not mere restatements (*anuvāda*). Nor do they possess an independent operation...

[If it were otherwise,] those words would be designated as "pramattagīta" (the songs of the intoxicated), being devoid of any denotable meaning; therefore, it is better that they possess the capacity to denote the action (*kārya*), even by relinquishing mere predominance.
This has been well said, but it is incorrect. For an injunction (*vidhi*) does not have [mere] proximity (*saṃnidhi*) as its basis for eligibility (*adhikāra*).

Does the injunction for the Jyotiṣṭoma grasp everything that is merely recited? No, it grasps only that which is fit to be grasped; however, the *samit* and other [subsidiary acts], whose objects are their own specific effects, do not deserve to be grasped.
But is it not the case that, due to conflict with the grasper (*grāhaka*), there is no predominance for the *niyoga* (obligation) whose object is the *samit* and others? Or rather—

Why is it that the *grāhaka* (the recipient) itself is not set aside, given the contradiction with the perception of its predominance? In this case, because the predominance of the *niyoga* (the injunction) is perceived from the mere hearing [of the word] alone and is thus independent, whereas the apprehension of the *grāhaka*—resulting from the consideration of other sentences—is dependent and therefore its perception of predominance is weaker; consequently, one must assume an independent qualification (*adhikāra*), as in the case of the *Rātri-satra* and similar rites.

If [the relationship between] auxiliary and principal were real, then the status of the *prayāja* and other rites as auxiliaries and the status of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and other rites as principals would not be tenable; thus it was well said that "the relationship of auxiliary and principal cannot be determined.

Having provisionally accepted the relationship of auxiliary and principal, he states another refutation: "Even if the relationship of auxiliary and principal were real, in the case of the occasional..."

It has been stated that if this [injunction] were not eternal, then because the purpose of the injunction would not be fulfilled through its performance, there would follow the consequence of fruitless effort. Furthermore, what is [the nature of] the state of being enjoined?
If it is the state of being enjoined, that too is accomplished solely through the injunction. If it is the state of being the master...

Since there is nothing performed by the master that he does not enjoy, both types of entitlement would be equally restricted to the completion of the action. Therefore, it is impossible to resolve the distinction between the optional (*kāmya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) entitlements based on whether they are restricted to the completion of the action or restricted to its performance; thus, the matter must be resolved otherwise.
That is explained as follows:
Since the occasion, such as the act of living, is common [to all], time is the distinguishing factor.
When that occasion has arisen, there is a necessity to perform the ritual action for the sake of that occasion.

Furthermore, this "qualification" (adhikāra) cannot tolerate being [defined as] a "separation" (vivāra), since you state that its accomplishment occurs even when the application of the occasional rule (naimittika) is deficient in its constituent parts (aṅga). To this he says: "And what is this qualification, the accomplishment of which is spoken of by you? The words "is spoken of by you" are to be supplied as the ellipsis. The proponent of a partial view (ekadeśin) says, according to his own technical terminology: "If it is an injunction" (niyoga). He refutes this:
Its accomplishment has been examined. For it was stated in this context that the mandate (*niyoga*) itself is not the object to be accomplished;
rather, the object (*viṣaya*) is what must be accomplished.

"Because it would entail the absurdity that the person to be enjoined (niyojya) is also the enjoiner (niyoktṛ). He states this in another way: if one objects that the status of being enjoined must be abandoned, he replies: "That [status] is also established solely through the injunction itself. Only when one understands the injunction whose object is the performance of an action (bhāvārtha) does one attain the status of being enjoined; one would not proceed to the performance [of the act] merely for the sake of attaining that status."

Having rendered the technical definition (paribhāṣā) useless, he states the worldly meaning of the term *adhikāra*: "If it means ownership (*svāmitā*). The intention is that in common usage, this word *adhikṛta* is well-known as signifying a master (*īśvara*). He refutes this: "One who does not enjoy anything produced by that [authority] is not a master; for in this way, the occasional (*naimittika*) ritual action becomes possible for the person."

O Master, if that action serves his benefit; for this kind of benefit is twofold: the attainment of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful. And in your view, occasional (naimittika) action is not conceived as following the attainment of the beneficial or the avoidance of the harmful.
As for what is said—that from an occasional action another quality of the primordial person (puruṣa) arises—let it indeed arise, but...

Furthermore, this qualification [of the person] is not itself of the nature of happiness, nor is it the cause thereof. If, out of fear of this [conclusion], one were to admit that even a contingent [act] serves as a benefit to the person, then both qualifications would result in being aimed at an action (*kāryaniṣṭha*).
The word *iti* has the sense of "therefore. He concludes the subject under discussion: "Therefore, it is not aimed at an action."

The distinction between the entitlements for optional (*kāmya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites can be determined by their respective states of being performed with a specific desire or without such a desire. He provides a transition to his own view: "Therefore, it must be resolved otherwise. That is stated:
because the occasion, such as living, is the same, time is the differentiator."
In that case, the purpose of the sign is that once [the child] is born, the ritual action must necessarily be performed.

If eligibility were dependent solely upon the Vedic revelation (*śruti*), then it would follow without distinction that even the blind, the Śūdras, and others would be eligible for optional (*kāmya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites; furthermore, there would be a transgression of eligibility for the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*) who do not constantly perform the *agnihotra*. However, for us, eligibility does not depend solely on the revelation, but rather on the auxiliary factors (*aṅga*).

[Page 246] It depends on the capacity [of the agent] in accordance with the instruction. Thus, those who lack the capacity—such as the blind, the Śūdras, and others among the three higher castes (traivarṇika)—who are unable to observe the prescribed times such as midday or evening, have no entitlement [to the rite]. Now, if this is so...

Just as in the case of optional rites (*kāmya*), it might be argued that in the case of occasional rites (*naimittika*) as well, the phrase "when [the cause occurs]" would apply in accordance with the instruction regarding the subsidiaries (*aṅga*).

To this, it is replied: First, let your honor explain this when questioned: regarding the claim that in the case of the optional rite, the qualified performer (*adhikārī*) is one capable of performing all the subsidiaries, is that understood directly from the words of the scripture, as in the case of the "one desiring heaven" (*svargakāma*)?

Or is it due to the requirement of the instruction regarding the subsidiaries (*aṅga*)?
