In that regard, first of all, the reciters do not study a word—such as the term "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*)—that is capable of encompassing all the subsidiaries. Now, if it is argued that the instruction [of the ritual] must follow the instruction regarding the subsidiaries, because such instruction would be untenable for one who lacks the capacity, since the capacity is a concomitant factor when verbal roots express their meaning; as, for example:

In the case of the injunction "he cuts with the *sruva*," even though the substance and other factors are not explicitly mentioned, they are nevertheless connected by virtue of being implied as that which is possible; likewise, although the capacity to perform all subsidiary rites (*sarvāṅgopasaṃhārasāmarthya*) is not explicitly stated, it will be connected as a qualification of the qualified person (*adhikṛtaviśeṣaṇatayā*), since it is not something to be directly enjoined.
This is appropriate in the case of optional rites (*kāmya*), because there is no obstacle to the presumption (*arthāpatti*) regarding the capacity to perform all subsidiary rites.
There is no contradiction, because an obstacle to the occurrence [of the action] is possible, and the word "desirer" (*arthin*) is possible even when [the person] is capable;
for it has not been stated that "one who desires heaven must be capable. However, in this case, there is a contradiction with the scriptural statement regarding the occasion (*nimitta*).
To explain: in the injunction "one should sacrifice as long as one lives," life (*jīvana*) connected with the phrase "as long as" (*yāvat*) is the occasion for the duty to perform the act.
It will be demonstrated later that when a certain condition exists, the effect necessarily occurs, while the other case is merely figurative.

Therefore, since there is the cognition that "when the occasioning cause (*nimitta*) exists, it must indeed be performed and not left unperformed," the necessity of performance follows from the connection with the cause;
this is because of the requirement to follow the injunctions regarding the auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) as they relate to the cause. This is due to the specific capacity for their inclusion.

It is understood that [the rite] is prescribed in the *Udbhava-samādhi*; and since it is impermanent, its necessity follows as an invariable concomitant (*nāntarīyakatva*). Furthermore, there is not even a single preeminent person (*puruṣadhaureya*) so endowed with fortune as to be able to perform the *Agnihotra* throughout his entire life, both morning and evening, without hindrance and with all its parts intact.

[The opponent claims] it is capable; however, this is because obstacles such as illness, thirst, and negligence are necessarily and invariably present, as are the suffering and mental distress that coexist with them. Furthermore, there is a contradiction between the capacity for the instruction on the cause and the capacity for the inclusion of all constituent parts [of the ritual]. Since the cause is based on Vedic revelation (*śruti*), the capacity must be described in a manner consistent with that revelation.

But surely the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) have also been heard [in scripture]. Why, then, should even they be considered as having been heard with the same necessity? Following the authority of many scriptural texts, it would be better to abandon a single text concerning the occasion (*nimitta-śruti*), according to the maxim: "One should sacrifice an individual for the sake of the family. Is this poor occasion-text merely a song of negligence, or rather, should we abandon the primary [text] instead?
Does it rely on a secondary causal status (*gauṇa-nimittabhāva*), such that [the rite occurs] only when that exists and not when it is absent?

To this it is replied: First of all, the direct scriptural injunctions regarding the constituent parts (*aṅga-śruti*) are not in conflict with the scriptural injunctions regarding the occasion (*nimitta-śruti*).
For the performance of each particular constituent part is not impossible when the occasion exists. [Objection: But [it is stated] as if it were obligatory (*nityavat*)...

There is a contradiction in saying that these are not auxiliary parts (*aṅga*). It is true that they are heard as eternal injunctions; however, being independent of the primary injunction, they are not capable of impelling the performance of the auxiliaries. For it is thus with the realization of the auxiliary (*aṅgabhāvanā*) [p.

First, one who is entirely incapable of the aforementioned application is excluded from the qualification [to perform the rite] by virtue of being too distant; such a person cannot be understood as being subject to the injunction (*niyojya*) for that purpose. Consequently, the expectancy for a result (*bhāvya*), which is a constituent part of the capacity [to act], not finding a result within its own sentence and perceiving no human goal (*puruṣārtha*) because it has been brought about by a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*), [remains unfulfilled].

Deprived of its expressed meaning, the subordinate *bhāvanā* (*aṅga-bhāvanā*) requires an end to be accomplished (*bhāvya*) consisting of human purpose (*puruṣārtha*). And the principal *bhāvanā* (*pradhāna-bhāvanā*), which possesses a causal basis (*nimittavatī*) and has as its object that which must necessarily be performed, having obtained the eternal desired end and its means, requires a cause for the assistance to its own means. Thus, this subordinate *bhāvanā*, having attained an end to be accomplished characterized by the assistance to the instrument (*karaṇa-upakāra*), [serves] the principal [action].
And cultivation (bhāvanā) comes to rest only after obtaining assistance from the instruments (karaṇa).

Consequently, regarding the subsidiaries (aṅga)—which are the means for providing that assistance required by the primary injunction (pradhāna-vidhi)—even though their performance is obtained through the acquisition of the qualification belonging to the person authorized for the primary act, their cessation must be established in accordance with the non-primary [subsidiaries]. However, in case of conflict with those [non-primary ones], there is no performance due to the absence of the qualification belonging to the person authorized for them.

The essential nature of the injunctions regarding the subsidiaries would not be lost due to the impossibility [of their performance]. Nor is it the case that the primary rite, because of its connection with a specific occasion (*nimitta*), must necessarily be performed; for it is not fit to be connected with an occasional completeness of subsidiaries, due to the contradiction between a permanent (*nitya*) and a non-permanent (*anitya*) connection.
But how, one might ask, can the primary rite itself be connected with an occasion? For even the *Agnihotra* is not [performed] when it is devoid of its subsidiaries.

[The rite] must be performed for as long as one lives, until death, because obstacles may arise. If it is argued that, by the force of the injunction, the performer must be skillful, then that [requirement] applies equally even regarding the completeness of the subsidiary parts (*aṅga*).

It is not so; for that which has a connection with a specific occasion (*nimitta*) must necessarily be performed, and since that [connection] belongs to the primary act (*pradhāna*), it is that [primary act] alone [which must be performed].

Likewise, since there is no existence of anything else in that essential nature, the skill of the performer is possible [only therein], but there is no scriptural mention of a condition (*nimitta*) regarding the subsidiaries (*aṅga*). For if that were so, they too would necessarily have to be performed.

If it is argued that because of their connection with the primary rite (*pradhāna*), they too must necessarily occur, [we reply] no; for [the requirement] is limited by the fact that they are not necessarily to be performed.

Or rather, when one does not insist on the necessity of the actual completeness of the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) according to the primary injunction (*pradhānavidhi*), because of the connection [of the subsidiary] with the phrase "as many subsidiaries as there are"; then, in this way, the scriptural statement of the occasion (*nimittaśruti*) residing in the primary sentence first brings its own object into a state of complete integration with the primary, thereby [subordinating] even the numerous scriptural statements of the subsidiaries (*aṅgaśruti*) that are favorable to itself.

By establishing it thus, one does not fall into a state of inferior practice by means of these [auxiliaries]. Nor is it the case that, as with a deficiency in other auxiliary parts, the performance of the primary rite becomes possible even after the lapse of time; for although it is an auxiliary (*guṇa*), its inclusion within the occasioning cause (*nimitta*) will also be explained later. Furthermore, there is no entitlement (*adhikāra*) for the blind, Śūdras, and others, because [the rule applies] as long as one lives (*yāvajjīva*).

Regarding the injunction "one should perform the *agnihotra*," once the goal (*sādhya*) and its means (*sādhana*) have been obtained through the productive urge (*bhāvanā*), the inquiry as to "how" is satisfied by the instructions on the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*), which generate assistance for one's own instruments. In that regard, because it is impossible for one who lacks the capacity to carry out the performance in accordance with the instructions on all the auxiliaries, and because even for one who possesses the capacity, such performance would be untenable if the state of having experienced those [auxiliaries] has not occurred; [the capacity must be established].

The capacity for the performance of the primary rite together with all its constituent parts constitutes the qualification (*adhikāra*), as in the case of rites performed for specific desires (*kāmya*). This capacity and its manifestation are understood as qualifiers of the qualified person (*adhikṛta*). In that regard, since there would be a contradiction with the scriptural injunction regarding the occasion (*nimitta-śruti*), one must necessarily avoid such a contradiction; therefore, let only the non-manifestation of one [of the two] be relinquished, but not the capacity for the constituent parts (*aṅga-sāmarthya*).

Because it would entail the undesirable consequence of the loss of both [options], it is established that there is no entitlement for blind persons, Śūdras, and the like, nor is there an occasional lack of entitlement for those afflicted by diseases that can be remedied.

First, there is the cognition of entitlement (*adhikāra*) for one who possesses the capacity, based on the scriptural injunction. And this cognition of entitlement results in the conclusion that it is not [permanent], because capacity is non-eternal; otherwise, if the one entitled were required to perform the rite with all auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) complete, there would be no performance [of the rite] when such completeness is impossible. Otherwise, since the entitlement is of a certain kind, a performance of a different kind [would not follow from it].

Because it is scriptural, there is no performance [of the rite] due to a lack of qualification; therefore, once again, there is a requirement for capacity (*śakti*) in order to determine qualification. For it has been stated that capacity is a part of the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). This is what he says: "As for one who is absolutely incapable of the aforementioned performance, such as a Śūdra..."

The lame and others are excluded from eligibility by a long distance. Why? He says: because such a person cannot be understood as being fit for the injunction (*niyojyatayā*). Therefore, having regard for the teaching of the auxiliary factors of capacity (*śakti*), the understanding of eligibility belongs first and foremost to the capable person. He clarifies: "And this understanding of eligibility does not exist in the case of the occasional rite (*naimittika*)."

The sense is that [the capacity] is concluded to be non-eternal because of its impermanence, and because that which is not contingent upon external causes must necessarily produce its effect; furthermore, there is a contradiction between "necessarily" and "not necessarily. Now, one might object: let it be that the capacity for the performance of all auxiliary parts is non-eternal, yet even so, the attainment of entitlement (*adhikāra*) should be concluded through that very capacity alone, for it is the capable person who is entitled.

To refute the claim that one might somehow employ [the rite] even when unable to bring together all the constituent parts due to some obstacle, he says: "Otherwise, if there were an absence of the bringing together of all constituent parts for the qualified person, there would be no performance; 'otherwise' means according to what is possible. If the cognition of qualification were to terminate at this point alone...

This is the meaning. Why? He says: because eligibility pertains to something different—that is, eligibility belongs to one who is capable of performing [the rite] endowed with all its constituent parts (aṅgas).
Since a performance lacking constituent parts is not sanctioned by the scriptures, it is not to be performed; for there is no eligibility for one whose constituent parts are deficient.

This is what is meant: when there is a common understanding based on the application of a specific qualification (*adhikāra*), the performance is considered scriptural (*śāstrīya*); however, in this case, even though there is a difference in subject matter due to the association of contradictory properties characterized by the completeness or incompleteness of auxiliary elements (*aṅga*), the performance is considered intuitive (*prātibha*). He concludes: "Therefore, once again, there is a dependence upon capacity (*śakti*)."

This is for the purpose of arriving at the comprehension of the qualification (*adhikāra*). Regarding the phrase "in view of capacity" (*śaktyapekṣā*): since there is a contradiction with the eternal scriptural injunction (*nitya-śruti*) regarding the connection of the temporal restriction (*yadā*) to that scriptural mention of incapacity—which was obtained through the inability [of the agent] to perform the subsidiary acts as taught—the incapacity here refers to the requirement of another connection. Thus it is said, "in view of capacity. And by means of the capacity, which is the object (*viṣaya*), one [reaches] the subject (*viṣayin*).

He defines the "hearing of capacity" (*śakti-śruti*). For example, in the statement "fire is cognized from smoke," there is an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the cognition of smoke by means of the smoke itself.

Now, why is the hearing of capacity required for the sake of reaching the conclusion regarding the understanding of entitlement (*adhikāra*)? Because once the understanding of entitlement has reached its conclusion in a case devoid of any specific restriction, the performance [of the rite] subsequently occurs according to one's capacity (*yathāśakti*). Capacity—

To show that [the capacity] itself will determine [the application], he says: "The capacity (śakti) is the scriptural statement of capacity (śakti-śruti); it is a part of the means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa) and a part of the injunction (codanā)," as stated by the Teachers. And thus, the conclusion regarding the understanding of entitlement (adhikāra) occurs precisely through its inclusion therein;
this is the meaning. For if it were not a part of the injunction, the capacity would be merely an object of cognition (prameya) and would not serve to determine the performance.

"Is postulated," is the ellipsis. This is the underlying intention here: for the ascertainment of reality is the function of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because that [ascertainment] has no other means of valid cognition. That [ascertainment] would have to depend either on time or on its constituent parts (*aṅga*). Among these, regarding the constituent parts:

In the case of dependence (*saṃśraya*), there is a contradiction with the verbal text because of the omission of other auxiliary factors that have been understood from the words. However, regarding time (*kāla*), since other times are not denoted by the words, there is no contradiction whatsoever. And this absence of contradiction exists because, in the case of an entitlement (*adhikāra*) without a specific occasion (*animitta*), the meaning of the word consists merely of "this [is to be done] by this [means] in such a manner. But when there is an occasion (*sanimitta*), it depends on the occasion.
There is a contradiction with the Vedic revelation (*śruti*). For when that [result] is attained, the fact that the action has that [attainment] as its motive is subverted.

If it is argued that in the other case as well there is a contradiction with the *śruti* "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*), it has already been stated: neither is there a specification of a particular person, nor is there a capacity; thus, by the perception of what is incompatible with the cause, the determination of performance is set aside. Now...

If it is argued that the knowledge of capacity (*śaktijñāna*) itself, being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), would determine the correct application [of words], then why is there a scriptural mention of capacity as merely a part of the injunction (*codanā*)? To this he says: "Because that application is not established by any other means of valid cognition, the knowledge of capacity is not the means of valid cognition."

Now, the proponent (pūrvapakṣin), considering that [the performance of the rite] occurs only when [the capacity exists] and not when it does not exist—thus regarding it as a causal condition (nimitta) in accordance with the instruction on the subsidiaries (aṅga) as if they were permanent—reflects: "And that capacity is based either on time or on the subsidiaries; or rather, is it based on time? This refers to the point at which one is able, having regard for the capability of bringing together all the subsidiaries.

Having reflected thus, [the author] determines the position that [the subsidiaries are related] "by way of being constituent parts" (*aṅgataḥ*), after first refuting the opposing view that they are related "by way of time" (*kālāt*).

In that regard, if one were to rely on [subsidiaries] by way of being constituent parts, there would be a contradiction with the Vedic word because it would entail the abandonment of other constituent parts understood from the word. However, if [they are related] by way of time, there is no contradiction, because other times are not the meaning of the word. This is because the constituent parts are taught as if they were eternal (*nityavat*).

If that [condition] were not abandoned, there would be a contradiction with it. However, when there is the restrictive adjunct "when" (*yadā*), since other times are not taught, there is no contradiction with the instruction; thus, in the case of optional (*kāmya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites, "when" alone is appropriate.
He refutes this: "And this non-contradiction applies to an entitlement (*adhikāra*) that lacks a specific occasion (*nirnimitta*). Why? Because this—

The meaning is that because the verbal meaning consists merely of "this is to be cultivated," "by this instrument," and "with such a specific procedure," the necessity of performance is not necessarily understood. However, when there is a conflict with the scriptural statement regarding the occasion (*nimitta*), and since that occasion has already arisen, the status of the action as being contingent upon that occasion would be contradicted; therefore, [the rule applies] when it has arisen, and thus it pertains to the archetype (*prakṛti*).

By means of these two conditions, he explains [respectively] non-acceptability and the nature of being a cause (*nimittatā*). The word *ca* (and) has the sense of *api* (even/also) and indicates a contradiction.
It will be stated that the meaning of "being a cause"—namely, "it certainly arises when [the condition] exists, and it does not arise [when it does not]"—is not what you have asserted.
Furthermore, there is no contradiction with the rule regarding the [auxiliary] factors (*aṅga*); this is the intended meaning, as has been explained in detail.

A bystander challenges the proponent: "If it is argued that there is a contradiction with the scriptural injunction regarding the 'desire for heaven' (*svargakāma*) even in the other case as well. The meaning is this: the scriptural injunction concerning the seeker (*arthiśruti*), which functions without restriction toward anyone who seeks [the result]—whether capable or incapable—is violated when it is restricted solely to those who are capable. He provides the resolution: "It has been stated," referring to the meaning of the word *kevala*.

This was stated previously [in the passage] beginning with "due to the absence of worldly transaction" (*vyavahārābhāvāt*), etc., while accepting that the word *arthin* denotes the qualified person (*adhikārin*). However, in the ultimate sense, this [passage] does not aim to establish the qualified person; rather, it aims to establish the specific object to be accomplished (*bhāvya*) required by the productive urge (*bhāvanā*). It will be explained later in this very work that the understanding of the qualified person follows as a matter of course (*arthāt*).

This is what is intended here, because it is that which is to be established (*sādhya*). Nor is there performance at all times; for it is understood that the duty is to be performed at a specific time when the occasion (*nimitta*) arises, since that [duty] is implicitly qualified by a specific time.
Because it enters into the cause (*nimitta*) of that [action]. As it has been said:

"Time is not a quality (*guṇa*), for this is the cause. The meaning is that it is not merely a quality. But other auxiliary factors (*aṅga*) are not like this, because of their inequality and because of the difference in the mode of expression (*vacanavyakti*).
And it is said in the *Bhāvanāviveka*: "Therefore, since there is no status of being an eligible agent (*adhikārin*), how could there be opposition to that?
Thus he demonstrates: "Nor is the mention of the person intended here, because the focus is on the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*)."

Having stated this verse (*kārikā*), he provides a brief introductory transition to its meaning: "And there is no performance [of the rite] continuously. Right here he raises an objection: "If, by virtue of the scriptural injunction regarding the occasion (*nimitta*), the rite were to be performed according to one's capacity even when lacking auxiliary elements (*aṅga*), then, since time such as 'evening' is also prescribed as an auxiliary element, in the absence of that..."

Since the cause for living exists at the time of midday and other such occasions, there would follow the performance of the *agnihotra* sacrifice; or, if it were not performed then due to the absence of its evening and other constituent parts (*aṅga*), then it would follow—as in the case of optional (*kāmya*) rites—that it should not be performed at all even when other parts are present. This is what has been reached [as a prima facie view]. That is now refuted by this: "nor is there performance as a continuous stream."
Thus [it is said]. Because the obligation to perform [the rite] is understood as being contingent upon a specific time [as its] occasion (*nimitta*). This is what is meant:

although this time is a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the performance, because it is not something to be intentionally undertaken (*anupādeyatva*), it qualifies the person entitled to the rite (*niyojya*), just as the capacity to include all subordinate elements [qualifies one]. Therefore, in the absence of that [time], there is no entitlement (*adhikāra*) to the Viṣṇu-steps and so forth at midday or other such times.

"...as in the case of the lame and others due to the absence of wealth. Now, an objection is raised: time is heard as a subordinate factor (*aṅga*), not as a qualification of the person entitled (*adhikṛta*). For instance, an injunction (*vidhi*) consists in setting in motion one who has not yet acted; it [operates] upon a person to be impelled once that person has understood the primary rite together with its subsidiaries. Therefore, how can there be an understanding of entitlement for one who possesses that [time]? To this, he says:

Because it is qualified by time through its meaning; for although time is heard as a subordinate factor (*aṅga*), it nevertheless qualifies the subject under discussion (*adhikṛta*). For an injunction (*vidhi*), which consists in the instigation of one who has not yet acted, having as its object the primary rite together with its subsidiaries as understood by the person to be impelled (*pravartya-puruṣa*), strives to conceive of that person to be impelled as qualified by an element that is not itself to be undertaken (*anupādeya-vastu*).

And because its subject matter is in conflict with the characteristics of being non-adoptable (*anupādeyatva*) and being that which is to be enjoined (*vidheyatva*) due to the opposition between "attainment" (*prāpti*) and "acquisition" (*āpti*), it is unable to accept [the injunction] as a qualification; furthermore, since the entitlement (*adhikāra*) is understood according to the specific application (*viniyoga*), one must follow the capacity for the integration of the primary rite along with its subsidiaries, which is inseparable from that [entitlement], and the capacity of the non-adoptable subsidiaries serves as the occasioning cause (*nimitta*).

Furthermore, even a subsidiary element (*aṅga*) is grasped as a qualification of the person who is to perform it. Moreover, time cannot possess the capacity to bring its own action to completion in the same way that the collection of other subsidiary elements does; for since capacity is a property of the effect, and the effect is characterized by its completion, it is illogical for that [capacity] to be something not to be undertaken (*anupādeya*). Indeed, the ritual act is performed in time, not in the ritual act.

Time [is a factor]. Therefore, even though time is a constituent part [of the rite], when there is a requirement for a specific person to be prompted by the injunction, the understanding that the performance belongs to one possessing that [time] arises by implication from its qualification [by time]. Consequently, there is no performance at all times.
Why? To this he says: because that [time] also enters as a causal condition (*nimitta*).
And the relation is of the nature of delimiting a single enjoined agent (*niyojya*), just as there is a co-inherence in a single individual instance between a universal and a quality.
For the subsidiary parts (*aṅga*) are to be adopted, while the occasioning cause (*nimitta*) is not to be adopted. One should perform these by means of these, or these [results] by means of these.

The syntactical structure (*vacanavyakti*) applies to all the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*). In the phrase "this being present," it refers to the occasion (*nimitta*); therefore, other auxiliaries are not capable of entering into that occasion. However, time (*kāla*), though not something to be directly undertaken (*anupādeya*), is logically able to enter into the occasion even while being an auxiliary, because it shares the same syntactical structure. Now, [if one asks] whether there is merely a restriction to the occasion...
Why is this not accepted? [Because] even in the case of an optional rite (*kāmya*), it occurs by virtue of the desire at that time. Is this not merely a practical purpose (*prayojana*)? True.

However, the relationship [of identity] between "the cow" and "white" is the cause for grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). The venerable Teacher also accepts this very point; thus he says: "It has been stated that time is not a quality (*guṇa*), for it is a causal condition (*nimitta*). But [one might object]: [The objection continues: "But..."

Fearing that the independent established doctrine (*svatantra-siddhānta*)—that time is an auxiliary of the performance (*prayogāṅga*)—would be undermined, he explains: the meaning is "it is not merely an accessory" (*guṇa*). Furthermore, its status as a "condition" (*nimitatva*) is figurative (*bhākta*) due to its connection with a condition, and not its actual essence, because there is no evidence for such a conceptualization. Now, if time, even as an auxiliary, is not a condition...
Why is it that the others are not also [included] as such members? To this he says: "But the other members are not like this.

Why? Because of the inequality of the cause. Why is that? Because of the difference in the mode of expression (*vacanavyakti*). What, then, is the reason for the difference in the mode of expression? To this he says: "For the other members are things to be adopted (*upādeya*)."

From time [as the cause], the motive (nimitta) is not something to be adopted; hence, there is a difference in the mode of expression (vacanavyakti). He demonstrates this: "One should perform those [rites] with these [means]"—this is the mode of expression regarding the subsidiaries (aṅga). Indeed, when the assistance for the performance (karaṇopakāra) is being rendered by the subsidiaries, since they do not exist as unperformed, they too must be performed to some extent. This, then, is the adoptability (upādeyatva) of the subsidiaries.

Therefore, in this case, two modes of expression are appropriate. One mode of expression is: "When these [factors] exist, even though they are not within the scope of human effort, these [results] occur.

Consequently, due to this difference in the mode of expression, other auxiliary factors (*aṅga*) are not capable of entering into the status of a condition (*nimitta*). Time, however, is not something to be brought about (*anupādeya*); therefore, it is similar to a condition.

It is logical that time, like other auxiliary factors (*aṅga*), enters into the causal condition (*nimitta*) through its specific mode of expression (*vacanavyakti*). Just as a rite is enjoined with respect to a non-auxiliary causal condition, so too it is enjoined with respect to time; however, this does not apply to other auxiliaries. Thus it is established that, like a causal condition, time is a qualification of the person entitled to perform the rite (*adhikṛta*), and not an auxiliary factor itself.
Here, an objector from the side raises an objection: Why is it not accepted that there is merely a withdrawal of the occasion (*nimitta*)?

Time is connected as a primary auxiliary (*aṅga*), whereas the occasion enters [the rite] only subsequently by implication; what is the use of this circuitous process? For, according to the scriptural hearing (*śruti*) "as long as life lasts" (*yāvajjīvam*), this life—which has extended [to the end of one's existence]—is itself [the occasion] by the scripture alone.

The rule regarding time will be restricted to specific times. The meaning is: let this not be a scriptural injunction regarding time (*kāla-śruti*) nor even a scriptural injunction regarding auxiliary factors (*aṅga-śruti*), but rather it should be understood as a scriptural injunction regarding a causal condition (*nimitta-śruti*).
He refutes another objection from a bystander: "Even in the case of an optional rite (*kāmya*), [it occurs] by desire for that time. This is the meaning.

If this were a scriptural statement of occasion (nimitta-śruti) such as "on the full moon" or "on the new moon," it would not be connected with the optional (kāmya) rite; nor can a single sentence convey both its status as an occasion and its status as an auxiliary (aṅga), due to the resulting inconsistency (vairūpya). Furthermore, if it were connected to both by way of being an occasion, then [the rite] would also be [performed] for the sake of the optional result.

There would be the consequence of having to perform the ritual application according to one's capacity; or else, if there were no connection, the optional rite would result in being performed at an indefinite time.

The reason [for this] is that the scriptural statement regarding lifelong performance does not have a meaning exceeding [the general rule], and that even the principal rite serves as a subordinate element for its subsidiaries.

Thus, since there is no contradiction, in the case where there is no specific occasion (*animitta*), the basis for the capacity is "whenever" in terms of time; however, when an occasion exists (*nimittavati*), because of the contradiction with the occasion, it is "just as" in terms of the subsidiary elements, specifically in terms of time.
He refutes this as follows: "But surely this is the purpose. This is the underlying intention:

if, through the examination of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it turns out that what is desired is of indefinite time, let it be so; what harm is there for us who follow the authority of the *pramāṇas*? A *pramāṇa* never conforms to a purpose, because it is the *pramāṇa* that holds sway over [the purpose].
Regarding the phrase "of that":

the proponent of the ultimate conclusion (*paramasiddhāntin*) says—"True; the meaning is that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not dependent upon a purpose. However, the reason is that the scriptural injunction for lifelong performance (*yāvajjīva-śruti*) possesses no meaning beyond [the general rule]. This is the underlying intention here: in that context, there is indeed a general scriptural statement.

Where it is restricted to a specific instance, it possesses a meaning that exceeds the general rule; for example, the general scriptural injunction "He divides the sacrificial cake into four parts" is restricted to the *āgneya* cake by the specific rule "He divides the *āgneya* into four parts. In that case, if only "He divides [the cake] into four parts" were heard, and not the specific "He divides the *āgneya* into four parts," then [it would apply to all cakes]. If it were not [restricted] to the *āgneya*, [the general rule would remain unrestricted].

Even for one [who holds the opposite view], both [the injunctions] would become purposeful only if the rite were performed on the occasion of either the full moon or the new moon; however, in that case, it would neither apply to one who is not alive nor to one who lives for his entire life. Since the occasional rite (*naimittika*) must necessarily be performed when the occasion (*nimitta*) arises, it follows that the scriptural statement regarding "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīva*) would have no meaning beyond what is already implied. Thus, there is the consequence of redundancy.

Now, it might be argued: if the phrase "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīvam*) were not recited in connection with the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, then—since the two groups [of rites] would each be connected to the occasion [of the sacrifice] individually—they would each come to be the object of the qualification [for performance]. To prevent this contingency, the meaning of the sentence is "as long as one lives, [one should perform] the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices. For by this...
It is argued that the six sacrifices are brought under a single scope of eligibility (*adhikāra*). Even so, the phrase "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīvam*) would be redundant;

one should simply have read "one should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices" (*darśapūrṇamāsābhyāṃ yajeta*). Furthermore, there is no qualification based on the desire for heaven (*svargakāma-adhikāra*) here in the form "that [result] would be heaven"; for that [qualification] is already established by the injunction "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*svargakāmo yajeta*).

Regarding the verbal expression: this solution is not possible in the case of the injunction "one should perform the *agnihotra* as long as one lives. For once the *agnihotra* has been established by the rule "one offers the *agnihotra*," and the time-conditions characterized by evening and morning have been prescribed by the rule "one offers the *agnihotra* in the evening and in the morning," the sentence "one should offer the *agnihotra* as long as one lives" would be redundant.

"By way of a consequence (*prasaṅgāt*)," he adds another reason: "and because even that which belongs to the context (*prakaraṇin*) is for the sake of the subsidiary (*aṅga*). Indeed, this primary efficient force (*bhāvanā*), which consists of the accomplishment of what is to be achieved, requires assistance for its own means; it therefore accepts whatever has fallen within proximity (*saṃnidhi*) as a subsidiary, by way of assisting its own means. And in that context...

A scriptural injunction regarding time (kāla-vidhi-vākya), when heard, makes known that [the time] is a subsidiary (aṅga) to its own scope, not that it is a conditional occasion (nimitta); for the principal rite does not stand in need of a subsidiary. Therefore, it is elegant to conclude that a scriptural injunction regarding time, aided by the context (prakaraṇa), is the authority for the time’s status as a subsidiary, and not for its status as a conditional occasion.

[253] But what is this that is contradicted? It is the substratum of capacity in terms of time. From what is it understood whose [capacity it is], and how is the relationship between the cause and the effect established? Furthermore, what is the nature of its connection with the effect?

If it is the case that [the effect occurs] "when this exists," what contradiction is there? For even in terms of time, when that substratum of capacity does not exist, that action certainly does not exist. On the other hand, if it is argued that [the action] is necessarily performed only when that [substratum] exists, then there would be a contradiction. However, such is not the meaning of "efficient cause" (*nimitta*). For an efficient cause is indeed a reason (*hetu*), and it is not necessarily [the case that the effect must occur whenever the cause exists].
Causes possess effects, but an effect does not exist when its cause is absent; therefore, there is no contradiction.

He concludes the subject under discussion along with its cause: "Thus, because there is no contradiction, in the case of that which is without a cause, [the manifestation occurs] by power according to time; but in the case of that which has a cause, due to the presence of a cause, it occurs as a constituent part according to time."
This is easy to understand.

Having thus explained the first half of the verse, he raises an objection as a prelude to introducing the second half, beginning with "But what, moreover... (*kiṃ punar iti*). The word "what" (*kim*) is used here in the sense of an objection. In that context, "But what, moreover, is this... [is the question].
That which obstructs its cause at a particular time is the implication of its own nature (*svarūpākṣepa*), based on the locus of power;

"of what [is it the cause]? is the implication of another related entity (*saṃbandhyantarākṣepa*); and "how is the relationship between cause and effect understood? is the implication of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇākṣepa*). Among these, he analyzes the implication of its own nature: "If, first of all, when something exists... Who?
There is a contradiction regarding time; the phrase "by means of the locus of power" is to be understood as the ellipsis. He demonstrates the absence of contradiction:
for even with respect to time, that action does not occur when that locus of power is absent, but rather only when it is present.
Now, it might be argued: it is not being determined that the action is performed only when it is present and not when it is absent, but rather...
He says that there is a contradiction regarding the cause in the case of non-performance, [expressed as]: "it is indeed performed, it is not not performed. He then states:

"Now, when that [cause] exists, it is indeed performed. He refutes this: "There might be a contradiction, but such is not the meaning of the word 'nimitta' (cause). For a cause is indeed a *hetu* (logical reason). What follows from that? Causes do not necessarily produce their effects."

[The suffix *kta*] has been discarded; therefore, the meaning of the causal factor (*nimitta*) is exactly as before: "only when [the cause] exists, not when it does not. And thus there is no contradiction; so he says: "But the effect does not exist when the cause is absent; therefore, there is no contradiction. This is intended: for the relationship between word and meaning is dependent upon the determination of usage in the world, and the word "cause" (*hetu*)...

An effect is applied only when [the cause] exists, not when it is absent. Indeed, worldly people do not fail to recognize that a seed situated in a granary, having failed to produce a sprout, is not the cause. Therefore, just as the relationship between the pervaded (*vyāpya*) and the pervader (*vyāpaka*), although dependent on both, is understood in the case of the pervaded as "existence indeed" by virtue of its connection with the pervader, and not as "non-existence."

And it is established that [the relation] does not exist elsewhere because of its nature as a pervading connection; likewise, the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) must also be defined such that the effect exists only when the cause exists and not when it is absent, and thus the priority (*prāgbhāva*) of the cause over the effect—not its non-existence—must be determined. Consequently, this word "efficient cause" (*nimitta*) is used; therefore, it does not have that [other] meaning.

Thus it is said. To analyze what was raised by the question "Of what?", he says: if action were the cause, then the injunction for the commencement of action would be purposeless, and all verbal instruction would likewise be purposeless.

If [the soul] were caused by action (*karman*), then because action would proceed from that very cause, the injunction (*vidhi*) would be purposeless; for even from an unascertained cause, one observes the occurrence of that which possesses a cause, and thus there would be an absence of human effort (*puruṣakāra*). Nor does its production arise from a cause, because it is eternal. When that [cause] exists, there is no cognition [of it], because [cognition arises] only from a sentence (*vākya*).

Because that [result] is established, ritual action would be useless. If it is argued that "it occurs only when [the cause] exists"—that is, the fruit of the ritual action arises only when that [cause] is present—then there is no contradiction regarding the performance of all constituent parts. Or, if it refers to the qualification (*adhikāra*), we say no; for qualification arises from the injunction (*niyoga*). That very connection with the injunction is what constitutes the cause of that qualification. If, then...

Now, one might object: why is the word useless? For the word will cause one to understand the cause, and from that understanding of the cause, a person will apply themselves to action. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Because even from an unascertained cause, there is no human effort [resulting] from the mere perception of what possesses the cause. This is the intended meaning: namely, that...

Let it be understood by the word "api" (also/even) that even ignorance, when not appropriated, is insufficient for the production of its effects; just as substances, qualities, and actions are each their own respective effects of action, yet this [ignorance], such as life-force and so forth, is not an effect of action.
Therefore, action is the cause merely by its existence, and thus human effort and its investigation are purposeless.
Now, it is understood that "the cause" refers to the injunction (*vidhi*). [The author] refutes this: its production does not arise from a cause. Why?
Because of its eternality and because it is inherent. For the injunction regarding action is simply its status as a means to the highest good (*śreyas*).
And this [status] is not imposed upon the action by a cause such as the need for livelihood; rather, it arises solely from its own cause.

The means to the highest good (*śreyas*) arises from ritual action (*karman*); and it has already been stated that living and so forth are not caused by ritual action—this is the intended meaning. Now, [an objection is raised]: "Let it not be [caused] by the injunction (*vidhi*), but it will be [caused] by the cognition thereof. To this he says: "When that [injunction] exists, there is no cognition of that [result]. Why? Because that is established from the sentence alone. Now, as for the cause of the result...

The word "it is said" (*ucyate*) is supplied [from the previous context]. He refutes this: [it would lead to] the futility of ritual action (*karmavaiyarthyam*). For when the cause (*nimitta*) exists, the result necessarily arises. Again, he raises an objection: if it is argued that the fruit of the action occurs only when that cause is present; [the reply is: no, for the dependence upon action does not destroy the status of [the cause] as a cause.
The sense is that it does not obstruct it, as is the case everywhere.

This is true; however, he says that what was intended [by the opponent] is not so: "There is no contradiction when all the constituent parts are combined. This has been explained by the word *nigada* (the explanatory prose). Now, the connection is: "[this is] the cause for the qualification (*adhikāra*). This is what is meant: the cognition that arises in a person—that this ownership over the ritual action is the producer of that very result which he desires.

Regarding the phrase "from the cause" (*nimittāt*), he refutes it: rather, entitlement (*adhikāra*) arises from the mandate (*niyoga*). Understanding the mandate, the person—who perceives himself as the one to be enjoined (*niyojya*) directed toward the object of action, which is the verbal root-meaning (*bhāvārtha*)—comes to know his own ownership over that verbal root-meaning, which is the object of the mandate, solely through the power of the mandate itself.

"What is the purpose of a cause? is the meaning. True; the state of being enjoined implies ownership (*svāmitva*) directed toward the meaning of the ritual act (*bhāvārtha*). However, that very state of being enjoined—the person's connection with the mandate (*niyoga*)—does not occur without a cause.
Therefore, he raises the doubt: "In that case, there will be the existence of a cause"—that very connection with the mandate... [is] that.

The opponent objects: "If, then, the mandate (niyoga) is caused by that [condition], there is no comprehension of the condition from the mandate. This is the intended meaning: when one states that the connection of a person with the mandate has living and so forth as its cause...

The injunction (niyoga) is caused by that [condition], but the cognition of the condition does not arise from the injunction itself. Since it is expressed by the word as depending upon a condition already established, there is dependence.

Alternatively, the status of being a condition belongs to the qualification of the person to be enjoined (niyojya) by implication; for when that [qualification] exists, there is entitlement (adhikāra).
And in this case, neither perception nor other means of knowledge apply, nor does verbal testimony (śabda), because that [verbal testimony] is primarily concerned with injunctions (vidhi),

and because its object is positive existence (bhāva), and because it exceeds the three factors [of action]. For, in that context, since there would be an injunction of the rite being enjoined with respect to the result, or an injunction regarding the occasion for that [result], or an injunction of both, there would be a syntactical split (vākya-bheda).

He speaks of the mandate (*niyoga*) itself as being preceded by the [understanding of the] occasion (*nimitta*). For it is not understood merely as "this is to be done" (*kāryam*), but rather as "this is my duty to be done. Thus, the comprehension of the mandate is precisely the comprehension of the task as related to oneself. Therefore, one who asserts that the connection with the mandate is preceded by the understanding of the occasion, says that the mandate itself is preceded by that [understanding].
And consequently, the comprehension [of the object] would not arise from the mandate (*niyoga*) as its cause. [Objection: Let it not be so; what is the fault? [Response: To this he says:
"That [mandate] is spoken of by the word as depending upon a previously established cause"; thus there is dependence.
For the cause of the mandate must be either an efficient factor (*kāraka*) or a signifier (*jñāpaka*); a third mode of being a cause does not exist.

Since there is no such thing as a "time" (yāma), if it were the agent [of the injunction], the performance of ritual acts would be rendered useless; therefore, its status remains that of a mere indicator (*jñāpaka*). Consequently, because the mandate (*niyoga*) is already understood by means of a cause that is already established, the verbal expression would be dependent upon that [pre-existing cause];
thus, the undesirable consequence follows that the word lacks authoritative validity (*aprāmāṇya*).

Now, it might be argued: "We do not say that the understanding of the mandate (niyoga) arises from the comprehension of a causal sign (nimitta), whereby we would be subject to such a consequence. Rather, the word itself, independently, makes known the mandate for one who possesses life.
This is because the qualification of the person to be enjoined (niyojya-viśeṣaṇa) is required first by the mandate, and [the state of] living serves as its delimiting factor."
[This is] the connection. However, it is said that living and so forth are indeed the conditions (*nimitta*) that qualify the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*).

For only when that qualification of the person to be enjoined exists is there a cognition of the mandate (*niyoga*) as being connected to oneself, and because ownership (*svāmitā*) in the ritual act is understood, the entitlement (*adhikāra*) of the agent is established. Thus he says: "Now, by implication, the condition [is derived] from the qualification of the person to be enjoined..."

Because of the context, [the word] "existence" (bhāva) refers to that [condition]. Consequently, it is possible for the desire for heaven (*svargakāmanā*) also to function as a causal factor (*nimittatva*).

Nor does there arise any contradiction regarding the performance of all auxiliary parts (*sarvāṅgopasaṃhāra*) in this case, as there would be in the instance of the injunction "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīvam*). This is the meaning.

Having thus analyzed the question "of what [is this the cause]?", he analyzes the question "from what [does it arise]?"—and here, perception and the other means of knowledge do not apply to the status of being a cause for life and so forth. Now, one might object: "Let perception and the others indeed not apply; but the Word (śabda) will apply.
To this he says: "Nor even the Word. Why? Because its primary function is that of an injunction (vidhi). Nevertheless...

Why is there no status as having a cause (*nimitta*) as its object? To this he says: "And because that injunction has existence (*bhāva*) as its object, and the word 'existence' denotes productive activity (*bhāvanā*), since it is derived from the root *bhū* with the suffix *ṇic* and the affix *ac* according to the rule *eraj*. If it were argued: "Let the injunction have productive activity as its object; however, by virtue of its connection with that [activity], it also takes the cause as its range, and thus the word is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) therein."
It is said: That in whose arising there is a necessity for the performance of an action is its cause. How so?

When something exists, that which necessarily follows is the primary cause; the other, however, is a cause by way of metaphorical designation (*bhaktyā*). This is the distinction between their respective states.

Because of the connection; and since between the secondary and the primary, the understanding rests on the primary, its necessary establishment [is required]. To the objection that [the injunction] will intend that [connection] as its cause, he says: "And because of its being beyond the three factors. Once the connection with the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) is established, the cause would have the status of an injunction (*codanā*); however, that very [connection] is not established because of the excess over the [standard] triad of the end (*sādhya*), the means (*sādhana*), and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*).

This is the meaning. He analyzes the phrase "of this" [as follows]: there, because the action being enjoined with respect to a cause is enjoined with respect to a fruit that is constantly desired, the ellipsis is: "because of the injunction regarding that fruit, and because of the injunction regarding the cause. Both...

"But if both [the fruit and the cause] were injunctions, or if it were an injunction of action regarding the fruit and the cause, there would be a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*). The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the objection.
Having thus raised the objection, he introduces the second half of the verse as the response, saying: "It is said: where..."

When [the son] is born, there is the necessity of performing the rites; this is the occasion (nimitta). By the word "jāte" ("when born"), he indicates that the birth is not something to be brought about (anupādeya), but rather serves as the condition for the occasion. He states that the occasion consists in the necessity of performing the rites, saying "the necessity of performing the rites.
By the inclusion of the term "necessarily" (avaśyam), he demonstrates that an occasion is that in whose presence [the rite] necessarily occurs and in whose absence it does not.

And by speaking thus, the manner in which the occasion (*nimitta*) is connected as a qualifier of the injunction (*vidhi*) in the form of something to be performed (*kartavyatā*) has also been indicated by implication as a way of construing the meaning of the sentence. He asks about most of what was stated previously:
"How? The answer: That in the presence of which [the effect] necessarily comes to be is the primary cause (*hetu*). But [one might object]: "Is it not the effect (*kārya*)..."
Ordinary people employ the word "cause" (hetu) with the intention that [the cause] exists only when [the effect] exists and not when it does not;

in that case, how can this be the primary cause? To this he says: "But the other [is so called] figuratively, by way of indication (lakṣaṇā). It is true that even when it does not produce an effect characterized by smoke and so forth, the word "cause" is applied to fire and the like; however, it is not on account of this that it [is the primary cause].

This is the primary meaning. Indeed, this word "cause" (hetu), which functions specifically toward whatever effect it produces, ought not to function [metaphorically] everywhere. For the word "staff-bearer" (daṇḍin), whose application depends upon the qualification of a staff, never applies to Caitra or others who lack a staff. Therefore, that alone is called a "cause" in relation to which [the effect] arises when it exists.

An effect certainly comes into being; however, that which, when present, sometimes produces it and sometimes does not produce it, cannot be the instrument (*karaṇa*). Furthermore, how can an instrument be the cause (*hetu*) for the application [of the term]? For the word "cause" is not applied to that which will produce [the effect] or has produced it, because an instrument that is not currently functioning lacks existence. And if that which is non-existent were the occasion for the application [of the term], then...

Because of this consequence. Therefore, it is correct to say that the word "cause" (nimitta) is used in its primary sense in the case where something necessarily arises when [the cause] exists, whereas in other cases it is used figuratively. He states the reason for this secondary usage (lakṣaṇā): "because of the connection with a specific state of those [factors].
For it is only seeds and so forth, having acquired a particular state through their mutual conjunction, that invariably produce the effect.
This is the position of the Śālinas. As even outsiders have said:

"Nothing arises from a single cause; rather, everything arises from a causal complex (*sāmagrī*). Therefore, either specific states or those possessing specific states are the efficient causes (*nimitta*).
[It follows] precisely from the force of the context. For that alone would not be a cause (nimitta) in the presence of which the rite would not be performed;
and the necessity of performing the ritual action is understood as pertaining to one who performs it with all its constituent parts intact, not to one whose limbs have been omitted.

It is appropriate [to perform it], never that which is a means to what is harmful; therefore, it is understood that "action" (karman) is that which is always desired as a means, when endowed with its constituent parts according to one's capacity. Furthermore, the causality (*nimittatā*) of the injunction (*vidhi*), which consists in the state of being something to be done, is such that when that [injunction] exists, for one who performs it in whatever way possible, it invariably accomplishes the destruction of sin, which is always the desired goal.

[The terms] are denotable. However, where that particular state does not exist [at present], there the term is used figuratively (lākṣaṇika) by some means of connection with a different state, such as "it was" or "it will be. Now, one might object: "Let it be figurative;
nevertheless, why is that very [figurative sense] not the logical reason? To this he says: "And between the secondary and the primary, the understanding [of the word] applies to the primary."

Therefore, the necessity of performance must be established. Why? Precisely because of the force of the occasion (*nimitta*). He demonstrates this very force by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*): for that would not even be an occasion upon which the rite could not be performed. Consequently, it is established that in the case of a rite contingent upon an occasion (*naimittika*), there is a performance according to one's capacity (*yathāśakti-prayoga*), due to the contradiction [otherwise] with the inclusion of all auxiliary parts (*sarvāṅga-upasaṃhāra*).

And he says that it is always the means for what is desired: "The necessity of performing the rite (*karma*) is perceived and cannot be set aside; it applies to the entire collection of its constituent parts (*aṅga*), and never to that which is merely a means toward what is desired. By implication, this means that an occasional rite (*naimittika*) is understood to be a rite that is always the means for what is desired, when it is endowed with its constituent parts according to one's capacity. For what occasion?

Regarding what was stated [previously], he provides the following answer: "And the status of being a cause (nimittatā) excludes the necessity of performing the action (kartavyatā) which consists in the injunction (vidhi-rūpā), namely the necessity of performing it for the sake of a result.
Now, it was argued that this [injunction] is eternal; to that he replies: "While that exists, for one who performs [it] in whatever manner..."

The mind always accomplishes the destruction of sin that has been intended. This is the underlying intention: it is true that an injunction (*vidhi*) is a property of the action (*karman*) consisting in being the means intended by the agent (*kartṛ*). Furthermore, although that [property] is natural to that which is about to arise from its own causes, nevertheless, because it must necessarily be performed when the occasion (*nimitta*) exists, it is accomplished in some way or another, thereby fulfilling the agent’s intended purpose regarding what has been undertaken.

It indeed accomplishes the fruit characterized by the exhaustion of defilements. This is what is meant: when the causal sign (nimitta) exists, action arising from its own causes possesses all its constituent parts; otherwise, it does not attain the status of being a means for the agent’s desired end or the status of being something to be performed.
Thus, the status of being "to be performed" constitutes the means for achieving what the agent desires.
"Because it is heard as the cause for that injunction.

Regarding what was said—that there is a lack of evidence for its being a cause—we accept the absence of anything other than the word, but not the absence of the word itself. Now, the word has the injunction as its primary meaning; therefore, in the injunction, [it refers] to the *bhāvanā* which has that [injunction] as its object.

Or rather, [the word] is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with respect to its constituent parts because of its connection to them. Nor is any one of these [parts] the cause; how then is the word a means of valid cognition in that regard by virtue of being an injunction (*codanā*)? To this he says: "Even though there is a distinction from the [actual] entity (*bhāva*), the fact of being cognizable by the word which constitutes the injunction is the cause"—this is the connection. By the word *bhāva*, he refers to the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) endowed with the three factors.

Now, it may be argued that because the *nimitta* (condition) is not something to be adopted (*anupādeya*) and is not something to be enjoined (*avidheya*), there would be the consequence of a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*);

furthermore, even in the absence of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), it is still cognizable by the word (*śabdaprameyatva*). This is because even that which is not to be enjoined enters into the injunction in the same manner as that which is enjoined.

Because it possesses two types of qualifiers; for this very reason, when this [qualification] is connected with the ritual action (*karman*), there is no room for an alternative, which is logically sound.
Now, some consider qualifications such as "living" to be like "heaven" and so forth—[qualifications] belonging to the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) by means of the mandate (*niyoga*).
Because the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) is required first. For in the world, there is no injunction (*niyoga*) that does not depend on a specific person to be enjoined. [Objection:

How can that which is to be indicated (*uddeśya*) be the object of the word that constitutes the injunction (*codanā*)? To this he says: "Even though it is not something to be enjoined, it is like that which is enjoined. This is the intended meaning (*abhisaṃdhi*): There is no such rule that only that which is to be enjoined (*vidheya*) can be the object indicated by the purpose of the injunction.

Thus [it is argued]: because it would follow that an injunction (*vidhi*), that which is not to be enjoined (*avidheya*), and that which is not intended as a goal (*anuddeśya*) would lack the status of being the meaning of an injunction (*codanārtha*). Rather, that which the injunction makes known as a cause (*nimitta*) is also its object, just like the injunction itself. [Objection: A word is an authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by virtue of being an injunction when it makes known an injunction or that which is to be enjoined; however, a cause is neither an injunction nor that which is to be enjoined. Therefore, how [can it be the object]?

In that regard, is verbal testimony a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by virtue of being an injunction (*codanā*)? To this he says: "Because of its entry into the injunction. Why is that [the Vaiśvānara sacrifice] itself not something to be enjoined? To this he says: "Because it is a qualification of the injunction. This is the intended meaning:
the ritual act of the twelve-potherd cake for Vaiśvānara is to be performed without distinction, whether the birth of a son has occurred or not.

Furthermore, it would not be necessarily applicable. By this reasoning, when the duty is established as something to be performed only upon the birth of a son— using that birth as a *nimitta* (occasion)— it follows that the occasion, though itself neither enjoined nor intended as a goal, yet, being unintended and unenjoined, takes on the status of a qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*) by its own nature.
And since the qualification has been expressed, the status of the word as an injunction (*codanā*) is established.
Regarding what was asked—how its connection with the occasional factor (*naimittika*) comes about—the answer is stated:
"For this very reason, there is no room for an alternative (*vikalpa*) regarding its connection with the ritual act (*karman*), because it is not something to be enjoined (*avidheya*)."
Because it functions as a qualifier, enters into the injunction, and is an object of knowledge through the word, it has a connection with the injunction; for this very reason,

regarding the relationship between the occasion (*nimitta*) and the action (*karman*) to be enjoined, the dilemma was raised as to whether the action is enjoined with reference to the occasion, or whether the occasion is enjoined with reference to the action— and the fault that follows therein [was addressed].

That entire [objection] is without foundation. The meaning is that the contingency of an option (*vikalpa*) is based on a connection with something to be enjoined (*vidheya*); it cannot occur when there is no connection with something to be enjoined.
Therefore, the argument is sound.
Thus, he refutes what was stated previously—that life and so forth are connected as the occasioning condition (*nimitta*) from the very beginning.

He says: But surely [the Mīmāṃsakas] consider qualifiers of the person to be enjoined, such as "living" and so on, just like "heaven" and so on? He offers the reason that this is not established by mere reflection alone: because the person to be enjoined is required first by the mandate (*niyoga*). This is the meaning: for an effect, whose existence depends upon being performed, does not culminate in its true nature if it is not being executed.

Furthermore, performance cannot exist without an agent, and agency does not exist without entitlement (*adhikāra*), and such entitlement is indeed observed. In its absence, there would be no comprehension at all; rather, that [entitlement] is precisely the qualification for it.

On account of the context of truth (*satya*), [the phrase "as long as one lives"] stands as a causal condition (*nimitta*); whereas heaven and so forth stand as the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*) because they are objects of desire.

This is not sound, because the qualification is untenable. For there is no one whatsoever who is ever enjoined as qualified by "as long as one lives," nor is anyone ever enjoined as qualified by various seasonal times such as spring.

Since the notion "this is my duty" arises only with reference to a person who is to be enjoined (niyojya) as the one who understands the task, the distinction of the person to be enjoined as the knower of the task is not established by the mandate (niyoga) itself, nor by the task, nor by the performance prompted by nothing else. Because of its intrinsic nature, the mandate requires the person to be enjoined first as its very cause; furthermore, since the distinction of the person to be enjoined cannot be established without a qualification, the qualification—being the cause—is [the primary factor].

Since that [obligation] is established as something to be accomplished, its initial connection is first and foremost as a qualification of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), and not as a causal occasion (*nimitta*).
This is well-established even in common worldly usage; since the Veda is preceded by that [worldly usage], how could it not be established there as well?
With this intention, he says: "For in the world, an obligation (*niyoga*) is never seen that does not depend on a specific person to be enjoined."

The meaning is that, on the contrary, in both the world and the Veda, an injunction (*niyoga*) is observed to function according to its respective context even without a [perceptible] sign (*nimitta*). Now, one might object: "Exclusion does not follow from mere non-perception. To this he says: "In the absence of that [sign], and in the absence of a specific person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) who is the cognizer, there would be no cognition at all. This was stated by the Teacher: "For indeed, without aiming at Devadatta or Yajñadatta..."

"The optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth function [to denote an injunction]. Now, if the occasioning cause (*nimitta*) were also a qualification of the person entitled to perform the rite (*adhikṛta-viśeṣaṇa*), then, because there would be no connection [of the rite] with that as its occasioning cause, the rite would not be occasional (*naimittika*); thus, a contradiction of one’s own established doctrine (*svasiddhānta*) would result. To this, he says: "But that very qualification of the person, when it exists, stands as the occasioning cause because of the entitlement [to the rite] being contingent upon it."

The meaning is as follows: although life and so forth are qualifiers of the qualified person (adhikṛta), since the entitlement [to perform the rite] exists when they are present, they possess the status of a "condition" (nimitta) by implication; thus, because of that connection, the ritual action is "conditional" (naimittika). Therefore, how could there be a contradiction with the established conclusion (siddhānta)? Now, one might object: "In this way, even heaven and the like would have the status of a condition, and consequently, even a rite performed for a specific desire (kāmya) would result in being classified as conditional. To this, he says:

"But heaven and so forth, however, exist as objects of desire by virtue of being that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*); this is the ellipsis. This is the intended meaning: even though heaven and so forth are qualifiers of the qualified person (*adhikṛta*), they do not possess the status of a *nimitta* (occasioning condition). This is because there is a contradiction with their status as a *sādhya*, which is brought about through connection with the root *kam* ("to desire"); furthermore, the status of being a *nimitta* must necessarily coexist with [the state of] being already established (*siddhatā*).

Because [the cause] is excluded by the perception of something incompatible with its pervader; and since the status of being a motive for living and so forth is already established, the distinction between optional (*kāmya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites is proven.
The proponent of the established doctrine refutes this view of a partial authority: "This is not sound. Why? Because of the qualification..."

Because [that] is untenable. He states that very point: "For there is no one whatsoever who is ever qualified by 'as long as life' (*yāvaj-jīvanam*), nor is anyone qualified by various spring seasons. This is the meaning: "life" (*jīvanam*) is said to be the maintenance of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). And that word, being used here in conjunction with the word "as long as" (*yāvat*), refers either to [the duration of] those [lives]...

Whether one were to assert that the lives of all living beings, or the life of a single person for as long as it lasts—in regard to these, the refutation of the first two alternatives is as follows: for it is not the case that [the word "all"] refers to as many persons or as many lives as there are.

Neither "being alive" (*jīvana*) nor "dwelling [in the village]" (*vasan*) is a qualifying attribute (*viśeṣaṇa*), because being alive is not something that requires to be stated (it is already established), and because there would be no syntactic connection (*ananvaya*) with the terms "as long as" (*yāvat*) and "repetition" (*vīpsā*). Nor is it a restatement (*anuvāda*) of two things already established; for even in the case of one who is alive, eligibility belongs only to him who desires heaven, since there is no contradiction due to the adjunct "when he is able" (*yadā śaknuyāt*), given that the performance of the ritual depends upon the sequence [of other duties].

There is no loss of a constituent part [of the sentence]. Therefore, as long as the repetition (*vīpsā*) and its meaning cannot be construed [with the subject], life (*jīvana*) cannot be a qualification of the agent; rather, the singular number is intended to refer to the genus (*jāti*). Consequently, it is possible for some single individual to be qualified by that [genus]. Regarding the refutation of the third alternative: "at some time" (*kadācit*). For [the action] is not scattered across the three times.

A person who possesses life is possible at some time; for whether [the qualification] is possible or not invariably present, the qualification is meaningful. But how could it be meaningful if it were impossible? Thus, [the person] is characterized by various spring seasons. For, by means of another sentence—"One should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma in the spring"—the connection of the Jyotiṣṭoma with a specific time is indeed enjoined.

The intention is that the scriptural statement has the purpose of indicating a specific characteristic (*nimitta*). Now, it might be argued: "It is not the case that both [terms] are qualifications of the person entitled to perform the rite (*adhikṛta*), but rather they are 'living' (*jīvana*) and 'spring' (*vasanta*); and these two are possible [to occur together]. To this he says: "Neither mere living nor mere spring is the qualification. He states the reason why mere living is not a qualification there:

Because life is not [suitable] to be expressed [as a qualification]. It is true that there is possibility [of its occurrence], but there is no deviation [from it]. Indeed, for one who is not living, the status of being subject to an injunction (*niyojyatā*) is impossible—that which would be delimited by "living. Therefore, because there is nothing to be delimited for this [injunction], the meaning is that life cannot be expressed as a qualification. And [the term "living"] is common to both the state of living and the spring season.

He adds another reason: "And because of the non-connection (*ananvaya*) of 'as far as' (*yāvat*) and 'repetition' (*vīpsā*. The meaning is that since it was stated previously that [the two] cannot coexist at one time in relation to a single person, there would follow the consequence that the use of 'as far as' and 'repetition' would be the mere babble of a madman, due to their lack of connection.

This might be so; even though the verbal status of being qualifiers of the subject under discussion belongs to "living" (*jīvana*) and "spring" (*vasanta*), nevertheless, in terms of the actual sense...

The status of being a condition (*nimittatva*) also exists. When one objects: "Since the occurrence of the conditional (*naimittika*) must happen whenever the condition (*nimitta*) is present, these two [terms] are merely restated (*anūdyete*) for as long as the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*) applies; so how can there be a lack of syntactical connection (*ananvaya*)? To this he says: "And it is not a restatement of two things already established. Why? Because even for one who is living, there is an entitlement (*adhikāra*) [to the rite] just as there is for one desiring heaven (*svargakāma*). When...

[The phrase] "he would be able" [is used] because of its connection [to the context]. Now, an objection is raised: since the necessity of performance is understood through the fact that [the action] is a cause by its very nature (*ārthataḥ*), the connection with the phrase "when he would be able" is untenable due to contradiction; to this, he replies: "Because there is no contradiction. This is what is meant: first of all, in the state of being a qualification of the eligible person (*adhikārin*), life and so forth are not [connected] with the phrase "when" (*yadā*).

There is a contradiction if it must be stated that [the ritual] exists as a causal factor (*nimitta*) in the ultimate sense. And since that [causal status] is contradicted by the capacity to incorporate all auxiliary parts—which is obtained through the force of the scriptural injunctions for the various auxiliaries taught as if they were permanent—it cannot even establish its own existence, much less a contradiction. Therefore, it must be interpreted in accordance with that [capacity].

It remains so; nor is there any contradiction with the injunctive statement (*adhikāra-vākya*). For that statement does not, independent of the scriptural mention of its cause, convey the necessity of performance. Nor is it impossible without that [cause], such that one would have to assume it from the very beginning. Therefore, since there is no contradiction, the requirement of the injunction for the sequence and its limits remains unimpeded; thus, when it is possible—

Because it is something to be expressed, and because the phrase "every spring" does not constitute a connection with time, nor does it serve as a qualification of the person entitled to perform the rite (*adhikāra*).
Therefore, that which serves as the cause is indeed a *nimitta* (an occasional occasion). For instance:
There is no connection between the two; for that [condition] would not even be a *nimitta* (occasioning cause) if the action were not performed when it exists.

Furthermore, since the qualification of the person entitled to perform the act (*adhikāriviśeṣa*) is established by the fact that the injunction (*niyoga*) possesses a *nimitta*, there is no lack of comprehension. Therefore, the *nimitta* exists as a qualifier of the person entitled to the act, but it is not a *nimitta* while being a qualifier of the person entitled to the act. This is the literal [meaning].

And because of the status of [the action] as a causal factor (*nimittabhāva*). For the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth denote that [action], since it is recorded in various Smṛtis that "one who intends to break [something] should burn it. In that context, setting aside the literal meaning of the word, the word is not deprived of its status as an auxiliary (*aṅga*), because it is subordinate to another purpose through its connection with the phrase "by the power of the word" (*śabdasāmarthyāt*). This has been stated: "Because the injunction (*niyoga*) depends on everything up to the sequence [of performance]."
There is no loss of a constituent part [of the sentence].

Furthermore, he states by way of a conclusion that this must necessarily be accepted even by you: "Therefore, as long as [the repetition] has the sense of distributive iteration (*vīpsā*), because it lacks syntactic connection (*ananvaya*) and because living is not denotable [as a specific qualification of the agent], 'living' is not a qualifier of the agent, just as in the expression 'in every spring' (*vasante vasante*)."
