Thus, there is no connection with time (*kāla*), nor are these [terms] qualifiers of the qualified agent (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*). Just as for you [the Mīmāṃsakas], "living" (*jīvana*) is not a qualifier of the agent because it lacks syntactic connection with the word *yāvat* and cannot be expressed due to the absence of anything to be excluded,
so too the phrase "in every spring" (*vasante vasante*) does not constitute a connection with an action, because the distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) lacks syntactic connection.

This is the meaning. He concludes his own view: "Therefore, the instrumental cause alone is the instrumental cause; it is not a qualification of the qualified person (adhikāriviśeṣaṇa) at the outset"—this is the meaning. Why? Because, as follows: there is no connection between those two [terms] and the distributive repetition (*yāvad-vīpsā*). Why? From what...?

[Objection: "If it is a causal factor (*nimitta*), does it not lack [logical] concomitance (*ananvaya*)? To this he says: "For that cannot be a causal factor in the sense that the action would not be performed even when it exists. This has been stated previously. [Objection: But was it not said that the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) must first be required by the injunction (*niyoga*)? To this he replies: "The injunction possesses a causal factor; for that person in whom that causal factor exists, there is the duty (*karma*)."

There is no non-comprehension regarding the "duty to be performed" (*kartavyatā*), because the qualification of the person entitled to perform it (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*) is established. Indeed, we shall explain later in this very work that it does not exist at the outset. Since the qualification of the person entitled is obtained through the force of the scriptural statement of the occasion (*nimittaśruti*), there is comprehension; thus, there is no non-comprehension of the duty to be performed—this is the meaning. By this, the following is stated:

To this he says: "Therefore, the occasion (nimitta) is first understood as a qualification of the qualified person (adhikāriviśeṣaṇa), whereas it is not the case that the qualification of the qualified person is first understood and then [becomes] the occasion by implication. Now, since there is no syntactic connection for the two meanings of "as long as" (yāvat) and "repetition" (vīpsā), let there be the status of occasion for "living" (jīvana) and "spring" (vasanta); but not for...
To the objection that there is no such authoritative evidence regarding house-burnings and the like, he says: "And because the status of being a cause is based on scripture.

The intention is that the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) alone is the source for understanding the status of these as causes; however, for the sake of brevity, even those [causes] mentioned up to the "island" have been set forth. He demonstrates this scriptural basis: "For the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth [indicate] 'one should burn,' 'one should break,' or 'one who is beginning [the rite]' [in the case of a breach]."

In that case, they express that cause through the recollection of the indicative mark (*nimitta*). The optative suffix (*liṅ*) in "he should burn" (*dahet*) and the word "when broken" (*bhinne*) are directed toward that cause;
therefore, to follow the literal function of the words by asserting that the other meaning follows from the sense (*arthāt*) is improper. And as for the cause...

It has been stated in the *Bhāvanāviveka* that "the fruit is indeed a qualification of the qualified agent" (*sadadhikāriviśeṣaṇam evaṃ phalam*), meaning that it is a qualification of the qualified agent while being the fruit, and not [merely] a qualification of the agent.

[The word] "darśapūrṇamāsau" is in the locative case (*saptamī*). In the phrase "one who is about to begin the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices," the locative is used in the sense of a cause (*hetu*) according to the rule: "The locative is used for the purpose of indicating a characteristic or a cause of an action" (*lakṣaṇahetvoḥ kriyāyāḥ*).

Regarding the suffix *lakāra*: although in the expression *yāvajjīvam* (as long as one lives), the suffix *ṇamul* is prescribed by the rule *yāvati vindajīvoḥ* even when [the action] is directly the cause (*nimitta*), nevertheless, because it is remembered [by grammatical tradition] that this suffix occurs when there is a connection with another verbal root meaning having the same agent (*samānakartṛka*), it indicates that living is connected with other verbal root meanings such as the oblation (*homa*) and so forth. And this [connection] is not something other than the relationship between the cause and the effect (*nimittanaimittikabhāva*).

The suffix *ṇamul* denotes the state of being a cause (*nimittabhāva*). Nevertheless, why should the word "cause" (*nimitta*) not be intended as a qualification of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*)? Indeed, it is not the case that in every instance a word must refer only to its directly expressed meaning; therefore, he says: in this context, the word "cause" (*nimitta*), having set aside its status as a cause for the literal meaning of the words, refers instead to a qualification of the qualified subject (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*) which constitutes the intended meaning of the words; and that...
By this, it is shown that the acceptance of an untenable position occurs through implication (*arthāt*), [namely] that the state of being a cause (*nimittabhāva*) constitutes the meaning of the word.

He demonstrates the abandonment of the tenable [position]: "but not that which has that as its primary referent" means not that which has the state of being a cause—which has become the meaning of the word—as its primary referent;

rather, it has the qualification of the qualified person (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*) as its primary referent through implication. In this manner, following the literal function of the word (*śabdavṛtti*) is improper.

By that [statement], the meaning is "unworthy. In some readings, it says: "In that case, having abandoned the literal meaning of the word, the word is intent upon something else; however, by the power of its own capacity (*sāmarthya*), it is intent upon that [other] through the force of the sense (*artha*). Its meaning is as follows: It is precisely this deliberation (*vimarśa*) that is being examined—is the word, having abandoned its status as the cause for the literal meaning, intent upon something else, namely a specific qualified person (*adhikārin*), while by its own capacity it is intent upon that [other] object?

Having deliberated whether the specific qualification refers to the occasion (*nimitta*) or whether the word itself refers to the occasion by implication, he determines that it is the occasion: "It is logical to follow the primary function of the word. When it is possible for it to refer to its own denotation (*abhidheya*), it is not logical for it to have another [indirect] referent. Furthermore, it has been explained that the occasion is indeed the denotation. Therefore, it refers to the occasion."

The meaning is that it is indeed correct. Now, one might object: "If this were so, the term *svargakāma* (desirer of heaven) would result in being intended merely as a qualification of the qualified person (*adhikārin*), for it does not indicate heaven as the end to be accomplished (*bhāvya*), but rather as a qualification of the person.
To this he says: "And just as a causal condition (*nimitta*) is a qualification of the qualified person, so too is the fruit (*phala*) a qualification of the qualified person."

It has been stated in the *Bhāvanāviveka* that the fruit [of an action] cannot be a qualification of the person entitled to perform it (*adhikāriviśeṹ�aṇa*). For *bhāvanā* is the production of something; therefore, it too cannot be defined without some entity to be produced. Furthermore, the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), which is expressed by the same word, cannot be accepted as the object to be produced (*bhāvya*), because it is brought about by the injunction (*vidhi*) itself.

Because it depends upon that which is to be brought about for the sake of the human goal (puruṣārtha), and because the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha) is suffering—being the opposite of that [goal]—it is displaced from there; since the object to be brought about (bhāvya) is required first of all, the word "one who desires heaven" (svargakāma) brings about the predominance of its qualification, just as in the case of "the staff-bearer recites the injunctions. This has been established in the *Bhāvanāviveka*.
Although that [determination] was required previously, it occurs only later than the state of being an undertaking (*pratipatti*), because it depends upon performance (*anuṣṭhāna*);
and thus, the determination follows at the very end of the sequence.
But if this is so, since every injunction is accompanied by its desired result, there would be an absence of an original injunction (*utpatti-codanā*).

And thus it might be argued: just as the word "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) refers to that [result] because the end to be achieved (*bhāvya*) is required first, so too the scriptural mentions of conditions (*nimitta-śruti*) must refer to the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), because the person to be enjoined is required first by the mandate (*niyoga*).

[Otherwise,] they would follow [as consequences], or else a distinction must be stated; therefore, he says: "Even though that qualified person (*adhikārī*) is the one to be enjoined (*niyojya*) and is required first, the cognition of this qualified person occurs only after the cognition of the primary rite together with its subsidiaries. This is the underlying intention here: it is not the case that something is cognized first simply because it is required first; rather, [it is cognized according to the sequence of the means of knowledge].

That which is capable of being practiced is what must be cultivated; however, that capability is not a qualification of the person entitled to the practice (adhikārin). Why? Because the specific qualification depends upon the knowledge of what is to be performed. Indeed, neither mere desire for the goal nor mere capacity alone constitutes a qualification for the person entitled to the practice. Let it not be so.

There is no entitlement for the lame, the Śūdras, and others; rather, since the determination of entitlement is established according to the specific application [of the ritual], the qualified person must be one capable of performing the principal rite together with the integration of all its constituent parts. Thus, the lame, the Śūdras, and others lack entitlement. Furthermore, this capability consists in being endowed with the entire collection of auxiliary parts, up to the sequence whose determination depends upon those [auxiliaries] within their respective scope.

Since the primary factor (pradhāna) has that [niyojya] as its object, it requires knowledge of that [niyojya]. Consequently, even though the niyojya is required first, it cannot be understood immediately; rather, it is logically determined only after one has fully comprehended the nature of the bhāvanā’s duty, the instrumental cause, the result, and the procedure (itikartavyatā). This is also consistent with the Great Sage [Jaimini], who, immediately after the definition of sequence, [established the definition of the niyojya].

He states that this very [definition] is accepted when one formulates the definition of *adhikāra* (qualification): "And likewise, following the sequence of this specific qualification, there is a further investigation beyond the inquiry into the collection of primary and auxiliary elements. By this, those who do not describe the relationship of the definition of *adhikāra* as being characterized by *avasara* (the occasion) due to the relationship of the signified and the signifier (*jñāpya-jñāpaka-bhāva*) are [refuted].

Those [objections] are to be understood as refuted; for while the former [arguments] serve as indicators by way of an investigation into the scope of their respective authorities (*adhikāra*), this [present argument] is that which is to be indicated. Furthermore, there is no restrictive reason why an indicator must consist of only a single defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇārtha*). Thus say the venerable masters of the Vārttika: "The authority (*adhikāra*) pertains to the cognition of the task to be accomplished."

It may be so. Since it has been stated that the primary action (pradhāna) must be performed together with its constituent parts (aṅga) up to the limit of their sequence, everything remains perfectly coherent for now. Furthermore, even regarding the injunction (vidhi) as the means to a desired end, there is the syntactic connection "when one is able" (śaknuyāt) in the case of optional rites (kāmya), whereas in the case of occasional rites (naimittika), it is "as far as one is able" (yathā śaknuyāt); thus, in that context, it is precisely the status of being a means to a desired end [that is intended].

Regarding the term "injunction" (*vidhi*): an objection is raised therein—"But if this is so, then since [the injunction] is present everywhere, the originative injunction (*utpatti-codanā*) would consist in the existence [of the act] due to its connection with the desired end.
This is the meaning: if the injunction is the state of being a means to what is sought after, and that [state] is the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth."

Even in originative injunctions such as "The cake on eight potsherds is for Agni," since there is an understanding of an injunction and that [injunction] consists in being a means to what is desired, the result is understood from that very source; consequently, because these would function as injunctions of entitlement— like the statement "One desiring heaven [should sacrifice] with the Darśapūrṇamāsa"—
it would follow that there is no such thing as an originative injunction.

Because they are independent of one another, even when in proximity, there would be no repetition for the sake of a result; thus, there would be a distinction of rites (*karmabheda*) in every case, and it would not be for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*). Furthermore, in the injunction "one offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*), there would be no connection between the accessory (*guṇa*) and the result.

It might be argued: "Nothing other than pleasure and so forth is desired, and since that [pleasure] is heaven (svarga), animals and the like would have no scope because they are excluded from heaven. Or, "They too may be included by virtue of being means of attainment (upādāna). Furthermore, heaven would then be eternal.
"Let there be an absence of injunctions for its production; what does that matter? To this, he says: "And thus, mutually..."

Because [the action] is independent, even when it is present, there is no repetition of the scriptural statement for the sake of a result; thus, in all such cases, there would be a difference of ritual acts (*karmabheda*).

This is the meaning: indeed, for those originative statements (*utpattivākya*) which are intent upon establishing the essential nature of a ritual act, that nature inherently requires something to be produced, since it cannot arise otherwise. And for those [statements] intent upon establishing the connection between the ritual act and its result...

Since sentences that require the cognition of their own specific forms can enter into mutual relation, it is logical that when there is a restatement in a sentence of result—occurring in proximity to a rite enjoined by an originative sentence—it serves the purpose of connecting that very same rite with a result; thus, no separate rite should be postulated. However, when the injunction consists precisely in being the means to a desired end, then...

Therefore, since it arises from that very [source] through production or acquisition, it has no need for a statement of result (*phalavākya*). Furthermore, a statement of result, being already occupied by the result mentioned in its own sentence, is incapable of requiring a connection with another action and its result; thus, it would necessitate the assumption of an entirely different action for the sake of connecting with a result. Consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of a distinction between actions (*karmabheda*) in every case. He states another such consequence:

Furthermore, the *prayāja* and other such rites would not serve the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*). For when a desired fruit is obtained through what is directly stated in the scripture (*śruti*), it is impossible for there to be a connection with a fruit characterized as an "assistance to the performance" (*karaṇopakāra*) obtained through the context (*prakaraṇa*). The point is that scripture is more powerful than context.

He adds another point of consequence: in the injunction "one offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*), there would be a connection between the accessory (*guṇa*), namely the curd, and the desired result. For here, by distinguishing between what is already established and what is not, in the case of the statement "for one desiring sense-power [one should offer] with curd," the oblation is not rendered fruitless by this much; rather, it possesses that result because it has its own result obtained through its own specific scriptural statement.

Nor is it tenable that curd is enjoined as a separate action from the one under discussion, characterized by a specific result; for it is impossible for that very same action to be both the object of an injunction for a result at that moment and the subject of an injunction regarding the curd. Therefore, it follows that the curd, which has the oblation obtained through the context as its substrate, is connected with the result.

This is correct. Furthermore, if the injunction (*vidhi*) consists in being a means to what is desired (*samīhitasādhanatā*), then for men, that which is desired is pleasure alone—not pain, nor that which is neither pleasure nor pain, because the latter are respectively objects of aversion or indifference. And that [pleasure], when unrestricted, is indeed heaven (*svarga*). If it were restricted, it would be merely worldly. Nor is it the case that in the statement "one desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Citrā," the [heavenly result] is already established by the very hearing of the word "should sacrifice" (*yajeta*).

The desired object [of the action] is understood as being delimited by animals and the like. Nor is this delimitation [derived] from its connection with the word *paśukāma* (desiring cattle), because that would depend on the consideration of another word and thus be cognizable through the sentence (*vākya*); whereas heaven (*svarga*) is more powerful because it is perceived from the mere hearing of the direct statement (*śruti*). Furthermore, since the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) has no requirement once it has obtained a *bhāvya* (the end to be produced) in the form of a desired object presented by its own word...

Because of that very fact: since [the result] is established as a qualification of the person exactly as heard in the text, and not as something to be brought into being (*bhāvya*), there would follow the consequence that animals and the like could have no connection with the *Citrā* sacrifice and others due to the exclusion of heaven. Thus he says: "And nothing other than pleasure and so forth is desired.
What follows from that? Since that [pleasure] is heaven, because of the exclusion of heaven, there would be no room for animals and the like. Or else, another...
To say that one intends one thing but does another is a contradiction. First of all, it is not merely for the sake of qualifying the person;
therefore, what remains for the *bhāvanā*? Its very status as being for the sake of the person (*puruṣārthatā*) is the qualification. Even so—

And in the case of a causal factor (*nimitta*), the action itself is what must be accomplished. Otherwise, there would be a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) between the causal factor and the result, due to the discrepancy of having both "living" and "the oblation" as things to be performed—namely, "by means of living, the oblation [is to be performed]" and "by means of the oblation, the result [is to be attained]. Since there are two objects to be aimed at (*uddeśya*), they cannot be connected within a single sentence;

rather, this [term "oblation"] is connected with the word "desire" (*kāma*). In that context, if it were not connected as a result, it would follow that the statement was merely the idle chatter of a careless person.

Therefore, he says that this [injunction] has the fruit as its primary object: "Or rather, those [animals] such as cattle would also be [the result] because of their being the material cause (*upādāna*). The sense is that even so, since heaven must necessarily occur, the combination [of both results] would follow as an undesirable consequence for you.
He concludes his own position: "Therefore, why [is it] not distinct from the *bhāvanā*? Why [is it] the *bhāvanā*?"

It indicates the object to be brought about (*bhāvya*). That is to say, when the state of being a means to what is desired (*samīhitasādhanatā*) is not the injunction (*vidhi*), nor is "being a human goal" (*puruṣārthatā*) itself the qualifier; rather, the meaning is that it is not qualified by "being a human goal" alone, but also by something else. In some readings, it says: "being a human goal is indeed the qualifier. In that case, [the following] is the answer to certain [objections regarding] words: "But even in your own view, it is only the productive operation (*bhāvanā*)."

It brings forward that which is to be produced (bhāvya) according to the injunction; since the scope for [other] things such as cattle is difficult to find, the qualification by the human goal (puruṣārtha) follows after those words. This is the meaning: for in our view, because it is the very nature of the productive operation (bhāvanā), only the "thing to be produced" in general is understood; thus, when there is a requirement for its specific nature, it is [fulfilled] by the human goal itself, such as cattle, which is subordinate to the ritual action (aṅguṇatayā).

It is logical that the "what" (kimaṃśa) portion should be qualified; however, in your view, there is no requirement for a qualification of the result to be attained, since heaven itself is understood as that specific result. Thus, what was stated—that an occasional rite (*naimittika-karma*) is a means to an eternally desired end—is also refuted; so he says: "And even so, since the 'what' portion remains unqualified..."

In the case of an occasional rite (*naimittika-karma*), action alone is to be accomplished, not the human goal (*puruṣārtha*). For the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) of an occasional rite, which requires an object to be accomplished (*bhāvya*), is unable to take up a human goal as that object; instead, it finds its fulfillment by taking up the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) itself, which is denoted by its own word. This is the meaning. [Objection: But if the human goal were the object to be accomplished for this [productive urge], what would be the fault? To this [it is said]:

He says: Otherwise, if the eternality [of the rite] and its status as a means to a desired end were [both] intended, there would be a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*) regarding both the occasion (*nimitta*) and the fruit (*phala*), as well as the action (*karman*) to be undertaken, because of the difference in the mode of expression (*vacanavyakti*). He demonstrates this very point: "When the occasion exists, it is the action itself that is understood as the object to be enjoined (*vidheya*) by virtue of being the objective (*bhāvya*) of the productive urge (*bhāvanā*). For such is the mode of expression manifested therein.

For when the condition (nimitta) of being alive exists, the oblation (homa) must be performed. However, when the action is enjoined with respect to a result (phala), since the result—unlike the condition—is unestablished and is perceived as something to be accomplished (sādhya), if the action were also to be accomplished, there would be no connection between the two, because one [of them] must serve the purpose of the other; thus, it is not desired that the action [be for the sake of] the production of another, namely the result. Therefore, regarding the action in relation to the result...

Because of the relationship [of the act] as an instrument (*karaṇa*), such a statement suggests that the fruit [is attained] by means of the oblation (*homa*). This constitutes a lack of uniformity (*vairūpya*).

Consequently, there would be a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*). To avoid this lack of uniformity—namely, that the ritual action (*karman*) will be enjoined with reference to the fruit—the author says:
"Because two things intended as objects (*uddeśya*) cannot coexist in a single sentence. For the determination [of meaning] is dependent upon common worldly usage.

This is the course of the sentence. In common worldly usage, a prescriptive sentence is completed with respect to each individual object of reference (*uddeśya*). Indeed, it is established by one's own experience that we are not able to designate another object with the very same effort by which we intend to prescribe a single object; therefore, the meaning is that two objects of reference cannot coexist within a single sentence.
Because of dependence. For it is not easy for the destruction of the impure and the avoidance of the miserable states to arise from a single [cause], nor is there non-action.
And thus, since the nature of karma is well known, there is indeed the absence of a [fixed] constituent, and not the undertaking according to one's power.
It is said:

Every injunction consists of origination (*utpatti*), application (*viniyoga*), purpose (*artha*), performance (*prayoga*), and qualification (*adhikāra*); it is not divided [into separate parts] because of its specific focus on that [single goal].

It should be understood that the objector’s underlying assumption is that because it is contradictory for a single thing to possess both the status of an indicator (*jñāpaka*) and the status of a causal factor (*nimitta*), it is also impossible for the causal factor to be a qualification of the injunction (*vidhi-viśeṣaṇatva*). Nor does this lead to the consequence of a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*). He states another [consequence] that follows: "For indeed, from a single [cause], the destruction of evil and the avoidance of non-performance are not easily attained. When—

When the action is enjoined with respect to the *nimitta* (the occasioning cause), it cannot then be enjoined with respect to the fruit (*phala*). Nor is the mere injunction of its own nature a cause for the engagement of a discerning person; therefore, one must assume that a loss [of merit] occurs upon its non-performance, since engagement is established out of fear of that [loss]. But when it is enjoined with respect to the fruit, then that very [action] destroys the evil (*durita*); thus, for that purpose, many...

The objection is that, due to the consequence of excessive conceptual complexity (*kalpanā-gaurava*), it is the ritual action (*karman*) alone that is the object to be brought about (*bhāvya*) by the productive urge (*bhāvanā*), and not even the desired result. This objection also gives rise to another; thus he says: "And in this way, there is indeed no status as a subsidiary (*anaṅgatva*) for the occasional rite (*naimittika*)," meaning there is no connection with the subsidiaries. Why? Because the nature of the ritual action is already known (*prajñātatvāt*). [It is] beneficial (*upakāraka*).
Indeed, subsidiarity (*aṅgatā*) is pervaded by assistance (*upakāratā*), and that assistance must exist either in the essential nature (*svarūpa*) or in the effect (*kārya*) [of the action].
It cannot first be in the effect; for it has already been stated that if an action were merely an assistant to another action, there would be no effect for the occasional (*naimittika*) rite.

By the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), subsidiarity must be defined as the production of the essential nature of the rite; yet that is not possible, because [the nature] is already known (*prajñātatvāt*).

The meaning is that being an auxiliary (*aṅgatā*) is pervaded by being helpful both through its means and its form; therefore, in the absence of that [helpfulness], it will not exist. He says this is not only a lack of being an auxiliary, but another consequence has also arisen: "In the case of an occasional rite (*naimittika*), there is no undertaking of auxiliaries according to one's capacity. He refutes this:

Every injunction consists of origination, application, purpose, performance, and qualification; it is not divided [into separate categories] because there is no distinction in its being directed toward that [single goal].

Even in the case of an injunction (*vidhi*) where the means are already established, there is no absence of origination (*utpatti*) and so forth; for when they occur simultaneously, there is no contradiction, since every injunction consists of origination, application (*viniyoga*), performance (*prayoga*), and qualification (*adhikāra*). [Objection: But on this view, being "consisting of performance" is untenable, for it is the cognition of what is to be done (*kartavyatā*) that impels one to action.

The understanding [of an action] as a means to a desired end does not constitute its being "to-be-done" (*kartavyatā*). For "being to-be-done" is defined as "being achievable through effort" (*kṛtisādhyatā*).

Here, "being a means" implies "already established" (*siddhatā*); and it is impossible to establish the identity between "being established" and "being to-be-accomplished," which are as contrary in nature as fire and snow, for that would entail the absurd consequence of the three worlds being one. Furthermore:

If "ought-to-be-done-ness" (kartavyatā) is intended to mean "being a means to what is desired," then since that which is desired is itself without dispute as being "ought-to-be-done," it would follow that it is a means to what is desired. [This applies even to] the mass of extremely harsh rays scattered by the midday sun during the summer season.

The injunction (*vidhi*) does not consist merely in the state of being a means to a desired end, but rather in the agent’s *evaṃkāra* (the act of saying "so be it"). And this is the cognition of instigation (*pravartanā*).

For those whose bodies are emaciated by the unbearable torment inflicted by calamities, who close their eyes to the circle of the sky, and who long for the rising of clouds—sudden, deep as the flow of water, and exceedingly beautiful with the luster of fresh tamāla garlands—they do not [long for] the [mere] means to a desired end.

And they do not consider this [the Kārīrī sacrifice] to be something that ought to be performed. Furthermore, farmers whose crops have been withered by drought do not understand the Kārīrī sacrifice—which, though it is a means for obtaining the desired rain completed by the sacrificer—as something that ought to be performed.
Therefore, because of contradiction and deviation, being a means for what is desired does not constitute "that which ought to be done" (kartavyatā).

If it is not something that must be done, how can it cause one to perform it? Thus, the injunction (*vidhi*) is not merely of the nature of application; to this he says: the injunction is not merely the state of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatā*), but rather [it is] for the agent. [The agent] is incapable [of acting otherwise]. We do not say that the state of being an effect (*kāryatā*) is merely the state of being a means to a desired end, such that we might be reproached in this way; rather, [we say it is] that which is a means to the desired end for the agent.

Whatever is to be done by it [the agent] cannot belong to one who does not act, for the reality of an agent is untenable in the absence of action. Nor is there a contradiction between the states of being "to be accomplished" (*sādhyatā*) and "already accomplished" (*siddhatā*), because they belong to different times. Indeed, prior to the commencement of activity, there is neither the state of the action being completed nor the state of its being performed; rather, the state of being performed belongs to what follows, while the state of being completed belongs to what immediately precedes it. And the word [denotes] an entity existing in all three times.

As the object [of the injunction], it is able to denote its status as a means existing at the time of accomplishment (*siddhatā*) and its being pervaded by effort (*kṛti*) existing at a time prior to that—even though these do not exist at the present moment. And precisely that which is pervaded by effort is the means for that effort; thus, there is a grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the status of being a means to the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) and the status of being a means to the desired end (*iṣṭasādhana*), such that one who desires [the result] acts.

Thus, for those who state that the injunction (*vidhi*) is the fact of being a means to what is desired by the agent (*kartuḥ iṣṭasādhanatā*), it is expressed as the state of being a means to a desired end that is co-inherent with the same object as the duty (*kartavyatā*); it is not merely the state of being a duty (*kartavyatāmātra*). For otherwise, since the state of being a duty would be no different even in the case of the fruit (*phala*), it would follow that the fruit itself would be an injunction. Furthermore, the duty of the fruit is not within the scope of the word; for people understand this for themselves.

The fruit is that which must be accomplished by the person; however, the word itself does not produce enthusiasm in the person toward the fruit, nor is the fruit the object of his effort, though it may be the means to achieve it. Furthermore, since ignorance regarding the existence of that fruit is not the cause for engagement, the knowledge of that [fruit] alone is the injunction (*vidhi*).

For what reason, then, is this accepted? To this he says: "The word *evam* (thus) is the causal factor for instigation (*pravarttanā-pratyaya*). This is the underlying intention: immediately upon hearing the instruction, "One desiring rice should cook," or "One should not give a finger to a serpent," there occurs in the person being instructed an inclination toward cooking, or [an avoidance] in one who was about to offer a finger to a snake.

And having observed his cessation from that [activity], the ignorant conclude: "Surely a cognition whose object is the cause of this man's engagement has arisen. For instance: this engagement of this person must have a cause, because it is an engagement, like [any other] engagement; and this [engagement] is preceded by a cognition, because it is an independent engagement, like our own engagement.

Furthermore, the cognition under dispute has as its object the state of being a means to what is beneficial or harmful, which is inherent in the same substratum as the state of being something to be done or not to be done; because it is a cognition that causes activity, like the cognition that causes our own activity. For instance, in the case of suckling at the breast and so forth, having understood the state of being a means to what is beneficial—which is inherent in the same substratum as the state of being something to be done—I engage in activity; likewise [in the case of fire].
And from the prohibition, having understood that the state of being a non-duty is co-inherent with the same object as being a means to what is undesirable— thinking "I have desisted"— [one acts],

because otherwise there would be no cause for desisting. This is because [the object] is established either by itself or by something else, and for this very reason its operation is not to be depended upon.
Because there would be no engagement even with the means for achieving what is desired. As it has been stated:

"The fruit of the scripture belongs to the performer, because that is its defining characteristic"—that is, because the scripture is defined by its being the means for the fruit of the performer. And therefore, [the word] is a synonym for *vidhi* (injunction).

The performance of an action is understood from the scripture; and for an action whose purpose is transcendental (adṛṣṭa), its specific nature is also dependent upon the scripture, because it was not previously established prior to the injunction. Furthermore, there is a formal application (viniyoga) because that which is required is the means to what is required. And there must be some qualified person (adhikārī) to be impelled, who is the master for whom this [action] is the means to achieve his desired end. This is perceived in every case.

The state of being "to be done" (*karttavyatva*) is the fitness for action (*kṛtyarhatva*), while its opposite, "not to be done" (*akarttavyatva*), is like *adharma*. It is precisely these two—the means to what is beneficial and the means to what is harmful—that become the objects of the cognitions of incitement and dissuasion, because those [cognitions] have that [fitness/unfitness] as their purpose.
Furthermore, since these two states do not exist prior to it but arise immediately after the cognition of the word, they accept that very cognition as their cause.

Therefore, since an incentive arises in this way and not otherwise—and since the incentive for action is the seed of engagement—it is established that an injunction (*vidhi*) does not consist merely in the fact of being a means to a desired end, but rather pertains to the agent.
Why does it not take another form? To this he says: "Otherwise, because the injunction would not be the cause of engagement..."

Because it exists [by itself]. Why? Because it is established by its own nature, independent of human effort, when the breeze—fragrant with the scent of a lotus bud opening at that very moment—rises to the tip of the nose; or otherwise, when the sound of the fifth note (*pañcama*) is being played on a lute (*vallakī*) or a harp (*vipañcī*) by a diligent musician, and it reaches the path of hearing of another person. Thus, [the object] is established.

For even toward that which accomplishes a desired end, there is no engagement if its operation is not required. To show that this is also the view of your own Great Sage (Maharṣi), he says: "It has been stated [in the *Pūrva-Mīmāṃsā-Sūtra*]: 'The fruit of the scripture accrues to the performer, because that is its defining characteristic. How is this not already stated here? He replies: "Because the scripture is defined by its being the means for achieving the fruit for the performer. Now, as for the scripture...

Dispelling the doubt that this is not a matter of injunction (*vidhi*), he concludes: "And therefore, from the scripture which is synonymous with injunction, the performance of the ritual action is understood; thus, the rule of application (*prayogavidhi*) is established. [The opponent asks: "Let it be then merely the nature of application; what is the need for it to be for the sake of origination (*utpatti*)? To this he replies: "Of that which has an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), [the knowledge comes] from scripture..."
The specific nature of that performance is also understood. Why? Because [the action] was not previously established prior to the injunction.

It demonstrates its purpose as being for application (*viniyoga*): application occurs because [an action] is the means for what is required. Indeed, the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and others are traditionally taught in the context of injunction;
an injunction is the state of being a means required by the agent. Consequently, those suffixes follow the verbal root.

When heard, they bring forward the desired object of the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) as that which is to be accomplished; and since the meaning of the verbal root— which is colored by the efficient force— is not inherently established as either the means for accomplishing the desired portion of the object engaged in by the efficient force, or as the means for accomplishing the desired efficient force itself, [the suffixes] denote this very status through direct statement (*śruti*).

The meaning is "the state of being for the purpose of application" (*viniyogārthatvam*). The sense is that demonstrating that something is a means to a result and its corresponding productive activity (*bhāvanā*) is precisely what constitutes demonstrating its being "for the sake of that" (*tādarthya*). He shows that it consists in the nature of an injunction (*adhikriyā*): "And there must be some person to be impelled, an authorized master (*svāmin*), for whom this [act] is a means to his desired end. For an injunction, when analyzed, consists essentially in the impelling of an agent.

The nature of the means to the goal has been established. And that [means], by enjoining an agent who must proceed toward action—an eligible person (adhikārin) characterized by a specific fruit born from the desire produced by the means such as sacrifice, and who is the master (svāmin) regarding the ritual—is called "eligibility" (adhikāra). This is because there is no such thing as an agent who does not possess eligibility; for mere status as a means to what is desired [does not constitute eligibility].

In these four types of injunctions (*māna*), the primary purport (*aidamparya*) differs. Consequently, there is a distinction between injunctive sentences regarding production (*utpatti*) and so forth.

And that primary purport arises from the connection with specific words such as attainment (*prāpti*) or particular suffixes (*upapada*). In some cases, there is a focus on all four; for example, in the case of the *udbhid* sacrifice.

"One should sacrifice" (*yajeta*). [This is] because nothing else [is available] from another source, and because of the connection with the word for the result (*phala*). In some cases, there is a threefold purpose, as in the sentence concerning the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, because the origin [of the rite] is obtained from elsewhere. In some cases, there is a twofold purpose, as in the case where, due to the impossibility of [the injunction] consisting merely in instigation (*pravartanā*), there would follow the contingency of the loss of its status as an injunction (*vidhi*). Now, is it not the case that every injunction...

Lest there be mutual contradiction among the origination and other [states] from the formless [state], and lest there be a split in the injunctions regarding origination and so forth—since the fourfold nature is understood in its entirety from each individual sentence—he says:

"And while this tetrad is perceived everywhere, the primary intent (aidamparya) differs; by that very [difference in intent], there is a distinction between the injunctions for origination and the others. Even though...

The meaning is this: although every injunction consists of these four elements, nevertheless, due to the diversity of sentences, there is a distinction between injunctions of origination (*utpatti*) and so forth, because they aim at four, three, two, or one [of these elements] according to their capacity and lack of difference in their essential nature. He demonstrates that very diversity as the cause for the specific purport (*aidamparya*): "It is distinguished by connection with attainment, a qualifying word, or a particular [element]," which is to be supplied [to the previous statement]; thus, among the four, one or another is distinguished.

The meaning is: because [the action] has not been previously established, and because it is connected with specific qualifying adjuncts such as "one desiring heaven" (*svargakāma*). He illustrates the differences in the lack of primary intent (*anai-damparya*) caused by those factors: "In some cases, there is intent toward all four, as in 'one should sacrifice with the *udbhid* [instrument]. Why?
Because among the four [factors] which are all of the nature of injunctions, not even one is obtained from any other source. But surely...

Since the suffix [in the word *yajeta*] expresses both the form of the action (*karmarūpa*) and the injunction (*vidhi*) consisting in being a means to a desired end (*samīhitasādhanatā*), it is logical that it possesses the character of enjoining both the origination (*utpatti*) and the application (*viniyoga*) [of the rite];

however, its having the character of conferring entitlement (*adhikāra*) is untenable, because the nature of that entitlement is not understood from it. Nor [is it untenable] by virtue of its being of the nature of instigation (*pravarttanā*).

It is now established that the person entitled to perform the rite (*adhikārī*) is merely one who is impelled by the injunction (*vidhi*). This is because the status of being such a person does not belong to a mere universal. For it has been stated that the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth operate without specifically intending Devadatta or any other individual.

Furthermore, the word "desiring cattle" (*paśukāma*) is sufficient to specify that particular [person], as it refers to the agent (*bhavya*) implied by the productive urge (*bhāvanā*). Nor can a single entity possess both [the nature of the impeller and the impelled].

[Otherwise,] there would be an impossibility of "otherness" (paratva). And thus, in the absence of that [otherness], the injunction (vidhi) would not consist of the application [of the means]. To this, he says:

"And because of the connection with the word denoting the fruit. The phrase "one desiring cattle" (paśukāmaḥ) is the word denoting the fruit; and since that [word] provides the object to be accomplished (bhāvya) for the productive activity (bhāvanā) established by the injunction, it also implies the qualified person (adhikārin) when there is a requirement for such a specific qualified person.

It leads [to the result]. And thus, the fact that the specific agent possesses the capacity to accomplish the desired end is established by cognition. In this way, they impel the agent—who is the one qualified to act—and thereby attain the nature of being an instigation (*prayoga*). Thus, it is established that [the Vedic injunctions] have fourfold purport.

As for their having a threefold purport, as in the case of the *jyotiṣṭoma* sentence, it is because of the origination [of the rite], which consists of the knowledge of the form of an action not yet performed.

Because [the details] are obtained from other sources— such as from the sentence "one should sacrifice with Soma"— in some cases there is a dual purpose, namely the purpose of qualification (*adhikāra*) and the purpose of application (*viniyoga*), as in the case of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sentences. [The origin (*utpatti*) is known] from such passages as "the cake on eight potsherds for Agni," and the performance (*prayoga*) is known from such passages as "one should sacrifice on the full moon day with the Paurṇamāsī [offering]."

Because of its establishment. Regarding the reading "in some cases it refers to three, in others to two," the meaning is as follows: having presented the view that it refers to three, the word "or" (*vā*) rejects that position, thereby accepting that it refers to two. Where?

In the sentences concerning the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, since both the origin (*utpatti*) and the application (*yoga*) are established from other sources, they have in some cases a single purpose, as in "one offers the Agnihotra" and "one should sacrifice on the full moon day. Nor is there an application to a fruit, because it is impossible to perceive a specific fruit that has not been specified. In the absence of such a specification, there is no cognition of a specific qualified person (*adhikāriviśeṣa*), and thus no qualification (*adhikāra*).

[The injunction] is also [of that nature]. For this very reason, there is no [separate] performance-injunction (*prayoga*). Indeed, when the status of being a means to the desired end (*iṣṭasādhanabhāva*) is not established, the cognition of performance does not become firmly grounded;
nor can [performance] exist without a determined performer. Therefore, the cognition of performance arises from the sentence concerning the result alone.

Consequently, in the case of "He offers the Agnihotra," the injunction has as its primary object the essential nature of the ritual act (*karmasvarūpa*); the other factors, however, are merely understood [incidentally].

Devotion to a single [aspect] is as follows: for example, in the case of "He offers the Agnihotra," there is devotion to the origin (*utpatti*), whereas in "One should sacrifice with the Paurṇamāsī on the full moon day," there is devotion to the performance (*prayoga*). Now, one might ask: how can the sentence concerning the Agnihotra have devotion to its origin, given that by the verb—which expresses the injunction (*vidhi*) as the means to what is desired by the agent—it [indicates] that which is desired?
Since the application (*viniyoga*) of the oblation, the qualification (*adhikāra*) of the performer, and the performance (*prayoga*) based thereon have already been stated, he says:

"There is no application with respect to the fruit. Why? Because it is impossible to cognize [the fruit] when its specific nature has not been specified. This is the underlying intention here: it is true that, by the very nature of an injunction, the fruit is merely something desired; however, it does not follow from this alone...

The application (*viniyoga*), which is a constituent part of the performance (*anuṣṭhāna*), must be established; for that [application] would consist in the cognition "this is to be done by means of this. And that [cognition] does not occur without a word expressing a specific desired object. For this very reason, it is said that there is no focus on qualification (*adhikāra*) either, because in the absence of that [specification], there is no specification of the fruit, and consequently, there is no cognition of a specific qualified person who desires that fruit.

There is no *adhikāra* (entitlement). It negates the state of being intent upon performance (*prayoga-paratā*): since there is no *viniyoga* (application) that becomes an *adhikāra*, for that very reason there is no performance. Why? Because when the status of the action as a means to a desired end (*iṣṭa-sādhanatva*) is not established—and in the absence of *viniyoga*—the cognition of performance does not become established; nor does it belong to one whose performer has not been determined. Ani... [text fragment]
The connection with the preceding [sentence] is as follows: "the cognition of performance, characterized by the specific qualified agent who has been defined, becomes established.

Therefore, the cognition of the performance arises from the very sentence stating the result. He concludes: "Thus, the injunction [in the sentence] 'one offers the Agnihotra' has for its primary purport the essential nature of the rite. Now, it might be argued that by the very nature of an injunction, the other elements [of the sacrifice] are also understood in a general sense.

The case endings do not signify a lack of intention to express [the qualifiers]; rather, by their very power, they will convey the specific qualification, just as in the Piṇḍapitṛyajña. Therefore, he says: "Even though the case-endings are perceived, they are not intended to be expressed. This is appropriate in the case of the Piṇḍapitṛyajña, because those specific qualifications are not established from any other source, and in their absence, the injunction itself would be untenable; thus, there is the expression of those specific qualifications.

Regarding the phrase "the conceptualization of the word 'iti'," the sense here is that since the application of the ritual procedures is already established by other scriptural statements (*vacana*) that are recited, it is more appropriate that those [words] which are perceived [in the text] be considered unintended (*avivakṣita*), given the inherent nature of an injunction (*vidhi*).

He provides an example of being intent solely upon the performance: in the case of "at the full moon," because it is not subordinate to anything else, it is intent upon the distinction between the performances.
Indeed, this [injunction] does not concern origination (*utpatti*), since origination is already understood from such [texts] as "the cake on eight potsherds for Agni" (*āgneyo 'ṣṭākapālaḥ*).

Nor does it concern application (*viniyoga*) or qualification (*adhikāra*), since both of these are established by the very [text]: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices" (*darśapūrṇamāsābhyāṃ svargakāmo yajeta*).
Although the performance (*prayoga*) is also established from that very sentence, nevertheless, there is no distinction [between the injunctions regarding them].
It ought to be established; for instance, the statement "by means of the Darśapūrṇamāsa" would imply a single performance for all six sacrifices, and in this context,
by the statement "on the full moon day," at that specific time, on the Paurṇamāsī— [p.271]

[The terms] may even be unintended [as primary referents]. However, because the phrase "at the full moon" (paurṇamāsyām) is not subordinate to anything else, it refers to a distinction in performance. In the case of the cleansing (saṃmārga), sprinkling (prokṣaṇa), and so forth, however, it refers to their origin and application. Through the medium of rice (vrīhi) and other materials, when the constituent parts of the sacrifice under discussion are obtained, the phrase "at the full moon" is intended to enjoin the three rites designated as the *Paurṇamāsī*, and the phrase "at the new moon" (amāvāsyāyām) [enjoins them] at the time of the new moon.

In a case where [the text] is intent upon enjoining three acts of naming, a distinction in performance (*prayoga-bheda*) is understood due to the difference in time; for time serves as the delimiter of performance. Since this [distinction] cannot be obtained from any other source, the text is indeed intent upon the distinction of performance. Furthermore, while the originative injunction (*utpatti-vākya*) provides the mere essential forms (*svarūpa-mātra*) of the three [offerings] such as the Āgneya—which serve as the means (*karaṇa*) subordinate to the connection with time—their connection with that [time] occurs through those [means].

He states, by way of another method, that even the subsidiaries, when accompanied by those [primary acts], possess the status of being instruments (karaṇa), and thus are subordinate to an injunction: "In the case of cleansing, sprinkling, and so forth, there is subordination to the originative and applicatory injunctions. This is the intended meaning: "He cleanses the cup with the fringe of the ten-fold filter" and "He sprinkles the rice grains"—herein lies the act of cleansing (*saṃmārga*).

And sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) is enjoined; since its essential nature is not obtained from any other source, the sentence is intent on its origination (utpatti) because it makes that known. Nor is the subservience (aidamarthya) of sprinkling and so forth to something required understood from any other sentence, and thus it is also intent on their application (viniyoga). Furthermore, because an injunction is seen immediately, heaven and the like are not directly required [as the purpose].

It is understood. For, due to the connection with the phrase "that which one is capable of," whatever capacity is perceived in something toward that which is required, by that [capacity] must that [requirement] be accomplished. Here, the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) of sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), as enjoined by the injunction "he sprinkles the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*), proceeds to accept the rice-grains—which have been rendered primary by the direct statement of the accusative case—as its immediate objective (*sādhya*).
Being directly unable to attain the state of being required for those [subsidiaries], the *satī* (the primary sacrifice) seeks the human goal even through a mediated sequence.

If, however, it does not obtain that [goal] even through a mediated sequence, then—reversing its course and breaking the syntactical connection (*viniyogabhaṅga*) as in the case of "he offers the flour-meal" (*saktūn juhoti*)—it would instead postulate that the sprinkling and other such acts are themselves what is directly required. But there exists a mediated sequence.

There is the attainment of a settled conclusion. For instance, in the injunction "one should sacrifice with rice," rice is prescribed as the instrument (*sādhana*) by way of a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the sacrifice already established in context. And it is not logically possible for rice to be the direct instrument of the sacrifice, because its place is occupied by the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) which is prescribed at the originative injunction (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*). Furthermore, sacrifices such as the Āgneya are characterized by the substance of rice in the same manner as [the injunction] "one should sacrifice with Soma."

Because of the excessive complexity of enjoining another ritual act, it is therefore appropriate that these [grains] are enjoined as the material cause (*prakṛti*) for the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), which serves as the means for the *Āgneya* and other sacrifices under discussion. Consequently, since rice grains are required as the material cause for the sacrificial cake substance— which itself serves as the means for the fruit-yielding sacrifice— it follows by the force of the injunction that one must not bypass the essential nature of the rice.

Consecrations such as *prokṣaṇa* (sprinkling), which are connected through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) with the form of the sacrifice that possesses a fruit, are enjoined by the very sentences such as "he sprinkles the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*), where they are required. And thus, even in the case of barley (*yava*), the *prokṣaṇa* and other rites are indeed directly taught (*aupadeśika*). This is because [barley] possesses the status of being the material cause (*prakṛti*) for the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), which serves as the means for the fruit-bearing sacrifice.
"Because there is no distinction between fear and protection.
Now, why does this not also result in being intent upon ritual performance (*prayoga*)? To this he says: "By way of rice and so forth" [p.

Because the performance [of the rite] is established by the injunction of the instrument (*karaṇavidhi*) alone; and because there is a cognition of entitlement for one who is already entitled. Some maintain that in the case of the *samidh* and other [offerings], the intent is merely toward their origination (*utpatti*), since the application (*viniyoga*) is based on a scriptural statement (*śruti*) inferred from the context (*prakaraṇa*). However, it is the scriptural statement itself—inferred here from the context—that effects the application; this very injunction is the application.

Since the performance of the sacrifice is established by the injunction regarding the instrument itself once the basic form of the sacrifice and its instrumental components have been obtained, the injunction "one should sacrifice with the Paurṇamāsī on the full moon day" and "with the Amāvāsyā on the new moon day" prescribes a distinction in the performance of that which has become the instrument— namely, the Paurṇamāsī and the Amāvāsyā. And [it is impossible for there to be a performance] of that which lacks a procedure (*itikartavyatā*).

The phrase "the state of being that" (tadbhāvaḥ) causes the instrument to be performed; it causes precisely that which has a procedure (*itikartavyatā*) to be performed, not by way of the rice-grains (*vrīhi*) and so forth. Thus, he states the specific door for those factors that provide assistance through direct contact (*saṃnipatyopakāraka*). Now, why does this not fall under the category of the qualification (*adhikāra*)? To this he says: because there is no cognition of a qualification for one who is qualified for that [instrument], namely, one who is qualified for the instrument.

For the sentence stating the fruit, by enjoining the fruit upon the means, authorizes the agent who desires that fruit for the performance of those means. Since the procedural requirements (*itikartavyatā*) are those which enter into the means, it follows by the very force of the injunction of the fruit that the one authorized for the means is also authorized for those procedural requirements; for in their absence, there would be no efficacy as a means toward that end.
The meaning is "because of the [specific] application.

Here, he introduces the view of a certain school of thought: some maintain that in the case of the *samit* and other such items, there is only a focus on their originative injunction (*utpatti-vidhi*).
If so, from where does their application (*viniyoga*) arise? To this, he says: "Because it is based on a scriptural text (*śruti*) inferred from the context (*prakaraṇa*)."

Regarding the *niyoga*: this is the meaning. When the statement "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices" is uttered, there arises for the principal efficient force (*bhāvanā*)—which has already obtained the desired end and its means—a requirement for the assistance of that means. It is in response to this requirement that the injunction is applicable; thus, whatever [subsidiary] such as the *samid* offerings happens to occur in proximity to it, [is understood as part of the procedure].

Having postulated a single syntactical unity by means of a statement that—due to its being an auxiliary to the accomplishment of its own object—induces the state of *aidamarthya* (subservience to that purpose), which includes the distinction between the principal and the subordinate, the direct Vedic injunction (*śruti*) inferred from the context (*prakaraṇa*) alone is the allocator, and not the [direct] statement such as "He offers the *samidh*s. For from this [direct] statement, the subservience to the principal is not understood; rather, it is the *samidh*s [that are understood].

[The sentence] "dīnām" [is incomplete]. Therefore, some maintain that the sentences concerning the *samit* and other [fueled-sticks], like the statement "he offers the *agnihotra*," are intended solely for the purpose of origination (*utpatti*).
Now, why is it that the context (*prakaraṇa*) itself is not the direct applicator? To this he says: "It is only the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*)."
In this context, however, it is determined that the *prakaraṇa* (context) is not directly the factor that effects application (*viniyojikā*). This is the underlying intention (*ākūta*) here:

*Prakaraṇa* is the statement of that which is to be performed (*kartavya*) when it possesses a requirement for the procedure (*itikartavyatākāṅkṣā*); and that [statement] consists in the production of the sense of "being for the sake of this" (*aidamarthyāpādana*). Furthermore, "being for the sake of this" is application (*viniyoga*). As for that which, being otherwise untenable, would lead one to postulate a supporting factor—that constitutes syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*).

And it is established in the world that one should go to that which brings about such a result. Furthermore, a statement whose meaning is otherwise untenable does not achieve syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) through another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) intended for determining its application (*viniyoga*), but rather through another scriptural statement itself.
For this very reason, those learned in the science of grammar (*śābdika*) are seen to supply an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) when a statement requires a complete sense.

If *śruti* alone is the means of application and not *prakaraṇa*, then why is there a separate category called *prakaraṇa* as a basis for injunction distinct from *śruti*? [Objection: But since *śruti* and the others are themselves the means of application, what is the need here for an injunction (*vidhi*)? [Reply: This is not so.

For application (*viniyoga*) consists in being for the sake of that (*tādarthya*), and that [application] arises from an injunction (*vidhi*). However, direct statement (*śruti*) and the other [means of proof] are merely causes for establishing a relationship. Has the Great Sage [Jaimini] presented a means of knowledge for the relationship itself? To this he says: "In the case of that which is to be inferred from context (*prakaraṇa*).

Although there is no difference in terms of being a "direct statement" (*śruti*), nevertheless, what is directly perceived is called "direct statement," whereas in the case of a direct statement inferred from context, [the relationship] exists because it is rooted in that [perceived statement].
Thus, the distinction is that context (*prakaraṇa*) is said to be the factor that effects application (*viniyojaka*).
Having set forth this view of a certain school, he refutes it: "But this injunction itself is the basis for application.
The word "but" (*tu*) sets aside the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*). It is not a direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) inferred from context that effects application.
However, the injunction regarding the fuel-sticks (*samid*) and the rest brings about their subservience (*aidamarthya*) toward that which is desired.

Nor is it the case that, as in the statement "one offers the *agnihotra*," there is a lack of injunctive force due to the non-specification of a particular desired end; for even in the absence of such specification, the nature of an injunction itself leads to the understanding of subservience toward the desired end, and of that [injunction].

Because of the qualification by context (*prakaraṇa*). In the absence of an injunction (*vidhi*), there would be the undesirable consequence that the meaning of the verbal root alone would be the object to be produced (*bhāvya*) by the productive operation (*bhāvanā*), due to its being expressed in the same word; consequently, it would be impossible for it to serve the purpose of [producing] what is desired. However, in the originative sentence of the *Agnihotra*, although the mere fact of something being desired is obtained through the very nature of an injunction, the specific nature of that [desired end] is obtained from another source.

It has been stated that because [the meaning] is already understood, the sentences are not intended for application (*viniyoga*). Therefore, the meaning is that the sentences concerning the *samidh* and other offerings are intended for both origination (*utpatti*) and application.
Here, an objection is raised: "But are not direct assertion (*śruti*) and the other means of proof themselves the factors that effect application? What is the need here for an injunction (*vidhi*)?
For, having begun with the words 'Now, therefore, the definition of the subordinate' (*athātaḥ śeṣalakṣaṇam*), it is precisely direct assertion and the others that are defined as such."

The meaning is "because of the instruction. He refutes this: "This is not so; for application (viniyoga) consists in being for the sake of that (tādarthya). [The opponent asks: "What follows from that? [The author replies: "And that [being-for-the-sake-of-that] belongs to the injunction (vidhi). [The opponent objects: "In that case, the direct statement (śruti) and the other means of proof are of no use. To this he says: "But the direct statement and the others are causes merely for establishing a relationship. [The opponent asks: "Is it not the case that being-for-the-sake-of-that itself is the relationship? To this he says: "And the relationship is that of the locus and the located (āśrayāśrayi)."

The state of being a subordinate element (*bhāva*) and so forth is of many kinds; however, that which is characterized by the status of being a *śeṣa* (subordinate) is understood solely through injunction (*vidhi*). Thus he says: "But [the status of] being for the sake of another is [known] from injunction.

If this is so, how then are direct statement (*śruti*) and the other means of application (*viniyojaka*)? The meaning is that the capacity to apply [a factor] does not consist merely in establishing a general relationship, but rather in establishing absolute subservience to another.

The answer is as follows: When threshing and the like are performed for the sake of another according to the injunction, and that [other], such as rice (*vrīhi*), is understood through direct statement (*śruti*) and other means to be connected with that [threshing] and so forth, then that threshing and the like is "for the sake of that"—meaning it is for the sake of the rice and so forth—because of this understanding. This is the underlying intention here: direct statement and the other means do not themselves make known the state of being for the sake of another; rather, [it is known] by means of the remnants of the *prayāja* offerings.

In the case of the statement "he sprinkles the oblations," let it not be that the remnant of the *prayāja* is a subordinate element (*guṇabhūta*), nor let the primary oblations (*pradhānahavīṃṣi*) be so;

for the two case-endings denote the instrument and the object, thereby establishing that status. However, when subordination to another purpose depends upon an injunction, then, because of the injunction "he sprinkles," the desired goal of the act of sprinkling [is established].

Because that purpose is established by the word *prati*, and because the remnant of the *prayāja*— which has already attained the status of being subordinate to the *prayāja*s— cannot function as a remnant (*śeṣa*) with respect to these oblations (*havis*), there would be a contradiction regarding its disposal (*pratipatti*). Furthermore, this would involve a definition based on the essential form (*svarūpa-lakṣaṇā*) of that which has not become primary.

The relationship between the subordinate (*śeṣa*) and the principal (*śeṣin*) is manifold, such as the relationship between locus and located (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*), and so forth; however, subservience to another (*pārārthya*) is the defining characteristic of the subordinate. How then are direct statement (*śruti*) and the other means of application (*viniyojaka*) effective? It is because one understands through them that "this belongs to that," based on the cognition that something whose subservience to another is being established by an injunction is related to that [principal] by way of direct statement and so forth. Nor has it been stated that the definition of the subordinate consists of both characteristics.

Because that [injunction] has that [the nature of the object] as its domain. And that state of being intent upon the essential nature (*svarūpa*) was examined in the section on the definition of difference (*bhedalakṣaṇa*), since difference is dependent upon it. For an injunction intent upon the essential nature differentiates the ritual action;
otherwise, there would result an improper alteration of the meaning of the base noun—which is the primary element—in accordance with the meaning of the case-ending.

However, since the remnant of the *prayāja* offerings that have been employed there and completed is intended as the *rocanī* (the shining surface) because it does not conflict with its function as a mere oblation (*homamātra*), and since other scriptural passages enjoin the spreading (*upastaraṇa*) and sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*) of the sacrificial materials for the purpose of moistening them,
a further sprinkling would result in an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), which is not intended; therefore, [one should use] the remnant of the *prayāja*.

The meaning of the statement is that [the word] "kṣārayati" (he causes to flow) refers to the oblations (*havirṣu*). Consequently, the meaning is as follows: since the direct assertion (*śruti*) and the other means of proof establish a relationship through their own inherent capacity, they are called the authorities (*pramāṇa*) regarding subordination (*pārārthya*), because they determine that subordination—which has already been established by the injunction—within its specific context.
This is also why the Great Sage, having commenced with "Now, therefore, the definition of the subordinate" (*athātaḥ śeṣalakṣaṇam*), [proceeded in this manner].

By stating "Jaimini [says] that even ritual acts [are subordinate], because they exist for the sake of the fruit," [the author] describes the subordinate status of the ritual act based on the injunctive suffix; and by subsequently establishing through *śruti* and other means those factors that demonstrate subservience to another, he has stated that the definition of subordination consists of both types: the mere injunctive suffix and *śruti* and the rest together with an injunction.
How can there be unity of definition even when there is internal differentiation? To this he says: "Because the injunction has that as its object.

The meaning is that even when subsidiarity (*śeṣatva*) is understood through direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) and so forth, it is still said to be enjoined therein. Furthermore, these [points] such as having the essential nature as the primary referent were not merely imagined by us; rather, they are approved even by the venerable Great Sage (Jaimini), for such is his investigation.

He says this: "And that [discussion] regarding the focus on the essential nature (*svarūpa*) has been considered in the definition of difference (*bheda-lakṣaṇa*). Why? Because difference is dependent upon that focus on the essential nature. Why is it dependent upon that? To this he says: "For an injunction focused on the essential nature differentiates the object (*karman*) and the productive operation (*bhāvanā*). For focus on the essential nature consists in making known an essential nature that was previously unknown; it is not...

And since it is possible for that [object] to be made known by something other than itself, that which is being made known is established as distinct from it; the point is that otherwise there would be no distinction.
Now, he demonstrates the consideration of the difference between the two types of *bhāvanā* based on their having the essential nature (*svarūpa*) as their primary object—that is, *tatparatā*.
By the passage beginning with "ceti" and ending with "vyāpriyate," [the author] states: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice by means of the Jyotiṣṭoma.
In that regard, it is traditionally taught: "One should sacrifice with Soma," "He offers the oblations with sacrificial fees," and "He gives gold to the Ātreya.

In this context, the following is considered: Are the meanings of the verbal roots, such as giving and so forth, [all equally] part of a single productive activity (*bhāvanā*) expressed by the injunction "one desiring heaven should sacrifice"?

Are they enjoined as distinct from one another, or is there a distinction in the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) corresponding to each verbal root-meaning? What is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*)? Since the productive activity is denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), and since that suffix is uniform everywhere, it is impossible for there to be a plurality of things denoted without a plurality of denoters; otherwise, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Furthermore, the meanings of the verbal roots—though denoted by various different roots—are distinct from the productive activity itself.

And even when a single word is employed, since there is a fixed rule regarding the sequence of the base and the suffix within the nature of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*), the denotation of the meaning is understood through the suffix in relation to the meaning of the base; thus, it is perceived when the connection has been established.

Since no other word is available in its pure form, it is impossible for [the suffix] to have the purpose of enjoining the meaning of the verbal root; furthermore, since a difference in the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) does not entail a difference in the efficient force itself when there is only one such force, and because the verb in "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*svargakāmo yajeta*) expresses a more clearly defined efficient force by taking up a specific object to be accomplished (*bhāvya*), it follows that [the subsequent injunction] refers back to the efficient force enjoined by that [original injunction].

The meanings of the verbal roots, such as giving (*dāna*) and so forth, are enjoined [as the means]. It has been stated that there is no non-enjoinment of gifts on the grounds that they are excluded by a sacrifice enjoined at the time of origin (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*); for in cases such as "one should give" (*dadyāt*) or "one should offer" (*juhuyāt*), the productive energy (*bhāvanā*) cannot be denied to have those [gifts] as its constituent elements, due to the recognition of those same verbal suffixes. And thus, since the injunction of giving and so forth is understood within that [productive energy], [the objection is refuted].
It follows, therefore, that there is only one efficient force (*bhāvanā*) qualified by the meanings of all the verbal roots.

This being the position reached, it is replied: even though they are presented by a single word, because of the rule of priority and posteriority between the stem and the suffix within the nature of the efficient force, the meaning of the efficient force is expressed by the suffix in dependence upon the meaning of the stem.

This refers to that denotation. What is meant is this: although this verbal suffix (*ākhyātapratyaya*) is indeed one and the same, nevertheless, when employed in relation to various roots, it denotes its own meaning as colored by the respective meanings of those roots—such as "one should sacrifice," "one should give," or "one should offer oblations"—thereby expressing *bhāvanās* that are mutually distinct and differentiated by the differences in the meanings of their respective roots.
He shows this. If it is asked: "How can the difference between one verbal root-meaning (*dhātvartha*) be the cause for the difference in the productive operation (*bhāvanā*)?"—the answer is: No.

For that [productive operation] has that [verbal root-meaning] as its object, and its determination is dependent upon it. Indeed, the productive operation is a self-activity characterized by the departure from indifference; and because it perishes very quickly, it differs according to the mutual differences of those [root-meanings].

Furthermore, these [suffixes] are not defined by their own intrinsic form (*svarūpa*); rather, they are defined through the mediation of the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) which is their object. Nor does a suffix denote its own meaning in isolation, independent of the meaning of the verbal base (*prakṛti*), because a suffix used alone is ungrammatical (*asādhutva*) and thus unfit for usage. However, when following a verbal base, it denotes its own meaning as something distinct, colored (*uparakta*) by the meaning of that base.
