The establishment of the distinction between mental dispositions (*bhāvanā*). Therefore, when the meaning of the suffix is perceived as having its connection established and its delimitation established, the verbal roots (*dhātu*)—which constitute the "connections" (*anubandha*)—belong to the mental disposition because they are distinct words. Since these [roots] pertain to different verbal roots and are thus distinct, they also differentiate the mental disposition; this is the meaning.

For in this way, the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) would not differ according to each verbal root (*dhātu*), provided that the suffix denoting cultivation expressed it in its pure form following the verbal root; but since this is not the case, he says: because a pure nature of cultivation is not obtained, and for the reason that it would be impossible for [the suffix] to be intent upon the application of the meaning of the verbal root, there can be only a single cultivation of heaven.

Because it is impossible for there to be a distribution of the meanings of various constituent elements (*dhātu*). A distinction in the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) delimited by sacrifice can never become one delimited by giving. Therefore, as for what was stated by the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) even according to the "single-part" theory (*ekadeśimata*) on page 276:
Since it is untenable for [the Veda] to be intent upon the application of multiple verbal root-meanings, there can be no application of multiple root-meanings to a single *bhāvanā*;

therefore, the entire Veda constitutes a single sentence and a single *apūrva*. However, this is not the case with the *samit* and other such offerings, because they are not subservient to anything else.

Even if the phrase "three oblations" (*tisra āhutīḥ*) refers to their essential nature, there is still a distinction based on number. He states that the objection—that this [distinction] is not a valid reason—is refuted by the rejection of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) we have previously set forth: "Not in a single productive urge (*bhāvanā*), because of the employment of various root-meanings; and thus the entire sentence is one, and the transcendental result (*apūrva*) is likewise one, [constituting] the production of action."
The sense is that the difference in the *apūrva* (the unseen potential) follows from the difference [in the action].

Having thus established the difference between actions by means of a different word (*śabdāntara*), he now states it by means of repetition (*abhyāsa*): "In that regard, in the passages such as 'He offers the *samidh*s,' the word *yajati* (he sacrifices) is repeated five times; therein, is there one single productive activity (*karmabhāvanā*)?"

Or rather, are there exactly five? What is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*)? Since the difference in the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) is expressed through the difference in the suffixes attached to the verbal roots, and since a difference in the meaning of the verbal root is untenable without a difference in the verbal roots themselves, the efficient force enjoined by the first statement of the efficient force—"He offers the *samit* oblations" (*samidho yajati*)"—is subsequently restated (*anūdyate*) by the following [sentences] while it remains present in the mind. And it is not...

There is no restatement [of the action] because there is no purpose [in doing so]. Since it is impossible to challenge that what is established by a means of valid cognition lacks a purpose, and because it would lead to the undesirable consequence of postulating multiple *apūrva*s, one ritual act consists of a single *apūrva* with intermediate operations.

This being the position reached, it is replied: "But in the case of the *samid* and other [offerings], there is a distinction because they do not have another as their purpose. This is the point here.

[Objection: It is argued that the sentences concerning the *samidh* and other [subsidiary rites] are mutually independent; thus, although all of them are equally entitled to primacy, they are studied sequentially because simultaneous study is impossible. However, this sequence is not what determines their application (*prayojaka*). For such a sequence would only exist if there were syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) among these mutually independent elements. Now, if there is an absence of primacy...

Since there is no such thing as "that which has already been obtained," of what would this be a restatement (*anuvāda*)? For mere reversal (*parivṛtti*) lacks the capacity to set aside the status of an injunction characterized by the commencement of what was previously uncommenced—which is the default rule (*utsarga*). Indeed, when a quality (*guṇa*) is heard, there arises a requirement for a restatement of the action (*karmānuvāda*) out of fear of the prolixity (*gaurava*) of enjoining an action qualified by that quality; it is in this context that reversal is of service.

Just as in the sentence "He offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*), which—by way of restating the oblation enjoined in "He performs the Agnihotra" (*agnihotraṃ juhoti*)—is intended for the injunction of the curd, there is no differentiation [of the rite] on account of the accessory (*guṇa*). This is because words such as *samit* and so forth, being names of rites (*karmanāmadheya*), lack the status of denoting an accessory; and since names stand in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the root *yaj* (to sacrifice), they are dependent upon it.

Because [the rites] are established as distinct, there is no differentiation of injunctions based on nomenclature here, as that would not serve as a proof for a difference in ritual acts. Therefore, since this repetition does not have another purpose and is intent upon establishing unknown ritual acts, it differentiates the acts—which serve as the adjuncts (*anubandha*) to the productive urge (*bhāvanā*)—and thereby differentiates the productive urge itself; this is established.

Now, the distinction based on number is being explained. In this regard, the example is: "He offers three oblations. Concerning this, the following inquiry arises: Is only one act of meditative realization (*bhāvanā*) regarding the oblations enjoined, or are there three?
If that were so, it would not be the case; for even in the absence of that [number], the accomplishment [of the rite] occurs through repetition.

What, then, is established? Since "juhoti" (he offers) is injunctive, and since it expresses a productive activity (*bhāvanā*) whose object is the meaning of a single verbal root, and because there is no repetition [of the act itself], the plural numbers found in "tisraḥ" (three) and "āhutīḥ" (oblations) [must refer to repetitions].

It is argued that since the injunction "he offers" is established even by the repeated performance of a single oblation, and because there is no difference in the subordinate elements (*anubandha*), it follows that there is only one productive operation (*bhāvanā*).
This being the position reached, it is replied: although the phrase "three oblations" refers to the essential nature [of the act], on account of the number...
This is the distinction. This is the underlying intention: this would be so only if the word "juhoti" (he offers) alone were the injunctive element.

However, since the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*) is the object of the injunction, and because linguistic usage does not proceed by means of the mere word-meaning (*padārtha*) alone, it is the sentence itself that is injunctive by way of expressing the word-meanings. Furthermore, in the case of "He offers three oblations," the number "three" [is subordinate].

It is logical that the nature of the action, which is not understood from any other source, being enjoined, differentiates the homas—which serve as its adjuncts—because multiplicity is necessarily based on a plurality of things inhering in a single substratum, and because such multiplicity is impossible in a single act; and since, if one were to resort to repetition (abhyāsa), the term "juhoti" would involve a figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) of repetition by means of the sacrifice, it therefore differentiates the homas and, by extension, differentiates the productive activity (bhāvanā) directed toward them. Thus, [the action is established as distinct].
The distinction has already been enumerated.

However, the Commentator, fearing that it would be difficult to establish [the point], cited the example of "seventeen animals dedicated to Prajāpati"; that too has been presented here. In this regard, the following is considered: Is Prajāpati the deity of these [animals]?

Is it that [the word] *prājāpatya* is derived with *prajāpati* as its deity? In this regard, if the formation of the *taddhita* suffix occurs after the formation of the *ekaśeṣa* (the single-remainder compound), as in the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*), then there is a single connection of the deities with seventeen animals;

thus, because of the singularity [of the deity], there is only one efficient force (*bhāvanā*) for the sacrifice. Alternatively, if the *ekaśeṣa* occurs after the *taddhita* suffix has been formed, as in the opposing view (*para-pakṣa*), [then...]

That being the case, since there are many relations between Prajāpati and the sacrificial animals, there are as many sacrifices as there are such relations; consequently, there are that many distinct *bhāvanās* (productive operations). What, then, is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? That the formation of the *taddhita* derivative occurs after the formation of the *ekaśeṣa* compound. If that were so, only one *apūrva* (transcendental result) would be postulated, because the ritual action is one. However, if there is a plurality of actions, then there must be many *apūrvas*.
"They may be so conceived.

This being the position reached, it is replied: "Seventeen"—even though they are identical in their essential nature (*svarūpa*), there is a distinction based on number. This is the underlying intention here: because the number one is the default (*autsargika*), [the mantra] "Prajāpati is the deity of this" also [applies].

It flashes forth [in the mind], and there is also the fear that they might involve the conceptualization of many unprecedented elements (*apūrva*). Thus, when this doubt arises, a resolution is reached through a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) postulated by presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*), namely: "The modification should be performed according to the archetype" (*prakṛtivad vikṛtiḥ kartavyā*). Once this is determined, it is proper to say "of this one" (*asya*) and not "of these" (*eṣām*). For instance, in the archetype—the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice—eleven portions (*avadāna*) are prescribed.

In that context, it is established that the animal serves as the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) by way of the portions to be cut off (*avattahṛdayādyavadāna*). This must be extended here by the statement "as in the archetype" (*prakṛtivat*). In that regard, if there were a single sacrifice consisting of seventeen animal substances, then this group of eleven portions would be performed upon one [animal], and that alone would be the means of accomplishing the sacrifice.

The sixteen animals would be rendered useless. If it were performed by distributing [the portions], even then, since the group of eleven cuttings (avadāna) pervades eleven animals, the six remaining ones would be useless. Nor [is it possible] for [the cutting] to apply to each of all [the animals] individually.
Even a subordinate quality (guṇa), by precluding mere application due to its prior connection, brings about that very [primary] purposefulness.
It is logical that there is a "group of portions" (avadānagaṇa) in the case of animals, because the portions are enjoined as the means for the sacrifice. And here too—

The status of being a means belongs to seventeen [animals] collectively, not individually, because that [status] does not exist in each one separately. However, since there is a distinction of sacrifices for each animal (*pratipaśu*), it is logical that the group of portions to be cut off (*avadānagaṇa*) applies to each one; thus, the *ekaśeṣa* (single-remainder) formation occurs after the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) has been applied. Consequently, it is established that there is a distinction in the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) due to the numerical distinction of the adjuncts (*anubandha*). Now, if even when the word refers to the essential nature [of the action], the distinction arises solely from number, [then...]

In that case, the word’s own form (*svarūpa*) would not be its primary referent. The reply is: No; for if that status of having the own form as the primary referent were absent, then since the number could still be accomplished through repetition, the principle that "the meaning of a word is that toward which the word is directed" would imply that the own form would not be the word's meaning. Consequently, the number would be accomplished even by means of repetition.

However, if the purpose is to establish the essential nature of the *bhāvanā* as delimited by the oblation (*homāvacchinnabhāvanā*), then because "he offers three oblations" (*tisra āhutīr juhoti*) has that very [nature] as its denotation,

and because the word is intent upon that, while the repetition (*abhyāsa*) is distinct from it, the word would not abandon its status as being intent upon the essential nature if there is a possibility of indicating it through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Therefore, regarding the status of being intent upon the essential nature—
The meaning is this: by way of refuting the characteristic of repetition (*abhyāsa*), even where there is a distinction based on number, there is no connection with form (*rūpa*).

He states that there is also a distinction from a quality (*guṇa*) which was not possible in the previous [case], with the words beginning "the quality also" and ending with "brings about. This is recorded in the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*): "One pours curds into heated milk; that is the *āmikṣā* for the Viśvedevas."

In this context, by the statement "The *āmikṣā* belongs to the Viśvedevas," a sacrifice is enjoined, inferred from the relationship between the material (*dravya*) and the deity (*devatā*). Immediately following that, it is recited: "The *vājina* for the Vājins. Regarding this, a doubt arises: is the *vājina* enjoined as an accessory (*guṇa*) to the previously mentioned rite, or is a distinct rite (*karmāntara*), qualified by its own material and deity, being enjoined?

What is the conclusion? Since enjoining a different action qualified by a different substance and deity would entail the fault of excessive injunction (*vidhigaurava*) and the fault of postulating a new unseen potency (*apūrva*) for a different action, there is no different action; rather, it is the application of the *vājina* substance to the previous action. Nor [can it be argued] that because the quality of *āmikṣā* is enjoined at the time of origin (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*), it excludes [the *vājina*] therein...
It is not tenable that the *vājina* (curd-whey) occupies another ritual action (*karmāntara*) because it finds no room [within the same action].

Since both sentences proceed simultaneously, and since the *āmikṣā* and the *vājina* are taught equally in their production (*utpatti*), it is impossible for the *āmikṣā* alone to possess the status of being "taught at the time of production" (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*). Therefore, how could the *vājina* be contradicted by this? Nor is it the case that...

Regarding the term *vaiśvadevī*, it must be stated that the Vedic connection with *āmikṣā* (curd-mixture) is stronger than the connection with *vājina* (whey), which is understood through syntactical context (*vākya*) in the phrase "for the Vājins, the whey. This is because there is no difference between the two in terms of being understood through syntactical context, as both are cognitions dependent upon other words. Indeed, when *vaiśvadevī* is uttered, [the connection with *āmikṣā* follows] without...
The hearers determine that *āmikṣā* is the primary referent. Or, even if it were directly stated by the Vedic text (*śrautatva*), nevertheless, the word *vājinam*—
through its etymological derivation as "that which belongs to them" (*tad-eṣām*)— refers to the Viśvedevas who are connected to it, since *vāja* means food and *āmikṣā* is that food.

The name (*saṃjñā*) also, arising from a new cognition produced by the cessation of the previous cognition and by the mere contradiction regarding the application of qualities such as "having a thousand sacrificial fees" (*sahasradakṣiṇa*), brings about that very same [result]. As for the gods, since the *vājina* is enjoined for the Viśvedevas by depending upon the connection with the *āmikṣā*, [it follows that there is no contradiction].
The objection that the *yāman* [offering] is not set aside by the *āmikṣā*, but rather is combined with it, and thus it is not a separate ritual action (*karmāntara*),
but rather the application of the quality of *vājina* to the very same prior rite—
this being the position reached— is now addressed: even though it is a quality, because of its connection with the prior [rite], it has as its sole purpose the specific application [of that quality].

"By setting aside that [other] priority, it brings about this [other]. This is the underlying intention here: this would be the case if the *āmikṣā* were not denoted by the word *vaiśvadevī* through the force of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*), for the secondary derivative is traditionally taught to refer to the meaning of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*)—namely, "its"—and since a pronoun refers to a proximate specific entity, the application of the secondary derivative occurs there [to that specific entity] and not to the Viśvedevas.

It does not exist among the gods, nor even in a mere relationship with them. [Objection: If that is so, then why do we not understand *āmikṣā* from the word *vaiśvadevī* alone, or why do we require the word *āmikṣā*? [Reply: We do not understand it because the denotation of the word ending in a *taddhita* suffix does not reach its completion; and we require [the word *āmikṣā*] for the sake of completing that denotation. It is completed...

For a word (*pada*) that denotes [an object] is capable of producing a cognition of its meaning only when it refers to a specific [object] in proximity; thus, depending upon that proximity, it requires another word—such as the word *āmikṣā*—to bring about that proximity. Why, then, would there be a contingency of cognizing *āmikṣā* from the word *vaiśvadevī* alone, or why would there be independence from it? And therefore, even though other words exist...

In a state of mutual expectation, that word which denotes its meaning independently of other words is stronger and more authoritative than the implied meaning because it is apprehended by the first-occurring word which possesses the nature of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). However, that which is understood through the sentence after the denotation of the word has been completed and the meaning of the word has been grasped is weaker, as it is apprehended by the sentence which is not directly perceived. Thus, [the word *dadhi*] conveys the quality characterized as *āmikṣā*, which is apprehended through direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) by means of the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*).

Because it is obstructed, the *vājina*—which is not connected with the prior ritual act—prevents its own application there and leads exclusively to the purpose of enjoining the nature of another action within its own scope. Furthermore, the *āmikṣā*, whose status as an independent means is known through the eternal [scriptural injunction], cannot tolerate either an option (*vikalpa*) or a combination (*samuccaya*) with the *vājina*. Nor is it fixed in the state of being a horse.
The word *vājī* may somehow function through etymological derivation (*yoga*) as having a dependent application (*sāpekṣavṛtti*) when explained in reference to the Viśvedevas;

and while the assumption of an authoritative injunction (*vidhi*) involves a certain complexity (*gaurava*), it must indeed be accepted rather than [rejecting the injunction] on the grounds that the means of knowledge lacks a valid object.
Thus, the distinction based on quality (*guṇa*) is established.

Since the order of the enumeration is not intended [to be significant], he now states the distinction of names in accordance with that, beginning with "The name also... and ending with "...leads. Now, there is this [sacrifice] called Jyotis, and this [sacrifice] called Viśvajyotis; one should sacrifice with this [Viśvajyotis] which has a thousand-fold sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Regarding this, there is a doubt: Is the phrase "one should sacrifice" a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma mentioned in proximity?

Is this for the purpose of enjoining the quality characterized by a thousand-fold sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), or rather is a different ritual action (*karmāntara*) qualified by that quality being enjoined? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? Because of the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma, it is simpler to enjoin merely a quality;
furthermore, the word *jyotiḥ* is seen to be used in reference to the Jyotiṣṭoma in the passage: "In every spring, [one should sacrifice] with the Jyotiṣṭoma" (*vasante vasante jyotiṣā*).

Since it is established in the world that a name can be indicated by a portion of its name— as the word *Bhīma* indicates *Bhīmasena*— even when occurring in a different context, the word functions solely as a synonym for the purpose of excluding other cognitions.

Indeed, since the word *atha* signifies immediate succession (*ānantarya*), and since that [succession] is untenable in the absence of a connection, and because the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) of one hundred and twelve is not prescribed as part of the original injunction (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*), it follows that this [statement] is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the very sacrifice under discussion for the purpose of prescribing the quality (*guṇa*) characterized by a thousand-fold fee; it is not [an independent injunction]. This is because, being equally enjoined (*sama-śiṣṭatā*), an option (*vikalpa*) with that [original fee] is logically possible.

When it is argued that this is a different ritual action (*karmāntara*), it is said in reply: Even the name, because it arises from a new cognition produced by the interruption of the previous cognition and because it is not in conflict with the mere application of qualities such as "having a thousand-fold sacrificial fee" (*sahasradakṣiṇatva*), leads back to that very same [action]. This is the meaning: it would be [the case] if there were an application of qualities in the previous [action].

If yoga were indeed that same context, it would be interrupted; for it is established in common experience that even when in close proximity, a different name perceived as having a meaning unconnected with the preceding cuts off the cognition of the prior action and generates a cognition of something new. It is never the case that one says, "Give a cow to Devadatta, and then [give] gold to the gods."

Just as people understand from the word "deva" (god) that Devadatta is the recipient of gold, so too, when the word "yajeta" (one should sacrifice) is heard later on, it does not produce that same cognition because it is separated by words whose meaning is unrelated; therefore, being incapable of merely enjoining an accessory (*guṇavidhi*), it enjoins a distinct ritual action (*karmāntara*) qualified by an accessory. And how could it be that, due to an inconsistency in one place...

Since the word *jyotis* is applied to the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice by virtue of its essential characteristic (*cillakṣaṇā*), it should, whenever possible, be understood as referring to that very sacrifice. Just as the word *gaṅgā* in the expression "the hamlet on the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*) does not function in its secondary sense (*jaghanyavṛtti*), it likewise does not do so in the expression "the fish in the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgāyāṃ matsyaḥ*). Thus, the word *atha* here signifies the commencement of a new topic (*adhikārārthaḥ*) within a different context.
The word "this" (eṣa) is also appropriate for referring back to that very [action] which is about to be enjoined; thus, it is established that there is a difference based on a different name.
Now, he states the difference based on context (prakaraṇa): "another context" (prakaraṇāntaram). [This refers to] the Kuṇḍapāyinām Ayana.

It is traditionally taught: "One should offer the Agnihotra for a month. Regarding this, there is an inquiry: Is the monthly characteristic being prescribed as a quality (guṇa) by referring back to the obligatory Agnihotra, or is it a distinct ritual action altogether? In this regard, since the word "Agnihotra" denotes the obligatory Agnihotra and is not established as denoting a different ritual action, [it must refer to that very same rite].

Furthermore, it would be unjustifiable for a single word to have multiple meanings, and if one were to resort to secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), there would be the undesirable consequence of abandoning the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) when a primary sense is possible.

Moreover, since the word "juhuti" can function as a mere restatement of the general nature of an oblation (*homa*), when there is a requirement for a specific detail, even if that detail is specified by the term "Agnihotra," there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) because the offering is understood through the very nature of the oblation itself. And although "juhuti" implies a plurality of agents, the action [remains unitary].

Because there is recognition [of the rite] through its essential nature and because it is not destroyed, even in that case of the obligatory [Agnihotra], since it would be impossible for the word "month" to be construed with the meaning of the object [of the action] due to conflict with the scriptural injunction "as long as one lives," it follows that this is an injunction for the repetition of the optional Agnihotra—which is to be performed in the evening and morning—as a subordinate element. This being the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), it is said in reply: "The difference of context [indicates] the exclusion of the notion of [that] other [rite]."
It functions precisely through its intended meaning (*tātparya*). This is the underlying intention here: this would be so if time were present in the action;
however, because it is not interrupted by that [time], there is no such intended meaning, and thus there is no interruption. And in this way, regarding the action...

It would have to be enjoined; however, it does not deserve to be enjoined because it is not something to be undertaken (anupādeya). Rather, the action is to be enjoined at a specific time. And if it is to be enjoined, why not something else? Because the scope of an injunction is that which has not [already] been established. If it is argued that this same contingency applies to the statement "one performs the Agnihotra in the evening and in the morning," we say no; for in that case, by virtue of occurring within that specific context, the fire-altar is already clearly [established].

In the case of the *hotṛ* [recitation], because it is subject to an exception by means of the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) that it refers to the essential nature of the ritual action (*karmasvarūpa*), its scope is limited merely to the application [of the mantra] at specific times such as evening; therefore, its general character is set aside. However, in this case (the present context), because the continuity of that cognition is interrupted by the recitation in a different section (*prakaraṇāntara*), there is no such exception. Consequently, since the general rule remains uncontradicted, it is impossible to remove the fact that the subject matter concerns the essential nature of the ritual action. And as for the name...

Because it is incapable of re-identifying the meaning of the verb— as consisting of a sequence of many agents enjoined as delimiters within the scope of the injunction— it is established in accordance with that [meaning]; and since the primary application of the word *para* (other) to something else is untenable, even though it is secondary, it serves to fulfill the properties of the occasional *agnihotra* which requires a corresponding different object.

The application [of the ritual] will be appropriate. Therefore, even in the case of a different context (*prakaraṇāntara*), because of the interruption of the mental impression (*buddhiviccheda*) caused by that which is enjoined as distinct from the action being prescribed, it functions for the sake of that very nature of the action—which is the primary object of the injunctive sentence—this being its essence (*tattva*). Thus, it is established that there is a separate action (*karmāntara*).
Regarding the word "you" (*tvam*):
however, in such cases where there is no distinct context (*prakaraṇāntara*), there is no intent toward the essential nature of the ritual action;
rather, it is solely intent upon the connection with the injunction itself. Thus he says: "Because of the lack of interruption in its proximity, there is recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*)."

"Because there is no interruption, there is no intentionality [to establish a new rule], nor is there a focus on the essential nature [of the act]; thus, the lack of interruption means it is focused solely on the application (*viniyoga*).
For example, with reference to the *Aveṣṭi* sacrifice, this is taught: 'One desiring food should cause [another] to sacrifice with this. In that regard, there is a doubt:
Is this *Aveṣṭi* enjoined as a separate ritual action (*karmāntara*) for the sake of this result, or is this merely an application of the [already established] sacrifice to the result?"

Thus [the question arises]: what is the prima facie view? Since it is impossible to enjoin the fruit as something to be accomplished because it is already the objective (uddeśya), the ritual action must be enjoined therein. This is because there can be no mutual relationship between two things that are both objectives. If, however, another action is being enjoined, this being the prima facie view, it is replied: True, such would be the case if there were no recognition; but here, since the text is recited in the immediate proximity of the Aveṣṭi sacrifice, [it refers to that very same sacrifice].
It is established that this more distinct recognition, by subverting the view that the text is concerned with the essential nature of the action as a general rule,

brings about the conclusion that it is concerned solely with the injunction; thus, it has been demonstrated through six means of proof that [the text] is concerned with the essential nature of the action, serving as a counter-example to the "different context" (prakaraṇāntara) principle.
If this [section] is intended to establish that the subject matter is the essential nature of action (*karma*), how then is difference (*bheda*) the purpose of the definition? To this he says:

"And thus, while the action is that which is to be enjoined, its differentiation is an introductory topic (*upoddhāta*). Even though difference alone is the purpose of the definition, nevertheless, its comprehension is impossible without first establishing that this very [action] has the essential nature as its primary referent.

Thus it has been stated. Therefore, for the sake of establishing the distinction under discussion, this introductory section (upodghāta) teaches that the six means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) have their own intrinsic nature; by means of the principle of a "conclusion established by implication" (*adhikaraṇasiddhāntanyāya*), the distinction is thereby demonstrated. Thus, the distinction is for the purpose of showing they are not identical.

The state of being subject to injunction (*vidheyatva*) is an introductory elaboration on its specific varieties. However, the focus on application (*viniyoga*) will be discussed in the third book (*adhyāya*). For it has been stated that the subservience [of one thing] to another does not arise from *śruti* and the other means of proof alone. Nor is that [subservience] established without recourse to performance (*anuṣṭhāna*). And performance belongs to the injunction (*vidhi*). Therefore, that too is intended to be expressed. True; however, since that is established through the injunction of performance (*prayogavidhi*), this [present discussion] is concerned solely with application.

Thus, having first demonstrated that the purpose of an injunction (*vidhi*) is production (*utpatti*), which is the subject matter of the second chapter, he now illustrates its purpose as application (*viniyoga*), which is the domain of the third chapter: "The focus on application (*viniyoga-paratā*) of an injunction is considered in the third *lakṣaṇa*. [Objection: But this would indeed be considered if the injunction were the agent of application (*viniyojaka*). It is not so.

This is so because only direct assertion (*śruti*) and the other means of proof are the factors that effect application. For it has been stated that "direct assertion and the rest are the causes for application"; therefore, he says: "For subservience to that purpose does not arise from direct assertion and the rest alone.
Indeed, it is not mere relationship that is being considered here, but rather subservience to another (*pārārthya*), as it is said: "Now, therefore, the definition of the subordinate (*śeṣa*)."

"The remainder [is subordinate] because it exists for the sake of another. Furthermore, that [subordination] does not apply solely on the basis of direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and so forth; for instance, one who is going to a village stops at the roots of trees along the way. In cases such as "He sprinkles the sacrificial oblations with the remnant of the *prayāja*," their subordination is not established by the authority of those [means of proof], since they are observed to deviate from it. And thus, it is the same even in cases such as "He threshes the rice-grains."

Even though the efficient force (*bhāvanā*), while requiring an object to be brought about (*bhāvya*) by its very nature, would— due to the employment of a coreferential term (*samānapadopādāna*)— opt for the form of the rice-grain (*vrīhi*) by abandoning threshing (*avaghāta*), it is nonetheless more remote from this wretched state of being a means to the transcendental result (*apūrva-sādhana*). Therefore, the injunction (*vidhi*), which consists in the status of being a means to what is desired by the agent and is perceived in acts such as threshing, presents that which is desired as the object to be brought about (*bhāvya*).
Even though threshing is proximate, one bypasses it because it is not the intended goal and approaches the rice-grains (*vrīhi*).

Having approached them as well, since even their form is not the intended goal, one does not rest with that alone; rather, one necessarily resorts to the state of being the material cause (*prakṛti*) of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), which is the means to the intended goal and the instrument for accomplishing the sacrifice. And the status of being its means [is established] through threshing.

It makes this understood for him. And in this way, threshing is established as being directly enjoined (*aupadeśika*) even in the case of barley, because the status of being the material cause (*prakṛti*) of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), which serves as the means of accomplishment, is no different in both cases.
The meaning is that when there is such an injunction, the purposefulness (*tādarthya*) does not depend on direct statement (*śruti*) and the other means of proof, as was stated previously.

Now, it may be argued: let there be no such purposefulness [of the acts] based on the Vedic texts alone; rather, it is the primary injunction itself—being recognized in the case of acts such as *avaghāta* (threshing)—that, because it lacks any other purpose once its application (*viniyoga*) is established, directly takes as its object even those things that are not themselves the direct subject of the injunction, by way of their being the immediate, unseen result characterized by the removal of husks, which is required by the sacrifice that serves as the means to the *apūrva*.

To dispel the doubt that one might establish the purposefulness (*aidamarthya*) of the threshing and other such acts—which have entered [into the ritual]—by taking them as being for the sake of that [final result], and thus assume an intermediate injunction (*antarvidhi*) just as in the case of threshing and so forth, he says: "Nor is their being for the sake of that [result] established by performance without reliance [on an intermediate step]. Indeed, it is not the case that threshing and the like are for the sake of the primary act merely because they are performed; rather, they are for its sake [only when so directed].
[The acts] being performed. Why? Because their performance is based solely on the fact that they serve that purpose (the principal act).
[Objection: Let it be so; nevertheless, what does this have to do with the present case? To this he says: "And the performance is [based on] the injunction.

That is, on the intermediate injunction (*avāntara-vidhi*) whose direct object is the act of threshing (*avahanana*). Here is the underlying intention: for, in the view that this is an *apūrva-vidhi* (an original injunction),...
It has been explained above that although the procedure for all [the subsidiaries] is established, it is not an original injunction (*apūrva-vidhi*).

Thus, as stated regarding the mandate (*niyoga*), the injunction of the subsidiaries is a restatement (*anuvāda*); yet, since no subsidiary can exist without being enjoined, [the injunction is required] for the sake of its status as a subsidiary.

"It must be enjoined"—this refers to the stage of investigation. However, in the context of an injunction (*vidhi*), because it depends on what is required by the agent, all of this is like a magical illusion.
For there is no recognition of the primary injunction (*pradhāna-vidhi*) in cases such as *avahanti* (threshing) and so forth, as there is in the case of the *samidh* and other subsidiaries. Nor...

Indeed, that very injunction which establishes the status of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices as a means toward a desired result can likewise be the injunction establishing the status of acts such as *avahanti* (threshing) as a means toward the assistance of the principal act, which itself possesses a desired result; for there is no contradiction characterized by mutual exclusion [between these two]. Therefore, if the injunction of the principal act were accepted... [the threshing would be included].

Consequently, since acts such as threshing would attain the status of primary rites—just like the Āgneya and other sacrifices—their being subsidiary (śeṣatva) could not be defined by their subservience to a primary rite. Therefore, to establish that status, an intermediate injunction (avāntara-vidhi) must be admitted for acts such as threshing, just as one is admitted for the Samidh and other subsidiaries. In this way, even acts such as threshing possess the quality of being "enjoined" (vidheya) by virtue of being the direct object of an injunction.

Furthermore, it will not be postulated as something to be employed for the sake of accomplishing a ritual injunction (*vidhi*) by any means whatsoever. Nor is it logical to claim that an object of knowledge (*viṣaya*) is that whose very accomplishment is the purpose [of the cognition], because according to our view, [the cognition] does not even operate upon a single part of the object; thus, due to this contradiction, it is impossible for this [proposed definition] to be its defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). To explain: even in the case of the primary [object],...

Even the mere accomplishment of the injunction (*vidhisiddhi*) is a purpose, because that [injunction], having the intermediate operation of the *apūrva* (unseen potency), has the accomplishment of the fruit as its ultimate purpose; this is even more so in the case of the particle "eva" (only). Therefore, although there is no distinction between the *samit* offerings and the threshing (*avaghāta*) etc. insofar as they are objects of an injunction, a distinction must be understood characterized by their connection with different intermediate operations of the *apūrva*. This...

And the Great Sage stated this very distinction: "They [the means] are twofold. Therefore, since performance is understood from that [statement], and since that [performance] is impossible without an injunction, an intermediate injunction is established for acts such as threshing.
If this is so, then that performance is also intended to be expressed; and thus, in cases such as "one threshes the rice-grains," [the performance is intended].

[Objection: The established [distinction] would be contradicted. [Response: True. However, since the performance [of the ritual] is established through the injunction of performance (*prayoga-vidhi*)—such as "One should sacrifice on each full moon" (*paurṇamāsyāṃ paurṇamāsyāṃ yajeta*)—this sentence, "He threshes the rice-grains" (*vrīhīnavahanti*), etc., is concerned solely with the application (*viniyoga*). And the use of the word "solely" (*mātra*) excludes the performance because it was suspected [of implying it], but it does not [exclude the application].
[The objection concerns] re-arising [of the injunction], because the established status of the focus on that specific rule remains uncontradicted. This is what is meant:

since every injunction possesses four forms, it does not have as its sole purpose the origination [of the action] and its application; rather, while the performance (*prayoga*) is understood as being inseparable from the injunctive sentence, it is not intended [by the injunction] because that [performance] is established through other means. [Objection: But it does not exist. [Reply: It does exist.

If it is asked how intermediate [means of proof] such as direct statement (*śruti*) and the rest function as causes for application (*viniyoga*), he says: "For it is not the case that the purposefulness [of a thing] arises from *śruti* and the rest alone; thus, in the absence of an injunction, they are not authoritative. This being established, there is an intermediate injunction regarding acts such as threshing (*avaghāta*). Since the performance of threshing and so forth is established through other means once an intermediate injunction exists, the [author] maintains that there is no intention to express [the details of the act] otherwise.

He presents the following argument: "Since it has been stated that 'the injunction regarding the subsidiaries is a restatement (anuvāda) of the performance,' and because that [performance] is established from another source, a subordinate injunction (avāntara-vidhi) must be postulated for the application of the subsidiaries such as *avaghāta*.

In this regard, having raised the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) argument that—since application (viniyoga) is based on direct scriptural statement (śruti) and the like, whereas an injunction (vidhi) consists merely in impelling action—the status of being a subordinate element (śeṣatva) belongs only to substances and the like, and thus the injunction is not the agent of application; [the author replies] that even the form of impulsion is difficult to obtain if there is no application. Therefore, according to the method to be stated in the sūtra "But it is not effective because it is for the sake of that" (asādhakaṃ tu tādarthyāt), there is indeed application.
The potential has been stated.
He recites the very words of the Teacher: "And that which is not enjoined does not become an auxiliary; therefore, for the sake of being an auxiliary, it must be enjoined.
In that regard, the venerable Great Sage, having commenced with "Now, therefore, the definition of the auxiliary," [proceeds] right at the beginning.

In formulating the *Bādaryadhikaraṇa*, it is stated that subservience (*pārārthya*) is dependent solely upon injunction (*vidhi*), and that this is accepted as the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇārtha*).

This is expressed by the passage beginning with "Therein" (*tatra*) and ending with "is said" (*uktā*). Here, the example is the scriptural injunction: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices" (*darśapūrṇamāsābhyāṃ svargakāmo yajeta*). For in this case, heaven, the person desiring it, and the sacrifice are understood; among these, each is a subordinate element (*śeṣa*) to the others.

It is now deliberated whether or not there exists a state of being a subordinate (śeṣibhāva). In this regard, since the application (viniyoga) is based upon direct scriptural statement (śruti) and other means of proof, it is as follows:

the accusative case-ending in the word "vrīhīn" (grains), by expressing that the grains are the most desired object, makes known that the purificatory rite characterized by sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) is for their sake. The same applies to the words "ekahāyanī" (one-year-old cow) and "aruṇayā" (red one).

It is logical that the instrumental case-ending denotes the subservience (*tādarthya*) of substances and qualities toward an action; thus, substances, qualities, and purificatory acts possess the status of being subordinate (*śeṣa*), because there exists valid evidence for this. However, as for the sacrifice, heaven, and the person desiring heaven, there is no evidence—such as direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) or any other means of proof—to establish their status as subordinate.

[Objection: "Granted that other [means of knowledge] may not be authoritative, but the injunction (*vidhi*) shall be. To this he says: "Because an injunction consists merely in instigation (*pravarttanā*). Since we observe a person's activity immediately following the hearing of an injunction, there is evidence that an injunction is merely an instigation; it does not, however, function as a connector (*viniyojaka*). Therefore, [the injunction applies] only to substances and so forth.

Having raised the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) objection that the injunction is not an allocator because the "remainder" (śeṣabhāva) does not exist with respect to heaven, the sacrifice, or the person, [the author] replies: even if it has the form of instigation (pravarttanā), it is difficult for it to be non-allocating; thus, according to the logic to be stated later in the sūtra *asādhakaṃ tu tādarthyāt*, the capacity for allocation is attributed to the injunction. This is what is meant: it is true that [the injunction] has the form of instigation...

The injunction (*vidhi*)—its very nature as such is difficult to establish without its being an instigator (*viniyojaka*). Indeed, it was explained above that there can be no status as a motivator (*prayojakatva*) without being a means sought by the agent; and we shall explain this very point while commenting on the *svargakāmādhikaraṇa* with the words, "But [the action] is not the means, because it exists for the sake of that. This being so, if one desires heaven...

When the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) is understood from the optative suffix (*liṅ*) in "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), being colored by that injunction, it—by virtue of that very coloring—would set aside even the object denoted by the same word, namely the ritual act, because that act is painful and cannot be the locus of the agent's desire; instead, it would grasp heaven as the goal (*bhāvya*), which is denoted by a different word and is a qualification of the person, precisely because it is something desired. Having thus obtained the desired goal, [the efficient force proceeds].
Depending upon a means, by the force of the injunction itself, one applies the action to the status of being a means for what is desired;

therefore, who other than the injunction is capable of prescribing the application (*viniyoga*)—namely, that an action exists for the sake of a result? This very point has been stated [by Jaimini]: "Jaimini [says] that even actions [are for the sake of results], because they exist for the sake of results. And that very [application], which consists in the status of being a means intended by the agent, [directs] toward the sphere of the result...
Bearing the agent’s effort, it makes known its purpose for that [result], because effort is untenable in the absence of the result being something to be produced by the agent.
No conscious person ever desires, "May heaven obtain itself," but rather, "May it be obtained by me."

If it is suspected that the injunction (*vidhi*) alone is the applicator and that the direct statement (*śruti*) and other means are not causes [of application], the dependence upon *śruti* and the rest is stated subsequently.
In the fourth [book], however, there is an investigation into the status of subsidiaries as factors of performance and the determination of their number.

How so? The purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) is dependent upon the performance of the injunctions for that sacrifice; however, the activity [toward a result] is based on the desire of the person (*puruṣa*). For it is precisely the quality of being experienced as agreeable that constitutes the "desirability" (*kāmyatā*) of those things sought after (*kāmya*); this is because things whose nature is experienced as disagreeable become objects of aversion or indifference. Therefore, the result possesses a purposefulness toward the person (*aidamarthya*).

And it has been said: "The fruit [is enjoined] because it serves the purpose of the person. Thus, that very injunction, carrying the factor of the agent, establishes that the person who possesses primacy with respect to the fruit—that is, who holds the status of the qualified performer (adhikārin)—possesses the status of being subordinate to the ritual act as its means, by virtue of being the agent (kartṛtva) or the causal factor (kārakatva) with respect to that action. This is what was stated: "And the person [is subordinate], because he exists for the sake of the ritual act."
Diti: Therefore, it is established that even the Great Sage (Vyāsa) agrees with this.

Now, one might raise the objection: "Since the application (*viniyoga*) has already been examined by this very section that was begun, and since the purpose of the definition is thus completed, the subsequent elaboration is useless. To dispel this doubt, he says: "The injunction," etc.

[This is] concluded by the words "stated by [the author] on the day... The meaning is as follows: It is true that the application (*viniyoga*) based on injunction (*vidhi*) has been examined by this [section], but the purpose of the definition does not terminate with this much alone, because what follows is intended as a response to an objection. To explain: if the injunction were the means of application, then since the application would be established from that alone, there would be no need for the direct statement (*śruti*) and the other [means of application].

It was suspected that those [subsidiary acts] are not causes for the purpose [of the main sacrifice], because their being a cause consists merely in a relationship, which is subject to deviation regarding that specific purpose.
To this, the reply is: True; nevertheless, an injunction is not capable of enjoining anything without assistance.
For an injunction, even while enjoining, does not say "one sprinkles" without also saying "the rice-grains"; thus, its conformity [to the main purpose] is established.

Without a direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) upon rice grains, the injunction "one desiring cattle should sacrifice" (*yajeta... paśukāmaḥ*), and the act of sprinkling with the remains of the *prayāja* offerings (*prayājaśeṣeṇa*)—all these would be unable to establish the application of the sacrifice for the fruit of cattle or the sprinkling upon the *prayāja* remains, even if they were reversed, without the status of being a previously established subordinate element. Therefore, it is the *śruti* alone that is the applicator (*viniyojaka*).
Since it depends upon the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) and other means as its auxiliaries, its purposefulness is established by the subsequent detailed exposition regarding that dependence.

Thus, having explained in the third [chapter] the application of the auxiliaries through the direct statement and other means, and having established their status as constituent parts (*aṅga*), [the fourth chapter proceeds].

In the fourth [section], there is an inquiry into the number of subsidiaries (aṅga) pertaining to performance. This is the meaning: since it is well-established in both common worldly usage and the Veda that an injunction (vidhi), by its very nature as an impelling force, possesses the quality of causing performance, its essential character need not be further deliberated upon. Therefore, the inquiry concerning the number of subsidiaries pertaining to performance is undertaken: how many subsidiaries are to be performed by means of the injunction, and how many are not?
By the phrase "from another cause" (*nimittāntarāt*), even this much, the performance [of an action] dependent upon an injunction has indeed been considered.

Now, one might object: the author of the Sūtras, by promising at the outset—"Now, therefore, [follows] the inquiry into what is for the sake of the sacrifice and what is for the sake of the person"—states that the subject matter of the chapter is the inquiry into what is for the sake of the sacrifice and what is for the sake of the person, and not the inquiry into the number of subsidiaries pertaining to the performance. This is the intended objection.

[Page 286] Regarding the human purpose (*puruṣārtha*): therein, one must consider which [act] is performed by virtue of an injunction for a sacrifice (*kratuvidhi*), what extent of the activity of instigation to perform belongs to the injunction for the sacrifice, and which [act] belongs to the person, based on other causes for that injunction not required [by the sacrifice]. This is also the inquiry into the instigator (*prayojaka*) and the non-instigator (*aprayojaka*).
The extent of the operation of the injunction for the performance of a sacrifice (*kratvanuṣṭhānavidhi*) is determined as follows:
namely, the injunction for the performance of the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifice, being for the sake of the *āmikṣā* (curd-mixture), implies the performance of the act of bringing curds (*dadhyānayana*).
How so? The answer is: that which has the sacrifice as its purpose (*kratvartha*) is performed in dependence upon the injunction of the sacrifice.

The purpose of man (*puruṣārtha*) is that which functions based on the desire of a person. For, by means of the sacrifice—which is the subject of the injunction—the injunction itself is indicated as its object; thus, "that which is desired" means "that which is being caused to be performed. Therefore, that which is dependent on the injunction for its performance is for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*). In the same way, when a person also [performs an act] due to their own connection [to it], or because of another cause...

The meaning of that [sūtra] is that something other than the injunction (vidhi) is perceived, namely those things being desired and being performed by it. Therefore, the human goal (puruṣārtha) is an activity based on human desire.
Having explained the meaning of the words of the sūtra, he states how the inquiry is established upon it: "In that regard, of what [is there a sacrifice]?"

What is performance according to the injunction? This very point he elucidates: to what extent does the ritual injunction (*kratu-vidhi*) have the function of enjoining the various constituent parts (*aṅga-jāta*), or for which person is there non-expectancy due to another cause for that injunction?
That other cause, which is the object of that injunction, is connected to the person; therefore, this is not the introductory aphorism (*pratijñā-sūtra*).

The meaning is that there would be a contradiction. Now, one might object: "Granted that there is no contradiction with the *pratijñā-sūtra*, why would the inquiry into what is *prayojaka* (the motivator) and what is *aprayojaka* (non-motivator) not be inconsistent with the inquiry into the number of subsidiaries (*aṅga*) pertaining to performance (*anuṣṭhāna*)? To this he replies:

"Even by means of the inquiry into what is *prayojaka* and what is *aprayojaka*, [one determines] precisely the extent of the operation of the injunction for the performance of what subserves the sacrifice (*kratvartha*)."

It is maintained: the meaning is that the extent of the operation of the injunction regarding the performance of the ritual (*kratvanuṣṭhāna*)—namely, that its operation is "this much" and not "that much"—is precisely what is determined. He provides an illustration of that very determination along with its supporting reasoning, beginning with "For instance" (*tathā hi*). In the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices, it is recited in the *Vaiśvadeva* section: "She pours curd into hot milk; that..."

"Vaiśvadevyāmikṣā, vājibhyo vājinam. In this regard, there are two rites: in one, the *āmikṣā* is the oblation and the Viśvedevas are the deity; in the other, however, the *vājina* is the oblation and the Vājins are the deity. Since the curdling of the milk (*dadhyānayanam*) is understood [to apply] here, a doubt arises: is this injunction for the Cāturmāsya sacrifice intended for both purposes?
Does it enjoin the bringing of curds, or rather [the bringing of milk] for the sake of the *āmikṣā*? For that purpose, there is this doubt regarding the cause:

is *āmikṣā* simply milk conjoined with curds, or is it something other than milk? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? It is [something other], because of the difference in color, configuration, designation, and indicative marks; and because of the pronoun "this" (*eṣa*), as in "this is the Jyotiṣṭoma."

Since it is also logical [to view *āmikṣā*] as a distinct entity from the *vājina*—as will be explained according to the established method—the *āmikṣā* is the curd-mixture derived from milk combined with curds.

From the addition of curds, both this *vājina* and the *āmikṣā* are produced. Since both are grasped by the injunction for the performance of the Cāturmāsya sacrifice as the means for two separate rites, the pair constitutes the Cāturmāsya itself.

The conclusion reached is that the injunction applies without distinction. This being the position, it is replied: The injunction for the performance of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, by virtue of having the *āmikṣā* as its purpose, enforces the bringing of curds (*dadhyānayana*), and not for the sake of the *vājina*;
for that [curd] which is produced as a by-product for the sake of the *āmikṣā* is what enters into [the ritual]. This is the underlying intention: this would indeed be so if the *āmikṣā*...
It does not serve as a means for the horse, because only that which is produced as a secondary by-product of that purpose enters into it.
Likewise, this applies to the seventh step, which is brought forward as an inseparable concomitant of the act of purchasing. Similarly, the sacrificial cake—

The substance would not belong to the class *kṣīra* (milk), for even though there is a difference in [qualities] such as color and so forth, the class *payastva* (milk-ness) is recognized through its taste. For a class is manifested by the form and configuration of the curdled milk and the milk, and thus it differs when those differ; this [class], however, is manifested by a specific taste, and therefore its difference or non-difference follows the difference or non-difference of that [taste].

This must be so. For this very reason, even though there is no difference in color and other qualities between water and *sauvīra* (vinegar), people determine a difference in genus (*jāti*) based on the difference in taste; likewise, ordinary people do not conclude that two samples of milk—one thick and the other thicker—belong to the same genus because they lack recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) based on taste. Furthermore, even when things belong to the same genus, [the distinction is made] by means of gender and so forth.

Likewise, the production of the *āmikṣā* is established by the statement "the *āmikṣā* is milk," and since the addition of curds (*dadhyānayana*) is enjoined for both the *vaiśvadeva* [offering] and the milk,
it is thereby enjoined for the *āmikṣā*. Since practical application follows such injunction,
the injunction for the performance of the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices mandates the addition of curds for the purpose of the *āmikṣā*, and not...

Because it serves the purpose of the *vājina* (curd-whey), and since its taste is distinct such that it cannot be recognized as being the same substance as the milk, it constitutes a different class of entity; therefore, it falls within the scope of the application of bringing curd for the sake of the *āmikṣā*. Since it is produced as a secondary result (*anuniṣpanna*) and enters into that [process], there is no separate performance [of the act]. This is the operation of the injunction for the performance of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices.
By this, only the measure (parimāṇa) is established.
He adds another example with the word "thus" (evam): it is heard in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, "He purchases Soma with a red, one-year-old, yellow-eyed cow; he steps out six steps after her."

"He takes up the seventh footprint. "If they should proceed toward the *havirdhāna* sheds, then they should smear the axle with that [dust]. Regarding this, there is a doubt: Does this injunction for the performance of the *Jyotiṣṭoma*—which serves both the purpose of the purchase and the purpose of taking the dust from the seventh footprint as a means for smearing—enjoin the leading forward of the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*), or does it enjoin it solely for the purpose of the purchase?

What is the prima facie position? Since both [the purchase and the footprint] are accomplished by the leading forward of the one-year-old cow, and because the statement "she steps out six footprints" is recited between the mention of the purchase and the mention of the dust of the footprints, there is no distinction in its application to either;
thus, it follows that it is the motivator for both purposes. To this, it is replied: [it is] for the purpose of the purchase, being an incidental consequence of the leading forward.
The connection is with the preceding [clause], "because of the seventh step's being entered into that," and with the following, "therefore there is a separate performance.
This is what is meant: this desire would be fulfilled if an independent one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*) were heard of in the sentence regarding the taking of the dust;
however, that [cow] which belongs to the sentence "He buys Soma with a one-year-old cow" is proximate [to the action].
Since the cognition [of the seventh step] is revolving in the mind, its connection with the statement regarding the taking of dust must be understood by way of dependence;

and because it is proximate for the purpose of purchasing the Soma, the seventh step—being inseparable from that—enters into the act of carrying for the sake of the purchase. Therefore, it is not enjoined as a separate performance by the injunction of the Jyotiṣṭoma.
The determination of the extent of the performance of the injunctions is established.
He states another example with the word "likewise" (*tathā*). The New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) exist; regarding them, this is recorded in scripture:
"He cooks [the rice] on a potsherd" (*kapāle śrapayati*), and "With the cake-potsherd (*puroḍāśakapāla*), he scatters the husks" (*tuṣān upavapati*). Here, an inquiry arises.
However, because the remaining *kapāla* comes into contact with it by means of the scattering of husks (*tuṣopavāpa*), and because the northern half is a single part [of that same vessel],
there is no separate performance; for the part to be taken (*upādeya*) is connected to that very whole which has already been appropriated (*upātta*).

Is this rule of application (prayogavidhi) a motivator for the use of the potsherd (kapāla) without distinction for both the purpose of the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) and the purpose of scattering the husks (tuṣopavāpa),
or is it a motivator only for that which serves the purpose of the sacrificial cake? In this regard, since the status of being a motivator follows the specific application (viniyoga),
and since the application is established by the injunction "he bakes upon the potsherd" for the husks and by the injunction "with the cake-potsherd" for the sacrificial cake—

Regarding the statement "he scatters the husks," since there is no distinction in the scattering of husks and because it is possible to designate that which is common to both [the husk-scattering and the cake-preparation] by means of even a single sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), it follows that the potsherd (*kapāla*) is employed for the sake of both. To this, it is replied: the potsherd is not for the sake of the scattering of husks, because its contact with them occurs only through its being a remnant of the sacrificial cake.
The connection with what follows is that there is a separate performance (*pṛthag-anuṣṭhānam*). This is the underlying intention here:

this would be possible if, in the sentence concerning the placing [of the cake] (*upavāpa*), one had heard a mention of the *kapāla* alone, as in the sentence concerning the cooking (*śrapaṇa*); however, what is heard is its connection with the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), namely, "with the *kapāla* of the sacrificial cake" (*puroḍāśakapālena*). Nor can its connection with the future sacrificial cake be anything other than [this].
Because of its purpose. If this is so, then the application of the *kapāla* (potsherd) to the scattering of husks is like that of the remnant of the *puroḍāśa* cake.

Nor is there a contradiction regarding the disposal (*pratipatti*) characterized by the application of what has already been applied; for by the word *puroḍāśakapāla*, it is the essential nature of the potsherd itself that is indicated. Furthermore, there is no extension (*prasaṅga*) of this function to other potsherds, because [the potsherd] is established as being for that specific purpose.

Because it is precisely the related locus (*sthāna*) that is being indicated. Indeed, in the expression "the hamlet on the Gaṅgā," the word "Gaṅgā" does not indicate the bank of a pond. For this very reason, he says "of the *kapāla*"; fearing that [the rule] might over-apply to another *kapāla*, he restricts it to the remnant of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*). And thus, regarding future [cases]...

Since the potsherd (kapāla) has been brought forth by the injunction of performance specifically for the sake of the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), its contact with the primary rite occurs even through the scattering of husks; however, this does not apply to a mere potsherd that is not for the sake of the sacrificial cake. Therefore, there is no separate performance [of the scattering], and thus the limit of the performance (prayogeyattā) is established here as well.
He states another example: "And of the latter half," etc. Regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard in the scripture:

"One cuts off [the portion] for Sviṣṭakṛt from the northern half. In this regard, the following is considered: Is the northern half also employed for the sake of the Sviṣṭakṛt offering by the performance-injunction (*prayogavidhi*), or rather, is it [employed] from that very [portion] which was already employed for the sake of the Āgneya sacrifice?

Is it also accomplished by means of the *puroḍāśa* cake? What is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*)? [It is not accomplished], because it is impossible for the *puroḍāśa* cake dedicated to Agni to be connected with another deity, and because this would contradict the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭa*). Indeed, the learned do not employ for one purpose that which was intended for another. Furthermore, since the purpose [of the sacrifice] necessarily implies both objects [the deity and the material], it has the capacity to entail [the use of the original material].

When it is argued that a separate substance must be employed for the sake of the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, the following is stated: Since the "northern half" (*uttarārddha*) is but a single part, and since that which is to be taken (*upādeya*) is connected only to the specific portion already taken (*upātta*), there is no separate performance [of the offering]. This is the meaning:
From the scriptural statement "from the northern half," this sacrifice is understood as one that takes a portion; and that which takes a portion [cannot be performed] independently.

Ordinary people do indeed accept a composite whole [as the object]. For instance, a boy sent to fetch a piece of a sweetmeat (*modaka*) does not go for the sake of the entire sweetmeat; nor does the sender become angry with him for failing to do so. Indeed, when the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering—which requires a portion to be cut from the rear half—is expected, it is performed only after the primary sacrifice has been completed by means of the mere cutting of the portions (*avadāna*) from the material procured for that primary sacrifice.

For if it were an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), there would be performance based on the injunction for the application of the sacrifice and its subsidiaries, such as the *juhū* ladle; whereas in the case of an injunction of a result, as in the instance of "being made of *parṇa*-wood," that [performance] would be absent. Therefore, the explanatory praise is for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), while the injunction of a result is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*).

And even though its performance is dependent upon an injunction, the quality of being made of *parṇa* wood—being enjoined for a purpose other than that which is the object of the injunction governing the performance of the sacrifice—is for the sake of that [sacrificial ladle], and not for the sake of the sacrifice itself, such as the upper portion [of the ladle]. For this very reason, the sacrifice performed with such a ladle does not bring about a contradiction with established practice. Or, even if such a contradiction were to exist, scripture (*śruti*) is more authoritative than practice (*ācāra*).

It is established. Therefore, since the northern half of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), which is a subordinate element included within the injunction for the performance of the primary purpose, is connected to the sacrifice, there is no separate performance; thus, the measure of the performance is proven. This concludes the section on attainment (*sagāpti*).

If the purpose of the definition were merely to determine the extent of the operation of the injunction regarding the performance (*prayoga-vidhi*), then the investigation into the fruit-injunction (*phala-vidhi*) and the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) would indeed be irrelevant here; therefore, he says: "For if they were *arthavādas*, then qualities such as being made of *parṇa*-wood would have their performance based on the injunction for the performance of the sacrifice that has *juhū*-ladles etc. as its auxiliaries; however, in the case of a fruit-injunction, that [basis] is absent."

If, however, the quality of being made of *parṇa* wood (*parṇamayītva*) were enjoined for a result based on the ladle (*juhū*) and other implements as its substratum, then in the absence of that [result], there would be an absence of performance—that is, an absence of execution—constrained by the injunction for the performance of the sacrifice. Indeed, here there is a statement not situated within a specific ritual context (*aprakaraṇādhīna*), which says: "He whose ladle is made of *parṇa* wood does not hear an evil report. Regarding this, there is a doubt.

Is this an injunction regarding a fruit, or is it an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*)? Just as from the statement, "He whose food is digested does not suffer from diseases," one understands that the absence of disease is the result of eating after digestion, so too from this [text], one understands that the state of being made of *parṇa*-wood is the cause for hearing verses of praise.

And all people take pleasure in that; therefore, even without a connection to ritual action (*karman*), it is understood that the hearing of the "fame of one free from evil" (*apāpaśloka*) is a fruit.

Thus, when it is argued that this is an injunction regarding a fruit (*phalavidhi*), the following is stated in reply: An injunction of this kind is not an injunction of a fruit, for the relationship of cause and effect is not understood through mere positive concomitance (*anvaya*) alone, because of the possibility of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Why?

However, those who follow the authoritative means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*) maintain that when something is possible upon the existence of another, yet does not occur even when other [conditions] are present if that [specific cause] is absent, then it is the effect of that [cause]. This [case], however, follows from another means of knowledge, such as the example of a worn-out vessel;
but here, even that is not present, because the opposite is also possible, and there is no non-deviation (*avyabhicārin*).

Regarding the injunction for the connection of the *parṇamayī* (palāśa-wood) nature with the ladle (*juhū*) that has attained its desired purpose for the sake of another, there exists a specific form; however, it is in its general form that it depends on human desire, and by this much alone it is for the benefit of man (*puruṣārtha*). This is the true meaning intended here by the Teacher: for men’s desire is indeed twofold—either when the specific means is unknown, or the opposite thereof.
And therein, when the specific means are unknown, an effort is produced directed solely toward that which is intended as the goal.

That effort—because it lacks the determination of a specific means for the object of desire and thus consists merely in the sense of "this ought to be done" regarding the result alone—is called a "general inclination," since its object is merely the thing to be aimed at. Nor is this...

It is devoid of an external object; activity extends only as far as the fruit itself. Indeed, the specificities of one's self, body, speech, and gestures do not penetrate into the nature of the fruit. As the Master has said: "For one who desires the fruit, the agent’s exertion consists in the direct realization of the fruit. And such valid cognition of the fruit, by virtue of its connection to the fruit, is a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) only with respect to its own means.

[Page 290] Therefore, it is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*). And the extent of its activity has been considered in this very manner. As for the primary cause (*pradhāna*), although its engagement proceeds from injunction in a specific form, it is in a general form with respect to the person; it is by this much alone that it is for the sake of the person.

The requirement for the subsidiaries (*aṅga*), however, follows after the knowledge of the instrument (*karaṇa*); since that knowledge and its injunction proceed even from a general perspective, and because [the performance] depends upon it, the subsidiary is for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*). But then how is this? A certain person, being motivated by a human goal (*puruṣārtha*), undertakes [an action]. That too is merely a general effort toward the necessity of performing the means thereto, without having yet ascertained the specific details.
It is produced. Nor should it be said that there is no "ought-to-be-done-ness" (*kartavyatā*) other than desire;

for even when desire exists toward each respective object, a discerning person does not necessarily perceive it as something "to be done. Furthermore, those free from deceit cannot claim that desire is something to be perceived through the internal organ (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*), since it is the opposite of that [perception].

Because it has as its object a specific means (*upāya*), it generates an effort that is distinguished precisely by the previously mentioned fruit. In this regard, the activity in its general form—being of the nature of mere inclination—occurs even prior to the injunction; thus, like the initial inclination toward the fruit, it is not based on the injunction (*vaidhī*). However, the activity in its specific form does not occur without the injunction, and is therefore based on the injunction. This may be so; yet, one who is being swept away by the current of the river of desire...

If this conscious agent has its activity obstructed by the dam of ignorance regarding the specific means to that fruit, then let him merely be made to understand those specific means; thereafter, through the breaking of that dam, the stream of his desire will flow toward the specific means as a specific activity.

Thus, there is no need for an application-injunction (*prayoga-vidhi*) concerning the scope of the principal injunction (*pradhāna-vidhi*). But if this is so, then that [application] itself would extend to the limit of the principal act.

If it is argued that the knowledge [of the means]— which was previously obstructed by a lack of specific knowledge regarding the constituent parts (*aṅga*)— becomes the motivator for those parts merely through its own attainment,

then the injunction of application (*prayogavidhi*) would not have the constituent parts as its object. Alternatively, if it is held that activity toward the parts, even in its non-general form, is not already established prior to the injunction due to the presence of desire, then why is this activity, which possesses a specific form, directed toward the means?

Is it established? No, for the establishment of a particular does not follow from the establishment of a general, because they are distinct. Therefore, although there is equality regarding the fruit, its means, and its auxiliaries insofar as they are objects of activity prompted by a general desire, the activity toward the fruit is of a purely general nature; there is no other kind of activity. And since that [general activity] arises prior to the injunction, it is not brought about by the injunction (*vaidhī*).

However, the desire for the means in its general form is the cause [of activity]. Although activity occurs prior to the injunction, it takes a specific form through the injunction; this occurs once there is an understanding of that [means], because in the absence of such understanding, activity is impossible even if the desire exists. Nor is the mere injunction the cause of activity, since one who lacks desire does not act even by means of a hundred injunctions.
