Therefore, since the injunction (*vidhi*), acting in conjunction with a previously arisen desire, is the cause of a specific engagement toward the primary act, the primary act— characterized by this specific engagement dependent on the previously arisen desire— is the human goal (*puruṣārtha*). As for the subsidiaries (*aṅga*), although the injunction acts in conjunction with desire as the cause of a specific engagement (for if desire were absent, effort would be impossible), nevertheless, in their absence...

Because bodily and vocal activity do not arise in that [state], and because there is an absence of an effect when there is an absence of a cause, even so, since the prescription of the means for the desire to know the constituent parts and the desire to act is impossible prior [to that], it is dependent upon the injunction; thus, that [injunction] is the cause. Since even activity in its general form is dependent upon that, activity is subordinate to the injunction (*vidhyadhīnapravṛtti*).

"Therefore, it is for the sake of the sacrifice. This is the distinction of the auxiliaries (*aṅga*) from the means (*upāya*). Regarding this, he says: "The requirement for auxiliaries follows after the knowledge of the instrument (*karaṇa*); and that knowledge [of the instrument] arises from the injunction (*vidhi*). Thus, because activity depends both specifically and generally upon that [injunction], and because it is dependent on the injunction, the auxiliary is for the sake of the sacrifice.

[Is it that] "the instigator (prayojaka) is for the sake of the sacrifice (kratvartha)"? How so in this case? For here, both the thing to be instigated (prayojya) as being for the sake of the sacrifice and as being for the sake of the person (puruṣārtha) have been mentioned.
In that regard, it should be stated thus: "one thing to be instigated is for the sake of the person, and another is for the sake of the sacrifice. This is not [the case].

[This is] a fault. "Puruṣārtha" (for the sake of the person) and "kratvartha" (for the sake of the sacrifice) form a coordinate compound (*samānādhikaraṇa-samāsa*), because the analysis (*vigraha*) is "that which has the person as its purpose. This is what is meant: for some [action], a certain person is the one to be prompted; such is the meaning. Even in the case of a sacrificial injunction, there is something that prompts and something that does not prompt, as in the case of *āmikṣā* and *vājina* by way of their respective means.

Here, an objection is raised: "In that case, how is this statement made by the author of the Bhāṣya to be understood? [He says: 'A certain thing is a motivator (prayojaka) when it serves a human purpose (puruṣārtha), and it is a non-motivator (aprayojaka) when it serves the purpose of the sacrifice (kratvartha)'? Not understanding the intended meaning, he asks:
"How is this so here? The objector clarifies his own intention: "[It refers to] the primary injunction and its other..."

For here, the *nimitta* (occasion) and the *prayojya* (that which is to be prompted) are stated to be for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) and for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*). In that regard, one might say: "The *prayojya* is something for the sake of the person," and so forth. He refutes this: "This is not a fault. In the Bhāṣya passage stating "the prompter (*prayojaka*) is something [for the sake of the person]," there is a coordinate compound (*samānādhikaraṇa-samāsa*) meaning "that which is for the sake of the person and for the sake of the sacrifice. [Thus,] *puruṣārthaḥ*...

The object (*viṣaya*) is the locus (*āśraya*) of both desire (*kāma*) and the occasion (*nimitta*); "the ritual (*kratu*) is the purpose" because of the analysis [of the compound] as "the object of the injunction for the ritual. He clarifies this very point: this is what is meant. For some action—whether it be optional (*kāmya*) or occasional (*naimittika*)—some person, being either desirous or possessing the occasion, is the motivator (*prayojaka*). That very [person] is the agent of the action.

He clarifies [the meaning] for the benefit of his students by means of a summary: the sense is that some action—whether optional (*kāmya*) or occasional (*naimittika*)—is to be performed by someone who has a desire or who possesses a specific occasion. Someone explains [the sūtra], inserting a certain word, as "that which is not a motivator is for the sake of the sacrifice" (*kratvartha*), [meaning] that even for the injunction of a sacrifice, something may be to be performed.

Just as the bringing of curd is for the sake of *āmikṣā*, whereas the bringing of curd for the sake of *vājina* serves no [independent] purpose; by this, the author of the *Bhāṣya*'s mode of expression is explained. However, that which proceeds from the desire of a person is for the sake of man (*puruṣārtha*), and that which proceeds from the injunction of a sacrifice is for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*)—this alone is established.

Some say that that which has a status as a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*) based solely on its being adopted [in the injunction] is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), whereas that whose activity is dependent upon the injunction of a ritual (*kratu*) is for the sake of the ritual (*kratvartha*); this alone is established. Others say that that which has a status as a subordinate element based solely on its being adopted is for the sake of the person, such as the fruit of a sacrifice.

[The injunction] is either with respect to the fruit or with respect to the qualified agent (*adhikārin*). For in this case, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such as direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and so forth [to establish this directly]. However, since an injunction (*niyoga*) having sacrifice as its object is perceived as being qualified by the goal of heaven (*svarga*), it is understood—by the principle of "otherwise inexplicability" (*anyathānupapatti*)—that sacrifice possesses the nature of being a means to heaven, and that heaven possesses the nature of being an object of enjoyment for the qualified agent.

It implies the status of being a *śeṣa* (subordinate). Such a status as a *śeṣa* constitutes being for the sake of the person (*puruṣārthatā*). However, when there is an application by means of direct statement (*śruti*) and so forth, that which possesses a status as a *śeṣa* based on the context of inclusion (*upādāna*) is for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), such as singularity and so on. For number, by its very nature, delimits the object to be numbered; thus, by the mark (*liṅga*) characterized as the capacity of the thing itself, it is connected to the essential form of the animal.
The status of being for the sake of the qualified person (*adhikāra*) arises from the mere recitation in proximity to the qualified person; thus, it follows from the qualification itself.

Consequently, in order to fulfill its purpose for the self, the qualification itself implies the connection with the animal that has become an instrument; this is the status of being a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*) based on implication (*aupādānika*). And when there is such an application (*viniyoga*), it brings about precisely the state of being for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvarthatā*).

[Page 292] The bringing of curd (*dadhyānayana*). In that context, it has been shown that performance regarding the portion of the fruit—that "in which there is pleasure"—does not arise from an injunction.
Regarding the purpose, the fruits of the *śyena* sacrifice and others are unwholesome (*anartha*). Furthermore, by virtue of being a subsidiary of the ritual (*kratvaṅga*), that subsidiary—

Regarding enumeration: thus, that for which the purposefulness (*aidamarthya*) consists solely in its being instrumental to the attainment [of a result] is *puruṣārtha* (for the sake of the person); however, when there is an application (*viniyoga*), it is *kratvartha* (for the sake of the ritual). This sūtra, "That in which there is joy," is intended to provide a definition for these two through direct statement (*abhidhāna*) and implication (*lakṣaṇā*). To those [who hold this view], he replies: "In that in which there is joy"—that is, regarding the portion consisting of the fruit, performance does not proceed from an injunction (*vidhi*).

Thus it has been shown. Indeed, when there exists a treatise devoted to defining the principles of logic (*nyāya-lakṣaṇa*), it is not appropriate to define merely the categories of things (*padārtha*) if such [a definition] is possible; nor is it even tenable [to do so]. Furthermore, the relationship of subsidiary and principal (*śeṣa-śeṣitva*) between heaven and sacrifice, as well as between the qualified person and heaven, cannot be established through *aupādānika* (implication by necessity). For *aupādāna* is said to be the implication of the mandate (*niyoga*), and not...

Just as it has been demonstrated in the *Niyogaparīkṣā* that there is no inconsistency in the *niyoga* even without a direct connection between those entitled to the sacrifice and heaven, so too the scriptural injunction (*vidhiśruti*) itself, when combined with the mention of one who desires heaven (*svargakāma*), constitutes the application (*viniyoga*) of heaven, the sacrifice, and the person, each according to its respective role. This is application.

By explaining the operation of the injunction (*vidhi*), this has been demonstrated. Therefore, that which we have stated—namely, that the purpose of the ritual is for the sake of another—is indeed superior.
Now, the meaning of the Sūtra is stated: in the passage "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma," [heaven] is the end to be accomplished (*bhāvya*).

[He] is led to heaven; regarding this, there is a doubt: does the injunction impel the person toward the factor of the fruit (*phala*) as well within the efficient force (*bhāvanā*), or not? In this regard, because the injunction has the efficient force as its object, and because the efficient force—devoid of its three constituent parts—is incapable of being enjoined due to its lack of executability, [the injunction must operate] upon the efficient force endowed with its three constituent parts. And among these, in the case of the efficient force...

It might be argued that since the portion consisting of the "how-to" (netikartavyatā) is enjoined, the portion consisting of the "end to be accomplished" (sādhyāṃśa) is likewise enjoined; thus, just as with the means and their subsidiaries, the injunction impels the person toward the fruit as well. Consequently, because the performance [of the fruit] would be dependent on the injunction, it could not be considered a human goal (puruṣārtha). To this, we reply: It is true that the productive activity (bhāvanā), endowed with its three constituent parts, is enjoined. Nevertheless, regarding that which has not yet been set in motion...

An injunction (*vidhi*), whose nature is to impel, will abandon even that which has been undertaken and brought forward. For it has been said: "The subordinate elements (*guṇas*) should indeed be enjoined, provided they are not already taught by another [means]. Furthermore, the person is impelled toward the fruit; for it was stated previously that the impulse toward the fruit is not distinct from the general impulse caused by desire. But as for its means (*upāya*), if...

Desire is the cause of general activity; thus, even before a formal injunction, there exists such activity. Nevertheless, that which consists of specific forms—namely, specific bodily and verbal actions—is not yet attained prior to a specific injunction, and is therefore enjoined. Since one has already engaged in the fruit [of the action], one is not impelled toward it by an injunction; thus, its status as a human goal (puruṣārtha) is established.

He states the purpose of the deliberation: the purpose is that the result of the Śyena sacrifice and others is non-beneficial (*anartha*). For if the performance of the portion consisting of the result were enjoined—as in the prima facie view—then malevolent magic (*abhicāra*), being understood as something required by the agent and as a means to an end, would not be non-beneficial. However, if, on the other hand, the result is not what is enjoined...

Just as the subsequent position [of the opponent] establishes the status of being a mere mental resolve (*mānatva*), so too, in that case, there is no comprehension of it as something to be performed.

Consequently, the non-performance expressed in the injunction "one shall not kill" proceeds without obstruction. And since that which is not to be performed results in suffering, it is established that the fruit of the *śyena* sacrifice and similar rites is harmful (*anartha*).

And by virtue of being the object or non-object of the injunction for the performance of the sacrifice (*kratu-prayoga-vidhi*), they are determined through the definition of the "auxiliary" (*śeṣa-lakṣaṇa*). The distinction between that which is for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) and that which is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*) is established by an inquiry into whether something is an auxiliary to the sacrifice or not. Once it is established that something is indeed an auxiliary to the sacrifice, the injunction of the sacrifice [is fulfilled].

This is because [the fifth book] investigates only the extent of the operation of the rules for performance (*prayoga-vidhi*). For this very reason it was stated that the third subject matter has been transcended.
But what is considered in the fifth [book]? Is it not the case that the order [of performance] is established by means of direct statement (*śruti*) and so forth? Yes.

[Objection: "If the scope of the operation of the injunction (*vidhi*) is being considered here by way of whether [an action] serves the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratu*) or the purpose of the person (*puruṣa*), then the investigation primarily concerned with the application (*viniyoga*) of the *godohana* vessel and so forth is irrelevant. To this, he says:

"Furthermore, because the acquisition of the substance *godohana* and so forth is a subordinate member (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice, and because number and so forth are subordinate members of that [acquisition], [the discussion concerns] the injunction for the performance (*prayoga*) of the sacrifice."
The states of being an object and not being an object have been shown; however, they are not intended here according to their respective order.
Some say that the material cause (*upādāna*) itself, as distinct from the means of knowledge such as direct statement (*śruti*), is the allocator of oneness and so forth;
to them he says: "that too" means by the definition of the subordinate (*śeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) through direct statement and the rest. For it is thus:

In the case of the acquisition of materials for milking and so forth, the injunctive suffix itself is the scriptural statement (*śruti*) regarding their being for the sake of the human goal; and in the case of [the number] oneness and so forth, there is the scriptural statement of the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā-śruti*) indicating that they belong to the animal sacrifice which has become the instrument. Now, one might object: since this [instrumental suffix] is uttered following the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), it is capable of denoting oneness as residing solely in the meaning of that stem, and not as residing in the instrument; therefore, is it not the case that the instrumenthood is not its meaning?

Let it be so; nevertheless, even then, let [the word] denote only that which resides in the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) alone. But surely, are these two—the instrumentality and the oneness—entirely unrelated to one another? For one who says "it was previously true" cannot intend to denote both simultaneously. Indeed, even if capable, the word *akṣa* does not, all at once, intend multiple meanings that are mutually unrelated.

It is used in common worldly practice. When it is said, "Bring the dice," people do not at once understand three dice; rather, they understand only one due to the force of context and so forth, or in its absence, they hesitate. If it is argued that they understand two or three dice—either as "the two dice" (*akṣau*) or "the dice" (*akṣān*)—this is not so, because of the connection through the grammatical device of *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one).

[Objection: "In this case as well, there exists a relationship between the instrument and its singularity, characterized by their co-inherence (*samavāya*) within the meaning of a single nominal stem (*prātipadika*). [Response:

Is this [relationship] the cause for the operation of denotation (*abhidhāna*), or not? If it is not, what is the use of denoting it? If it is the cause—albeit in a manner that is virtually non-existent—then either the instrument itself possesses that singularity, or the singularity belongs to that which is the instrument.

It is established that subsidiary status (*śeṣatva*) is not based on the act of taking up (*aupādānika*), because it is obtained through the third *śruti* (the instrumental case). Thus, here, prior to the investigation into similarity and dissimilarity, the purposes of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) and the person (*puruṣārtha*) are distinguished by means of an inquiry into whether something is a subsidiary of the sacrifice or not. Subsequently, once the unity of the subsidiary has been established, there follows an inquiry solely into the extent of the operation of the injunction for the performance of the sacrifice, as in the case of bringing curd (*dadhyānayana*) and so forth.

However, the determination of the extent of performance occurs by way of [distinguishing] between that which subserves the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) and that which subserves the person (*puruṣārtha*). And precisely because the subsidiariness (*śeṣatva*) of [properties such as] singularity and so forth is characterized not by the principle of "inclusion" (*aupādānika*), but rather by direct statement (*śruti*) and the other [means of proof], for this very reason the Commentator, at the commencement of the discussion regarding similarity and dissimilarity, says: "The subject matter of the third [book] has been transcended," meaning by virtue of being a subject matter belonging to the means of proof of the third [book].
The state of being an object of the third [cognition] occurs and not otherwise; the meaning is that its status as an object has been explained accordingly.
Now, intending to begin the investigation of the fifth chapter, he first raises an objection regarding its subject matter—at the beginning of the fifth [chapter].
This is not sound. It has been stated that Dharma is a beneficial purpose characterized by Vedic injunction (*codanā*), and that it exists in exactly four stages.

Sequence (*krama*), however, is distinct from those; for it is not the object of the injunction regarding performance (*prayoga-vidhi*), because it is not something to be performed. Why then is this considered a meaning of the word? Indeed, there are these four stages of the injunction, and among them, the second, third, and fourth...

In the first three chapters, the origin (*utpatti*), application (*viniyoga*), and form (*rūpa*) [of rituals] have been determined; and in the sixth chapter, the qualification (*adhikāra*) will be determined.
What else remains that would fall within the scope of the fifth chapter? This is the intended objection.
The respondent, however, speaking with the following intention, says: "But what about the sequence (*krama*)? Ah, my friend, it is quite gross!"

"This is the sequence. However, this is not within the scope of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it is not the domain of the four stages of injunction (*vidhyavasthā*), because it is not based on verbal testimony (*aśābdatvāt*), and because perception and the other means of knowledge are too remote from it. Furthermore, the elders do not accept anything devoid of a means of valid cognition in Mīmāṃsā; thus he asks: "By what means of valid cognition? [The answer follows: "By the hidden intention of the composer..."

The author of the *Saṃdhi* says: "By means of direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) and so forth. The meaning is that the sequence [of ritual acts] is established by authoritative means such as the word "first" in the rule "the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer takes the first draught," the scriptural mention of the *ktvā*-suffix in "having initiated the *gṛhapati*," and other factors characterized as will be explained hereafter. The objector states his own view: "This is not sound; [it is based on] injunction (*codanā*)."

Dharma is that which has the characteristic of being an object; and since that [characteristic] consists in expressing an injunction (*vidhi*), and because an injunction possesses four forms, it has been stated above that it exists in exactly four stages. This is true, but what follows from this? To this he says: "And the sequence has its essence in transcending those [stages]. Why? Because this is not the domain of the injunction regarding performance (*prayoga-vidhi*). Regarding this, the author of the *Vivaraṇa*...

He states the reason: "Because it is not something to be performed" (*ananuṣṭheyatvāt*). For performance (*anuṣṭhāna*) is indeed the ritual application (*prayoga*); that injunction (*vidhi*) would either cause the performer to engage in the activity of performance, or it would direct the causal factor (*kāraka*) through its penetration into that activity. However, sequence (*krama*) is neither an activity nor a causal factor for an activity, because it is obtained through the accumulation of the performance of those activities and their causal factors. [Objection: In that case, the injunction for the eleven *prayāja* offerings...

Regarding the number eleven, which is constant: this too is obtainable only through the accumulation resulting from the performance of constituent elements (padārtha) in their proper sequence; thus, it is neither an action (vyāpāra) nor a causal factor (kāraka). Here, the number eleven is not enjoined with respect to the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, but rather their repetition (*abhyāsa*), which is characterized by them. And that repetition is indeed a repeated action. Nor [is it enjoined] with respect to the full moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*).

The injunction regarding performance (*prayoga-vidhi*) prescribes the performance (*prayoga*) that is to be executed; however, at that time, the injunction "what is the ritual act? does not have the object of execution within its scope, and this sequence—whether belonging to the third [book] or the fifth—is not something to be executed. Therefore, it is not an object of the injunction regarding performance.
The author of the *Nibandhana* states the reason: "because it is not the meaning of the word" (*aśabdārthatvāt*). This is the underlying intention here: although...

An injunction has as its object the meaning of the verbal root; nevertheless, it does not directly impel the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) toward the external object of the cow, but rather toward itself. And this very quality of impelling toward itself consists in the cognition of that [injunction] in its indirect form. It is precisely the possession of that cognition by the person that constitutes his status as one to be enjoined. Furthermore, that injunction is of the nature of a task (*kārya*).

When the meaning of an action (bhāvārtha) is being understood, it is connected with every purpose—such as the action itself, substance, quality, number, sequence, and so forth—and thus, while being a purpose itself, it is denoted by its own word. Furthermore, words that denote actions and the like express their own meanings only as they have entered into service for that [purpose]. This is what is called "apprehension by the grasper" (grāhakagrahaṇa). And therefore...

Because it cannot be defined as "this" apart from the successive items themselves; for it is the objects (padārtha) that are performed in succession, but not the succession itself, nor the injunction of application (viniyoga-vidhi), nor the injunction of origin (utpatti-vidhi). For this very reason, it is not the injunction of qualification (adhikāra-vidhi).

Even while impelling [the agent], this injunction (vidhi), failing to achieve its own establishment without those [factors such as the bhāvārtha], implies all of them; for, since it lacks self-establishment without them, its status as something to be accomplished (sādhya) would otherwise be untenable. This is precisely what constitutes their being the objects of the injunction. As it has been said in that very [text]: "That which is employed for the sake of accomplishing that [injunction] is what is enjoined."

Regarding the term "hāra" (conveying): that very thing must be brought forward by that [injunction] for its own establishment, which, for the sake of establishing that, has been made subservient to this purpose by the injunction; and that which has been made subservient is what is mentioned in proximity to it.
In this regard, in the proximity of an applicatory injunction (*adhikāravidhi*) such as "The first draught belongs to the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer," there is that which is presented by its own word.

Let it be that sequence (*krama*), being a real entity (*padārtha*), is the object of injunction (*vidheya*) according to the third book [of the *Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtra*]. But how can that which belongs to the fifth book—being not the direct meaning of the word (*aśabdārtha*) such as "having initiated the householder" (*gṛhapatiṃ dīkṣayitvā*) and so forth—be employed for the sake of accomplishing that [sequence], since it lacks the purpose of serving that end?
Nor does the verbal suffix *-ktvā* in "having initiated" (*dīkṣayitvā*) express anteriority in time, as in the case of "having opened his mouth, he sleeps" (*mukhaṃ vyādāya svapiti*).

Because there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) in this case; for the opening of the mouth occurs only at times other than sleep, and one cannot explain it by intending those moments subsequent to the opening of the mouth while asleep, since the relationship between word and meaning is determined by worldly convention. For even during the moments preceding the opening of the mouth, the mouth [remains open] for those who are asleep.

Even when one cries out while beating one's breast, saying "he sleeps with his mouth open," the usage [of the suffix] does not cease; thus, having the same agent (*samānakartṛkatā*) is the invariable meaning of the suffix *-ktvā*. Furthermore, regarding a verbal root that expresses an action having the same agent, worldly speakers employ the suffix *-ktvā* only in that case where [the action] is used first. For example:

Since the application [of a word] is for the purpose of conveying meaning, and the performance [of an action] follows that very understanding, how can there be the conceit that the temporal sequence is the intended meaning of the word?
This sequence is not the literal meaning of the word; thus, it is correct to say that it is "not to be enjoined" because it is not something to be performed.

Granted that sequence itself may not be something to be performed (*anuṣṭheya*) independently like an action; nevertheless, it will exist as that which delimits what is to be performed. For instance, actions are delimited by a sequence;

therefore, since it serves as their delimiter, sequence will be performed just like unity and so forth. To this, he says: "Apart from that which possesses sequence, [it cannot be grasped] as a specific 'this-ness' (*idantayā*)."
Because it cannot be determined. That which delimits what is to be performed is itself what is to be performed; and that which is enjoined is what must be performed.

Since it is the constituent elements (padārthas) that are enjoined, and not their aggregate nor the sequence which delimits that aggregate, the meaning is that one does not perform the constituent elements by relying upon the sequence. Nor can the sequence itself be performed independently; thus he says:

For it is the ritual acts (*padārtha*) that are performed in sequence, not the sequence itself. The plural number in the word *padārthāḥ* indicates that sequence rests upon a collection (*samudāya*) which is a single entity inhering in a plurality [of acts]. Consequently, since sequence is neither to be performed *per se* nor as part of anything else, it is established that sequence is not within the scope of the injunction of performance (*prayogavidhi*).
But surely the injunction of performance (*prayogavidhi*), the injunction of origin (*utpattividhi*), or the injunction of application (*niyogavidhi*) would not prescribe [the order],

because there is no person to be enjoined (*aniyojyatva*). And while such an injunction might exist regarding the order of the Vedic text (*śrauta*), which is its specific object, it could not apply to the meaning (*artha*) and so forth.

[Objection: That [the injunction] would apply to something else is impossible. [Reply: It is said: it has been stated that the meaning of an injunction is performance (*prayoga*). And a difference in sequence is a specific kind of performance.
For instance, it is said that "the ritual elements (*padārtha*) are performed in a sequence. [Objection:

This [sequence] does not fall within the scope of performance, because [the injunction] is concerned with the essential nature of the relationship [between the act and its result]. To this he says: "Nor..."

The phrase "the object of either the application injunction (viniyoga-vidhi) or the origin injunction (utpatti-vidhi)" is to be supplied [to the question]. Why? Precisely because it is not to be performed [independently]. This is the intended meaning: this entire injunction is fourfold in form; however, it has been stated that its designation differs according to whether it is directed toward that [specific aspect] or another. Therefore, even in the cases of the origin and application [injunctions], they are pervaded by the performance (prayoga).

And because there is an absence of application in the sequence [of the stages], by the exclusion of the pervader (*vyāpaka*), there is the exclusion of the two pervaded factors (*vyāpya*), namely arising and cessation.

Now, why is it not the case that this is the subject matter (*viṣaya*) of the qualification (*adhikāra*)? To this he says: "Not of the injunction of qualification. Here too, the word "subject matter" is supplied from the context. Why? Because of the lack of a person to be enjoined (*aniyojyatva*). Mā...

Furthermore, an injunction regarding entitlement (*adhikāravidhi*), which has as its domain that which is to be performed (*anuṣṭheya*), does not have the sequence as its object; moreover, the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) must be conscious, and it is quite absurd to claim that a sequence possesses consciousness. Nor can it be the occasioning cause (*nimitta*), because it is not established prior to the performance. Therefore, because it is not something to be performed, because it is not a constituent element of the ritual action (*apadārtha*), and because it is not a person to be enjoined, it is not the object of an injunction.

Regarding the word "sequence" (*krama*): [The opponent objects,] "But the reason—that it is not the meaning of a word—is unestablished (*asiddha*), because sequence is the meaning of the suffix *-ktvā* in the word *dīkṣayitvā* (having initiated). And thus, there would be an injunction intended for that [sequence]. To this he says: "And while there might be an injunction intended for a restriction of sequence based on what is heard (*śruta*), such an injunction intended for that [sequence] is impossible in the case of [the meanings of] words and so forth. This is the meaning.

It has been stated that priority [of one action over another] is not the meaning of the suffix -ktvā because of its deviation [from the rule]; thus, the reason "because it is not the meaning of a word" (*apadārthatvāt*) is not unestablished (*asiddha*). Even granting [the opponent's position], it is said: since the temporal sequence (*krama*) derived from the fifth case-ending is a qualification of the substratum (*dharmin*) distinct from what is directly expressed by the words (*śrauta*), the reason "because it is not the meaning of a word" is not partially unestablished (*bhāgāsiddha*). This applies to cases such as those involving purpose (*artha*) and so forth.
"Because it pervades the sequence. Having thus raised an objection, he provides the resolution: "It is said: the application (prayoga) has the sense of an injunction (vidhi).
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "And the distinction of sequence is a specific mode of application (prayogaviśeṣa). This is the meaning: for by means of a sequence...

The application (*prayoga*) is specified; it is distinguished from other applications. For instance, those very same word-meanings, when employed in a different sequence, produce a cognition of a difference in the sequence of application, just as phonemes (*varṇa*), despite their identity, produce a cognition of distinct words such as *gave*, *vega*, *nadī*, *dīna*, *ajara*, and *rāja*. Otherwise, there would be no difference in the cognition of the meaning.
"But if there were no difference in the causes, it would follow that the difference in the effects is accidental.

Now, it has been stated that individual constituent elements (*padārtha*) are enjoined, not their collection; for that collection is accomplished through the performance of the constituent elements. And since sequence depends upon that [collection], it does not apply to each constituent element individually, because it cannot be determined within them. Therefore, it concerns the constituent elements...

An injunction does not have sequence as its object. Nor is this the meaning of the word, such that it would be something to be enjoined by virtue of being employed for the sake of accomplishing that [action], through the implication of its being for the purpose of the task; therefore, he says: "For instance, by means of sequence...

It is said that "the ritual elements (padārthas) are performed. This is the underlying intention here: as for the claim that "sequence is not a property residing in the ritual elements, because it cannot be defined in each one of them individually," that is incorrect. For we observe that conjunction, disjunction, number such as duality, and so forth—though not definable in each individual instance—are nonetheless properties residing in the ritual elements.

Now, [the opponent argues] that it is because [the universal] is not perceived. That is incorrect; for, like conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and so forth, it is perceived as residing in the objects [it qualifies]. To explain: conjunction and the like, while depending on two distinct objects, are not determined in only one of them, nor do they depend on a collection [of those objects]. Furthermore, for you [the opponent], there is neither the cognition nor the designation "the collection is conjoined."

Rather, it is either "this is conjoined with that" or "these two are conjoined. However, conjunction and the like possess a co-inherence (*samavāya*) within a single composite object (*samudāya*). Furthermore, sequence—which is synonymous with priority and posteriority—possesses a specific basis in each individual entity even more so than those [conjunctions]. Nevertheless, its definition depends solely upon the cognition of a second entity.

The sequence is equivalent to its conjunctions and so forth; therefore, it exists as that very form as a secondary function (*dvitīyavṛtti*) characterized by priority and posteriority, or else it functions as a property of individual entities alone. In either case, it functions only as a property of individual entities and not as a property of a collection, because it is perceived in that way. Indeed, there is no such thing as "the collection of actions is prior" or "the collection of actions is posterior."

Alternatively, one action is "prior" in relation to another action, and another action is "subsequent" in relation to that [first]; or rather, priority and posteriority themselves are defined by the objects possessing limits (avadhimat), and their extension is sequence (*krama*). Since this is perceived in the case of sound, actions, and so forth, it is accepted as being dependent upon them. Therefore, although [sequence] exists in each individual object—
The injunction is specific to each individual act, even though it relies upon the injunction of performance (*prayogavidhi*).

Furthermore, since simultaneous performance is impossible, if that [injunction] were to prescribe the performance of all [acts] together, it would result in a loss of authority—like the instruction to adorn oneself with the jewel from the crest of the serpent Takṣaka as a remedy for fever. Therefore, by the phrase "as far as one is able," the various distinctions of sequence brought forward are combined into a single set of constituent elements (*padārtha*).

It prescribes the difference in performance and also prescribes the sequence; indeed, if this [sequence] were not prescribed, it would be impossible to prescribe the performance of the constituent elements as qualified by that [sequence].
As for the view that "precisely because it is required by the injunction, it is therefore not itself enjoined," [that is incorrect].
It will be explained [later]. For there is no restrictive rule that whatever is required by an injunction must itself be enjoined.

Since the qualification (*adhikāra*) is also something to be established, it is the agent alone who is enjoined for the sake of its accomplishment. However, because a distinction in sequence is required, and because the injunctions, the cognizer, and this [sequence] are perceived while nothing else is perceived, [the sequence is established] based on perception.
And because it is performed [only] after [the injunction has been understood], the injunction is respected by those who act with foresight.

To this, it is replied: What, then, do you consider to be that which is to be enjoined (*vidheya*) which is not present here? Has it not been stated that it is "that which is undertaken for the sake of accomplishing the sacrifice"? What does this "for the sake of accomplishing that" mean?

If that [sequence] were the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), then how could there be plurality for that which is unitary? For it is not a causal factor (*kāraka*). If it is argued that it is so because it delimits the causal factor, then sequence too is exactly like that, insofar as it delimits the object to be performed, and the object to be performed is a causal factor. Furthermore, it has already been stated that this [sequence] does not depend upon a collection (*samudāya*). Now, if it is not...
"For the sake of its accomplishment" means that the instrument (kāraka) for that purpose is what is to be enjoined; however, that which has attained the status of being for that purpose is twofold:
by way of application (viniyoga) and by way of procurement (upādāna). Application is derived from the third [book], while procurement is derived from the fourth.

However, regarding oneness (*ekatva*) and the like, both types of subsidiarity (*śeṣatva*) belong to the word-meaning; yet it has been stated that sequence (*krama*), which is derived from the fifth [case-ending], is not the word-meaning. If one asks, "In that case, does 'one should sacrifice with the Viśvajit' (*viśvajitā yajeta*) also lack the status of being a word-meaning?"—then, in the case of "having initiated" (*dīkṣayitvā*) as well, how could even the state of prior time (*pūrvakālatā*), though denoted, be somehow considered the word-meaning?

The Vedic sequence (*śrauta-krama*) is specifically enjoined because it is employed for the sake of accomplishing that [result]. Furthermore, what is the reason for the claim that only that which is directly expressed by the words is employed for the sake of accomplishing that? If you say it is because its subservience to that purpose is understood [from the text], we say no; for how could the word that expresses it make known its subservience to that purpose?

Or is it a word that denotes an object to be performed (*anuṣṭheya*)? The first alternative is not tenable; for it has already been stated that being for the sake of something [else] does not follow from the mere presence of direct assertion (*śruti*) and so forth. However, a word denoting an action to be performed expresses its own meaning as connected with whatever purpose happens to be immediately present in the mind, and by means of that purpose, [it conveys its sense].

Since the word—or the act of bringing [the object] near—is useful merely for the purpose of making that [object] present, and since such presence can be achieved through other means such as the object itself, what utility is there in its being conveyed by the word? Therefore, it is not the case that this [order] is non-injunctional simply because it is apprehended through another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), for the word alone, assisted by the object and so forth, possesses authority. Otherwise, for one who maintains that sequence is not denotable...
Furthermore, it would follow that sequence (*krama*) is unfit for investigation by the scripture because it is not characterized by an injunction (*acodanā-lakṣaṇatva*).

As for what is said—that being subject to an injunction (*vidheyatva*) is pervaded by *prayukti* (the motive for performance), and that *prayukti* does not exist in sequence because sequence occurs subsequent to it; for this very reason, this [topic of sequence] is investigated immediately after *prayukti*. Therefore...

It is argued that "the application (prayukti), which pervades the state of being enjoined (dheyatva), by receding in due order, causes the pervaded state of being enjoined to recede as well—just as the perception from afar of a single-stone mountain region excludes the *śiṃśapā* tree [from being that mountain].

This is incorrect, because it is unestablished that [the cognition of the injunction] occurs at a time subsequent to the application; for this person is indeed enjoining the application even as he speaks.

The procedure for performance (*prayogavidhi*) prescribes everything that cannot otherwise be established through the connection with the performance, provided it has not been obtained from another source; and since *krama* (sequence) is of such a nature and is delivered by direct statement (*śruti*) and other means, how could it be subsequent to the performance? Therefore, the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) is unestablished (*asiddha*). Nor [is it unestablished] in its own form in the fourth [chapter].

The application [of the mantra] has been examined; rather, it was stated that [the determination of the application] is by means of the number of the items being employed. That cognition is the cause for understanding the restriction regarding the difference in sequence. This is to say: because there would be no ascertainment of the number of the items being employed. Furthermore, the sequence is not understood in the same way as the items themselves; it would be subverted if other items were to intervene. By means of the ascertainment of the sequence...
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of not understanding the limit [of the sequence]. Nor is there a limit in the sequences themselves, because that state remains unchanged.

Therefore, this investigation into the sequence does not occur after the performance [of the ritual], but rather after the determination of its limit; for it has that as its cause. Consequently, the sequence—which is subordinate to it—must be enjoined as resting upon the objects being employed.
This is now [addressed]. This has already been stated: for it is said that the constituent elements (*padārtha*) are performed in a sequence.

Although [the order] is not something to be performed in its own nature (*svarūpeṇa*), nor is it directly expressed by words (*aśabdopātta*), the meaning is that it is to be enjoined (*vidheya*) in the injunction of those [elements] because it serves as their delimiting factor (*avacchedakatayā*). And how even such a thing can be an object of injunction has been demonstrated.
"From below"—though we were afraid of this great extent, we have nonetheless fallen into it. Therefore, let this matter rest for now.

And thus, because it is an object of the injunction regarding performance (*prayoga-vidhi*), sequence (*krama*) does not transcend the character of being defined by scriptural injunction (*codanā-lakṣaṇatva*). In that regard, first considering that sequence—being unascertainable as a specific "this" apart from the constituent parts—is neither something to be performed, nor something to be applied, nor something to be produced, one might doubt its status as an object of injunction; however, it is indeed an object of the injunction regarding performance.

[The objection] has been shown. However, by the subsequent section, the purification of the example is accomplished because of the attainment of the category of *dīkṣā*. And thus, he says that what was challenged—the fact that [the sacrifice] is not characterized by an injunction (*codanālakṣaṇatva*) because it falls outside the scope of the fourfold operation of injunction—is refuted by demonstrating that it is indeed the object of the operation of the performance-injunction (*prayogavidhi*): "And thus, the performance..."

The sequence continues: because it is not an object of an injunction (*vidhi*), it does not possess the characteristic of being defined by a scriptural mandate (*codanā-lakṣaṇatva*). Having thus purified the object of knowledge (*prameya*), he demonstrates the nature of the inquiry: therein, first, considering that [the Self] cannot be employed, cannot be applied, and cannot be produced—because it is not determined as "this" through a sequential process—he raises the doubt regarding its being an object of an injunction.

The status of being the object of the injunction for application (*prayogavidhi*) has been shown; the connection is that it was "shown first. This [point] regarding the objection and its refutation has already been explained. He states another interpretation (*varṇaka*), beginning with "by the subsequent interpretation" and ending with "has been done. And here, the subsequent...
The purification of the examples has been accomplished by means of this commentary; thus, the purpose of the treatise is established through its beginning, middle, and end.
An example therein is as follows:
"Those who are the sacrificers in a sacrificial session (sattra) are themselves the officiating priests (ṛtvij)"—so it is recorded in the sacred tradition (āmnāya).

Having initiated the Gṛhapati, the Adhvaryu initiates the Brahman; then the Udgātṛ; then the Hotṛ; then the Pratiprasthātṛ, having initiated him, initiates the Gāthin, and so forth, ending with "the Hotṛ initiates the Grāvastut for the Brahman, or a religious student sent by his teacher."

In this regard, a doubt arises: is it the initiation (dīkṣā) qualified by each respective ritual item that is enjoined, or is it the sequence? Since the sequence is already implied by the very injunction of the initiation qualified by each respective item, and because no separate [injunction] for the sequence is perceived, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the initiation itself is what is enjoined. To this, he replies: "Since there is no other thing to be enjoined, it is the sequence alone that is enjoined."

Because the act of initiation (*dīkṣā*) is already established as being performed by the sacrificer, and since initiation is obtained for the *gṛhapati* and others through the force of the general rule (*codaka*) itself, it need not be enjoined in the sūtra. Now, one might object that sequence (*krama*) is also not the literal meaning of the word and thus should not be enjoined;
for it has been stated that the suffix *-ktvā* does not express priority in time. To this, he replies:
Because even that which is inexpressible, yet somehow cognized—namely, the performance of a specific sequence—is the meaning of the injunctive suffix (*vidhi*).

This is the point: why is it that the suffix *ktvā* does not have "prior time" as its meaning? If it is argued that this is because we observe its usage even in the absence of such [prior time], then surely, if that were the case, "having the same agent" (*samānakartṛkatva*) would also not be its meaning.

Indeed, it is sufficient [to say] that the suffix occurs after a verbal root even in the absence of a prefix (*upapada*), because we observe its usage in the sense of mere prohibition, as in *khalūktvā* and *alaṃ bhuktvā*. If it were argued: "We do not claim that a word lacks meaning simply because of such deviation;
let there be no pointlessness for multi-meaning words like *akṣa* and so on, but rather, the meaning of a word is that which cannot be obtained through any other means."

It has been stated that duration (*sthiti*) is obtained through the condition of usage (*prayogopādhi*) and consists in the sequence of prior and posterior time. This being the case, however, the requirement of a common agent (*samānakartṛkatā*) is not [required], for even that [requirement] deviates from the meaning of the suffix *-ktvā*. What, then, is the condition of usage?
Even when there is a common agent, the suffix *-ktvā* occurs only with respect to that verbal root whose meaning is employed first.

Even though it is inexpressible, since the meaning of the injunction is that the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) must be performed according to a specific sequence, there is no purpose in prescribing a particular agent (*kartṛ*) in relation to the *adhvaryu*. Furthermore, because there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) from enjoining multiple matters simultaneously.

However, because the ritual element of initiation (*dīkṣā*) is repeated for each primary offering (*pradhāna*), there is a single purpose for the injunction regarding the specific performance; thus, when that is enjoined, it applies to worldly [actions] and not elsewhere. True, this would indeed be the case if the restriction of performance were established, but such is not the case.
For that [restriction] must be understood either from grammatical exposition (*anvākhyāna*) or from common worldly usage (*loka*). It cannot first be derived from the suffix *-ktvā*.

There is no grammatical explanation by anyone that [the gerund] must necessarily follow the verb; nor does common usage employ only that which ends in *ktvā* as the prior member. For we observe the use of words ending in *ktvā* even after verbs in the works of poets, sages, and the Vedic tradition. Therefore, because it cannot be established otherwise, just like the requirement of a common agent (*samānakartṛkatā*), the priority [of the action]— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The full argument would conclude that priority is not an inherent property of the gerund itself, but rather a result of the speaker's intention to express a sequence of actions.]
The ultimate truth is that priority of time (*kālatā*) is for the sake of that [action].

Let it be so; even if it is not directly denotable, since it is somehow perceived, and because there is no other thing to be enjoined, that very priority must indeed be enjoined. And thus, this priority of time for the suffix *ktvā* would be as useless as the teeth of a crow.
[This is] the consideration of the designation.

Now, it might be argued: "Let the initiation (dīkṣā) not be enjoined; however, since it is obtained through the general rule (codaka), the specific agents such as the Adhvaryu and others will be enjoined in relation to it. What, then, is the purpose of an injunction regarding sequence? To this, he says:

Because the connection with the *adhvaryu* would be redundant in an injunction regarding a specific agent; for in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the initiation (*dīkṣā*) is understood as belonging to the *adhvaryu*, so what is the purpose of an injunction here connecting it to the *adhvaryu*? It is because that [connection] is already established. Furthermore, because there would be a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*) from the injunction of multiple things: "The *adhvaryu* [initiates] the *gṛhapati*, the *adhvaryu* the *brahmān*, the *adhvaryu* the *hotṛ*," and so on—[all these] are many.

"...lest the sentence be split in the injunction of those [individual] objects. Now, one might ask: even so, why is there no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) when the initiation (*dīkṣā*) is repeated for each object? To this he says: "But because the act of initiation (*dīkṣā*) is repeated with each principal element (*pradhāna*).
For me, the co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) with the word "initiation" is what is being enjoined. Indeed, initiation is a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). That...

"Because it is a subordinate element (*guṇatva*), it recurs for each sacrificer"—this is the meaning established by logic. Thus, he states that there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) in the injunction of the sequence, because there is a single purpose: "because the injunction of the specific performance has a single purpose.
That by which the performance is specified is the "specific performance," namely, the sequence. This is the view of the Teacher who speaks thus.

"Sequence is intended to reside in multiple entities, just like conjunction and so forth. Someone says: "There is no restriction regarding the injunction for the Adhvaryu priest. Some explain its meaning as follows:
for here—

Because of the injunction that "those who are the sacrificers are the officiating priests" (*ye yajamānāste ṛtvijaḥ*), the officiating priests are excluded from their priestly functions by the prescription that the sacrificer performs them; thus, it is the sacrificers themselves who, by performing the respective duties of those priests, acquire the designation "officiating priest," but there are no actual Adhvaryus and so forth present here in reality. Therefore, by whichever [sacrificer], wherever, and whenever...

The office of the *adhvaryu* performed by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*)—who, by virtue of that act, assumes the designation of *adhvaryu*—must not perform another subordinate *adhvaryu*-function, because of the prohibition: "One who is already purified does not purify. As for the other [functions], they are performed by someone else, since there must be a distinction among them.

Thus, there is no cause for restriction whatsoever. Therefore, by this statement, it is restricted that the initiation (*dīkṣā*) performed by the *adhvaryu* priest belongs to the *gṛhapati*, and he alone performs the initiations of the *brahmā* and others. In the same way, the restriction regarding the *pratipat* and other elements [of the ritual] also follows; thus, there is no lack of further things to be enjoined. This must be considered: how is it that there is no cause for restriction?
Now, if there is no regulating authority (*niyāmaka*) here, then even Brahmā and the others would be indeterminate. For instance:

he who is Brahmā by virtue of performing the functions of Brahmā becomes a Hotṛ, Neṣṭṛ, and so forth, by virtue of performing the functions of the Hotṛ, Neṣṭṛ, and so forth. Likewise, a Hotṛ and the rest become Brahmā, Neṣṭṛ, and so forth, by virtue of performing the functions of Brahmā, Neṣṭṛ, and so forth. The same applies to the Neṣṭṛ and the others.

Since there would be no fixed rule regarding those who are enjoined and the objects of the injunction—such as the *brahman* priest being the *iṣṭṛ* and so forth, and Brahmā himself being the *adhvaryu* and so forth—upon what basis could the injunction be postulated? Indeed, by the rule for the initiation (*dīkṣā*) of the *adhvaryu*, other priests such as the *iṣṭṛ* and others must be excluded from the *brahman* and other roles. In that case, regarding the initiation of the *brahman* and others, [what would be the status of] those who are to be excluded?
Because there is no fixed restriction regarding the *neṣṭṛ* and others, as well as the *adhvaryu* who is the object of the injunction, it is impossible to distinguish them through confusion;

nor is it possible [to distinguish] the threshing of rice by means of confusion with such acts as piercing with a pointed instrument or tearing with the nails, as expressed in the rule "one threshes the rice."

A restrictive rule (niyama) is thus postulated. Therefore, whatever portion of the ritual action a sacrificer has first commenced, that entire portion must be completed by that very sacrificer alone; it should not be accepted as being performed by another sacrificer acting as a priest, because such lack of restriction would lead to the undesirable consequence of inconsistency. This follows from the force of the context (*prakaraṇa*).

For the grammarians (śābdāḥ) maintain that even propriety (*aucitya*) is a means for determining the meaning of a sentence. Therefore, since propriety itself is the cause of restriction, it need not be prescribed by rule; this [objection] is so gross that it was not refuted by the Teacher.

However, others think as follows: since the consecration (*dīkṣā*) belongs to the Adhvaryu, and because the Adhvaryu is already established for the Gṛhapati and others through the general rule of consecration, the specific injunction regarding the Gṛhapati and others serves as an exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) of him from those other roles.

And the statement of a restrictive rule (*niyama*) regarding that very exclusion is made figuratively (*bhaktyā*), based on the similarity of excluding others. This is what they mean by "figurative application" (*bhakti*).

To refute that, he says: "Because of the prohibition, 'one who is not purified does not purify. Since a positive injunction is possible there, the threefold fault of *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification) is set aside; thus, rather than stating that, the contradiction with the scriptural statement is shown, because since the initiation of the Adhvaryu is prescribed immediately after the initiation of the Hotṛ, how could the initiated Adhvaryu—who is himself purified—[purify] the Adhvaryu and the others?

"He should purify" means "he should initiate. Therefore, a restrictive enumeration (*parisaṃkhyā*) that has prohibition as its result is untenable in the case of a prohibition, because there would be no purpose for it;

this is the meaning. Nor is it the case that the Pratiprasthātṛ is not already established in the initiation of the Adhvaryu, such that the statement "the Pratiprasthātṛ [should initiate] him" would be enjoining the Pratiprasthātṛ; for another [priest], namely the Pratiprasthātṛ, initiates the other, namely the Adhvaryu.

It causes [the other] to perform [the rite] even without a verbal injunction. For in the archetypal (*prakṛti*) ritual action, the Adhvaryu’s assistants—the Pratiprasthātṛ and others—are indeed prescribed. When, however, the Adhvaryu is incapable due to being occupied with another task or because of the impossibility of performing the action upon himself, then his duties are performed by those assistants, such as the Pratiprasthātṛ.

It is established that [the deities] such as Dayā perform [this]. Therefore, since it is a contradiction for an agent to act upon itself, he is unable to initiate himself; thus, he must be initiated by his own *puruṣa*. And his own *puruṣa* is his...

Because a non-Brahmin lacks the qualification for the office of officiating priest (*ārtvijya*), and because those in the subsequent stages of life (*uttarāśramin*)—as well as the student (*brahmacārin*)—are dependent upon their teacher (*ācārya-paratantra*). Furthermore, although the injunction regarding the ritual materials (*arthādi*) pertains to the constituent elements of the action, nevertheless, since the Pratiprasthātṛ is already established by virtue of requiring that specific form and purpose, he need not be enjoined [again]. Now, it may be argued that there are many men belonging to the Adhvaryu class.
He says: "Because there will be an injunction for the Pratiprasthātṛ among them, therefore there would be a distinction.

Among those men belonging to the Adhvaryu, "yato" means "of whom"—the suffix *tasi* is used here in the sense of all case-endings (*sārvavibhaktika*). There would be a distinction characterized by being more proximate (*antaraṅga*), and that other person purifies [the offering] in the office of the Adhvaryu (*ādhvaryave*).

Indeed, since there exist many other officiants, such as the Pratiprasthātṛ and others, who are prescribed for that ritual action when [the Adhvaryu] lacks the capacity, and they are arranged in a progressively more external order, it follows that the first among them—the Pratiprasthātṛ—is internal (antaraṅga). Therefore, the restriction [that he must perform it] need not be enjoined, because it is already established; this is the meaning. Now, one might object: "But in the case of the Unnetṛ’s initiation, since the Adhvaryu and the others have already been purified, [the Unnetṛ would be] unavailable..."

Since the status of being a *kāśa* would entail the contingency of applying [the rule] to any person whatsoever, it is specified that "a Brāhmaṇa" is the one so enjoined; therefore, he says: because the office of officiating at a sacrifice (*ārṭvijya*) does not belong to a non-Brāhmaṇa. The meaning is: since officiating at sacrifices is prescribed as the unique duty of a Brāhmaṇa alone, how could it apply elsewhere? Furthermore, once a Brāhmaṇa is established, since there is no distinction among the four stages of life (*cāturāśramya*), by the Brāhmaṇa...

Since the term "fellow-student" (*saha-brahmacārin*) is subject to ambiguity, this statement is made for the purpose of excluding monks (*bhikṣu*), forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*), and others; hence he says:
"And of those in the higher stages of life. The phrase "due to the absence of officiating at sacrifices" (*ārtvijyābhāvāt*) is drawn over from the previous context here as well.

Officiating at sacrifices is not for the sake of livelihood, because that mode of subsistence is prohibited for monks and forest-dwellers. Nor is it for the sake of bestowing favor, [as they have no dependents].

The phrase "one who does not undertake [acts of] injury or favor" means that acts of favor are prohibited; nor is the expression "sent by the teacher" intended to prohibit the student's independent engagement in activity, for his [independence] is already established by another scriptural injunction.

He states that there is dependence on the teacher (*ācārya-pāratantrya*), because the religious student (*brahmacārin*) is dependent upon his teacher. Therefore, for these reasons, since there is no other thing to be enjoined and since the sequence (*krama*) is worthy of being enjoined, the purpose of the injunction regarding the sequence is established by the subsequent explanatory section (*uttara-varṇaka*).
The construction of the text is such that the purity of the illustration has been established, as in the example: "One kills the leopard for its skin.
Now, he states the necessity of the sequence characterized by the meaning, beginning with the words "In matters of meaning," etc., as required.
[This is] the end [of the section]. Here is an example: "He offers the Agnihotra; he cooks the gruel.
In this regard, there is a doubt: is the sequence of the offering and the cooking unrestricted, or is the offering to follow immediately after the cooking? Regarding this:

Since both injunctions are intent solely upon enjoining the mere ritual acts of offering (homa) and cooking (pāka), and as before there is an absence of direct scriptural statement (śruti), and since the two actions— the offering in the form of *yavāgū* and the act of cooking for that purpose—
fall within the scope of the objects of knowledge (*prameya*), they lack the authority to determine a fixed order; furthermore,
because the offering can be accomplished even with other substances, there is no evidence for a rule of sequence, and thus there is no restriction.

To this, he says: although the injunction regarding the materials and so forth is primarily concerned with the meaning of the words (*padārtha*), it nevertheless depends upon the purpose consisting of that very form [of the action].
The connection with what follows is: "The specific performance (*anuṣṭhāna*) establishes the sequence. This is the meaning:

although there is no direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) regarding a specific sequence, nevertheless, the injunction for the oblation (*homa-vidhi*) must enjoin an oblation that is not yet fully characterized.

The efficient agent requires a substance that possesses that specific form—as in "he cooks gruel. Since it is illogical to enjoin the act of cooking as a subordinate factor with respect to gruel for no purpose, the gruel stands in need of a purpose. And thus, fire...

Furthermore, there is an expectation for the purpose of the rule regarding the order of recitation as established by the injunction for Vedic study (*svādhyāya-vidhi*); and once that order is known, the meaning "one performs the *agnihotra* with rice-gruel (*yavāgū*), and that [gruel] by means of cooking" becomes established. Nor can rice-gruel that is not yet prepared serve for the *agnihotra*; thus, even an injunction focused on the ritual act (*padārtha*) depends upon the purpose consisting of the nature of that act.

That is to say, it is a collaborator with the object (*arthasahakārī*) insofar as it makes known a specific sequence of priority and posteriority, yet its validity (*prāmāṇya*) is not necessarily established [by that alone].

For even the object of cognition (*prameya*) is seen to possess validity; as the authorities on epistemology have said: "The scale, though itself an object of cognition, possesses validity. Therefore, it is established that the sequence pertaining to the object (*ārtha*) must also be enjoined.

Regarding the phrase "in the case of meaning and so forth," he states that the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*), which was indicated by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) and follows in sequence, is what must be observed:
"In the case of Vedic study (*svādhyāya*). An example here is: "He offers to the *samidhs*, he offers to *tanūnapāt*," and so on.

In this regard, there is a doubt: should these *samit* and other [subsidiary rites] be performed according to a fixed order, or according to the order of the textual recitation (*pāṭhakrama*)? Since there is an absence of direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) or logical purpose (*artha*), and since the order of recitation is already established as applicable by virtue of its being an unavoidable and inherent factor, the *samit* and others should be performed without a fixed order, as the [recitation] does not serve as a restrictive factor.
To this, he says: "And it depends on the purpose of the restriction regarding the order of recitation as established by the injunction for Vedic study.
The connection with what follows is: "The injunction establishes a specific mode of performance. By the injunction for Vedic study...

Indeed, since these sentences have been presented in a specific sequence, it is not appropriate to accept their inclusion merely because the order is unavoidable when a purpose for that sequence is possible. And a purpose does exist: namely, the restriction of the specific order of the *samidh* and other offerings as required by the injunction regarding performance (*prayogavidhi*). Nor is the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*) incapable of serving this function here.

For instance—the sentences are recited in a sequence, and by that very [sequence], their meanings, though previously unperceived, are also revealed; because the sequence of the effect conforms to the sequence of the cause, and because the cognition of those meanings is produced by the cognition of the sentences, and because wise people perform actions according to their understanding. Therefore, this is the order of recitation.
Even by means of the rule for private recitation (*svādhyāya-vidhi*), [the order] is set aside because it lacks a purpose and that [purpose] is impossible;

therefore, let it be established as having its purpose defined by the rule of application (*prayoga-vidhi*) regarding the regulation of the sequence of the *samit* and other [subsidiary rites]. Thus, the establishment of the sequence is achieved through the sequence of the rule of application, which conforms to the sequence of the text. However, in cases involving multiple distinct qualifications (*adhikāra*), there is a difference in sequence.
Even when [the texts] have been recited, since there is no inclusion within a single injunctive statement (*prayoga-vacana*), no sequential order is possible among those that are unconnected;
thus, even the requirement for a purpose (*prayojanākāṅkṣā*) produced by the injunction for Vedic study (*svādhyāya-vidhi*) vanishes due to the impossibility of such a [sequential] application.
However, the purpose of the restriction regarding the order of recitation—which is made known by the injunction for Vedic study—is the literal meaning (*akṣarārtha*) itself.

And there is the injunction for the performance contingent upon that. By means of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), he states that the restriction of the order of performance is indeed what is to be enjoined: "It is already known," etc. In the Vājapeya sacrifice, one immolates seventeen animals dedicated to Prajāpati.

Thus it is heard. In that context, these seventeen constituent parts are subsidiaries of the Vājapeya sacrifice; they are established by the injunction for the performance of the Vājapeya as being performed together, and they are also obtained through the rules of extension (*codaka*). It has been determined that the ritual properties (*dharma*), such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and so forth, which belong to these [subsidiaries], must likewise be performed together with their substrates (*dharmī*) and not one by one; rather, they are to be completed in their entirety all at once.
Being thus obstructed,
and not subverting the understanding of concomitance already attained by itself, it establishes a specific performance;
therein, because there is no authoritative means of knowledge for a restrictive rule (*niyama*), the first ritual act should be performed upon any animal whatsoever.

Success! Regarding the second and subsequent items, there is a doubt: should these be employed according to the fixed order of words from the first item, or according to the sequence of the first item? In this regard, since performance is preceded by cognition, and at the time of comprehension, just as there is the performance of the first item, so too is there the performance of the second and subsequent items.

Since the sequence depends on the rules of order, just as with the first [action], the second and subsequent ones would also have their order of performance dependent upon human will; this being the prima facie view, he says: "The injunction of performance, following a sequence already determined, establishes a specific mode of execution. Why is it followed? To this he says: "And that which is understood by itself, together with..."

"Not completely obstructing the existence [of the subsidiaries]. The word "ca" (and) indicates the reason. For, by the injunction for the performance of the Vājapeya sacrifice, all the constituent elements (*padārtha*) are brought together as being employed toward the binding [of the sacrificial post].
Yet, their simultaneous performance is not possible, because of the connection with the phrase "as far as he may be able. It is such [a sequence] that is resorted to.

To whatever extent that action is strictly obstructed by the injunction, there is no partiality or aversion toward the sprinkling and other rites obtained through the force of the injunction (*codaka*), such that one would bring some of them into proximity or exclude others. Therefore,
observing that the bringing into proximity of all [the rites] is equal, even while setting aside [some], one does not create an interruption.

Considering [the order] as something to be avoided, [the agent], having secured as a cooperative cause the sequence of the first object's performance— which, although external, arises from a cognition whose sequence is dependent on human will— restricts the performance of the second and subsequent objects within the very midst of the ritual application according to that same sequence, in order to ensure equality in proximity to the primary [act]. Otherwise, there would be an inequality among the constituent elements (dharmas).

There would be an excessively long interval between the performances. To explain: from the very moment the first ritual item is performed, if the second and subsequent items are then performed, there would be an interval of sixteen moments (paramāṇus) between the performance of the second and subsequent items and the quality associated with the object of the activity of the first item.

Because it is unavoidable, the injunction regarding the performance (*prayogavidhi*) indeed permits [this]. However, starting from the seventeenth animal and proceeding in reverse order through the second and subsequent ritual items (*padārtha*), there would be an interval of twenty-two [steps]. This same discrepancy should be observed in other cases as well. And since the injunction regarding the performance is equal in all instances, it does not permit that [irregularity].

Since the primary factor—the coexistence already understood by oneself—is not absolutely sublated by mere proximity; otherwise, there would be sublation due to inconsistency. Therefore, it is established that the injunction of performance (prayogavidhi) sets forth the sequence (krama), which is a specific form of execution, and thus the sequence of performance is also something to be enjoined.

Another interpretation: In the *Sādyaska* sacrifice, it is heard in the scripture, "One sacrifices the animals together. Since that [sacrifice] is a modification (*vikāra*) of the Soma sacrifice, those three animals are also subordinate members (*aṅga*) of the Soma sacrifice, following the *Agnīṣomīya* and the *Savanīya*.

Since those [offerings] are already established by the force of the water-libation (udaka-prāpta), their simultaneous performance (sahatva) is what is being enjoined as something not previously obtained. And because of that injunction, the original order of recitation (pāṭhakrama) is set aside. Furthermore, their simultaneous occurrence takes place at the time of the Savanīya offerings, and the time for the Savanīyas follows immediately after the ritual encircling (parivyāṇa).
The entire point has been understood from the statement, "having encircled the sacrificial post with the threefold cord.
However, this remains in doubt: are all three animals to be employed at the time of the *savanīya* sacrifice?

Should the *mānasas* be performed without a fixed order, or rather, should the *āgnīṣomīya* and *anubandhya* follow after the *savanīya*? In this regard, since the scripture prescribes the simultaneous performance of all three at the time of the *savanīya*, an order necessarily follows from the requirement to achieve their coexistence. And regarding that order, there is the sequence immediately following the *parivyāṇa*.
In the case of non-restriction (aniyama), however, that [sequence] exists in some instances; thus, there is no absolute sublation (atyantika-bādha).
Therefore, when it is argued that between restriction and non-restriction, non-restriction of sequence is superior here, it is further taught in reply: "It is well-known."

Following the sequence: for at the very time of its production, the sequence of the *savanīya* [offering] is indeed determined to occur immediately after the *parivyāṇa* (encircling), just like its temporal status. That sequence, moreover, cannot be abandoned as long as no powerful subverting factor (*bādhaka*) intervenes, provided it does not fall outside the body of the *savanīya*. But surely, its contradiction with the requirement of simultaneity (*sahabhāva*) is the subverting factor?

Therefore, he says: because their coexistence is prescribed in the place of the *savanīya*, the two animals approach the *savanīya*, but they do not displace the *savanīya* from its own place. Being together with the *savanīya* which possesses its innate position, they establish their own coexistence without contradicting it; they do not, however, cause the *savanīya* to move from its own place. Thus...

Because coexistence is established even through contradiction, since it is precisely those things that coexist which constitute the object of the undertaking. Thus, it is understood: "Sacrifice the animals together. Since this understanding of coexistence derived from the injunction remains uncontradicted and constitutes the object of a single undertaking, it has been stated that the order of position (*sthāna*) also falls within the scope of the injunction.
Likewise, there is another alternative: where two principal acts are enjoined simultaneously, as in "There are two Sarasvatī offerings;
this indeed is a divine pair. In that case, a doubt arises: are the subsidiaries of these two [to be performed] without restriction?

Should they be performed in their own sequence, or according to the sequence of the performance of the primary acts? On this point, since the injunctions for the subsidiaries follow the injunction for the primary, and because that [primary] injunction prescribes two primaries simultaneously—thereby lacking any internal sequence—there is no rule of sequence even for the subsidiaries whose performance is prompted by the injunction for the primary; such is the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa).
Furthermore, it is presented again:
following the established order, whether there is indeed a sequential recitation of the pairs of *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* mantras for Sarasvatī and Sarasvant,
or whether there is no such sequential recitation.

Even in the absence of a specific restrictive rule (*niyama*), when a particular sequence for the primary acts has been ascertained, the injunction of performance (*prayogavidhi*), following that sequence, establishes a specific order of execution for the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) as a restrictive rule of sequence: namely, that whatever primary act is performed first, its subsidiaries must also be performed first.

Now, one might object: since the primary injunction is incapable of fixing the order even for its own two primary elements due to the prescription of each of those two primaries, how much less could it fix the order of their subsidiaries? To this, he says: "And not utterly subverting the concomitance already understood from its own [text]. The intention here is this: this simultaneity belongs to the act of prescription, not...
