Because if the injunction were to teach an execution that is impossible due to incapacity, it would result in the invalidity of the word; for, due to the connection with the phrase "as one may be able," the performance-injunction (prayogavidhi)— which ordains the necessary sequence and the absolute proximity between the two primary acts, as well as the mutual proximity of their respective subsidiaries with those two primaries— extends as far as...
Since an intervention occurs due to the inevitability of non-proximity, one permits only that much intervention and no more;
thus, it is indeed a constituent part of the formal application (*prayoga*). This was considered previously. True; it is the limitation of the number of things to be employed.

The sequence that is not [otherwise] applicable is indeed a specific mode of performance. Therefore, since it is not established by the preceding [topic], this consideration of the specific mode of performance constitutes a distinct purpose for the definition. Furthermore, even a mere husk [of doubt remains]. And according to the sequence of the primary acts and the sequence of the subsidiary acts, there occurs an interval of separation as far as permitted.

If there were no restriction, however, then anything additional would be permitted; yet the injunction regarding performance (*prayogavidhi*) does not tolerate that. Therefore, lest the coexistence already understood from the context be violated, the very injunction of performance—aided by the order of the principal acts (*mukhyakrama*)—is itself the authority for the restriction of the order of subsidiaries.
Thus it is established that even in the absence of a specific rule, the order must be enjoined.

Therefore, he concludes that the objection raised—that because sequence is not within the scope of the fourfold operation, it cannot be characterized by the Vedic injunction (*codanā*)—is refuted by the fact that sequence is a specifier of the performance (*prayoga*): "Therefore, sequence is indeed a subsidiary element of the performance. Now, if sequence is a subsidiary element of the performance, then [it should have been discussed] precisely in the fourth book, which deals with the consideration of performance.

He raises an objection, saying that because it has already been "considered" (*cintita*), it does not necessitate another chapter: "That was considered previously. He replies: "True, what was considered was the consideration of the constituent parts of the performance (*prayoga-aṅga*). Furthermore, the extent of those constituent elements which are to be performed was also considered; however, the sequence (*krama*) is not like that," he says, "it is not [a part of the performance]."
As for the sequence [of the ritual], since it is devoid of independent activity (*avyāpāra*), if it is not something to be employed (*aprayojya*), then what is it?
To this he says: it is simply a particularity of the performance (*prayoga-viśeṣa*). How the performance is qualified by this has already been explained above.

He concludes: therefore, because it was not established by the previous [argument], this [sequence] must be understood as a particularity of the execution (*anuṣṭhāna*). And thus, there is no single definition...

He states "the state of being *ṇatva*" as follows: because there is a distinction between the general application (*prayogagata*) and the specific application (*prayogaviśeṣa*), even though the status of being the object of the injunction of application (*prayogavidhi*) is the same [in both cases], the meaning of the definition (*lakṣaṇārtha*) differs. Otherwise, however, due to the similarity in the determination of the meaning of the injunction (*codanārtha*), the entire treatise (*śāstra*) would constitute a single chapter. Thus, by this [section] beginning with the second and ending with the fifth...

By means of the *Dhyāyavyūha*, which is intent upon defining the constituent parts of the injunction (*vidhi*)—namely, origination (*utpatti*), application (*viniyoga*), performance (*prayoga*), and form (*rūpa*)—it has been established that the ritual action (*karman*), as the object of what is to be done, must be performed with all its auxiliary limbs (*sāṅga*).
Now, it is determined who the agent (*kartṛ*) and the qualified performer (*adhikārī*) of that action is; for qualification (*adhikāra*) is also [a function of] the agent.

In this sixth [chapter], the qualification-portion (*adhikārāṃśa*) of the injunction (*vidhi*)—which consists of the duty whose nature is the accomplishment of meditative concentration—is being determined. Now, one might object: since the agency and ownership of a person desiring heaven are already obtained from the very hearing of the word "desiring heaven" (*svargakāma*), what is there left to be determined here? To this, he says: "one capable of performing all the auxiliary parts... (*sarvāṅgopasaṃhārasamartha*).

The meaning is that even if [the person] is thus incapable, his specific qualification is now being examined. Now, one who has fallen into doubt is worthy of examination; yet here there is no doubt, because the eligibility of a seeker who lacks capacity has been refuted by other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, doubt arises only when there is an unsettled state regarding non-perception; therefore, he says:

Because capacity (*śakti*) is scriptural, it is distinguished by being either scriptural or non-scriptural. This is what is meant: for an agent desiring heaven, the scripture [teaches] that the ritual act is the means to the desired end; since agency would otherwise be impossible without capacity, if the scripture also makes known that capacity, then that [capacity] too must have its knowledge dependent upon the scripture.

In the sixth [chapter], however, the aspect of qualification (*adhikārāṃśa*) is examined. This is because capacity—whether one is capable of performing all the constituent parts (*sarvāṅgopasaṃhāra*) or not—is determined by whether it is scriptural (*śāstrīya*) or non-scriptural (*aśāstrīya*). In that regard, just as it is required...

The state of being a means (*sādhanatva*) is the cause for engagement, and nothing else; the same applies to feasibility (*śakyatva*). Feasibility, too, enters into the form of the injunction (*vidhi*), which consists of instigation (*pravartanā*), as the state of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatā*) as understood from the scripture (*śāstra*). Thus, for anyone who desires [a result], the action is a means to what is desired and is feasible. And the action, as apprehended from the scripture, is to be carried out according to possibility, provided there is no contradiction with other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

"Stay" is stated as a universal injunction (*sarvādhikāra*). Since the root *sthā* (to stay) pertains to an object within the scope of other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it is not [itself] unestablished; thus, the scripture (*śāstra*) possesses purposefulness. Furthermore, even though it follows the form of an injunction (*vidhi*), it does not constitute the primary meaning of the scripture. For an injunction operates by aiming at anyone who merely desires [the result], and since there is no restriction, that action is capable of being undertaken by all who seek it.

And because there is the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), and because the firm understanding of the scripture establishes that even gods, sages, animals, the deaf, the blind, the dull-witted, and *śūdras* possess the capacity to perform those respective portions [of the ritual], it appears that eligibility for a particular sacrifice belongs to whoever is able to perform it in whatever way they can; thus, the action is the means for accomplishing the desired goal according to one's ability. Now, if there were no such capacity...

However, even that which is accessible through scripture (*śāstra*)—the scripture merely makes known the fact that the agent has understood the means of accomplishment, depending upon what has already been established by other means of knowledge (*māna*). Therefore, the scripture remains operative only with respect to that person whom those other means of knowledge have directed toward the goal; for that [scriptural] teaching is dependent upon them. Thus, by this sequence, the capacity [of an action] may be either scriptural or non-scriptural.
The exposition is concluded.

He takes up the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): In that regard, just as the state of being a required means (*apekṣita-sādhanatva*) is the cause of engagement and nothing else, so too is the state of feasibility (*śakyatva*). This [feasibility] is also understood from common worldly experience through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Thus, feasibility as well—

The sense is that, just as the capacity to accomplish a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatā*) enters into the form of an injunction (*vidhi*) whose nature is to impel action, so too the scripture would be non-authoritative with respect to that [capacity] if it were dependent on such [an inability]. Now, since the scriptural mention of the auxiliaries (*aṅga*) as being obligatory (*nitya*) is not subject to option, the capacity of the primary rite (*pradhāna*)—just like the completeness of its auxiliaries—is also within the scope of the injunction. And yet, even by a thousand scriptures, animals and the like [cannot be made to perform it].
He concludes in order to refute the claim that [an action] can be rendered capable [of being performed]:

"And thus, since there is no restrictive authority (*niyāmaka-pramāṇa*) for the delimitation of being a means to a desired end as cognizable through scripture, every means to a desired end is [potentially] available to anyone who desires it; and an action, though understood from scripture, may in some cases be merely possible."

Due to the observation of contradiction with other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the fear of invalidity, [the ritual] is established according to the possibility of non-contradiction with other *pramāṇas*— namely, that for whichever person is able to bring together as many auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) as possible, his primary rite (*pradhāna*) can achieve the desired result by means of only those many auxiliaries. Thus, through the reinforcement of the meaning understood from the verbal testimony, there is qualification for all [persons].
It has been stated.

He now introduces the established conclusion (siddhānta): "But because power (śakti) is not an object of other means of knowledge (pramāṇa), it is not already established; therefore, since the scripture (śāstra) possesses its own purpose, even that which conforms to the form of an injunction (vidhi) does not constitute the subject matter of the scripture. The word "but" (tu) sets aside the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa).

[The word] is understood through verbal expression as depending upon a capacity that is cognizable by another means of knowledge (*mānāntara*). Yet, there is no fault of such dependence, just as there is none when [a word] depends on the form of an object that falls within the scope of another means of knowledge. Otherwise, everyone would be capable of performing all the constituent parts [of a ritual].
It might be asked: "How is there a systematic arrangement according to possibility? Is it not because of contradiction with other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?

If this is argued, then alas, the word (*śabda*) would lack authority. One must accept that the subject matter of the treatise (*śāstra*) is a specific nature of categories established by definitions and other means of valid cognition, which serves as a means for understanding and is not within the scope of anything else. And thus, it does not belong to one who lacks the capacity [to understand].

"The cause for engagement [is established] because there is no agent. It is understood that one who is incapable cannot be prompted toward that [action]; thus, there is a qualification based on capability (*samarthādhikāra*). And when such a qualification exists, the question arises as to "to whom" it belongs; this very point was established previously. But how, then, was its non-existence suspected? Here, some [hold]:

Because the agent is yet to be accomplished, verbal suffixes primarily express actions— which consist of a means for accomplishing what is already established— and which are set in motion by a result.

This would be so if the capacity (śakti) were understood from scripture; however, this is not the case. For scripture provides what has not been previously established. Moreover, the capacity, like the fact that something is a means to a desired end, is not unestablished by other means of valid cognition.
Therefore, even though the capacity is accompanied by the form of an injunction, scripture does not take it as its object because it is already established; rather, it [takes] that...

He says that [the Vedic injunction], depending upon what is established by other means of knowledge, makes known the fact that the means [of action] has been prepared by an agent—a fact not previously attained:

"The injunction, however, is understood through the word as depending on that which is cognizable by other means of knowledge. Now, if this is so, does it not follow that the scripture lacks authority due to its dependence? To this he replies: "And thus there is no fault of dependence," just as...

The meaning is this: if there were a dependence on other means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*) regarding the nature of the objects that fall within its own scope, then such dependence on other means of knowledge would indeed undermine its validity;

however, it does not do so with respect to its own causal complex (*svasāmagrī*), for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Furthermore, it has already been stated that even though "fitness" (*śakyatā*) is connected with injunctions (*vidhi*), it is not the subject matter (*viṣaya*) of the scripture (*śāstra*). Otherwise, if the scripture were to have fitness as its subject matter, [the aforementioned consequences would follow].
Therefore, due to the absence of a restrictive authority (*niyāmaka-pramāṇa*), all claimants would be presented at once by the word "claimant" (*arthi*);
consequently, everyone would be capable of performing the entire set of constituent parts (*sarvāṅga-upasaṃhāra*). How, then, could there be a restriction according to what is possible?

The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) objects: "If it is argued that this is because of a contradiction with other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara-virodha*)," [the response is: "In connection with the word 'claimant'..."

Because, by that method, the capacity of all [beings] beginning with animals is established, and because that [capacity] contradicts other means of valid cognition (*māna*). The reply is: "In that case, alas, verbal testimony (*śabda*) would lack authority. For the scripture (*śāstra*) is that which provides the means for understanding the specific nature of an object—characterized as its 'denotability' (*śakyatā*)—which is established through definitions and other means of valid cognition."

That [object] must be accepted as having no other scope [than that]. And thus, when there exists a determining means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends the capacity [to act], the qualification based on capability is established. As for what was previously examined—whether or not there is a qualification—he states the connection here: "And when the qualified subject (*dharmin*) exists, for whom is there capability?"

The determination of its specific nature is possible only in this way and not otherwise; thus, that very existence of eligibility (*adhikāra*) has been established previously. Now, one might object: since eligibility for those such as the "desirer of heaven" (*svargakāma*) is understood from injunctions such as "one desiring heaven should sacrifice," how can its non-existence be suspected, such that it must be investigated?

To this he says: Here some [maintain] that a sentence has action as its primary element and consists of a single meaning. For it is action alone that is brought about, whereas [the substance] is established by its own nature.

Those who maintain that [the Veda consists of] substance and quality consider that there is no syntactic connection (*asamanvaya*) of the fruit within the sentence. Consequently, due to the absence of a fruit, there is an absence of entitlement (*adhikāra*). For indeed, in rites devoid of fruit, there can be no one who is enjoined (*niyojya*) nor any owner (*svāmī*).
But how is there a lack of syntactic connection with the fruit? Because the action is perceived as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), and thus there would be two things to be accomplished.

[This is] because of the inherence of the flavor (*rasa*). For instance: if the sacrifice and so forth are themselves the action (*kriyā*), then they alone are understood as being primary in their nature as having prior and posterior parts. Or, even if there is an action distinct from them which takes an object and has the result (*bhāvya*) as its primary element, nevertheless, it is those [sacrifices and so forth] that are [the action]. Why? Because of the necessity of their sequence (*paurvāparya-niyama*). [This is known] from the suffix.

Because they denote their own meaning as connected with the meaning of the verbal root, they are perceived as being in a state of accomplishment (*sādhyatvena*). Otherwise, since the substance would be what is accomplished, the operations denoted by the verbal suffixes would be [the means of] accomplishing what is already established.
They are expressed primarily as being impelled toward the fruit (*phala*) by that very fruit.

He explains: indeed, according to the usage of words, a sentence is that in which the entire manifestation of action has a single meaning and a single purpose. Furthermore, in reality, it is action alone that is manifested as having the nature of something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), because of the principle that "substance, which is established by its own nature, exists for the sake of what is to be accomplished" (*bhūtaṃ bhavyāyeti nyāyaḥ*); thus they say that heaven and so forth are subordinate (*guṇabhūta*) to that [action].

They consider there to be no connection with the fruit. However, if there were a connection by way of being the fruit, then because heaven and so forth would be primary, the action would not be primary; and if both were primary, the well-known worldly principle of having a single purpose (*ekārthatva*) would be lost—this is the sense. Now, one might object: "Let there be no fruit; what is that to us? To this he says: "And thus, regarding the fruit..."

Due to its existence [as a mere action], there is an absence of entitlement (*adhikāra*). Why? Because no one can be enjoined to, nor can anyone be the owner of, actions that are fruitless. And only that which serves as a benefit to someone becomes "one's own" (*svam*); since a fruitless thing does not do so, how can it become the property of an owner? Furthermore, an owner is said to be one who possesses an entitlement (*adhikārī*). This is not the case here.
The meaning is that even a discerning person would not undertake an action that is fruitless, nor would one who is subject to an injunction do so.

Now, an objection is raised: "Surely the sentence has the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) as its primary meaning, and since the productive operation requires an object to be produced (*bhāvya*), it will be connected with the fruit as that which is to be produced. To this, he replies by asking: "But how is there no connection with the fruit? He then provides the solution:

Because the action, which is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), is understood as that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Now, why is it not the case that both the fruit and the action are to be accomplished? To this he says: "Because the two things to be accomplished do not coexist. It is logical that from a single sentence, even between two entities to be brought about, it is the action alone that is to be accomplished, and not the fruit; therefore he says: "For instance, if..."

Sacrifices and the like are indeed actions (*kriyā*); nevertheless, it is they alone that are understood as being primarily constituted by a sequence of prior and posterior stages, and at that time there is no requirement for another object to be brought into being (*bhāvya*). Even if one were to assume an action distinct from those [stages], such an action would always require an object; yet, even when there is a requirement for an object to be brought into being, because that object is subordinate, it is still those very sacrifices and the like [that are primary], and not [the action].
[The opponent asks: "But if both [the root-meaning and the suffix-meaning] are to be brought about, what is the distinction? Having this intention, he asks: "Why?

Because of the rule of priority and posteriority (*paurvāparya-niyama*). This is because the suffix expresses its own meaning as connected with the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), and because the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*) is perceived as that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*). This, then, is the distinction from the result (*phala*). Otherwise...

If the meaning of the verbal root were not something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), then there would be no distinction from words denoting substances or qualities; for, as denoting an already established entity (*siddhārtha*),
it would be indistinguishable from words for qualities, and because such a position is not accepted.

Regarding the phrase "upon the arising of which": [the instrumental case is used] because of its connection with the act of direct realization (sākṣātkaraṇa), as in the expression "he cooks with wood. Now, one might object: "Would this not be the case even when there is a connection with another object (karman)? No;

for even in the case of an object, there is a recollection of it as a *kāraka*, and it connects with the action precisely by virtue of being a *kāraka*. This is because, according to the word, it exists as something that has already come into being (*bhūtataya*).

Because of the act of reaching [the goal]. However, the state of being the most desired (*īpsitatamatva*) is the object of another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Thus, let there be fruitfulness in the case of those things whose fruits are perceived; but in the case of sacrifices and the like, there is no fruit such as heaven, because of the lack of connection [with perception] and the absence of any other means of knowledge. And so it has been said: "those [actions] are twofold. Otherwise, they would simply be of one kind.

Thus, first of all, in the connection of substances with an action, there is a relationship as a quality (*guṇa*), not as a result (*phala*); for words denoting substance and quality differ from verbs (*ākhyāta*) which express that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*). By this [definition], those [words] are called verbs for which no form is perceived in their own usage at the time of their production, according to the Great Sage.

By means of the Sūtra: nor is that [the mention of the object] intended for the sake of mere meditation (bhāvanā), because when the meaning of the noun is connected with the meaning of the verbal root, it serves to establish a required relationship since its purpose is already perceived in the world. And therefore, the verbal root-meaning possesses the status of being the "thing-to-be-accomplished" (sādhya) because of its direct connection with the instrument, as in the case of "he cooks with wood. Indeed, there can be no connection with an instrument for that which is not itself something to be accomplished.

It follows that the wood cannot function as the instrument (*karaṇatva*) with respect to the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) denoted by the verb, because according to your own view, that force is already occupied by the cooking (*pāka*) which is expressed within the same word. Nor can there be a connection with the efficient force implied by the cooking, since the connection with cooking is perceived directly. Indeed, one does not say, "The pot is made by the jar; he cooks with the wood."

The understanding of the relationship is uniform. Therefore, because [the fuel] is directly related to the cooking and so forth by the words "with wood" (*kāṣṭhaiḥ*), it is correct that those [factors] alone are to be accomplished in their own form.
But then, in a case such as "he cooks rice with wood," where another object (*karman*) is perceived, there [the wood] is not [related to] the meaning of the verbal root.
There would be two things to be accomplished (*sādhya*), for it is not possible for there to be two things to be accomplished within a single sentence;

thus [the opponent] objects: "But this would not be the case because of the connection with another action. He replies: "No, because even in the case of an object (*karman*), its status as a *kāraka* (participant in an action) is traditionally taught. This is because [an object] is connected to an action precisely by virtue of being a *kāraka*. This is the underlying intention: both [the action and the object] exist in the case of rice-gruel (*odana*) and so forth as *kārakas*..."

[There is] both the state of being the agent (*kartṛtva*) and the state of being the most desired object (*īpsitatamatva*). In that regard, when there is a connection [of the object] as a *kāraka*, there is no loss of its being something to be accomplished by the action (*kriyāsādhyatva*).
Nor is rice and so forth understood from the word as having a temporal sequence—as in "the rice is cooked"—but rather as something already established (*siddhatayā*); thus he says:
"because it is presented as an existing entity by its own word. Now, if the word does not denote the most desired object...

"How can there be a cognition of that [object] as being the most desired (*īpsitatamatva*)? To this he says: "But the state of being the most desired is the object of another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

And thus, while in the case of visible results such as cooking rice and so forth, let the result belong to the agent; however, in the case of sacrifices and the like, how could heaven and other such results—which are not the literal meaning of the word—belong to him? Consequently, because there is no connection with the status of being a result, the injunction (*codanā*) and so forth cannot apply there.

It is appropriate [to speak thus], because no other means of knowledge is possible. And so, some actions such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and the Prayājas are primary because their results are yet to be accomplished (*sādhyatvena*); whereas others, such as the *avaghāta* (threshing) and so forth, whose results are established by other means of knowledge, are subordinate with respect to their results.
Thus it has been stated that these [actions] are twofold: those that are subordinate and those that are primary.

By the Great Sage. Otherwise, if it were admitted that all [subsidiary acts] possess fruit, then the fruit for all of them would necessarily be of one and the same form, because they are subordinate with respect to the fruit, just like the act of husking and so forth.

This is correct. In reality, there is no connection [of the sacrifice] with the fruit as its result, because human effort has the sacrifice and so forth as its object, whereas heaven and so forth have no such connection; and because the sacrifice and so forth cannot function as an instrument (*karaṇa*), since no other operation (*vyāpāra*) is observed in them. Furthermore, since an entity (*bhūti*) is not itself an operation, and because a person’s injunction applies to what is possible, it is illogical to say "one should produce heaven."

Furthermore, this would entail the consequence that [the result] must necessarily be performed; for it is accepted that the fruit (*phala*) is not something to be enjoined (*avidheya*), whereas sacrifice (*yāga*) and the like are taken to be what is enjoined (*vidheya*). Indeed, an injunction (*vidhi*) does not directly concern the sacrifice or the fruit as the object of activity (*pravṛtti-viṣaya*); rather, activity is the productive urge (*bhāvanā*).
And that word which is the cause of the activity directed toward a particular object is called an "injunction" (*vidhi*). In that regard—

There is no such cultivation (*bhāvanā*) based on what is already known that could be enjoined. Even assuming there were a distinct *bhāvanā*, [the author] connects the Sūtra here after having clarified the object of knowledge (*prameya*): "In this way, first of all, when substances are connected with an action, their relation is as a subordinate factor (*guṇatva*), not as a result (*phala*) such as heaven and so forth; this is established by the word. Not only this...

There is no connection with the result, either verbally or in reality. Why? Because the human effort, which is the *bhāvanā*, has the sacrifice and so forth as its object; for that reason, there is no connection with heaven (*svarga*) and the like. A person is never observed to be actively engaged in heaven, but rather in the sacrifice. Therefore, the sacrifice alone is what is to be accomplished by him, not heaven. Now, [if it is argued...]

One might argue that even though sacrifice is accomplished through human effort, it will still serve as the instrument (*karaṇa*) with respect to the fruit, and thus the relationship [between the sacrifice and the fruit] will be established;
to this, he says: "Because no other operation (*vyāpāra*) is observed in the case of sacrifice and the like, their status as an instrument is untenable.

For the status of being an instrument is pervaded by connection with an action (*kriyā-yoga*); and since such an action is not observed, the status of being an instrument is excluded from sacrifice and the like.

The meaning is that it also causes [the agent] to desist. Now, one might object: "But surely the very coming-into-being (*bhūti*) of the sacrifices and other such acts is their operation; and from that, they possess the status of being *kārakas* (factors of action) and instruments (*karaṇas*). To this he replies: "Because coming-into-being is not an operation. For an operation must have an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) that possesses that operation, and that inherent cause must already be established. If it were not yet established, it would be something yet to be brought into being (*bhāvya*).

Existence does not inhere in this [heaven]. Indeed, things such as sky-flowers do not possess activity. Even that which is already established cannot be something that "will come to be. Space never comes into being. Therefore, existence is not an activity. Furthermore, if heaven were something to be brought into being (*bhāvya*), then the person would be the one enjoined (*niyojya*) toward it; yet he is not [enjoined] by means of that [heaven].

He says: "It is possible"—for if [heaven] were merely possible, there would be no justification for the injunction to a person that "one should produce heaven. Furthermore, if heaven and the like were dependent on desire, then because there is no rule that desire must necessarily occur, it would not follow that they must necessarily be performed. However, if they were dependent on an injunction, then since desire is not the governing factor and the injunction is eternal, [the performance of the action follows].

He says that because it would be prescriptive, there would necessarily be an obligation to perform [the act]: "And because of the consequence of [imposing] an obligatory duty. Furthermore, this is because it is accepted that the fruit is not something to be prescribed. If it is argued that "the desire for that [fruit] is indicated by the purpose [of the act]," such that one thinks, "This must be done by me," [we reply that this is not so], because no prescription of the sacrifice and so forth is heard [in the texts]. As it has been said: "But he does not know the means."

Therefore, because of that expectancy, it is taught [in the injunction] "by means of sacrifice. And this is appropriate, as he says: for an injunction (*vidhi*) has activity as its object because its nature is to impel, and it does not [directly apply] to the sacrifice or the fruit. Furthermore, activity is the productive urge (*bhāvanā*).
And since the word is the cause of the activity directed toward that [sacrifice], and because activity toward the fruit is caused by desire, [the injunction does not apply directly to the fruit].
Thus it is said. Furthermore, the engagement with the form of the object must be enjoined; nor is that [engagement] directed toward the means [alone].

There is no non-conjunction between the sacrifice and the fruit—the two being the object of the cultivation (bhāvanā)—and there is no other fruit [to be produced] than that which arises from the power of the injunction itself.
For that [action] as well, it is not so, because of its non-inherence; because of the dissimilarity [of action], the state of being a means (*sādhanabhāva*) is difficult to comprehend;

nor can it be established through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), for that would result in the loss of the definition of action as "that which is characterized by effort" (*ceṣṭā-lakṣaṇatva*). This is because such [effort] culminates in the state of being the goal (*sādhyatva*);
and because in the world, an action that is fruitless is never observed to be a goal, while the state of being a means necessarily entails the state of being a goal.

Because it precedes [the result], it is logically impossible for it to imply that [result]; for that which is yet to be accomplished (*sādhya*) lacks the capacity to imply its own means (*sādhana*). Even if it were to imply it, there would be no one-eyedness (*kāṇatva*) in the agent-form required for the sake of accomplishment. How then can there be another [activity] directed toward the result? He says: "And there is no second *bhāvanā* whatsoever that has the result as its object."
It is enjoined. Or, let it be so; nevertheless, the subject at hand is not established. Therefore, he says:

even though there is a second *bhāvanā*, there is no inherence (*asamavāya*) between the sacrifice and the fruit, which are the object and the result of that *bhāvanā*. Now, let there be no connection between the fruit, which is an already existing entity, and the object of a separate *bhāvanā*; however, by the force of the injunction, the sacrifice [is connected].

One might argue that [the injunction] will be connected with another fruit imagined [for it], as in the case of the Viśvajit sacrifice and others; to this he says: "There is no other fruit either, due to the force of the injunction. Why? Because even for that [imagined fruit], there is no connection with a word for a fruit heard in the text in this manner.
Why? Because of the cause of dissimilarity (*vairūpya*), since the status of being a means (*sādhanabhāva*) would be difficult to comprehend. Never indeed [can it be understood] all at once...

It is logically untenable for the sacrifice, as heard in scripture, to be both the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), because of this contradiction. Therefore, it is difficult to understand how a sacrifice, which is heard as something to be accomplished, can possess the status of being a means.
This might be argued: from the injunction (*codanā*), the sacrifice and so forth are understood as things to be accomplished, and by implication (*arthāpatti*), the result [is established].
It is understood that [the action] possesses the status of being a means; let there not be a discrepancy [in the definition]. Therefore, he says: "Not from presumptive testimony (arthāpatti). Why?

Because of the loss of the character of being defined by Vedic injunction (codanā). If the status of being a means to the fruit were cognizable through presumptive testimony, it would lack the character of being defined by Vedic injunction.
Consequently, there would be a contradiction of the proposition that "Vedic injunction alone [is the source of Dharma]. Furthermore, presumptive testimony is not a Vedic injunction.

It is not correct to say that "that which is characterized by an injunction (*codanā*) has that [dharma] as its object" on the basis of being the root [of knowledge]. For an injunction, which culminates merely in the performance of sacrifices and the like, cannot be established without being a means to a fruit; thus, it lacks the status of being the root for *arthāpatti* (presumption).

He states this because [the injunction] culminates in the state of being something to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Now, if one objects: "The state of being something to be accomplished for that which lacks a fruit is inconsistent with what is understood from the injunction."

He states this regarding the point that the injunction (*codanā*) itself, which conveys the state of being something to be accomplished (*sādhyatva*), does not terminate [its function] until it serves as the seed for the postulation of a result:

"Because an action without a result is never seen in the world to be something to be accomplished. This is because the author of the Dharmaśāstra prohibits it, saying, "One should not perform useless exertion" (*na kurvīta vṛthāceṣṭām*). Now, just as for others [the result] is understood from the word as being a means (*sādhana*), [so too is the action to be accomplished].

[The opponent argues: "Just as sacrifice and the like imply their own status as that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), so too in our view, [the means] perceived as that which is to be accomplished will imply their own status as the means (*sādhana*). To this he replies:

"Because the status of being a means, such as sacrifice and the like, is preceded by the status of being that which is to be accomplished; for it is impossible for that [status of being a means] to exist in what has not been performed."

Now, this application of the objection (*ākṣepayoga*) applies to the view of those who maintain that [the object] is the means (*sādhana*) by virtue of being the word (*śabda*). However, in the view of those who maintain that it is the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*), there is no capacity for the means to imply [itself] because the state of being the goal (*sādhyatva*) is what stands foremost. This is easy to understand. If one should think that even the state of being the goal (*sādhyatva*) is not possible without being a causal factor (*kārakatva*) with respect to the accomplishment (*siddhi*), then [there would be] the state of being the means (*sādhanatva*).

[Page 313] What, then, is injunction (*vidhi*) now? What is its nature here? Injunction is merely the act of impelling; it does not touch upon the benefit or harm of the person. Why? Because of the non-deviation of its cognition. And thus, from the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth—

[The meaning of the optative suffix is] the comprehension of an impulsion (*preraṇā*). Although being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatā*) is the cause of activity, the word, however, does not touch upon that specific form [of being a means];

rather, it settles upon the mere cause of activity. This is because [the word] conveys that form [of impulsion], whereas such [being a means] is absent in cases such as commands (*praiṣa*), and because the mere act of instigating activity (*pravartanā*) is never absent [from the word's function]. Furthermore, there is the fault of [the word] having multiple meanings; nor is that specific form [of being a means] [the primary meaning].
That [cognition] arises from cognition alone, because it can also arise from delusion and so forth.

[Objection: Even so, since an instigation (*pravartanā*) must have a specific object to be instigated (*pravartya*), and since that [object] must necessarily be anticipated beforehand, it will imply [the existence of the agent]. To this, he says: "Even in the case of implication, for the sake of establishing [the instigation], the form of the agent is established because it is the cause."
Because [the probandum] exists. This has been established: that the probandum is not an agent (*kāraka*).

Even granting this—let it be an agent—it follows from that very fact that, since it is the *kartṛ* (agent) with respect to the accomplishment [of the result], it would project only itself and not the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*); such is the meaning. If [it be argued that] sacrifices and so forth...

"It is merely the state of being something to be accomplished (*sādhyatva*), and not the state of being a desired means (*iṣṭasādhanatva*); how then, at this point, is there an injunction (*vidhi*)? The proponent (*pūrvapakṣin*) says: What does it matter here? An injunction is simply the act of impelling (*pravartanā*), not the state of being a desired means; consequently, it does not touch upon either human benefit or harm. Why? The answer is: because of its cognition. But surely [it is] the desired..."
Since the state of being a means (*sādhanatā*) is also understood [from the word], he says: "And because of non-deviation. He explains this by the phrase "of the understanding":

"And thus, from the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth, there is the comprehension of an instigation (*preraṇā*). Now, let that be granted; however, is this [instigation] not based on the state of being a means to what is desired? To this he replies: "Even though being a means to the desired is the cause of activity, the word, however, does not touch upon that."

One becomes attached to that [word] merely as the cause of activity. Why? Because it is understood in that form. He explains this by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) through the phrase "because of non-deviation" (*avyabhicārāt*). This is because in cases such as commands (*praiṣa*), that [cause of activity] is absent; for there is an absence of being the means to a desired end (*abhimata-sādhanatva*). And since the mere act of impelling (*pravarttanāmātra*) is non-deviant [with respect to activity], while in some cases there is commanding (*preṣaṇā*) and in others...

One might argue that in some cases the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) will be an injunction (*adhyeṣaṇā*), while in others it will be the state of being a means to a desired result (*iṣṭasādhanatā*), because such is the understanding in each respective instance. To this he replies: "Because of the fault of having multiple meanings. Indeed, when [the meaning] is simply instigation (*pravartanāmātra*), it is not tenable for there to be multiple meanings; the sense is that it would entail the burden of postulating multiple potencies (*anekaśakti-gaurava*). Now, [one might object: "But [the meaning] is not the state of being a means to what is desired..."
He refutes this: since the state of being a means to what is desired exists everywhere—in all cases such as commands (*praiṣa*)—either directly or through a causal chain, he says:
"And in those cases, it is not from the mere cognition [of the command] that the state of being a means to what is desired becomes the cause of cognition";
this is the meaning.

In this context, a certain proponent of the Mīmāṃsā school says: "Even so, since instigation (*pravartanā*) has as its object a specific person to be instigated (*pravartya*), that very person must be expected first; thus, priority belongs to him over the instrument (*karaṇa*) and other factors. Nor can it be said that words such as 'one desiring heaven' (*svargakāma*) are incapable of fulfilling this requirement of expectation. He continues: "And of the words 'one desiring heaven'..."
This is because of the capacity for that dedication. It is that very [agent] who is set in motion and dedicated by them, not the specific object of the means (*sādhana*).
The sense is that it will subsequently be connected to the action as its agent (*kartṛ*).

And because words such as "one desiring heaven" (svargakāma) have the capacity to present that [result], it is that very thing which is presented by them, not a specific means. What follows from this? It is that the qualification (*adhikāra*) of one who desires [the result] is established. Indeed, it is so; however, there can be no accomplishment of activity (*pravṛtti*) in the absence of a fruit. And qualification is for the sake of activity. [Objection: But would it not be purposeless?

Thus, there would be no purpose for the instruction [of the Vedas]. If its meaning were real, it would not be purposeless; but if it were unreal, what else could it be? Or rather, it is not purposeless because its purpose is the accomplishment of the qualification for the knowledge of the Self (ātmavijñāna). Indeed, this person, by his very nature, is possessed by passion and other afflictions; being engaged in acquiring sense-objects through means that yield visible results, he remains intent on attaining them, taking their side.
The protector is not capable of either understanding or contemplating the reality of the Self as taught, wherein the manifold expansion of sense-objects has dissolved;

rather, being instructed by the teachings on action, having brought about the destruction of performed desires, having desisted from natural activity and become established in scriptural activity, he is self-controlled, his mind unassailed by desires.

The proponent (pūrvapakṣin), with the following intention, asks: "What follows from this? The partial proponent (ekadeśin) replies: "The qualification of one who desires [a result] is established. The meaning is that, consequently, the connection [of the injunction] "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" becomes logically consistent. The proponent refutes this: "For it has been stated that there is no qualification for a fruitless [action]; having granted [this point]..."

It is also said: "Indeed, it is so; however, there can be no establishment of activity when the fruit is absent. [The opponent objects: "Let there be no activity, but let the qualification (*adhikāra*) be established. To this he says: "Qualification is for the sake of activity; if there is no activity, the qualification is useless. [The opponent objects: "In that case, the instruction itself would be purposeless. The answer is: "When the purpose exists..."

It is not purposeless. But if it were not so, what would its purposelessness be? Or rather, he says that even in this way there is no purposelessness: "Or, because its purpose is the accomplishment of the qualification for the knowledge of the Self, it is not purposeless. But how are all these injunctions for that purpose? To this he says: "This person indeed is the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña)."
By nature, one is possessed by passion and the like; as the Blessed One Akṣapāda said: "Because the birth of one free from passion is not observed.

Therefore, when one engages in the acquisition of sense objects through means that yield visible results, such as service and the like, his mind is drawn toward them, he becomes partial to them, and is always impelled by them. Consequently, he does not have his attachment for sense objects dissolved.

Even when the reality of the Self is taught, those possessed of a mind are not able— having withdrawn the senses— to direct the flow of the intellect toward the Self alone in order to comprehend, ascertain, or define it; how much less, then, can they perceive it directly?
"Let it be so; nevertheless, what is the use of instructions regarding ritual duties? To this he replies:

"But the instruction regarding ritual duties is for the twice-born of the three castes, aged eight years and so forth, who, though established daily in the manual of rituals beginning at the hour of Brahma and ending at nightfall, have their hearts captivated by theft, gambling, pursuit of women, hunting, and the like."

Having eliminated desire through the instruction regarding the concern for his wife and attendants, he then desists from natural activity; and just as with the concern for his attendants, so too with that which is scriptural, he begins every day at the Brahma-muhūrta.

Such a person is capable of understanding and reflecting upon even such a reality of the Self as has been taught. Indeed, the injunctions regarding ritual action (*karmavidhi*) have as their purpose the qualification for the knowledge of the Self (*ātmajñāna*), as evidenced by direct perception. Thus, the status of a scripture (*śāstratva*) arises either from the instruction of one who is to be enjoined (*niyojya*) or from the teaching of what is beneficial. However, when desire (*kāma*) is the goal to be accomplished—which is natural and permeated by passion and other such impulses—[the situation differs].

By showing a means toward worldly activity (*pravṛtti*) and thereby giving one’s own hand [to assist], the word [of the scripture] transcends the status of being a true treatise (*śāstra*). For in that case, the person would not be instructed; rather, he would be permitted to act according to his own will. Even if the treatise teaches what is beneficial, it nevertheless incites one toward desirable objects that are by nature connected with suffering by showing them as a means.
Otherwise, the word would not be one that provides beneficial instruction.

[Objection: In that case, even an injunction regarding knowledge (*jñāna-vidhi*) would be a mere teaching (*anuśāsana*). [Response: No; because knowledge has a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*) and, by its very nature, is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*), like the act of wiping (*saṃmārga*) and so forth. It is with this very point in mind that it is said: "And it must be performed..."

One who is established in the ritual procedure (*karmapaddhati*) until the end of the evening, being self-controlled and whose mind is unassailed by desires, is able to realize and define even such a reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*), which has dissolved the manifold expansion of sense objects.

Now, one might object: just as an action to be accomplished (*sādhya-kriyā*) is not connected with an object to be accomplished such as heaven (*svarga*) and so forth, so too [is it not the case] regarding the knowledge of the Self?

Even by way of the accomplishment of action (*kāryasiddhi*), what indeed is the distinction between these two? To this he says: "In this way, by means of what is seen [in the world], the injunctions regarding ritual action have as their purpose the qualification for the knowledge of the Self. This is true; the connection is not verbal (*śābda*), but rather, when brought forward by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is not rejected by the word, just as in the case of "one threshes the rice" (*vrīhīnavahanti*). Such is the sense. Thus...

And its status as a *śāstra* (treatise) arises from its being an instruction (*anuśāsana*) for those who are to be instructed; "instruction" means the turning away from activities that are tainted by the sufferings of transformation, pain, and latent impressions through the teaching of alternative modes of activity. Therefore, this is the meaning. He states another way: "or because it is an instruction on what is beneficial. This refers to the qualification for the knowledge of the Self, which consists of eternal bliss.

The purpose of accomplishment is the knowledge of ritual action; the meaning is that [the Veda] serves this through its instruction. Otherwise, however, the traditional scripture (āmnāya) would not possess the status of a treatise (śāstra); thus he says: "But with regard to desire"—desire is that which is desired, such as heaven and so forth.
When that is to be accomplished, the Word (śabda) bestows its own hand by showing the means for natural activity, which is impelled by passion and the like.

It transcends the nature of a treatise (*śāstra*). Even if one so desires, one might not engage [with it] due to a lack of knowledge regarding the means (*upāya*), for engagement occurs only through the knowledge of the means. Therefore, the meaning is: if even such a work is a treatise, what else could possibly not be a treatise? Why does it transcend the nature of a treatise? To this he says: "For at that time..."

A person would be merely instructed; however, if he were permitted to act according to his own will, then the scripture’s nature as a teacher—characterized by the turning away from what is harmful—would not exist. Thus it has been stated that [the scripture] would lack the characteristic of being a teacher. Furthermore, even if the scripture teaches what is beneficial, nevertheless, by inciting one toward desirable ends such as heaven—which are connected with suffering—by showing them to be the means [to attainment], it does not lead to what is beneficial.
The word would be an instruction (*upadeśa*). [The opponent] objects: "In that case, even an injunction regarding knowledge (*jñāna-vidhi*) would be nothing but an instruction (*anuśāsana*).

For in that case as well, liberation (*mokṣa*) cannot be connected as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), just like heaven and so forth; nor can one who desires liberation (*mumukṣu*) be the qualified person (*adhikārī*). This is the meaning.
He refutes this: No, because knowledge has a visible purpose. And that was stated previously:
"By its very nature, one who possesses pleasure is not to be made to possess pain," and so forth. This is the meaning: because one's own body and so forth are momentary...

Because it is invariably associated with suffering, the sacrifice, as a means to that [desire], would indeed not be something to be performed due to its nature as suffering. However, that which has as its purpose the manifestation of the cessation of the entire manifold of suffering and results in happiness must be performed. But if one describes it in this way, does it not follow that the qualification for the rite is abandoned? True; yet there is no other [qualification].
This is being examined, not merely accepted as a premise. Furthermore, it will be explained later on how there is a qualification (adhikāra) in the sense that "one should perform the sacrifice.
To this, it is said:
For it is indeed particulars that are the meanings of words, even when there is an observed conformity of form;
moreover, the cognition of an injunction is not meaningful without the capacity for what is desired.

Because it is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*), like the act of wiping and so forth. Just as the act of wiping is dependent upon the object being wiped, so too is cognition dependent upon the object of knowledge (*jñeya*); this is established by experience—this is the meaning. And with this very point in mind, your honor stated: "That which is to be performed is accompanied by pleasure, and that which is not to be performed is accompanied by pain," and so on. Now, [an objection]: [The text continues: ...nanu... [the objection begins].

Even though heaven and hell are the fruits [of actions], this statement by the author of the Bhāṣya regarding what is to be done and what is not to be done is indeed appropriate; therefore, he says: "This is the meaning. Because heaven and so forth are momentary and are accompanied by suffering, the sacrifice that is their means would itself be something not to be done, as it would be characterized by suffering. [Only] when the entire manifold of suffering has been dissolved...
However, the manifestation [of the Self], which has happiness as its fruit, must be performed for its purpose.

He objects: "But in this way, since it is a fruit through a traditional succession, is it not the case that the absence of entitlement (*adhikāra*) regarding ritual action (*karman*) is not absolute? To this he says: "By describing it in this manner, is not entitlement itself indeed granted? [The opponent replies: "No."

[The opponent] says: "True; however, it is the logical principle (*nyāya*) that is being examined, not our own admission (*abhyupagama*). We do not assert the lack of qualification (*anadhikāra*) based on mere admission, but rather on the basis of logic. That [logic], moreover, establishes the inherent lack of qualification for those injunctions regarding ritual action (*karmavidhi*), but it does not preclude their entry into another sphere of qualification. Therefore, for those who follow them..."
The meaning is that the acceptance [of the injunction] is logical only when that [result] is perceived.

Having thus presented a semblance of a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣābhāsa*), he first states his own intended position regarding its purposelessness: "And it will be explained later on how, in the case of 'one should perform a sacrifice,' the purpose is according to the qualification [of the agent]. Thus ends the prima facie argument.
Having thus established the conclusion, he says: It is replied:
"Indeed, even when there is a perceived conformity of form, it is specifically the particulars (*viśeṣa*) that are the meanings of words;
and the cognition of an injunction is not purposeful without the capacity for the desired [result]."

[Page 317] First of all, the universal (sāmānya) is not the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, because in common usage only particular instances—namely, commanding (*preṣaṇa*), requesting (*adhyeṣaṇa*), permitting (*abhyanujñā*), and instruction (*upadeśa*)—are perceived; and because distinctions such as delusion (*moha*) and the like are understood [to exist apart from them]. For activity does not...

In some cases, there is an understanding of the cause alone. When a general term is used in the absence of a specific means of knowledge, there is a comprehension of that [general] alone. Therefore, the meaning of a word is not merely that much; rather, it is invariably accompanied by a particular, just as the sense of agency in words like *tṛn* is invariably accompanied by habitualness (*tācchīlya*). Otherwise, there would be no cognition of the employment of the agent.
This follows as a consequence. Nor are the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) the meaning of the word, because those that are not perceived cannot function as differentiators.
Indeed, by one who considers that the meaning of a word is merely the instigation of another, the status of heaven and so forth as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*) was rejected;

he now refutes that very point: first of all, the universal (*sāmānya*) is not the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and the like. [Nor are] command (*preṣaṇā*), entreaty (*adhyeṣaṇā*), or permission (*abhyanujñā*)...

Because in the world, only the qualifiers of the instruction—such as the *liṅ* suffix—are perceived; indeed, people do not understand a mere incitement devoid of the specific qualifications of the instruction and so forth. Nor is it the case that they fail to perceive even the "cowness" (*gotva*) in the phrase "A cow should not be touched with the foot"; rather, they waver regarding the denotata among various objects such as the substance, the word, and so on, just as they do with words like "artha. Those who do comprehend [the meaning], however, [perceive it as follows]:

They do not cause one to understand that [injunction] as being merely colored by the instruction; for it is not the case that when one proceeds from the instruction "one who has a fever should eat wholesome food," there is an understanding of mere incitement, and the comprehension of the instruction is preceded by that [incitement]. If incitement alone were the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*), then its specific varieties would be understood through implication; consequently, there would be a distinction between the instruction and so forth, just as there is in other cases.

He says this because there is the undesirable consequence that even delusion (*moha*), being an object of cognition, would result in being a cause for activity such as salutation; [he states the reason: "and because other distinctions such as delusion are understood.
Now, let it be granted that the impelling force (*pravartanā*) is indeed colored by specific qualities; nevertheless, why is it not that alone?
What is the meaning? To this he says: for there is nowhere a cognition consisting merely of the cause of activity.

Indeed, the status of being a general term is pervaded by the capacity to convey only the general, provided that there is an absence of a specific means of knowledge [to determine the particular] and that the relationship [between word and object] has been grasped. Therefore, in the manner stated here, the capacity to convey only the general is excluded.
The optative suffix (*liṅ*), being coextensive with itself, also excludes the status of being a general term. This is what he says:
"From a general term, when there is an absence of evidence for a particular, there is the cognition of that [general] alone;
and in some cases, when a certain particular is sublated, there is the cognition of a particular preceded by the cognition of the general. In every respect, [this is so].
There is indeed an understanding of the mere essence (*tanmātra*). He concludes: "Therefore, the mere essence is not the meaning of the word.

Rather, it is only that which is connected with a particular [quality], just as the agency of words like *tṛn* is connected with habitual disposition (*tācchīlya*). Nor is this example unestablished; therefore he says: "Otherwise, if the distinctions such as habitual disposition were not mentioned..."
If only agency were expressed, then, as in the case of [the rule regarding] the *tṛc* and *aka* suffixes, there would be the undesirable consequence of its application to every agent whatsoever.

As for what some say—that injunctions (*praiṣa*) and the like are not the meanings of words because they are merely limiting conditions (*upādhi*), whereas the meaning of the word in all cases is "that which prompts action" (*pravartakatva*) since it is never abandoned—in response to that, he says: "Nor are the limiting conditions such as instruction (*upadeśa*) and so forth the meanings of the words. Why?

Because those that are not perceived do not effect differentiation; for even by those who accept these as limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), their status as differentiators must be admitted, since there is no cause for the cognition [of difference]. And because it ends with that, this word "common" (*samāna*) is denotative of that.

Because it is remembered [in scripture]; because genus (*jāti*) and the like are also limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*); and because it would follow that the meaning of a word is merely "existent" (*sat*). Even granting this, it is said: since a general injunction has a particular as its ultimate referent, one must accept a particular; for in the absence of such a particular, it is impossible for something to function as a limiting adjunct. Furthermore, that which is not apprehended cannot serve as a differentiator.

For a cognition does not arise without its qualifier having been apprehended. Now, one might object: "The denotation of the qualified (upahita) depends upon the perception of the qualifier (upādhi), but it does not depend upon the [qualifier] being its own object of representation. To this he says: "Because there is no other cause for the cognition [of it]. The meaning is that the very expression of the qualified implies the object of representation by virtue of the context. Not only is this logically established, but there is also recollection.

He states that the *Kātyāyana* rule applies here: "Because it ends in that [suffix], this word having a common form (*samāna-śabda*) denotes that [meaning]," according to the traditional rule (*smaraṇa*).

The two kinds of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) are those whose locus is identical with the qualified object (*upahita-samānādhikaraṇa*) and those whose locus is different from it (*tad-vyadhikaraṇa*). For example: *dṛtiḥ hariḥ paśuḥ* ("the skin is a tawny animal") and *gārgikayā ślāghate* ("he boasts by means of being a Gārgya"). In that context, the word which has a common form is the one that is identical.

That which has a substratum (*adhikaraṇa*) as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is to be called "ending in a suffix" (*pratyayānta*), such as *dṛtihari* (one who carries a skin) or *paśu* (an animal). However, that which does not have the same word [as its base]—that is, which is non-co-referential (*asamānādhikaraṇa*)—is not so called, such as in the case of *gārgikayā ślāghate* ("he praises with the skill of a Gārgya"). For in the expression *gārgikayā*, the suffix *bun* is prescribed by the rule governing praise and the like; therefore, that which ends in this suffix is not co-referential with *gārgi*.
The meaning is: by what [quality] is praise (ślāghā) expressed?

This might be argued: "It is a settled principle that the meaning of a word is that which cannot be obtained from any other source. Furthermore, limiting adjuncts (upādhi) are obtainable from elsewhere and ought not to be the denoted meaning (vācya). Why? Precisely because they are obtained from common worldly usage. Thus...

Indeed, elders employ the word *dṛtihari* only with respect to an animal, and not elsewhere. If it is asked, "From what does this restriction of its usage arise?"—it is not so; for since worldly usage is beginningless, it is not subject to questioning.
Therefore, limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) are merely external; they do not enter into the denotation itself. Hence he says: "cowness and so forth."

Because even names are conditioned by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), it would follow that the meaning of words is simply "Being" (*sat*). If, on the other hand, you argue that [the word's meaning] is not the referent of the word because it is understood from worldly usage which is beyond questioning, then alas, even "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth would not be the referents of words;
it would follow that the meaning of words such as "cow" is merely "Being. For those words would then function solely with respect to pure Being.

Since the specific adjuncts (upādhi) such as "cowness" (gotva) are established precisely through the restriction of usage, there will be no unjustified polysemy. Nor would they denote "Being" (sattā) itself; that too will be understood from the very restriction of usage, and consequently, there would follow the undesirable consequence that all words are non-denotative. Even though the usage of the elders is beginningless...

Since the application [of a word] is for the purpose of conveying a meaning, one who employs it is subject to censure if it fails to convey that meaning. Indeed, elders do not employ words merely because they ought to be employed; rather, they employ them in order to convey a meaning.
Therefore, the restriction on the use of words such as "cow" with respect to things such as "cowness" is justified by their denotative capacity, and not otherwise.

In that case, this [objection] applies equally to all adjuncts (*upādhi*), because of the insistence on that point. Furthermore, there is no restriction regarding the usage of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth. By this, the nature of *yogarūḍhi* (etymological-conventional) is established in cases such as *paṅkaja* ("mud-born"). Nor does it follow that there would be denotability (*vācyatva*) for adjuncts that are not in grammatical coreferentiality (*asamānādhikaraṇa*). In those cases, there are words expressing praise and so forth.

Because it would follow that the application of the intermediate suffixes would occur at all times. For those who receive the guest-offering (*pādya*) do not employ merely the word *gārgikayā*; rather, that [suffix] applies to anyone whatsoever, or to someone specific. In every case, however, there is a negation of distinction.

Through *māna* (inference), general cognition becomes meaningful. In that regard, for those who do not depend on desire (*iṣṭa*) or its capacity (*tacchakti*), but follow mere intention (*abhiprāya-mātra*), as well as for those who do depend on them while awaiting their conformity, the causes of activity—namely, command (*preṣaṇā*), entreaty (*adhyeṣaṇā*), and permission (*abhyanujñā*)—are not to be understood as originating from human intellect. Nor are delusion (*moha*) and the like [to be understood] as contradicting cognition.

For if those [meanings] were presented, they would not be causes for activity; thus, the comprehension of the impulsion (*pravartanā*) would be frustrated by the presentation of delusion (*moha*). There would be a complete reversal: there would be no "desirability" (*iṣṭatā*) regarding the action, because that would contradict direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Furthermore, if it did not convey even the state of being a means to what is desired (*iṣṭasādhanatā*), it would simply fail to be a communicator at all. This is because the general cognition [of the word's meaning] depends upon the particular...

Because [the word] would be meaningless upon the cessation [of the object], it would follow that it is false; and since that [falsity] is untenable in the absence of two causes [for error], the elders attain praise from that alone. Therefore, qualifiers such as "instruction" and so forth, or "having that character" and so forth, must be expressed, for otherwise there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga). Thus, even while accepting the mere expression of incitement (pravartanā),...

[The injunction] is released [from its general form]. Since a general injunction has a specific intent, it is the specific alone that is to be established. And that [specific] may be either some particular one or all, because there is no distinction; for example, in "one should cook rice in a pot," it could be any particular pot or every pot. Or, as in "a Brāhmaṇa is not to be killed," it refers to the Brāhmaṇa class in general. Or it may refer to a particular individual, as in "bring a man."

"Surā is to be carried"—this is the understanding of the Śūdra. In every case, the cognition of a universal (sāmānya) is meaningful only through the disappearance of specific distinctions (viśeṣa), because a universal devoid of particulars is impossible. Thus, since commands and the like are excluded by what has been established, and since there is no possibility of confusion regarding anything else, he says that the instruction alone remains as the object of conviction: [The text continues: "Therefore, the teacher, having first presented the general rule (*utsarga*) and then the exception (*apavāda*), concludes with the statement: 'In this way, the Śūdra shall carry the liquor. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the word *surā* here refers to the substance itself, not to the act of carrying; for otherwise, the Śūdra would have to perform two actions simultaneously, which is impossible. Moreover, the Śūdra’s own cognition is that "I am to carry the liquor," and not "I am to carry the act of carrying. Therefore, the Śūdra’s cognition is directed toward the substance, not toward the action. Consequently, the Śūdra’s cognition is established solely through the exclusion of the specific [act of carrying] and the non-exclusion of the substance. Thus, the Śūdra’s cognition is indeed valid. This is the sense. And so it is said: "The Śūdra shall carry the liquor. In this way, the Śūdra’s cognition is established through the exclusion of the specific and the non-exclusion of the substance. Therefore, the Śūdra’s cognition is indeed valid. This is the sense. And so it is said: "The Śūdra shall carry the liquor. In this way, the Śūdra’s cognition is established through the exclusion of the specific and the non-exclusion of the substance. Therefore, the Śūdra’s cognition is indeed valid. This is the sense. And so it is said: "The Śūdra shall carry the liquor. In this way, the Śūdra’s cognition is established through the exclusion of the specific and the non-exclusion of the substance. Therefore, the Śūdra’s cognition is indeed valid. This is the sense. And so it is said: "The Śūdra shall carry the liquor. In this way, the Śūdra’s cognition is established through the exclusion of the specific and the non-exclusion of the substance. In that regard, for those servants who do not depend on their own desire or interest, but act solely in accordance with the intention of the one who sends them or the one who requests them, and for those students who do not depend on themselves but look toward the favor of the one who commissions them or the one who instructs them— being aware only of the intention to grant permission— the causes of their activity are the commands, the requests, and the permissions; for such an injunction does not derive its authority from human power.
They are not to be taught. He states that delusion (*moha*) and the rest do not apply [in this context]: "Delusion and the rest are not causes of activity.

Why? Because they are opposed to knowledge (*bodha*). He explains the opposition: "For if those [delusions] were being taught, they would be causes of non-activity; thus, the knowledge of how to instigate action would be destroyed by the teaching of delusion, and the opposite would occur."

Only cessation would follow as a consequence; for those who rely on authoritative means of knowledge never engage in acts such as bowing to a caitya once they have understood it to be a mere fabrication of illusion and delusion, nor do they desist from them once they have engaged. If it is argued that "being a means to a desired end" (*iṣṭasādhanatā*) is the cause of engagement, he says: "Being a means to a desired end is not the cause of engagement in an action. Why? Because [it is] perceived...

Because of contradiction. Furthermore, if it did not indicate that [the action] is a means to achieve what is desired, it would simply be non-informative. For when a particular [object] is negated by perception, even the universal ceases to exist; thus, [the word] would be useless, lack an object, and consequently fall into falsity.
[The opponent asks: "Let it be false; what is the contradiction? To this, he says: "And of that, because of the two reasons..."

Because it would be illogical [to claim] that there is an absence of defects in the cause and an absence of subverting cognition when [the result] exists; and here he applies the aphorism of the Great Sage (Pāramarṣa-sūtra): "But it is not effective because it is for that purpose. He explains this: "It would be ineffective if the action did not find an accomplisher; the meaning is that it would lack an agent. He states the reason for this very point:

Because it is for that purpose. He explains: because the word of injunction has as its sole purpose the act of impelling, there is no comprehension of its being a means to pleasure. [Objection: Let there be no such comprehension; even so, why would the action not be effective? To this [he replies on p. 320]:

As it has been said: "But [the Veda] is not a means of accomplishment because its purpose is that [pleasure]. This means that the ritual action would not be a means of accomplishment if it did not find an accomplisher, for there would be no one entitled to perform it. This is because [the Veda] exists merely for the sake of instigation (*pravarttanā*), since the word does not convey that pleasure is the means [to the end], and because human efforts are for the sake of pleasure. In the absence of a distinction...

Thus, the qualification [for action] is established as being based on the means of achieving pleasure. Furthermore, at the time when all specificities are set aside, the sentence would be non-probative—that is, non-informative—because a general injunction has an undifferentiated meaning.
But was it not stated that the instigation (*pravartanā*) to be manifested by the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth is a property of the agent (*prayoktṛdharma*)?

True; [therefore] a command (*ājñā*) and the like are not an *upadeśa*. But surely, even an *upadeśa* consists of an intention to favor (*anugraha-abhiprāya*), and thus it does not transcend being a property of the agent.
This is not sound. For in the case of an *upadeśa*, the intention lacks the quality of being a cause for activity, as is the case with commands (*praiṣa*) and the like.
For instance:
"In the case of commands and the like, the power of the action does not conform to the [agent's] intention;
rather, one engages in activity after having understood the power of the action in the instruction."
For, disregarding the capacity of the object in both commands and requests, and paying no heed to its specific nature, he says:

"And because human efforts are for the sake of pleasure. Since desire is absent when pleasure is absent—because desire is concomitant with pleasure—and since effort is absent in the absence of desire, it is like the absence of smoke when there is an absence of fire.

This is a general statement. However, if the status of being a means to attainment (*prītisādhanatva*) were established without qualification, then the qualification would be proven; yet, when all specific qualifications have been set aside, the sentence would be non-probative, meaning it would be non-informative and fail to produce understanding. Why? Because a general injunction has a general meaning, and a general [category] cannot exist without specific instances; thus, it would be without a subject matter (*nirviṣaya*).
Because it has already been refuted. In this context, he recalls the objection stated previously: "But was it not said? [The meaning is:

"The incitement (*pravarttanā*) to be expressed by the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth is understood; however, it is not a property of the employer (*prayoktṛdharma*), just as [the agent] is restricted in the case of the causative suffix (*ṇic*).
The sense is that since the incitement of the employer is impossible, there is no such incitement. This point is established.

He states that [the Veda] is a means of accomplishment: "True; while the quality of being an agent, such as a command (*ājñā*) and so forth, does not exist at all in the Veda, instruction (*upadeśa*) certainly does. He objects: "But since instruction also consists of the intention to favor, it does not transcend the status of being a quality of an agent.
For instance, the great seers (*maharṣis*), disregarding their own interests, [act] for the attainment of what is beneficial and the avoidance of what is harmful for others..."

The meaning is that since those whose intention is to favor [others] by means of the characteristic of avoidance formulate an instruction, the instruction itself is merely a quality of the speaker. He refutes this: "This is not sound. Why? Because, as in the case of commands (*praiṣa*) and the like, the intention lacks the status of being a cause for activity within the instruction. To explain:"
For in the case of commands and the like, the power of action does not conform to the intention [of the speaker];
rather, one engages in activity after having understood the power of action [inherent] in the instruction.
For in the case of commanding or requesting, you do not depend upon the capacity of the object toward the accomplishment of one's own desired goal;
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that all words would necessarily have known objects.
