But in that case, the *codanā* would itself be the object of knowledge (*prameya*), whereas it is intended to be the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), since it is stated that "Dharma is a matter characterized by *codanā*. Therefore, the *artha* (matter) which is the cause of activity— namely, the object of action residing in the cognizer, inferable from the act of engagement, self-evident, and denoted by the word which is the nature of the means of knowledge— is the *codanā*.

Disregarding the specific details of that action—namely, its purpose and object—and acting solely out of compliance with the [agent's] intention, one who exerts some effort thinking, "This commander is pleased; he will do something desired by me," proceeds as one who follows the intention. Even in the case of permission (*anujñāna*), although...

Activity proceeds from the fruit of an action; nevertheless, it requires conformity with the [teacher's] intention. He states the distinction of instruction from commands and the like, which does not depend on such an intention: even when there is instruction accompanied by the intention to favor, one does not engage in activity if the action lacks the capacity for the desired result and so forth. However, having understood the capacity of the action, [one recognizes] the non-deceptiveness of the instructor.

By the mere absence of a cause for deception— that is, by the reason consisting in the mere absence [of such a cause]— the speaker proceeds to utter speech that possesses a true object even when there is no intention to deceive. Therefore, because the engagement in instruction follows the existence of the state of being a means to achieve the desired object within the scope of that engagement, and because it does not follow the [speaker's] intention, the meaning of a word is not the intention to favor.
"But it is now [argued] that the meaning of the word is the action as being the means to what is desired.

He raises an objection: "The presentation of that [action]—that is, the presentation of its being the means to what is desired—is not possible without the intention of favor; therefore, the intention is the meaning of the word. He refutes this: "No, for one who is neutral..."

This is because we observe questions and the like even in such cases. Generally, indeed, one who has approached with a desire to know is instructed by the teacher with the intention of favoring him; however, since we observe instruction given by a neutral teacher to a neutral questioner, there is an instance of deviation (vyabhicāra), and thus instruction does not necessarily imply the intention to favor.

Thus [it may be argued]: "Let there be no over-extension (*vyabhicāra*); nevertheless, it does not follow that [the suffix] has the purpose of conveying intention (*abhiprāya*). For it is not the case that whatever instruction (*upadeśa*) does not occur without something else must have that as its purpose; rather, it is that which cannot be obtained otherwise (*ananyalabhya*). Otherwise, since the establishment of all words depends upon the knowledge of their meanings, they would all have the purpose of conveying knowledge. To this he says: "And it is not so by that much alone."
There would be the consequence that [the means] is the meaning of the word.

Now, he raises an objection: "If this is so, since it is the state of being a means to the desired [end] that constitutes the impulsion (*pravarttanā*), then the impulsion itself would be the *codanā*;
and because that [impulsion] is the meaning of the word, the *codanā* would be merely the object of cognition (*prameya*). Yet, the *codanā* is intended to be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)."
Because "dharma" is defined as that object which possesses [injunctional] characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), the proponent states his own position under the guise of a conclusion:

"Therefore, the object—which is denoted by the word as its means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), which is to be inferred from the effects of engagement and comprehension, which has action as its domain, which resides in the cognizer, which is self-evident, and which is the cause of engagement—is the *codanā* itself in the form of a means of valid cognition; thus, this is not my [unique] position."

This is a contradiction of the thesis. Since the injunction (*codanā*) is expressed by a word that is itself a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the very understanding that arises upon its engagement is the action; it is that [understanding] which is to be inferred. Thus, the possibility of grasping the relationship [between word and meaning] occurs with respect to an action, and therefore its capacity to impel one toward action is established. "Residing in the cognizer" means that for the cognizer, it is caused by that [injunction].

Because it is the basis for the causal conditions for the engagement with the object-domain. Regarding the term "self-cognizable": this [objection] that it is based on words is irrelevant, because the word is designated as *codanā* (an injunction) precisely because it is the cause of engagement. Thus, it is called *codanā*.

"Speech is that which instigates action. In cases where its authority resides in the word itself, let it be so; what is the use of this internal excrescence? For there is no contradiction whatsoever for the word in such instances.
Let its authority be like that of other word-meanings; the mention of a specific qualification is useless. Where [is this]?

And what is its source of validity (*prāmāṇya*)? If it is in respect to the object, no; because that [object] is established by other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, even in the absence of that [external object], there is the cognition of a relation (*saṃsarga*) that is unprecedented, just as occurs in common worldly experience. If it is in respect to being a means to an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*), let that belong to the word itself. Moreover, if it were an effect of the word, there would be the application of words by one who has not mastered their usage. As for being made known by the word...

It has been stated that [the view] of one who holds [the Veda] to be the cause is incorrect. Furthermore, inference does not function through the comprehension of its own object; the meaning is that since this cognition is self-cognizable (*svasaṃvedya*), it too is of that same nature. He refutes this: "This is trivial. Why? Because it is declared that a sentence which is the cause of activity is *codanā*. *Codanā* refers to an action."

The meaning is that the Bhāṣyakāra’s statement that "the injunction is the speech" (pravartakaṃ vacanam) contradicts his own designation of the injunction as the "meaning of the speech" (vacanābhidheyā codanā). Furthermore, since the authority (prāmāṇya) of this [injunction] is accepted, let it belong to the word itself; what is the use of this internal excrescence (antargaḍu), which is devoid of any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)? [For authority resides] in the word alone regarding the resulting knowledge (pramā).

Because it is capable [of being understood]. However, since that [injunction] is not even perceived in its own form, there is no contradiction whatsoever for the word in that regard. If it is argued that, by virtue of its being expressed by the word as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the understanding of the connection between the person to be impelled (*niyojya*), the means (*sādhana*), and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) occurs through the force of its own expectancy and not otherwise, then it exists as a means of valid cognition.
To the objection that "this [instrument] must be sought as the denotation," he says: let there be validity for it as having another word-meaning; the mention of a specific [instrument] is redundant.

For in that very way, even though an action (kriyā) is not denoted as a means of knowledge (pramāṇa) by its own word, it nevertheless brings about its own connection with a suitable and proximate factor (kāraka) through the force of expectancy (ākāṅkṣā); so too does a factor (kāraka).

The meaning is that, just as in the case of the action [expressed by] "Caitra cooks rice in a pot," so too [the statement] "this will also cause one to understand" makes the specification of its being a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) redundant.
Thus far, it has been stated taking the object as established without investigation; now, however, he investigates the object itself.
And where does its authority reside? [The opponent] raises an objection: "In the object, such as the sacrifice. [The author] refutes this:

"No, because it is established by another means of knowledge. Now, if it is argued that it resides in the connection between word-meanings which is not perceived through other means of knowledge, he says in response:
"Even for a previously unknown connection, there is cognition in its absence, just as in the world. In the world, [one sees] rice in a cooking pot...

The word "cooks" is understood even in the absence of the connection between action and its factors (kriyākāraka-saṃsarga), and even in the absence of the meaning of the *codanā* as you define it; this is because [the understanding occurs] even when sacrifices and the like are not seen to be means (*sādhana*) or means to the highest good (*śreyas*). He refutes this, saying:
"Let it be the word itself [that effects it]. Furthermore, is the difference in meaning (*arthabheda*) produced by the word or made known by it? If it were an effect of the word...

The application of words is not established [in this way]. Being made known by a word does not constitute a logical mark (*liṅga*), because that which has another cause or another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) lacks the nature of a mark; for it would be the result of a mark, and that would lead to an infinite regress. Nor is it [established] through the comprehension of the object.

[The existence of the self] is established from words regarding objects; yet it is not by means of one's own activity, because that [activity] is absent [prior to knowing the self], which would involve mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). If activity were the object of knowledge, words would be useless; if the word itself were the object of knowledge, inference would be redundant. However, having inferred another’s activity, one who has understood the connection between words and their meanings perceives [the object] from the word for himself and acts; thus, neither [of the two means] is redundant.

If it is argued [that this is possible], we say no. Because through the activity of another, one only perceives the cause of activity in general, and since the specific [cause] is not determined, that [argument] is incorrect; for if sacrifices and the like possessed an unseen potency (*adṛṣṭa*), it would be impossible to perceive their relationship [to the result]. If it should be said:
"Having grasped the distinction in meaning known as the 'injunction' (*codanā*) by means of inference, the relationship of the word will be grasped therein."

To this he replies: "And inference does not have the relationship [between sign and signified] grasped through its own apprehension. For inference indeed arises from the perception of a mark (liṅga); therefore, it cannot be the cognition [of that relationship], because that [cognition] is not itself the mark.
Furthermore, it is impossible for the means of knowledge and its result to be one and the same. Now, [if it is argued that it is grasped] by a single mark consisting of one's own apprehension..."

Having produced one cognition, it will produce another cognition that serves as the object of the injunction; thus, the status of being the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and its result (*phala*) would be established based on a distinction [between two cognitions].

To this, he says: "Because of infinite regress" (*anavasthānāt*). Since there is no other cause for the cognition that serves as the inferential mark (*liṅga*), one must state that its own subsequent cognition is its cause. And in this way:
The meaning is that there would be an infinite regress, as for that [cognition] there would likewise be another cognition of itself.
If it were argued that the cognition whose object is the meaning of the word will be the mark (liṅga) for this [injunction], he says in response:
"There is no inference of the injunction from the cognition of the object. Why? Because that [meaning] is established from words denoting the object.

Because the realization of the object in the form of the meaning of the [Vedic] statement is established. This is the underlying intention: this inference does not have a perceived particular (dṛṣṭasvalakṣaṇa) as its object. For nowhere has an injunction ever been observed through the realization of an object.

Why? Because an inference based on general observation (sāmānyatodṛṣṭa) must be accepted as having the perception of color and so forth as its logical mark (liṅga), just like the case of the sense organs and so forth.
Let it be so; however, that is untenable, because the effect characterized by the comprehension of the object is established from the words denoting the object themselves.

If it is argued that it is established through "activity" (*pravṛtti*), that too must be either one's own or another's. Regarding this, he refutes the first alternative: "The inference of the *codanā* [is not] by means of the mark of activity that is not one's own."

Why? Because that [object] would be absent due to the absence of its cause. Or, if the cause for cognizing it were the injunction (*codanā*), there would be mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). Now, if it is argued that the object is inferred precisely from the arising of another cause for activity, and thus there is no mutual dependence, to that he replies: "If the object is to be known through activity, inference is useless, since it is already inferred from the activity of another."

If it is argued that there is no redundancy because one acts after understanding from the word "self" (svayaṃ-śabda) the connection with the known [object], and thus neither the word nor the inference—which has activity as its mark—is redundant; [the author] refutes this: No, because through the activity of another, which is the effect, one only understands the cause of activity in general, since the specific [cause] is not determined.

Because there is the cognition of the mere [object] itself (*tanmātra*). [Objection: Let there be the cognition of the mere object; what is lost for us? To this he says: "Because activity is impossible through the cognition of the mere object. For if some specific cause of activity were cognized within oneself, that very cause would be inferred in another as well from the observation of activity. But [such a cause] is not known.

Because of the association [of words with their objects], once one has understood the word, activity becomes possible; for when that [word] has as its sole mark the mere inclination toward activity, there is the cognition of the expression of its cause. This is because activity is not possible through the apprehension of that alone. Indeed, it is not the case that everyone [acts] toward everything.

It is the cause of activity, and because its nature is not caused by anything else. If it is argued that it is "caused by inference" because activity is preceded solely by verbal testimony, then why is it not simply "established by the means of valid cognition that is inference," since the understanding from a word is preceded by inference itself?

Furthermore, no cause for activity other than the "unseen" (adṛṣṭa) is inferred; for such a cause would depend on what has already been established, whereas activity can be accounted for by means of visible causes. Moreover, those specific conditions that depend upon a cognizer must have an objective basis (ālambana) to be specified; and it is capable of being established through another means of valid cognition.

This is because [the object] is inferred merely through its existence; the meaning is that since the specific nature (*svarūpa*) is not apprehended, even that which is apprehended by means of a word cannot serve as a cause for activity. Now, why does that which is apprehended merely as a universal (*sāmānya*) not become a cause for activity?
To this he says: "For not everything is a cause for activity for everyone. Indeed, specific instances such as commands (*ājñā*) and the like are not all [causes].
They cause everything to proceed; however, it is only a certain determination of its specific quality (*viśeṣa*) that is the cause of activity, not the mere universal (*sāmānya*) alone.

The meaning is that, since the universal is indistinguishable everywhere, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that all [words], such as commands and so forth, would cause everyone to act toward everything. Furthermore, because the activity of a word is dependent upon the cognition of a relation (*sambandha*), it is a means of valid knowledge (*māna*).

And because that [activity] is impossible without the apprehension of a relationship, and because its nature is not caused by anything else. He raises an objection: "If it is argued that [the activity] has sound as its cause, since it is inferred from an activity preceded by sound. He refutes this:
"Since the cognition arises from sound only after inference, why is it not simply based on the means of knowledge that is inference?"

This is the underlying intention: a word whose connection has been grasped by a particular cognizer with respect to a particular object causes that very cognizer to understand that very object. And that cognizer, placing before him his own means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) which was operative at the time the relationship was determined and which has that object as its domain, understands the object from the word; thus, he considers the word to be merely a reminder (*smāraka*).

Therefore, in this case, if one has grasped the related motivator for activity by means of inference, then surely the meaning of this [Vedic injunction] must also be understood by placing inference itself before it. And thus, the optative suffix (*liṅ*) would be a mere restatement (*anuvāda*) of that [inference]. Nor can inference, which is the cause of activity based on the comprehension of the meaning of the optative suffix, be the cause for the comprehension of the [injunction] itself.

It is now appropriate to consider that [the object] exists as something previously established; for it resides within a different cognition. And a cognition residing within one activity does not re-cognize a cognition residing within another activity—even if they share the same object—lest there be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Therefore, he says: "It has inference alone as its means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Here, there is not even a scent of comprehension through scripture (*āgama*).
The word "eva" (only/just) has this meaning: the cause of activity, which is indeed perceived through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) within one's own self, must be inferred in another;

it is not, however, something to be understood solely through verbal testimony (*śabda*) that has never before been experienced. Thus he says: "Moreover, no cause of activity other than what is [already] seen is inferred from verbal testimony, because every instance of activity depends upon a prior established [cause]."

The meaning is: "because of the operation of that inference, which has as its mark the activity based on words. If it is argued, "Let there be no inference; rather, an unseen cause, never before observed, will be postulated as the reason for the activity [of the word] through the otherwise inexplicability of the activity of other words," to that he says: "Because that is established even by means of perceived causes. And as for what was said, "it resides in the cognizer."

Is this "condition" (pratyaya) intended as something distinct from the object, or is it that very object? Those who say it is a "condition," let us consider them. Even if it is accepted as a distinct entity, if it were eternal, then everyone would always and everywhere be entitled to [the result].

And that [Vedic injunction] lacks a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇaka*), because from a word there is no cognition of a mandate (*niyoga*) for anyone anywhere. Even if it were non-eternal, the word would not be something to be produced (*kārya*), due to the faults already mentioned. If its production were due to a cause or a desire, there would be the undesirable consequence of it being produced even after the ritual performance has been completed. If it were to persist as long as the cause lasts, then even for one who has completed the performance, there would be activity prior to the experience of the result.

It may be so. Therefore, the injunction is indeed the former one. In that case, it is not logical for the activity associated with the sacrifice to be the visible cause, since that [activity] is presented by the word as being subordinate to that [injunction].
He replies: "And by whichever specific conditions it is supported as being dependent upon a cognizer, by those very conditions its objective support (*ālambana*) must be stated;

for it is impossible that it be without an objective support (*nirālambanatva*). Nor is that [objective support] anything other than the means toward the desired end. Thus, our desired conclusion is established."

Furthermore, its being cognizable by no other means of knowledge (*ananyapramāṇakatva*) must be established; yet this cannot be done, because it is either established through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) or because it is an object of inference (*anu meyatva*). He refutes another alternative by considering it: even if one accepts that it is a distinct entity, if it were eternal, then—since there would be no distinction [in its nature]—it would, by virtue of residing in all persons, by its capacity, and by its commonality as an object for them, always [be so].

Furthermore, by virtue of being eternal, everyone would be authorized for everything at all times and in all places, because it is impossible for an effect to be delayed when its efficient cause is present. Moreover, that [eternity] lacks any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), since the cognition of an injunction for someone regarding something arises from the word itself, which is accepted as a means of valid cognition. Even if [the Veda] were non-eternal, the status of being an effect is invariably concomitant with it; therefore, it is an effect of speech.

Or it might be an injunction (*niyoga*), or an effect caused by desire (*kāmanimittakārya*). In that regard, it cannot be an effect of the word, because of the faults already stated, such as [the argument] beginning with "because it would lack the status of a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇatva*). Furthermore, if it were produced from a cause—either from desire or otherwise—then even when the causal agent has perished, the effect would not perish; consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the effect would persist even for one who has completed the performance of the rite.

Now, if desire (*kāma*) is not the efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*), but rather the inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*) sharing the same substrate as the effect, then the effect would perish upon its destruction—just as a cloth perishes from the destruction of the conjunction of the threads. To this, he replies: "If [the action] were to persist as long as the efficient cause [desire], then even for one who has performed the application [of effort], there would be continued activity prior to the experience [of the result]. This...

The intention [of the opponent] is as follows: Because it is a specific quality of the self (*ātman*), this injunction (*niyoga*) has the conjunction of the self as its non-inherent cause (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*), just like cognition (*buddhi*) and other qualities; it does not, however, have desire (*kāma*) as its non-inherent cause. Rather, desire is merely its instrumental cause (*nimitta*). Furthermore, the means of accomplishing what is beneficial (*hitasādhanatā*) alone constitutes the injunction (*vidhi*). Nevertheless, there exists some instrumental cause for it.

The destruction of which is the cause of the destruction of the effect, just as the destruction of enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) is the cause of the destruction of duality (*dvitva*) and so forth. To this it is said: "As long as the cause persists, there would be activity even for one who has performed the effort, prior to the experience [of the result]. He concludes the subject at hand: "Therefore, the former alone is the means for accomplishing what is desired by the agent."

This is the injunction (*vidhi*). And that being established, the meaning of sentences such as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices" must be described in accordance with it. However, in the view of the opponent, it would be the reverse; thus he says:
"An activity conjoined with the sacrifice cannot be a visible cause."
When that [object] is communicated by means of a word through its being directed toward it;

If, indeed, in an activity colored by sacrifice, the sacrifice itself is apprehended as the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) by virtue of coloring the existence of that activity, then— since it is proximate and denoted by the word as the primary referent— the nature of being the cause of the desired result is not the meaning of the injunction (*vidhi*) therein.

[The agent] would act [even toward what is not desired], because that [undesired result] is not intended [by the injunction]. In that case, if the injunction were not intended to be significant, there might somehow be activity in the world toward something either fruitful or fruitless. As it has been said: "But [an action] is not effective [toward its result] because it is for the sake of that [result]," since human efforts are for the sake of pleasure (*prīti*). However, when the meaning of the injunction is not connected [to the result], the causality of pleasure [does not constitute] effectiveness.

"One would not attain [the result]"—if, on the other hand, by the force of the injunction (*vidhi*), the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) were thus the instrument (*karaṇa*) because it culminates in the desired end, this would follow from its being invariably concomitant with that [result]. But if there is no reason to disregard the injunction, the operation of the object [is not intended];
for if it were presented by the word as being intent upon connection with an operation, such as "the task" (*kārya*) and so forth, as follows:

Regarding the first position: the operation consisting in the state of being a means to the desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatā*), which is understood through the injunctive suffix (*vidhipratyaya*), would be contradicted.

He elaborates on this point: if, indeed, the sacrifice were grasped as being inherent in the operation that is colored by the sacrifice—in the form "one should effect the sacrifice" where the sacrifice exists as the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) by way of coloring that operation—then that operation would be grounded in that [sacrifice].

Since that [action] is to be explained by another as a restatement (anubhāṣaṇa) through the word "liṅ-ukta" (expressed by the optative suffix), the nature of being a cause of the desired (iṣṭahetutā) cannot coherently apply there as the meaning of the injunction (vidhyartha). Now, if it is argued that even in the case of a sacrifice—which is itself something to be accomplished—what kind of activity could exist such that there would be no contradiction with its being a cause of the desired? To this he says: because that sacrifice and so forth are not themselves desired, the action is suffering (duḥkha).

Such is the experience of the world. Now, one might object: "Just as in the world there is activity by a person even when there is no intention to instruct—as in the case of a command and so forth—so too in the Veda such activity will occur even without an intention to instruct. To this, he says: "In that case, if the injunction were not intended, how could there be [activity] toward something fruitful or fruitless in the world, given the disposition of the person to be obeyed?"

[Otherwise] there would be activity [based on that]. However, in the case of the Veda, which is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*), because there is an absence of human intention, even if that [intention] were the motivator, it should be understood that no activity would occur if the injunction (*vidhi*) were not intended to be expressed.
This is because a specific injunction is the cause for the negation of other alternatives; just as the statement "he sees with the left eye" implies [the exclusion of seeing with] the right.

A prohibition of seeing [the fruit] is understood there. To that point also, he applies a Sūtra of the Great Sage: "But it is not the means of accomplishment, because it exists for the sake of that. He explains this: "Since human efforts are for the sake of pleasure, and since the cause of pleasure is not attained by one who does not perform the injunction, [the sacrifice] would not reach the performer. This is easy to understand. [The word] "one should sacrifice" (yajeta).
An injunction is understood merely as the state of being a means to what is desired; likewise, there is the state of the sacrifice being that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*).

If the injunction were intended to be expressed [as the primary object], the state of the sacrifice being that which is to be accomplished would be lost. Furthermore, there is no reason for deciding [which must be abandoned] that an injunction cannot be intended while abandoning the state of being that which is to be accomplished, since both are equally established by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and thus indistinguishable.

Therefore, he says: "Now, if it is thus [the case], then by the force of the injunction (*vidhi*), the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*)—whether desired or undesired—is the instrument (*karaṇa*);

for in that case, there is no attainment of an obstacle. Even when the injunction is intended to be expressed, the understanding of the sacrifice as the thing to be accomplished (*sādhya*) is logically consistent; because it was previously unestablished, its status as the thing to be accomplished follows from its being the means (*sādhana*) once it has been established.
Because it is inseparable from that;
at that time, since the sacrifice is not intended, there is no room for the sacrifice—which is essentially the primary element—to be subordinate to anything else. The manner...

Even though it is presented as being necessarily concomitant with the injunction by virtue of its own capacity—due to the fact that [the injunction] has no other scope while [the result] does have scope—it follows as the object in the form of the instrument (*karaṇa*).
For an operation aimed at the desired end (*iṣṭa*) is not thereby aimed at that [instrument], nor is one aimed at the sacrifice (*yāga*) thereby aimed at the desired end. Thus, first of all, this...
The connection with the fruit [of the action] occurs through the power of the injunction (*vidhi*), as expressed by the term "wins" (*jetā*). And because:
the status of being the object of the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) is first understood in the form of a desire;
therefore, even though heaven (*svarga*) is already established [as a desired end], it connects [with the action] by way of being that fruit.
For indeed, the commencement of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is desire, according to the principle that "whoever desires something, that they do.

He explains the verse: "But if, due to the absence of a reason for not intending an injunction and because of the absence of a means of accomplishment, the operation toward the object is neither desired nor undesired, then, since the sacrifice itself is undesired, one would be intent upon something other than the sacrifice that is desired."

In the context of the operation, the sacrifice does not lack scope as the primary element. Now, one might object: "Precisely because there is no other scope, the sacrifice will be connected as the primary element itself by setting aside its status as being for the sake of another desired end; otherwise, it would be impossible for it to be something to be accomplished.
To this, he says: "Because there is scope for the sacrifice to be that which is to be accomplished even in another manner."

The meaning is that, because an injunction (*vidhi*) cannot be purposeless, it is logical that the function of the operation (*vyāpāra*) must indeed have the intended [result] as its goal. Now, if it is asked: "Even if there is no possibility [of the injunction being purposeless] in either case, what is the reason for the decisive determination (*vinigamanā*)? To this he says: "By virtue of capacity" (*sāmarthyāt*). By virtue of the capacity of the cognition of the injunction—which has no other scope—the sacrifice, being presented through its inherent connection (*nāntarīyakatā*) as a mode of existence (*vṛtti*), attains the status of the object (*viṣayatva*).

It follows as the nature of the instrument (*karaṇa*). Although human effort proceeds with a desired end in view, nevertheless, if it does not take the sacrifice and so forth as its object, it does not lead to that desired end; therefore, by way of being inseparable (*nāntarīyakatayā*), the status of being an "end to be accomplished" (*sādhyatva*)—defined as being pervaded by the effort engaged for the sake of the desired object—is established for the sacrifice and so forth within an operation that is not itself the primary purpose. This is the meaning.

[Objection: But why does the state of being directed toward sacrifice (*yāgaparatva*) not also exist in a verbal activity that is directed toward what is desired (*iṣṭapara*)? [Response: He says: "For a verbal activity directed toward what is desired is not one directed toward that [sacrifice], nor is one directed toward sacrifice one directed toward what is desired. This is because we do not observe a single [verbal activity] expressed once to have both as its object; for in the world, the cognition of the relationship between word and meaning is rooted in that [usage]. Upa...
He summarizes: "In this way, one should abandon suffering"—thus, by virtue of the injunction, there is a connection with the result.

He says "and because" to show that it is not only by virtue of the injunction, but also through its connection with ritual action (*karmin*), that heaven and so forth become the object to be realized (*bhāvya*):
"First, the state of being the object of cultivation (*bhāvanā-karmatā*) is understood in the form of a desire."
Even though heaven is already established, it follows as a result through its connection with that [action].
He shows that desire is the precursor to the state of being the object of cultivation (*bhāvanā*): "Whoever desires something, he does that.
Thus, desire is the commencement of cultivation; by means of it, the effort of cultivation is initiated.

And thus, since it is to be accomplished by that cultivation (*bhāvanā*), even heaven and the like, though already established, are connected to the cultivation only as its objects—just as rice and other grains are connected through their relation to the agent—and not otherwise. As it has been said:
"Because of the connection with each object" (*pratyarthaṃ cābhisambandhāt*). That is, the human activity is directed toward each thing that is being sought.

It is connected [to the verb]. Therefore, because of the impossibility of [the agent] being the object, heaven (*svarga*) and so forth are connected as the objects of that action; otherwise, there would be no syntactic connection (*ananvaya*). Thus, since the mere injunction "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) requires a fruit, and since heaven and so forth cannot be otherwise integrated [into the sentence], the action is understood through that connection as the means (*sādhana*) for heaven. But how [is this so]?

The efficient force (*bhāvanā*) is connected with heaven as its qualifier; or, if it were connected [with another], how could there be the status of being a qualifier for another, or even a compound? For there can be no connection with the efficient force for that which is devoid of connection with it, or for that which depends on a connection with something else. Indeed, a compound is not appropriate for that which has become a subordinate factor (*guṇabhūta*).

This is not a fault; for the word "staff-bearer" (daṇḍin) enters into a relationship with the qualifier by implication. And because of that connection, the compound is not corrupted even when there is a relation with another [word].

Since effort (*prayatna*) is preceded by desire (*icchā*), that action is the "action of desire" (*icchākarma*). Even though heaven and the like are already established [as objects], they are connected to the *bhāvanā* as its object (*karma*) precisely in their capacity as the object of desire; they do not connect otherwise as qualifiers of the qualified person (*adhikṛta*). Just as rice and the like, through their connection with the agent as an object—as in the case of the connection with the accusative case—are construed within the *bhāvanā* solely in their nature as things to be accomplished (*sādhya*), so too is heaven and the like. This is precisely the point here.
He applies the aphorism of the Great Sage (*pāramarṣa-sūtra*): "And because of the connection with each respective object. He explains this:

the human activity is connected directly toward that which is being sought; therefore, by virtue of its connection with the act of seeking, heaven and so forth are connected as the objects of that activity. Otherwise, if it were established otherwise, there would be no syntactic connection (*ananvaya*). He concludes:

Therefore, it is not only that one should sacrifice (*yajeta*) because [the injunction] depends upon a result; rather, even for the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) as presented by the injunction, the state of being something to be accomplished (*sādhya*) is brought about through its connection with an agent such as heaven, since otherwise [the action] would not be properly integrated. He concludes:

"And thus, because of the connection as something to be accomplished, there is the operation of the ritual act (*karmavyāpāra*). For 'one who desires heaven' (*svargakāmaḥ*) is indeed a qualification."

Heaven is understood from the word; how then can it be related as the primary element to the *bhāvanā*? Or, if it were so related, how could the *bhāvanā* be subordinate to another, or how could there be a compound (*samāsa*)? This is because there would be a lack of syntactic capacity (*asāmarthya*) due to mutual expectancy. He states this very lack of capacity: for there is no connection with anything else for that which is devoid of a connection with it [the *bhāvanā*] and devoid of a connection with the person (*puruṣa*).

Alternatively, the connection with the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) belongs to that which is dependent on something else. However, a compound is indeed observed even for a principal element when it is dependent on a connection with another, as in "the king’s man is handsome" (*rājapuruṣaḥ śobhanaḥ*). To this he says: "For a compound is not appropriate for that which has become a subordinate member (*guṇabhūta*). He refutes this: "This is not a fault."
By implication, that which is intended as a qualifier enters into a relationship like a staff;
or, through connection with that [qualifier], there is no fault in the compound even when it relates to something else.
Indeed, heaven is not related to the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) independently of its connection with the person desiring heaven;

rather, it is that very heaven, as the primary element qualified by the desire, that enters into the relationship. Just as in the case of the injunction "the staff-bearer recites the *praiṣa* formulas," it is the staff [that qualifies the agent].

The staff-bearer (*daṇḍin*) is the primary [referent]. However, that which is related to him is not intended to be expressed as having its own independent nature, because it is subordinate to him. And in this way, the compound is also established. For if an independent entity were related to another, a compound could not occur due to the impossibility of such a relation, as it would involve dependence (*sāpekṣatva*). But when there is a relation to another through the medium of that [primary referent], there is no loss of the state of being a single meaning (*ekārthībhāva*).

For if heaven were connected with the productive operation (bhāvanā) independently of its relation to a person, then the verbal cognition of the person's connection would be contradicted. Or, if the word "desiring heaven" (svargakāma) were directed solely toward the person, then heaven would not be connected with the productive operation. Since neither of these two [extremes] is the case, he says: "Indeed, not..."

Heaven, which is independent of the lineage [of the agent], is connected to the *bhāvanā* (efficient force), so that the verbal cognition of it as a qualification of the person (*puruṣa*) would not be contradicted. However, that very heaven, being primary as a qualification, enters into a relationship with the *bhāvanā*. For if the word "desirous of heaven" (*svargakāma*) were primary in its referent (*viśeṣya*), then heaven would, by virtue of the person, [be subordinate] in the *bhāvanā*.
It is connected [to the subject]; however, this fault does not apply when this [term] is intended as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). Where is such intentionality toward a qualifier observed?

To this he says: "Just as in the case of *daṇḍī praṣānanvāha* (the staff-bearer recites the directions), the staff is primary, and thus he is the 'staff-bearer' (*daṇḍin*). Just as in the case of *maitrāvaruṇaḥ praṣānanvāha* (the Maitrāvaruṇa priest recites the directions), although the recitation of the directions is already established for the Maitrāvaruṇa, [it is specified that] the staff-bearer recites the directions.

Just as in the case of the word "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*), because it is impossible to enjoin the substantive characterized by the attributes of Maitrāvaruṇa, and because the attribute— the staff— is not already established and must therefore be enjoined,

the word "staff-bearer" is intended to enjoin that [staff]; so too here, since the agent who brings about the action is obtained through the very implication of the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) in the injunction "one should sacrifice," and thus is not something to be enjoined, and since the productive urge requires a specific object to be brought about (*bhāvya*), [the word "heaven"] refers to heaven and the person.

It is elegant [to hold] that the scriptural injunction "one who desires heaven" (svargakāma) refers to that [heaven], because the qualifier, being of an unestablished nature and being an object of an action, is fit to be brought into being (bhāvya), and because it is not established by any other means. Now, if the scriptural injunction "one who desires heaven" refers to the qualifier, then there would be a connection between heaven and the qualified [subject].

If it were not expressed through its own verbal form, it would have no connection with the efficient force (*bhāvanā*), because [the word] is intent upon that [other thing]. To this he says: "But that which is connected to it is intent upon it"—meaning it is intent upon the connection with the efficient force; it is intended precisely in its own right, intended precisely as referring to itself. For connection is the opposite of non-connection, but it is not the same as being intent upon something else.

The meaning is "contradictory. He avoids the contingency of there being no compound by stating: "And thus, the compound is also justified. Regarding the phrase "and thus": he explains that very point through both negative and positive concomitance (*vyatireka-anvaya*). For, in the case of an independent *puruṣa* (Self) that is indifferent to its own relation [to anything], since it is impossible for it to have a relation with another, a relation with a *puruṣa* is impossible; therefore, the compound [is not possible].

It would not [be possible]. At the time of the compound, even though heaven is devoid of connection with anything else, it still depends on a connection with the *bhāvanā* (efficient force); nevertheless, because of that dependence, the compound would not occur. But neither of these two [conditions] exists here.
He states the logical connection (*anvaya*): "But by way of its connection—that is, by way of its connection with the person—there being a connection with another through that medium..."

There is no obstruction to the formation of a single integrated meaning (*ekārthībhāva*), nor is there any obstruction to the capacity to express the meaning of the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*). Therefore, the compound is justified. However, if a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) were not compounded because it is "dependent" (*sāpekṣa*) and thus "incapable" (*asamartha*)—even when it enters into the action by way of its connection with the qualified object (*viśeṣya*)—then no qualifier at all would be included in this type of compound.
The compound *parodha* is thus appropriate; otherwise, every instance would be a descriptive determinative compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*).
For if it did not touch upon the function of that [object], it would be purposeless; or, if it did touch upon it, the compound could not exist because of its dependence on another word.

As for the claim that "when the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is the thing to be accomplished (*sādhya*), there can be no co-inherence (*samavāya*) of another thing to be accomplished," [the response is as follows]: First, in the case of the productive urge (*bhāvanā*), there is indeed such co-inherence by its very nature, because it has the form of having a goal (*bhāvya*) as its primary element. Even regarding the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), if its status as something to be accomplished were intended primarily through the productive urge, that would be precluded by the injunction (*vidhi*). On the other hand, if it is merely the state of being an object of the productive urge [that is meant],...

This is the same even in the case of other instruments (*karaṇa*). For it has been stated that an instrument is indeed the sphere of the agent’s activity in all cases; because that which is to be produced is an instrument by its very nature as a substance, quality, or word-meaning, whereas there is no taking up of what is already established. [The sacrifice and so forth] color the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) precisely through the verbal suffix (*śruti*), being its specific qualifiers.

He says that it must be so; otherwise, every qualifier would necessarily be a non-compound. Now, why should it be a non-compound? For there will be some qualifiers that refer solely to the qualificand, such as in the case of "Bring the blue lotus. To this he replies: because that qualifier, such as "blue" and so forth, does not touch upon the function [of the qualificand], such as bringing and so forth.

Because it would be redundant. For in this way, as much as is said when one says "bring the lotus," since the qualifier would have no effect on the action (*kārya*), it follows that the qualification of the lotus itself would be purposeless. Alternatively, if the qualifier were to touch upon the action, then according to your own view, the compound would be impossible because of its dependency (*sāpekṣatva*).

As for the objection raised—that if the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyātārtha*) is what is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), then another thing to be accomplished, such as heaven (*svarga*), cannot be inherent in it—this must be examined: is it said that another thing to be accomplished cannot be inherent when the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) is the thing to be accomplished, or rather when the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), such as sacrifice (*yāga*), is the thing to be accomplished? In that regard, concerning the *bhāvanā*...

The inherence of that [effort] in the form itself is the connection with the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Why? Because its nature consists primarily of the object to be brought into being (*bhāvya*).

For effort (*bhāvanā*), although it is itself of the nature of an action to be accomplished, necessarily requires an object to be brought into being (*bhāvya*) because it would otherwise be logically untenable without one;
this requirement follows from its very essence. Indeed, there is no possibility that there could be an act of production without another [object].

[The opponent argues: "There is something yet to be produced. Therefore, when there is an expectation for something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), a connection with another thing to be accomplished is not tenable.

Now, if the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is what is to be accomplished, there can be no inherence of another thing to be accomplished [within it], because that [root-meaning] itself is what is to be accomplished—either because the verbal productive energy (*bhāvanā*) is directed toward that, or because it is the object of the *bhāvanā* which is engaged in activity for the sake of the fruit. First of all, the *bhāvanā* does not [inhere] in the form of its own primary purpose.

He states that this is because it contradicts the understanding of the injunction (*vidhi*): "If the intention [of the injunction] were directed toward the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), then its status as the goal (*sādhya*) would be set aside by the injunction. On the other hand, if it is merely the state of being the object of an activity (*bhāvanā*) engaged for another purpose, then that is common even to other instruments such as axes and the like; for they too bring about the state of being split in two."
They have as their object an operation characterized by the raising and lowering [of an axe] directed toward a specific place, and these are the cause.

Likewise, sacrifices and the like, although they are themselves to be accomplished (*sādhya*) as objects of a productive activity (*bhāvanā*) directed toward another end, will be connected with other things to be accomplished by way of being causes—just as axes and the like are connected with pieces of wood that are being split in two. And this has not yet been proven.
He says that this is established elsewhere: "Indeed, in all cases, the instrument (karaṇa) is the object of the agent's activity," as stated in the *Bhāvanāviveka* [p.

This is because it is understood [from the scripture]. Its twofold nature, however, is caused by the existence or non-existence of the *apūrva* (the unseen potency). It is not contradictory for sacrifices to be the object of human effort even with respect to heaven, just as an axe is the object [of effort] with respect to a tree to be cut.
Nor is there a lack of causal operation (*vyāpāra*) in sacrifices and the like, since that is understood from the word itself; this is also the case for the arising of cognitions and lamps.

And as for what they urged—that if the verbal root (ākhyāta) has the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*), there would be no distinction from substance-words (*dravya-śabda*) and quality-words (*guṇa-śabda*) because it would have an established meaning (*siddhārtha*)—to that he replies: "But there is a distinction between the meanings of substance-words and quality-words, because the meaning of the verbal root, being something to be accomplished (*niṣpādya*) by its very nature, is not already established; for there is no taking up (*upādāna*) of what is already established."

However, in the case of items such as the *godohana* (milk-pail), they are employed because their purpose is already established elsewhere. Not only from the perspective of the object (*vastu*), but also from the perspective of the word (*śabda*), this [the root-meaning] is understood as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*). This is because it is the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛtyartha*), because it is invariably perceived prior [to the suffix], because it enters into the very form [of the action], and because, by coloring the *bhāvanā* which is itself in the state of being accomplished, it serves as its qualifier—just as in the case of "Śābaleya" and so forth.

He says "cows" as if by way of the qualifier "cow-ness"—for when sacrifice and the like, which color the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) in its form as something to be accomplished, are perceived as qualifiers of that [urge], there is an understanding of their being the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*).

However, this is not the case for substances and so forth, which are expressed by separate words; their status as qualifiers arises through their inclusion therein, acting as delimiters (*avacchedaka*) of that [urge].

However, it should not be thought that this is based on the generality of being an object of cultivation (*bhāvanātva*). And thus, because the form of the result (*sādhyarūpa*) is perceived through the entry of the operation (*vyāpārāveśāt*), the status of the wood and so forth as the instrument (*karaṇabhāva*) is established directly with respect to the meaning of the root *pac* (to cook) in expressions such as "he cooks with wood" (*kāṣṭhaiḥ pacati*).
This is what is indicated.

Although it was objected that, because action is subordinate as the means for accomplishing all desired ends, the twofold division [into primary and subordinate] would be lost due to this subordination of the action, he refutes that: "The twofold nature, however, is caused by the presence or absence of the *apūrva* (unseen potency).
Even when there is dependence on something else, that which possesses the *apūrva* is primary, such as the *Āgneya* sacrifice and the *Samid* offerings."

Where that [transformation] is absent, such as in the case of threshing and so forth, or sprinkling and so forth, those things possess the status of being qualities or actions. However, the author of the Vārttika has stated that the *apūrva* resulting from a restriction arises from the restriction itself, and not from the action.

Furthermore, it has been said that, in reality, heaven and the like do not possess the status of being the objective (*bhāvya*), because human effort is directed toward the meaning of verbal roots such as "sacrifice" (*yāga*).

Regarding the argument "because it is an object," he refutes it as follows: It is not contradictory for human effort to have sacrifice and the like as its object even when heaven is the goal to be accomplished, just as an axe has a tree as its object when felling is the goal. For if that which is to be brought about (*bhāvya*) must be directly within the scope of human activity, then even things well-known in the world as being brought about, such as the splitting [of wood] into two, would no longer be so.

[The axe, etc.,] would be that which is to be brought about (*bhāvya*). For even they are not directly the objects of human activity; rather, it is the axes and so forth themselves, being raised and brought down, [that are the objects]. Nor are those [axes] what is to be brought about; rather, they are the means for that [result].

Even in the case of human activity directed toward the axe, its status as that which is to be brought about (*bhāvyatva*) arises because it proceeds with the aim of the result-portion, namely, the splitting in two.
The same applies to heaven and the like as well; for there too, human activity directed toward objects such as sacrifice proceeds with the aim of attaining heaven and so forth.
As for what was stated—that sacrifices and the like are not instruments because they are non-activities, and that their "operation" (vyāpāra) is not a produced effect—[that is also incorrect].
To this he replies: "Nor is it the case that sacrifice and the like lack causal operation (avyāpāratva). Why? Because sound and so forth are perceived as means (sādhana).

Otherwise, since [the result] would be inexplicable otherwise, there must be an intermediate operation called *apūrva*, established by presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) for the sake of accounting for that [perception].

Because its status as an activity (*vyāpāra*) is accepted. Nor is it impossible because heaven is eternal, for it is absolutely non-existent [in the present] such that it would be unachievable. If it is argued that this is due to ignorance of the means, then for that very reason it is made known. Nor is it so because of the postulation of a necessity to act. If it is asked: "How can it have an activity when the ritual action (*karman*) has ceased, since that [action] was not dependent upon it?"

In that case, are the production-apūrvas (utpattyapūrvas) of the Āgneya and other rites not the intermediate operations (avāntaravyāpāra) of those very rites—the Āgneya and others—when the qualification-apūrva (adhikārāpūrva) is to be generated? For they do not exist simultaneously with the Āgneya and other rites, since the supreme apūrva (paramāpūrva) arises from them only after they have ceased; and this is so even for the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices, which occur together.

In order to fulfill the instrumental capacity understood from the words "by means of the Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices" regarding their own nature (*svarūpataḥ*), when one postulates a verbal expression for them,

the lack of operation (*avyāpāratva*)— which is unestablished because they are not inherent in that [result] but are dependent upon it and constitute its intermediate function— is equally applicable to the sacrifices (*yāga*) and so forth as well. This has been explained in detail in the *Nyāyaparīkṣā*.

And he says that there is neither existence (*bhūti*) nor activity (*vyāpāra*), because this is observed in the case of the lamp of knowledge and the like—by such statements as: "Since even the arising (*utpatti*) of the lamp of knowledge and so forth is admitted to be an activity, therefore the very birth (*janma*) of the cognition with respect to its object is accepted as its activity. [Objection: But how can that which is unestablished (*asiddha*) be the agent of becoming? [Reply: It is not unestablished, because of the material cause (*upādāna*).

Because [the cloth] is established by means of its form (*rūpa*). It is the very threads, engaged in the production of a cloth and characterized by a collection (*pracaya*) of specific prior and posterior conjunctions, that are called "cloth" through metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) because they serve that purpose. And since these [threads], having been set in motion for that purpose, possess the occurrence of the process of becoming the cloth, there is no operation of something unestablished. Furthermore, the process of becoming (*bhavana*) is of two kinds.
What is it? [The production of some things] depends solely on the mere existence [of their object], as is the case with the cognition’s pervasion of its object of knowledge (*jñeya*).

[The production of] others, however, occurs after they have already arisen, through the coming together of a collection of auxiliary causes (*sahakāri-grāma*), as is the case with the visual consciousness of form and so forth by the eye and other [faculties]. For the eye does not perceive form merely by virtue of having arisen; rather, [it perceives it] through the object and light.

[This occurs] due to the convergence of auxiliary causes (*sahakāri-pratyaya*). For indeed, the status of being a means (*sādhana*) is never observed for those that are devoid of activity (*nirvyāpāra*).

In that regard, when an effect is dependent on the necessity of certain factors, then in order for that [effect] to be produced, some manifest (*pratyakṣa*) factor possessing origination and possessing an imperceptible (*parokṣa*) operation must be admitted; it is through connection with that [operation] that their status as a means is established. As for that which is intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), however...

An effect has its origin dependent upon its material cause (*mātrā*); no other operation exists therein. Nor can there be the status of a means (*sādhana*) for that which is devoid of operation; therefore, birth itself is accepted as the operation in that case. And its agency (*kartṛtva*) therein has been established. Furthermore, operations do not produce a result immediately after [the thing] has arisen; rather, once it has arisen—
When the prior conjunction has been destroyed by disjunction during the operation, the subsequent conjunction arises;
thus everything is clear. As for what was said—that the injunction "one should produce heaven" is an impossible instruction—that is untenable, for it is twofold.
For [an entity] would be unfit for action either because of its absolute existence, like space, or because of its absolute non-existence, like a sky-flower.

Yet neither of these two conditions exists in the case of heaven and so forth; thus he says: "And heaven is not eternal," because it is not absolutely non-existent such that it would be impossible [to attain]. Now, let there be no unfitness in its essential nature; however, [it might be unattainable] due to ignorance of the means.
He raises the objection: "It will be something that must be performed"—if it is argued that this is because of ignorance regarding the means (*upāya*). He refutes this:
"For this very reason, it is made known by the injunction; and therefore, once the means is known, it will be possible [to perform it].

This is a logical consequence (*prasaṅga*). Because there is a restatement (*anuvāda*) regarding the portion of the result (*phala*), and because there is a synthesis (*upasaṃhāra*) of the instrumental portion (*karaṇa*), there is an injunction (*vidhi*). It is just as in the case of "He offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*). Furthermore, since the impulse to action (*pravṛtti*) directed toward the result has the sacrifice as its object, the word serves as the cause;
thus, the sacrifice is enjoined. For a person’s engagement in the ritual act is not one thing, while their engagement in the instrument is another. [The sacrifice is the] instrument.

Thus engaged, one becomes engaged in the fruit. Engaging in the action itself, one engages in the instrument. Therefore, because the meaning is understood in this way, there is no pointlessness, nor is there any other purpose [beyond what is stated], such as "one desiring heaven should perform a sacrifice. Since the word culminates in the sacrifice, there would be a loss of what is heard and an assumption of what is not heard due to its inherence therein, resulting in a lack of authority.

And because of [the presence of] conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). Nor is the perceived purpose—the realization of the self through ritual acts for one whose desires have been fulfilled—the [sole] motive.

As for what was said—that there would be the consequence of [the rites] being mandatory because a person is dependent on injunctions—he replies to that: "Nor is there the consequence of their being mandatory, because heaven and other such results are restated [as already known], and because the instrumental portion [of the action] is subsumed [within the context]."

Regarding the injunction (*vidhi*): An injunction, whose inherent nature is to bring about what has not yet been attained, prescribes that specific aspect of the *bhāvanā* with which it is connected, provided that aspect has not already been established. Since the aspect of the result (*phala*) is already established, the injunction functions as a restatement (*anuvāda*) of that, and operates instead upon the aspect of the means (*sādhana*), which is not yet established. To illustrate this very point, he says: "He offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*).

The meaning is as follows: just as an injunction, even though its objective is the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of the oblation, restates the element of the oblation already understood from the originative statement (*utpattivākya*), "He offers the Agnihotra," and is intent upon establishing that [cultivation], so too is this [present case].
Furthermore, as for what was said—that an injunction has activity as its object, and if activity were to have the fruit as its object, then the fruit would be enjoined—[that is not so].

"It is not the sacrifice; if it were the object of the sacrifice, there would be no fruit. To this, he says: "We do not say that [the activity] does not have the fruit as its object; rather, because activity has the fruit as its object precisely because that [fruit] is its goal, and because the sacrifice is the verbal cause (*śābda-hetu*) as the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by virtue of being pervaded by the purposefulness toward the fruit—since the status of having the sacrifice as its object is otherwise unestablished—the sacrifice [is indeed the object]."

It is enjoined. Now, if the engagement in sacrifice is thus enjoined, from where does the connection with the fruit arise? To this he says: For a person’s engagement toward the fruit in an action is not one thing, while the engagement toward the instrument is another.
Through engagement with the instrument, there occurs engagement with the fruit; by that very means, the fruit is accomplished. [This applies] to the fruit in the action itself.
Since it is impossible for that [activity] to be established otherwise, one engages in the performance [of the rite] as its necessary concomitant (*nāntarīyakatayā*).

Therefore, he concludes by refuting what was brought forward by the opponent—that there is pointlessness due to the absence of a connection with a result and a lack of *ādhikya* (additional benefit)—by demonstrating that such a connection with a result is indeed possible: "Thus, because the meaning is understood, there is no futility. Previously...
He states that the view of those who hold only one side of the argument is untenable: "Nor is the purpose [of scripture] the entry into the qualification for the knowledge of the Self.

Why? Because, according to your own view, since the verbal testimony rests solely on the necessity of performing the sacrifice—in the form 'one desiring heaven should perform the sacrifice'—the intent (tātparya) is directed toward that alone; therefore, the entry into the qualification for the knowledge of the Self would lack authority."

Alternatively, if that were the case, there would be the abandonment of the scripturally enjoined necessity of performing sacrifices and the assumption of an entry into the knowledge of the Self that is not so enjoined. Now, one might argue: "This fault would indeed apply if [the Self] were to be understood solely through the word; however, the realization of the Self is actually perceived as the purpose of ritual actions.
To this, he says: "And the realization of the Self is not merely a visible purpose accomplished by rituals for one whose desires have been fulfilled."

By means of eradication, one who is self-controlled and whose mind is not agitated by desires possesses a well-ascertained knowledge of the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*). This has already been explained in the section on the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). In that regard, how do the injunctions for ritual action eradicate desire? What is that desire?
[Page 334]

Because the self-reality (*ātmatattva*) is well-ascertained by one who has eradicated desire, is self-controlled, and whose mind is not agitated by desires; for if indeed actions are for the purpose of eradicating desire, and once that is accomplished, the seeker of desire requires no further purpose, then the injunction regarding action is solely intent upon that [eradication]. Thus, there is no evidence for it being intent upon anything else. Nor is it the case that such a work would lack scriptural authority (*aśāstratva*).

Because it denotes that which is beneficial (*śreyaḥ*). Since the beneficial consists of the nature of pleasure (*prīti*), and since pleasure regarding objects of desire is experienced within each individual self, [the Veda teaches this]. Furthermore, enjoyment is not the means of eradication; for there is no satiety in desires. Now, if it is argued that [the Veda teaches this] by way of the cessation of other activities, even in that case, if one who possesses desire were to accomplish [his goal] through sacrifice and not by some other means, [then the Veda would be teaching the beneficial].

What is the distinction regarding the desire-side of the mind? And how, in the case of an activity directed toward the cessation of desire, can there be the exclusion of other [desires] when no specific alternative has been prescribed? Is it that one who possesses desire should perform the sacrifice but not the desire itself—by abandoning both [the sacrifice and the desire] through the enjoyment of that [sacrifice], or rather by the instruction of another course of action [which excludes the desire] from those [activities] that are natural?

Is it by turning away from active engagements? Not the first alternative, as he says: "If indeed [the acts] are for the purpose of destroying desire, then a person who has fulfilled his desires through those very actions by means of enjoying them is one who has accomplished his purpose (kṛtī) and does not require any further objective. And that which is not desired is not accepted by an injunction."

And thus, the injunction regarding ritual action is indeed intent upon that very action conveyed by its own words; for if it were intent upon something else, there would be no evidence for it, because [the injunction] does not depend on desire, whereas this [desire] is the opposite of that. As it has been said: "If it were intent upon desire, there would be a contradiction with the scripture. To this, he replies: "And it is not the case that it is non-scriptural."

Why? Because the elders maintain that a scripture (*śāstra*) is a collection of words that denotes the highest good (*śreyaḥ*). And since injunctions regarding desires (*kāma-vidhi*) are likewise [scriptures], he says: "Because they denote the highest good. Now, one might object: "How can things that are merely attractive at first sight, yet result in misfortune, have the nature of the highest good? To this he replies: "Because the highest good consists in the form of pleasure (*prīti*). For the highest good is the realization of the person's [true] self.

The worldly consensus is that common experience is the basis, and the scripture is its instruction; thus, it is purely worldly. Nor are these people subject to such critical inquiry that they would not respect desire and greed. However, objects of desire such as cattle and heaven are not themselves of the nature of joy; for he says: "And because the joy in desires is experienced by each individual within themselves. Furthermore, enjoyment cannot possibly be a means of eradication [of suffering].

For there is no satisfaction for a person through desires such as those for heaven and the like. In the phrase "of desires" (*kāmānām*), the genitive case is used in connection with a word expressing "satiety. Thus it has been said: "Desire is never extinguished by the enjoyment of desired objects," and "The passions increase in accordance with the practice of enjoyment, as do the skillfulness of the senses. This is the second [point].
He restates the opponent’s position: "Now, [it is argued that] by the cessation of other activities... He refutes this:

"In that case as well, if one who possesses desire (kāmī) were to accomplish his desire through sacrifice rather than by some other means, what distinction is there? And if the cessation of desire is merely a mental state occurring during activity, what is the point? Furthermore, how can there be a cessation of other [means] when the injunction is already established by way of an option (pakṣeṇa)? For the injunction does not apply to one who already possesses the desire."
Previously, they were unable to comprehend the various means for attaining desire— such as the distinctions between sacrifices and the like, or the accumulation of the various limbs of ritual—
just as worldly people cannot understand the causes for removing husks, such as threshing and so forth; whereby those [means] are compared to worldly means for attaining desire.
Specifically, regarding the literal, indicative, and other types of meaning: if the intent is to enjoin a sacrifice, there is no prohibition of desire;

if the intent is to prohibit desire, there is no injunction for a sacrifice. Since both are incompatible, the cessation of desire would follow only by implication. Furthermore, if there were a contradiction with all worldly activity, then even injunctions for ritual action would become purposeless.

Since the object [of ritual action] is achievable through visible means, and since the enjoyment of the fruit is inherent [to one's nature], the meaning of the sacred tradition (āmnāya) would effectively be the doctrine of inherent nature (svabhāvavāda) adopted under a disguise. Therefore, this is a grave censure: that ritual injunctions, by means of what is visible alone, lead to the qualification for the knowledge of the Self. Scripture is the instruction of those who are to be enjoined.

Thus, even the injunction regarding knowledge (*jñāna-niyoga*) is merely an instruction for the person to be enjoined (*niyojya-anuśāsana*); therefore, no realization of the Self (*ātma-pratipatti*) arises from it.

If there were an option (*vikalpa*), then—as in the case of threshing (*avaghāta*) and other such acts—there would be the contingency of its application being optional (*pakṣe prāpti*). It should be understood that this was stated while provisionally accepting the possibility of such optional application. However, the sacrifice is not enjoined as a means to [fulfill] a desire; rather—

He says that it is merely this much: "One who desires [objects] should perform a sacrifice in order to turn away from those objects. To this he replies: "Two things are difficult to obtain, especially when one involves a primary (śrauta) sense and the other a secondary (lākṣaṇika) sense. Since the primary sense of 'one should perform a sacrifice' is possible, it is not proper to adopt the secondary sense of 'the cessation of desire'."
The meaning is "to rely upon. Now, he demonstrates the very possibility [of this]: if the intent is the injunction for sacrifice, there is no prohibition of desire;

if the intent is the prohibition of desire, there is no injunction for sacrifice. Just as in the sentence "The fat man does not eat by day," which is intent on the prohibition of eating, it follows by implication that his eating is prescribed at night; so too here, by implication...

[The cessation of desire]. Why? Because here, even for both [the fat man and the sacrificer], there is no concomitance (*asamavāya*). For a prohibition of eating during the day for one who is fat is not possible together with not eating at night;
therefore, by implication, it is understood that "he eats at night. However, sacrifices and the like are not [understood] when desire has ceased.

The meaning is that they do not occur in the context of worldly activity (*pravṛtti*). Or, even if it be granted that [the scripture] has both as its purport, nevertheless, since all activities having visible purposes are obstructed by injunctions such as those for sacrifice, rice and other materials to be accomplished by them would be impossible; consequently, sacrifices and the like would also cease to exist due to the absence of their means. Thus he says: "And when all activities having visible purposes are obstructed..."

Even if ritual procedures were established, they would be useless, because the purpose of sacrifices and the like can be accomplished through visible means. Furthermore, since sacrifices and such do not produce results, and because service and the like are inconsistent [in their results], pleasure, pain, and so forth—which are accepted by the Lokāyatas as being natural—are the meaning of the Veda; this is what has been accepted through a different formulation of the statement.

He says [in response]: "Because the enjoyment of the fruit is inherent, the doctrine of inherent nature (svabhāvavāda) itself would effectively be resorted to under the guise of the meaning of the sacred tradition. He concludes: "Therefore, this is a grave position: that the injunctions for action, by means of perception alone, lead to the qualification for the knowledge of the Self. Furthermore, if qualification were not admitted...

The nature of a scripture (*śāstra*) consists in the instruction of those who are to be enjoined (*niyojya-anuśāsana*), as is the case with the injunctions for sacrifices and the like; by that same logic, the injunction regarding knowledge (*jñāna-niyoga*) also consists in the instruction of those to be enjoined, being intended solely to enjoin that "the knowledge of the Self must be performed.
Therefore, the result would not be the realization of the Self, but rather its complete pervasion.

If it is argued that [the injunction is necessary] because [the act] has knowledge as its intrinsic nature (*jñānasvabhāva*), [we reply: no, because the injunction would be redundant. If it is argued that it is like the case of threshing (*avahanana*) and so forth, [we reply:

no, because [the injunction] serves the purpose of restriction (*niyamārthatva*). There is no restriction to a specific type of knowledge, since even in the alternative case [of knowledge arising from other sources], it is not already established [by another means]. This is due to superimposition (*samāropa*).

And because of this possibility, there is no determination of the true nature [of the action]. Therefore, when the meaning of the verbal root is not the means (*sādhana*), the accomplishment of the modification (*avikāra*) is not established.
Furthermore, it has been stated that its status as a means is due to the injunction (*vidhi*).
Thus ends the Vidhiviveka composed by the venerable Mahāmahopādhyāya Maṇḍanamiśra.

An objection is raised: "Because it is of the nature of knowledge. He refutes this: "Because an injunction would be purposeless. Again, an objection is raised: "It is like the case of threshing and so forth. He answers: "No, because the injunction for threshing and so forth serves the purpose of restriction (*niyama*). If it were argued that here too, in the realization of the Self, the knowledge of the Self is restricted [to a specific means]," [the response follows].

To this he replies: There is no restriction to a specific kind of knowledge. Why? Because it would not be attained even in the case [of the opponent's view]; for indeed, immediately after the knowledge [of the self], the realization of the self is not possible through that very knowledge of the self. Furthermore, if the knowledge of the self were something to be enjoined, then since even a contrary cognition could be considered "knowledge of the self," it too might be subject to injunction; thus, there would be no definitive determination of reality. He says: "By way of superimposition."

Because of this possibility, there is no determination of the true nature [of the action]. He concludes: "Therefore, when the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is not itself the means of accomplishment, the qualification (*adhikāra*) is not established. Suppose the meaning of the verbal root is the means of accomplishing the result, and let the qualification be established;
even so, what follows for the injunction (*vidhi*)? To this he says: "And its status as a means is what is called the injunction."
Thus ends the Nyāyakaṇikā, a commentary on the Vidhiviveka, composed by Ācārya Vācaspatimiśra.
